Most studies evaluating the effects of MUF have demonstrated improved patient outcomes in the pediatric heart
surgery population (77–79). Speciﬁcally, it has been
shown to decrease postoperative blood loss and transfusion requirements in this group (6,78,80–82). Studies
have also demonstrated increases in arterial blood pressure (77,82–84) and cardiac output (78,82,83), improved
pulmonary function (84–88), reduced postoperative ventilator requirement (6,78,88), and fewer days in the intensive
care unit (78). It has also been shown to improve myocardial contractility (83,89) and decrease myocardial
edema (90). Investigators have hypothesized that these
improvements were due to decreased myocardial water, increased viscosity and systemic vascular resistance,
removal of anesthetic agents and/or vasodilators, removal
of myocardial depression factors, or stimulation of the
sympathetic reﬂex by removing water from the aorta (66). After several studies detected inﬂammatory mediators in
the ultraﬁltrate, most research efforts have focused on
the correlations of blood and ultraﬁltrate levels of these
mediators and the improved outcomes (91,92). The results of these studies have been inconclusive, but they
suggest that the removal of inﬂammatory mediators during MUF is at least in part related to the improved
outcomes (93). MUF seems to be most effective in pediatric patients, probably due to the large prime volume
relative to the patient’s blood volume. A few studies
have demonstrated the positive effects of MUF in adult
patients, but the effects do not extend past the immediate postoperative period (72,94–96). Currently there are
no large prospectively randomized studies corroborating
clinical outcomes and the removal of inﬂammatory mediators (97).

HEMODIALYSIS DURING
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Hemodialysis uses a microporous membrane material in a
hollow ﬁber conﬁguration similar to previously described
ultraﬁltrators. Hemodialysis differs from ultraﬁltration in
that a dialysate solution is passed through the nonblood
side of the membrane. Hemodialysis removes diffusible

6. Ultraﬁltration and Dialysis
123
solutes based on a concentration gradient established
by the dialysate solution. Because the blood is under
pressure when ﬂowing through the hemodialysis circuit,
water and solutes are also removed by convection, as in
ultraﬁltration. Hemodialysis during CPB was ﬁrst reported
by Soffer et al. in 1979 (98). Theory and Indications
Consider a tank partitioned into two compartments separated by a semipermeable membrane. Each side contains a
solution with dissolved solutes. Diffusion across the membrane is the net movement of molecules from a region of
higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. If there are no other forces, diffusion goes on until the gradient becomes zero. Diffusion rate is directly affected by
blood and dialysis ﬂow rate, temperature, membrane surface area, membrane thickness and solute concentration
gradient, and indirectly by viscosity and solute molecule
size (22) (Fig. 9). Hemodialysis during CPB has been utilized in patients
with end-stage renal disease or those who have renal
insufﬁciency (35). In recent years the number of patients
presenting for heart surgery with these comorbidities has
increased (99). Circuit Design and Management
Although hemodialysis can be performed by attaching a
conventional hemodialysis machine to the CPB circuit,
this would require an additional technician and unnecessary complexities to the procedure. A more common
approach is to position the dialyzer in parallel to the
extracorporeal circuit, similar to where the ultraﬁltrator
would be positioned. Indeed, an ultraﬁltrator can also be
used for dialysis, but it must be modiﬁed by removing the
plug from the extra efﬂuent port. Dialysate solutions have
been as simple as 0.9% sodium chloride (100), or may be
more complex and require a continuous source of water
to be used for mixing the concentrated dialysate. Others
have utilized premixed peritoneal dialysate and premixed
hemodiaﬁltrate (101,102). The premixed solutions may
FIGURE 9. Diffusion is the movement of solutes in a solution
from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower
concentration. either be set up to recirculate through the dialyzer in
which the bag is changed periodically, or set up as a
‘‘one pass system’’ in which it ﬂows through the dialysate
compartment into a collection canister to remove the solutes more efﬁciently (102).

To achieve the most efﬁcient
diffusion rate, the concentration gradient should be maximized by conﬁguring the dialysate to ﬂow counter to the
current of the dialyzer blood ﬂow. Optimally, the dialysate
ﬂow should be three times the blood ﬂow. However, if
the dialyzer blood ﬂow is 300 to 400 mL/min, this would
require 900 to 1,200 mL/min of dialysate ﬂow. Dialysate
ﬂows during CPB are generally in the range of 200 to
300 mL/min. Outcomes
Hemodialysis is effective in removing potassium and other
small molecular weight solutes. Studies on patients with
renal failure have determined that hemoﬁltration treatments are as effective as hemodialysis in removing small
molecular weight solutes such as urea and electrolytes. However, hemoﬁltration can more efﬁciently remove the
middle molecule solutes compared with hemodialysis, because middle molecule removal is accomplished primarily
by convection rather than diffusion (51,103). MISCELLANEOUS USES
OF ULTRAFILTRATION
Ultraﬁltration and Hemodialysis in
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
Critically ill patients undergoing long-term extracorporeal
membrane oxygenation (ECMO) often present with ﬂuid
overload due to renal insufﬁciency or failure (104). Because these patients often have limited vascular access,
the ultraﬁltrator or dialyzer is incorporated into the
extracorporeal circuit (105,106). Because the circuit is closed in ECMO and the patient
is only on partial bypass, they are still dependent on their
native cardiac output. If too much ﬂuid is removed from
the vascular space the patient may become hypovolemic,
causing the ECMO ﬂow as well as the patient’s native
cardiac output to decrease. Systemic Inﬂammatory Effect with the
Use of a Semipermeable Membrane
SIRS is triggered during heart surgery owing to contact
with the artiﬁcial surfaces of the CPB circuit, ischemiareperfusion
injury,
and
operative
trauma
(46,107). Myocardial dysfunction, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, neurologic complications, and bleeding are at
least partially attributed to this SIRS (108).

II. Equipment
The older cellulose and modiﬁed cellulose hemodialysis and ultraﬁltration membrane materials have been
shown to increase inﬂammatory mediators and initiate
complement activation (109,110). The newer synthetic
membrane materials such as polysulphone invoke minimal complement activation (110). Expression and elimination rates affect blood cytokine
and other inﬂammatory mediator levels (7,111,112). Most cytokines have a low molecular weight, and numerous studies have demonstrated that many of these
inﬂammatory mediators are present in the ultraﬁl-
trate (103,113–115). In fact, cytokine elimination has been
correlated to the duration of the ultraﬁltration procedure
and the amount of ﬂuid removed. However, several studies
failed to demonstrate signiﬁcant reductions in plasma levels despite levels being detected in the ultraﬁltrate (116). Other studies have shown minimal levels of cytokines in
the ultraﬁltrate, but signiﬁcant reductions in plasma levels. This may be explained by the adsorptive properties of the
membrane materials. Many of the synthetic membranes
are able to bind complement regulating proteins such
as factor B, factor D, ß2m, C3a, and C5a (114). The anti-
inﬂammatory cytokine IL-10 is also removed by ultraﬁltra-
tion, but to a lesser extent than the other proinﬂammatory
mediators owing to its larger molecular weight (117). To date, no large prospective randomized studies
have correlated reductions in complement factor and
proinﬂammatory cytokines to clinical outcomes (118). Inconsistent results may be explained by use of various
protocols and equipment, different end points, patient
type, and measurement techniques (39,75). KEY POINTS
■CPB presents challenges to the management of
hemodilution, electrolyte levels, as well as ﬂuid shifts
because of the capillary leak associated with the
systemic inﬂammatory response. ■Ultraﬁltration can reduce hemodilution by removing
excess body water, and can also be utilized to
concentrate the residual CPB circuit blood as in
MUF. ■Z-BUF functions like hemoﬁltration by removing
plasma water but, as opposed to ultraﬁltration, the
amount of water removed is in excess of what is
necessary to reverse hemodilution. ●As additional water is removed, it is replaced with
a balanced electrolyte solution. ●Z-BUF can be used to correct certain electrolyte
imbalances. ■Use of Z-BUF and/or MUF have demonstrated
improved post-CPB outcomes and reduced levels of
inﬂammatory mediators. ■The conventional dialysis circuit is simpliﬁed for use
in the extracorporeal circuit. ●Dialysis can be used to manage patient volume
and electrolyte imbalances, similar to Z-BUF or
hemoﬁltration.

●Ultraﬁltration appears to more efﬁciently remove
middle molecule uremic solutes than dialysis. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

7
◗Mechanical Circulatory Support Devices
Richard G. Smith and Jack G. Copeland
CLINICAL APPLICATIONS
AND MANAGEMENT
In 2006, there were three basic applications for circulatory
support devices practiced in the United States, where the
U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) oversees their
use: (a) as a bridge to recovery, (b) as a bridge to transplantation, and (c) as long-term support for nontransplant
patients (destination therapy). It is estimated that 1% of
the approximately 700,000 patients annually undergoing
cardiac surgery in the United States receive a circulatory
support device exclusive of an intra-aortic balloon pump
(IABP). The overwhelming majority of this support is in
the bridge to recovery application, for which there is a
25% to 30% rate of successful weaning from the device
and functional recovery. Orthotopic heart transplantation is still acknowledged
as the best therapy for end-stage congestive heart failure
(CHF). In the United States, approximately 2,000 to 2,500
patients undergo a heart transplant each year, and an additional 25% to 30% die while waiting for transplant (1). The International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation Registry for 2005 reported that 48% of those who
received a heart transplant required intravenous inotropic
support and that 27% required some type of circulatory
support [21% of these mechanical support devices were
left ventricular assist devices (LVADs)] (2). The ﬁrst FDA approval of a device for long-term support for nontransplant patients was given in 2002 and
was based on the Randomized Evaluation of Mechanical
Assistance for the Treatment of Congestive Heart Failure
(REMATCH) study results (3). The approval of destination
therapy has attracted new devices for long-term support. The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
(CMS) has designated approximately 70 centers that meet
their approval criteria for payment for this application. In
the world, the longest support of this type has exceeded
5 years (4). The spectrum of devices discussed in this
chapter ranges from the IABP to the total artiﬁcial heart
(TAH). Each system is described in detail. Patient Selection, Initiation of Support,
and Outcome
Patients with severe cardiac failure are at once diverse,
each having a unique medical history and pattern of organ
dysfunction, and homogeneous, all sharing many aspects
of CHF, low-output syndrome, and cardiogenic shock.

They have frequently been treated with maximal medical inotropic and afterload reduction therapy, and have
also often been treated with an IABP. For those who continue to decompensate, a number of possible solutions are
available. Patient selection is the most important factor in determining survival with mechanical circulatory assistance. The younger the patient, the better the chance of survival. Experience with the use of postcardiotomy devices for
cardiac recovery has shown that patients younger than
60 years have a survival rate of 21% to 31%, whereas patients older than 60 years have a survival rate of 12%. The
survival rate for patients older than 70 years is 6%. Other
factors that contribute to the success of these devices include the performance and selection of the device, and the
skill, experience, and judgment of the clinical team in the
use of these devices (5). Various criteria have been applied in the past as guidelines for the placement of ventricular assistance (Table 1). Considered together, these criteria function as a deﬁni-
tion of cardiogenic shock (6). They are presented as basic
guidelines, and do not exclude such other parameters as a
requirement for high-dose inotropic support, systemic hypotension (mean arterial pressure <60 mm Hg, systolic
<80 mm Hg), respiratory distress, waxing and waning
state of consciousness, failure to separate from cardiopulmonary bypass, and metabolic acidosis. Common to all
these patients is a global picture indicating inadequate perfusion of organs and tissues as a result of cardiac failure. Prompt institution of mechanical circulatory assistance is
of great importance. Prolonged hypotension (>12 hours) is
associated with multisystem failure and poor recovery (5). To assess simultaneously the physiologic need for and the

Availability of Devices
In 1976, an amendment to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetics
Act gave the FDA the responsibility to oversee clinical trials. Inherent in this regulation is the requirement that the
FDA must ensure that anticipated beneﬁts to the individual
patient, and to society at large, outweigh the risks involved
in subjecting patients to an unproven device. Before any
clinical trials begin, the FDA reviews an application [Investigational Device Exemption, or (IDE)] submitted by
the sponsor of the proposed study. The IDE application
includes a description of the device; details of materials
and manufacturing; a description of any bench and animal
testing; results of and conclusions derived from these tests;
and a protocol of the proposed clinical trial, including indications, criteria for patient selection, methods proposed to
evaluate the results, and a patient informed-consent document (10). A local institutional review board oversees each
clinical study. The institutional review board is expected
‘‘to apply local community attitudes and ethical standards
in making a judgment that the beneﬁts to subjects and the
knowledge to be gained outweigh the risks’’ (11). Because devices that existed before 1976 did not require
an IDE application, any device that can demonstrate
‘‘substantial equivalence’’ to a preamendment device may
be exempted from the IDE requirement by ﬁling a request
for exemption (510k). Importantly, the device categories
of balloon pumps, centrifugal pumps, and resuscitative
systems do not require an IDE application because similar
technology existed before 1976. Although centrifugal

incorporated, its use for ventricular assistance did not. Because of the absence of a rigorous clinical study with
these exempted devices, issues involving patient selection,
complications, and informed consent are unclear (12). Once the IDE study is concluded, the accumulated data
are submitted to the FDA for premarketing approval. The
FDA staff and a panel of non-FDA experts review all data
presented by the IDE sponsor. Approval at this point is
the prerequisite for marketing any new device. Another
path for limited FDA approval was added in 1997. The
Humanitarian Device Exemption (HDE) permits limited
marketing of a device to fewer than 3000 patients, by
ﬁling a humanitarian use designation, once the company
has proven that no other device can meet the need. Complications of Circulatory Support
Systems
Bleeding
Bleeding can be quite signiﬁcant at the time an intrathoracic device is placed, especially if cardiopulmonary
bypass (CPB) has taken more than 2 1
2 hours. Activation of
platelets and the coagulation system during exposure of
the blood to artiﬁcial surfaces and turbulent ﬂow patterns
of the heart–lung machine may lead to a severe coagulopathy characterized by platelet dysfunction. Once surgical
bleeding has been controlled, bleeding from suture lines,
conduits, and raw surfaces, as a result of deﬁciencies in
the coagulation system, becomes the next major clinical
undertaking. Clear professional communication between
the surgeon, anesthesiologist, hematologist, and blood
bank may prove to be lifesaving if persistent bleeding
continues. Prompt control of bleeding is necessary to decrease the incidence of end-organ dysfunction as a result
of transfusions. Dilution of the coagulation factors to less than half the
normal concentration as a result of the nonblood prime
used for CPB appears not to adversely affect hemostasis. However, persistent dilution by more than 50%, coupled
with the consumption that is encountered during prolonged surgical operations requires the administration of
coagulation factors, either in fresh-frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate. The use of cell-salvage devices helps return
red cells from the operative ﬁeld back into the circulation,
but it contributes to hemodilution and platelet dysfunction in that any procoagulant factors and platelets are lost
in the washing process. These issues are fully discussed as
applied to CPB elsewhere in the text, and are not different
for assist device-associated bleeding.

In the postoperative period, brisk bleeding or tamponade can decrease cardiac ﬁlling and thereby prevent
ﬁlling of any circulatory assist device. The same criteria
used for routine surgical operations should be applied
for reoperations when devices are implanted. Evidence of
tamponade in the face of rapid bleeding, a sudden decrease
in chest tube drainage, and ongoing bleeding of more than
200 mL/hour for longer than 3 to 4 hours are commonly accepted criteria for reoperation. Bleeding may also become
a signiﬁcant problem at the time of removal of assist devices. Dense, immature adhesions between the device and
intrathoracic organs tend to cause diffuse hemorrhage. Thromboembolism
Protocols for anticoagulation differ among institutions
using mechanical assist devices, mainly because no single
regimen seems to be more effective than any of the
others. Many agents have been used at different times
after implantation, and in varying combinations. These
agents include heparin, warfarin, aspirin, dipyridamole,
and ticlopidine. A typical regimen may start with continuous intravenous infusion of heparin to maintain the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) at 50 to 60 seconds. Dipyridamole
may be started simultaneously with heparin. The patient is maintained on heparin and dipyridamole unless
a relatively long implant time is anticipated. In this case,
warfarin is favored over heparin, with maintenance of the
prothrombin time (PT) at approximately 18 to 22 seconds
[international normalized ratio (INR), of 2.5 to 3.5.] Aspirin is also started very early to decrease platelet adhesion. Since the early 1990s, at the University of Arizona,
the authors have adopted the multidrug approach that
is individually tailored, through use of multisystem monitoring to minimize both thromboembolic and hemorrhagic complications. The multidrug therapy consists of
an anticoagulant, intravenously administered heparin followed by conversion to warfarin; a platelet-stabilizing
agent, dipyridamole; a platelet antiaggregant, aspirin; and
an anti-inﬂammatory agent, pentoxifylline. The use of
thromboelastography (TEG) is probably the best available
indicator of overall coagulation mechanisms, and calculation of the thrombodynamic potential index provides a
measurement of the coagulability of blood by examining
the rapid phase of clot formation (13). Other factors that appear to be involved in the development of thrombus within devices are low or reduced blood
ﬂow and infection. The low-ﬂow state and the contact of
blood with an artiﬁcial surface may accelerate thrombus
formation.

Infection can lead to a hypercoagulable state,
with activation of inﬂammatory cells and mediators leading to the formation of thrombus. Infection within a device,
on valves or adherent thrombus, is more likely to be seen
after prolonged periods of support. The risk for this complication in ‘‘nonpermanent’’ implants appears to be low. The brain is by far the organ most sensitive to thromboembolism, and therefore is the organ most often

affected by it. Fortunately, irreversible neurologic damage has not been a common clinical observation during
the use of circulatory assist devices. Transient ischemic
attacks have been among the more frequently reported
events. Embolism to the kidneys, ophthalmic artery, lung,
and heart through the coronary arteries has also been
documented. Embolism to other organs, such as the liver,
should be expected to be more difﬁcult to document. On
the basis of current experience, thrombosis, thromboembolism, and infections are increasingly common beyond
30 days and may be interrelated (14). Infection
Patients who need circulatory assistance are at risk for
the development of infection, not only because of the
presence of a large foreign body but also because of their
often debilitated and malnourished state. Improvement of
the nutritional status of the patient should be considered
of great importance. Prophylactic antibiotics should be
routinely used during the perioperative period. A common
practice is to begin administering a combination of
vancomycin and gentamicin before surgery and continue
the drugs until the chest tubes are removed. The rate of infection is directly related to the duration of circulatory support. It appears that pneumonia
and mediastinitis are the most prevalent infections encountered. Infection of the support device itself often
involves the inﬂow and outﬂow conduits and the drivelines. Such infections require systemic antibiotics and
surgical debridement. Fungal infections, with Candida and
Aspergillus organisms, have been reported in immunosuppressed patients who required circulatory support. Infection in these patients increases the rates of morbidity and mortality (2.5%–31%). However, many of these
patients can be successfully treated with antibiotics and
become good candidates for cardiac transplantation. A
recent study looked at infection issues between patients
implanted with the Thoratec Heartmate vented electric
LVAD and smaller axial LVADs (15); the study showed
lower rates of infection and infection-related deaths with
improvements in patient selection, patient management,
device durability, and device design. Another study (16)
showed that LVAD-associated infection can be prevented
by adhering to evidence-based infection control and prevention guidelines, meticulous surgical techniques, and
optimal postoperative surgical site care. The authors have
seen a reduction in serious infection over time with the
CardioWest TAH owing to increased knowledge in patient
management and device design (17). Hemolysis
Hemolysis is commonly observed during extended CPB.

Chronic hemolysis can be associated with anemia and
a requirement for transfusions, which may sensitize a
potential transplant patient to tissue antigens and thereby
create a less compatible potential recipient. Chronic
hemolysis can also be associated with chronic renal
failure. None of the currently approved devices, when
used as recommended, produces excessive hemolysis
(free hemoglobin >10 mg/dL). Most clinical hemolysis
is related to patient-speciﬁc, not device-speciﬁc, parameters (18). In the bridge to transplant setting, drive parameters of devices should be set to minimize blood trauma
while achieving a blood ﬂow index of 2.5 to 3.5 L/min/m2
body surface area. Blood transfusions should not be given
unless the hematocrit falls below 20%, and then blood that
has been in storage for less than 1 week should be used,
and administered with a white blood cell ﬁlter. Multiple Organ Failure
Multiple organ failure is multifactorial. Many ‘‘device
patients’’ are in some degree of cardiogenic shock preoperatively. This may persist if the device fails to produce the
desired increase in cardiac output. Many of these patients
have clinically signiﬁcant bleeding during placement of
the device and require large amounts of blood products. Postoperatively, many will require inotropic support for
the ﬁrst 24 to 48 hours to maintain an adequate output. The presence of sepsis compounds multiple organ failure. Renal failure in this patient population is associated
with mild azotemia and abnormal clearance of free water. Its onset is associated with a high mortality. Massive transfusions may be associated with adult respiratory distress
syndrome. Hypoxemia is usually one of the ﬁrst manifestations of pulmonary failure. Increased intrapulmonary
shunt and decreased compliance are common clinical accompaniments. Jaundice is the most common evidence of
liver failure. Although an elevated bilirubin level may represent hemolysis, elevations in the levels of liver enzymes
may help make the diagnosis of liver failure. Gastrointestinal failure presents as gastrointestinal bleeding or ileus. The outcome of patients with multiple organ failure is well
known; the more organs involved in failure, the higher the
mortality. CIRCULATORY SUPPORT DEVICES
Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump
The IABP is at present the simplest and most frequently
used mechanical circulatory support device. It was ﬁrst
introduced by Moulopoulos et al. (12) in 1962 and then described clinically by Kantrowitz et al. (19) in 1968. It offers
the least complicated means of circulatory assistance.

Operation of the balloon is timed with the electrocardiogram
or aortic pressure waveform. It inﬂates during diastole

balloon and progresses to the proximal and distal end simultaneously. This pattern propels blood proximally and

(Fig. 1) include augmentation of diastolic pressure, decrease in afterload, and decrease in myocardial oxygen
consumption (20). Use of the IABP improves cardiac function, augmenting cardiac output by approximately 10% or
500 to 800 mL/min. It is generally used in combination
with inotropic agents, which are usually at near-maximal
levels at the time of IABP insertion. The IABP has many therapeutic uses in modern
medicine. It is widely used in left ventricular failure following CPB for revascularization or valve replacement. It
is also used in cases of cardiogenic shock in patients
on maximal inotropic support while awaiting cardiac
transplantation (21), cardiogenic shock following myocardial infarction, or intractable angina. Other limited
uses include left main coronary disease, ventricular dysrhythmias, right ventricular failure (22), septic shock, and
pulmonary embolus. In cases of right ventricular failure,
the IABP can be placed in the pulmonary artery. This is
performed in the operating room with the heart and great
vessels exposed (22). Contraindications for the use of the IABP include aortic
valve insufﬁciency, aortic aneurysm, and severe aortoiliac
or femoral disease precluding insertion of the balloon. Augmentation of the diastolic pressure will cause an
increase in regurgitant ﬂow across an incompetent aortic
valve, resulting in left ventricular distension. The same
augmentation or passage of the balloon may perforate the
aortic wall in patients with an aortic aneurysm. The IABP is usually inserted percutaneously in one of
the femoral arteries by the Seldinger technique (23) and
advanced into the descending aorta just distal to the origin
of the left subclavian artery (Fig. 2). If the femoral artery
pulse is not palpable, especially after bypass, insertion
may require a femoral artery cutdown.

In cases of severe
obstruction of the iliac and femoral vessels, the IABP
may be placed directly into the ascending aorta, in the
operating room, and advanced into the descending aorta. The advantages of the IABP are that (a) it is a nonIDE
device, (b) it is inexpensive, (c) it is easy to insert and use,
(d) there is much experience in its insertion and minimal
surveillance is required (physicians, perfusionist, nurses),
and (e) anticoagulation is not absolutely necessary (recommended during weaning). The disadvantages are that
(a) it has a complication rate of 20%; (b) there is a limited
increase in cardiac output; (c) there is no effective preload
reduction; and (d) there is limited effectiveness in cases of
tachycardia, dysrhythmias, and right ventricular failure.

External ventricular assist devices can be divided into
pulsatile and nonpulsatile. The pulsatile include the Thoratec pVAD (Pleasanton, California), the ABIOMED BVS
5000, and AB 5000 systems (Danvers, Massachusetts). The
nonpulsatile centrifugal systems include the Medtronics
BioMedicus pump (Eden Prairie, Minnesota), CardiacAssist TantemHeart Percutaneous Ventricular Assist Device
(Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania), and Levitronix CentriMag System (Waltham, Massachusetts). The family of paracorporeal pumps provides univentricular or biventricular pulsatile ﬂow. A system of two or
four cannulas provides inﬂow and outﬂow to the blood
pumps (Fig. 3). The Thoratec ventricular assist device is
a pneumatically driven paracorporeal prosthetic ventricle. This system has been very successful when used as a
bridge for cardiac transplantation (24) (Fig. 3). Better device ﬁlling is obtained if the pump inﬂow cannula comes
from the patient’s left and right ventricles (25). BjorkShiley valves sit at the inlet and outlet of each ventricle
and provide unidirectional ﬂow. A polyurethane sac divides the blood chamber from the air chamber within the
prosthetic ventricle. When the device is used as a bridge
to transplantation, and sacriﬁce of a sizable portion of
the left ventricular apex will thereby have no long-term
consequence, the inﬂow to the left ventricular device may
be anastomosed to an apical left ventriculotomy. The
stroke volume from each paracorporeal ventricle is approximately 65 mL. The pneumatic drivelines connect to
a console a few feet from the patient. Anticoagulation is
recommended. The Abiomed BVS 5000 system is also a paracorporeal,
pulsatile pneumatic device that can provide biventricular
support (Fig. 4).

Each blood pump, for right- or left-sided
heart support, consists of two polyurethane chambers. Each chamber is separated from the other with trileaﬂet
polyurethane valves. Blood ﬂows continuously in both
systole and diastole by gravity from the atrium to the
ﬁrst chamber within the blood pump. From there, it ﬂows
passively across an inlet valve into the active ventriclelike chamber, where it is pneumatically propelled into
the great vessel composite cannula with a distal Dacron
conduit. The pumps are operated by a console that
determines the pulsatile rate and the systole-to-diastole
ratio based on the compressed air ﬂow into and out of
the chambers. The system maintains a stroke volume
of 82 mL. It was designed as a support for hearts that
have sustained reversible damage, particularly in failed
attempts at weaning in CPB situations. Patients must
be at bed rest with this pump, which can be used for
univentricular or biventricular support. Anticoagulation
is maintained with intravenous heparin during the full
duration of assist (26). The AB 5000 has been introduced
with a stroke volume of 95 mL and one third less priming
volume of the BVS. The advantages of the paracorporeal systems are
the following: (a) right, left, or biventricular support;
(b) versatility for bridge to transplant; (c) useful in smaller
patients; (d) feedback and control of cardiac output of
the device; (e) easier implantation; and (f) commercial
availability. The disadvantages of these systems include
the following: (a) cannulas limit ﬂow to 4 to 6 L/min;
(b) hemolysis, thromboembolism, bleeding, and infection
are associated complications; and (c) anticoagulation is
required.

The World Heart Novacor ventricular assist device (Oakland, California) and the Thoratec HeartMate XVE ventricular assist device are useful implantable devices for
bridge to transplant and destination therapy applications. They required more than 20 years of research and
development, which was funded by the National Institutes

ventricle.

electrically driven pump with a solenoid that moves a

cirrhosis, unresolved malignancy, severe blood dyscrasia,
severe cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease,
prior cerebrovascular accident or transient ischemic
attack, acute systemic infection, and positive result on
human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) antibody test. Another type of internal LVAD under investigation in
the United States is the axial ﬂow pump. The Thoratec
HeartMate II, MicroMed DeBakey VAD (Houston, Texas),
and the Jarvik 2000 FlowMaker (New York, New York)
are all in current studies for bridge to transplant and
destination applications. Each of these devices uses the
principle of an Archimedes’ screw, which is in essence
an impeller pump that spins at very high revolutions per
minute (RPM) to impart forward ﬂow to the entrained
blood. The earliest versions of these devices were inserted
through the femoral artery and placed across the aortic
valve so that blood was entrained from the left ventricular
cavity and propelled into the ascending aorta. The current
devices function similarly, although placement is now typically through the apex of the left ventricle. The advantages
of these systems are their small size and durability. The advantages of implantable ventricular assist devices are mobilization of patients, long periods of support,
and high cardiac output capability. The disadvantages are
that (a) they require a median sternotomy with extension
into the upper abdominal wall or abdominal cavity; (b) ﬁt
problems are possible in smaller patients; (c) they cannot
support the right ventricle; (d) they are expensive; and
(e) complications of bleeding, infection, or thromboembolism can occur.

Total Artiﬁcial Hearts
The TAH provides complete support of the circulation,
but removal of the native heart is required. This device
has been used to provide permanent support; however, its
most important role is to serve as a bridge to cardiac transplantation. The ﬁrst implantable experimental design was
introduced in 1958 (32,33). An artiﬁcial heart was ﬁrst
used clinically in 1969 by Cooley et al. (34), who used
the Liotta heart to support a patient for 64 hours until
a donor heart became available. The use of the TAH as
a permanent device was initiated by Jarvik et al. (35). In
1982, the Jarvik 7 was implanted in Dr. Barney Clark (36),
who survived for 112 days. The Jarvik TAH was ﬁrst
used successfully as a bridge to cardiac transplantation by
Copeland et al. (37) in 1985 in a 25-year-old man with idiopathic cardiomyopathy (37,38). The TAH was also used by
the same surgical team in patients with viral and ischemic
cardiomyopathies, and in adults with congenital heart
disease (39–41). TAHs are currently manufactured by SynCardia Systems Inc (Tucson, Arizona) and ABIOMED. The
prosthetic ventricles are made of polyurethane. Mechanical heart valves (Medtronic-Hall, Minneapolis, Minnesota)
sit at the inlet and outlet of the ventricles to provide unidirectional ﬂow. A four-layered segmented polyurethane
diaphragm separates blood and air. This diaphragm retracts during diastole and is displaced forward during
systole, which propels blood out of the prosthetic ventricle. Compressed air provides the energy for displacement
of the diaphragm (Fig. 7). Dacron-covered pneumatic
drivelines pass through subcutaneous tunnels to the left
epigastrium. The drivelines are connected to 6-ft plastic tubing, effectively tethering the patient to a mobile
console. The console contains pneumatic drivers and a
computer to continuously monitor cardiac output, air
pressure curves, and ventricular ﬁlling volume curves,
and also displays trends. The console is mobile within
the hospital, allowing cardiac rehabilitation, diagnostic
studies, and even limited outdoor activity (walking with
assistance). A portable pneumatic driver will soon allow
more mobility, and possibly enable out-of-hospital lives
for these patients (42). FIGURE 7. Total artiﬁcial heart (pneumatic).

Implantation techniques emphasize hemostasis (43)
and the facilitation of explantation. Ventriculectomy is
started on the ventricular side of the atrioventricular (A-V)
groove. Both ventricles and the A-V valves, except for 2 mm
of valve tissue beyond the annuli, are excised. Strips of
teﬂon felt one half inch wide are then whipstitched around
the outer edges of the atrial cuffs, taking care to include,
in the stitch, all remaining epicardial fat and A-V groove
vessels. The coronary sinus is closed from inside the right
atrium. The atrial quick-connects are then sutured to the
Teﬂon felt–bolstered atrial cuffs. In the area of the atrial
septum, the left cuff is sutured in place, followed by the
right cuff. The two cuffs are on either side of the septum,
creating a double suture line in this area that is not
buttressed by Teﬂon felt. Next, measurements of lengths
for the great vessel conduits are approximated by placing
the ventricles in the mediastinum. Usually, the aortic
conduit is approximately 2.5 cm and the pulmonic conduit
approximately 5.5 cm. The great vessel conduits are then
anastomosed to the great vessels. Before attaching the
ventricles, an expanded polytetraﬂuoroethylene (e-PTFE)
‘‘neopericardium’’ is created using e-PTFE 0.1 mm in
thickness. Three 15 × 20 cm sheets are anchored with
nonabsorbable sutures to the most posterior aspects of
the pericardial reﬂection on the left pulmonary veins, the
diaphragmatic surface, and the cavae. These are folded
out of the way until ventricular attachment is completed,
then they are brought anteriorly to cover the device
completely. The ascending aorta and aortic anastomosis
are also encircled with a sheet of e-PTFE membrane. These nonreactive sheets greatly facilitate explantation
by creating surgical planes for aortic control, right atrial
cannulation, and device removal. They also minimize the
amount of adhesion formation and pericardial thickening
caused by the device. Once the ventricles are attached to the quick-connects,
de-airing is done with the patient in steep Trendelenberg
position. Pumping with the device is gradually increased
as CPB ﬂows are decreased. Positioning of the ventricles is checked and modiﬁed if necessary to assure that
the inferior vena cava and left pulmonary veins are
not compressed. This is conﬁrmed by transesophageal
echocardiogram as the chest is closed. Before closure,
complete hemostasis must be assured and the neopericardial tent is closed over the ventricles.

The ventricles of the
TAH are set for incomplete ﬁlling but complete emptying
with each stroke. The atrial pressure on each side determines ventricular ﬁlling. As atrial pressure increases, a
higher stroke volume and cardiac output are obtained. An
atrial pressure of 5 mm Hg provides a cardiac output of
4 to 5 L/min; an atrial pressure of 10 to 15 mm Hg may
result in a cardiac output as high as 12 L/min at the same
heart rate. A comparative study of neurologic events and infections
among three TAH devices showed similar stroke rates
and frequency of transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) per
patient year for the three devices. Infection rates in 40
patients, accounting for over 8.38 patient years, were
low [four positive blood cultures, and three positive
mediastinal cultures at explantation in the absence
of clinical (purulent) mediastinitis]. From a functional
perspective, postimplant these patients were extubated on
day 3, out of bed on day 3.5, and walking more than
100 ft without pause and discharged from the intensive
care unit on day 11. All survivors attended regular cardiac
rehabilitation sessions featuring treadmill walking and
exercise bicycle riding. The past decade has seen signiﬁcant advances in the
understanding of the pathophysiology and pharmacologic
approach to the treatment of CHF. These developments
have lead to a ‘‘shift to the right’’ of the mortality curve
for CHF, with patients living longer and with improved
quality of life. Unfortunately, once patients reach the steep
or rapidly declining phase of the mortality curve, that is,
being classiﬁed as American Heart Association/American
College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) Class D and New
York Heart Association (NYHA) Class IV CHF, their
decline continues in an accelerated manner. Patients
with Class IV CHF face a 2-year mortality risk of
greater than 75%. At that point in their natural history,
medical therapy is of limited value. It is exactly for
this group of maximally medically managed patients
with persistent and worsening CHF that the ﬁeld of
mechanical circulatory support has emerged. Over the
years, devices have been developed with progressively
increasing hemodynamic support capabilities. However,
when complete biventricular failure occurs, replacement
of total heart pump function is needed. It is for this
situation that the TAH has been developed.

Rationale for the Total Artiﬁcial Heart
The artiﬁcial heart arose from the unmet clinical need
for a device or system capable of completely restoring
systemic and pulmonary blood circulation and organ perfusion pressure in patients with failed circulatory systems
due to irreversible biventricular dysfunction. Early in the
history of TAH development, the vision was for creation of
such a device as a long-term permanent cardiac replacement. While this was a laudable initial goal, it proved
to be too big a technical, clinical, and social leap in the
early days of TAH development. With the eventual parallel
improvement in survival after heart transplantation, as a
result of the advent of effective antirejection pharmacology, a new and unforeseen rationale for the TAH arose. The growth of transplantation, with inadequate instant
donor heart availability, created the need for a ‘‘bridge,’’
rather than a permanent device, capable of sustaining
the life of a patient until a donor heart could be procured. Currently with advances in TAH development, both

of these visions, that is, short-term ‘‘bridge’’ and longterm ‘‘destination therapy,’’ are back in the minds of the
medical and technical community and are being actively
addressed. FUTURE DIRECTIONS
CHF affects approximately 4 million people in the United
States. Approximately 3% to 10% of these patients will
die each year because of the complications of CHF. It is
estimated that $3.1 billion/yr would be required to support
every patient needing a circulatory support system. It is
thought that treatment of patients with circulatory assist
devices may enable them to return to the work force
and contribute to society an income that is greater in
value than the total investment on support systems. Many
new models of assist devices will appear during the next
few years. The technology that has been developed and
the knowledge that has been acquired with all types
of circulatory assist devices represent one of the great
achievements of humankind. The quest for new materials,
new power supplies, and better devices will undoubtedly
open new frontiers to bring about changes to the human
life as we know it. KEY POINTS
■Appropriate patient selection and early initiation
of support are key to the successful utilization of
circulatory support devices. ■Major complications of the use of circulatory support devices include bleeding, thromboembolization,
infection, hemolysis, and multiple organ system
failure. ■Between 35% and 70% of patients receiving circulatory support device therapy will recover to be
weaned successfully from support or to the point
of transplantation. Approximately 60% of patients
who received mechanical support with the intent of
bridging to transplantation actually received an allograft organ, and of these, 88.5% were subsequently
discharged home. ■Device categories include intra-aortic, internal ventricular assist (single or dual ventricular), external
ventricular assist (also single or dual ventricular)
devices, and the TAH. ■Intra-aortic devices are the intra-aortic balloon
counterpulsation pump and the axial pump. ■Internal assist devices may be univentricular or
biventricular, and they may have atrial or ventricular supply sites with corresponding outﬂow vessel
discharge sites. Power supply may be compressed
gas or electrical. ■External devices include centrifugal pumps and two
paracorporeal pulsatile pumps (Thoratec ventricular
assist
device
and
ABIOMED
ventricular
assist
device). ■Current TAHs are pneumatically driven biventricular
devices that require excision of the native ventricles. ■Indications for the use of a support device are key to
patient criteria and therapeutic targets.

■Intra-aortic devices may be the ﬁrst line, but are
largely limited to short-term support. ■External devices provide longer-term support, but
may limit patient mobility. In general, these are best
suited for situations in which myocardial recovery is
anticipated. ■The internal devices appear to be the current choice
when transplantation is the target therapy and
a bridging interval is required, provided patient
characteristics meet device criteria. ■The TAH necessitates that the native ventricles
are excised with device implantation, so that only
permanent device dependence and transplantation
are left as therapeutic alternatives. REFERENCES

Invasive Cardiac Surgery
Matthew L. Kolz, John M. Toomasian, and Christina T. Mora Mangano
The
advent
of
minimally
invasive
cardiac
surgery
(MICS) coincided with the substantial improvements
in endoscopic equipment and novel operative methods appearing in the mid-1990s. Currently, minimally
invasive approaches continue to represent the minority of cardiac procedures. However, numerous centers
in the United States and abroad have embraced minimally invasive techniques believing that a decrease in
end-organ morbidity, a reduction in pain and scarring, and a reduced duration of recovery time may be
achieved with these methods. Minimally invasive techniques have been applied to coronary artery, aortic valve,
mitral valve, congenital heart disease, and atrial ﬁbril-
lation surgery. The incisions have diverged from the
traditional sternotomy to totally endoscopic procedures
done through thoracoscopic ports, with partial sternotomy
and minithoracotomy incisions falling between those
extremes. While not the focus of this chapter, coronary revascularization without the support of cardiopulmonary bypass
(CPB) is the most commonly performed minimally invasive cardiac procedure. This has been termed minimally
invasive direct coronary artery bypass (MIDCAB) or offpump coronary artery bypass (OPCAB). These techniques
have been widely described (1–3), and appear to be
cost effective. However, the superiority of on-pump versus off-pump coronary revascularization continues to be
hotly debated (4). Irrespective of an individual’s advocacy,
most surgeons (and anesthesiologists) agree that ‘‘beatingheart’’ coronary surgery represents a far greater technical
challenge (5). To access the potential advantages of minimally invasive techniques without forfeiting the support and safety
inherent in extracorporeal support, surgeons, anesthesiologists, and perfusionists have developed methods to
provide CPB in a minimally invasive environment. The
present chapter outlines the considerations and innovations permitting the application of CPB in procedures
conducted with a minimally invasive approach. INCISIONAL APPROACHES
FOR MINIMALLY INVASIVE CARDIAC
SURGERY
The location of the heart within the middle portion of the
mediastinum creates a surgical challenge for operative
exposure. Minimally invasive techniques have modiﬁed
methods to access the heart despite it being surrounded
by the thoracic skeleton (sternum and ribs), thoracic
muscles, and lungs. These techniques vary depending on
the speciﬁc heart surgery. A minimally invasive approach
for isolated aortic valve surgery includes a traditional
intercostal incision in the right anterior second or third
intercostal space.

The skin incision is made three to four
ﬁnger-breadths in width, overlying the rib interspace. The
intercostal incision is undermined to an extent greater
than length of the skin incision. Following the placement
of a soft tissue retractor, a specialized ﬂexible rib spreader
is advanced 3 in. The surgeon excises the anterior
mediastinal fat and incises the pericardium longitudinally. Sutures placed along the pericardial edges are placed
under tension outside the incision, thereby marsupializing
the aorta into the center of the wound. An upper ministernotomy incision (Gundry-style incision) is also used for aortic valve and aortic root procedures. This incision can be extended to a ‘‘J’’ shape, with
a partial sternal incision into the right fourth intercostal
space. In several centers, this approach is reserved for
patients requiring an extensive aortic root procedure, for
those who have an extensively calciﬁed ascending aorta,
or for patients in whom it may be necessary to cannulate
the aortic arch. Minimally invasive mitral valve surgery can also be
achieved through a small right anterior thoracotomy in
either the third or fourth intercostal space. For women,
a fourth interspace, inframammary incision may be preferred. However, in this lateral approach to the mediastinum, access to the heart may be obstructed by the
diaphragm. In this situation, a heavy traction suture

placed in the central tendinous portion of the right hemidiaphragm can lower the diaphragm and improve exposure. Traction sutures in the incised pericardial edges provide
an operating ﬁeld from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the
ascending aorta. Some surgeons advocate the use of a parasternal
incision. With this approach, an incision is made adjacent
to the sternum in a sagittal plane and several ribs
are transected for exposure. Alternatively, transverse
thoracotomy incisions of varying lengths can provide
exposure to heart through spreading the ribs and entering
the pleural space. These latter two approaches may not
fulﬁll some deﬁnitions of ‘‘minimally invasive’’ procedures. Finally, port-access cardiac surgery provides the ability
to operate on the heart through small incisions, ‘‘ports,’’
between the ribs. A ‘‘pure’’ port-access approach to cardiac
surgery with CPB demands the use of aortic and central
venous bypass conduits introduced through a peripheral
or extrapericardial location. Each of these techniques
provides different exposures to the heart through the
mediastinum and has advantages and limitations (Fig. 1). Although the surgical incisions developed for MICS
may appear straightforward, the challenge to institute
complete CPB in a closed chest or an extremely limited
operative ﬁeld is substantial. The approaches and technologies that have evolved to arrest and exclude the heart
from the central circulation, cannulate the aorta for systemic ﬂow, divert venous return to an extracorporeal site,
and provide respiration and heat transfer for MICS are
discussed in the subsequent text. Importantly, many surgeons and clinical groups have
adopted—mixed and matched—various components of
different systems designed to allow MICS. There are a
number of components that can be used together although
they were not part of an original MICS system. ANESTHESIA MANAGEMENT

echocardiography must assess and monitor cannula
placement with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). In some institutions, anesthesiologists place endocoronary
sinus retrograde cardioplegia catheters (ECSCs) through

term fast-track anesthesia has been used to designate a
paradigm shift away from the high-dose narcotic techniques previously used for cardiac surgery toward more
balanced techniques utilizing moderate doses of narcotics,
shorter-acting muscle relaxants, and an increased use of
potent volatile anesthetics, and sometimes regional techniques for postoperative pain control (7). Both MICS and
‘‘fast-track’’ anesthesia have been advocated in leading
to decreased intubation periods, decreased intensive care
unit stay durations, and decreased costs. CANNULATION AND MYOCARDIAL
PROTECTION STRATEGIES
Venous Cannulae and Venous Blood
Return
Traditional CPB utilizes direct cannulation of the right
atrium and ascending aorta for venous and arterial
conduits, respectively. During MICS, the limited exposure
to these structures has provided an incentive for an
evolution of cannulation strategies (8). Extrathoracic vascular cannulation has been widely
used in long-term extracorporeal respiratory or cardiac
life support (9,10), portable or emergency bypass for
supported angioplasty (11), resuscitation from exposure
hypothermia (12), surgical clipping of giant cerebral
aneurysms (13,14), and cardiovascular rescue (15,16). The jugular vein, carotid artery, or femoral vessels are
acceptable vascular access sites for connection to the
heart–lung machine. Vascular access cannulas used for
extrathoracic circulatory procedures are typically smaller
and longer than standard right atrial cannulas, and some
can be inserted percutaneously. Although this method
of partial support for the circulation can be maintained
for a prolonged period of time, total cardiopulmonary
support through peripheral cannulas is difﬁcult to achieve
for sustained periods (17). Unless the left ventricle is
completely decompressed, the heart continues to eject
blood.

If the surgical procedure provides access to the right
atrium, it may be cannulated directly with a large-bore
cannula and drained through gravity siphon. However,
many surgeons have found it advantageous to utilize
the femoral vein to guide an endovenous drainage
cannula (EVD) into the IVC and right atrium. The right
femoral vein is preferred over the left as it provides a
straighter path for cannulation passage, which may be
done percutaneously or through a femoral vein cut down. The EVD contains multiple holes which are guided into
the right atrium by ﬂuoroscopic or TEE guidance. The extended length and reduced diameter of extrathoracic venous cannulae increases the resistance to
blood return. The issue of inadequate venous return
during MICS requires the attention of the surgeon,
perfusionist, and anesthesiologist. All must recognize
the multiple, frequently covert, technical challenges and
mishaps—kinked or obstructed catheters, excessive negative pressure on venous return catheters, and/or increased
venous capacitance—that can lead to inadequate venous
return and in turn, inadequate oxygen delivery. To optimize venous return during MICS, the anesthesiologist must assess ongoing venous compliance and
capacitance and central venous pressure (CVP). With the
placement of retractors and/or cannulae used for MICS,
the measurement of CVP is challenging. Some recommend the use of the distal port of the pulmonary artery
catheter to measure true CVP. Because poor venous return
from the superior vena cava (SVC) may compromise cerebral blood ﬂow (mean arterial pressure - central venous
pressure = cerebral perfusion pressure) the adequacy of
venous return from the upper body should be monitored. Ultrasonic ﬂow monitors can assist in assessing venous return. Raising the lower limbs above the level of the heart
may prevent venous pooling and improve drainage to the
central circulation. Despite interventions to optimize venous return, traditional gravity drainage usually diverts
only 75% to 80% of the venous return to the heart. To address this problem, most institutions employ some form
of augmented venous blood return to provide complete
cardiopulmonary support. Assisted venous drainage (AVD) enhances the drainage
siphon to increase the venous blood ﬂow to the heart–lung
machine. A variety of methods is available to implement
AVD, but two different techniques are widely used:
kinetically assisted venous drainage (KAVD) and vacuumassisted venous drainage (VAVD) (18–21). KAVD utilizes a centrifugal or kinetic pump between
the venous drainage cannula and the venous reservoir.

The
kinetic pump generates a siphon, which enhances venous
return. This method improves venous drainage by 20% to

8. Cardiopulmonary Bypass for Minimally Invasive Cardiac Surgery
143
40% in comparison with a gravity siphon (18). With KAVD,
venous blood is actively pumped into either an open or
closed venous reservoir. The inertia of the kinetic pump
regulates the siphon. As the pump speed is increased, more
suction is generated. Monitoring pressure in the venous
conduit at a point proximal to the kinetic pump inlet
directs the perfusionist in regulating the amount of siphon,
which can be controlled manually or automatically (20). Excessive negative pressure can cause cavitation, blood
trauma, and hemolysis and may lead to collapse of the
right atrium around the venous cannula, impeding venous
return (21). In this clinical circumstance, the perfusionist
can stall the applied negative pressure on the venous lines,
thereby releasing the entrapped atrial tissue or venous
intima. Subsequent reapplication of a reduced amount of
negative pressure should optimize venous return. Greater
diligence
must
be
exercised
to
prevent
air microemboli with minimally invasive bypass techniques (22,23). Negative pressure on venous return lines
results in air entrainment from a number of sites. Because
small bubbles are not very buoyant, they advance readily through the entire perfusion circuit and are expelled
through the aortic cannulae. Perfusionists must be diligent
in alerting the surgical staff to inadequate venous return. KAVD has successfully supplemented venous return in
MICS and in other cardiothoracic procedures (18–20). Von Segesser et al. have evaluated the factors affecting
venous blood return using peripheral versus right atrial
blood return and KVAD (24,25). They found that venous
return was greatly dependent on CVP (greater CVP values
are associated with improved return) and the type of
cannula used. In their experimental model of ‘‘light house’’
type 24-Fr, 28-Fr, or 38-Fr catheters versus a percutaneous
type 28-Fr, the percutaneous catheter performed best
under low CVP conditions and KVAD. This same group
of investigators developed a so-called Smart Canula
(Smartcanula LLC, Lausanne, Switzerland). This cannula
was developed for peripheral access venous drainage and
addresses the problem of inadequate venous return with
MICS techniques. The size of traditionally sized cannulae
is limited by the size of the vein used as a portal for
the central venous drainage. For example, an adult open
cardiac procedure permits the placement of a 36- to 41-
Fr catheter in the IVC and the SVC.

Peripheral venous
access ports (jugular, femoral) will accept cannulae of 24
to 28 Fr. The Smart Canula is made from a shape memory
alloy that is stretched over a hollow mandrel to reduce
its proﬁle. The ‘‘compacted’’ cannula is fed over a guide
wire into the peripheral access vein. When the tip of the
catheter reaches the central venous location, the guide
wire and mandrel are removed and the cannula expands
to its predetermined diameter or the diameter of the host
vessel (Fig. 2). Von Segesser et al. reported on their use of the
Smart Canula in ﬁve patients undergoing redo cardiac

case, supraoptimal ﬂows were achieved and represented
values 20% greater than ﬂows obtained with traditional
cannulae (26). The other form of AVD, VAVD, utilizes a standard
vacuum suction source to enhance venous return. Applying vacuum to an open (hard-shell) venous reservoir
applies suction to the entire venous drainage system to
increase venous return. VAVD requires close regulation
of the vacuum source to avoid the negative pressure
variations found in most hospital wall suction systems. Avoiding excessive VAVD negative pressures limits blood
trauma and hemolysis (22,23) and prevents venous reservoir cracking or implosion. Step-down vacuum regulators
maintain precise vacuum pressures. Positive and negative pressure relief valves must be incorporated into the
reservoir to prevent both overpressure and underpressure
and to ensure consistent extracorporeal ﬂow rates. VAVD
cannot be applied to closed systems utilizing a (soft-shell)
venous reservoir bag. Aortic and Arterial Cannulation, Aortic
Occlusion, and Cardioplegia in
Minimally Invasive Cardiac Surgery
Once venous blood has been collected into the venous
reservoir, it is pumped through the heart–lung machine
and returned into the systemic arterial circulation. Arterial
cannulation strategies are dependent upon the surgical
procedure, but include aortic cannulation and peripheral
vessel cannulation. When surgical exposure allows for
direct ascending aorta cannulation, it is usually the
preferred approach as the technique and results are
essentially the same as that used for conventional cardiac
surgery.

Some modiﬁcations to the technique may be
utilized by the surgeons due to the limited exposure and
include smaller or tapered cannulae. When direct ascending aortic cannulation is not possible, peripheral cannulation may be achieved at brachial,

axillary, and femoral arterial sites. Femoral cannulation
has served as the standard due to ease and cosmetic scarring considerations. Risks of femoral cannulation include
embolization due to retrograde aortic ﬂow, femoral or
aortic dissections due to vessel manipulation, and femoral
vessel injury with hematoma. Transesophageal echocardiographic assessment of the descending aorta is essential
before cannulation to rule out extensive aortic atheromatous disease and to observe for dissections and aortic
injury. Contraindications to femoral cannulation are discussed in a later section. Traditional surgical techniques utilize an aortic cross
clamp placed through a median sternotomy to provide occlusion of the aorta from the surgical ﬁeld. While this may
be possible with some minimally invasive approaches,
two alternative methods have been developed to occlude
the aorta when the surgical ﬁeld does not allow direct
clamping of the aorta. The ﬁrst has been the development
of endoclamps that obstruct the aorta from an intraluminal location. The ﬁrst endoclamp was developed in
the mid-1990s by Heartport (Heartport, Inc., Redwood
City, CA, USA) (8,27–30). The endoclamp and the entire port-access cardiac surgery (PACS) system developed
by Heartport are now available through CardioVations
(EndoCPB System) (Ethicon, Inc., Somerville, NJ, USA). The endoaortic clamp (EAC) is an inﬂatable, polyurethane
aortic occlusion balloon containing individual lumina that
allow antegrade cardioplegia administration, aortic root
venting, and aortic root pressure monitoring (Fig. 3). The
catheter is passed through the lumen of the femoral artery
cannula into the aorta and positioned in the ascending
aorta by ﬂuoroscopy or TEE. A similar type of endoclamp
that can be placed directly in the ascending aorta is also
available (SOFTCLAMP arterial cannula) (CardioVations
(SOFTCLAMP SYSTEM) (Ethicon, Inc., Somerville, NJ,
USA) (Fig. 4). In addition to antegrade delivery through the ENDOCLAMP Aortic Catheter, retrograde delivery of cardioplegia is possible through an ECSC. This catheter is
inserted through a jugular venous sheath, because direct
right atrium cannulation is not possible, and advanced
into the coronary sinus with ﬂuoroscopic or TEE guidance. Manual inﬂation of an occlusion balloon on the end
of the catheter facilitates the retrograde administration of
cardioplegia. Estech (Estech, Danville, CA, and USA) developed a
second type of endoclamp [Estech-remote access perfusion (RAP) clamp] that also uses a balloon to occlude
the ascending aorta and can provide antegrade cardioplegia and venting of the left ventricle.

In contrast to the
EndoCPB System, the Estech-RAP approach permits antegrade aortic blood ﬂow from a port just distal to the
balloon. Some clinicians suggest that the Estech system
affords greater stability and is less likely to migrate intraoperatively. Moreover, antegrade blood ﬂow is likely
superior to retrograde perfusion. Blood ﬂow originating
at the level of the femoral artery is more likely to be
associated with aortic dissections, embolic phenomenon
and compromised perfusion to the lower extremities (31)
(Fig. 5). In 1997, Chitwood et al. introduced a modiﬁed aortic
cross-clamp (Chitwood transaxillary clamp) that could be
used in restricted-access cardiac surgery procedures. The
Chitwood clamp was designed to be inserted through an
additional port in the right third or fourth intercostal
space with the posterior jaw in the transverse sinus (32). Cardioplegia may be given retrograde through a catheter
placed into the coronary sinus through a purse string
suture in the right atrium or anterograde if the coronary
ostia are accessible. Some surgeons advocate the use
of a modiﬁed aortic cross-clamp over endovascular
aortic occlusion devices. One study comparing restrictedaccess aortic cross-clamps versus aortic endoclamps
found similar clinical outcomes but reported that the
endoclamps were associated with greater operative costs
and an increase in complications (33). PERFUSION MANAGEMENT DURING
PORT-ACCESS CARDIOPULMONARY
BYPASS
Perfusion management algorithms for CPB for restrictedaccess cardiac surgery follow conventional protocols for
pump blood ﬂow, anticoagulation, temperature management, myocardial protection, and acid–base regulation. However, the cannulation strategies discussed may require additional expertise, monitoring, and instrumentation. This is especially demonstrated by port-access
cardiopulmonary bypass surgery (PACS) which utilizes
femoral venous and arterial cannulation. With PACS, gravity-dependent venous drainage initiates partial CPB. Once a stable blood ﬂow is achieved,
AVD is begun. The magnitude of the venous siphon is
gradually increased. Pressures of −50 to −80 mm Hg are
usually adequate without causing venous conduit ‘‘chatter’’ or collapse. In contrast to what occurs in conventional
CPB, several minutes usually elapse before a steady state
of extracorporeal circulation is established. To facilitate EAC balloon inﬂation, the pump ﬂow is reduced while full venous decompression is maintained in an
effort to decrease the systemic pressure and keep the heart
empty, which prevents left ventricular ejection against the
EAC balloon as it is inﬂated. The occlusion balloon is
inﬂated with a mixture of contrast dye and saline solution
(10%–30%).

The approximate correlation between aortic
diameter and inﬂation volumes of endoarotic clamps are

With EAC inﬂation, cardioplegia solution can be
infused antegrade or retrograde through the EAC distal
vent/cardioplegia lumen or through an ECSC, respectively. Pressures must be monitored to ensure proper catheter
positioning. Following cardioplegia infusion, the aortic
root can be vented through the EAC aortic root lumen. To ensure the safety and adequacy of perfusion, the surgical team (surgeon, anesthesiologist, and perfusionist)
must monitor venous drainage, arterial inﬂow, myocardial decompression, cardioplegia, cardiac venting rates,
aortic balloon occlusion, and cerebral perfusion. In addition, TEE and ﬂuoroscopy are used to assess the
catheters (34,35). The continued attendance of an anesthesiologist skilled in TEE is crucial to the management. Following completion of the surgical procedure, the
EAC is deﬂated. To facilitate this, the extracorporeal ﬂow
is reduced and the EAC balloon contents are aspirated
into the inﬂation syringe. The aortic root is usually vented
following deﬂation of the balloon. With deﬂation, blood
ﬂow to the coronary arteries is reestablished. As the patient warms to 37◦C, the left ventricle is permitted to eject,
ventilation is reestablished, the patient is weaned from
bypass, and catheters are removed. Overall, perfusion management is more complex and
requires a greater number of monitors and instruments
during PACS than during a traditional CPB procedure.

In
addition to monitoring of the usual perfusion parameters
(e.g., arterial venous pressure and CVPs, blood ﬂow, venous reservoir volume, cardioplegia and circuit pressures),
careful monitoring of the position and function of the

endovascular catheters is required. Venous siphon pressure, endopulmonary and endoaortic root vent ﬂows, EAC
balloon pressure, and the relation of the aortic root pressure and the systemic arterial pressure are all inﬂuenced
by management of the heart–lung machine. Changes and
manipulations to the circuit are often very subtle, and
more time and more precise technique are required than
in traditional CPB. Surges in systemic or cardioplegia
ﬂow can potentially dislodge the endovascular catheters,
which require repositioning to prevent patient injury. Constant vigilance is therefore necessary to maintain proper
function of the PACS system. PERFUSION MONITORING
AND TROUBLESHOOTING
Two aspects that should receive special attention during
minimally invasive port-access CPB are monitoring the
position of the EAC during bypass and monitoring for
air removal at the end of bypass. Migration of the
EAC is one of the major concerns in operating the
system. During retrograde CPB, the ﬂow tends to push
the balloon toward the aortic valve (Fig. 7). This can
result in loss of occlusion, damage to the aortic valve,
prolapse of the balloon into the left ventricle, and
ineffective delivery of antegrade cardioplegia. Conversely,
delivery of antegrade cardioplegia tends to push the
balloon cephalad and occlude the innominate artery and
possibly the left carotid artery. Balloon migration can
also damage the aortic wall or dislodge atheromatous
debris or plaque. In most instances, TEE adequately
monitors EAC position during CPB. However, cardiac
manipulation, particularly during mitral valve procedures,
can make observation by TEE difﬁcult, and ﬂuoroscopy
can be used to assess balloon placement if TEE ﬁndings
are inconclusive. Preventing proximal migration depends
on removing excessive slack from the EAC catheter during
placement, ensuring that balloon inﬂation pressures are
adequate, avoiding excessive aortic root vent ﬂow rates,
and changing systemic arterial perfusion ﬂows gradually. Monitoring the systemic regional perfusion is important, as distal balloon migration can occlude the cerebral
vessels. Monitoring of innominate artery and cerebral
perfusion can be carried out by a number of methods. Table 1 lists these methods and their limitations. Arterial pressure should be monitored in the right radial,
brachial, or axillary artery because this pressure will fall
if distal EAC migration partially or completely occludes
the innominate artery.

Simultaneous pressure monitoring
in an artery supplied by the innominate artery and in
one distal to (but not supplied by) the innominate artery
(usually the left radial or either femoral artery) will demonstrate balloon migration. The clinician should recognize
that partial innominate artery occlusions may be difﬁcult
to detect and that preexisting right-to-left or arm-to-leg
pressure differences can complicate interpretation. Transcranial Doppler monitoring of the right middle cerebral
artery, can also be used to detect distal migration and may
identify partial innominate artery occlusions more readily than does regional arterial pressure monitoring (36). However, transcranial Doppler equipment is expensive,
expertise is required for its placement and interpretation,
and a signal cannot be obtained in 10% to 20% of patients even in the presence of pulsatile ﬂow. Carotid or
temporal artery pulse wave Doppler can also be used, but
continuous monitoring is difﬁcult to maintain for long
periods. Electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring should
theoretically provide information about the adequacy of
cerebral perfusion, but no data are available regarding its
utility in this clinical setting. Similarly, bilateral cerebral
transcranial oximetry may reﬂect acute changes in unilateral cerebral O2 delivery following balloon occlusion of
the innominate artery, but again no data are available. The prevention of distal migration depends on adequate
balloon inﬂation and avoidance of high aortic root

A number of conditions preclude the use of PACS (Table 3). These conditions largely relate to the potential for vascular
injury with the Port-Access system, difﬁculties in maintaining the correct catheter position, and the potential for
retrograde embolization of particulate matter.Both preoperative screening and intraoperative TEE (and occasionally arteriography) identify patients who are inappropriate
candidates for a PACS approach. Peripheral vascular disease and aortic atheromatous
disease predispose to retrograde embolization of atheromatous plaque and retrograde arterial dissection. The
increased incidence of aortic dissection in the ﬁrst group
of patients managed with the Port-Access system initiated recommendations for patient screening, EAC and
guide wire design changes, and modiﬁed insertion techniques. Tortuous femoral and iliac arteries, which make
it very difﬁcult to place the endovascular system, increase
the risk for vascular injury. Therefore, preoperative arterial screening is recommended for all patients with
coronary artery disease (or risk factors for ischemic
heart disease), age of 55 years or more, or weight of
less than 60 kg. At the time of operation, the anesthesiologist should examine the thoracic aorta (by TEE)
for evidence of atheromatous disease, especially mobile
plaque. Grades 3 to 5 atheromatous disease of the aorta
is a contraindication to PACS. Because inﬂation of the
EAC results in balloon pressures of 250 to 350 mm Hg,

SURGICAL PROCEDURES
AND OUTCOME DATA
Despite the fact that it has been in development since
the mid-1990s, MICS still represents the minority of
cardiac procedures. Restricted-access cardiac procedures
continue to evolve in the hands of skilled surgeons,
ambitious anesthesiologists, and able perfusionists who
push the boundaries of cardiac surgery by specializing in
what might be termed niche techniques. Coronary Revascularization
Recent years have seen advances in interventional cardiology for the treatment of coronary artery disease. This
has provided increased incentive for cardiac surgeons to
utilize less invasive surgical techniques, which has fueled
the development of minimally invasive coronary surgery
into two divergent directions. One of these directions has
been to minimize the incision size while utilizing mod-
iﬁed bypass techniques. The second direction has been
to avoid the CPB machine—often referred to as MIDCAB
grafting or OPCAB grafting. As noted earlier, there is scant
consensus regarding the superiority of one approach over
the other. Performing coronary revascularization through portaccess techniques has been proved feasible using femoral
artery and venous cannulation techniques with a minithoracotomy approach (37). However, these techniques have
decreased in popularity as a result of increased complexity
and operating times. Mitral Valve Surgery
When performing intracardiac procedures, surgeons do
not have the option of avoiding CPB and therefore, the
focus is on limiting the incisional trauma. The major
decision is to perform the surgery using a conventional
