DURING CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
The ability of a drug to produce its effect depends
on the ability of free (unbound) drug to reach its
receptor and bind with that receptor to transduce the
signal (153,154,244). A number of factors may affect the
ability of drugs to reach and interact with their receptors
during cardiac surgery and CPB. Protein Binding
In the blood, drugs exist as free (unbound) drug in equilibrium with the bound (i.e., bound to plasma proteins) drug. Free drug interacts with the receptor to produce drug effect (56,155). Drugs are bound primarily to the plasma
proteins albumin (acidic drugs) and α-1-acid glycoprotein
(α1AGP) (basic drugs, e.g., fentanyl, lidocaine), an acute
phase reactant (154). The concentration of α1AGP rises
during stress, including stress during the systemic inﬂam-
matory response following CPB (47,143,225,226,245–249),
and this reduces lidocaine (246,249), quinidine (143,249),
and propranolol (249) free drug concentrations following CPB, as marked by the return of arrhythmias despite
adequate measured total drug concentrations. Changes in protein binding are clinically signiﬁcant
only for drugs that are highly protein bound (58). The
degree of drug–protein binding depends on the total drug
concentration, the available protein concentration, the
afﬁnity of the protein for the drug, and the presence of
other substances that may compete with the drug or alter
the drug binding site (250,251).

Measurement of total drug
concentrations in plasma during CPB may therefore fail
to elucidate the true picture of changes in drug effect
unless measurement of the unbound concentration is also
reported (Fig. 14) (53,55,58). The degree of protein binding may be altered by
pathologic states existing before CPB, for example, acute
myocardial infarction (MI) (248), renal disease (252),
and diabetes (253), or as a result of changes occurring during CPB, for example, development of the SIRS
leading to a reduction in albumin production and an increase in α1AGP concentrations (47,143,246,249). Renal
failure and liver disease reduce plasma albumin concentrations (254). The afﬁnity of albumin for drugs such as
phenytoin, thiopentone, and diazepam may be reduced
in the presence of chronic disease states, for example,
cirrhosis (63,226,254,255). Heparin is administered before and during CPB to
prevent clot formation. Heparin releases free fatty acids,
which may in turn displace drugs from protein binding
sites and increase free drug concentrations to enhance the
pharmacologic effect (26,37,38,256). Tissue Binding
Following drug administration, free drug penetrates into
tissues where it may bind to tissue proteins. Certain
tissues, for example, those of the heart and lung, may have
an afﬁnity for certain drugs (38,40,41,77,203–207,257). This has two relevant pharmacodynamic consequences. Tissue binding may limit access of a drug to its receptor
if that tissue is not the site of the desired drug action,
thereby potentially limiting the magnitude of effect (206). The tissue may also serve as a drug reservoir, thereby
extending drug effect, particularly if the tissue (e.g., lung)
is out of circuit during CPB (Fig. 17) (41). Changes in
plasma-free drug concentrations occurring as a result of
protein binding, for example, hemodilution during CPB,
are buffered by redistribution of drug from tissue stores
to plasma (16,18,53,54). Age
Adult cardiac surgical patients are frequently elderly,
deﬁned as age greater than 65 years. Independent of
pathologic processes, aging is associated with a variety of
physiologic processes that may inﬂuence drug effect (63). The function of organs such as the heart and blood ﬂow
to the kidneys and liver are reduced (258). These factors
may reduce drug clearance (259). Elderly humans have
increased adipose tissue, which may serve as a reservoir
for lipid soluble drugs. Albumin concentrations may be

11. Changes in the Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Drugs
207
reduced to cause higher free drug concentrations when
standard doses are administered (63,259). Central nervous system (CNS) sensitivity to drugs in
the elderly has been investigated. CNS sensitivity to
barbiturates may be unaltered in the elderly (260), but
reductions in dose are required because of a slower return
of drug from the effect site to the central compartment
(a pharmacokinetic difference) (261,262). In contrast, a
true difference in CNS sensitivity to opioids (fentanyl,
alfentanil, and remifentanil) (263–265) and to volatile
agents (266) has been described in the elderly. For
the elderly patient undergoing CPB, a reduction in
dose to limit the high free drug concentrations and
the potential for prolonged or toxic drug effects seems
prudent. At the other end of the age spectrum, infants and
children may have altered drug effects owing to differences in distribution of body fat, immaturity of clearance
mechanisms, and disease-related changes in drug handling (87,267–280). The degree to which they may have
differences in drug sensitivity has received little scientiﬁc
scrutiny, but differences appear to exist (281). It cannot be assumed that doses of drugs considered adequate
in adults undergoing CPB will sufﬁce for the pediatric
population (269,271,282,283). Central Nervous System Penetration
For anesthetic agents, the site of drug effect is presumed
to be the CNS. Differences in CNS pharmacodynamic
effects between drugs have been measured by utilizing
the time difference between peak plasma concentrations
of drugs and their effect on the electroencephalogram
(EEG) (284). A hysteresis (i.e., less time to equilibrium
with alfentanil) has been observed between the peak
plasma concentration of fentanyl versus alfentanil and
the shift in the spectral edge frequency of the EEG (285). A similar time lag has been observed as drug concentrations fall, and differences between drugs have been
detected. Most likely, this represents disposition of the
more lipophilic fentanyl to highly lipophilic brain tissue preventing fentanyl concentrations from rising at the
CNS opioid receptors and prolonging time to peak effect,
that is, a pharmacokinetic difference. This hypothesis is
substantiated by the demonstration that hysteresis for
sufentanil (another lipophilic opioid) more closely approximates that of fentanyl than the more hydrophilic
alfentanil (286). A similar rationale has been used to
describe differences in onset of action between midazolam and diazepam (284,287).

Utilization of these time
differences and concentrations can be measured and
modeled, and has led to the development of computer
programs with a rate constant (Keo) designed to target
stable drug concentrations at the effect site compartment (receptor level) (79,86,281,288). Such programs have
been utilized in studies of drug administration to target concentrations during general (86,90,251,289) and
cardiac surgery (74,86,89–91,271). By providing stable
plasma concentrations, determination of concentration
versus effect relations during CPB can be made by utilizing various monitors of CNS activity, such as auditory
evoked potentials (AEP) (290) and the bispectral index
(BIS) (31,57,73,74,79–84,88,89,91,167,291,292). Temperatures
Hypothermia produces a number of pharmacodynamic
effects. Anesthetic requirements are reduced by hypothermia (21,31,168). Changes in receptor afﬁnity, for
example, decreased opioid receptor afﬁnity (293) and
nicotinic acetylcholine receptor sensitivity (294), occur during hypothermia. The action of neuromuscular receptor blocking agents is enhanced, which may
reﬂect a pharmacodynamic and a pharmacokinetic effect (22,23,27–29,188,197,295–298) (Table 4) (7). Use of hypothermia may attenuate release of the excitatory neurotransmitters glutamate and glycine (299),
thereby exerting a cerebroprotective effect. The implications of such an effect on drug action are unknown,
but hypothermia has not reduced the incidence of neurocognitive deﬁcits in most [but not all (300)] prospective
randomized clinical trials (157,167). Acid–Base and Electrolyte Changes
Regardless of the strategy used to manage the patient’s
acid–base status during CPB (219–222), altered tissue
blood ﬂow produces tissue acidosis during CPB (301,302). ◗TABLE 4 Muscle Relaxants and Hypothermic

III. Physiology and Pathology
This may affect the response to catecholamines (303). The
degree of ionization and protein binding (hence free drug
concentrations) of weak acids and bases may also be affected by the blood gas management strategy employed
during CPB (Fig. 18) (224). Changes in pH may also affect
electrolyte balance. Calcium, magnesium, and potassium
concentrations decline during CPB (304–310), and associated muscle weakness, arrhythmias, and enhanced
digitalis toxicity may ensue. Whether intraoperative replacement of calcium (311,312) or magnesium (313,314)
reduces these complications, for example, arrhythmias, is
still debated. Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Volatile anesthetic agents are commonly employed during
CPB, usually in combination with intravenous anesthetic
agents to avoid hemodynamic aberrations (315–317). Volatile agents may disrupt ion channels and intracellular
transduction mechanisms (318–321). The anesthetic requirements for volatile agents are reduced by a yet uniden-
tiﬁed mechanism following CPB in dogs (322) (323,324),
although the nature of the priming solution (acetate) may
prove important by acting as a supplemental anesthetic
agent (324). In man, using the brain’s electrical activity ‘‘depth of
anesthesia’’ monitors [which may be problematic in terms
of sensitivity (31,56,291)] to examine the independent
role of CPB in reducing anesthetic requirements has
yielded mixed results. Yoshitani et al. demonstrated a
greater pharmacodynamic effect for a given concentration
of propofol pre- versus post-CPB under normothermic
conditions (57). Similarly, Takizawa et al. showed an
enhanced effect of propofol for a given dose following
normothermic CPB—in part related to an increased free
(but not total) drug concentration during CPB (56). However, Ahonen et al. examined the need for propofol to
maintain a ﬁxed BIS in a group of patients randomized
to on- versus off-pump surgery, and could not detect any
difference in anesthetic requirements (325). Mets et al. examined the concentration–effect relation for isoﬂurane
in combination with a computer-driven infusion of
fentanyl designed to maintain a constant effect site
concentration of 3 ng/mL and noted a 25% reduction
in the concentration of isoﬂurane required to maintain a
stable BIS level post- versus pre-CPB (326). Whether there
is an independent difference in anesthetic requirements
related to the use of CPB requires further investigation. Receptor Density
The number of receptors available for interaction with
a ligand will determine the magnitude of drug effect. Patients presenting for cardiac surgery frequently
have CHF (1,2,317).

In this clinical setting, there are
reductions in the number of cardiac β-receptors, defects in receptor transduction, and impaired synthesis and
reuptake of norepinephrine (128,138,327,328). Chronic
β-adrenergic receptor agonist administration has a pharmacodynamic effect (329,330) and therapeutic failure, including increased mortality (331). Chronic administration
of β-adrenergic receptor blocking agents in this condition
improves morbidity (332,333) and mortality (332–334),
hence patients with CHF typically take these agents preoperatively. As a consequence of both a reduced number
of receptors and pharmacologic blockade of β receptors,
β-adrenergic agonists may exhibit reduced pharmacodynamic effects during and following CPB (335,336). Discontinuation of β-adrenergic receptor blocking
agents in patients treated for angina pectoris and CHF
in the perioperative period may lead to β-adrenergic
receptor
upregulation
and
increased
adrenergic
responsiveness (337,338). Increases in myocardial oxygen
demand due to increased heart rate and contractility may lead to worsened symptomatology or even
death (339). A retrospective database analysis suggested
that continuation of β-adrenergic receptor blocking agents
might also have a neuroprotective effect (340). It is
generally recommended, with only a few exceptions,
for example, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, that chronic cardiovascular medications including β-adrenoceptor receptor blocking agents be continued
until surgery commences (337). Changes in receptor density and function may occur
very quickly (126), and have been observed to occur
during the conduct of cardiac surgery (42–45,341,342). The density and function of the β-adrenergic receptor has
been examined the most. β-adrenergic receptor function is
impaired following CPB (343,344). Possible mechanisms
include ischemia-reperfusion injury (345,346) and acute
β-adrenergic receptor desensitization (347,348) occurring
as a result of the catecholamine release accompanying
CPB (174). At the cellular level there is a reduction in GRK
activity (124). Attempts to ameliorate the β-adrenergic
receptor dysfunction have included the administration of
β-adrenergic receptor blocking agents during CPB (349,
350), use of warm blood cardioplegia (351), and the
use of high spinal anesthesia (352). Further work is
required to elucidate the mechanisms and identify the best
therapeutic options to reduce these undesirable changes
in receptor density and function. THE SYSTEMIC INFLAMMATORY
RESPONSE SYNDROME
Cardiac surgery and CPB initiate a systemic inﬂammatory
response as a consequence of operative trauma, blood
contact with a foreign surface and complement activation,
development of ischemia and reperfusion injury, and the

11. Changes in the Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Drugs
209
presence of endotoxin (47,48,353–361). The magnitude of
the response is inﬂuenced by a number of factors (46,
47,354–356,362,363), including genetics (364–366), and
may have an adverse effect on clinical outcomes (8,
367,368), including the development of multiple organ
dysfunction syndrome (MODS) (66,68,193,211,212,369–
371). The pathophysiologic mechanisms by which this
occurs are gradually being elucidated (372–382). Attempts to ameliorate the inﬂammatory response are
of interest because of increasing recognition that inﬂam-
mation may have a profound effect on drug handling by
the body (8,383). As part of the inﬂammatory response, cytokines are released, including tumor necrosis factor alpha
(TNF-α), interleukin 1 (IL-1), IL-6, IL-2, IL-8, IL-10, interferon γ (IF-γ ) and nitric oxide (NO) (47,384). Each of these
cytokines subserves a number of functions (377), but those
that are relevant to this discussion include the alteration
in gene transcription to increase the production of acute
phase proteins by TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 (377,385) [which
may reduce free drug concentrations (143,246,249)] and
inhibition of drug metabolism through the inhibition of
cytochrome P-450 activity (386–388). The metabolism of most clinically important drugs,
including those utilized for the provision of cardiac
anesthesia, is restricted to a relatively small number of
cytochrome P-450s (cypP-450): 1A2, 2A6, 2C8, 2C9, 2D6,
and 3A4 (94,386,389,390). Of particular note, cypP-450
3A4 (CY3A4) is partly responsible for the metabolism of
many of the opioids (391), propofol (392), and exclusively
for the metabolism of midazolam (98,393,394). Factors that affect CY3A4 function can have a sig-
niﬁcant effect on drug metabolism. These include in-
ﬂammatory cytokines (395,396), endotoxin (397,398),
drugs (399–406), food (407), hypoxia (408), neurotransmitters including adrenaline (409), CPB (410,411), preexisting disease (412,413), and race (414,415). The variability
in drug handling seen during cardiac surgery may be partly
explained by these factors. Myocardial depression may be induced by IL-6 (416–
418) and NO (417), which may alter the distribution
of drugs. Activation of neutrophils with generation of
oxygen-derived free radicals may injure tissue, particularly
endothelium, leading to a capillary leak syndrome that
may affect volume of distribution for drugs and penetration to receptors (419–425). Reductions in liver blood ﬂow
may reduce clearance of drugs with a high hepatic extraction ratio, for example, fentanyl (30,209,210,301,426–428). The inﬂammatory response may have some pharmacodynamic effects as well.

TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6
are endogenous pyrogens (377,429,430) that may produce an anesthetic-sparing effect (431). Inﬂammation
induces
brain
swelling
(432,433),
which
intuitively
would be expected to reduce anesthetic requirements. Inﬂammation may also alter drug penetration across the
blood–brain barrier. Animal studies have demonstrated
that inﬂammation causes changes in brain cypP-450 activity and alterations in the activity of p-glycoprotein,
which is thought to be responsible for the blood–brain
barrier (49,50,434–439). Agents employed during cardiac surgery may affect
the intracellular signaling pathway(s) following stimulation by inﬂammatory cytokines. For example, agents that
increase intracellular cAMP (e.g., catecholamines, phosphodiesterase inhibitors, glucocorticoids, opioids) will
reduce TNF-α production (47,440,441). Clearly, the systemic inﬂammatory response during
CPB could signiﬁcantly impact drug pharmacokinetics
and pharmacodynamics. Strategies designed to ameliorate the systemic inﬂammatory response require further
investigation (47,48). SPECIFIC DRUGS
The actual inﬂuence of the factors outlined earlier on
the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drugs
administered during hypothermia and CPB have been
investigated for a number of agents. An overview of the
results of some of these investigations are provided in the
commentary given later and in Table 5. However, caution
should be exercised in the interpretation and comparison
of the reported results because they may be inﬂuenced by
a variety of factors including the coadministration of other
agents (e.g., vasoconstrictors and vasodilators that might
alter the volume of distribution and clearance), differences
in anesthetic techniques (changes in cardiac output and
tissue distribution), type of oxygenator (differential drug
uptake), use and magnitude of hypothermia (changes
in distribution and pharmacodynamics), hemodilution
(changes in protein binding), nature of the priming
solution (blood colloid or crystalloid and implications
for drug binding), and so on. Antiarrhythmic Agents
Lidocaine is frequently administered during cardiac
surgery, usually just before release of the aortic crossclamp, to prevent ventricular ectopy. Review of data in
Table 5 suggests that the bolus dose of lidocaine administered should be increased (from 1.5 to 2.5 mg/kg) to
ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved (36). If an infusion is subsequently initiated, the free drug concentration may decline over time despite adequate total
free drug concentrations because of enhanced protein
binding by the acute phase reactant protein α1-acid glycoprotein (140,141,246). This effect appears to be maximal
3 days after CPB in uncomplicated cases. Should ectopy
occur during this period, an increase in infusion rate
is warranted.

Other drugs with high protein binding to
α1-acid glycoprotein may be similarly affected (143).

11. Changes in the Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Drugs
245
Antibiotics
Infection is a devastating complication following cardiac surgery because it increases morbidity, mortality,
and hospital costs. The primary causative bacteria are
Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Although the choice of prophylactic antibiotic used usually reﬂects the local pattern of antibiotic resistance and
surgical preference, whatever drug is employed for antibiotic prophylaxis must achieve and sustain therapeutic
serum and tissue concentrations [minimal inhibitory level
(MIC)] against these organisms during surgery and CPB. Examination of Table 5 reveals that this is not always the
case (442,444,462,463,466,471,472,474,480,481,577). Failure to achieve therapeutic MIC in plasma/serum and tissue
may result from an inadequate dose or from inappropriate timing of an otherwise adequate dose. Alternatively,
as a result of changes in pharmacokinetics during CPB,
decreased clearance of some drugs, for example, aminoglycosides, may lead to toxic drug concentrations (447,448). Agents utilized for antibacterial prophylaxis during cardiac surgery have been examined in a meta-analysis (578). This review conﬁrmed that prophylaxis reduces infections,
but found equivalent efﬁcacy with short (up to 24 hours)
or long periods (i.e., days) of prophylaxis and with ﬁrst-
or second-generation cephalosporins. There may be some
advantage in the use of cefamandole, because it appeared
to have better tissue penetration (451,462). It should be
noted that, for most second-generation cephalosporins
(e.g., cefazolin, cefamandole), there is a considerable
(>30%) reduction in plasma concentration at initiation of
CPB (457,473). In areas where there is a high prevalence
of methicillin-resistant Staphylcoccus aureus (MRSA), an
alternative class of antibiotic for prophylaxis (e.g., vancomycin) should be chosen; the guidance for dosing can
be found in Table 5 (231,478,480,482,577,579). Antiﬁbrinolytic Agents
Cardiac surgery—with or without CPB—generates a coagulopathy owing to the release of tissue factor and contact
activation generated by the interaction of blood with
nonendothelial surfaces, as well as from hemodilution. Contact activation leads to ﬁbrin generation, ﬁbrinolysis,
and to platelet activation (372,380,580,581), and consumption or sequestration. Antiﬁbrinolytic agents are often
utilized prophylactically to reduce the coagulopathy generated by surgery and CPB (581). Although these agents
effectively reduce blood loss, their relative cost/beneﬁt ratio is still under debate (582–586) (Chapter 25). The use
of many different dosing regimens may account for some
of these differences (Table 5), and the resolution of these
difﬁculties will require a multicentre randomized clinical trial utilizing pharmacokinetic principles to achieve
comparative plasma drug concentrations.

β-Adrenergic Receptor Blocking Agents
Sill et al. illustrated the importance of maintaining chronic
β-adrenergic receptor blocking agent therapy (500). If
changes in propranolol pharmacokinetics reﬂect those of
other β-adrenergic receptor blocking agents (501), one
should use caution when reintroducing these agents after
cardiac surgery. Digitalis Glycosides
Results of studies listed in Table 5 suggest that, provided
digoxin is continued until the day of surgery, adequate
tissue concentrations are sustained during CPB (257,504,
587). Glucocorticoid Agents
Glucocorticoid agents are commonly employed during
cardiac surgery to ameliorate the stress or inﬂammatory
response associated with CPB (47). However, a critical
analysis of relevant studies could not demonstrate any
beneﬁt for their use in this context (588). Pharmacokinetic
studies suggest that methylprednisolone hemisuccinate is
rapidly converted to the active agent methylprednisolone
even during CPB (Table 5) (511). Inotropic Agents Including
Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors
The pharmacokinetics of amrinone administered during cardiac surgery have been studied (273–275,277,589),
but the thrombocytopenia occasionally associated with
its use (590) has made milrinone the most commonly
employed phosphodiesterase III inhibitor during cardiac
surgery (591). In contrast to amrinone (276), milrinone
appears to bind minimally to the CPB circuit (519). Although dosing recommendations can be made on the basis
of pharmacokinetics (520) (Table 5), results show considerable variability. These studies are complicated by the
fact that most of them have involved pediatric populations, which differ from adults in clearance capabilities
(immature liver/renal function) and volumes of distribution (differences in fat tissue/lean tissue ratios) (519,520). We suggest that the dosing regimens utilized in the studies
given in Table 5 serve as guides, with knowledge that they
may be affected by age, disease, and CPB. Doses should
be adjusted on the basis of the hemodynamic response to
therapy. On the basis of these considerations, it is suggested that an appropriate initial infusion regimen would
be a loading dose of 50 µg/kg with a maintenance infusion of 0.5 µg/kg/min. Upon initiating phosphodiesterase
inhibitor therapy during CPB, one should anticipate the
need for a vasoconstrictor, such as norepinephrine, to
sustain the systemic blood pressure to partially offset the

246
III. Physiology and Pathology
vasodilation induced by these ‘‘inodilator’’ agents. Uptake
by a membrane oxygenator has been demonstrated for
dopamine (513), but the degree of uptake probably lacks
clinical signiﬁcance. Intravenous Anesthetic Agents
Studies of changes in pharmacokinetic parameters of
intravenous anesthetic agents, including thiopental, midazolam, and propofol, mirror those observed for the
opioids, that is, reductions in total drug concentrations on initiation of CPB, with rapid readjustment
of free drug concentrations to approach those present
before initiation of CPB, and reductions in drug clearance and increased volume of distribution leading to
an increased elimination half-time following termination of CPB (12,31,37,52,53,55–57,142,148,227,229,272,
292,325,522–525,529,535). Utilizing computer-driven infusions to maintain constant plasma concentrations, the
independent anesthetic effects of hypothermia (31) and
CPB (57,325) have been described. Neuromuscular Receptor Blocking
Agents
It is perhaps in this class of pharmacologic agents that the
most contradictory evidence exists for changes in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics during hypothermic
CPB. Table 5 shows studies where requirements for muscle relaxant are increased (22,538) or reduced (297) for the
same agent (pancuronium). Most likely, this represents
the confounding pharmacodynamic effects of hypothermia on the function of the neuromuscular junction,
which probably vary with the magnitude and duration
of hypothermia (23,27,29,182,295,543,592). For agents
such as atracurium, mivacurium, and doxacurium, decreased plasma concentrations of the metabolizing enzyme cholinesterase may play a greater pharmacokinetic
role than the use of CPB per se (184,593). In addition,
changes in clearance and volume of distribution for drugs
metabolized or cleared by other mechanisms may alter
their pharmacokinetics (195,543,593). The importance of
monitoring neuromuscular function by use of a twitch
monitor is evident given the changes in function and
kinetics demonstrated for this class of drugs. Opioids
Review of studies on opioid administration during cardiac surgery (Table 5) shows, in general, a normal
decline in concentrations of drugs administered before
CPB, reduction in concentrations at initiation of CPB,
with rapid readjustment of free drug concentrations
while on CPB, and relatively stable plasma concentrations during hypothermic CPB. Increases in plasma
concentrations occur at termination of CPB, likely from
washout of the drug sequestered in the lungs, and
reduced drug elimination occurs after CPB probably
as a result of increased volume of distribution and
reduced clearance (41,51,54,78,185,198,203,206,271,280,
546,547,550,557,558).

Changes in pH as a result of blood
gas management are more likely to affect fentanyl and
sufentanil concentrations, with decreased concentrations
of fentanyl observed at neutral or high pH likely secondary to increased absorption by the circuit (224), and
decreased sufentanil concentrations observed when pHstat blood gas management was employed, likely due to
increased tissue penetration as a result of changes in
the degree of ionization of the drug (555), and reduced
remifentanil clearance due to hypothermia (33,185). Opioids exhibit little capacity to suppress the stress response
during CPB (551), so concomitant adjuvant agents [such
as halogenated agents (594), sedative/hypnotics (83,537),
or vasodilators (551)] are required to control hemodynamics (83,551,595). Pharmacokinetic models permit the use of computerdriven infusions to achieve targeted plasma drug concentrations during cardiac surgery with CPB. Opioids have
received the most scrutiny in this regard. In an elegant series of studies, the Winnipeg group has explored the effect
of CPB on opioid pharmacokinetics. Using a computercontrolled infusion and pharmacokinetics derived in other
surgical populations, they examined the concentrationeffect relation for fentanyl and sufentanil when used in
the presence of isoﬂurane (83). They determined that
concentrations of sufentanil above 1.25 ng/mL and fentanyl above 13.3 ng/mL minimize isoﬂurane requirements
but do not provide additional control of hemodynamics. They next determined that a three-compartment model
was adequate for delivery of sufentanil by computer
infusion (82), and that although CPB had effects on
pharmacokinetics, these could largely be ignored for all
practical purposes in the clinical arena (73). Similar results were found for fentanyl (81,82). In effect, a simple
infusion scheme can be utilized to maintain adequate
concentrations of opioid during cardiac surgery without
adjusting for CPB (93). It should be emphasized that this
applies only to the relatively short-term administration of
opioids during the intraoperative period. More prolonged
infusions of opioids for sedation/analgesia in the intensive
care unit (ICU) may be affected by CPB-induced alterations in the clearance and volume of distribution of these
agents. Signiﬁcant binding of opioids to some types of oxygenators (principally silicone) occurs, but is of limited
clinical importance (perhaps other than during initiation
of CPB) because of a rapid redistribution of drug from
peripheral storage sites (15–17). To prevent a reduction in
opioid concentrations at the time of initiation of CPB, one
should consider supplementing opioids at this point.

11. Changes in the Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Drugs
247
Vasodilator Agents
Signiﬁcant uptake by the oxygenator can be demonstrated
in vitro for nitroglycerin (10), but this appears to be of
little clinical signiﬁcance in vivo (564). When sodium
nitroprusside is administered during hypothermic CPB,
cyanide concentrations are consistently elevated—at times
to toxic concentrations (24,186,566). Volatile Anesthetic Agents
In general, wash in and wash out of volatile anesthetic
agents is rapid (146,147,233,571,572), but this process
slows with hypothermia (13,147), and may be affected by
the type of oxygenator employed (13,14,19,61). Uptake by
the oxygenator is of particular concern as it may lead
to insufﬁcient anesthetic delivery to the patient (61). Before employing a new type of oxygenator, it would seem
prudent to verify that sufﬁcient anesthetic gas transfer
occurs to maintain anesthesia. This can be determined
by monitoring the gas concentration at the outlet port
of the oxygenator (234). For initiation of CPB, overpressurization with high inspired anesthetic concentrations
and high gas ﬂows may increase the anesthetic level more
rapidly (146). Before termination of CPB, concentrations
of volatile agents should be reduced in order to minimize
myocardial depressant effects while still maintaining adequate anesthesia to prevent awareness. Supplementing
anesthesia at this time with a benzodiazepine such as midazolam, may help prevent awareness while minimizing
myocardial depression at this critical juncture. As compared with the pre-CPB state, concentrations of volatile
anesthetic agents required to achieve similar levels of
anesthesia may be diminished following CPB (326). SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION
This chapter has reviewed basic pharmacokinetics and
pharmacodynamics. The potential role of hypothermia
and CPB in altering drug disposition and action has been
examined and relevant studies presented. Understanding
these concepts and the potential for alteration of drug
effect by CPB allows for appropriate adjustment in drug
regimes to prevent unwanted complications, including
inadequate levels of anesthesia, prolonged muscle relaxation, infectious complications, and arrhythmias. Further
work to elucidate the role of ameliorating the occurrence
of SIRS during surgery and CPB, and its effects on drug
pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, is required. KEY POINTS

mathematical terms, of the processes involved in
handling a drug once it is introduced into the
body. ●Volume of distribution
●Clearance
●Elimination half-time

■Pharmacodynamics is the description of how a drug
reacts with the body to produce its effects.

●Receptors
●Second messengers
●CPB-induced changes
■Pharmacokinetic changes are induced by the following:
●Hemodilution
●Hypothermia
●Perfusion ﬂows
●Acid–base status
●Sequestration
■Pharmacodynamic properties are changed by the
following:
●Binding (to tissue, proteins, apparatus)
●Age

●Temperature
●Receptor density
●Acid–base status

toward baseline during CPB. ●Intravenous anesthetics (benzodiazepines, propofol, barbiturates): Concentrations decrease with
onset of CPB, but free drug concentrations rapidly
return toward baseline during CPB. ●Neuromuscular

◗Embolic Events
Robert A. Baker and David A. Stump
Do no harm is the ﬁrst rule of medicine. Regrettably,
we often ﬁnd that a negative outcome following cardiac
surgery was caused by the very team that was striving
to extend a patient’s life. Too often we may extend a life
at the cost of reducing the quality of the life we saved. In the last two decades massive gains in knowledge and
technology have removed much risk from cardiac surgery
procedures, but there is still much to be accomplished. The
frequency of mortality and stroke have been reduced to
such a low frequency that they have become difﬁcult to use
as research outcome measures. However, careful analysis
using sophisticated behavioral or radiologic diagnostic
techniques reveals that a substantial number of patients
still incur brain injury. No level of brain damage is
acceptable if it can be avoided. Optimizing patient outcomes drives improvements in
clinical practice through ongoing research and development. There is no place where this effort is more evident
than in the continuing quest to reduce adverse outcomes
from embolic events, either through prevention or by
amelioration of their impact. Reports indicate that the incidence of clinically obvious stroke after cardiopulmonary
bypass (CPB) procedures is 1% to 5%, while magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) studies suggest that a new cerebral infarct may occur in as many as 30% of those same
patients (1–5). There has been extraordinary improvement in technology, equipment, techniques, and management of CPB
since its clinical introduction in the 1950s. Most of these
improvements have been directed toward reducing the
amount of embolic debris attributable to the CPB apparatus itself. It is critical to identify the sources of the various
types of emboli that may contribute to a negative
neurologic outcome, because the CPB apparatus is not
the sole source. For example, the patient is a major
contributor. Approximately 50% of patients undergoing
coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) have experienced
a cerebral infarct before the surgery (4,6), many of
which are either completely subclinical or they would
require sophisticated neurologic or neuropsychological
testing to detect. Trauma to the aorta during surgery
contributes to brain infarctions up to 1 month after
surgery.

Preexisting cerebrovascular disease will continue
unabated, because CABG surgery does not affect the
progression of atherosclerosis in other vascular beds. Gross (i.e., potentially visible to the naked eye) air
embolism, a common occurrence in the earlier days of
cardiac surgery, is now rare, so other categories of emboli
contribute more importantly to adverse patient outcomes. These include gaseous microemboli (GME), particulate
debris of various composition, and biologic material. An
embolus can be deﬁned as deformable (conformal) or nondeformable (particulate). A lipid droplet or microgaseous
bubble will change shape to ‘‘stick and slip’’ as it progresses
through the vessel, dividing into smaller units to eventually
pass through the capillary bed while wreaking endothelial dysfunction along its path. A nondeformable embolus,
such as a calciﬁc or atherogenic particle, will travel until its
girth exceeds the vessel’s ability to deform. If a deformable
embolus has preceded the nondeformable particle, it will
have initiated an inﬂammatory cascade which may cause
the particulate embolus to ‘‘wedge’’ sooner than would
have been the case in a pristine vessel, thereby causing a
larger zone of ischemia. Current technologies, including membrane oxygenators, arterial ﬁlters, blood surface coatings, bubble traps,
emboli detection systems, and other extracorporeal circuit
design features have decreased the incidence of emboli delivered to the patient, yet embolic events still occur whenever CPB is employed (7,8). Emboli have traditionally been
classiﬁed into three categories: biologic, foreign material,
and gaseous, each of which has the ability to distribute into
and obstruct arterial vessels throughout the body. They
may arise as integral components of the circuitry and
priming solutions used to perform bypass, from interactions between blood and foreign surfaces, or be created or
introduced into the system by practitioners. Device manufacturers have attempted to address device design aspects
that generate emboli, just as surgeons and perfusionists
have adopted speciﬁc surgical and clinical practices to
reduce the likelihood of emboli generation. These efforts

have likely contributed to an appreciable decline in morbidity associated with CPB (9). In spite of these successes,
emboli remain a major cause of morbidity associated with
the use of extracorporeal circulation for cardiac surgery. This chapter reviews the detection, pathophysiology,
prevention, and treatment of emboli associated with CPB. ETIOLOGY OF EMBOLI
Many discussions about the origin of emboli focus heavily
on sources that are clinically irrelevant in that they no
longer exist in modern perfusion practice. Accordingly,
only brief reference will be made to these sources. Foreign Material
Foreign material can be present in multiple components
of the extracorporeal circuit and in the priming solutions
used for bypass, or they may arise from the interaction
of various components either prebypass (e.g., pumptubing interaction) or while on CPB. These foreign
bodies may arise during manufacturing or assembly
of circuit components. A variety of different materials
have been found in CPB circuits, including cotton ﬁbers,
plastic or metal particles, antifoam, and ﬁlter and tubing
materials. Similarly the operative ﬁeld can be a source
of foreign materials, including talc, bone wax, bone
fragments, muscle fragments, microﬁbrillar collagen,
calcium particles, and surgical thread (10,11). Table 1
lists the impressive variety of nongaseous emboli that
have been reported during CPB. Braun et al. (12) reported elevated serum aluminum
concentrations postoperatively in patients who had undergone CPB. This aluminum contamination was associated
with use of speciﬁc manufacturers’ aluminum heat exchangers. A decade later Challa et al. (13) reported that
postmortem concentrations of aluminum and silicone
were higher in the brains of patients who died after

Roller pumps have produced foreign matter emboli
from so-called spallation. Spallation is deﬁned as the
release of fragments (often >300 µm diameter) of
tubing into the circuit that can potentially embolize
into the patient. These emboli were thought to be more
common with silicone-based rubber tubing than with
tubing of polyvinyl chloride or polyurethane base (14–17).

However, recent scanning electron micrograph studies
suggest that spallation remains prevalent even in new
generation biopassive tubing (18). The widespread clinical
application of membrane oxygenators instead of bubble
oxygenators has reduced or eliminated antifoaming agents
as a signiﬁcant source of emboli. Gaseous Emboli
Gross air embolism is now uncommon because of
safeguards and changes in clinical practices that have
ensued from identiﬁcation of their most frequent causes. It is likely that the most frequent cause has been perfusion
inattention leading to the emptying of the venous reservoir
and concomitant pumping of air into the patient. Other
causes include introduction of air into the aortic root
from the cardioplegia delivery tubing and cannula, cardiac
contractions before intracardiac de-airing is complete,
and accidental reversal of ﬂow in the left ventricular
venting system (19). A 1986 report about the major
mechanisms of CPB air embolism included factors such
as low CPB reservoir levels, damaged extracorporeal
circuit components, pulsatile ﬂow devices, and perfusion
interventions (20). More recent surveys (21,22) have
indicated that iatrogenic air embolism continues to occur
during CPB, although the incidence has been greatly
reduced (20). GME may originate from a number of sources during
bypass, including the extracorporeal circuit and oxygenator, and from the way clinicians perform both the surgery
and the extracorporeal perfusion. Persistent GME often
adhere to the quiescent areas (i.e., areas of potential stasis) of the oxygenator, reservoir, ﬁlters, and circuitry which
can be released into the arterial infusion tubing (subsequently referred to as the arterial line) upon initiation of
bypass or an abrupt shock to the circuit (23). Changes
in circuits and the addition of ﬁlters have been employed
to remove GME, yet several recent studies have clearly
identiﬁed that gaseous emboli can still be delivered to the
patient (7,24,25). Historically bubble oxygenators were a common source
of embolized oxygen microbubbles. These GME were usually 400 µm or less in diameter, showing a wide variation
in size (23,26–32). Bubbles with diameters greater than 35
to 40 µm were reportedly associated with CPB morbidity,
unlike those of smaller diameters (33,34). Design changes,
along with chemical defoaming agents and arterial line

ﬁltration, signiﬁcantly reduced the numbers and sizes of
GME produced by bubble oxygenators. Membrane-type blood oxygenators signiﬁcantly reduce
or eliminate GME (27,35,36). Physical damage to the
membrane material may allow release of gas bubbles into
the blood, or areas with elevated transmembrane pressure ratios may cause bubble formation on the blood side
of the membrane. Quinn et al. (37) described a counterdiffusion phenomenon whereby bubbles could be formed
at the membrane surface. It is important to recognize that
membrane oxygenator–reservoir systems vary in their ability to handle and remove air introduced into the venous
side of the circuit. Arterial and venous blood reservoir levels correlate inversely with GME production (27,38–41). Sparked by clinical observations, Mitchell et al. found
a signiﬁcant increase in gaseous microembolic activity
when venous reservoir levels were lowered, although the
reservoir level remained above the manufacturers’ recommended minimum (40). Subsequently this same group
of investigators demonstrated signiﬁcant variation in venous air handling by different hard-shell venous reservoirs
while also quantifying the emboli removal capacities of
these oxygenator circuits when coupled with an arterial
line ﬁlter (41). In these latter experiments air was introduced artiﬁ-
cially into the venous side of the circuit, although in vivo
the origin of venous air entering the extracorporeal circuit varies. Unfortunately, despite the impediment to gas
transmission imposed by the capillary tubules in the membrane oxygenator, air entrained into the venous line can
pass through the oxygenator to the arterial side and hence
into the patient (24,25,42,43). Willcox et al. demonstrated
that vacuum-assisted venous drainage augmented the rate
and amount of air entrainment into the circuit almost 10-
fold when compared with gravity venous drainage (25). (Fig. 1). Jones et al. (24) evaluated ﬁve CPB circuits composed
of components from different manufacturers to determine
their ability to remove GME arising from a ﬁxed quantity of entrained venous air in vitro. With all circuits,
the introduction of a ﬁxed volume of air (60 mL) into
the venous side of the circuit resulted in the detectable
GME in the arterial line downstream from the arterial
ﬁlter. In addition, they demonstrated that the design
characteristics of each component impacted the resultant embolic load, while also demonstrating signiﬁcant
differences among manufacturers. More recently, Dickenson et al. (44) demonstrated major differences in the way
four different commercially available circuits handled air.

demonstrated the effect of failure to adequately de-air the
venous line before going onto bypass. Similarly venous
air entrainment resulting from loose pursestring sutures
around venous cannulae insertion sites has been shown to
be a source of GME during bypass. Maneuvers to reduce
this such as retying single pursestrings or using double
pursestrings have been shown to signiﬁcantly reduce these
GME (49). Air emboli can be introduced into the patient’s arterial blood when the cardiac chambers are opened to the
atmosphere for valvular, atrial septal, or ventricular septal repair. Pearson (31) characterized ‘‘surgical air’’ as air
entering the arterial circulation during cannulation of the
left atrium, aorta, and right atrium or vena cava immediately following removal of the aortic cross clamp and
after resumption of blood ejection from the heart. The
type of cannula and its placement can have a large impact
on whether air from the arterial line migrates to the head
or descending aorta. In the presence of an atrial septal
defect or with placement of a left atrial or left ventricular vent cannula, air may be introduced directly into
the systemic circulation (50). When open cardiac surgical
procedures are performed, air may remain on the luminal
surfaces of the heart or be trapped within the muscular trabeculae. Cardiac ejection should be avoided until
complete blood ﬁlling and de-airing maneuvers occur. Residual air has been reported for extended periods using transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) even when
careful de-airing attempts have been employed (51,52),
and upon resumption of cardiac contractions cerebrovascular gas has been detected with transcranial Doppler
(TCD) ultrasonography (51). Taylor et al. 1999 (7) demonstrated that a large number
of embolic events previously thought to be of unknown
origin (8) in fact resulted from interventions by the
perfusionist during activities such as administration of
drugs or solutions or blood sampling (Fig. 2). Later work
by the same group demonstrated that appropriate removal
of air before injections or solution administration could
signiﬁcantly reduce this embolic load (49). This work
reinforces the concept that the membrane oxygenator
circuit does not entirely remove the gaseous embolic load
delivered to it. It also highlights that different perfusion
groups using different apparatuses and techniques report
substantial differences in detectable emboli.

Gaseous and particulate emboli are commonly reported
with cardiotomy suction (53,54). Inherent to all suctioning
procedures is the mixing of air with the blood, forming
relatively large bubbles, often with a foam-like matrix. These bubbles are not only larger than the GME produced
by the oxygenator but consist of air (mostly nitrogen) and
hence are more persistent than oxygen gaseous emboli
and often coalesce with other blood products or aggregate
material (55). The increased stability (persistence in the

reabsorption will depend not on the Ideal Gas Law or

bubble will be reabsorbed, depending up its shape, in 29
to 32 minutes (58). A 200 µ foam particle may take many
hours to disintegrate. Figure 3 demonstrates the geometric
principles of gas embolus reabsorption. A bubble will travel at a slower velocity than the blood
in a large vessel and then approximate the velocity of
the blood in smaller vessels until it contacts the vessel
walls.

At this point it ‘‘sticks and slips’’ until it stops. The difference between the arterial and venous pressures,
when great enough, will cause the bubble to shred into
smaller bubbles which will then repeat the process until
they reach a size that is easily reabsorbed or they pass
through the capillaries and then regroup. An increase
in arterial pressure may merely bulge the bubble. In a
car, such a ‘‘vapor lock’’ in a brake or fuel line makes
the brakes fail or the engine stop. The Trendelenburg
position, which can move air from cerebral to spinal

arterial circulation. This was demonstrated by Rodriguez
et al. who showed in children that the Trendelenburg
position failed to decrease the cerebral microembolic
load as compared with the horizontal head position (59). Although design changes such as improved defoamer
material, revised ﬂow patterns, and integral ﬁlters have
reduced but not abolished embolus transmission from the
cardiotomy suction circuit ﬁltration, utilizing 21-µ ﬁlters
in that circuit substantially reduces its embolic load (60). Gaseous emboli may also be produced by processes
known as gaseous or vaporous cavitation (61,62). Cavitation involves hydrodynamic phenomena that consist of
bubble nucleation, growth in volume, and then ultimate
collapse (63). The bubbles or cavities contain gas or vapor. True vaporous cavitation is an extremely transient phenomenon. Gaseous cavitation, similar to effervescence, is
more common in gas-nucleated ﬂuids, including blood,
that are subjected to tensile, ultrasonic, or supersaturating pressures (64). In these conditions, bubble growth is
achieved by mass transfer of gas molecules by diffusive
mechanisms and occurs with lesser pressure reductions. Vaporous cavitation occurs when a vacuous space is created in blood, for example, within the negative pressure
regions that develop behind the roller pump heads, where
pressures drop suddenly to below liquid vapor pressure (65,66). Early model centrifugal pumps reportedly
produce fewer GME than roller pump heads (67). Similar cavitating phenomena can occur at arterial
injection sites or at stenotic regions in the circuit
where vortices are created with turbulent ﬂow and
negative pressures spontaneously develop (68–70).

In their
review of cavitation phenomena during CPB, Kuntz and
Maurer (71) evaluated a number of factors involved with
GME production at the arterial cannula site. Such factors
include Reynolds number, kinetic energy, hydrostatic and
line pressure, temperature, PO2 levels, cannula size, and
ﬂuid ﬂow rate. The authors concluded that excess blood
gas tensions should be avoided and that larger bore
arterial cannulas were less likely to be associated with
GME production at cavitating velocities. In addition to the
formation of GME, cavitating phenomena are extremely
traumatic to red cells and can cause platelet activation,
granule release, and cell lysis (63). Vapor bubbles are also
reported with transmyocardial laser revascularization,
as detected with TEE and TCD (72). Although both
studies detected cerebral vascular emboli, neither reported
adverse gross neurologic deﬁcits or decreases in mean
cerebral blood ﬂow velocity or jugular bulb oxygen
saturation. Similarly GME have been studied in patients
following mechanical heart valve placement, where emboli
have been detected in the cerebral circulation using TCD. The rate of embolus production appears to relate to valve
design. These microemboli do not appear to cause overt
neurologic injury, but recent evidence suggests that they
may produce neuropsychological deﬁcits (73–75). Bloodborne Biologic Emboli
Bloodborne biologic microemboli (hereafter referred to as
bloodborne emboli) associated with CPB consist primarily
of autologous aggregates of cells and cell products of various types (76,77), of which one etiology may be associated
with GME as described earlier. Cellular products include
microthrombi containing ﬁbrin/ﬁbrinogen, lipid material,
protein (denatured or not), bone or muscle fragments, and
so forth. Platelet, neutrophil, and red cell aggregates are
also commonly observed during and after bypass. Bloodborne emboli can derive from homologous transfused
blood, which accumulate in this blood proportionate to
storage time (78,79). Fibrin formation occurs when inadequately anticoagulated blood contacts a foreign surface,
thereby activating factor XII to factor XIIa and thereby
initiating the coagulation cascade. Heparin blocks coagulation within the cascade at multiple points, mainly by

generated during CPB and are found in capillaries of
the kidneys, lungs, heart, brain, liver, spleen (88), and
in pericardial blood (89). These emboli are released as
a result of trauma to the fat cells in the epicardium
and other sites within the surgical wound (90,91) and
can occur without CPB after median sternotomy or
thoracotomy (31). Fat emboli may be observed directly
using microscopy (Fig. 4) or can be inferred from
increases in serum concentrations of total lipids, free
fatty acids, triglycerides, or lipases. It has been estimated
that two thirds of the fat emboli developed within a
CPB circuit enter through cardiotomy suction (91). Fat
emboli typically contain denatured of plasma lipoproteins
and lipids and vary from 4 to 200 µ in diameter (89). The fat molecules that come out of solution consist
of chylomicron aggregates (92) or free fat–containing
triglycerides and cholesterol (91). A number of fatty
acids and other lipid molecules have been linked with
postperfusion lung parenchymal damage or alterations in
surface properties (93,94). Generation of immiscible fat,
however, is reduced by hemodilution (90). Brooker et al. (95) demonstrated the relation between
the return of shed blood and brain emboli. Avoidance
of fat emboli by reducing cardiotomy suction blood
return is effective, however, techniques to eliminate fat
microemboli in processed blood have had mixed success.

In a prospective comparison of cardiotomy suction blood
and cell salvaged processed blood, while the fat embolic
load was reduced by blood processing (centrifugation
and saline washing) there was still an abundance of fat
emboli in both the processed and cardiotomy suction
blood returned to the patient. Passing the blood through a
21-µ ﬁlter before returning it to the patient eliminates
fat emboli (60). Jewell et al. also reported that cell
salvage processing reduces fat content compared with
unprocessed blood from cardiotomy suction (96). Kincaid
et al. (97) demonstrated wide variability in the ability of
different cell savers and ﬁlters to prevent fat embolization
(Figs. 5 and 6). As plasma proteins come into contact with foreign surfaces within the extracorporeal circuit, denaturation can
occur (92). This process alters immunologic and complement proteins (98,99). Blood contact with foreign surfaces
also activates platelets, which leads to aggregate formation and subsequent thrombocytopenia as platelets are
consumed in this process (53,100–102). Platelet aggregates are also commonly observed in stored whole blood,
packed red cells, and stored platelet concentrates (79). Although many aggregates are likely to disperse within the
circulation (102), their embolic potential has manifested
in various organs, including the brain.

Signiﬁcant decreases (30%–50%) from preoperative
platelet counts are usually observed early in CPB as the
platelets adhere to the surfaces within the circuit (103)
or to the gas–blood interface of GME (104). Functional
changes and decreased platelet counts have been associated with postoperative bleeding, whereas circulating
aggregates may provide a causative link with postoperative neurologic dysfunction (105). Preservation of platelet
numbers and a reduction of aggregate formation has
been reported with prostacyclin use (106,107). Reducing
platelet sensitivity to aggregation associated with heparin
administration (108) may be assisted by prostacyclin therapy, thereby reducing the microembolic risk associated
with bypass (109,110). Surfactants have been reported
to attenuate platelet–bubble and platelet–platelet binding,
and as such may have a clinical role in attenuating some
of the sequelae associated with GME (111). Platelet aggregation is associated with release of biogenic amines
such as serotonin and other bioactive mediators such as
thromboxane, which not only produce vasoconstriction
but may also further promote adhesiveness and aggregate
formation. Release of histamine from platelets and mast
cells may promote changes in microvascular membrane
permeability to plasma proteins, promoting interstitial
edema formation (112). Neutrophil aggregation during CPB may lead to complement activation (99). Hicks et al. (102) and Ratliff
et al. (113) found aggregated leukocytes in the lungs of
dogs undergoing bypass, and their presence was difﬁcult
to prevent clinically, although damage to other organs
was not reported. Complement-mediated neutrophil aggregation appears to depend on the nature of the foreign
material that the neutrophils contact (114). After aggregation, lysosomal enzyme release increases microvascular
endothelial permeability to protein, especially in the lungs,
contributing to the postperfusion lung syndrome (115). Upregulation of adhesion molecules and the subsequent
adherence and activation of neutrophils with CPB has
been reviewed by Hall et al. (116). Patients who possess cold-reacting antibodies, usually
of the immunoglobulin M (IgM) class, may be at risk
for red cell aggregate microembolization with cold cardioplegia or other hypothermic techniques used during
open-heart surgery (117–119).

Manipulation of the aorta
serves as a major source of bloodborne emboli during
CPB, and the risk associated with this manipulation is
well established (120–123). MEASURING EMBOLIC EVENTS

with real-time data collection as a component of clinical

be accurately measured in the operating room. Commercially available gross air embolus detection systems
available on heart–lung machines have been available for
many years and recent surveys indicate high levels of usage (135–137); however, their ability to detect microemboli
has not been established. Ultrasonography Devices
Ultrasonography devices are most commonly used to
detect emboli both clinically (including transcranial,
transesophageal, and transthoracic) and in research environments, owing to their ability to detect emboli as a
result of a change in the reﬂected Doppler energy. This
phenomenon was ﬁrst described by Austrian physicist
Christian Johann Doppler in 1942, when he recognized a
change in the frequency of sound waves when an object
was moving toward or away from an observer. A common
example of this phenomenon is the change in pitch of a
train whistle as the train approaches or departs. Doppler
ultrasound devices emit a sound signal from a piezoelectric crystal, and this sound signal reﬂects from the moving
blood cells. The frequency of the reﬂected signals differs
from that of the transmitted signal in proportion to the
blood velocity. This results from the difference in sound
frequency between the ultrasonography beam transmitted
into the tissue, and that returned by reﬂection from red
blood cells. The resultant Doppler shift allows the velocity
of the blood to be determined through the Doppler principle [Doppler equation: f = (2 × f × v × cosine θ)/C (f is
the frequency of transmitted ultrasound beam, v is the
velocity of red blood cells, C is the velocity of sound in
soft tissue, and θ is the Doppler angle, the angle at which
the ultrasonography beam intercepts the tissue)]. With
Doppler devices, these frequency shifts typically occur
within the audible range (0–10 kHz). The audio signal
contains both amplitude and frequency information, and
the degree of reﬂection of the sound waves is a function
of the difference in acoustic properties of the reﬂecting
particles.

Ultrasonography allows noninvasive differentiation of circulating particles from the background blood
ﬂow. Microemboli, whether solid or gaseous, are more
effective in scattering sound because of the difference in
density between the particle and the surrounding blood or
tissue. Gas bubbles are much more efﬁcient at scattering
ultrasound than more rigid particles, such as red cell
aggregates or microthrombi, especially at the smaller
diameters (138). A detailed review of ultrasonography
techniques can be found in a number of textbooks (e.g.,
Cerebrovascular Ultrasound in Stroke Prevention and Treatment. Andrei V Alexandrov, 2004, Blackwell Futura, New
York (139). Ultrasonographic Doppler devices used for detection
of microemboli emit pulsed or continuous-wave sound
waves. With pulsed systems, short energy bursts (approximately 2 µs) are emitted at rates in the order of
1,000 pulses per second. Particles along the beam path
are then set in motion, reﬂecting the sound waves at a
speciﬁc depth from the emitting ultrasonographic transducer, whereas the regions in front of or behind this
preset depth are not affected. This technique enables the
operator to focus the beam to a speciﬁed depth. Using
pulsed Doppler systems for microemboli detection highly
depends on the particle diameter (140,141), angulation of
the ultrasonic transducer (23,56,142), and incident pulse
length (140,141). Blood ﬂow rate also has an important
inﬂuence on pulsed Doppler systems in that the pulse
echoes usually represent the product of the pulse frequency and the time that the bubble resides within the
sampling ﬁeld (141). Some devices take this feature into
consideration by making the pulse-repetition frequency
proportional to the blood ﬂow (143). With continuouswave ultrasonography, the emitted beam is continuous,
and the particles are soniﬁed along the entire length of
beam penetration. Ultrasonography imaging systems have gained widespread support in detecting circulating microemboli. Transthoracic, transesophageal, and transcranial ultrasonography devices enable localization of microemboli
within their respective acoustic ﬁelds. The B-mode
(2-dimensional mode) enables the operator to view the
emboli within the heart chambers, although the M-mode
(linear or 1-dimensional mode) permits some degree of
quantiﬁcation of emboli, because the x-axis represents
time and relative counts are possible (144). TEE has been
shown to be particularly effective in detecting GME during
and after CPB and is useful in determining the adequacy
of de-airing maneuvers (145,146).

The closeness of the
esophagus to the myocardium and aorta enables TEE to
obtain an acoustic window without interference from the
chest wall, ribs, and lungs without interfering with the
surgical ﬁeld (147–149). TCD can be used in the intraoperative setting to

with the highest incidence of surgical air had the highest

higher counts of CPB-generated emboli had greater decrements in cognitive function than did those with those with
lower counts. Overall, the CPB-generated emboli were
relatively well tolerated. Yao et al. (156) compared the efﬁcacy of simultaneous

the aortic arch in 20 patients undergoing CPB. Emboli
signals were obtained from all patients, with mean total
signal counts from the aorta being 77% greater than
cerebral emboli counts. Overall, 83% of emboli signals
were detected during aortic cross-clamp and partial
occlusion clamp placement. Recent investigations have
further explored the timing of embolic events during the
perioperative period. Rodriguez et al. (48) demonstrated
a direct relation between the amount of air in the venous
cannula before initiation of bypass and HITS in the MCA
at the initiation of bypass. Quantiﬁcation and Discrimination
of Emboli
Quantiﬁcation of microemboli in vivo is difﬁcult using TCD ultrasonography techniques, and currently no
automatic online embolus detection system can detect
and classify emboli with adequate sensitivity and speci-
ﬁcity.

Currently the ‘‘gold standard’’ is manual assessment
using the criteria described in the preceding text. Difﬁ-
culties arise from the similarity between random energy
increases in Doppler signal (energy) that occur and signals reﬂected from red blood cell clusters, as well as
from variations between diastole and systole and from
artifact introduced by the recording system (e.g., with
movement) (157). Signiﬁcant limitations exist in the ability to quantitate the size or number of microemboli
present in vessels or the bypass circuit (134,153,158,159). Figure 7 depicts potential causes for signal differences
