to develop techniques that discriminate between gaseous
and solid microemboli while simultaneously quantifying their size and/or numbers continues. Techniques
that have been attempted include use of multifrequency
devices and sophisticated signal analysis of spectral patterns (160–162), measuring the intensity of the reﬂected
signals (163,164) and looking at the harmonics and subharmonics of the ultrasound signals (165). None of these
techniques have been able to reliably classify or quantify
emboli. Russel and Bruchner (166) have recently reported on
multifrequency TCD designed to speciﬁcally discriminate
between solid and GME by using two frequencies (2 and
2.5 MHz) to insonate. The applicable principle is that
solid emboli will reﬂect more ultrasonographic power at
the higher frequency than at the lower frequency and
that gaseous emboli will do the opposite. In vitro studies
demonstrated high discrimination ability and the authors
concluded that it was possible to discriminate solid and
gaseous using multifrequency TCD. However, a subsequent validation study by Markus and Punter (167) failed
to conﬁrm the reliability of the technique, while recognizing that the dual frequency allowed better discrimination
than a simple intensity threshold ultrasound system. Recently, Luna Innovations began marketing a device
for detecting emboli in the arterial inﬂow line, grossly
based on the device used by Stump et al. (42,168),
the embolus detection and classiﬁer (EDAC) Quantiﬁer. The EDAC employs a broadband ultrasonographic pulse
(1.0 ms), which minimizes the duration of the signal
and effectively isolates echoes from individual signals. Through complex ﬁltering algorithms, the acoustic signature of emboli can be categorized by size and determined
to be either gaseous or nongaseous. The EDAC is highly
resistant to artifact. Studying Emboli In Vitro
Numerous studies have examined different aspects of the
CPB circuit in an attempt to provide useful information
to the perfusion community about the equipment that we
use. A signiﬁcant component of these studies relates to
the ability to measure, quantify, and describe the emboli
handling characteristics of the circuits. Study designs
address the speciﬁc question posed by the researchers. Recent studies have investigated air introduced into the
venous side of the circuit (24,25), into the sampling
manifold (169), and into other components of the CPB
circuit (24,45). Other studies have evaluated the inﬂuence
of hematocrit and temperature upon different detection
systems (170–172).

Areas of particular interest raised
by these studies include the different technologies used
to measure emboli as well as the method of emboli
generation. To date there are no standards for the design
of in vitro experiments examining the critical questions
regarding emboli handling by CPB components (173). Numerous devices have been used to measure emboli
in in vitro circuits, including modiﬁcation of clinical
Doppler devices (25,169,170) and speciﬁcally designed
devices (24,42,44,168). Many of these devices have utilized
pulsed 2 MHz Doppler waves with probes mounted onto
circuits using locally designed purpose-built mounts or
commercially available brackets. The studies by Jones
et al. (24,42) and Dickinson et al. (44) report on the EDAC
Quantiﬁer, a device which utilizes 4.5 MHz waves and
advanced ultrasonographic technology to noninvasively
count and classify emboli. The report of Jones et al. discusses the ability of an earlier iteration of the device to
discriminate between different types of particles, whereas
Dickinson et al. focus on accurate counting of emboli. The methods used to generate an experimental embolic
load currently lack experimental design consensus. Various ingenious emboli generation techniques have been
developed (24,25,44,169). The most contentious issue may
be the CPB circuit priming solution in which the experiments are performed. Various priming solutions have been
used, including expired human red cells (25,171), animal
blood (24,44,161,167,172) water, saline, and other solutions (170). Recently the use of a glycerin-based solution
has increased in popularity (45,161,175). Other studies
have observed the ultrasonographic properties of artiﬁ-
cial solutions mimicking blood such as Orgasol. Orgasol
has similar physical and acoustic properties to human
blood; however, such solutions are not without limitations (176,177). Other factors inherent to these studies
that must be reported include ﬂuid ﬂow rates, temperature, hematocrit (if appropriate), gas ﬂow, arterial line
pressure, and reservoir volumes. Such studies have provided important information such as the venous reservoir
design issues highlighted by Mitchell et al. (40), the impact
of vacuum-assisted venous drainage on embolic load (25),
and the ability of circuit components to handle embolic
loads (24,44). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Injury is not a ‘‘normal’’ or acceptable consequence of
any medical procedure. Adverse embolic events following
cardiac surgery have generally focused on the catastrophic
outcomes associated with stroke; however, a full spectrum
of adverse neurologic and cognitive outcomes has been
reported.

Functional Change Associated
with Embolic Events
It is generally accepted that postoperative cerebral dysfunction after the use of CPB is largely attributable to

12. Embolic Events
271
microembolism and/or hypoperfusion (178). Individual
differences in patient tolerance to CPB make it difﬁcult to
deﬁne safe thresholds for ﬂow and pressure. The brain has
been the focus of many studies evaluating adverse surgical outcomes after CPB, which has been facilitated by the
large number of available tests that have the capacity to
assess cerebral damage (179,180). Histologic studies have
also shown embolic material in the kidneys, heart, liver,
lungs, and spleen after CPB (88,89). Histologic examination of the brains of patients who died after open-heart
surgery has demonstrated ﬁbrin, fat, muscle fragments,
calcium, and platelet aggregate microemboli (181). In
these studies, fat emboli were detected in 80% of the cases
and their presence was independent of perfusion variables, whereas nonfat emboli were related to the duration
of CPB. Some authors have speculated that the period of
greatest risk may occur at the initiation of CPB, when hypotension and an initial microembolic load may combine
to induce cerebral injury (182,183). In 1990 Moody et al. (184) reported focal microvascular
dilations or very small aneurysms, which they named
small cerebral capillary and arteriolar dilations (SCADs),
in both dogs and humans after CPB. As most of the
dilatations appeared empty, those authors suggested that
they contained gas bubbles or fat emboli which had been
removed during processing. The authors also proposed
that these SCADs may represent the anatomic correlate of
neurologic deﬁcits reported in cardiac surgical patients. Cardiotomy suction has been implicated as an important
source of lipid emboli that can lead to formation of SCADs
found in the brain and other organs (95,124). Brown
et al. (185) reported a direct relation between embolic
load and CPB duration. They also demonstrated that the
embolic load declined over time after bypass. Neuropsychological testing has demonstrated that cerebral dysfunction is present both immediately after surgery
with CPB and as long as 5 years afterward (186). One can
easily oversimplify the pathologic implications of these
ﬁndings, however. Either a single large embolus or a multitude of microemboli can shut down blood ﬂow to a
similar volume of tissue in a watershed area. The patient’s
anatomy plays an important role in determining outcome
as well.

In a patient with a dense capillary bed, a microembolus may not cause infarction, whereas a patient with a
paucity of capillaries may develop a clinically signiﬁcant
infarction lesion from a relatively small embolus. Between
15% and 20% of the population is born with only one posterior communicating artery in the Circle of Willis. The
consequences of a brief reduction in ﬂow from one carotid
artery in such a patient is much more severe than in patients with a complete Circle of Willis; therefore variability
in arterial anatomy may also explain variability in patient
outcomes resulting from similar embolic insults. Gaseous microembli ‘‘stick and slip’’ as they are
extruded through the vascular bed. Lipid droplets tend to
be ‘‘conformal’’ as well, taking the shape of the vessel. The
rate at which a microembolus passes through a vascular
bed is determined by the relative ratio of the arterial and
venous pressure. Gas bubbles ultimately resorb. When
a gas bubble’s length reaches approximately three times
its width, its surface tension destabilizes and the bubble
fragments into smaller emboli that work their way further
down the vascular tree. Even a short-lived microembolus
damages the blood vessel in which it resides (187). If the health of a patient’s endothelium is impaired,
an embolus may occlude the vessel much earlier than in
a normal vessel. According to Swank and Seaman (188)
the endothelium can be injured by the presence of a microembolus as small as 20 µ in diameter. In sufﬁcient
quantities, such microemboli can cause complications
such as increased pulmonary vascular resistance from
endothelial lysis induced by the widespread release of enzymes from damaged platelets and neutrophils. Damaged
blood vessels allow blood to leak into surrounding tissues. Lipid microemboli disrupt the blood–brain barrier
(BBB) and also cause leakage of ﬂuid into the peritoneal
space, which suggests that all endothelial surfaces exposed
to microemboli are injured (189). Efforts to prevent the
changes in vessel permeability through the use of aprotinin show some promise, suggesting the possibility that,
even if we can not prevent embolization, we may be able
to ameliorate their deleterious effects by protecting the
endothelium (190). Diabetic patients have a chronically
inﬂamed endothelium that may respond differently than
nondiabetic endothelium. Microbubbles irritate the endothelial surface to induce blood–brain barrier breakdown
(BBBB).

Lipid microemboli causes such BBBB, which is
accompanied by increases in CSF inﬂammatory markers
as well as blood leakage into CSF (191). We do not yet know whether an irritated vessel will stop
an embolus sooner than a pristine one, perhaps increasing
the ultimate size of an ischemic infarction. The Hammersmith group (192,193) and others have
graphically demonstrated that endothelial irritation results in neutrophil adhesions that retard the passage of
blood through the vessel and affect permeability. Fifteen
to 20 minutes after an initial insult, leucocytes begin
to transmigrate through the vessel into the interstitial
space. Such changes in permeability may interrupt the
BBB to allow blood into brain tissue (76,188). In a
closed container such as the skull, extravascular blood
cells can collapse the perivascular space around penetrating arterioles. This perivascular space normally carries
metabolic waste to the brain surface where it is transported to the saggital sinus. Reduction in waste transport
can then render the local tissue environment toxic. Therefore, a cascade of events starts with the passage of a
microembolus to cause endothelial irritation followed
by rolling neutrophils and the transmigration of leucocytes into the brain, culminating in the breakdown of

272
III. Physiology and Pathology
the BBB, blood in the CSF, and brain swelling. This cascade may explain the swollen brains shown in the images
of Harris (192,193) and the enlarged cerebral ventricles
described by Kohn (196). Some misinterpretation of central nervous system
(CNS) injury etiology may occur because similar changes
in cerebral function are reported after a multitude of
nonembolic factors, for example, anxiety, sleep deprivation, drugs, cerebral edema, or hypoxemia (194,197–199)
can induce the same neurobehavioral abnormalities. Patients
undergoing
the
same
procedure
can
have
similar adverse outcomes from different etiologic factors (179,180,200). The issue is further complicated by
the fact that variations in study design can account
for wide variations in the incidences of neurologic dysfunction after CPB (e.g., prospective versus retrospective
studies, randomization methods, time lapse between preand postsurgical evaluation, and the neuropsychological
tests performed). In most contemporary reports, stroke rates after CPB
range from 1% to 5% (1,195,201–204). This contrasts with
neurobehavioral deﬁcit rates ranging from 30% to 70%
in the immediate postoperative period (194,205,206). It
may not be mere coincidence that these neurobehavioral event rates are very similar to the new infarct
rate reported by a sensitive diagnostic technique such as
diffusion-weighted MRI (207). Recent reviews detail the
subjects of neurologic and neuropsychological morbidity
and their prevention during cardiac surgery (208,209). Occult visual ﬁeld defects after cardiac surgery may be explained by ocular embolization to the retina (133,210)
or by microemboli to the occipital cerebral circulation (211). For a number of years biochemical markers have
been used as surrogate markers of damage induced by
embolic events following cardiac surgery. To date the ideal
marker has not been identiﬁed. Serum concentrations of
the cerebral isoenzyme of creatine phosphokinase brain-
AQ1
type (CPK-BB) can be elevated in patients undergoing
open-heart surgery (212–214), and this rise was prevented
by the use of an arterial line ﬁlter (215). Other CSF
and serum enzymatic protein markers of brain injury
have been reported in 6% to 50% of cardiac surgery
patients (214,216,217). Neuron-speciﬁc enolase and S-100
proteins have been widely used to estimate brain injury
after cardiac surgery; however, their signiﬁcance and
relation to embolic phenomena need to be more clearly
deﬁned. Jonsson et al. (218) demonstrated the inﬂuence
of extracerebral sources of S-100 arising from cardiotomy
blood and from subsequent retransfusion of shed blood.

The use of biochemical markers as indicators of brain
injury from CPB holds great promise, but this ﬁeld
is plagued by methodological issues that can obscure
the interpretation of the relation between biochemical
markers and cerebral outcomes (219). PREVENTION
We know from recent studies that in routine clinical practice it is highly improbable that embolic events can be
eliminated. However, an awareness of factors responsible
for their etiology may allow perfusion teams to minimize
the number of emboli generated and their consequences
during clinical CPB. Undoubtedly the routine use of ﬁl-
tration (prebypass, venous reservoir, cardiotomy reservoir
and arterial line) has been responsible for a major reduction in the embolic load delivered to patients. Similarly
adoption of new technologies as they become available
(e.g., membrane oxygenators) and awareness of strategies
to minimize the embolic load (e.g., avoidance of venous
air) have decreased embolus production as well. Impressive improvements in extracorporeal circuit
technology have also decreased embolic loads delivered to
patients. It is imperative that clinicians choose appropriate
technologies when selecting extracorporeal circuits for
clinical use. It cannot be overemphasized that each
component of the circuit can contribute importantly to
the embolic load experienced by the patient. Recent
studies (24,25,47,170) highlight variations that occur in
emboli-handling characteristics of different membrane
oxygenators and circuits and also minicircuits (220,221). Surprisingly, to date no reduction in embolic load has been
associated with enhancements to the biocompatibility of
the circuit (220,221). Perthel et al. (222) recently reported
a signiﬁcant reduction in micoemboli delivered to the
patient when a dynamic bubble trap was inserted into the
circuit distal to the arterial line ﬁlter. Filters in the CPB circuit have long been recognized
as an important safety feature. The original LilleheiDeWall bubble oxygenator incorporated four standard
intravenous infusion set screen ﬁlters on the outﬂow
side of the arterial settling reservoir (223). Similarly Kolff
et al. (224) and Gross et al. (225) relied on arterial ﬁlters
for particulate trapping and air removal. The seminal
work of Swank et al. (226,227) in the mid-1960s led
to the use in 1970 by Hill et al. (228) and others of
the Swank depth ﬁlter ﬁrst for ﬁltration of cardiotomy
blood (227) and later for arterial blood (228). Further
work by Solis et al.

(53) in the early 1970s evaluated
the effectiveness of screen and depth ﬁlters using a
microparticle counter and concluded that cardiotomysuctioned blood contained a much greater volume of
microaggregates than either arterial or venous blood in
the extracorporeal circuit. Further, such microaggregates
found in the cardiotomy-return blood were more resistant
to deaggregation and therefore posed the greatest potential
risk to the patient. This latter ﬁnding is receiving
signiﬁcant recent interest. Page et al. (229) conﬁrmed the
beneﬁt of depth ﬁltration of cardiotomy-suctioned blood
during clinical perfusion to reduce embolus transmission
to patients.

273
The beneﬁt of arterial line ﬁltration, has been demonstrated by decreased quantities of microemboli and by
improved patient scores on neuropsychological tests after CPB (56,151,152,230–234). Loop et al. (56) evaluated
four arterial line ﬁlters utilizing ultrasonographic technology, allowing the quantiﬁcation of the efﬁciency of
different types of ﬁlters. Padayachee et al. (151) additionally demonstrated the beneﬁcial effect of a 25-µ arterial
ﬁlter over a 40-µ ﬁlter. Pugsley et al. (152) demonstrated a
reduction in the number of microemboli delivered to the
cerebral circulation, measured with TCD, with the inclusion of a 40-µ arterial line ﬁlter. Contemporary studies
have conﬁrmed the importance of the arterial line ﬁlter in
removing emboli although circuit design has evolved and
improved (24,25,44). Leukocyte-depleting ﬁlters further
reduce embolic load as compared with traditional arterial
line ﬁlters (235). The importance of prebypass ﬁltration
with 0.2 µ pore size for the removal of microemboli and
other contaminants has also been emphasized (236). Surprisingly, recent surveys reveal that arterial line ﬁlters are
not universally employed, although usage appears to be increasing over time. Between 1992 (237) and 2003 (135), a
survey from Australia and New Zealand revealed changes
in the clinical use of various ﬁlters, with the use of prebypass ﬁlters increasing from 58% to 97%, and arterial
line ﬁlters from 66% to 94%, which reﬂects a similar
evolution in the United States (136,137). Similarly, with
the use of prebypass ﬁlters increasing from 58% to 97%,
reﬂected the importance of ﬁltering the circuit before
establishing bypass as emphasized by Reed et al. (239)
in 1974. Recent studies demonstrating the adverse effects of
perfusion interventions underscore the need to mange
interventions appropriately (146). Blood ﬁltration techniques have evolved substantially since the development
of modern blood banking and transfusion practices in
the 1930s (240,241). In 1983, 94% of cardiac surgical
teams reported the use of ﬁlters for bank blood added
to the CPB circuit (242), while 97% ﬁltered cardiotomysuctioned blood and 78% ﬁltered blood in the arterial
line during both adult and pediatric perfusion. Because
of the potential for ﬁlter occlusion with inadequate anticoagulation, several questions on this survey were posed
regarding its management. Blood coagulation status was
monitored by more than 95% of the respondents, who
most often performed the activated coagulation time at
least every 30 minutes during CPB.

Forty percent also
reported ﬁltration of the cardioplegic solution, probably
as a result of reports of particulate emboli contained in
these solutions (243–246), this low adoption is reﬂected in
recent surveys (135). A pharmacologic panacea for protection against injury
during the use of extracorporeal circulation has been the
‘‘holy grail’’ of investigators in cardiac surgery for many
years. Numerous agents have been proposed as beneﬁcial
in reducing the injury associated with bypass; however, no
agent has emerged as the ‘‘gold standard’’ for protection. Adequate heparinization to maximize anticoagulation
and minimize microclot emboli during bypass remains
integral to any protective strategy (247–250). A number
of drugs have been associated with improvements in
cerebral protection in various clinical and experimental
settings, including isoﬂurane (251), barbiturates (252),
remacemide (253), lidocaine (254,255), aprotinin (256),
and piracetam (257). The putative mechanisms for their
beneﬁt are widely divergent. To date no reproducible
advantage has been reported. Royston (258) reviewed
pharmacologic interventions aimed at reducing platelet
and neutrophil emboli during CPB. Alpha (α)-stat acid–base management during hypothermic CPB more closely maintains cerebral autoregulation
than pH-stat management, during which higher cerebral
blood ﬂow occurs as a result of a higher PaCO2. Lower
cerebral blood ﬂow during α-stat management reduces the
transmission of microemboli to the brain without compromising cerebral oxygen delivery, thereby favoring the
α-stat approach to minimize cerebral injury (259). In a pig
model, Plochl and Cook (210) manipulated PaCO2 to vary
cerebral blood ﬂow during periods of high embolic risk,
and demonstrated that lower PaCO2 signiﬁcantly reduced
the cerebral embolic load. Prevention of gross air embolism from either the
bypass circuit or operative ﬁeld has been the subject
of numerous reports (260–262). The variety of safety
devices with proven efﬁcacy includes arterial line ﬁlters,
bubble traps, air bubble detectors, low-level alarms, and
one-way valves for the vent or arterial ﬁlter purge line. Arterial-line ﬁlters and air bubble detectors are both
highly effective in preventing air embolism (20). Clear
lines of communication and the use of protocols during
CPB are equally important to the prevention of air
embolism (263). Systemic air embolism can also be prevented by insertion of a vent into the left ventricle (264) or by needle
aspiration of the pulmonary veins and cardiac chambers
before reinstitution of circulation after CPB (127).

Flooding the surgical ﬁeld with carbon dioxide also reduces
air embolism at the operative site (265–267). One group
used TEE in cardiac valve surgeries to demonstrate that
carbon dioxide ﬁeld ﬂooding eliminated the residual intracardiac gas (that remained even after careful de-airing
maneuvers) to disappear within 1 minute in 86% of cases
and within 1 to 24 minutes in the remaining cases (52). However, CO2 is a potent cerebral vasodilator, so monitoring PaCO2 is necessary to avoid an increase in cerebral
blood ﬂow that could paradoxically increase the delivery
of emboli to the brain despite the impressive decrease in
gas content in the left atrium and ventricle (268). Other
maneuvers include closure of the left atrium while the suture line is under blood or saline, lung expansion to clear

pulmonary venous blood, and placement of the patient
in the Trendelenburg position (269), Milsom and Mitchell
described a novel dual vent left ventricular de-airing technique (270). The patient’s ascending aorta, which is typically the site
of arterial cannulation for CPB, constitutes a major source
of particulate emboli during cardiac surgery. The ascending aorta, which may contain signiﬁcant atherosclerotic
lesions, is also cross-clamped and manipulated during
CPB. Atheromatous plaques may be dislodged during
these maneuvers (271,272). A recent multicenter study
investigating adverse cerebral outcomes after coronary
bypass surgery (195) found the presence of proximal aortic atherosclerosis to be a strong predictor of stroke. Alternative cannulation (273–275) or venting sites have
been proposed, as well as the so-called no-touch technique (276). Intraoperative epiaortic ultrasonographic
scanning to deﬁne the extent of disease in the aorta is becoming increasingly popular. One randomized trial from
Toronto demonstrated that distal aortic arch cannulation
decreases embolic load (277). Hammon, et al. compared three different, but commonly practiced, methods of manipulating the aorta
during CABG surgery (278). Clamping the aorta multiple
times with partial occlusion clamps resulted in a fourfold increase in particulate emboli detected in the carotid
artery with almost twice the number of patients (57%)
demonstrating neurobehavioral deﬁcits 6 months postoperatively when compared with either a single cross-clamp
technique (29%) or off-pump group (32%) of high risk
patients. A patient undergoing multiple clamps had 3.5
times the chance of displaying neurobehavioral dysfunction. Further analysis revealed that approximately 15%
of patients ﬁrst manifested neurobehavioral deﬁcits after leaving the hospital. Based on Leary’s work which
demonstrated that almost one third of septuagenarians
will experience a new ‘‘silent’’ cerebral infarct every year,
these delayed deﬁcits could be explained as a natural progression of preexisting vascular disease (279). A secondary
analysis assessed ‘‘persistent’’ deﬁcits (those present at
1 week, 1 month and 6 months) as the outcome. These
results indicated that only 11% of patients in the single
cross-clamp group experienced brain dysfunction after
surgery compared with 32% in the multiclamp group. The type of aortic crossclamp used may also importantly
inﬂuence embolic load (Fig. 8). Embolic burden can be reduced by either discarding
shed blood or by using different methods to process shed
blood (135).

Kaza reported the high rate of fat emboli in
pericardial suction blood and demonstrated that passing
shed blood through a 21-µ ﬁlter before returning it to
the patient eliminated fat emboli (60). This ﬁnding was
supported by Jewell et al., who demonstrated signiﬁcant
reduction in the fat content of recycled blood following
cell salvage processing (96). Embolic activity

TREATMENT OF EMBOLI
The lack of effective treatment options for neurologic dysfunction caused by microemboli delivered during CPB
underscores the importance of prevention and reduction
in embolic loads as the mainstay of perfusion-related interventions. Some protocols exist for the management of
gross air embolism, although the recommended maneuvers are supported more by common sense and anecdote
than by demonstration of improved outcomes. These
maneuvers may include retrograde cerebral perfusion, induction of hypothermia, pharmacologic intervention, and
the use of hyperbaric chambers (280). Treatment protocols have been proposed (281) and used with considerable
success (282–285). The importance of having a plan for
this rare event has been emphasized, as this can make the
difference between severe injury or death and uneventful
recovery (263,281,286). Pharmacologic interventions have
not yet been proved to improve outcome following gross
air embolism. Hyperbaric oxygenation is considered the
most effective treatment of gross air embolism (287–294),
although access to such a treatment facility may be limited (20). CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE TRENDS
Embolic events continue to underlie adverse outcomes
from surgery utilizing CPB. Major advances have occurred
in the technology available to clinicians to improve the

12. Embolic Events
275
practice of cardiac surgery with CPB. Diligence and acceptance of responsibility will assist in the early adoption of
technologies shown to reduce the embolic load delivered to
the patient. Such reductions in embolic load will favorably
impact neurologic outcomes, be they frank stroke or subtle neurobehavioral changes, and will attract the interest
of researchers and clinicians. The adoption of individual technologies can cause controversy, yet clear evidence
supports many of the practices reported in this chapter as
mechanisms for reducing the embolic load. As new technologies continue to be developed, clinical investigations
will need to quickly, rigorously and accurately evaluate
these advances to provide the best outcomes for patients
to undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB. Preventing embolic events remains our best hope for improving brain
outcomes following cardiac surgery, as treatment of brain
damage after the event continues to be an elusive goal. KEY POINTS
■Adverse outcomes are associated with embolic
events. Reducing these events through prevention
or by ameliorating the focal impact of an embolus should be a major goal of contemporary clinical
perfusion practice. ■The three categories of emboli are biologic, foreign
material, and gaseous. ■Cardiotomy suction blood carries an embolic load
that needs to be taken into account when that blood
is returned to the patient. ■All circuits do not handle embolic load in the
same manner. Filters, cardiotomies and biopassive
surfaces can inﬂuence embolus-carrying capacity
and dissemination. ■Filtration systems are effective in reducing embolic
load. Filtration of cardiotomy and arterial blood are
the most important techniques for reducing emboli
during CPB. ■GME may be produced by rapid injection of drugs
or blood into the CPB circuit. ■Surgical manipulation may introduce multiple emboli, so careful handling of the aorta and arterial and
venous cannulae is essential. ■TCD is most common clinical modality used for
detecting microemboli. ■The most striking manifestation of an embolic event,
stroke, is relatively uncommon, but more subtle
neurobehavioral changes occur with alarmingly high
frequency. REFERENCES

◗Endocrine, Metabolic, and Electrolyte
Responses
Scott G. Walker and John F. Butterworth
Surgical procedures using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)
produce physiologic alterations not found in other major surgical procedures. During total CPB, the heart and
lungs are not perfused and can neither secrete hormones
nor make their normal contributions to drug metabolism. Exposure to the extracorporeal pump, oxygenator, and
tubing traumatizes cellular blood elements, causes plasma
proteins to be adsorbed and removed from the circulation,
and stimulates an immune response, as is well described
in other chapters. Hemodilution (from blood-free priming
solutions) and heparin anticoagulation alter the concentrations of electrolytes, hormones, and serum proteins in
the blood during CPB. Finally, moderate to profound hypothermia is often used during CPB, reducing the rates of
biochemical reactions and further perturbing hormonal
responses. Other features of extracorporeal perfusion contribute
to the endocrine, metabolic, and electrolyte alterations. Nonpulsatile perfusion may change the distribution of
ﬂow, both among and within organs. As a consequence,
some hormonal alterations during CPB can be lessened or
prevented by pulsatile perfusion. CPB increases ‘‘stress’’
hormones disproportionate to the apparent levels of physiologic disturbance, and it remains unclear which factor—
hypothermia,
hemodilution,
decreased
perfusion
of
endocrine glands, or denaturation of hormones by foreign
surfaces—most contributes to these changes. Additionally,
some hormone concentrations increase above normal levels after termination of bypass, with the return of pulsatile
warm perfusion to endocrine glands (1). Consistent with
expectations, some data show that deeper planes of anesthesia attenuate or eliminate the exaggerated endocrine
responses to CPB and reduce mortality (2). Finally, an interest has recently developed in the use of spinal and epidural anesthesia for cardiac surgery, and these techniques
have long been known to inhibit the neuroendocrine response to abdominal and lower extremity surgery (3). The literature regarding endocrine, metabolic, and electrolyte responses to CPB is difﬁcult to summarize because
of marked variations in patient populations, perfusion and
cardioplegia techniques, perfusate temperatures, priming solutions, and anesthetic and adjuvant drugs. Early
hormone assays were often not speciﬁc for intact active hormones. Where possible, this chapter emphasizes
the most recent studies in which contemporary anesthesia, cardioplegia, perfusion, and hormone measurement
techniques were used. PITUITARY HORMONES
The anterior portion of the pituitary gland secretes
hormones that regulate the adrenal cortex, thyroid,
ovaries, and testes.

Several aspects of pituitary response
are considered in subsequent sections. Gonadotropin
responses during CPB have not been reported using
modern surgical or analytic techniques (4–6). Pituitary apoplexy, a rare but potentially devastating
complication, has been reported after CPB (7–11), typically in patients with pituitary adenomas. These patients
demonstrated varying combinations of ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, nonreactive and dilated pupils, decreased visual
acuity, and visual ﬁeld defects, in addition to the characteristic hormonal deﬁcits. Although ischemia, hemorrhage,
and edema of the gland are usually blamed for pituitary
failure after bypass, no speciﬁc etiology is identiﬁed in
most patients. The diagnosis can be conﬁrmed with cranial
computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging
(Fig. 1). Hormonal replacement and prompt hypophysectomy are indicated, and experience suggests that the latter
may be performed safely early after cardiac surgery (7). Vasopressin
Vasopressin, or antidiuretic hormone (ADH), secreted by
the posterior pituitary gland, is a potent regulator of renal water excretion (12). At high concentrations, ADH
may increase peripheral vascular resistance and decrease

Catecholamines
The catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine are
products of the adrenal medulla and (in the latter case)
of peripheral sympathetic and central nerve terminals. Marked elevations of plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine concentrations occurring during CPB may
underlie many hemodynamic sequelae of bypass, including peripheral vasoconstriction and shifts in intraorgan
blood ﬂow (21,24–27). With hypothermia, the plasma
epinephrine concentrations may increase as much as
10-fold over the prebypass concentrations; norepinephrine
concentrations typically increase to a lesser extent (fourfold) (2,21,25,27), and deepening hypothermia attenuates
these events (Table 1). In early studies, peak increases in
both norepinephrine and epinephrine occurred when the
heart and lungs were excluded from the circulation (26,27). However, norepinephrine and epinephrine were found to
peak at different times. In a later study, patients undergoing cardiac surgery were randomly assigned to have
CPB with mild (34◦C) or moderate (28◦C) hypothermia. With both bypass temperatures, peak norepinephrine
concentrations were observed after release of the aortic
cross-clamp and rewarming, whereas peak epinephrine
concentrations were observed at the target hypothermic
temperature (28). Neonates, infants, and young children,
much like adults, demonstrate marked increases in catecholamine concentrations during CPB (2,29–31). ‘‘Deeper’’ planes of general anesthesia (whether accomplished with larger doses of synthetic opioids, addition
of a propofol infusion, higher concentrations of volatile

Some increase in catecholamine concentrations during
and after bypass may be unavoidable with current
anesthetic and surgical techniques; nevertheless, higher
doses of opioids, inhaled general anesthetics, and epidural

Secretion of cortisol is one of the central features of the
metabolic stress response (23). In the classic studies, by
Hume et al. (38), of patients undergoing major surgery
(without bypass perfusion), cortisol concentrations rose
quickly to a maximum and then slowly returned to baseline 24 hours postoperatively. It is therefore not surprising
that even the more recently employed ‘‘off-pump’’ coronary revascularization procedures are associated with
increases in serum cortisol and other markers of the
stress response, despite the lack of a CPB interval (39). It is apparent, however, that CPB modiﬁes cortisol responses to surgery. Total plasma cortisol concentrations
typically decrease immediately upon initiation of bypass, likely as a consequence of hemodilution (40–43)
(Fig. 8). During bypass, cortisol concentrations return
to values signiﬁcantly above baseline values (2,40–44). After CPB, patients exhibit markedly elevated concentrations of cortisol (both free and total) for more than
48 hours (43–45). Free cortisol remains elevated for 24
hours. Tinnikov et al.

(46) studied 14 children undergoing
repair of ventricular septal defects with deep hypothermia
and circulatory arrest without the use of extracorporeal
circulation. Maximal perioperative concentrations of cortisol and minimal perioperative concentrations of cortisol
binding globulin were recorded at the ﬁrst assessment
after circulatory arrest. Therefore, hypothermia and circulatory arrest initiate a cortisol-stress response even in
the absence of bypass perfusion. Cortisol responses during bypass appear to be perfusion temperature dependent. Taggart et al. (47) showed
that the rise in cortisol concentration during CPB can be
blunted by perfusion with blood at 20◦C rather than at the
more usual 28◦C. Cortisol concentrations during bypass
were decreased by deeper planes of anesthesia in both
adults and children (2,43,44) (Fig. 9). Stenseth et al. (34)
found that compared with high-dose fentanyl anesthesia
alone, high-dose fentanyl anesthesia plus thoracic epidural anesthesia resulted in a delayed increase in cortisol
concentrations during coronary artery surgery and lower
concentrations during bypass. Similarly, Moore et al. (35)
found that thoracic epidural anesthesia combined with
sufentanil 20 µg/kg was associated with markedly lower
cortisol concentrations compared with sufentanil anesthesia alone. On the other hand, spinal anesthesia failed
to attenuate cortisol responses in children undergoing
correction of congenital heart defects (compared with intravenous general anesthesia) (3) and in adults undergoing
coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (compared with
inhalational general anesthesia) (36). CPB modiﬁes adrenocorticotropic hormone responses
in surgical patients. In the previously mentioned study

foreign surfaces of the extracorporeal membrane, reperfusion injury, and endotoxemia may be attenuated by
large doses of exogenous glucocorticoids (52). This in-
ﬂammatory response triggers tissue injury in the heart,
kidneys, hemostatic system, and especially the lung, which
is the only organ exposed to the entire cardiac output. Previous investigations have studied small numbers of
patients undergoing cardiac surgery, randomized to variable doses of different corticosteroids (most commonly
1 mg/kg dexamethasone or 30 mg/kg methylprednisolone)
initiated at varying intervals between induction of anesthesia and the start of CPB (52). Unfortunately, few of
these studies have addressed outcome issues such as
morbidity and mortality, intensive care unit or hospital
length of stay, and other aspects of hospital resource
utilization. Results generally demonstrate an amelioration of the inﬂammatory response, with decreases in
cytokine formation [tumor necrosis factor and the interleukin 1 (IL-1), IL-6, and IL-8] but inconsistent effects
on C3a and elastase concentrations.

Leukotrienes such
as LTB4 are decreased in a dose-dependent manner (52). In addition, large doses of methylprednisolone can block
upregulation of neutrophil integrin adhesion receptors,
whereas dexamethasone decreases endothelial production
of certain adhesion molecules (53). Clinically, glucocorticoid therapy may result in an increased cardiac index
and decreased systemic vascular resistance (54). Dietzman et al. (55) showed an improvement in tissue perfusion
and a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance when a
large dose of glucocorticoid was given just before bypass (56). Routine glucocorticoid supplementation has
also been advocated as part of an accelerated recovery
program (57), albeit without much supporting evidence. A recent small study has shown that patients who underwent cardiac surgery and were receiving glucocorticoids
had shorter lengths of hospital stay and improved quality
of life as compared with patients not receiving glucocorticoids (58). In summary, current data nearly uniformly demonstrate large increases in cortisol and adrenocorticotropic
hormone concentrations with initiation of bypass. These
increases may be attenuated by deeper planes of general
anesthesia or addition of thoracic epidural (but apparently not spinal) anesthesia to general anesthesia. Pulsatile
perfusion does not appear to reduce these exaggerated
responses. Moreover, it is not clear whether elevated corticosteroid concentrations during bypass are deleterious

Natriuretic peptides are a family of biologically active peptides that were ﬁrst isolated from cardiac atria and include
atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP, a-type natriuretic peptide),
brain natriuretic peptide (BNP, b-type natriuretic peptide),
and c-type natriuretic peptide (CNP), among others (72).

ANP and BNP are expressed in cardiac myocytes. The designation of BNP as ‘‘brain’’ natriuretic peptide derives from
its initial discovery in porcine brain, but the role of BNP
and ANP in the central nervous system remains unclear. ANP is produced and stored predominantly in the atrium. BNP is present in both atrial and ventricular tissue, but in
myocardial disease states the ventricle becomes the primary source of secretion of BNP, which is occasionally
referred to as ventricular natriuretic peptide (VNP). The
nervous system and endothelial cells are the major sites
of expression of CNP, which has signiﬁcant vasodilatory
paracrine effects on the blood vessels. The heart is not a
signiﬁcant source of CNP. ANP is released in response to
atrial distension, whereas BNP levels tend to be elevated
in the presence of ventricular dysfunction. Other stimuli,
some of which are commonly associated with CPB, may
promote ANP and/or BNP release, including myocardial ischemia (73), catecholamines, endothelin-1, prostacyclin,
and cytokines (74). Both peptides increase glomerular
ﬁltration, inhibit renin release, reduce aldosterone concentrations in blood, antagonize renal vasoconstrictors
(such as vasopressin, norepinephrine, and angiotensin),
and reduce arterial blood pressure. They regulate vascular
volume by increasing sodium excretion and decreasing vasomotor tone (75). Within the heart, natriuretic
peptides regulate myocyte growth and inhibit ﬁbroblast
proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition. Natriuretic peptides have an anti-ischemic (preconditioninglike) function, and inﬂuence the coronary endothelium
and vascular smooth muscle proliferation and contractility through activation of guanylate cyclase (76,77). Atrial Natriuretic Peptide
Despite evidence that stimuli associated with CPB may
promote the release of natriuretic peptides, plasma ANP
has been measured before, during, and after CPB, with
conﬂicting conclusions. Patients with cardiac valve lesions, especially those with arrhythmias and congestive
failure, may demonstrate elevated preoperative ANP concentrations, whereas coronary artery surgery patients may
have normal preoperative ANP concentrations (78–82). In one study, no signiﬁcant changes were noted during
induction of anesthesia or during CPB; however, after
separation from CPB, both arterial and venous concentrations of ANP increased in those patients who underwent
coronary artery surgery (82). In contrast, most other studies found signiﬁcant alterations of ANP concentrations

during bypass, particularly during aortic cross-clamping. Curello et al. (80) measured ANP in patients undergoing
either coronary artery bypass or mitral valve replacement for mitral stenosis. Although there was no change
in ANP concentrations during bypass in the group undergoing coronary surgery, patients undergoing mitral valve
replacement demonstrated signiﬁcantly reduced concentrations during CPB. After release of the aortic clamp,
ANP concentrations in both groups of patients rose to
values equal to those found preoperatively in the patients
undergoing mitral valve replacement (80). Nearly identical responses were observed by Northridge
et al. (83) in their study of 12 patients undergoing aortocoronary bypass grafting with hypothermic
nonpulsatile perfusion. In another study, arterial concentrations of ANP decreased signiﬁcantly after aortic
cross-clamping (84). Interestingly, this study also found
evidence for ANP release from the brain during bypass. Ashcroft et al. (79) found a signiﬁcant reduction in ANP
concentrations during bypass, with return to baseline values postoperatively. Haug et al. (85) studied 33 patients
undergoing coronary artery surgery and found signiﬁ-
cantly increased concentrations of ANP after CPB, with
a further increase measured at the end of surgery, which
was maintained in the measurements 24 hours after the
operation. Pasaoglu et al. (86) found that ANP concentrations were elevated (relative to normal values) before
induction of anesthesia for coronary artery surgery. ANP
concentrations increased signiﬁcantly (relative to baseline values) after surgical incision and remained elevated
during and after surgery, with the highest mean values recorded on the ﬁfth postoperative day; however,
no measurements were made during CPB. In 16 patients undergoing aortocoronary bypass grafting or mitral
valve replacement, ANP concentrations decreased significantly during hypothermic extracorporeal perfusion and
aortic cross-clamping (81). More recently, Kostopanagiotou et al. (87) studied patients undergoing mitral or
aortic valve replacement, and although ANP levels were
elevated preoperatively in this population (relative to normal values), these levels did not change before, during,
and up to 1 week after surgery. Patients with arrhythmias, particularly atrial ﬁbrilla-
tion, are prone to elevated ANP levels and may require
an interval of CPB for surgical palliation through the
maze procedure. Perioperative decreases in ANP levels
have been implicated in the frequent manifestation of
postoperative ﬂuid retention in these patients (87–90). However, this phenomenon may be more related to increases in plasma arginine vasopressin and aldosterone
than to changes in ANP levels (91).

tiﬁed secretion of ANP into the left atrium and its
clearance by the lungs in adults and children (84,92). ANP concentrations declined signiﬁcantly during aortic
cross-clamping, but rebounded rapidly after release of the
aortic clamp (80,83,84). Multiple studies in both children and adults demonstrated

Clinicians seeking reliable outcome predictors in patients
with heart disease have recently taken signiﬁcant interest
in BNP, levels of which have shown to be positively
correlated not only with the presence and severity of heart
failure, but also with myocardial ischemia in the absence
of congestive heart failure (CHF) and postoperative
morbidity, including risk for atrial ﬁbrillation, need for
support, and death (98–102). Although the preponderance of the literature seems
clear in this regard, a few studies contradict the trend
of elevated baseline BNP in patients with heart disease. For example, a pediatric study demonstrated normal BNP
levels in 5 infants with CHF related to left-to-right shunting
before surgical repair using CPB (103). Signiﬁcant elevation of BNP in response to modiﬁed ultraﬁltration was
another unexpected ﬁnding of this limited study. However, a larger study of pediatric patients with congenital
heart disease did ﬁnd baseline elevations of BNP not only
in the plasma, but also in the pericardial ﬂuid of patients
with Qp:Qs ratios that are more than 2 (104). In contrast,
Terazawa et al. (105) found that baseline BNP levels were
signiﬁcantly higher in the patients in American Society of
Anesthesiologists’ physical status classiﬁcation II than in
those in class III or IV undergoing CABG. Like ANP, studies are somewhat contradictory with
respect to the effect of CPB on BNP levels. In Terazawa’s
study, ANP and BNP levels were both decreased relative
to baseline during CPB, and neither peptide increased
signiﬁcantly above baseline postoperatively. Neither ANP
nor BNP levels correlated with hemodynamic variables
before or after CPB. Berendes et al.

(106) also measured
ANP and BNP levels in patients undergoing either CABG
or valve surgery, and in a separate study (107) patients
undergoing CABG with or without adjunct thoracic
epidural anesthesia (Fig. 12). The results of both studies
were nearly identical with regard to ANP and BNP
levels. ANP levels increased signiﬁcantly during CPB, and
particularly during volume reloading after aortic crossclamping, but levels of BNP remained unchanged during
CPB. BNP levels became signiﬁcantly elevated compared
with baseline only in the patients undergoing CABG, and
not until several hours postoperatively. The degree of this
elevation correlated positively with both CPB time and
aortic cross-clamp time. Of note, both ANP and BNP
responses were attenuated when general anesthesia was
combined with thoracic epidural anesthesia. In summary, the preponderance of recent evidence
suggests that both the level and biologic activity of ANP
are reduced during CPB, especially during hypothermia
and aortic cross-clamping. Decreases in hormone concentration are most evident in patients with preoperative
elevations in ANP, which is especially common with valvular heart disease and atrial arrhythmias. Most patients
will demonstrate distinctly elevated ANP concentrations
(relative to those measured during aortic cross-clamping)
during rewarming and after discontinuation of bypass. Patients also fail to demonstrate the normal relation between
ANP concentrations and atrial pressure during bypass and
the early postoperative period or the normal response of
ANP to saline infusion after bypass. Finally, BNP levels
tend to remain unchanged during CPB, but are commonly
elevated in the ﬁrst 24 hours after CPB, especially in patients with pre-existing heart failure not related to valvular
disease. RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN-ALDOSTERONE
AXIS
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis regulates arterial
blood pressure, intravascular volume, and electrolyte
balance (108). In patients with heart failure, or with
conditions that place them at risk for heart failure, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis leads to
hemodynamic and renal dysfunction, inﬂammation, and
cardiac remodeling (109,110). The renal juxtaglomerular
apparatus secretes renin in response to sodium depletion,
falls in blood volume, or reduced renal perfusion. Conversely, increases in blood volume, renal perfusion, or
sodium load inhibit the release of renin. The sympathetic
nervous system stimulates renin release in response to
pain, emotion, and stress. Renin catalyzes the conversion
of angiotensinogen to the decapeptide angiotensin I in the
blood.

ACE present in blood vessel walls (particularly of
the pulmonary vasculature) catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (an octapeptide). Conversion
of angiotensin I to angiotensin II is nearly complete during a single pass through the lungs. Angiotensin II raises
blood pressure through two mechanisms: direct vasoconstriction and stimulation of aldosterone secretion by the
adrenal glands. Aldosterone stimulates the renal distal
tubules to reabsorb sodium and secrete potassium and

A variety of acute illnesses leads to alterations of peripheral
thyroid hormone metabolism. Characteristically, serum
concentrations of T3 (the active thyroid hormone species)
are reduced, thyroxine (T4) is normal or reduced, free
thyroxine is reduced, and thyrotropin [thyroid-stimulating
hormone (TSH)] concentrations are normal, producing
the so-called sick euthyroid syndrome (122). Multiple
studies have documented the presence of this syndrome
during and after CPB in adults and children. Recent
evidence conﬁrms that sick euthyroid syndrome is also
seen in patients undergoing normothermic (35 ± 1◦C)
CPB (123). In theory, the concentration of T3 would
be especially important for patients undergoing cardiac
surgery because T3 regulates the number of β-adrenergic
receptors and their sensitivity to agonists (124). Jones
et al. (125) demonstrated a frequent (>10%) incidence of
preoperative abnormalities in thyroid function in patients
undergoing CPB. Nevertheless, there appeared to be no
association between abnormal laboratory results and
adverse outcome (125). Before CPB, administration of heparin leads to small
increases in free T3 and free T4, because heparin displaces hormones from binding proteins (126–129).

Total
T3 concentrations drop precipitously with bypass and remain depressed 24 hours after surgery (27,124,130,131)
(Fig. 14). T3 values corrected for hemodilution (using
albumin concentration) are not altered by the initiation of CPB or by the initiation of hypothermic perfusion (27). Similarly, the free and the dialyzable fractions
of T3 increase after the onset of bypass and hypothermia (27,126). These alterations in T3 and T4 during bypass
are independent of thyrotropin-stimulating hormone secretion because adjustments in T3 and T4 concentrations
are normally delayed by 2 to 4 hours after a change
in thyrotropin-stimulating hormone concentration (132). 400

between thyrotropin and T3 during and early after CPB
than do patients undergoing cardiac repair without circulatory arrest. In other words, deep hypothermia with
circulatory arrest may better preserve the hypothalamopituitary axis than conventional hypothermic bypass
without circulatory arrest (139). Nevertheless, any bene-

decreased thyrotropin and T3 concentrations irrespective of whether circulatory arrest was used (139). Murzi

either repair of D-transposition of the great arteries or

unchanged immediately after institution of bypass but

may have clinical importance. T3 serves to regulate cardiac rate, contractility, and oxygen consumption. Cyclic
AMP production in response to β-adrenergic receptor agonists is markedly reduced in hypothyroid cardiac, adipose,
and hepatic tissue. Cyclic AMP regulates intracellular
calcium transients and myocardial contractility (147,148). Experimental studies have shown improved myocardial
contractility in animals receiving T3 after CPB (149,150). Patients with a preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction greater than 40% receiving T3 demonstrated significantly greater cardiac outputs after CPB than control
patients. Patients with preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction less than 40% receiving T3 required much
less dobutamine and furosemide than did control patients (151). On the other hand, two recent controlled
clinical trials showed that patients receiving T3 prophylactically were no more likely to require inotropic drug
support than those receiving placebo (152,153). Children undergoing correction of congenital heart disease
who received prophylactic liothyronine had improved myocardial function and reduced duration of stay in the
intensive care unit as compared with the placebo-treated
group (154). However, we urge caution in considering thyroid replacement in patients with chronic ischemic heart disease. Levothyroxine or liothyronine replacement therapy
may precipitate myocardial ischemia and infarction, or
even adrenal insufﬁciency. Indeed, patients with mild
to moderate hypothyroidism appear to tolerate cardiac
surgery without excess morbidity or mortality, although
practitioners must be cognizant of the potential for
delayed emergence from anesthesia, hypotension, bleeding, and the need for exogenous corticosteroids (155). EICOSANOIDS
The lungs are actively involved in the metabolism of vasoactive substances, including eicosanoids; therefore, the
separation of the lungs from the circulation during extracorporeal perfusion may signiﬁcantly alter the plasma
concentrations and kinetics of prostaglandins and thromboxanes (156). The endoperoxide prostaglandin H2 can
isomerize (catalyzed by isomerases) into PGE2, PGF2α, or
PGD2, or be chemically converted (catalyzed by either
prostacyclin or thromboxane synthetase, respectively),
into either prostacyclin (PGI2) or thromboxane (TXA2). The predominant prostaglandins formed in the bronchial
tree and in the pulmonary vasculature are PGE2 and
PGI2 (156,157). PGEs are dilators in most vascular beds. PGD2 and PGF2α are pulmonary vasoconstrictors.

In
addition to the synthesis and release of prostaglandins, the
lungs are a major site for metabolism of prostaglandins
of the E and F types (156). These substances are nearly
completely cleared during a single passage through the
pulmonary circulation. PGI2 can disaggregate platelets
and act as a potent vasodilator (156). Conversely, TXA2
potently stimulates platelet aggregation and vasoconstricts. Concentrations of 6-keto-prostaglandin F1α (the stable metabolite of prostacyclin) rose signiﬁcantly after
aortic and atrial cannulation and remained elevated
during CPB in children and adults (157–163). 6-Ketoprostaglandin F1α concentrations rose at the beginning
of bypass, continued to rise upon aortic clamping, but
decreased progressively after termination of bypass and
reperfusion of the lungs. There were no signiﬁcant differences between patients undergoing cardiac surgery
with or without bypass (161). One can compare the production of PGF2α in response to either oxidative stress
or inﬂammation by monitoring the concentrations of
speciﬁc metabolites (8-iso-PGF2α versus 15-keto-dihydro-
PGF2α). When concentrations of these two metabolites
were compared during and after CPB in adults undergoing various types of cardiac surgery, the data supported a greater concern for free radical–induced oxidative stress rather than inﬂammation per se in these
patients (164). TXB2 (the stable metabolite of TXA2) concentrations
increased and reached peak arterial levels just before termination of bypass, a markedly different pattern from
that seen in patients undergoing cardiac surgery without bypass (161) (Fig. 18). After completion of the cardiac repair and discontinuation of CPB, concentrations
of prostacyclin and thromboxane metabolites decreased
progressively (157–160,162,163). Compared with adults,
children have greater and more sustained increases in
thromboxane metabolites (160,162). Infants undergoing
extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, a form of longterm CPB, demonstrate increased prostacyclin metabolite
concentrations after initiation of therapy (165). With
continued use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation,
prostacyclin metabolite concentrations slowly fell. Prostacyclin metabolite concentrations rose again as the patients
were weaned from extracorporeal membrane oxygenation;
concentrations remained elevated for approximately 1 day
thereafter (165). Although increased concentrations of prostacyclin and
thromboxane during bypass may have important effects on
systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance and vasoreactivity, studies have not shown a consistent effect (157,160). Administration of the protease inhibitor aprotinin reduces
the surge in TXB2 associated with bypass but has no effect
on 6-keto-prostaglandin F1α concentrations (161). These
aprotinin-induced changes in prostaglandin metabolism
were associated with better-preserved platelet function,

Histamine
Elevated blood concentrations of histamine may produce
vasodilation and hypotension. Numerous drugs administered to patients undergoing cardiac surgery induce
histamine release, including opioids (especially morphine), muscle relaxants, antibiotics, heparin, and protamine (167). Current anesthetic practice favors the use
of agents that have a negligible likelihood of inducing
histamine release. In adults, plasma histamine concentrations rise at the time of systemic heparinization and
remain elevated throughout the period of CPB (168). Comparable measurements of histamine concentration in children are problematic because, unlike adults, children often

CPB to prevent excessive hemodilution (64,169). Marath

The availability of calcium ions in the sarcoplasmic reticulum determines the magnitude of the increased intracellular calcium concentrations during depolarizations,
which regulates the inotropic state of the heart (174). Calcium ions are also necessary for normal electrical
conduction and rhythm of the heart. Calcium in blood
exists in three fractions: ionized (approximately 50%),
protein bound (approximately 40%), and chelated (approximately 10%). The free ionized fraction is the physiologically active component.

is maintained within the normal range by parathormone
and 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol or vitamin D)
actions on bone and kidney. Parathormone secretion
is stimulated by decreasing ionized calcium concentration, overt hypocalcemia, and by mild hypomagnesemia. Parathormone secretion is suppressed by rising or normal (unchanging) ionized calcium concentrations and by
severe hypomagnesemia. Changes in the total and ionized calcium fractions
during and after CPB are inﬂuenced by the inclusion of
exogenous calcium salts or albumin or other blood products in the pump priming solution. Calcium salts are
frequently administered on discontinuation of extracorporeal perfusion. Clinical studies uniformly demonstrate
a fall in ionized calcium concentration on initiation of
CPB (176–189). When blood-free priming solutions are
used during bypass, both total and ionized calcium decrease as a consequence of hemodilution; ionized calcium
concentrations may further decrease if albumin (which
binds calcium) is added to the priming solutions (188). Total calcium, total magnesium, ultraﬁltrable magnesium
(analogous to ionized magnesium), and total protein likewise decline upon initiation of CPB (188). During cardiac
surgery, parathormone concentrations rise appropriately
in response to reductions in ionized calcium concentration
and in response to rising ionized calcium concentrations. Changes in the ionized calcium concentration and in
its absolute concentration regulate parathormone secretion. As has been demonstrated in other circumstances,
there is hysteresis in the relation between parathormone
and ionized calcium concentrations measured intraoperatively (188–190). When ionized calcium concentration
rises in response to increased concentrations of parathormone, secretion of parathormone will decrease at ionized
calcium concentrations below ‘‘normal,’’ which would
elicit increased parathormone secretion if approached
from a higher rather than a lower initial ionized calcium
concentration. Studies of parathormone concentrations using contemporary assays sensitive only to the intact hormone have
found reductions at the beginning of bypass, increases
to maximal concentrations during hypothermia, and a
slow return toward normal values as ionized calcium
concentrations approach normal values during rewarming (188). Some early studies, using assays sensitive to
both parathormone and biologically inactive fragments,
reported falls in parathormone concentration upon initiation of bypass, without appropriate increases in response
to hypocalcemia thereafter (179). Studies in adults have demonstrated that moderately
reduced magnesium concentrations do not inﬂuence the
response of the calcium-parathyroid-vitamin D axis during CPB (188).

Calcium and parathormone concentrations and responses were identical in patients receiving
magnesium salt supplements during bypass and in control
patients whose magnesium concentrations were permitted to fall without correction. Calcitriol (vitamin D) is
a fat-soluble vitamin; therefore, it is not surprising that
calcitriol concentrations are minimally altered by hemodilution and CPB or that this vitamin plays a minimal role
in the alterations in calcium concentration seen during
cardiac surgery (188). CPB is managed differently in infants and young children than in adults. Even with the use of smaller extracorporeal circuits, priming solution volumes represent a
much greater fraction of the child’s blood volume, and
blood products are often included in the priming solutions to avoid excessive degrees of hemodilution (63,64). Despite these differences, the responses of the calciumparathyroid-calcitriol axis in infants and young children
were similar to those in adults (189). Despite demonstrating much greater declines in ionized calcium concentration on initiation of CPB, parathyroid hormone concentrations in infants peaked at values similar to those achieved
by children and adults (188,189) (Fig. 21). Moreover,
parathyroid gland ‘‘sensing’’ of increasing and decreasing ionized calcium concentrations was also similar, with
infants and young children demonstrating hysteresis in a
manner similar to adults (188–190). Infants and young
children differed from adults in that ionized calcium
concentrations did not recover as completely before termination of CPB. This was likely a consequence of the considerably shorter duration of bypass in the children compared
with the adults studied, although impaired bone reabsorption in response to parathyroid hormone could not be
ruled out. There are important clinical implications from
these studies. Unlike the case of many other hormones,
parathormone secretion is minimally altered by hypothermic CPB (188,189). Ionized hypocalcemia, even to severe degrees, produced no obvious adverse effects during
these studies (184,188,189). Moreover, hypercalcemia may
lead to accelerated adenosine triphosphate breakdown (a
calcium-dependent process) and unnecessarily increase
contractility and myocardial oxygen consumption (191). Systemic hypocalcemia coupled with anoxic cardiac arrest and calcium-free cardioplegia may lead to a beneﬁcial
reduction in adenosine triphosphate breakdown (192). Rewarming and reperfusion after aortic clamp removal, essential for resynthesis of high-energy phosphates, should
be accompanied by minimal myocardial oxygen consumption. Exogenous calcium during this time might unnecessarily increase the myocardial inotropic state, leading to
depletion of adenosine triphosphate.

The empirical use of calcium salts at the end of CPB
(supposedly for inotropic support) remains a tradition in
cardiac surgery, despite limited evidence of clinical efﬁ-
cacy in controlled trials and the usual absence of serious
hypocalcemia in adult patients. In addition, excessive use
of calcium salts may cause perioperative pancreatitis (188,

Magnesium is the second most abundant intracellular
cation (after potassium) and is a key cofactor in enzyme
systems maintaining transmembrane electrolyte gradients
and energy metabolism, enzymes involved in synthesis
of second messengers (e.g., adenylyl cyclase), ion channels, and hormone secretion and action (e.g., insulin and
parathormone) (202). Much like calcium, magnesium in
the blood exists in three fractions: ionized (approximately
55%), chelated (approximately 15%), and protein bound
(approximately 30%). The ultraﬁltrable fraction includes
only the ionized and chelated fractions and, due to the
small contribution from the chelated ions, approximates
the ionized fraction (203). Because there is a dynamic
equilibrium between intracellular and extracellular magnesium, the magnesium concentration in blood may be
normal in the presence of magnesium depletion. Patients undergoing cardiac surgery frequently develop
hypomagnesemia, which may be due to insufﬁcient dietary intake, increased excretion (secondary to diuretics),
diabetes, aminoglycoside antibiotics, cardiac glycosides,
ethanol abuse, pancreatic disease, or administration of
citrated blood products or albumin (202,204–206).

Concentrations of blood magnesium decrease during and after
CPB in adults and children (188,189,204–208). During
CPB, total magnesium concentrations decline in concert
with the ultraﬁltrable fraction as a consequence of chelation by albumin and other blood products and hemodilution (188). Urinary excretion of magnesium during bypass
is not increased (205). Magnesium concentrations, unlike
calcium concentrations, once reduced during CPB, return
to normal only slowly in the absence of active treatment
because of the lack of a speciﬁc hormonal regulatory
system (188,189) (Fig. 21). Hypomagnesemia in the post-bypass period commonly
contributes to cardiac arrhythmias (206,208). Infusion of
magnesium salts prevents hypomagnesemia and its complications during and after CPB (188,208). During CPB,
cardiac muscle is preferentially depleted of magnesium
(compared with skeletal muscle). Magnesium may suppress arrhythmias by multiple mechanisms that include a
direct myocardial membrane effect, a direct or indirect effect on cellular potassium and sodium concentrations,
antagonism of calcium entry into cells, prevention of
coronary artery vasospasm, antagonism of catecholamine

action (209), or improvement of the myocardial oxygen supply/demand ratio (210). Magnesium may inhibit
the calcium current during the plateau phase of the
myocardial action potential. Finally, magnesium may also
inhibit arrhythmias by antagonizing accumulation of excess intracellular calcium induced by ischemia-related
mediators such as lysophosphatidylcholine (211). Supplemental magnesium decreases the incidence of
arrhythmias after cardiac surgery, as noted in the preceding text, and during myocardial ischemia or infarction (212–214). The Leicester Intravenous Magnesium
Intervention II Trial used 8 mmol of magnesium sulfate
acutely, followed by 65 mmol as a continuous infusion
over 24 hours in patients having an acute myocardial
infarction (215). This intervention signiﬁcantly reduced
both mortality (p = 0.04) and left ventricular failure
(p = 0.009), without producing excess hypotension. A
meta-analysis of 930 patients with myocardial infarction
concluded that intravenous magnesium reduced ventricular tachycardia and ﬁbrillation by 49% and decreased
overall mortality by 54% (216). Magnesium is a critical cofactor for numerous cellular enzymes, and partially regulates transmembrane
calcium movement (217). Magnesium salts dilate coronary arteries (218), regulate myocardial metabolism (217),
lower
systemic
vascular
resistance,
protect
against
catecholamine-induced myocardial necrosis (219), and
modify platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Clinically, magnesium salts are used for the treatment of both atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias (208,
212–214,220), coronary artery vasospasm, myocardial
ischemia (208,220), myocardial infarction (212–214),
pregnancy-induced hypertension, and even therapy for
bronchospasm (221). Moderate magnesium supplementation (intravenous
magnesium sulfate 1–2g/hr of CPB) maintains serum magnesium concentrations greater than 1 mM and has minimal effects on blood pressure in normotensive patients. Renal insufﬁciency may predispose to magnesium toxicity exhibited as deep tendon hyporeﬂexia, somnolence,
and even respiratory insufﬁciency. However, only very
high concentrations of extracellular magnesium directly
depress myocardial contractility. Magnesium potentiates
neuromuscular blocking drugs, which may produce clinical weakness and respiratory insufﬁciency in patients
with residual paralysis from previous administration of
neuromuscular blocking drugs. This may be particularly
important for patients who will be extubated soon after completion of cardiac surgery. An ill-timed bolus
of magnesium can produce ‘‘recurarization’’ of patients
with previously adequate neuromuscular function. Overall, magnesium salts represent a safe, moderately effective,
and low-cost therapy that may be used on a nearly routine basis for prevention or treatment of many atrial
and ventricular arrhythmias.

As long as there are no
neuromuscular concerns, the routine occurrence of hypomagnesemia during CPB and rapid renal excretion of magnesium allows the clinician to administer moderate doses
of magnesium salts empirically without the need for frequent measurements of magnesium blood concentrations. POTASSIUM
Maintaining normal blood potassium concentrations is
important in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Patients receiving diuretics may come in for surgery with
substantial potassium deﬁciencies; those with renal failure
may be hyperkalemic. During and after CPB, potassium
ﬂux is also inﬂuenced by myocardial protectant solutions
(cardioplegia), CPB priming solutions, renal function, carbon dioxide tension, arterial pH, hypothermia, insulin
treatment of hyperglycemia, catecholamine infusions, and
mineralocorticoids. Potassium depletion may occur in as many as 40% of
patients undergoing valve surgery (222,223). Hypokalemia
is frequent after CPB (224–227). Before the era of potassium cardioplegia, hyperkalemia was rare. Currently,
brief episodes of hyperkalemia may be more common,
especially immediately after the release of the aortic
cross-clamp. Hyperkalemia may also be more common
during true normothermic bypass than during hypothermic bypass due to the increased volumes of cardioplegic
solutions that are required (228). Loss of potassium during
CPB is related to urine ﬂow, implying that urine potassium concentration must remain nearly constant (229). Bumetanide produces less kaliuresis during CPB than
furosemide for a similar diuretic response (230). Increased
urinary potassium loss is characteristic of the post-bypass
period (231). Mofﬁtt et al. (232) reported that whole blood priming may cause greater reductions in serum potassium
than blood-free priming solutions. Maintenance of normocalcemia during CPB may better maintain potassium
concentration than the more usual techniques that tolerate mild hypocalcemia (233,234). The ionic constituents
of blood-free priming solutions (other than calcium and
potassium ions) have little effect on potassium concentration. Careful studies of potassium intake and output and
red blood cell potassium, rates of hemolysis, and serum
hemoglobin have shown that much of the fall in serum
potassium concentration is not accounted for by dilution
or excretion. Likewise, repeated studies have failed to
identify the organ into which potassium is lost from the
blood (235). In the absence of potassium cardioplegia, the fall in
potassium concentration during clinical CPB appears
to be proportional to the decrease in body temperature (236). Conversely, potassium concentration increases
with warming (237). Blood glucose concentrations rise

whereas insulin concentrations decline during hypothermic CPB (see earlier discussion on glucose metabolism). Insulin favors intracellular transport of glucose and
potassium. Increased concentrations of cortisol, aldosterone, and
catecholamines during CPB may contribute to hypokalemia. Cortisol and aldosterone increase the urinary
excretion of potassium. Catecholamines increase potassium uptake by skeletal muscles and decrease serum
potassium (238). β-Adrenergic blockade inhibits uptake
of potassium by the skeletal muscles but does not inhibit
the hepatic release of potassium by β-adrenergic stimulation (239). Hypokalemia during CPB may be lessened
if albumin is added to the priming solution, because the
negatively charged albumin molecules help maintain adequate blood concentrations of positively charged potassium (240). Potassium concentrations are monitored frequently
during CPB, although strict normokalemia need be
present only when normal cardiac electrical activity is
desired (241). Increases in systemic vascular resistance
have been observed with bolus intravenous potassium
injections of 8 mEq or greater during CPB. With smaller
bolus doses, an initial fall followed by a slight rise in
systemic vascular resistance is common (242). In summary, potassium concentrations rarely remain
constant during or after CPB. Hypokalemia, formerly a
frequent problem during bypass, is now uncommon due
to the widespread use of multiple doses of potassiumcontaining cardioplegic solutions. Postoperative potassium loss and hypokalemia continues to be common after
CPB, particularly with the more frequent use of insulin
infusions to maintain normoglycemia (243). METAL IONS: ZINC, COPPER,
AND IRON
Reductions in blood iron, selenium, and zinc concentrations and increases in copper concentrations occur as
part of the nonspeciﬁc ‘‘acute phase reaction’’ to trauma,
prolonged infections, burns, and major surgery (244). These reciprocal changes in zinc-selenium and copper
were observed in a recent study of 67 patients undergoing
CABG with CPB (245) (Fig. 22). In adults, zinc concentrations decline at the onset of CPB and remain low for 1
to 3 days postoperatively (246–249). Zinc concentrations
usually return to normal by the seventh postoperative
day. Urinary excretion of zinc is unaffected by cardiac
surgery. Taggart et al. (249) monitored the iron and
zinc concentrations before, during, and after coronary
surgery in 20 patients perfused at either 20◦C or 28◦C.

CPB produces widespread alterations in endocrine, humoral, and metabolic functions, some of which may be
lessened by the use of pulsatile CPB, larger doses or higher
concentrations of general anesthetic drugs, or addition of
thoracic epidural anesthesia. The magnitude and direction of these changes may be inﬂuenced by the duration
of bypass and the techniques used (such as the degree of
hypothermia, cardiac venting, and contents of the priming
solution). For the most part, the mechanisms underlying
these neuroendocrine alterations during bypass are poorly
understood. In only rare patients will the endocrine alterations inﬂuence the likelihood of a successful recovery
from surgery. However, the importance of these changes
may increase with longer durations of CPB or extracorporeal circulatory support. KEY POINTS
■A variety of pituitary-related hormonal activities are
inﬂuenced by CPB: ADH and adrenocorticotropin
levels increase markedly and TSH levels are typically
normal, but T3 and T4 responses to TSH are reduced,
consistent with ‘‘sick euthyroid syndrome.’’
■Adrenal responses affected by CPB include marked
increases in catecholamine, aldosterone, and cortisol
levels that can be attenuated to varying degrees by
deeper anesthesia, thoracic epidural anesthesia, and
pulsatile perfusion; the rise in aldosterone levels
is stimulated by activation of the renin-angiotensin
system. ■Hyperglycemia, hypoinsulinemia, and insulin resistance occur with hypothermic nonpulsatile CPB. ■Atrial natriuretic factor concentrations decrease
early in CPB but typically increase during rewarming. The secretion of atrial natriuretic factor in response
to the usual physiologic stimuli is blunted during and
after CPB. ■Ionized calcium concentrations decrease at the
onset of CPB and then rise slowly toward normal,
with physiologic parathormone responses to these
changes. Routine calcium supplementation upon
emergence from CPB is not recommended. ■Hypomagnesemia commonly occurs during CPB,
and prophylactic treatment of this deﬁciency with
intravenous magnesium supplementation reduces
the incidence of post-CPB atrial and ventricular
dysrhythmias, and may reduce the incidence of
coronary vasospasm and myocardial ischemia. ■Plasma potassium concentrations ﬂuctuate during
CPB under the inﬂuence of a variety of factors,
especially cardioplegia composition and dosing. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
