◗Cardiopulmonary Bypass and the Lung
Vivek K. Moitra and Robert N. Sladen
Pulmonary function in patients after cardiopulmonary
bypass
(CPB)
is
consistently
altered,
ranging
from
microscopic atelectasis of no clinical consequence to
fulminant acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Perioperative management of oxygenation and ventilation
can be challenging because multiple factors compromise pulmonary function, including atelectasis, pleural
disruption, impaired lung compliance, and the systemic
inﬂammatory response to extracorporeal circulation. CPB
represents a particular challenge to the patient with a
limited pulmonary reserve, who is particularly at high
risk for postoperative pulmonary complications. This
chapter will address the current state of knowledge of
pulmonary function in the setting of CPB, and outline
therapeutic approaches to the management of the lungs
during CPB. CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
AND PULMONARY MECHANICS
Pathophysiology of Atelectasis
Atelectasis is common after cardiac surgery and general
anesthesia, and several mechanisms have been proposed
to explain this phenomenon (1). In the anesthetized
patient, relaxation of the diaphragm and its cephalad
movement increase pleural pressures, which compress
adjacent lung tissue (2). Resorption atelectasis is possible
with airway obstruction when capillary uptake of oxygen
exceeds the rate of alveolar oxygen inﬂux. Absorption
is also possible in areas with low ventilation/perfusion
(˙V/ ˙Q) ratios. In the lung zones characterized by low
ventilation, the uptake of oxygen increases signiﬁcantly
as the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) increases (2). Atelectasis during CPB is also expected because the
lungs are collapsed and not perfused. Subsequently,
re-expansion and ventilation at the end of CPB is
seldom fully successful, and a variable degree of residual
atelectasis remains, ranging from microscopic to lobar in
magnitude. Anesthesia
After the induction of general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, mechanical ventilation initiates atelectasis
within 5 minutes (3). The relaxed diaphragm is displaced
cephalad by the abdominal contents, and gas ﬂow is preferentially distributed to the nondependent regions of the
lung. This causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and promotes hypoventilation and progressive microatelectasis of
the dependent lung zones. This process is uninterrupted
by the intermittent ‘‘sighs’’ that occur in the awake patient, and the monotonous mechanical ventilatory pattern
allows the extension of atelectasis from the alveoli to the
segments, lobules, and even lobes of the lung. Surfactant Depletion
Pulmonary surfactant covers the alveolar surface and
lowers surface tension to prevent alveolar and small airway collapse.

There is laboratory evidence that exposure
to anesthesia reduces surfactant function and increases
the permeability of the alveolar capillary barrier (4,5). Alterations in surfactant composition and function after CPB have been reported, but clinically signiﬁcant
changes in surfactant function have not been studied at
length (6,7). Because of an extensive surfactant reserve
and long turnover time, the role of surfactant depletion in
the setting of CPB is unclear. Atelectasis itself promotes
the production of proinﬂammatory cytokines, which decreases the synthesis of the surfactant (8). Anatomical Considerations and Position
During CPB, the heart rests on the immobile left lower
lobe. With blind bronchial suctioning, the catheter usually
enters the more direct right main stem bronchus, resulting in preferential right bronchial drainage. Traumatic
mucosal ‘‘pitting’’ induced by the suction catheter at the
carina causes secretions to dam up and promotes airway
collapse (9). When the pleural cavity is opened, blood and
ﬂuid can enter and compress the adjacent lung. In patients

who undergo coronary revascularization, dissection of the
left internal mammary artery (LIMA) mandates entry into
the left pleural space. All these factors account for the
60% to 70% preponderance of left lower lobe atelectasis
after CPB (10). The right lung can be compressed during
cannulation of the inferior vena cava. The supine position
is associated with a decrease in functional residual capacity (FRC) as abdominal contents push the diaphragm
cephalad and promote small airway closure. Signiﬁcant
atelectasis has been observed in the dorsal lung regions in
patients after cardiac surgery (11). Inspired Oxygen Concentration
The use of high-inspired concentrations of oxygen during the perioperative period can cause atelectasis (12–14). When the alveolar capillary concentration gradient increases and the capillaries rapidly absorb oxygen, atelectasis occurs. Although the degree of atelectasis varies at
different oxygen concentrations, it is most notable when
the FiO2 is more than 0.8 (15). Mechanical Ventilation
The use of low tidal volumes as a component of a protective
lung strategy has been advocated in the setting of
ARDS. Although this does protect against alveolar stretchinduced injury, it also promotes atelectasis. Pressure
controlled ventilation (PCV) is a ventilator mode that
limits peak airway pressures in the hope of decreasing
the risk of pulmonary barotrauma. However, if lung
compliance is very poor, the delivery of small tidal volumes
may promote the development of atelectasis. Comorbid Conditions
Heavy smokers with chronic bronchitis develop metaplasia of ciliated columnar epithelium to mucin-producing
goblet cells. Anterograde cilial clearance of mucus and
debris is impaired, surfactant production is diminished,
and small airways and alveoli tend to collapse. Obesity
causes a reduction in FRC and predisposes to atelectasis
before and after CPB. An increase in extravascular lung
water, whether due to congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema, increases the tendency for small airways
to collapse. Clinical Consequences of Atelectasis
It is common for the FRC to be decreased by as much
as 20% for up to a week after general anesthesia. Atelectasis induced by CPB, however, causes more severe
disruption of the bronchoalveolar tree and can decrease
FRC by as much as 40% to 50% (16). This causes a
substantial impairment of lung compliance and promotes
a pulmonary inﬂammatory response that contributes to
postoperative pulmonary complications (17–19). Impaired Oxygenation
The alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, or P(A-a)O2, is increased after CPB (20–24).

It increases to a maximum
after approximately 48 hours postoperatively, does not
return to normal for at least 7 days, and remains detectable for weeks after the surgery (25). Although intrapulmonary shunt (Qs/Qt) and venoarterial admixture
are increased after CPB, there is a poor correlation between the decrease in measured FRC and the increase
in Qs/Qt (26,27). Intrapulmonary shunt is worsened
in the setting of collapsed airways, which compromise
secretion clearance and predispose the patient to pulmonary superinfection and pneumonia. Regional areas of
hypoxemia from alveolar collapse increase pulmonary vascular resistance and may cause right ventricular dysfunction (28). Decreased Lung Compliance
A decline in lung compliance increases the alveolar
distending work of breathing. Loss of lung volume
lowers the FRC, that is, the volume remaining in the lung
at the end of a normal tidal ventilation. As a consequence,
the inspiratory and expiratory components of the breath
duty cycle occur within a less efﬁcient portion of the
pressure–volume curve (29,30). If severe enough, this can
lead to a substantial increase in energy consumption and
acute ventilatory failure, with continued requirement for
mechanical ventilation. Acute Lung Injury
The repetitive opening and closing of alveoli leads to
surfactant inactivation and atelectrauma, which has been
implicated in the development of ventilator-induced lung
injury (VILI). When alveoli are stretched by excessively large tidal volumes, inﬂammatory mediators and
neutrophils are activated, leading to increased alveolar
capillary permeability and hyaline membrane formation. Atelectrauma may be prevented or attenuated by
a protective lung strategy that limits tidal volumes to
curtail inspiratory alveolar stretch and adds positive endexpiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent expiratory alveolar
collapse. Prevention and Treatment
of Perioperative Atelectasis
Strategies to prevent and treat atelectasis in patients undergoing CPB have focused on recruitment maneuvers and
efforts to prevent derecruitment of alveoli. The resultant

313
modiﬁcations in mechanical ventilation may improve gas
exchange, increase FRC, and prevent atelectasis-induced
lung injury. Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
Ventilation
The use of static inﬂation of the lungs has been investigated to prevent the adverse effects of CPB on lung
function. The application of continuous positive airway
pressure (CPAP) at 10 cm H2O during CPB has been found
to improve postoperative PaO2, decrease P(A-a)O2, and decrease ventilation-perfusion mismatch up to 4 hours after
CPB and at the time of extubation (31). This response
is attenuated at lower levels of CPAP (32). In a similar
study, it was suggested that the lung expansion induced
by CPAP may preserve pulmonary mechanics by preservation of bronchial perfusion (33). It is also suggested that
static inﬂation of the lungs with oxygen might prevent
ultrastructural damage by sustaining cellular oxidative
metabolism (34). In small studies on animals, CPAP during CPB was found to be associated with lower pulmonary
lactate/pyruvate ratios and greater high-energy phosphate
concentrations compared with passive lung collapse (35). However, these ﬁndings have not been correlated with
signiﬁcant changes in gross lung function. Recruitment Maneuvers
There is considerable evidence that sustained inspiratory
recruitment maneuvers on CPB may inﬂate the collapsed
alveoli and improve arterial oxygenation and lung compliance (2,36–38). However, peak inspiratory pressures of
up to 40 cm H2O may be required. Although identical
‘‘Valsalva’’ maneuvers are routinely used after open-heart
procedures to expel air from the left atrium and ventricle,
there is a risk of disruption of the internal mammary graft
by excessive distension of the left lung, or rupture of a
bleb or weakened lung area. Sighs provided after separation from CPB can impede venous return and add to
hemodynamic instability. Open-Lung Concept
The recruitment maneuver has been extrapolated to the socalled open-lung concept (OLC), which requires an initial
period of PCV with high airway pressures (40 cm H2O)
with an inverted inspiratory:expiratory ratio (I:E, 1:1). This is followed by a protective lung strategy with low tidal
volumes and PEEP to minimize atelectrauma. Application
of the OLC to cardiac surgery has minimized post-CPB
atelectasis, improved FRC, and decreased the incidence of
postoperative hypoxemia (39).

Moreover, when the OLC
is commenced immediately after anesthetic induction and
tracheal intubation, the inﬂammatory response to CPB is
attenuated, with decreased levels of the proinﬂammatory
interleukins (IL), IL-8 and IL-10 (40). Impact of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
on Pulmonary Mechanics
There is considerable evidence that CPB has a deleterious effect on pulmonary mechanics (22,41–45), but it
may be difﬁcult to distinguish these from those induced
by thoracotomy, pleural resection, and pleural effusions. Decreases in vital capacity, FRC, lung compliance, and
pulmonary function have been shown to persist for more
than 3 months after surgery (46–49), although in several
studies the alterations have been considered to have a negligible clinical impact (50–52). To resolve the question of
the role of CPB versus cardiac surgery on pulmonary mechanics, trials have compared cardiac surgery with CPB
with off-pump coronary artery bypass (OPCAB) surgery. In
one prospective randomized trial of 197 patients undergoing cardiac surgery, OPCAB was associated with improved
oxygenation and decreased time to tracheal extubation. There were no differences in chest radiographs, spirometry, pneumonia, pleural effusion, pulmonary edema, or
mortality between groups (53). Although these beneﬁcial
effects have been conﬁrmed by some (54,55), others have
found no difference in pulmonary mechanics or oxygenation (56). Beneﬁts have been observed by the avoidance of
CPB in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in whom OPCAB or minimally invasive approaches
are associated with decreased atelectasis, reduced duration of tracheal intubation, and shorter length of stay in
the intensive care unit (ICU) (57). Airway resistance is consistently increased by CPB, and is more pronounced than
in patients undergoing OPCAB surgery (58). There have
been a number of reports of fulminant bronchospasm
during CPB (59–62). It is most likely related to contact
activation with an idiosyncratic excess activation of human C′5a anaphylatoxin, although other causes, such as
acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (‘‘cardiac asthma’’),
should be excluded (63). Operative technique and graft
selection can also alter pulmonary mechanics. Dissection
of the internal mammary artery with violation of the anterior chest wall and pleural cavity decreases FRC, as well
as the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), to a
greater extent than when saphenous vein grafts are used
alone (64,65). Lung retraction and pleurotomy, rather
than CPB itself, are the major architects of disturbed lung
mechanics during cardiac surgery (22,41).

ACUTE LUNG INJURY
Pathophysiology of Acute Lung Injury
Acute lung injury with fulminant noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is a rare but life-threatening complication

III. Physiology and Pathology
of CPB (66–70). After the advent of CPB in the 1950s, a
substantial proportion of deaths following cardiac surgery
was the consequence of a syndrome of acute respiratory failure, referred to as pump lung. Its morphology is
identical to that of the ARDS associated with other inﬂam-
matory syndromes, such as sepsis (71). There is diffuse
injury and swelling of the endothelial cells and pneumocytes, with an uneven distribution of surfactant (72). Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) after CPB demonstrates an
increase in IL-8 levels and neutrophil percentage (73). Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema results from increased
permeability of the alveolar capillary membrane, creating
a capillary leak syndrome with exudation of water and
protein into the alveolar space. It is distinguished from
cardiogenic pulmonary edema by the ﬁnding of normal
or low left atrial or pulmonary artery wedge pressures,
and a high protein concentration in the edema ﬂuid (albumin concentration ≥90% of serum albumin). In its most
dramatic form, its presentation is unique: a massive outpouring of frothy, proteinaceous ﬂuid from the tracheal
tube. Fluid loss may culminate in intravascular volume depletion and hypovolemic shock, with death resulting from
low cardiac output syndrome rather than hypoxemia (68). Even in patients with diffuse pulmonary edema and severe hypoxemia, aggressive restoration of intravascular
volume is mandatory, guided by close monitoring of left
ventricular ﬁlling pressure. The Role of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
in Acute Lung Injury
It was initially assumed that acute lung injury during
CPB is triggered by the embolism of particulate debris
into the pulmonary microcirculation. This in turn evokes
an inﬂammatory response mediated by complement activation, neutrophil migration, cytokine production, and
arachidonic acid metabolites. However, it soon became
apparent that ‘‘pump lung’’ occurs even when all the
perfusate is ﬁltered, suggesting a role for etiologies in
addition to, or instead of, microembolism. Contact activation of the blood by the extracorporeal circuit triggers
a series of ampliﬁcation cascades mediated by proteolytic
enzymes, especially serine proteases. It is initiated by
the activation of the circulating procoagulant, Factor XII
(Hageman factor), which triggers the intrinsic pathway
of coagulation, ﬁbrinolysis, and complement activation. The last results in the activation of C′5a anaphylatoxin,
a potent bioactive molecule that plays a central role
in mediating the acute inﬂammatory response. In addition, C′5a has spasmogenic and leukocyte-activating
properties (63).

Complement-exposed neutrophils become
‘‘sticky,’’ adhere to surfaces, aggregate, and may block the
microcirculation by margination and leukoembolization. The neutrophils degranulate and release highly reactive oxygen-free radicals and proteolytic enzymes, which
damage the endothelial cells. The net effect is a dramatic
increase in vascular permeability and capillary leak syndrome. Although its pathogenesis has been clearly elucidated, acute lung injury induced by CPB does not account
for all the lung dysfunction after cardiac surgery. The incidence of postoperative respiratory complications is not
signiﬁcantly different in ‘‘off-pump’’ cardiac surgery (74). The lung inﬂammatory response may be as much an
epiphenomenon of surgery on the heart, and its incidence
may be related to operator technique. Other factors also
contribute, for example, high FiO2 in the early postoperative period increases cytokine levels and augments the
proinﬂammatory response of alveolar macrophages (75). Anaphylatoxins and Complement Activation
Complement activation and the potential for pulmonary
dysfunction appear to be a consistent response to contact activation of blood in extracorporeal circuits, such as
leukophoresis and hemodialysis (76,77). Complement is
activated through two interrelated cascades, termed the
classical and alternate pathways. Ultimately C′3, the central component of the system, is cleaved. The resulting
fragments, called anaphylatoxins, cause smooth muscle
contraction and function as a major chemotactic factor
for neutrophils. They trigger the release of arachidonic
acid metabolites such as leukotriene B4, which increases
vascular permeability and provokes mast cell degranulation and induce the formation of neutrophil adhesion
molecules. A higher expression of adhesion molecules after CPB is seen in patients with diabetes, which may
increase the risk of postoperative complications (78). The
incidence and severity of postoperative organ dysfunction correlates with plasma complement concentrations,
duration of CPB, and the degree of elevation of C′3a
levels (79). Neutrophil Activation
Neutrophils are activated during CPB by complement,
shear stress, and contact with the CPB circuit (80–83). High levels of neutrophil elastase, a measure of neutrophil
activation, peak at the end of CPB and are associated
with increased intrapulmonary shunt and postoperative
pulmonary dysfunction (84). BAL demonstrates that neutrophil count, IL-8, and elastase concentration correlate
with decreased arterial oxygenation after CPB (85). Activated neutrophils migrate to the areas of inﬂammation and
ischemia where they release proteolytic enzymes and cytotoxins, causing direct lung damage and increased capillary
permeability (1,84,86,87). CPB also increases the production of neutrophil matrix metalloproteinase (MMP),
and MMP-9 degrades basement membranes.

There is increased expression of neutrophil intracellular adhesion
molecule-1 (ICAM-1) on pulmonary endothelium, which

14. Cardiopulmonary Bypass and the Lung
315
promotes sequestration of neutrophils and is linked
with the development of pulmonary insufﬁciency after
CPB (88). Cytokines
CPB induces leukocytes to release a variety of cytokines,
including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), IL-6, and IL-8. These exacerbate the inﬂammatory response by upregulating neutrophil adhesion molecules and promoting
the accumulation of parenchymal neutrophils (88). In
a prospective observational study, an increased plasma
level of IL-6 after CPB was predictive for postoperative
pulmonary infection (89). The lung itself may play a
role in the response to CPB and development of acute
lung injury (90). This is suggested by the ﬁnding of a
greater inﬂammatory response (i.e., proinﬂammatory cytokine levels) in the lungs (alveolar macrophages) than in
the systemic circulation (plasma monocytes). There may
also be a genetic predisposition to acute lung injury. Some
functional polymorphisms are associated with increased
levels of TNF-α, which may serve as a marker for an
enhanced inﬂammatory response after CPB (90). Arachidonic Acid Metabolites
The role of vasoactive arachidonic acid metabolites such
as thromboxanes, leukotrienes, prostaglandins (PGs),
and prostacyclins in acute lung injury is unclear (91). Thromboxane, a pulmonary vasoconstrictor, is released
from platelets activated by the extracorporeal circuit. The ﬁnding of greater thromboxane B2 levels in the left
than the right atrium at the end of CPB suggests that
thromboxane is produced in the lungs, perhaps in the
ischemic pulmonary tissue or intravascular hematologic
components (92). A disturbed balance between pro- and
anti-inﬂammatory arachidonic acid metabolites may play
a role in pulmonary injury. Inhibition of thromboxane
synthetase decreases the CPB-induced lung injury in
sheep (93). In patients with severe lung injury after CPB,
levels of thromboxane B2 concentrations are increased
relative to the levels of prostaglandin E2. Disordered Lung Metabolism
The lung is the only organ that receives the entire
circulation, and it plays an important function in the
production of angiotensin II, prostacyclin, and endothelin I. Pulmonary endothelin-1 is a powerful vasoconstrictor released during lung endothelial injury and is
implicated in the development of pulmonary hypertension after CPB (94,95). Increased pulmonary artery
pressures after CPB may result from the reduction of
nitric oxide production owing to pulmonary endothelial
dysfunction (96–98). The lung also inactivates bradykinin,
serotonin, leukotrienes, and norepinephrine. Bradykinin
is a potent vasodilator that is rapidly metabolized and inactivated by the pulmonary vascular endothelium.

During
CPB, serum levels of bradykinin are increased (99). Early resumption of blood ﬂow to the lungs may facilitate weaning from CPB in patients whose hypotension
is a result of a bradykinin-induced decrease in systemic
vascular resistance (SVR) (71). In contrast, it has been hypothesized that systemic hypertension after CPB is caused
by depressed clearance of neurohumoral substances, particularly norepinephrine, by the damaged lung (100). There is experimental evidence that diminution of the
lung’s ability to remove circulating norepinephrine and
prostaglandin E2 is directly related to the duration of
CPB (101). Pulmonary extraction of serotonin following
CPB is also decreased, and may also play a role in postoperative pulmonary complications (102). Prevention and Treatment of Acute
Lung Injury
Extracorporeal Circuit
Numerous attempts have been made to attenuate the
inﬂammatory response to CPB by modiﬁcation of the
extracorporeal circuit itself. Heparin-coated CPB circuits
improve biocompatibility and limit neutrophil activation
and its attendant release of complement activated mediators, cytokines, and proinﬂammatory enzymes, such as
secretory phospholipase A2 (103–107). Their use is associated with improvements in the post-CPB indexes, such
as pulmonary vascular resistance, lung compliance, shunt
fraction, and oxygenation, but this has not been correlated
with an improved clinical outcome (103–107). Membrane
oxygenators avoid the potential damage to blood components and plasma proteins caused by direct gas contact
in bubble oxygenators. However, a randomized study of
the two devices on 500 patients found that, although use
of the membrane oxygenator decreases extravascular lung
water, there are no demonstrable differences in intrapulmonary shunting, duration of ventilation, ICU stay, or
mortality (108,109). Hemoﬁltration
High-volume continuous hemoﬁltration is a means of removing ﬂuid and low molecular weight molecules from
plasma under a pressure gradient. Its application during
CPB could attenuate the inﬂammatory response by ﬁl-
tering the substances that cause acute lung injury (110). Hemoﬁltration removes endothelin-1, a pulmonary vasoconstrictor, and may thereby decrease the severity of
postoperative pulmonary hypertension (110–112). Improvements in postoperative oxygenation and duration of
mechanical ventilation have been observed with this technique (112,113), although it appears to be more effective in

316
III. Physiology and Pathology
pediatric than adult patients (114). A randomized prospective trial on 192 adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery
demonstrated that hemoﬁltration during CPB is more effective than placebo or steroids in decreasing the time to
tracheal extubation (115). Leukocyte Depletion
As discussed earlier, leukocytes play an intrinsic role
in the inﬂammatory response to CPB, suggesting that
leukocyte ﬁltration could attenuate pulmonary injury. Although several studies show a beneﬁt for pulmonary
function by leukocyte depletion during CPB (91,116–119),
this has not been a consistent ﬁnding (120). During
routine coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery,
total leukocyte ﬁltration during CPB results in a transient
postoperative decrease in white cell count, but this is
not correlated with improvements in pulmonary function,
respiratory index, or length of stay in the ICU (121). Mechanical Ventilation
During mechanical ventilation, excessively large tidal volumes and the repetitive opening and closing of alveoli
induce atelectrauma and VILI. As described in the section
on atelectasis, early application of the OLC appears to
decrease interleukin concentrations after CPB and could
attenuate the inﬂammatory response and acute lung injury (40). Although the use of protective ventilation with
low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg) has shown beneﬁts in patients
with established ARDS, the role of minimal alveolar distention to prevent CPB-induced acute lung injury remains
unclear. Compared with conventional tidal volumes, protective tidal volumes do not appear to decrease systemic
cytokine levels, postoperative pulmonary dysfunction, or
hospital length of stay (17). Once ARDS has become established, maintenance of oxygenation requires high levels of
airway pressure therapy (122,123). This is provided by
volume-controlled ventilation with extrinsic positive endexpiratory pressure (PEEPe), or PCV with inverse I:E ratio
and intrinsic or auto-PEEP (PEEPi). With either approach
the goals are to support the FRC, decrease Qs/Qt, and wean
a high FiO2. Corticosteroids
Under experimental conditions, corticosteroids consistently attenuate the inﬂammatory response to CPB by
decreasing concentrations of proinﬂammatory cytokines,
neutrophil activation, upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecule, and complement activation (124–127). Unfortunately,
the
clinical
beneﬁts
of
perioperative
steroid administration remain unproved. In fact, there
is some evidence that the perioperative administration
of methylprednisolone actually worsens oxygenation and
increases the duration of mechanical ventilation required
after cardiac surgery (115,128). Plausible explanations for
these adverse effects are steroid-induced sodium retention, increased lung water retention, and intrapulmonary
shunt (129).

Aprotinin
Aprotinin is a serine protease inhibitor administered
during high-risk cardiac surgery with CPB to decrease
perioperative bleeding caused by ﬁbrinolysis and platelet
dysfunction (130). It also attenuates the inﬂammatory
response to CPB that is triggered by contact activation. Experimental studies demonstrate that its administration decreases IL-8 levels, lung neutrophil accumulation, release
of TNF-α and neutrophil elastase, and upregulation of
neutrophil adhesion molecules (131,132). This translates
into decreased lung edema and improved lung compliance
and oxygenation after CPB (133–135). Some retrospectively analyzed data has been published that associates
aprotinin administration with an increased incidence of
renal failure and stroke (136), so its use in the individual
patient must be based on a risk–beneﬁt assessment. Inhaled Nitric Oxide
Endogenous nitric oxide production is reduced after CPB,
probably because of pulmonary endothelial dysfunction,
with diminished substrate or cofactor activity that lowers
nitric oxide production (73,137). Endothelial nitric oxide
maintains tonic vasodilation of the pulmonary vasculature, and a reduction in endogenous nitric oxide levels
potentiates pulmonary hypertension after CPB (96–98). Binding with heme compounds instantaneously inactivates the circulating nitric oxide. Inhaled nitric oxide
(INO) provides potent vasodilation in the pulmonary vasculature, but INO is inactivated before it can get into the
systemic circulation. As such, it is commonly used to treat
elevated pulmonary vascular resistance after CPB. INO
also has anti-inﬂammatory properties, it decreases the
levels of IL-8 and thereby attenuates neutrophil adhesion
and transendothelial migration, as well as the apoptotic
changes in the lungs during CPB (73,96,138–145). Prostaglandins
There is evidence that vasodilator prostaglandins such
as PGE1 may be more anti-inﬂammatory than corticosteroids during CPB, with a greater inhibition of intravascular pulmonary leukocyte aggregation, activation, and free
radical production (146). PGE1 increases cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) formation, which stabilizes
leukocyte lysosomes. Infusions of PGE1, prostacyclin, and
Iloprost (a more stable prostacyclin analog) during CPB
prevent platelet aggregation and thromboxane release,

14. Cardiopulmonary Bypass and the Lung
317
and decrease operative bleeding (147,148). However, these
agents are potent vasodilators and their use is limited
by systemic hypotension. These hypotensive effects are
much less pronounced with Iloprost than with other
prostaglandin analogs. PGI2, a known platelet inhibitor,
was shown to prevent occlusive ﬁbrin, leukocyte, and
platelet-based aggregates in pulmonary arterioles in dogs,
without signiﬁcant hypotension (149). However, these experimental ﬁndings have yet to be translated into any
proven beneﬁt on clinical outcome. Exogenous Surfactant
Pharmacologic preparations containing surfactant have
been used clinically in the treatment of hyaline membrane
disease in premature infants. However, both experimental
and clinical studies with exogenously administered surfactant during CPB have demonstrated no beneﬁts for
pulmonary function, and in fact resulted in deleterious
effects on gas transfer (150,151). KEY POINTS
■Several anesthesia-related effects predispose to atelectasis:
●Cephalad movement of the diaphragm with muscle
relaxation leads to ˙V/ ˙Q mismatch and microatelectasis with decreased PaO2. ●Surfactant production is decreased. ●High FiO2 contributes to atelectasis (resorption). ●Comorbid conditions such as chronic lung disease
and smoking are common. ■Clinical consequences of atelectasis:
●There is impaired oxygenation. ●Lung compliance is decreased. ●Acute lung injury may occur. ■Prevention and treatment of atelectasis:
●Use of CPAP (10–20 cm H2O) during CPB improves
postoperative PaO2. ●Sustained inspiratory pressure (recruitment maneuvers) may improve PaO2. ❍There are risks that include damage to LIMA
grafts, pulmonary barotrauma, and hemodynamic instability. ●OLC
❍This should be begun shortly after intubation,
with a period of pressure control ventilation
using high airway pressures and an inverted I:E
of 1:1. ❍Subsequently, the use of low tidal volumes (e.g.,
6 mL/kg) with PEEP may also be resorted to. ❍OLC may also decrease the inﬂammatory response to CPB. ■Prevention of acute lung injury:
●Use of heparin-bonded circuits and membrane
versus bubble oxygenators may decrease acute
lung injury. ●Hemoﬁltration decreases time to extubation. ●Leukocyte depletion is not consistently linked to
improved postoperative lung function after CPB. ●Administration of corticosteroids is generally not
beneﬁcial. ●The use of serine protease inhibitors may be
beneﬁcial. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

C h a p t e r
1 5
◗Immune System and Inﬂammatory
Responses to Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Mustafa Zakkar, Kenneth Taylor, and Philip I. Hornick
The development of the heart–lung machine in the 1950s,
together with the development of cardiac catheterization
and the usage of heparin, made open-heart surgery possible and contributed enormously to the treatment and
life expectancy of cardiac patients (1). Cardiopulmonary
bypass (CPB) provides a complex set of nonphysiologic
circumstances during which patients are subjected to severe physiologic alterations, with relatively few serious
adverse sequelae in most patients (2,3). CPB is far from
perfect, but, because our understanding of the inﬂam-
matory process associated with the extracorporeal circuit
has improved over the years and with the development of
different methods and agents to support the bypass machine, survival rates continue to improve, even with more
complex surgery. This chapter focuses on the complex
subject of immune and inﬂammatory responses related
to CPB. Immune responses offer protection to the organism
from a variety of pathologic insults. The immune system
comprises two fundamental features that act to effect
such protection by generating both innate and acquired
responses to the insult. The result is inﬂammation. Innate
immunity depends on a variety of immunologic effector
mechanisms that are neither speciﬁc for a particular
infectious agent nor improved by repeated encounters
with the same antigen. The innate system comprises
phagocytic cells (neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages,
and natural killer cells), endothelial cells, and soluble
factors such as complement, cytokines/chemokines, and
acute phase proteins. By contrast, the adaptive or acquired
immune response is mediated by T and B lymphocytes;
memory of prior exposure and recognition of speciﬁc
antigens along with speciﬁcity of the response are the key
features of this response. In practice, there is considerable
overlap and reinforcement between these two types of
immunity because the innate response can activate and
amplify the acquired response, which, in turn, is able to
direct elements of the innate system, such as phagocytes
or complement factors. Contact of blood with the artiﬁcial surface of the
CPB circuit, ischemia and reperfusion phenomena, along
with hypoperfusion of various organs during periods
of CPB, may initiate and aggravate the inﬂammatory
response (4). CPB is accompanied by the activation of
both innate and acquired immunity mounting a complex
inﬂammatory response.

CPB also induces the cellular
and humoral constituents of the immune system to
undergo quantitative and qualitative changes, leading to a
temporary immunodeﬁciency. THE SYSTEMIC INFLAMMATORY
RESPONSE TO CARDIOPULMONARY
BYPASS
Deﬁnition
At the outset, it is important to deﬁne what is meant by
the systemic inﬂammatory response in general and, more
speciﬁcally, in the context of CPB. On the basis of clinical and experimental studies, which indicate that various
conditions, both infectious and noninfectious, induce similar host response, the syndrome, ‘‘systemic inﬂammatory
response syndrome’’ (SIRS) was advanced by the American College of Chest Physicians/Society of Critical Care
Medicine (ACCP/SCCM) consensus conference in 1992 to
describe the common systemic response to a wide variety of insults (5,6). Two or more of the following clinical
manifestations must be fulﬁlled for the diagnosis:
1. Body temperature higher than 38◦C or lower than 36◦C
2. Heart rate more than 90 beats/min
3. Respiratory rate more than 20/min or PaCO2 less than
32 mm Hg
4. Leukocyte count more than 12,000 cells/mm3 or less
than 4,000 cells/mm3, or the presence of more than
10% immature neutrophils
Although it has been more than a decade since its inception, and despite criticism against the deﬁnition, it still

provides a useful framework in the approach to critically
ill patients (7) and remains capable of showing signiﬁcant
associations with physiologic deterioration combined with
increasing organ dysfunction. It is generally accepted
that CPB produces a ‘‘whole-body’’ inﬂammatory response (8,9). In its most severe form, a spectrum of injury
may be observed that includes one or more of the following clinical manifestations: pulmonary, renal, gut, central
nervous system, and myocardial dysfunction; coagulopathy and hemolysis; and pyrexia, increased susceptibility to
infections, and leukocytosis (9). Certainly, this ‘‘postbypass’’ syndrome would come
within the somewhat loose catch-all term of SIRS (4). However, the breadth of diagnostic criteria that permit
the inclusion or exclusion of CPB in the terminology
leads to the suggestion of yet another acronym to indicate the systemic inﬂammatory response after bypass
(SIRAB). The potential diagnostic criteria for SIRAB
would at least combine the noninfectious clinical picture(s) mentioned earlier with certain hemodynamic and
hematologic parameters, together with speciﬁc biochemical markers of inﬂammation. An obvious pitfall here is
distinguishing end-organ damage, for example, a stroke
or mesenteric infarction, due to inﬂammatory phenomena per se (microemboli, hyperdynamic circulation, etc.)
versus that due to suboptimal perfusion during CPB of
an organ system that already has a compromised vascular supply and little endogenous reserve. Until we deﬁne
speciﬁc criteria for the inﬂammatory response after CPB,
it will remain difﬁcult to accurately deﬁne its incidence
and prevalence and to properly apportion its pathologic
effects in terms of patient morbidity and mortality. Moreover, any strategies aimed at either therapy or prevention
can only be properly assessed in the light of established
criteria. Although it is widely accepted that a systemic in-
ﬂammatory response is induced in nearly all patients
undergoing CPB (10), the incidence and severity of the
response following CPB is variable; most patients experience few clinically adverse sequelae (2,3), and only a
minority develop severe hemodynamic changes or organ
failure (10,11). The speciﬁc degree of response is not predictable in a given patient, nor is its clinical sequelae. The
length of CPB is frequently, but not necessarily (11), regarded as a risk factor. Nonetheless, the adverse sequelae
of SIRAB do, in fact, account for substantial morbidity in
pediatric surgery, in the aged or inﬁrm, and in patients
undergoing long, complex surgical procedures (12,13).

Initiation of Systemic Inﬂammatory
Response after Bypass
SIRAB is initiated by a number of injurious processes that
impinge on both cellular and noncellular (humoral) elements of blood. These processes generate microemboli,
disrupt hemostasis, and lead to a generalized wholebody inﬂammatory response. Most importantly, they
set in motion a sequence of cytokine-mediated events
that activate vascular endothelium, allowing further
neutrophil-mediated inﬂammatory injury. The damaging
effects of CPB are most commonly attributed to contact
of blood with the foreign surface of the extracorporeal circuit. However, other factors, such as altered arterial blood
ﬂow patterns, shear stress generated by blood pumps, cardiotomy suction devices (including intracardiac venting),
tissue ischemia and reperfusion, hypothermia, relative
anemia, and the anticoagulation agents used during the
period of bypass, can play an equally important role in triggering tissue injury and an inﬂammatory response (14). This response may continue long after the discontinuation of CPB, and can manifest as a wide range of adverse
clinical outcomes (9), depending on the magnitude of the
inﬂammatory response (15). The repeated passage of blood through the nonphysiologic extracorporeal circuit leads to a ‘‘contact activation’’
response, which is initiated by the activation of contact protein cascades upon exposure of the blood to the
nonendothelialized surface of the CPB machine. Four
proteins are involved in the contact activation cascades:
coagulation factors XII and XI, prekallikrein, and highmolecular-weight kininogen (HMWK). The end result of
this activation is the formation of bradykinin, and the conversion of plasminogen into plasmin. This, in addition to
initiating ﬁbrinolysis, can trigger the classical complement
cascade. Therefore, multiple inﬂammatory mediators are
released upon exposure to the extracorporeal circuit (16). These responses disrupt hemostasis and lead to a generalized whole body inﬂammatory response, which is set
in motion by a sequence of chemokine-mediated events
that activate vascular endothelium and potentiates further
neutrophil-mediated injury. It is important to appreciate that none of the events
described here occurs in isolation. They occur simultaneously and frequently stimulate or catalyze other
reactions in the cycle of SIRAB, producing both proand anti-inﬂammatory effects (4,17), as the increase in
proinﬂammatory mediators is accompanied by phased
anti-inﬂammatory mediator release, such as interleukin
10 (IL-10) (18,19). Furthermore, some cytokines, such
as IL-6, might carry both proinﬂammatory and anti-
inﬂammatory properties (20).

The Cellular Components of Blood
Red Blood Cell
Tissue oxygenation is dependent on continuous oxygen
delivery, most of which is carried by the hemoglobulin
molecules in the red blood cells (RBCs). The use of an
extracorporeal circuit exposes the RBCs to a challenging

15. Immune System and Inﬂammatory Responses to Cardiopulmonary Bypass
323
environment, altering their integrity and function. Rheologic shear stress forces cause mechanical damage to
the RBCs, and induce ionic pump changes at the cell
surface and an abnormal accumulation of intracellular
cations (21). This reduces RBC deformability, which
is important for maintaining normal microcirculation. Furthermore, as a further consequence of membrane distortion, the RBC is susceptible to the membrane attack
complex (MAC) generated from the activation of complement (9), leading to haemoglobin leak. Free hemoglobin
in plasma may be damaging to tissue function by increasing plasma oncotic pressure and viscosity. Cytotoxic
oxygen-free radicals are also released after auto-oxidation
of hemoglobin. Adenosine diphosphate (ADP), released
from red cell lysis, may alter the function of platelets and
their ability to contribute to hemostasis (22). In addition,
arrhythmias may also develop as a result of potassium
released from the RBC. Lipid red cell membrane ghosts
may further occlude the microcirculation and lead to organ dysfunction (21,23). The ability of RBCs to aggregate
is signiﬁcantly reduced as a consequence of the dilution of
blood with priming solution. This can, in addition to compromising tissue oxygenation, trigger different signaling
pathways leading to endothelial activation (24). CPB may also inﬂuence hematopoiesis. Recent evidence indicates that inﬂammatory mediators have the
ability to up- or downregulate erythropoietin production (25,26), which not only controls the differentiation
and proliferation of the erythroid progenitor cells (27),
but also contributes to the premature release of reticulocytes (28,29). Vascular Endothelium
Under resting conditions, the vascular endothelium offers a relatively inert surface that regulates the passage
of intravascular substrates to the extravascular space and
ensures the unhindered ﬂow of cellular and serum components through the capillary network. These cells are
extremely sensitive to the stimulation associated with
CPB, such as hypoxia, surgical manipulation, cytokines
[IL-1B and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α], thrombin,
(C′5a), and lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), leading to activation with an increase in surface expression of E-selectin,
endothelial leukocytes adhesion molecule (ELAM), intercellular adhesion molecule-1(ICAM-1), and vascular
adhesion molecule (VCAM), which are mediators of leukocytes recruitment (30–33) (Fig. 1). ICAM-1, ICAM-2, and
VCAM-1 are members of the immunoglobulin superfamily. ICAM-1 contains ﬁve Ig-like domains and is expressed
at low levels on resting endothelium, but markedly induced in response to cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF-α.

ICAM-2 has two Ig-like domains and is constitutively
expressed on endothelial cells (34,35). VCAM-1 has a
N-terminal extracellular region comprising seven Ig-like
domains and is not expressed in resting endothelium,
but is induced by IL-1, 1L-4, and TNF (36,37). CPB also
reduces the ability of the endothelium to produce factors
important for promoting vascular patency and the prevention of thrombosis, such as nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin,
and adenosine, while the production of vasoactive factors
such as endothelin and angiotensin is increased, leading
to vasomotor and organ dysfunction (38). ICAM-1, VCAM-1

III. Physiology and Pathology
Leukocytes
The recruitment of leukocytes from the circulation to an
inﬂammatory site is a multistep process (Fig. 1) involving
members of several adhesion receptor families (39,40). CPB activates vascular endothelium, leading to rapid expression of members of the selectin family (41). These
are transmembrane molecules, expressed on the surface
of leukocytes and activated endothelial cells. Selectins
contain an N-terminal extracellular domain with structural homology to calcium-dependent lectins, followed
by a domain homologous to epidermal growth factor,
and two to nine consensus repeats (CR) similar to sequences found in complement regulatory proteins. Each
of these adhesion receptors is inserted through a hydrophobic transmembrane domain and possesses a short
cytoplasmic tail. The initial attachment of leukocytes from
the bloodstream during inﬂammation is afforded by the
selectin family and causes a slowing of downstream movement, culminating in a complete standstill (ﬁrm adhesion)
of leukocytes along the endothelium through transient,
reversible, adhesive interactions. There are three members in this family; P-, E-, and L-selectin. P-selectin is
stored, preformed, in Weibel-Palade bodies within the
endothelial cell and is released by exocytosis within minutes of activation by agents such as histamine, thrombin,
H2O2, and C′5a. The primary ligand for P-selectin is
PSGL-1 (P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1), which is constitutively found on all leukocytes. Other ligands include
CD24 and uncharacterized ligands. The transient interactions between P-selectin and PSGL-1 allow leukocytes
to roll along the endothelium. Accordingly, P-selectin is
largely responsible for the rolling phase of the leukocyte
adhesion cascade. P-selectin can also mediate capture
when L-selectin is not present. E-selectin mediates much
slower rolling than P-selectin. Depending on the level of
expression of E-selectin, rolling velocities range between
less than 5 µm/s and approximately 15 µm/s (42,43). E-selectin ligands on polymorphonucleus (PMNs) are not
well characterized. Other than PSGL-1, which is a ligand
for all three selectins in vivo (44), CD44 has been iden-
tiﬁed as a physiologic E-selectin ligand (45). L-selectin
contributes greatly to the capture of leukocytes during the early phases of the adhesion cascade. Following
capture, L-selectin is shed from the leukocyte surface
after chemoattractant stimulation. L-selectin interacts
with three known counter-receptors or ligands: mucosal
addressin cell adhesion molecule (MAdCAM)-1, glycosylation dependent cell adhesion molecule (GlyCAM)-1,
and CD34 (46,47). In conjunction with other molecules,
L-selectin’s function and inﬂuence in the adhesion cascade has been under scrutiny in many experiments using gene-targeted mice.

Transmigration is the next step
to follow and is mediated by adhesion molecule upregulation, including platelet endothelial cell adhesion
molecule (PECAM)-1, CD99, ICAM-1, CD11a/CD18, very
late antigen (VLA)-4, and endothelium-secreting chemoattractants (46). Neutrophils
Neutrophils are a central cell type in the mediation of
the systemic inﬂammatory response; their recruitment,
activation, and cytotoxic capability are an essential aspect of the body’s ability to ward off infection. Neutrophil
activation through interaction with activated vascular endothelium may be responsible for much of the clinical
sequelae of SIRAB. Activation of neutrophils during CPB
is shown by the loss of L-selectin and the upregulation
of CD11b/CD18 (Mac-1). Increased production of reactive
oxygen intermediates (47) and neutrophil-derived elastase
and similar molecules have also been reported (47,48). Studies in complement-deﬁcient dogs suggest that at least
some of the neutrophil activation seen in CPB is due
to complement activation (49,50). This process of neutrophil activation, ﬁrm adhesion, and sequestration can
lead to obstruction of capillaries and local ischemia (51). In addition, the release of cytotoxic products by activated
cells can cause direct cellular damage. These cytotoxins
include both preformed agents that are present in the
granules of neutrophils and newly synthesized molecules. There are two forms of neutrophil granules. The primary
or azurophil granules have a predominantly intracellular role. These granules contain various proteases and
myeloperoxidase (MPO) that convert hydrogen peroxide
to hypochlorous acid. The secondary neutrophil granules
are released from the neutrophil and function primarily
in an extracellular role. The secondary granules contain
a number of cell surface molecules, such as the receptor
for breakdown products of C′3b and for chemoattractants. They also contain soluble mediators of inﬂammation, including activators of the C′5 component and macrophage
chemotactic agents. In addition to causing obstruction in small vessels and
the release of preformed molecules, neutrophils (and
mononuclear phagocytes) synthesize novel substances,
including leukotrienes (48) and reactive oxygen intermediates (47). This synthesis can be readily detected
by a dramatic increase in the oxygen consumption of
the cells. These species are largely responsible for the
so-called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Ischemic injury occurs when the blood supply to a tissue is impaired or
suboptimal, which may occur with CPB. The paradox,
however, is that a more severe tissue injury occurs when
blood ﬂow is restored upon reperfusion.

The onset of
ischemia is accompanied by the depletion of cellular
adenosine triphosphate as a result of its degradation
by hypoxanthine. Normally, hypoxanthine is oxidized by
the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase to xanthine using
nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) in a reaction

cell types. Monocytes
Peripheral monocytes are another type of leukocytes involved in the systemic inﬂammatory process. They possess
migratory, chemotactic, pinocytic, and phagocytic activities, as well as receptors for IgG and C′3b. Upon
migration to tissue, they undergo further differentiation
to become tissue macrophages, which participate in
both speciﬁc and nonspeciﬁc immune pathways.

Recruitment of these cells can be as early as 1 hour
following insult (53) and is thought to be mediated
mainly by monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1),
although other factors such as C′5a play an important role. Upon activation, they play a pivotal role
in inﬂammation, serving as effector cells secreting cytokines (54). Macrophages can exhibit both pro- and
anti-inﬂammatory properties, depending on the signals
they receive, and it has been recently suggested that
these cells have the capacity to switch from one state
to the other and so can participate in both the induction and resolution of inﬂammation (53). Furthermore,
recent studies have shown an increase in plasma and
surface CD163 (which is a member of the cysteinerich scavenger family and is exclusively expressed by
cells of monocyte/macrophage lineage) levels in patients
undergoing CPB (54,55). CD163 mediates the internalization of hemoglobin–haptoglobin (Hb:Hp) complexes and
even free Hb when haptoglobin (Hp) binding capacity
is exhausted, demonstrating important anti-inﬂammatory
capabilities (54,56). Platelets
CPB is associated with a transient deﬁcit in platelet
function and number, which can cause a derangement
in postoperative hemostasis (57). The normal platelet
is able to adhere to a damaged endothelial cell or
the subendothelial layer. Adherence is achieved by a
bridge formed by a molecule of the multimeric form
of the von Willebrand factor from the endothelium to
the platelet at the glycoprotein (GpIb) receptor site. The platelet then undergoes a conformational change,
with exposure of different glycoproteins that include
the complex GpIIb/IIIa, which can bind to ﬁbrinogen. Fibrinogen is an important cofactor in platelet adhesion
and is essential for platelet-to-platelet binding that occurs
during irreversible aggregation. The aggregate is stabilized
by the protein complex thrombospondin. Thromboxane
A2 is also released, which produces vasoconstriction and
platelet aggregation. Numerous factors associated with CPB contribute to
the changes that occur in platelets. These include physical
factors (58) (such as hypothermia and shear forces),
exposure to artiﬁcial surfaces (59,60), the use of exogenous
drugs, and the release of endogenous chemicals (61,62). Hemodilution from pump priming ﬂuids contributes to
the early thrombocytopenia to a degree (63). However,
mechanical disruption, adhesion to the extracorporeal
circuit, and sequestration in organs can explain the drop
in the circulating platelet count, which can be 30% to
50% from baseline (64). The response of platelets to
CPB is complex and multifactorial, including a rapid

326
III. Physiology and Pathology
consumption of platelets during bypass (63), a decreased
reactivity to known agonists (62), an increase in the
concentration of the α-granule compounds in plasma (65),
and an increase in the stable metabolite of thromboxane A2
(thromboxane B) released from aggregating platelets (66). Morphologic changes, including spherical appearance and
the development of pseudopods, have also been seen as a
result of CPB (67).The observation that the bleeding time
is prolonged after a period of extracorporeal circulation
has been related directly to the time on bypass; however,
the time course of these observations and the precise
mechanism is less clear (68). It has been observed that
platelets of patients deﬁcient in the GpIIb/IIIa complex
did not bind to a foreign surface and that the proteins
adherent to the extracorporeal system were primarily
made up of fragments of the GpIIb receptor (69). This suggests that the GpIIb/IIIa complex is the most
likely adhesive glycoprotein affected by the extracorporeal
circulation (70). Platelets activated during CPB form conjugates both
between themselves and with leukocytes. P-selectin is
expressed by activated platelets, which contributes to
leukocyte conjugate formation by binding PSGL-1 (71). Activated platelets use this P-selectin/PSGL-1 adhesion
pathway to stimulate conjoined monocytes, thereby leading to secretion of the proinﬂammatory cytokines IL-1β,
IL-8, and MCP-1 (72,73). P-selectin also induces tissue factor expression and ﬁbrin deposition by monocytes, thereby
contributing to the evolution of thrombus (74,75). Evidence is accumulating that activated platelets attach to vascular endothelium and play an important role
in neutrophil adhesion and transmigration. Endothelial
cells express an adhesion molecule known as CD40 and
activated platelets express, on their surface, a complementary binding molecule (ligand) known as CD40L. This
transmembrane ligand protein is structurally related to
TNF-α and induces endothelium to secrete chemokines
and express further adhesion molecules. Substantial secretions of IL-8 (chemotactic for neutrophils) and MCP-1
(chemotactic for monocytes) were noted on platelets binding to the endothelium. Therefore, activated platelets
bound to endothelium are able to initiate recruitment
of neutrophils and monocytes (76). Some authors have
suggested that any platelet stimulation associated with
the initial phase of bypass is of little consequence and
that only a small proportion of the platelets proceed beyond the initial contact phase. The argument is based
on a number of observations. Zilla et al.

(77) found that
platelet release reaction products, such as α-granule constituents and thromboxane, increase progressively during
the course of bypass, suggesting that platelets are undergoing a lytic process throughout the period of perfusion. Whatever the case, all studies do agree that platelet functions are abnormal during the period of extracorporeal
circulation. Coagulation System
Activation of the coagulation cascade can be by either
intrinsic or extrinsic pathways, each of which consists of
a series of enzymes (Fig. 3). The intrinsic pathway begins
with the activation of factor XII upon contact of blood
with collagen in the damaged vascular wall, or exposure
to an artiﬁcial surface, and ends with the formation of
ﬁbrin through a cascade including activated factors XI,
IX, X, and thrombin. The extrinsic pathway is initiated by
exposure of blood to nonvascular tissue cells that express
a protein called tissue factor, which binds to factor VII and
activates it. This in turn activates factor X. Once factor Xa
is generated, the remainder of the cascade is similar to the
intrinsic pathway. With the activation of the coagulation cascade, the ﬁb-
rinolytic system is coactivated, which limits the amount of
ﬁbrin clot formed, and localizes clot formation to the site
of injury. CPB results in the activation of both clotting and
ﬁbrinolysis pathways. The process not only leads to ﬁbrin
formation and platelet activation, but also results in the
activation of vascular endothelium. Thrombin-mediated
endothelial cell activation elicits increased leukocyte adhesion due to the expression of the selectin family. In
addition, the factor VIIa-tissue factor complex and factor
Xa have been shown to activate cells through protease
activated receptors and this, in turn, generates cellular responses similar to those mediated by thrombin activation
of protease activated receptor-1 (78,79). CPB results in
increased ﬁbrinolytic activity caused by elevated levels of
factor XIIa and kallikrein, and has been linked to increased
postoperative bleeding time, blood loss, and reduction in
platelet adhesion and aggregation capabilities due to redistribution of glycoprotein Ib, and IIb/IIIa receptors (80,81). Coagulation cascade

Humoral Components of Blood
Kirklin and McGrifﬁn (3) initially hypothesized that
many of the deleterious effects of CPB were secondary
to the exposure of blood to nonendothelial surfaces
in the bypass circuit, which initiate a ‘‘whole body
inﬂammatory response.’’ He noted that this response was
characterized by activation of coagulation, the kallikrein
system, ﬁbrinolysis, and complement (3,13,82). We now
recognize the importance of cytokines (83) and the
combined effects of this humoral cascading in the
activation of endothelial cells and neutrophil adhesion. Inﬂammatory Cascades
The principal event is the activation of factor XII
(Hageman factor) to factor XIIa, which stimulates a
number of inﬂammatory systems (Fig. 3). After surface
contact, factor XII undergoes a conformational change
and becomes attached to a HMWK, which is one of a
class of proteins involved in the early stages of intrinsic
pathway activation and is a precursor of bradykinin. This complex attaches itself to the foreign surface (e.g.,
the CPB circuit) and, after limited proteolysis, releases
kallikrein, bradykinin, and also factor XIIa. This active
proteolytic factor can initiate the intrinsic coagulation cascade by exerting direct effects on factor XI, which binds to
the foreign surface and can also induce activation of factor VII, thereby further augmenting the intrinsic cascade
of coagulation. Factor XIIa is also involved in a positive
feedback system involving kallikrein. Factor XIIa releases
kallikrein from prekallikrein, and the former is, in turn,
able to act on factor XII to produce factor XIIa (84). Kallikrein can further activate neutrophils and, in so
doing, can produce further activation of inﬂammatory
cascades by producing oxygen-free radicals and proteolytic enzymes. Furthermore, kallikrein and bradykinin
can stimulate the ﬁbrinolytic system. Kallikrein stimulates plasmin production by its action on prourokinase
and bradykinin by releasing tissue-type plasminogen activator from the endothelium. Complement System
One of the most important immunologic mechanisms involved in the inﬂammatory process is the complement system (C′). It consists of more than 30 proteins that serve both
as an effector arm of the immune response and as a primitive recognition system capable of self-/non–self discrimination (85). Its functions include mediating inﬂammation,
opsonizationofantigenicparticles,andcausingmembrane
damage to pathogens. The complement components interact with each other so that the products of one reaction
form the enzyme for the next.

Therefore, a small initial
stimulus can trigger a cascade of activity with consequent
biologic activation and ampliﬁcation. The importance of
the complement system is seen in the fact that 5% to 10%
of serum proteins are complement components. There are three different pathways of complement
system activation (Fig. 4) (classical, lectin, alternative)
leading to a common terminal sequence. Each pathway
consists of a series of preformed, inactive proteins
that, upon activation, activate the next protein in the
pathway. This results in massive ampliﬁcation of the initial
activating event and to a cascade of different members
being activated; the primary trigger, therefore, leads to
the production of a large number of different effector
functions. Such an ampliﬁcation system needs tight
control, and so it is no surprise that nearly half the proteins
in the complement system are regulatory molecules. The classical and the alternative pathways both culminate in the production of C′3 convertase molecules, which
cleave the central component of the complement system,
C′3, into the active C′3a and C′3b fragments. The classical pathway, which is probably the least important to the
present discussion, is initiated by the binding of antibodies
to target antigens on an appropriate surface. The clustered
Fc regions of the antibodies are recognized by the ﬁrst
component of the classical pathway, C′1, thereby initiating the cascade of activation leading to the production of
the classical pathway C′3 convertase, C4b2a (Fig. 4). The
alternative pathway, which is the most primitive part of the
system, operates by a feedback loop in which the C′3b component interacts with factor B (and subsequent activation
of factor B by factor D) to generate the alternative pathway
C′3 convertase, C′3bBb (Fig. 4). Therefore, C′3 acts as both
a substrate and a component of the alternative pathway. The original C′3b that initiates the alternative pathway can
be generated either as a product of the classical pathway
(in which case the alternative pathway acts as an ampli-
ﬁcation loop for complement activation) or through the
spontaneous activation of C′3 that occurs at a low level on
a continuous basis. This ‘‘tickover’’ of C′3 activation means
that the complement system is continually being triggered
and, to prevent the consequent activation of the whole
cascade, it is necessary for cells to express regulatory
proteins that inactivate the alternative pathway C′3 convertase.

This system provides the complement cascade with
its primitive self-/non–self recognition system in which
surfaces (e.g., those of viruses and bacteria) that lack the
necessary regulatory components are ‘‘recognized’’ by the
alternative pathway, leading to the activation of the complement cascade and generation of inﬂammatory effector
mechanisms, as discussed in the subsequent text. The lectin pathway is homologous to the classical
pathway, but with the opsonin, mannan-binding lectin
(MBL), and ﬁcolins, instead of C′1q. This pathway is
activated by binding MBL to the pathogen surface, which
activates the MBL-associated serine proteases, and then
splits C′4 and C′2 into C′4b and C′2b, which bind together
to form C′3-convertase, as in the classical pathway.

The ﬁnal pathway of the complement system is the lytic
or terminal pathway. This pathway is initiated by C′3b,
produced by either the classical or alternative pathway C′3
convertase. C′3b activates C′5 to generate C′5a, a soluble
molecule, and C′5b, which is bound to the cell surface. This
leads to the subsequent binding to the surface of C′6, C′7,
and C′8 and the polymerization of C′9 to form the MAC,
which is able to create a pore through the membrane that
can result in target cell lysis. The MAC therefore forms a
transmembrane channel that allows the inﬂux of ions and
water into the cell, so that it becomes unable to maintain
osmotic and chemical equilibrium (78,86). There are a number of effects of activation of the
complement system. First, a number of proteins, most
notably the anaphylatoxins, C′3a, C′4a, and C′5a, are
produced. These molecules act through receptors on mast
cells and basophils, leading to their degranulation and
the release of a wide range of inﬂammatory mediators
(including histamine). They also act directly on smooth
muscle and endothelium, leading to muscle contraction
and an increase in vascular permeability. In addition,
C′5a acts as a chemotactic and activating agent for
neutrophils and other myeloid cells, leading to both their
recruitment and release of lysosomal enzymes, reactive
oxygen species, and other inﬂammatory mediators (87). In addition to the production of soluble molecules,
a number of components bind to surfaces after activation, including the MAC, whose role has already been
mentioned. Also, there are receptors for C′4b and, more
importantly, C′3b and its breakdown products. These are
involved in the opsonization of complement-coated particles and the clearance of immune complexes.

Activation of the complement system is observed during
or shortly after CPB, mainly through the alternative
pathway, and is induced by blood contact with the
nonphysiologic surface, and later by ischemia reperfusion. Protamine administration and the subsequent formation
of heparin–protamine complexes can further activate
the complement through the classical pathway. This,
in turn, mediates cellular damage, endothelial cell and
leukocyte activation, histamine release, increased vascular
permeability, and generalized inﬂammatory response (16). Further Contributions to Systemic
Inﬂammatory Response after Bypass
In addition to the inﬂammatory interactions that result from the bypass circuit, cardiogenic shock and
endotoxemia may further compound the response (88). Cardiogenic shock can further contribute to SIRAB, and

15. Immune System and Inﬂammatory Responses to Cardiopulmonary Bypass
329
prolonged nonpulsatile perfusion or periods of circulatory
arrest can also lead to diffuse end-organ ischemia (89). The
end-organ hypoxic insult likely causes endothelial cells,
circulating monocytes, and tissue-ﬁxed macrophages to
release cytokines and oxygen-derived free radicals that
drive this response. Once the patient is resuscitated from
shock and after hypoxic end-organs are reperfused, a form
of systemic ischemic-reperfusion injury results (88). Another form of inﬂammatory activation that results
from extracorporeal circulation and episodes of systemic
ischemia-reperfusion is endotoxemia. Endotoxin is frequently detected in high concentrations in the systemic
circulation after CPB (90). Endotoxin is a potent stimulant
of both complement and of endothelial cell activation, resulting in the surface upregulation of adhesion molecules
and tissue factor (91). Endotoxin is a potent agonist of
macrophage TNF release, which may explain why concentrations of this cytokine are increased in some patients
after CPB. Although the precise mechanism of endotoxemia after CPB is unclear, this may derive from a
translocation of bacteria from the gut, resulting from the
systemic stress of CPB and splanchnic ischemia (explained
later) coupled with impaired Kupffer cell function (92). The result is a transient endotoxemia that contributes to
the overall state of systemic inﬂammation after CPB. Endotoxin is also relevant in considering the ‘‘hyperdynamic circulation’’ and the associated profound fall in
systemic vascular resistance, which is sometimes seen after CPB (11). This condition is very similar to the early
phases of sepsis or endotoxemia (93). Until recently, it was
thought that endotoxin exerted its myocardial depressant
effects by reducing the response to adrenergic stimulation
by desensitization of the B-1 receptor (94). Recent data
indicate that G proteins (guanine nucleotide binding proteins) may, in fact, be the mediators of endotoxin-induced
defects in inotropic regulation (94). IMMUNE RESPONSE AFTER
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
The cellular and humoral constituents of the adaptive
immune system undergo changes in both function and
number after CPB. The concern is that postoperative
morbidity and mortality related to infection are partially
due to a loss of T and B cells and immunoglobulin
consumption resulting from CPB. This section examines
the effect of CPB on adaptive immunity and, speciﬁcally,
T-cell function. Immunodeﬁciency
and Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Numerous studies have demonstrated that a depression
of the acquired immune response occurs after surgical
procedures (95).

The degree of immunosuppression is
directly related to the magnitude and duration of the
surgical procedure and to the volume of transfused
blood (96). Therefore, one would expect that cardiac
surgeries would be highly immunosuppressive. The clinical prevalence of infections after cardiac
surgery indicates that duration of CPB is signiﬁcantly
correlated to the incidence of infections (97). The risk
factors for the development of infections identiﬁed in
general surgical patients are also applicable to those
undergoing cardiac surgery (98).The result of CPB is
a depression in immunologic reactivity, which makes
patients susceptible to perioperative infections, with the
development of septic shock as a possible, and frequently
fatal, result (99). In this study, whether sepsis was the
primary factor initiating the multisystem organ failure or
was the result of endotoxin and bacterial translocation
produced by a primary circulatory abnormality could
not be determined. With the advent of interventional
catheterization laboratory techniques and better medical
management of patients with coronary artery disease,
older and sicker patients are being referred for surgery. These patients comprise a group that is at higher risk for
the development of infections in the postoperative period. Of additional concern is the fact that any depression in the
acquired immune response may be detrimental, because
it could increase the susceptibility of patients undergoing
cardiac surgery (many of whom have prosthetic material
in the vascular system) to endocarditis. Under normal conditions, relatively low levels of
immunoglobulins and complement are sufﬁcient for
adequate opsonization of bacteria (100). However, if the
load of infectious microorganisms increases, as may occur
in patients undergoing open-heart surgical procedures,
then an imbalance may develop in the homeostasis of the
host defense. The quantitative and qualitative exhaustion
of humoral and cell-mediated immune mechanisms may
have an adverse effect on clinical outcome when an
additional injury occurs to a patient with a downregulated
immune system in the early postoperative period. It is,
therefore, not surprising that opportunistic pathogens are
frequently found in patients who have undergone cardiac
surgery and experiencing one or more perioperative
complications, for example, renal failure or low cardiac
output. This patient group is likely to develop sepsisrelated multisystem organ failure that can account for a
high proportion of perioperative fatalities (101). Humoral Immunity
In patients undergoing CPB, serum levels of immunoglobulins and complement are markedly changed (10,102,103).

in vitro (104). Leukocyte counts fall with the onset of
CPB. The sequestration of leukocytes in tissue is increased after their activation by anaphylatoxins C′3a and
C′5a. After CPB, the chemotactic ability of granulocytes is
impaired (105), which may also contribute to a higher susceptibility to bacterial infections. Other studies show that
not only the phagocytic function but also the metabolic
function of leukocytes is impaired after CPB (106). It is unclear what happens to B-cell numbers after CPB. Some investigators report no change (9) whereas others
demonstrated a drop (107,108). Roth et al. (109) reported
that relative levels (percentage) of B cells increase after
CPB, with no signiﬁcant increase in absolute numbers,
which can all be related to the hemodilution status
and immunosuppressive effect of trauma rather than of
immunologic origin (110). The secretion of IgG, IgM,
and IgA by B cells in response to pokeweed mitogen
is diminished after CPB (109). Recent work by Lante
et al. (111) showed that IgE levels did not change after CPB
until day 3; in contrast, both IgG, and IgM levels decreased
signiﬁcantly on day 1 and, although IgM returned to
baseline on day 5, IgG levels remained low. This was
associated with a reduction in the B-cell count on day 1
and a return to baseline by day 3. The bacteriocidal activity
of serum is depressed after CPB. Complement is consumed
and all components of humoral immunity are decreased as
a consequence of the hemodilution caused by bypass (112). Exposure of immune proteins to contact with gaseous
and foreign surfaces results in denaturation. Surface depolarizing forces result in the disruption of the sulfhydryl and
hydrogen bonds that stabilize the secondary and tertiary
structure of the protein molecules. The resulting unfolding of globular protein molecules may expose otherwise
masked chemical groups and create a randomly coiled
molecule. The macromolecules so formed then tend to
ﬂocculate. These changes in plasma proteins may also
lead to coalescence of serum lipids and an increase in
plasma viscosity because of protein denaturation (103). Natural Killer Cells
Natural killer cells are a heterogeneous subpopulation of
lymphoid cells that are not T or B lymphocytes. Natural
killer cells have been shown to produce cytotoxic responses in virus-infected cells and transformed target cells
(e.g., tumor cells).

Decreases in both number and function
of natural killer cells have been shown after CPB (113,114). Reticuloendothelial System
The reticuloendothelial system is made up of tissue macrophages in the spleen, lymph nodes, lung, and liver. These
cells are initially derived from blood-borne monocytes. The
normal function of the reticuloendothelial system includes
the clearing of bacteria, endotoxins, platelets, denatured
proteins, chylomicrons, plasma hemoglobin, thrombin,
ﬁbrin, ﬁbrin degradation products, thromboplastin, and
plasminogen activator from the circulating blood. The function of the reticuloendothelial system has been
shown to be depressed after CPB, which can be attributed
to the increased amount of microparticles generated by
CPB (115). T Cells
T cells are lymphocytes that develop in the thymus. This
organ is seeded by lymphocytic stem cells from the bone
marrow during embryonic development. Following T-cell
development, mature na¨ıve T cells leave the thymus and
begin to spread throughout the body. These cells then
develop their T-cell antigen receptors and differentiate
into the two major peripheral T-cell subsets, one of which
expresses the CD4+ marker (helper cells) and the other
CD8+ (cytotoxic cells). Proliferating T helper cells can
differentiate into two major subtypes on the basis of the
speciﬁc cytokines they produce, known as TH1 and TH2. T helper cells play a central role in the initiation and
regulation of the acquired immune response. T helper cells recognize antigen presented on the
surface of antigen-presenting cells in association with
class II molecules encoded by the major histocompatibility
complex (MHC). T-cell activation requires other speciﬁc
costimulatory signals generated by the antigen-presenting
cell. Cytotoxic T cells recognize antigen presented on the
surface of antigen-presenting cells in association with
class I molecules encoded by the MHC. T helper cells provide ‘‘help’’ in the form of lymphokine
secretion. Such lymphokines help B cells to divide, differentiate, and produce antibodies. The lymphokines are
also required for the development of leukocyte lines from
hematopoietic stem cells and development of cytotoxic
T cells. They also cause activation of macrophages, allowing them to destroy the pathogens they have taken up. Cytotoxic T cells are capable of destroying virus-infected
target cells or allogeneic (transplanted) cells. Morphologic Correlation
Scanning electron microscopy of T cells after CPB
shows profound alterations to the plasma membrane of
the T cells. There are decreased numbers of microvilli
and a decrease in the folded aspect of the lymphocyte
surface.

Furthermore, after CPB, the membrane does not
accommodate monoclonal microbeads. Quality and Quantity
Phenotypic changes induced by CPB have been investigated using standard commercially available leukocytelabeling
monoclonal
antibodies
together
with
