35◦C to 60 mL/kg/min at 20◦C. It is uncertain what
effect the decreased systemic pump ﬂow rate had on
the overall perfusion pressure (16). Because systemic
blood ﬂow was not maintained throughout the study,
it is also impossible to differentiate whether the observed
decrease of splanchnic regional blood ﬂow was due to
comparable decreases in systemic blood ﬂow or to changes
in temperature. These data indicate that neither liver
nor pancreatic blood ﬂow is effectively autoregulated
during hypothermic CPB. Because a control group (similar
surgery without CPB) was not included in the study, it is
impossible to conclude whether any baseline splanchnic
autoregulation exists through hypothermia or whether
this is lost secondary to CPB. Effect of Vasoactive Drugs
Maintenance of adequate splanchnic oxygenation is crucial for the prevention of sepsis and multiorgan failure,
probably secondary to increased intestinal permeability (17,18). Dopamine (DA) receptors in the gut mediate
splanchnic vasodilation, and some researchers have evaluated DA to improve splanchnic circulation. DA is still commonly used during cardiac surgery, both as an inotrope
and to preserve renal function, although the latter function is controversial. DA has been shown in dogs, pigs, and
humans to augment nonrenal splanchnic circulation as
well (19–21). In anesthetized dogs, a DA bolus (12.8 µg/kg)
directly vasodilated the superior and inferior mesenteric
arteries, left gastric artery, and superior pancreatoduodenal artery (19). In contrast, DA failed to vasodilate either
the canine hepatic or renal arteries. The lack of response
in the hepatic artery might be explained by a paucity or
absence of dopaminergic receptors in the hepatic arterial
bed (19). However, a similar lack of response in the renal
artery occurred despite a well-documented abundance of
dopaminergic receptors in the canine renal artery (and
an observed 50% increase in urine ﬂow) (19). In pigs, DA
increased superior mesenteric arterial ﬂow and, although
it did not alter hepatic arterial ﬂow, increased portal vein
ﬂow such that total hepatic ﬂow was augmented (21). In
one study of patients who had cardiac surgery, DA infusion, which was titrated to increase cardiac output by
25% above baseline, increased splanchnic O2 consumption despite no changes in systemic O2 consumption; this
was consistent with a selective positive effect on splanchnic energy metabolism associated with the stimulation of
cardiac output (22).

Overall, there is no clear effect of
DA on splanchnic circulation, with some reports of improved splanchnic blood ﬂow (23–28), some having no
effects (29,30), and some having decreased ﬂows (31–34). DA’s inﬂuence on splanchnic circulation has been evaluated in patients undergoing epidural anesthesia. Lundberg et al. (20) used electromagnetic ﬂow probes to directly
assess splanchnic blood ﬂow in nine patients undergoing
abdominal aortic aneurism repair. Epidural anesthesia
moderately decreased both splanchnic and systemic perfusion and arterial pressure, secondary to vasodilation. DA (4 µg/kg/min), although it had no apparent effect
on systemic or superior mesenteric artery hemodynamics in the absence of epidural anesthesia, reversed the
impairment of splanchnic perfusion secondary to epidural anesthesia (20). Equally important, the increase in
lactate production, presumably caused by ischemic intestine in one patient undergoing epidural anesthesia, was
reversed by DA infusion. DA eliminated the difference
between intestinal and systemic lactate production, indicating that the effect was speciﬁc for preservation of
splanchnic perfusion (20). Although these studies were
performed during an abdominal rather than a thoracic
procedure, and were performed on subjects not undergoing CPB, they underscore the insensitivity of systemic
markers to detect regional abnormalities in the splanchnic tissues, and that the splanchnic circulation can be
improved with low-dose DA during surgical procedures. Dobutamine is an adrenergic β1 and (to a lesser extent)
β2 receptor agonist, with no dopaminergic receptor activity. In patients under septic shock, dobutamine slightly
decreased hepatosplanchnic blood ﬂow (35). Hepatosplanchnic O2 consumption and release of tumor necrosis
factor-α were increased, but MEGX clearance, which is
an assessment of liver function, remained unchanged (35). Other studies have shown that dobutamine increases cardiac index, in large part by increasing heart rate, and
thereby increasing hepatosplanchnic blood ﬂow, without
changing the distribution of total ﬂow or altering the
splanchnic metabolic demands (36,37). Practical limitations for both DA and dobutamine
have led to development of the synthetic dopaminergic
drugs, fenoldopam and dopexamine, to improve splanchnic blood ﬂow. Fenoldopam is a speciﬁc DA-1 receptor
agonist. When administered to hypovolemic patients,
fenoldopam restored portal vein blood ﬂow to near baseline, maintained fractional splanchnic blood ﬂow, and
attenuated the accumulation of CO2 in ileal mucosa, an
indicator of improving tissue acidosis (38,39).

In patients
with septic shock and being treated with a combination
of norepinephrine and dobutamine, low-dose fenoldopam
infusion improved gastric mucosal perfusion as indexed
by intramucosal pH using gastric tonometry (18,40). Dopexamine is a β2 adrenergic receptor agonist that also
stimulates peripheral DA-1 and prejunctional DA-2 receptors, which, overall, produces systemic vasodilation (41). Reports on dopexamine are mixed, including both positive and negative effects on splanchnic blood ﬂow and
oxygenation (42–46). Dopexamine, which also markedly
increases heart rate, is not available in the United States. In summary, various inotropes and DA receptor agonists have different inﬂuences on splanchnic perfusion. DA increases splanchnic blood ﬂow in sepsis, but not

355
after CPB, and speciﬁc regional organ effects are varied. Dobutamine increases splanchnic perfusion only through
its positive chronotropic and inotropic actions on the heart
rather than any apparent splanchnic vascular effect, and
tachycardia may limit its usefulness in the patient undergoing cardiac surgery. Fenoldopam, which is currently the
most promising drug in this category, selectively vasodilates splanchnic vessels and improves microcirculation to
the dependent GI mucosa. Dopexamine increases splanchnic blood ﬂow in CPB, and can increase intracellular pH in
sepsis, but also induces tachycardia. Finally, preliminary
data indicates that low-dose prostacyclin may decrease
systemic O2 consumption and splanchnic O2 extraction
during CPB, although the mechanism and ultimate outcome effects are still unknown (47). Problems with Clinical Monitoring
Animal studies over the past 50 years indicate that
gross splanchnic circulation is adequately maintained
during CPB, but the methods utilized have assessed
neither microcirculatory adequacy nor the preservation of
cellular viability and physiologic function. Furthermore,
the young adult primate may not be an adequate model
for circulatory efﬁcacy in the elderly humans with diffuse
atherosclerotic disease, who are a growing segment of
patients undergoing CPB. One of the persistent difﬁculties
in CPB has been the inability to clinically monitor
in real time the integrity of perfusion and physiologic
function of splanchnic organs. Attempts have been made
to assess hepatic perfusion by uptake of indicator dye
such as bromsulphalein (BSP), which is speciﬁcally taken
up by hepatocytes (48), or continuous hepatic vein O2
saturation monitoring (49), but these have not been
integrated into the routine clinical care during cardiac
surgery with CPB. Reluctance to adopt routine dye
uptake or hepatic vein oximetry during CPB has been
based on the uncertainty of how tightly dye uptake or
O2 consumption is coupled to perfusion adequacy in
the anesthetized patient (50). A second problem with
hepatic vein catheterization is that it must be performed
with ﬂuoroscopic guidance, which involves time and
expense, with no proven record of efﬁcacy, limiting its
attractiveness to the clinician (49). A third splanchnic
monitoring technique, which has mostly been utilized in
the postoperative setting, is continuous measurement of
GI pH by tonometry (51–53). The limitation of tonometry
is that it remains technically difﬁcult to perform.

All three
of these potential methods to assess visceral perfusion
adequacy during CPB, despite future promise, remain
relatively obscure and scarcely utilized, pending further
research and/or technical development. Near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) has recently entered
the clinical arena for monitoring (Fig. 1). It is used to
monitor tissue O2 saturation in cerebral and in mixed

somatic tissues, using a noninvasive optical technique. For the cerebral reading, a pad with a paired emitter and
detector is attached to the forehead to monitor appropriate
wavelengths for saturated (735 nm) and desaturated
(810 nm) hemoglobin (54). A computerized algorithm,
speciﬁc for adult or pediatric patients, interprets the
data into a number that represents cerebral venous O2
saturation at a particular depth, correcting for values
obtained for skin and skull perfusion. Unlike pulse
oximetry, which reads a pulsatile signal and subtracts
out venous noise, NIRS reads continuously and is more
representative of regional cerebral mixed venous O2
saturation. Use of cerebral NIRS is supported by clinical
evidence suggesting a correlation between low cerebral
tissue O2 saturation index (rSO2i) and adverse neurologic
outcome (55). It has stimulated other studies looking at
alternative potential uses. Addressing the effects of CPB
on muscle perfusion, Soller et al. (56) compared muscle
PO2 and pH obtained from NIRS with invasive muscle
PO2 and pH, both measured at the thenar eminence from
human patients undergoing CPB. NIRS muscle pH and
PO2 were sensitive to changes in tissue perfusion during
CPB (56). Early investigations in burn patients are also
promising, showing the diagnostic value when used in
conjunction with other pertinent patient information. NIRS has been useful in pigs to help differentiate
superﬁcial, intermediate partial thickness, deep partial
thickness, and full thickness burns (57). In pediatric
cardiac patients, NIRS technology has been evaluated as
a monitor of ﬂank muscle and renal tissue bed perfusion,
with sensors applied to the ﬂank of neonates (Fig. 1). Hoffman et al. used, in the setting of deep hypothermic
circulatory arrest, the difference between regional rSO2i

of brain and somatic tissues to diagnose circulatory shock
and onset of anaerobic metabolism in visceral tissues (58). During adequate systemic tissue O2 delivery, somatic
rSO2i is 10% to 20% higher than brain rSO2i. When
systemic perfusion is decreased, blood ﬂow to the brain,
within limits, is protected by cerebral autoregulation, and
ﬂow is diverted from peripheral tissues. A reduction of
the tissue rSO2i difference to less than 10% indicates
desaturation of somatic tissues, most likely muscle, but
possibly also splanchnic, as these tissues become ischemic
and commence anaerobic metabolism (58,59). Fortune
demonstrated, using probes placed on the abdomen of
neonates, that NIRS had a 90% sensitivity to predict
surgical intestinal ischemia when used in conjunction
with cerebral NIRS (60). Soller et al. also demonstrated the
feasibility of measuring bowel, liver, and muscle pH using
NIRS in the setting of regional ischemia and hemorrhagic
shock in animal models (61,62). Naulaers correlated liver
tissue oxygenation index, transcutaneously measured with
spatially resolved spectroscopy (a variant of NIRS), with
mixed venous O2 saturation and blood ﬂow in different
parts of the splanchnic circulation in newborn piglets (63). To summarize, NIRS holds some promise as a monitor
for adequacy of splanchnic perfusion, especially in young
children. However the technology is still very new and
largely untried, for this indication, in the cardiac surgery
population. LIVER FUNCTION
AND CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
The liver serves many different functions and participates
in the following: (a) Cori cycle activity, with glucose
production and lactate clearance; (b) synthesis of plasma
proteins, such as albumin, coagulation factors, and
plasma cholinesterase; (c) immune function and clearance
of intravascular debris by Kupffer cells; and (d) drug
metabolism, principally by the cytochrome P-450 system. Because of the distinct and multiple functions of the liver,
it is difﬁcult to assess global liver function during or after
CPB with a single method. Clinical markers of presumed
hepatocellular damage have been selected on the basis of
enzyme leak from injured tissues and erroneously called
liver function tests, because their relation to the preserved
liver function remains unclear. The hepatic arterial buffer
response is a dynamic interaction between hepatic arterial
and portal venous blood ﬂow, helping to maintain total
hepatic blood ﬂow in the face of decreased portal blood
ﬂow (64). Substrate Metabolism by the Liver
Waldhausen et al.

(65) studied the relation between hepatic blood ﬂow and hepatic O2 consumption in dogs
undergoing normothermic CPB. They found that hepatic
O2 consumption is preserved at pump ﬂow rates as low
as 2.2 L/m2/ min. Below this rate of perfusion, which
corresponded to a hepatic blood ﬂow of approximately
110 mL/100 g liver/min, hepatic O2 consumption (and
blood ﬂow) was markedly curtailed (65). These authors
did not assess the consequent hepatocellular damage as a
result of liver hypoperfusion during CPB. It is unclear how
systemic ﬂow, liver perfusion, and hepatic O2 consumption
relate under hypothermic conditions. A major role of the liver is to regulate plasma glucose
concentration by varying its rate of glucose production. Normally, the liver increases glucose production when
challenged with glucagon. Kuntschen et al. (66) demonstrated that, during CPB in humans, the hyperglycemic
response to exogenous glucagon is impaired. These authors speculated that the failure of glucagon to provoke
hyperglycemia occurs secondary to compromised hepatic
glucose output, but they did not actually measure glucose
production by isotope dilution either across the liver or
at the whole-body level. It is possible, alternatively, that
glucose production during CPB is already maximally increased secondary to high circulating concentrations of
cortisol and catecholamines (67). In the absence of direct
assessment, it is unclear if hepatic glucose production is
abnormal during CPB, or to what extent the hepatic glucose output is due to gluconeogenesis versus glycogenolysis. Glycogenolysis is stimulated by catecholamines, even
in the absence of exogenous glucagon stimulation (67). General anesthesia with pentobarbital decreases hepatic
glucose production by 30% in rats (68). In the absence
of direct measures, the effect of CPB on the dynamics of
hepatic glucose production remains unknown. Hyperlactatemia after cardiac surgery is most often
due to excess lactate production (69,70). Decreased lactate
clearance is less likely, and necessarily involves severe liver
failure. Maillet et al. prospectively examined 325 patients
who had undergone cardiac surgery with normothermic
CPB and found that 20% exhibited a plasma lactate
concentration greater than 3 mM on admission to the
intensive care unit (ICU). Not only was hyperlactatemia
common but it also served as a risk marker for higher
postoperative ICU morbidity and mortality rates (71). Anderson et al. demonstrated that hepatic lactate removal
is maintained during normothermic CPB in dogs, despite
a rising plasma concentration, a ﬁnding consistent with
increased peripheral lactate production (48).

However,
the CPB conditions used by Anderson et al. differed from
common clinical practice in that it maintained normothermia and a high mean arterial pressure (75–110 mm Hg)
with high pump ﬂow (50–60 mL/kg/min). Hepatic lactate
clearance and lactate production rates remain to be tested
under hypothermic, low-ﬂow conditions. Glucose–lactate
cycling (the Cori cycle) dynamics during CPB have not
been reported, although such measurements could be a

17. Splanchnic Visceral, Metabolic, and Glucoregulatory Effects of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
357
potential probe to assess hepatic function during and after
this unusual physiologic circumstance. Protein Synthetic Functions
An iatrogenic heparin-induced coagulopathy immediately
before onset of CPB is currently a clinical standard. Commencement of CPB leads to a 30% to 40% dilutional decrease in plasma concentrations of all coagulation factors
except factors VIII and XI (72). Titrated administration
of protamine at the end of CPB is aimed to reverse the
heparin-induced component of coagulopathy. Decreased
plasma concentration of most coagulation factors, however, persists into the early postoperative period (72). The decrease in procoagulant factor concentrations is
paralleled by a comparable decrease in plasma concentrations of the anticoagulant factors, antithrombin and
plasminogen (72). In the postoperative study by Wolk
et al., a large interindividual variability in plasma concentration of ﬁbrinogen prevented the more than 50%
average reduction compared with the preoperative value
from achieving statistical signiﬁcance (72). Assuming that
the decreased plasma ﬁbrinogen concentration is real, the
extent to which this reﬂects increased consumption versus decreased hepatic synthesis in the affected patients is
unknown. An indirect marker for ﬁbrinogen consumption
is plasma concentration of ﬁbrin degradation products,
including D-dimer. Alternatively, hepatic synthesis of ﬁb-
rinogen can be measured directly to determine its role in
the hypoﬁbrinogenemia of the postoperative patient after
cardiac surgery (73,74). It would be interesting to compare
plasma ﬁbrinogen synthesis with more conventional measures of hepatocellular injury, the ‘‘liver function tests.’’
Performed simultaneously, they could elucidate the extent to which liver injury and functional impairment
contribute to decreased coagulation factor levels following CPB. Plasma ﬁbronectin is a glycoprotein that facilitates
phagocytic clearance of debris and microorganisms from
the vascular compartment. Although ﬁbronectin can be
synthesized by many tissues in vitro, the liver is the
principal source of plasma ﬁbronectin in vivo (75). Plasma
ﬁbronectin concentration is consistently decreased in
patients during and after CPB, but the etiology remains
uncertain (76–81). Potential mechanisms responsible for
this decrease involve ‘‘losses’’ through hemodilution, blood
loss, and redistribution into extravascular ﬂuids (76). Fibronectin is also consumed as it binds to heparin,
ﬁbrin, and cellular debris to facilitate phagocytosis (76). Another mechanism that could contribute to a post-CPB
plasma ﬁbronectin deﬁciency is intravascular proteolysis
by abnormally high levels of serum proteases (82). The
inﬂuence of hypothermic CPB on ﬁbronectin synthesis
is unknown.

Fibronectin has a very rapid turnover rate
in healthy humans, with a fractional synthetic rate of
approximately 30%/d (73,74). Further, its synthesis is
exquisitely sensitive to altered physiologic states such
as trauma (74), exercise (73), and starvation (83). The
mechanism by which normal plasma ﬁbronectin levels
are restored in the hours after separation from bypass is
equally complex. Extravascular stores of ﬁbronectin can
be remobilized into the vascular space (76), and urinary
diuresis reverses the effects of hemodilution. Studies
examining hepatic ﬁbronectin synthesis following CPB
are yet to be performed. Plasma cholinesterase levels are
also decreased during CPB, which is at least partially
due to hemodilution (84). Although the role of hepatic
synthesis was not tested directly, recovery of normal
plasma cholinesterase levels over the course of the ﬁrst 2
postoperative days is more consistent with concentration
secondary to ﬂuid diuresis from the vascular compartment
than hepatic biosynthesis of the enzyme, because synthesis
of plasma cholinesterase is slow, in contrast to that of
ﬁbronectin (84,85). The conclusion to be drawn from the
currently available data in adults is that, although there
may be a mild and temporary impairment of plasma
protein synthesis associated with hypothermic CPB, it
does not appear to have clinical signiﬁcance. It also
appears to be completely corrected, at least by indirect
assessment, by the ﬁrst postoperative day. Further work
is necessary to determine if recovery of normal levels of
plasma proteins occurs secondary to accelerated hepatic
synthesis or to other mechanism(s). The kinetics of plasma proteins in pediatric patients
are different from those in adults, because of variable
hepatic developmental stages in the pediatric population. The incidence of a pre-existing coagulopathy is more
common among pediatric patients than in adults undergoing cardiac surgery, and may complicate postoperative
hemostasis. Plasma concentrations of coagulation factors are decreased in the newborn, relative to those in
adults, most notably affecting contact factors (XII, XI,
prekallikrein, and high molecular weight kininogen) and
vitamin K–dependent factors (II, VII, IX, and X) (86). The newborn also exhibits decreased plasma concentrations of the coagulation inhibitors, antithrombin III,
heparin cofactor II, protein C, and protein S (86). It
is unknown how vulnerable the immature liver is to
the effects of CPB, in terms of inhibiting plasma protein synthesis below an already low baseline.

Marginal
preoperative plasma coagulation factor concentrations in
the very young pediatric patients make it difﬁcult to ascribe post-CPB coagulation problems to the effects of CPB
itself. Hepatic Drug Metabolism
The liver metabolizes many of the drugs that are administered to patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Clearance of these drugs could serve as another index of

358
III. Physiology and Pathology
hepatic function during and after CPB (87). Barstow
and Small reviewed a number of clinical liver function tests that assess different pathways of hepatic drug
metabolism (87). These include metabolite formation of
allopurinol, caffeine, lidocaine (MEGX), methacetin, and
aminopyrine (87). Many of these tests could be applied
to the patient undergoing cardiac surgery as probes for
liver function. Hepatic metabolism of fentanyl and midazolam is decreased by hypothermic CPB (88–92). Koren
et al. reported that hypothermic (20◦C) CPB virtually
arrested metabolism of fentanyl in children for up to
2 hours (89). Several groups of investigators have attempted to dissect the effect of hypothermia from that
of CPB. Koska et al. correlated the increased half-life
of fentanyl with a comparable 30% decrease in hepatic
blood ﬂow during normothermic CPB (92). Alternatively,
Koren et al. demonstrated that hypothermia decreased
fentanyl clearance by more than 70% in piglets, without superimposed CPB, concomitant with a 42% decrease
in hepatic blood ﬂow (89). Unlike fentanyl, metabolism
of theophylline, a low-extraction drug, is relatively unaffected by hypothermia (93). Two possible explanations
are that high hepatic-extraction drugs such as fentanyl
or sorbitol are more sensitive to hypothermia-induced
changes in hepatic blood ﬂow, or that different hepatic
enzyme systems have different temperature sensitivities. Midazolam clearance is decreased following CPB in both
adults and children (88,90). The role of hypothermia in the
metabolism of midazolam has not been addressed. Data
is also lacking on the duration of impaired hepatic drug
metabolism in the postoperative setting after CPB, under
either normothermic or hypothermic conditions. Not all drug metabolism is impaired after CPB, for
example that of nitroglycerin or lorazepam. Dasta et al. reported that clearance of nitroglycerin increased 20%
during and after CPB, although they could not exclude
the possibility of nonhepatic factors such as adhesion
of nitroglycerin to elements of the bypass circuit or
metabolism by erythrocytes and endothelial cells (94). CPB does not impair clearance of lorazepam, unlike the
related benzodiazepine midazolam (95). It is possible that
impairment of midazolam, but not lorazepam, during
CPB relates to their different mechanisms of hepatic
metabolism. The major pathway for metabolism of
lorazepam is conjugation with glucuronide, a process
relatively resistant to liver disease, whereas midazolam
must ﬁrst be oxidized by hepatic mixed function oxidase
before conjugation.

Identiﬁcation of the particular enzyme
system is important when attempting to evaluate hepatic
function with respect to drug metabolism. Fentanyl is
a good candidate for assessing liver drug metabolism,
because its metabolism is very sensitive to changes
associated with CPB and hypothermia, but other drugs
must be tested to probe different enzyme systems as
well (87). Markers of Hepatocellular Injury
Hepatic blood ﬂow has essentially no effective autoregulation during CPB (16), although hepatic O2 consumption is
maintained at systemic ﬂows as low as 2.2 L/m2/ min (65). There is no currently accepted monitor for on-line assessment of adequate hepatic perfusion. The traditional
methods for determination of adequate liver function, the
‘‘liver function tests,’’ include plasma levels of bilirubin
and enzymes found in high concentration in the liver. However, the time course for appearance of hyperbilirubinemia in relation to a hepatic ischemic insult, although
unknown, is probably delayed. This makes intraoperative assessment of hepatic function difﬁcult. Welbourn
et al. followed plasma enzyme patterns in 22 patients
during and after CPB with ‘‘mild’’ hypothermia (nadir
range, 19◦C–34◦C) (96). These authors reported that,
when corrected for hemodilution, plasma concentrations
of lactic dehydrogenase (LDH), hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (HBD), isocitrate dehydrogenase (ICD), and serum
glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) [now called
aspartate aminotransferase (AST)] all rise during CPB and
remain elevated postoperatively (96). However, the source
of the enzyme leak could not be ascribed to the liver,
and may have been largely due to myocardial damage. Serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT) [now called
alanine aminotransferase (ALT)] and ornithine carbamyl
transferase (a urea cycle enzyme), considered more spe-
ciﬁc markers of liver damage, are not usually elevated
during or after CPB (96,97). Intraoperative serum bilirubin levels have not been reported. A dye uptake technique,
such as BSP or ICG, which are speciﬁcally taken up by
the liver, has been used experimentally to assess the effects of CPB (48). It is difﬁcult, however, to distinguish
between the effects of hepatic hypoperfusion and hepatocellular dysfunction despite ‘‘adequate’’ perfusion using a
dye uptake technique alone. Under normal circumstances,
BSP uptake is a better marker of hepatic perfusion than
ICG, but this has not been veriﬁed under conditions of
hypothermic CPB. Estimation of hepatic blood ﬂow from
bolus ICG clearance correlates poorly with that directly
measured by ﬂowmeter in either healthy volunteers or
subjects with liver disease (50).

Dye uptake methods for assessing either liver perfusion or function must be carefully
validated before they are applied to patients undergoing
CPB. From a purely clinical perspective, there is no evidence that CPB is detrimental to the liver in most patients,
but that does not exclude the need for hepatic monitoring
during cardiac surgery. Liver dysfunction after CPB is often clinically heralded
by the appearance of jaundice (‘‘postpump jaundice’’),
which has an incidence of 10% to 20% (98–100). Postpump
jaundice usually occurs secondary to conjugated (direct)
hyperbilirubinemia (98), consistent with a defect in biliary excretion of bilirubin rather than a more proximal

17. Splanchnic Visceral, Metabolic, and Glucoregulatory Effects of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
359
hepatocellular process. Hyperbilirubinemia is maximal at
postoperative day 2 and resolves in most patients within
the ﬁrst week. In a prospective study of 248 patients,
Collins et al. found that the incidence of postpump jaundice was not associated with preoperative ethanol intake,
intraoperative hypoxia, hypotension, or hypothermia (98). It occurred most frequently in patients undergoing multiple valve procedures (with higher right atrial pressures),
and was associated with higher transfusion requirements
and longer pump times. Hyperbilirubinemia can alternatively be caused by hepatocellular failure to clear a normal
bilirubin challenge or by excessive bilirubin load overwhelming the normal hepatic function. Excessive bilirubin
challenge secondary to massive transfusion or intravascular hemolysis must be included in the differential diagnosis
of patients who develop postpump jaundice and who otherwise do not exhibit any evidence of hepatic injury or
failure. This can be ruled out by a predominance of direct
over indirect bilirubin in the plasma. Long duration of
CPB, in addition to being a risk factor for postpump jaundice, is associated with other markers of hepatocellular
damage, such as high postoperative plasma ICD concentration (96). Postpump jaundice can also occur in patients
undergoing uncomplicated surgeries, raising the question
of how better intraoperative monitoring of hepatic function could reduce its incidence. Jaundice after cardiac
surgery is associated with a 25-fold increase in mortality (98), whereas progression to fulminant hepatic failure
is uniformly fatal (101). Frank hepatic trauma during cardiac surgery has been
reported, involving inadvertent placement of thoracotomy
tubes (102), or manipulation of venous cannulas to
augment venous return drainage and during placement
of right atrial lines (103). Hepatic trauma can rapidly
lead to unexplained hypovolemia and require immediate
abdominal exploration. Hepatic Arterial Buffer Response
The hepatic arterial buffer response is a dynamic interaction between hepatic arterial and portal venous blood
ﬂows to maintain O2 delivery to the liver. The liver receives blood supply from both the hepatic artery (normally
∼25%) and the portal vein (normally ∼75%). Hypoperfusion of the liver through the portal vein leads to
tissue accumulation of adenosine, which in turn induces
vasodilation of the hepatic artery. In a study of hepatosplanchnic blood ﬂow control with modiﬁcations of
underlying perfusion in pigs, Bracht et al.

showed that
blood ﬂow redistribution totally restored hepatic perfusion when mesenteric blood ﬂow is selectively reduced,
whereas redistribution was only partially effective when
cardiac output was reduced and did not occur if all abdominal blood ﬂow was compromised (104). The effect of
CPB on this protective mechanism is unknown. PANCREATIC FUNCTION
AND CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Exocrine and Endocrine Pancreas
The pancreas has two broad functions, which are deﬁned
as ‘‘exocrine’’ and ‘‘endocrine’’ in nature. Exocrine pancreatic function involves synthesis and secretion of digestive
enzymes and other alimentary factors. A key enzyme in
the exocrine pancreas is amylase, which is released as
a proenzyme and activated within the pancreatic duct. Amylase is normally present in low concentration in the
circulation, but pancreatic injury leads to intravascular
leak of amylase, such that increased serum amylase concentration is a marker of pancreatitis. For maximal utility,
pancreatic amylase must be distinguished from its isoenzyme, salivary amylase. The relation between amylase and
creatinine clearance [amylase–creatinine clearance ratio,
(ACCR)] has been advocated to better quantitate pancreatic injury (105). However, this method has been criticized
in the setting of CPB, because CPB-associated alterations
in ACCR may be produced by alterations in renal function rather than pancreatic injury (106). A more speciﬁc
marker of pancreatic injury is plasma concentration of
trypsinogen activation peptide (TAP). There are no good
assessments of pancreatic exocrine function per se in the
acute intra- and postoperative settings. Endocrine pancreatic function involves secretion of insulin (from the β-cell) and glucagon (from the α-cell). Secretion of both insulin and glucagon is suppressed
during hypothermic CPB (66,107–110). Factors that
may play a role in the inhibition of hormone (insulin
and glucagon) are hypothermia and altered perfusion
(66,111). High circulating catecholamine concentration
also speciﬁcally inhibits insulin release (112), which is
not a sign of poor pancreatic function but rather an intact physiologic control mechanism. This contrasts with
glucagon release, which is normally stimulated by catecholamines (113). Recovery of ‘‘appropriate’’ insulin secretion occurs within 1 hour of separation from CPB,
and insulin generally remains at ‘‘normal’’ concentration
postoperatively (109–111,114). In contrast, peak glucagon
levels are delayed until the ﬁrst postoperative day (115). It
is unclear whether the slower response of glucagon levels
vis-`a-vis insulin levels represents a difference in functional
recovery of the α-cell as compared with the β-cell from
the effects of CPB, hypothermia, or general anesthesia.

Markers of Pancreatic Cellular Injury
The pancreas resembles the liver in that it has a high
metabolic rate (116), has no intrinsic autoregulation
of perfusion during CPB (16,117), and it is difﬁcult to
monitor its intraoperative perfusion and function during
and even after CPB. A variable spectrum of pancreatic

360
III. Physiology and Pathology
injury is associated with CPB. Nonpulsatile, hypothermic
CPB is followed by asymptomatic hyperamylasemia in
30% to 70% of patients (118–120). Similarly, an elevation
in ACCR is observed in 31% to 90% of patients undergoing
normothermic CPB (121). Alterations in ACCR, however,
may reﬂect alteration in renal function rather than
pancreatic injury (106). Haas et al. (122) reported that
serum concentration of pancreatic amylase was elevated
in 27%, and pancreatic ribonuclease in 13%, of 30
postoperative patients without clinical pancreatitis. In
the largest series studied to date, Fernandez-del Castillo
et al. prospectively followed up 300 consecutive patients
undergoing CPB and found a 27% incidence of pancreatic
cellular injury, deﬁned as hyperamylasemia accompanied
by a rise in pancreatic isoamylase (30%), lipase (10%),
or both (60%) (120,123,124). Ninety-nine percent of these
patients were completely asymptomatic (120). The incidence of clinical pancreatitis in adults (‘‘postpump pancreatitis’’) is 0.1% to 1% by either prospective
or retrospective analysis (120,122,125). Nonsurviving patients who underwent cardiac surgery more commonly
exhibited pathologic evidence of pancreatitis. In a study
of 209 patients who died within 10 days of cardiac
surgery, Feiner reported that the incidence of pancreatitis was 16% (126), whereas Warshaw and O’Hara
found an 11% incidence in 101 autopsies (127). The
pathology in both series was consistent with intraoperative pancreatic ischemia (126,127). Risk factors for
development of postpump pancreatitis include prolonged
duration of CPB, perioperative hypotension, low postoperative cardiac output, and perioperative administration
of calcium (120,122). It is unclear whether the association
with calcium administration is an independent risk factor
or merely an association, because of the frequent use of
calcium to treat of hypotension. However, pancreatitis has
been reported secondary to hypercalcemia in a variety of
medical conditions not accompanied by hypotension, such
as multiple myeloma (128), hyperparathyroidism (129),
breast cancer (130), iatrogenic calcium overload (131),
and vitamin D intoxication (132). Reber has suggested
that the leak of pancreatic enzymes into the plasma, secondary to calcium exposure, may be caused by increased
permeability of the pancreatic duct (133). Therefore, injudicious use of calcium, rather than appropriate correction
of (measured) hypocalcemia, appears to be a risk factor
for pancreatitis. Hypothermia has been considered as a
potential mechanism of pancreatitis, but studies linking
hypothermia and pancreatitis (134,135) are not controlled
for the preservation of blood ﬂow during hypothermia,
which is much better maintained during CPB.

Pancreatic injury after CPB may be even more common
in the pediatric population than among adults, and the
method of diagnosis may have to be different. Evidence of
pancreatic injury occurs in 4% to 8% of pediatric patients
following CPB (136,137), a signiﬁcant increase from the
reported incidence in adults. Pediatric patients, especially
infants, do not reliably exhibit hyperamylasemia in
combination with pancreatic isoamylase, lipase, or both,
which is diagnostic of pancreatitis in adults (138,139). Andersen et al. followed 21 infants and 25 children aged
1 to 16 years and found that a better marker of pancreatitis
in children is plasma concentrations of trypsinogen-2 and
trypsin-2-α1-antitrypsin, which are sensitive alternative
markers in adults and children (140,141). In contrast,
and unlike in adults, absence of hyperamylasemia did
not exclude pancreatitis in infants and children (140,141). Trypsinogen-2 is excreted by the kidneys, but trypsin-2-
α1-antitrypsin is not (142). In the Anderson study, levels
up to 150 µg/L reﬂect ‘‘normal’’ postoperative reaction,
whereas levels exceeding 300 µg/L most likely reﬂect
pancreatitis (143). In a report by Rodriquez et al., which
examined 131 patients between 7 days and 16 years
of age, 10% exhibited hyperamylasemia. These patients
were not stratiﬁed by age, but it is likely that they
represent the subset of patients older than 1 year. Of
those, 43% suffered shock postoperatively, the likely
pathogenic factor being intraoperative visceral ischemia. In general, the mechanism(s) causing pancreatitis in
pediatric patients are the same as those in adults. Implications of postpump pancreatitis are serious. Among adult patients exhibiting severe pancreatitis, the
mortality is 67% to 100%, and even mild forms of
postoperative pancreatitis have a 26% to 70% mortality
rate (120,125). There continues to be a real difﬁculty in
rapid intraoperative (and even postoperative (122)) diagnosis of pancreatic injury occurring with cardiac surgery. GASTROINTESTINAL COMPLICATIONS
There are neither good indicators of GI function nor spe-
ciﬁc enzymes that indicate GI injury in the perioperative
period. This has precluded intraoperative diagnosis of GI
ischemia and dysfunction. Even postoperatively, signs of
GI injury are very subtle, a factor that contributes to delayed diagnosis and treatment. Assessment of the effects
of CPB on the GI system has been limited to case reports
of severe injury, often resulting in patient death or resection of infarcted tissue.

Several retrospective analyses,
encompassing more than 13,000 CPB cases, have revealed
an overall incidence of GI complications following cardiac
surgery of 0.5% to 3% (1,101,144–147). GI complications
therefore occur at roughly the same rate as pancreatitis. The most frequent abdominal complication of CPB
in adults is GI bleeding, usually duodenal or gastric in
origin, accounting for 25% to 60% of overall GI complications (101,144–146). Mortality associated with GI
hemorrhage is 33% to 53% (101,144,145). Doguet et al. used a rat model to show an increase in the mesenteric endothelial response to α−1-adrenergic agonist with

17. Splanchnic Visceral, Metabolic, and Glucoregulatory Effects of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
361
systemic inﬂammatory response. This phenomenon might
contribute to an increase in mesenteric ischemic events
after CPB, particularly when vasopressors are used (148). The most common catastrophic GI complication after cardiac surgery is mesenteric ischemia, and its occurrence
has a reported mortality rate of 68% (1). Less common are duodenal ulcers, diverticulitis, colonic pseudoobstruction, intestinal ischemia or infarction, and splenic
infarction (101,149,150). Mortality associated with these
complications is comparable to that observed with GI
hemorrhage. Acalculous cholecystitis, which occurs in 5
patients per 1,000, has a reported mortality of 86% (101). Although GI complications after CPB in children are
not common, data are sparse and may reﬂect comorbidity
in the pediatric patients who are candidates for cardiac
surgery. Premature infants are at risk for necrotizing
enterocolitis (NEC) related to their prematurity. Factors
that shunt blood away from the systemic circulation, such
as left to right shunt, may worsen the predisposition to
NEC. NEC is a surgical emergency, which supersedes most
cardiac surgeries, because it leads to bacterial soiling and
consequent sepsis if left untreated. Patients who have
undergone cardiac surgery and still have a persistent
left-to-right shunt are at risk for postoperative systemic
(and GI) hypoperfusion and ischemia. In the postoperative
setting there have been some steps to protect the GI system
in children. Cisapride, a 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor
antagonist, decreases GI transit time and allows more
rapid return to enteral feeding (151). Histamine-2 receptor
blockers are used to prevent stress-related gastric ulcers,
particularly in patients with an expected longer recovery
period. The efﬁcacy of other GI interventions, including
early enteral nutrition, immunonutrition, and selective
digestive decontamination in children undergoing cardiac
surgery, has yet to be investigated (152). Risk factors for development of GI complications
include prolonged duration of CPB, low perioperative
cardiac output, embolic events, and valve surgery (with
possible portal congestion) (1,101,144,153). These risk
factors have also been identiﬁed for ‘‘postpump jaundice’’
and ‘‘postpump pancreatitis.’’ Not surprisingly, there
is a high coincidence of pancreatitis in patients with
‘‘postpump’’ GI complications (101,146). Low-ﬂow states contribute to GI ischemia by virtue
of ﬂow distribution. Ohri et al. demonstrated a decrease
in ﬂow to the jejunal mucosa by 40%, with decrease to
the serosa by 50% at initiation of hypothermic CPB (9).

During rewarming, O2 delivery falls approximately a further 50% whereas O2 consumption increases dramatically,
with a consequent decrease in intestinal mucosal pH (1). Tao et al. demonstrated a similar pattern during normothermic CPB and suggested that this may be in part due to
a diversion of blood ﬂow away from the ileum and colon
toward the foregut (1,13). These changes in ﬂow patterns
are accompanied by CPB-induced dysfunction in mesenteric endothelial cells with consequent hyperreactivity to
α agonists (1). This has implications for patients whose
separation from CPB is accompanied by an escalating
need for vasopressor therapy. Several clinical management strategies have been suggested to minimize intra-abdominal complications of
cardiac surgery. Off-pump coronary artery bypass graft
(CABG) technique theoretically reduces the mesenteric
hemodynamic lability, while concurrently avoiding cannulation and the risk of embolization. However, two
retrospective studies have failed to demonstrate a lesser
risk of GI complication in cardiac surgery performed without CPB (154,155). Other strategies that may help prevent
mesenteric ischemia include routine epiaortic ultrasonography to identify and avoid atherosclerotic areas in the
aorta (1), institution of a screening program for heparininduced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and active prophylaxis
against HIT with iloprost and dipyridamole (156), the use
of internal mammary-based pedicle grafts (157), proximal
anastomotic devices (158) to avoid clamping the aorta in
such patients, and paying meticulous attention to hemodynamic management in the perioperative period (1). The intestinal wall serves as a barrier to prevent intraluminal bacteria and endotoxin from migrating into
the vasculature. Decreased splanchnic perfusion disrupts
this barrier, increasing permeability and allowing endotoxin translocation. Rocke et al. (159) reported that
plasma endotoxin levels were increased transiently after
release of the aortic cross-clamp. The nine patients in
their study had an uneventful intraoperative and perioperative course (159), precluding an analysis of the role
of endotoxin in subsequent development of postoperative
sepsis. It is noteworthy, however, that the degree and time
course of endotoxemia in these patients closely resembles
the effect of 1-hour superior mesenteric artery occlusion
in cats (160). The magnitude of endotoxemia was directly
related to duration of CPB (159). Intestinal permeability
to intravascular proteins is also affected by CPB. Extravasation of plasma proteins into the interstitial space is
increased as much as fourfold during normothermic CPB
at 2.2 L/m2/ min in dogs, with the largest increase in permeability for large molecules (161).

CPB therefore induces
abnormal bidirectional ﬂux across the intestinal wall. The
signiﬁcance of increased endotoxin leak into the circulation is that this may occur in patients with the longest
CPB times, who are already at increased risk for GI and
hepatic injury. All these factors contribute to development
of postoperative sepsis and multiple system organ failure. The exact molecular mechanism by which prolonged CPB
leads to hepatic, pancreatic, and GI injury is unknown, but
could involve intestinal permeability. A second problem,
which may be related, is deﬁning an adequate visceral
perfusion for a given patient, and how this could be better monitored during CPB. One approach that has been

362
III. Physiology and Pathology
reported is to monitor the intraluminal pH of either stomach or colon by tonometry (51–53). Acidosis of either
stomach or colon as indexed by tonometry can be a reasonable marker of tissue ischemia (51–53). Early methods
proved cumbersome for assessing splanchnic perfusion
during CPB, and difﬁcult to master from both the technical and interpretive viewpoints; a new automated system
of air tonometry allows for frequent measurement of gastric regional CO2 of continuous air tonometry (162). This
is not generally utilized as an intraoperative monitor, but
may hold promise. The least invasive and perhaps most
sensitive indicator of a signiﬁcant GI event is still the patient’s complaint of abdominal pain. In the postoperative
setting, lighter sedation and fast-tracking patients when
appropriate may improve this ‘‘monitor’’ and allow earlier
surgical interventions for catastrophic GI events. NONCARDIAC
GLUCOSE–INSULIN–POTASSIUM
INTERACTIONS WITH
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Circulating Glucose and Insulin
Responses to Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Insulin secretion is regulated by the prevailing plasma
glucose concentration. Although insulin secretion is inhibited by α-adrenergic activity, which is increased during
surgery (110,112,114), there is generally good stability of
insulin and glucose metabolism during the pre-CPB period
managed by many different anesthetic techniques, including high-dose opioids (114,163), ketamine/diazepam (109),
or isoﬂurane/fentanyl (164). An exception to these ﬁnd-
ings occurs under halothane anesthesia, where there is
a progressive pre-CPB hyperglycemia to approximately
180 mg/dL with no substantial rise in plasma insulin (110). Glycemic control during the pre-CPB period in children
may differ from that in adults, because pancreatic insulin secretion in children does not increase effectively in
response to glucose challenge (108). Hyperglycemia accompanies initiation of CPB regardless of the anesthetic technique (109–111,114,163)
(Fig. 2). Without glucose in the pump prime, hyperglycemia indolently progresses throughout the duration
of CPB (115,163). Inclusion of glucose in the priming
solution, effectively constituting a large intravenous glucose challenge, exacerbates early hyperglycemia (110,114). Brandt et al. administered glucose 25 g in the prime,
increasing blood glucose concentration from 110 mg/dL
before CPB to 250 mg/dL at CPB onset (114). Interestingly,
despite no further glucose administration, hyperglycemia
persisted for 1 to 2 hours after separation from CPB, indicating poor glucose disposal.

with that of ﬂuroxene anesthesia (114), but this has
not been assessed in relation to more modern inhalation agents such as isoﬂurane, desﬂurane, or sevoﬂurane. Serum insulin concentration tends to increase along with
that of glucose, with patients exhibiting more marked
hyperinsulinemia in the setting of exaggerated hyperglycemia (114). The insulin secretory response, although
ultimately doubling the serum concentration during CPB,
is both slow and incomplete (109). When glucose is present
in the pump prime, the magnitude of hyperglycemia
is near maximal within the ﬁrst few minutes of normothermic CPB as the prime is distributed (109,110). In contrast, the rise in serum insulin concentration is
delayed and then restrained throughout the course of
CPB (109,110). Markedly high serum catecholamine concentrations, which occur during CPB, inhibit the pancreatic β-cell and could underlie at least in part the poor
insulin secretory response to hyperglycemia CPB (112). Hypothermia has a peculiar effect on glucose–insulin
interactions during CPB (Fig. 2) (66,163). During CPBassociated hypothermia, development of hyperglycemia
and insulin secretion are both suppressed, an observation
that led Kuntschen et al. (66) to surmise that hypothermia
directly inhibits hepatic glucose production. At rewarming
from hypothermic CPB, however, the magnitude of hyperglycemia of these patients actually exceeds that of patients
undergoing normothermic CPB, and relatively worse
glycemic control persists early into the postoperative setting (66,163). There is uncertainty as to whether (66,163) a
concomitantly exaggerated hyperinsulinemia exists at this
time. However, in patients in whom a marked hyperinsulinemia exists, it may reveal an underlying hypothermiainduced impairment of the peripheral (skeletal muscle)
glucose uptake response to insulin at a time when warmed
central circulation permits a full hepatic glucose production. Peripheral warming occurs more slowly than central
warming in the absence of aggressive convection warming
of the extremities. There may also be other humoral mechanisms, including a reduced ability of insulin to suppress
endogenous glucose production by the liver. Termination of CPB is followed by a continued rise
in plasma glucose concentration (Fig. 2). Infusion of catecholamines during weaning from CPB can exacerbate
hyperglycemia (165). Glycemic control further worsens as
the patient awakens from anesthesia and exhibits a full
endocrine stress response.

In the past it was not uncommon for a nondiabetic patient to arrive in the ICU after
cardiac surgery with a blood glucose concentration well
into the ‘‘diabetic’’ range (163,166). Each intraoperative
and postoperative stage of hyperglycemia is magniﬁed in
the patient with pre-existing diabetes mellitus, particularly patients with the type 2 ‘‘insulin resistant’’ diabetes
mellitus, for whom a comprehensive preoperative plan for
insulin management may not have been developed (166). Slowly, over a period of several hours to a few days,
plasma glucose concentration declines to the preoperative
value (109,114). Serum insulin concentration remains elevated after separation from CPB period, with maximal
concentration occurring within the ﬁrst hour (111). Hyperinsulinemia then slowly resolves over the ﬁrst several
postoperative hours to days (109–111,114). Hyperglycemia and Insulin Resistance
Coincidence of hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia occurs during CPB and extends well into the early postoperative recovery period. This pattern, known as insulin
resistance, indicates that even when it is present at a
reasonable concentration, circulating insulin fails to appropriately regulate glycemic status. Several ‘‘euglycemic
clamp’’ studies have measured insulin resistance in the
etiology of CPB-associated hyperglycemia. The essence of
the euglycemic clamp technique is that a primed, constant intravenous insulin infusion produces a steady-state
hyperinsulinemia stimulus while plasma glucose concentration is ‘‘clamped’’ at a constant level by titrating an
intravenous infusion of glucose (167–169). Glucose uptake is deﬁned as the amount of glucose infusion needed
to maintain euglycemia, and decreased glucose requirement versus control is a measure of insulin resistance. Two factors can contribute to insulin resistance: failure to
suppress endogenous hepatic glucose production or failure to stimulate peripheral glucose uptake. Unfortunately,
the isotope dilution studies that would be required to determine hepatic glucose production during CPB have not
been reported, precluding assessment of its role currently. It is erroneous to assume that a moderate insulin dose
that suppresses endogenous hepatic glucose production
in awake volunteers exerts a similar effect in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB, because much higher
insulin doses are required for hepatic suppression in type
2 diabetes mellitus or in septic patients (169,170). Approximately 60% of insulin-mediated peripheral glucose uptake
normally occurs by skeletal muscle, but this fraction is
reduced in the setting of type 2 diabetes mellitus (171).

Before CPB in nondiabetic patients, an insulin infusion rate of 5 mU/kg/min, which produces a serum insulin
concentration of 90 to 100 mU/mL, leads to a glucose
uptake rate that is 15% to 20% less than in healthy
awake volunteers at a similar serum insulin concentration (Fig. 3) (107,166,168,170,172). Insulin resistance is
induced by anesthesia and surgical trauma. Onset of CPB
further decreases glucose uptake by 25% to 30%, which
may or may not revert to pre-CPB levels by the time the patient arrives at the ICU (Fig. 3) (107,166). Similar data were
obtained in patients undergoing hypothermic CPB (66). Worse initial insulin resistance occurs in patients with
pre-existing type 2 diabetes mellitus (166). Intraoperative
glucose kinetics of diabetic patients in the pre-CPB period resemble that in the awake patients with diabetics

the magnitude of insulin resistance in nondiabetic subjects
actually approaches that of diabetic patients from the time
of sternal closure to arrival in the ICU (166). Several factors could underlie the marked insulin resistance during
CPB. The most likely factor would be elevated plasma
concentrations of the counter-regulatory hormones, cortisol and catecholamines. Glucagon plays a very minor
role, if any. Heparin can contribute to insulin resistance,
at least in part, because it stimulates lipolysis, leading
to a massive increase in plasma free fatty acid (FFA)
concentrations (173–175). Increased serum FFA concentration inhibits glucose utilization by the skeletal muscle (176–178). However, high-dose insulin infusion reliably
suppresses lipolysis and moderates intraoperative plasma
FFA concentrations (179). Further, the serum insulin
concentration required to suppress lipolysis is relatively
low compared with that for glucose control (180–182). The full extent to which insulin controls plasma FFA concentration after the large lipolysis-inducing heparin dose
associated with CPB is currently unknown, because they
exert antagonistic actions on the same enzyme–lipoprotein
lipase (175,183).

Extrarenal Potassium Metabolics
Potassium (K+) homeostasis, which involves regulating
serum K+ concentration within a relatively narrow range,
is accomplished chronically (and slowly) by the kidney
as K+ excretion into the urine. Acute changes in serum
K+ concentration involve redistribution of the electrolyte
between the intracellular compartment (where 98% of
total body K+ resides) and the extracellular compartment
including the serum. Transmembrane K+ shifts that can
cause very large changes in serum K+ concentration (at
least acutely) are accompanied by an immeasurably small
difference in intracellular K+ content. Two independent endocrine systems mediate transmembrane movement of K+
from the extracellular
to the intracellular compartment: β2-adrenergic system (184–186) and insulin (172,187). Both mechanisms
are rapid, decreasing serum K+ concentration within a
few minutes, and share Na+-K+ ATPase as the ﬁnal step
effecting cellular K+ uptake. β2 Adrenergic stimulation
induces hypokalemia by a G-protein mediated, cAMPdependent mechanism (188,189). Although the molecular
mechanism is β2 speciﬁc, either epinephrine or DA can be
used to treat acute hyperkalemia (184,190). Conversely,
β2 adrenergic blockade reduces the propensity to perioperative hypokalemia of cardiac surgery (191). Pederson
et al., using labeled 42K+, demonstrated that propanolol
increases serum K+ concentration by shifting K+ from
the intracellular to the extracellular compartment, without any effect on renal K+ excretion (192). Rosa et al. found that epinephrine infusion augments handling of
an intravenous KCl challenge, despite causing a 50% to
100% inhibition of renal K+ secretion, whereas pretreatment with propanolol interferes with disposal of a KCl
challenge despite increased renal K+ excretion (185). The
paradox of renal K+ handling is explained by the fact
that the rapid action of the transmembrane intracellular transfer into muscle and liver reduces plasma K+ to
the extent that there is no acute requirement for excess
K+ excretion, whereas if cellular uptake is prevented the
excess plasma K+ must be eliminated by the kidney. Although both the skeletal muscle and the liver participate
in catecholamine-mediated hypokalemia, the exact tissue
uptake distribution is unknown. More is known about tissue distribution of insulinmediated hypokalemia (Fig. 4). Most (70%–80%) of the
cellular K+ uptake in response to insulin stimulation

is taken up across the splanchnic bed, particularly the
liver (172,179). Skeletal muscle is the second most important tissue for insulin-mediated K+ uptake, but its
response time is considerably slower (172,187). Whether
insulin stimulates renal K+ excretion is controversial. Rossetti et al. (193), titrating KCl administration to
maintain eukalemia during a euglycemic clamp, reported
increased K+ excretion during hyperinsulinemia, but Furuya et al. (194), directly examining rabbit collecting ducts,
found that insulin inhibits K+ secretion in vitro. Maximal insulin-mediated K+ disposal occurs at a relatively
modest hyperinsulinemia (90–100 µU/mL), which is approximately one ﬁfth of that required for the maximal glucose uptake response (172). Insulin-stimulated K+ uptake
is mutually independent from insulin-stimulated glucose
uptake in both the liver and the muscle (172,187,195,196). K+ uptake in response to insulin is robust, remaining intact in such ‘‘insulin resistant’’ states as type 2 diabetes mellitus, acanthosis nigrans, obesity, uremia, sepsis, cirrhosis,
or hypertension (169,170,179,197–200). Cirrhosis causes
a rightward shift of the dose-response curve for insulinmediated K+ uptake, but maximum responsiveness at
pharmacologic insulin doses is preserved (179,201). Only
one rare disease, idiopathic nonazotemic hyperkalemia,
has been described in which insulin-mediated K+ uptake
is markedly disturbed and not accompanied by a defect
in glucose responsiveness (199). The molecular mechanism by which insulin promotes cellular K+ uptake differs
somewhat among tissues. In the liver, there is an intermediate step involving Na+ –H+ exchange by the sodium
hydrogen exchanger (NHE-1) transporter (and inhibited
by amiloride), whereas K+ uptake by skeletal muscle and
other tissues does not utilize the NHE-1 transporter and
is resistant to amiloride (Fig. 4) (202–205). Optimal K+ homeostasis depends upon an intact
β-adrenergic system, and can be impaired by adrenergic
β blockers (184). Basal insulin secretion also plays an
important role in maintaining K+ homeostasis, with K+
intolerance following either streptozotocin treatment in
animals or somatostatin in humans or animals (167). Abe et al. reported that serum K+ concentration rises
brieﬂy at initiation of CPB, coinciding with cooling and
administration of cardioplegia solution (206). Eukalemia
generally returns throughout hypothermic CPB, with
serum K+ concentration beginning to decrease but remaining within normal limits during rewarming (206). At the end of CPB, a marked hypokalemia ensues, with
a nadir 60 to 90 minutes following separation from
CPB (206). Abe et al.

calculated that 80% of the decrease
in serum K+ was due to intracellular sequestration during and for the ﬁrst hour after CPB (206). Regarding
the mechanism, Figure 5 superimposes the time courses
of serum insulin and catecholamines with that of serum
K+ concentration during and after CPB. Correlation of
rising serum insulin and falling K+ concentrations leads
one to suspect that insulin is the more likely mediator
of post-CPB hypokalemia than catecholamines (206,207). Because the liver appears to be a major storage organ for
serum K+ uptake, accounting for almost 80% of insulinstimulated K+ uptake (172,179), it is possible that the
absence of signiﬁcant hypokalemia during hypothermic
CPB may be due in part to impaired Na+-K+-ATPase
function in cooled hepatocytes to respond to either adrenergic or insulin stimulation (208). The direct inﬂuence of
hypothermia on K+ homeostasis during CPB remains to
be tested. There has been recent interest in the cardioprotective effect of sodium–hydrogen exchanger (NHE-1)
type blockade during cardiac surgery with CPB (209,210). It would be interesting to test whether an NHE-1 blocker,
such as zoniporide (211), attenuates hypokalemia after
CBP without altering the hyperinsulinemia necessary to
stabilize glycemic management. Alternatively, CPB can induce a sustained hyperkalemia. Risk factors for hyperkalemia during CPB are
potassium-sparing diuretics, preoperative hyperkalemia,
and ketone-prone (type 1) diabetes mellitus. Hyperinsulinemic type 2 diabetes mellitus is not usually a risk
factor unless the patient is absolutely insulinopenic, because these individuals are normally sensitive to insulin
in terms of its hypokalemic response despite the presence of ‘‘insulin resistance’’ for glucose metabolism. The
insulinopenic patient is prone to hyperkalemia during hypothermic CPB because it further suppresses an already
weak insulin secretion. Insulin Therapy in Cardiac Surgery
Insulin has been administered as a therapeutic drug during cardiac surgery with CPB in an effort to improve
outcome for many years. Insulin therapy was introduced
40 years ago in combination with glucose and potassium
as the glucose–insulin–potassium (GIK) technique (212),
but more recently insulin infusion has been aggressively
employed in the perioperative setting to achieve better
glycemic control. It is still not clear whether insulin improves cardiac outcomes directly or indirectly through
myocardial K+ uptake or better glycemic control. However, not all clinicians who used GIK employed an optimal
technique, which should ideally resemble the euglycemic
clamp with three different infusates, insulin, potassium,
and glucose.

Many authors report using GIK in a single
bag, with suboptimal consequent hyperglycemia during
and after CPB (164,213). Failure to account for the
different kinetics of insulin, K+, and glucose disappearance from the plasma puts the patient at risk for early
hyperglycemia, late hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, and hyperkalemia in the perioperative setting, sometimes in the
same patient (214,215). In one report, aggressive intraoperative K+ replacement during the GIK technique led to a
postoperative hyperkalemia-induced cardiac arrest (215).

The etiology was that after discontinuation of the GIK,
K+ infusion was continued to maintain a serum concentration of 4.5 mEq/L. Later, as hyperinsulinemia resolved,
K+ efﬂux from the liver (and muscle) overwhelmed the
capacity of the kidneys to excrete it and a concentration
of 7.6 mEq/L led to cardiac arrest (215). The GIK technique could be optimized, and best tested, by utilizing
the euglycemic clamp approach as described by Carvahlo
et al. (166), but by carrying out ‘‘clamping’’ of both glucose
and K+ plasma concentrations. Hyperinsulinemia could
be tapered in the postoperative setting, and the infusions
of glucose and KCl weaned as dictated by their respective
plasma concentrations. A recent landmark study by van den Berghe et al. (216)
has generated renewed enthusiasm for aggressive use of
insulin after cardiac surgery. These authors showed in
1,500 ICU patients, 60% of whom were status postcardiac surgery and only 13% had a previous diagnosis of
diabetes mellitus, signiﬁcant beneﬁts in several (noncardiac) outcome measures when glycemic status was tightly
controlled (target glucose range 80–110 mg/dL) versus
conventional treatment (target glucose 180–200 mg/dL). Outcome improvements were decreases in mortality
(42%), bacteremia (46%), renal failure (41%), transfusion
requirements (50%), polyneuropathy (44%), and durations
of mechanical ventilation and ICU stay (216).

Another
recent large study (3,500 patients) compared two groups
of CABG patients who received either subcutaneous insulin or insulin infusion, initially postoperatively and later
including the operative setting (217). Insulin infusion provided better glycemic control (average postoperative value
177 versus 214 mg/dL), and was also associated with improved outcome in terms of mortality (50%). The data also
showed that there was a progressive mortality rate (mostly
cardiac-related) with increased hyperglycemia from 0.9%
at an average glucose of less than 150 mg/dL to 14.59%
when the average glucose was more than 250 mg/dL (217). Gandhi et al., in a smaller retrospective study of 400
patients, showed speciﬁcally that intraoperative hyperglycemia, independent of postoperative glycemic status,
predicted worse outcome from cardiac surgery, as indexed
by mortality, postoperative infections, neurologic dysfunction, renal failure, cardiac complications, and pulmonary
complications, within 30 days (218). Another recent study
demonstrated that intraoperative GIK with tight glycemic
control, continued for 24 hours, attenuated the postoperative inﬂammatory response of C-reactive protein and
serum amyloid A, but did not affect the perioperative rise
in the concentrations of interleukins 6 and 8 (219). van
den Berghe speculated that the mechanism of action for

improved outcome with tight glucose control is probably multifactorial, involving, at least in part, several
steps by which hyperglycemia causes mitochondrial dysfunction (220). It could also involve modulation of the
inﬂammatory response. Although tight glycemic control has substantial literature support in the setting of CPB in adults, one should
be careful about extrapolating the beneﬁts of glucose control management to pediatric patients, where the few
available data are conﬂicting. In a retrospective study
of 34 patients undergoing deep hypothermic circulatory
arrest, Steward (221) showed that hyperglycemia paralleled worse neurologic outcomes. However, the Boston
Circulatory Arrest Study suggested that normoglycemia
during reperfusion was associated with worse neurologic
outcome, while hyperglycemia was associated with better
outcome (222). It is speculated that the immature brain
may be more vulnerable to substrate (glucose) deﬁciency,
and that ‘‘normal’’ blood glucose concentration during the
reperfusion period after cerebral ischemia in infants may
be insufﬁcient for complete cerebral recovery (86). Butterworth et al., recently published a randomized placebo
controlled clinical trial of insulin and attempted tight
blood glucose control versus placebo during CPB (223). This study, which included 381 nondiabetic patients, was
unable to demonstrate a clinical beneﬁt for insulin therapy and tight glucose control during CPB. It seems to
be well established for many groups of critical care patients, including patients undergoing cardiac surgery, that
maintenance of normoglycemia during the postoperative
period improves clinical outcomes. Extrapolation of this
strategy to the intraoperative CPB interval is not well
established despite the tempting logic of association. Technical problems encountered in an effort to obtain tight intraoperative glycemic control during CPB are
most commonly refractory hyperglycemia during the early
phase of CPB, and profound hypokalemia associated with
pharmacologic insulin therapy. Physicians have become
more aware that the insulin infusion at the end of the
critical care period should be tapered rather than abruptly
discontinued to minimize the risk of postoperative rebound hyperkalemia in the ICU. Hyperglycemia at the
onset of CPB can be due to the large glucose load if glucose is included in the pump prime. The hypoglycemic
response to insulin requires approximately 30 minutes
for any signiﬁcant effect and more than an hour for a
complete response (Fig. 6). Hyperglycemia is exacerbated
in the setting of pre-existing insulin resistant conditions
such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, hypertension, cirrhosis, or uremia (170,179,197,198,200).

Insulin-resistant
patients require more absolute insulin and longer time for
the hypoglycemic effect to become apparent (Fig. 6). The
hypoglycemic effect is increased by beginning the insulin
infusion during the pre-CPB period and titrating a separate glucose infusion to prevent hypoglycemia before CPB
is initiated. A hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp study
approach can be used to maintain tight glycemic control
throughout cardiac surgery with CPB, even in patients
with diabetes mellitus, because glucose is more quickly

(Figs. 6 and7). A K+ infusion set should be prepared in

Cardiac surgery with CPB exerts marked alterations in
the splanchnic circulation, and concomitantly leads to
a complex physiologic response of the endocrine and
metabolic environment. Most of these alterations are invisible to the anesthesiologists and surgeons caring for
the patient because of limitations in patient monitoring
in terms of regional blood ﬂow and substrate utilization. Because most patients do well postoperatively, there has
not been a rush to improve the system of monitoring. However, the changes in perfusion and metabolic function are profoundly important and must be understood
to advance the level of care in the future. In splanchnic perfusion and cellular viability, improved monitoring
would be expected to reduce the incidence of visceral
complications from the current 1% to 2% of patients. Although the relative number of patients affected appears to
be small at ﬁrst, the absolute number is substantial, and
the consequences of visceral complications are very serious. Understanding the metabolic environment, on the
other hand, will prove to be important because proper
manipulation of the complex alterations could reduce
the incidence of stroke and other systemic complications
(by better glycemic control), hypertension, postoperative
arrhythmias, and impaired myocardial performance (by
directing myocardial substrate utilization). Optimization
of protein metabolism, in particular, can lead to anticipated improvements in wound healing, immune function,
and recovery of normal coagulation status. There is a
solid and growing body of evidence that tight control of
glucose metabolism positively affects many processes not
previously known to be affected by the glycemic state. Much important work in both monitoring and regulation
of visceral functions during and after CPB remains to
be done. KEY POINTS
■Hypotension alters splanchnic blood ﬂow. ●Hypovolemic hypotension is more deleterious than
pharmacologically induced hypotension. ●Changes in total ﬂow do not necessarily reﬂect
changes in the splanchnic circulation. ■Assessment of the effect of clinical CPB on splanchnic
circulation is confounded by the associated effects of
hypotension and hypothermia.

●Normothermic CPB produces an overall increase
in GI blood ﬂow, a decrease in hepatic arterial ﬂow,
and variable effect on pancreatic perfusion. ■Rewarming decreases perfusion and O2 delivery to
the splanchnic viscera. ●It increases O2 consumption as temperature increases. ■The effects of CO2 on the splanchnic circulation
during CPB are inconclusive. ■Neither hepatic nor pancreatic blood ﬂow is effectively autoregulated during hypothermic CPB. ■Different inotropes have varying effects on the
splanchnic circulation. ●Only fenoldopam selectively dilates splanchnic
vessels. ■New advances in visceral monitoring include tonometry and near infrared spectroscopy. ■Hyperlactatemia after cardiac surgery is most often
due to excess lactate production. ■Dilutional coagulopathy occurs at the commencement of CPB and continues into the early postoperative period. ■Reduction in ﬁbronectin after CPB may be due to
losses, proteolysis, and decreased production. ■Hepatic drug metabolism is variably affected by
CPB, depending on the speciﬁc drug and its speciﬁc
enzyme pathway. ■Although there is no evidence that CPB is detrimental
to the liver in most patients, post-CPB jaundice and
rarely fulminant hepatic failure do occur. Hepatic
monitoring does not yet exist. ■Cardiac surgery with CPB induces a dynamic perioperative insulin resistance. ■Perioperative insulin resistance of glucose metabolism
is not accompanied by K+ disturbance. ■Tight glycemic control during and after CPB appears
to improve outcome measures in adults. The data is
conﬂicting in pediatric patients. ■Challenges to tight glycemic control with insulin
include iatrogenic hypokalemia and refractory hyperglycemia. ■Nearly a third of adult patients develop hyperamylasemia postoperatively. Ninety-nine percent of these
are asymptomatic. Calcium administration may be a
risk factor. ■Trypsinogen-2 and trypsin-2-α are better markers of
pancreatitis in children than amylase. ■GI
complications
after
CPB
surgery
are
rare
(0.5%–3%), but the mortality rate is high. ■Risk of developing NEC is increased in patients with
a left-to-right shunt.

17. Splanchnic Visceral, Metabolic, and Glucoregulatory Effects of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
371
■Disruption of the intestinal wall may occur from
decreased splanchnic perfusion, resulting in endotoxemia and sepsis. ■Surgical management strategies to decrease GI complications include epiaortic ultrasonography, screening (and prophylaxis) program for HIT, internal
mammary-based pedicle grafts, proximal anastomotic devices to avoid cross-clamping the aorta, and

1 8
◗Neurologic Effects of Cardiopulmonary
Bypass
David J. Cook
This chapter will provide an overview of the neurologic
effects of cardiac surgery and cardiopulmonary bypass
(CPB). First, the extent and nature of bypass-related
neurologic injury will be presented, emphasizing the
importance of patient demographics and comorbidities. In this context, etiologies will be considered. Second, basic
cerebral physiology during CPB will be reviewed. Third,
interventions having the potential to reduce neurologic
morbidity will be considered. Fourth, the applicability of
neurologic monitoring techniques for CPB will be brieﬂy
presented. THE POPULATION AT RISK,
DEMOGRAPHICS,
AND COMORBIDITIES
Cardiac surgeries requiring CPB are among the most
commonly performed surgical procedures in Europe and
North America. Studies describing more than 20,000 cardiac surgical patients indicate that signiﬁcant morbidity
may be experienced by 20% to 25% of patients (1–3). These
morbidities include cardiac and pulmonary failure, neurologic injury, renal insufﬁciency, bleeding, and infection. Complications have predictable adverse effects on duration and cost of hospitalization (4–7) as well as on patients
quality of life and functional capacity on discharge (7–9). When considering cardiac surgical neurologic morbidity, it is important to understand that many adult
cardiac surgical patients have preexisting risk factors
for stroke and cognitive impairment even without the
added risk of cardiac surgery and CPB. Cardiac or
noncardiac surgery superimposes incremental risk. The
recent European study of cognitive outcomes after noncardiac surgery superbly illustrated this risk (10). In that
study, 1,218 elderly patients undergoing major noncardiac
surgery underwent neurocognitive assessment preoperatively, before discharge, and at 3 months postoperatively. A large (n = 321) nonsurgical control group was also
enrolled. That study reported a 26% incidence of cognitive
dysfunction 1 week after surgery and a 10% incidence at
3 months. Cardiac surgery poses greater risks because cardiac surgical patients experience more serious neurologic
morbidity than age- and health-matched controls undergoing noncardiac surgery (Table 1) (9). Consequently, it
is useful to regard the perioperative period as an acute
neurologic stress in a subpopulation chronically at risk. There is general agreement about preoperative patientrelated factors that increase the likelihood of perioperative
stroke, but the role of many intraoperative factors is much
less clear. Preoperative risk factors include advanced age,
history of prior neurologic events, aortic atherosclerosis,
low cardiac output states, atrial arrhythmias, hypertension, and diabetes.

Advanced age, the most dramatic risk
factor, appears to magnify the other risk factors. The importance of this risk factor cannot be overemphasized,
because over the last two decades the number of cardiac
surgery patients older than 60 doubled and the percentage
of patients older than 70 increased sevenfold (11). The proportion of cardiac surgical patients older than 80 will grow
