intraoperatively between the end of rewarming and the
end of CPB (378–381). These levels appear to be related
to CPB time (379,382) and to patient age (382,383). Intracardiac operations result in higher S100 levels
than CABG procedures (384). Arterial line ﬁltration may
reduce S100 levels (378), and there appears to be some
correlation between embolization and S100 levels (383). Patients undergoing off-pump CABG have undetectable or
fractionally raised levels (379). The sensitivity or speciﬁcity of S100 as a marker for
cerebral injury has not been established, although it is
clear that levels measured at the end of CPB are not
speciﬁc (Table 7). Unfortunately, some extracranial tissues
can either release S100 or non-S100 substances that are
detected by current S100 assays, such that measured S100
values may not reﬂect cerebral events (385–387). A recent
study using mass spectroscopy, gel electrophoresis, and
Western blot analysis demonstrated that a variety of non-
S100 proteins in the surgical ﬁeld react with the S100
commercial immunoassay (388). This leads to problems
with test sensitivity and speciﬁcity. In a study by J¨onsson
et al., 93% of 515 consecutive patients had detectable
S100 at the end of surgery, but less than 10% showed
stroke, encephalopathy, or delayed awakening (382). In a study of 40 patients, 58% of patients showed
elevated S100 levels 1 hour postoperatively, but no patient
demonstrated overt cerebral injury (378). High levels of
S100 at 48 hours postoperatively have more sensitivity
and speciﬁcity for cerebral injury than early postoperative
measurements (382,389) because S100 values that are
very high 48 hours after surgery reﬂect size and predict
outcome of stroke (390,391). However, what therapeutic
intervention one might base on a 48-hour measurement
remains unclear. CONCLUSIONS
In adults, postcardiac surgical brain injury occurs because
the cardiac surgical population concentrates a variety
of neurologic risk factors. Surgery precipitates those
risks and imposes additional ischemic, physiologic, and
inﬂammatory stresses for which the patient may be unable
to compensate. Because neurologic morbidity derives from interaction
of the patient and the surgery, the greatest reductions in
morbidity may come from the application of risk stratiﬁ-
cation to decide who is best served by surgery and who
is not.

Although technical and pharmacologic innovations
such as off-bypass surgery, antiadhesion therapies, and
near-infrared monitoring are tempting, at present they
cannot effectively prevent stroke or signiﬁcant neurocognitive functional decline, hence tailoring the surgery to
the patients’ risk proﬁle or deciding not to take certain
patients to the operating room offers greater appeal. For the patients who undergo surgery, we must be
comprehensive and practical in developing an intraoperative management strategy. Because neurologic injury
derives largely from preexisting patient risk factors, multivariate analysis indicates that age and atherosclerotic
disease determine outcome. Although patient factors may
determine outcome in multivariate analysis, this is not
equivalent to saying that surgical, physiologic, and pharmacologic management is unimportant. We have a great

disease, regional blood ﬂow in focal ischemia, and the
potent effect of temperature on the cascade of injury. This
allows us to make well-informed choices about physiologic
management. Similarly, gas physiology can be applied to
facilitate absorption of bubbles or change the distribution
of CBF during periods of embolic risk. Echocardiography
can tell us when it is appropriate to remove an aortic vent,
and administering a barbiturate may be advantageous if
circulatory arrest must occur before adequate cooling. Our understanding of ‘‘postcardiac surgical’’ cognitive
decline is evolving. First, the best available evidence must
shift our attention away from CPB events as a primary
determinant if randomized studies of on- and off-pump
CABG result in equivalent cognitive outcomes. Second, if
patients undergoing interventional cardiology procedures
have the same cognitive outcomes as cardiac surgical
patients, it will appear that chronic cerebral vascular
disease may constitute the foundation of ‘‘postoperative’’
cognitive decline. Finally, it appears that cognitive decline
is a nonspeciﬁc event occurring in older patients following
noncardiac as well as cardiac surgery. The frequency and
severity may be higher in cardiac surgery simply because it
is more physiologically stressful than noncardiac surgery. Exquisite control of many physiologic variables is
possible during CPB and in the perioperative period. Until
effective interventions to improve neurologic outcomes
are more clearly identiﬁed, we will help our patients most
by understanding their risk factors and placing them in a
physiologic milieu that minimizes the impact of surgical
stressors while maximizing compensatory mechanisms. KEY POINTS
■Cardiac surgery patients undergoing CPB have a
higher risk for neurologic morbidity and mortality than noncardiac surgical patients. Risk factors
include age, preexisting neurologic disease, aortic
atherosclerosis, low cardiac output states, hypertension, arrhythmias, and diabetes mellitus. Advanced
age appears to be the most inﬂuential single risk
factor, with aortic atherosclerosis perhaps close behind. Preoperative cerebral imaging studies indicate
that over half of the neurologically asymptomatic
patients who present for CABG have preexisting cerebral pathology such as lacunar infarcts. ■A variety of physiologic circumstances surrounding
CPB may either predispose to or aggravate neurologic complications. Prominent among these factors
are perfusion ﬂows and pressures, the inﬂamma-
tory response to CPB, changes in CNS temperature,
acid–base management, metabolic disturbances such
as hyperglycemia, and embolic phenomena.

■Factors inﬂuencing CBF during CPB include CMRO2,
PaCO2, Hct, and MAP. Once MAP drops below a
critical threshold, CBF becomes pressure passive regardless of pump ﬂow in animal models. Human
studies also suggest that CDO2 may be compromised
at MAPs below 50 mm Hg during CPB, and possibly
at higher levels such as 60 mm Hg in patients whose
cerebral autoregulatory relations are abnormal. ■A variety of physiologic strategies have been attempted or suggested as ways to improve neurologic
outcomes following CPB. To date, the data supporting any speciﬁc strategy fall below the desired levels
of scientiﬁc rigor. However, there is sufﬁcient evidence to suggest the following during CPB:
●MAPs should exceed 50 mm Hg. ●There is no advantage to pulsatile ﬂow. ●Hyperglycemia should be avoided, but there is
controversy about the maximum acceptable blood
glucose level. ●Adults beneﬁt from α-stat acid–base management. Infants may beneﬁt from pH-stat management,
especially in the setting of deep hypothermia. ●Cerebral hyperthermia should be avoided. ■Despite some studies supporting prophylactic pharmacologic protective strategies such as thiopental,
the overall strength of evidence about pharmacologic
cerebral protection during CPB remains uncompelling. ■Studies have investigated a variety of cerebral monitoring strategies such as raw and processed EEG,
SjvO2, TCD, and transcutaneous NIRS. Available evidence to date fails to support any speciﬁc cerebral
monitor as a means to reduce neurologic complications of CPB. REFERENCES

HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
Historical perspective is particularly important in assessing the progression of techniques for hemodilution and
how they affect the physiology of extracorporeal circulation and the development of related complications. John
Gibbon (1), who developed the ﬁrst heart–lung machine
and performed the ﬁrst successful surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), envisioned a perfusion technique
employing a prime of normal composition (i.e., blood)
with ‘‘normal’’ ﬂow rates (70–80 mL/kg/min) and normal blood pressure. Kirklin et al. (2) continued Gibbon’s
original methods when he withdrew from this area of
research. Lillehei et al., ﬁrst in their procedures with controlled
cross circulation (3) and then with CPB (4), employed
signiﬁcantly lower ﬂow rates (30–35 mL/kg/min) than did
Gibbon. This modiﬁcation (based on the ‘‘azygous ﬂow
principle’’) (5) was derived from the observation that dogs
could survive when both the superior and inferior vena
cavae were occluded, because the azygous venous drainage
of dogs, unlike that of humans, still provided venous
return to the heart because of its more central conﬂuence
with the superior vena cava. In humans, this amount of
ﬂow (10% of normal cardiac output) proved adequate for
survival for up to 1 hour. This observation was rapidly
accepted and applied to the practice of CPB by many of
those who perceived the harm to blood elements by use
of high ﬂows and the excessive suctioning that results. Hypothermia was added to many high ﬂow rate and
most low ﬂow rate techniques to ‘‘protect’’ various organs,
although Lillehei’s original cross-circulation procedures
were carried out at normothermia (3). Despite lower ﬂows,
the priming solution for the extracorporeal circuit with
oxygenator remained the same—whole blood, which was
either freshly drawn and heparinized or collected into
citrated bags, but as fresh as possible. Spurred by animal research and the occasional emergent clinical experience with asanguinous prime, surgeons
began electively using crystalloid solution or plasmaexpanding colloids around 1960 to reduce or eliminate
blood from the prime (Table 1). Hypothermia was now
increasingly applied to protect organs from the ‘‘adverse
effects’’ of not only low ﬂow but also hemodilution. Nevertheless, the technique of hemodilution gained increasing
popularity; currently it is used almost universally.

It should be noted that the following discussion pertains
to short-duration, clinical CPB used in the aid of cardiac
surgery. Applicability of hemodilution to longer CPB
support times is discussed elsewhere. IMMEDIATE BENEFITS
OF HEMODILUTION
A main reason for employing asanguinous primes was to
reduce the severe strain placed on hospital blood banks
by the use of whole blood for priming CPB circuits. The need for at least two units of whole blood—and
possibly as many as ﬁve or six—just for use as prime
in each patient often caused severe logistic problems for
physicians trying to run an active cardiac surgical service. Many cases were postponed for lack of the correct type or
amount of blood. Crystalloid primes also improved access

OF HEMODILUTION
Rheology of Blood
A detailed review of the rheologic properties of blood
is beyond the scope of this chapter. However, some basic
deﬁnitions and concepts are required, because the changes
in blood rheology induced by hemodilution are central to
any discussion of hemodilution physiology. Exhaustive
reviews may be found elsewhere (12,13). A force applied to an area of a liquid conﬁned between
two plates, sufﬁcient to set the liquid in motion, is known
as shear stress. The velocity at which the liquid moves
in proportion to the separation of the plates is known
as the velocity gradient, or shear rate.

The shear stress
is proportional to the shear rate, and the coefﬁcient of
proportionality is the ﬂuid viscosity (Eq. 1). Shear stress = Viscosity × shear rate

For most uniform ﬂuids, such as water, viscosity is
constant; these are known as newtonian ﬂuids. The
viscosity of blood is not constant; rather, it depends on
the shear rate when ﬂowing (Fig. 1). Therefore, blood is
a non–newtonian ﬂuid. Lower shear rates are associated
with higher viscosity, because the cellular elements and
plasma proteins tend to aggregate, form rouleaux, and
resist ﬂow. This aggregation at low shear rates primarily
results from intracellular bridging by ﬁbrinogen; as ﬂow
rates increase, these bridges disintegrate. Non–newtonian behavior of blood is also inﬂuenced
by the effective cell volume (14). When solid particles
(cells) are added to a ﬂuid, they inﬂuence viscosity not
only by their absolute presence but also by their effect
on the surrounding ﬂuid. The effective cell volume is the
cell volume plus the surrounding ﬂuid that behaves as
though it were a part of the cell—much like the earth and
its atmosphere. Red blood cells are deformable, and as
shear rates increase, they tend to form ellipsoid shapes,
with their major axes aligned with the direction of ﬂow. This latter effect, combined with the disaggregation of red
cells, causes blood to behave in a more newtonian manner
at higher velocity gradients. One further concept about the behavior of ﬂuids is
important. The amount of shear stress that must be
applied to a stationary newtonian liquid to begin its
movement is at or near zero. For non–newtonian blood,
because of cellular geometry and aggregation, a force
known as the yield stress is required to induce ﬂow.

At
low shear rates, the yield stress represents part of the
viscous resistance and depends on both ﬁbrinogen and
hematocrit (15).

perfusion pressure would tend to increase viscosity and,
thereby, peripheral resistance. In turn, this would decrease
tissue perfusion. Hemodilution works to limit the adverse
effects of CPB by signiﬁcantly reducing blood viscosity
during bypass. Because there is a direct relation between
viscosity and hematocrit (12) (Fig. 1), reducing hematocrit
produces a marked decrease in total resistance and results
in an increase in tissue perfusion (Eq. 2B). For example,
in canine experiments, a decrease in hematocrit from
42% to 25% produces a 50% increase in ﬂow at the
same pressure (16). Extremes of hemodilution (hematocrit
<10%) permit blood to act as a newtonian ﬂuid (17).

Considerations in Oxygen Transport
Hemoglobin Physiology
Oxygen transport is the movement of molecular oxygen
from the atmosphere to the cellular mitochondria. This
movement depends on oxygen availability, cardiac output,
hemoglobin, tissue perfusion, and the tissues’ ability
to extract oxygen. Hemoglobin provides a tremendous
physiologic advantage to the process of oxygen transport
in that relatively larger volumes of oxygen can be brought
to the tissues bound to the hemoglobin molecule than
could be transported in a simple solution in the plasma. Reduction of hemoglobin concentrations to below normal levels still permits adequate oxygen transfer. In fact,
when oxygen transport is expressed as the product of cardiac output and oxygen-carrying capacity, and is plotted
against changes in hematocrit (Fig. 5), maximal delivery occurs at a hematocrit of approximately 30%; more
importantly, delivery decreases only approximately 10%
below normal between hematocrits of 20% and 50% (26). This preservation of oxygen delivery obviously depends

will decrease oxygen delivery, but this is usually well tolerated clinically. The lower limit to which hemoglobin can
be reduced under any circumstance without any compromise on patient’s safety is not known absolutely (discussed
later). On the basis of the earlier discussed oxygen transport concepts, a hemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL was
traditionally (and institutionally) accepted as adequate for
patients undergoing noncardiac surgery; however, it has
now been demonstrated that a level of 8 g/dL does not

The oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin is inﬂu-
enced by pH, PCO2, temperature, concentration of 2,3-
diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), and the speciﬁc type
of hemoglobin. These factors may shift the oxygen–
hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right (easier dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin—higher P50) or
to the left (more ﬁrmly attached oxygen—lower P50). Metabolic acidosis, hypercarbia, hyperthermia, increased
levels of 2,3-DPG, and anemia shift the curve to the right,
whereas metabolic alkalosis, hypocarbia, decreased 2,3-
DPG, and hypothermia shift it to the left. Abnormal forms
of hemoglobin may have a normal, increased, or decreased
afﬁnity for oxygen. The absolute clinical signiﬁcance of
each of these inﬂuences is not known. Physiology of Chronic Anemia
Chronic anemia, or reduction in the volume of circulating
red blood cells, tends to develop gradually and permit
compensation. These mechanisms include an increase
in plasma volume to maintain a euvolemic or even
hypervolemic state, an increase in heart rate and stroke
volume, and a passive (but real) increase in cardiac output
as a result of decreased viscosity. In healthy humans, this
occurs with little or no increase in myocardial oxygen
extraction (16).

Another compensatory mechanism is the
increased oxygen extraction by tissues, often associated
with a decrease in the afﬁnity of hemoglobin for oxygen
(produced by an increase in the 2,3-DPG level in the red
blood cells). This mechanism is not usually operative at
hemoglobin levels that are continuously above 7 g/dL (16). Reduction in physical activity with a subsequent decrease in oxygen consumption is an important additional
mechanism. Chronically anemic patients who are well
compensated may be compromised if metabolic demands
are increased (e.g., by enhanced physical activity, fever,
or an inability to increase cardiac output secondary to
intrinsic or acquired heart disease). In this context, anesthetized patients will demonstrate improved tolerance to
anemia because of reduced total body oxygen consumption (overall, ∼15%) and, especially, a reduced myocardial
oxygen demand (28). Hypothermia is an important physiologic method for reducing oxygen utilization by tissues
and has a greater or lesser role to play, depending on
the clinical circumstances. Again, anesthesia has a sig-
niﬁcant role because the compensatory mechanisms that
maintain normothermia, such as shivering, are blocked
by anesthesia and muscle relaxation. The acute anemia produced by hemodilution coupled
with lower than normal ﬂow rates at CPB initiation
must also be associated with operative compensatory
mechanisms to permit adequate oxygen delivery. These
include general anesthesia and muscle relaxation, normovolemia, improved microcirculatory perfusion as a
consequence of decreased viscosity, and, sometimes, induced hypothermia. Hemodilution and Complications
of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Despite the early success of open-heart surgeries in which
CPB was used, a high rate of complications was common.

Speciﬁcally, CPB was associated with postoperative neurologic, pulmonary, and renal dysfunction, which were
seen with both high and low ﬂow rates, and each was
attributed to a variety of physiologic or clinical factors. Neurologic dysfunction was thought to be associated
with low perfusion pressures. Stockard et al. (29) mathematically related an increased incidence of neurologic
complications to the degree and duration of hypotension. Pulmonary complications (postperfusion pulmonary in-
sufﬁciency, ‘‘pump lung’’) were attributed to parenchymal
hypoxia, pulmonary venous distension, the oxygenator itself, or other mechanical factors (30). Renal failure was
primarily related to low perfusion pressure and, secondarily, to low urine output during CPB (31). When Cooley
et al. (9) reported their ﬁrst 100 cases in which hemodilution with dextrose and water prime was used, they
anecdotally noted a reduction in postoperative cerebral,
pulmonary, and renal complications. Hemodilution may
have been instrumental in the reduction of morbidity
associated with CPB for each of these organ systems. The uncoupling of ﬂow and pressure with hemodilution, as discussed earlier, modiﬁes the relation between
perfusion pressure and neurologic complications. In all
the patients described by Stockard et al. (29), blood
prime was used for CPB. The relation between perfusion
pressure and the incidence of neurologic complications
has disappeared, because hemodilution has been universally adopted (32,33). Subsequent reports by Govier
et al. (34) and Prough et al. (35) have also demonstrated
the maintenance of cerebral autoregulation in patients
undergoing hemodilution at varying levels of ﬂow, temperature, and PCO2. Similar differences in reports of renal dysfunction
with and without blood priming are also revealing. Bhat
et al. (31) found bypass time, low perfusion pressure,
volume of urine formed during CPB, and hemoglobinemia
to be factors for postoperative dysfunction when blood
priming was employed. In the same year, Abel et al. (36)
found none of these factors to be predictive when
hemodilution was used. However, it did appear then
that in the absence of low cardiac output before or after
CPB or excessive perioperative transfusion, preoperative
renal dysfunction was the only predictor of postoperative
dysfunction (33). More recent evidence has made this
point debatable. Postperfusion respiratory failure still
occurs for multiple reasons, but these are often related
to extrapulmonary factors (37). The ‘‘pump lung’’ of the
1960s has markedly decreased in incidence, and this is at
least partly because of hemodilution techniques (9,38).

Another problem, referred to as homologous blood
syndrome, was blamed for both intraoperative and postoperative bleeding diatheses and also for contributing
to postoperative cerebral, pulmonary, and renal dysfunction (39). The syndrome was sometimes thought to
result from incompatibility or cross-reactions between
the patient and one or more of the multiple units of
donor blood used in the prime. More likely, with correct
donor–patient cross matching, it represented a reaction
occurring between units of homologous blood from different donors mixing together in the CPB circuit before
bypass. Whatever the exact mechanism, it too disappeared
with the introduction of crystalloid priming. Hemodilution is not solely responsible for the reduction
in complications associated with CPB. Other factors, such
as more accurate initial diagnoses, improved anesthetic
methods, better CPB equipment, and quicker recognition
and treatment of ventricular failure, have all contributed. Speciﬁcally, blood ﬁltering helps decrease pulmonary
complications (40), and less suctioning of the operative
ﬁeld helps reduce hemolysis and thereby decrease the
incidence of renal dysfunction. PRIMING SOLUTIONS
Crystalloid Primes
Currently, the use of a crystalloid priming solution is the
norm during CPB. There is probably as much institutional
variation in speciﬁc primes and components as there
is in cardioplegic solutions, because they both have
developed in an empiric manner. In general, modern
priming solutions have a similar electrolyte-to-plasma
content and a similar osmolarity. Balanced salt solution,
such as lactated Ringers solution, with or without glucose,
is a common, basic priming solution. Many believe that
the addition of colloid may be justiﬁed in perfusion
procedures of long duration to prevent the development of
excessive edema. In addition to institutional variations in
the types of priming ﬂuids used, differences in the volume
are also common, as a consequence of the differences
in priming requirements for the variety of oxygenators,
connective tubing, and arterial ﬁlters employed. Some
institutions have a ‘‘standard’’ prime volume that is used
for all adult patients, whereas others vary the volume
depending on the patient’s weight or body surface area. Each speciﬁc oxygenator-tubing system will obviously
have a minimum ‘‘safe’’ priming volume—that is, one that
will allow the initiation of CPB without undue risk for air
embolism and willpermit adequate ﬂow rates. The degree of hemodilution can be predicted based
on patient’s weight and hematocrit, the amount of
intravenous ﬂuids administered before CPB, and the
oxygenator priming volume.

The blood volume can be
calculated by multiplying the weight of the patient in
kilograms by 7% (for women) or 7.5% (for men) (Table 2). If use of the intended prime volume causes unacceptable
hemodilution, then packed red blood cells can be added
to the CPB circuit to compensate for its occurrence. Children, especially infants, present a special problem
because pediatric CPB circuits, even with efforts at

The degree of allowable hemodilution is an important consideration in the composition of the initial prime. There
are also large institutional variations in the range of ‘‘acceptable’’ hemodilution. In general, because hemodilution
has a salutary effect on perfusion and there is a theoretical decrease in microcirculatory ﬂow with hematocrit
above 30% (16), most centers try to achieve a hematocrit
below 30% during CPB. With priming volumes in the
range of 1,400 mL to 2,000 mL, this is easily achieved
in most adults. Patients with large blood volumes, high
hematocrits, or both, may require prepump phlebotomy
or additional dilution while on CPB (Table 2). Hypothermia also inﬂuences the acceptable range
of hematocrit, but guidelines are again institutional. Because of the viscosity–ﬂow relation and the inﬂuence
of hypothermia, it is appropriate to target a hematocrit
of less than 30% if the temperature is reduced to
30◦C, and lower hematocrits, generally below 25%, are
preferred if temperatures are to be reduced below 25◦C. Experimental evidence suggests that a hematocrit below
20% may be associated with an abnormal distribution
of ﬂow to the organs (41,42). However, a hematocrit
below this level appears to be well tolerated clinically,
with values in the range of 15% to 18% commonly seen
during the initial stages of CPB. Physiologic compensatory
mechanisms may be involved, in addition to the beneﬁts of
anesthesia and hypothermia.

Even extreme hemodilution
to a hematocrit below 15%, used by some centers for
hypothermic circulatory arrest or sometimes in patients
who are Jehovah’s Witnesses (11), appears to be clinically
well tolerated (43). However, this concept has been
challenged, at least in hypothermic circulatory arrest,
by researchers at Harvard who found improved cerebral
recovery in animal experiments in which the hematocrit

in infants maintained at higher hematocrit levels (45). When considering management of patients who have
hematocrit levels below an institutional minimum and,
speciﬁcally, if transfusion should be used, the reasons for
the resulting values must be evaluated ﬁrst. The multiple
factors listed in Table 3 will have an effect on the hematocrit value during CPB. Obviously, efforts to limit their
inﬂuence, including establishing meticulous hemostasis,
conserving intravenous ﬂuids, and minimizing priming
volume (if possible), can affect each patient differently. Also, the timing of blood sampling may have an inﬂuence. A
sample taken a short time after initiation of CPB may show
more apparent hemodilution than would a sample drawn
later, when equilibration between the prime and patient’s
blood volume has been achieved. The initial sample, even
if timed appropriately, usually has the lowest hematocrit
of all samples in routine CPB cases, because equilibration
and ﬂuid loss to the interstitial space tend to cause hemoconcentration asbypassprogresses. In general, transfusion
decisions should not be made on the basis of the ﬁrst hematocrit reading, unless the clinician is convinced that the
patient is hypovolemic and that treating the hypovolemia
with ﬂuid will reduce the hematocrit further and/or that
the value is far outside institutional norms. During CPB,
hemoconcentration (ultraﬁltration) devices in the circuit
may be used as an alternative to transfusion when patients
are anemic and have a very large circulating volume. Over the last several years, questions have been raised
concerning hematocrit levels during CPB and their association with outcome.

Several separate reports concerning
adult patients have described an association between nadir
hematocrit on CPB and an increased incidence of postoperative complications (46–51), including neurologic,
myocardial (low-output syndrome), pulmonary, and renal complications, longer hospital stays, and increased
mortality. Most studies show the strongest association
between nadir hematocrit on CPB and renal complications. However, other studies have found different levels
of hematocrit that appeared important, ranging from 14
to 25. All the authors of these studies advocate keeping

418
IV. Hematology
hematocrit levels above a certain value by various means
of limiting hemodilution, and none of them promote transfusion itself as a method of compensating for lower hematocrit levels. Some of these studies, and others (52,53),
also show an association of increased complications in
patients requiring transfusion, other than the commonly
known complications of infectious disease and transfusion reactions. It is easy to assume that, in addition to
their other morbidities, ‘‘sick,’’ high-risk patients will have
lower hematocrit levels and therefore will have more perioperative complications and require more transfusions,
with anemia being only a marker for their high risk. The
question of transfusion efﬁcacy and its absolute effect on
outcome remains unresolved (54). Another consideration in allowable hemodilution is
an acceptable hematocrit level for weaning from bypass. Here too, there is much institutional variation and few
hard data. Because maldistribution of coronary ﬂow
away from the subendocardium occurs experimentally
with a hematocrit at or below 15% (42,55), especially
if the coronary circulation is compromised, it would
seem prudent to separate from bypass with a hematocrit
above this level. Evidence of myocardial ischemia would
be a further cause to transfuse. An argument against
maintenance of a higher hematocrit (≥34%) is that
it has been associated with a greater risk of Q-wave
myocardial infarction, worsened left ventricular function,
and mortality after coronary artery bypass grafting (56). The safety of hemodilution, especially with crystalloid
solutions, was initially questioned because of fear of increased postoperative bleeding secondary to dilutional
coagulopathy. These fears proved unfounded in general,
even with extreme hemodilution (57). In polycythemic
patients with congenital heart disease, adequate hemodilution (hematocrit <30%) has been associated with a
decreased incidence of postoperative coagulopathies (58). Use of Glucose
For the last several years, there has been considerable
debate over intraoperative glucose management (59) and
intraoperative use of glucose-containing ﬂuids in general. Originally, data from a series of noncardiac surgical
cases showed an association between worsened neurologic
outcome and hyperglycemia (60). These data subsequently
affected the management of CPB prime because the use of
glucose-containing ﬂuids was widespread. However, more
recent data on management of intraoperative glucose have
shown improved outcomes, particularly in patients with
wound infections, when tighter control of blood glucose
concentration is maintained than when hyperglycemia is
treated in a less rigid manner.

A focus on more rigid
control of glucose levels in critically ill patients in the
intensive care unit has led to efforts by many to maintain
glucose levels during CPB that are less than some arbitrary
value by using insulin infusions and removing glucose
from crystalloid priming solutions (61). In contrast, Metz and Keats (62) have shown that the
addition of glucose to priming solutions raises the osmotic
pressure of the prime and signiﬁcantly reduces perioperative ﬂuid requirements and postoperative ﬂuid retention. Also, use of insulin infusions in patients on CPB has been
associated with postoperative hypoglycemia, which is another risk factor for neurologic complications (63). The
seeming lack of complications in the use of glucose during
CPB for many years may relate to the putative mechanism, as both animal and human data suggest that central
nervous system damage associated with hyperglycemia
occurs when either global or focal injury is followed by
immediate reperfusion of the ischemic area (64). Cerebral
injury after CPB, in the absence of low cardiac output, is
almost always embolic in origin, and areas affected would
not be expected to be reperfused immediately. Nevertheless, efforts at intraoperative glucose control—speciﬁcally
during CPB—are very appealing, despite the demonstrable
beneﬁcial effects with regard to ﬂuid requirements. The use of glucose may be advocated for patients in
whom the maintenance of high osmotic pressure in the
CPB prime is important and for whom use of bloodderived colloidal solutions may be restricted (such as
patients who are members of the Jehovah’s Witness faith). Colloidal Prime
A consequence of hemodilution in CPB is the decrease
in the plasma colloidal oncotic pressure secondary to
dilution of the circulating plasma proteins. This may
result, especially in the absence of glucose, in increased
movement of ﬂuid out of the vascular space and into
the interstitial and intracellular spaces, which can lead
to postoperative edema and be associated with lung
or other organ dysfunction. In an effort to attenuate
these changes, the addition of colloidal particles to a
crystalloid prime, or even the use of a colloidal solution
as the principal priming ﬂuid, has been advocated. Solutions used include 5% and 25% albumin, low and high
molecular weight dextran, 5% plasma protein fraction, 6%
hydroxyethyl starch, and human plasma.

These solutions
have been compared, in various combinations, with a
crystalloid prime alone or with each other. Differences
in lung water or total body water are reported between
groups, most notably immediately after bypass, but these
differences tend to diminish quickly in the immediate
postoperative period (65,66). The relative importance of
colloid in short-term CPB is therefore hard to judge,
and individual decisions can be made on the basis of
availability and cost. No signiﬁcant harm is associated
with synthetic or heat-treated colloid, but there is an
increased cost. Human plasma should not be used
without a speciﬁc indication, usually a clinically apparent

Additional components that have been used for varying
reasons in primes are listed in Table 4, with the rationale
for the use of each one. Much institutional variation exists
here as well. Experimental Priming Solutions
The use of oxygen-carrying solutions in CPB has paralleled
their experimental use as blood substitutes in noncardiac
surgery and has been conﬁned to four types: perﬂuorocar-
bons, cross-linked hemoglobin, polymerized hemoglobin,
and conjugated hemoglobin. The evaluation of these liquids, which can carry relatively large amounts of dissolved
oxygen in comparison with untreated human plasma, has
been under way for several years. Beneﬁts of their use
include their ability to permit oxygen delivery even in the
face of profound native anemia. Because they are insoluble in blood, perﬂuorocarbons
(also known as ﬂuorocarbons) must be emulsiﬁed before
use. They are nearly chemically inert substances with a
high natural solubility for oxygen. Their oxygen solubility
is linear, unlike that of hemoglobin, and because of this,
they are able to release oxygen in very low PO2 environments (67). The release of oxygen by perﬂuorocarbons
is not related to pH or temperature (68). Perﬂuorocar-
bon particles are small (0.118 µm), and their viscosity is
roughly half that of blood; these characteristics allow them
to bypass stiffened red blood cells readily and perfuse distal capillary beds (67). However, when perﬂuorocarbons
were used in patients belonging to the Jehovah’s Witness faith who were profoundly anemic, survival did not
increase (69).

Substitution of a hemoglobin-containing solution for
the transfusion of red blood cells would seem ideal
because of its natural oxygen-carrying capacity and
its osmotic activity in solution. Hemoglobin solutions
have a number of beneﬁts over banked blood: they are
readily available and have a long shelf life, and they
do not require blood typing or cross matching (70). Although hemoglobin solutions were thought to be free of
infectious contamination, this has been questioned (71). They do not cause immunosuppression, as blood can. The viscosity of hemoglobin-based substitutes, like that of
perﬂuorocarbons, is low. Bovine hemoglobin, chemically
cross-linked to prevent its ﬁltration by the kidneys, has a
low oxygen afﬁnity, similar to that of human hemoglobin
in erythrocytes (72). Despite promising theoretical advantages and a great
deal of effort by many researchers and organizations
over the last two decades, these blood substitutes are
not used clinically in the United States, mainly because of
unexpected safety concerns and unanticipated physiologic
effects, such as vasoconstriction. In fact, several clinical
trials of these products have been suspended and the
agents withdrawn. Although a few of these agents remain
at various stages of evaluation and some are used
elsewhere, none appears to be close to release in the
United States (73). ASSESSING ADEQUACY
OF PERFUSION WITH HEMODILUTION
The most notable effect of the use of modern asanguinous
priming solutions, as stated earlier, is a marked decrease in
perfusion pressure with institution of bypass. In almost all
instances, this is secondary to the resulting hemodilution
and corresponding decrease in viscosity, not to dilution
of circulating catecholamines or vasodilation (Fig. 2). Because hemodilution results in uncoupling of the relation
between perfusion pressure and blood ﬂow, the adequacy
of perfusion must be assessed by means other than blood
pressure. Standard ﬂow rates of 50 mL/kg/min or 2
L/m2/min are a tested reference, although they may be
modiﬁed by age, weight, or temperature.

420
IV. Hematology
Monitoring of organ perfusion is probably the most reliable method of determining adequate perfusion during
CPB with hemodilution; however, clinical methods of
monitoring are most often indirect and inadequate. Global cerebral function can be monitored by electroencephalographic means, blood ﬂow velocity by transcranial
Doppler, and oxygen saturation by near-infrared spectroscopy, but whether such monitoring confers the ability
to detect and modify an impending central nervous system adverse event is still open to question. The obvious
parameter of renal function, urinary output, is easily and
virtually uniformly measured, but clinical studies have
shown that the volume of urine produced during CPB has
little or no bearing on postoperative renal function. Measurement of arterial blood gases will monitor oxygenator
function, and measurement of mixed venous oxygen tension may detect inadequate perfusion. However, a normal
mixed venous oxygen tension does not ensure adequate
regional perfusion because it may not reﬂect local organ
conditions. SUMMARY
In summary, hemodilution probably represents the most
signiﬁcant advance in CPB technique after the development of the pump oxygenator itself. It permits the
maintenance of organ homeostasis under what would otherwise be often inadequate circumstances, with a resultant
decrease in complications and a conservation of blood resources. The absolute limits of hemodilution, however,
despite all that has been learned with more than 50 years
of CPB technique, are still signiﬁcantly uncertain. KEY POINTS
Hemodilution
■Advantages of hemodilution include the following:
●Decreased blood viscosity
●Improved regional blood ﬂow
●Improved oxygen delivery to tissues
●Decreased exposure to homologous blood products
●Improved blood ﬂow at lower perfusion pressure
(lower shear stress), especially during hypothermic
perfusion
■Hemodilution affects the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of drugs used during CPB,
predominantly by changing protein binding through
dilution of plasma proteins. ■Hemodilution decreases bypass-related complications (neurologic, renal, and pulmonary), but there
appears to be an association between a hematocrit
below a certain level and increased complications. CPB priming solutions
■Crystalloid priming solutions are the norm in the
present-day practice of CPB. ●The most commonly used solutions are ‘‘balanced
salt’’ or ‘‘physiologic saline’’ types. ●The use of 5% dextrose was common, but complications associated with hyperglycemia have led to
its withdrawal in most practices. ●Hyperglycemia during and after CPB may predispose the patient to neurologic damage and
infectious complications, but any adverse consequences of the control efforts are not deﬁned.

●Colloidal solutions (e.g., albumin, hydroxyethyl
starch) are widely used empirically as priming
components. ●Oxygen-carrying colloidal solutions of perﬂuoro-
carbons or hemoglobin have much promise, but
unanticipated problems with efﬁcacy and safety
have delayed their clinical use in the United States. REFERENCES

◗The Blood–Surface Interface
L. Henry Edmunds, Jr. Extracorporeal circulation (ECC) and open-heart surgery
(OHS) expose the entire blood mass to biomaterials in the
perfusion circuit and nonendothelial cells in the wound. Normally blood cells and proteins interface only with endothelium, which maintains the ﬂuidity of blood and the
integrity of the vascular system. Blood contact with nonendothelial surfaces, whether biomaterial, gas, basement
membrane, somatic cell membrane, or interstitial matrix,
potentiates thrombosis and triggers a defense reaction that
varies in intensity between patients and extracorporeal
systems, and as a result, hemostasis, ﬂuid balance, cellular
metabolism, and organ function are disturbed to varying degrees. This chapter presents a simpliﬁed overview
of the pathophysiological and biochemical challenges to
this homeostasis produced by the interaction between
circulating blood and nonendothelial cell surfaces in all
applications of ECC. Blood exists in ﬂuid and gel forms and its physical state
at any point in time depends on a delicate balance between
procoagulants and anticoagulants. Endothelial cells produce a long menu of anticoagulants and procoagulants,
which actively maintain this equilibrium (1,2) (Table 1). All extracorporeal perfusion systems tip this balance toward thrombosis, but the intensity of the stimulus varies
widely within and between perfusion systems. Only the
endothelial cell is nonthrombogenic; all other surfaces are
thrombogenic in comparison. Therefore, ECC is not possible without anticoagulation. Although new direct thrombin inhibitors are being tested
(3–7), for the moment heparin remains the best anticoagulant for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) because of wide
and generally satisfactory experience and because heparin
is rapidly reversed with protamine. CPB for OHS requires high concentrations of heparin to maintain the ﬂuidity of blood during perfusion. Unfractionated or standard heparin has both advantages
and disadvantages; protamine is the most notable advantage. Heparin, however, is a cofactor that does not
directly inhibit coagulation; heparin accelerates the actions of the natural serine protease, antithrombin (8). Antithrombin primarily binds thrombin; it absorbs to
factors Xa and IXa, but more slowly. During CPB the
latter is inconsequential. Low molecular weight heparin,
which is contraindicated for CPB (9), acts primarily on
factor Xa. Therefore heparin inhibits coagulation at the
end of the cascade after most coagulation proteins have
been converted to active enzymes. Antithrombin is a large
molecule (58 kDa) and heparin does not inhibit thrombin
trapped within clots (10).

Heparin is also an agonist for
several blood constituents: platelets (11–13), factor XII
(14), complement, neutrophils, and monocytes (15–17). Heparin concentrations are difﬁcult to monitor in the

Blood is a tissue that reacts with all nonendothelial
cell surfaces, including gas bubbles. Biomaterials are
created to minimize this reaction and to be tolerably
compatible with viable human cells and tissues. After a
half century of effort, no nonthrombogenic, unreactive
biomaterial exists. Nevertheless, a substantial number
of usable synthetic polymers, metals, ceramics, carbons,
treated biologic materials, and various surface coatings
have been developed for use as biomaterials (27–29). These
materials, including those used for ECC, are required to
meet demanding manufacturing standards for physical
properties; chemical inertness; absence of hemolysis,
immunogenicity, and toxicity; feasibility of fabrication;
ability to be sterilized; durability; and costs. None of
these materials are nonthrombogenic and none prevents
the formation of thrombin. Some biomaterials reduce
activation of complement and adhesion of platelets and
leukocytes. The interaction between heparinized blood and biomaterial surfaces is complex, dynamic, and speciﬁc for each
biomaterial and for each individual’s blood. Plasma proteins from bulk blood instantaneously (<1 second) adsorb
onto biomaterial surfaces upon contact (30) (Fig. 1). The
adsorbed proteins form a monolayer of selected proteins
that differ in concentrations from those in bulk plasma
(30–32). Adsorbed proteins ‘‘compete’’ for space on the
biomaterial surface and are tightly packed, irreversibly
bound, and immobile. Calculations indicate that the density of surface-adsorbed proteins is two to three orders
of magnitude greater than the density of proteins in bulk
plasma (33). The physical and chemical attributes of the biomaterial surface determine the intrinsic surface activity of the
adsorbed proteins and topography of the protein layer. Surface chemistry of solid biomaterials differs from the
bulk chemistry, and surface molecules are very reactive,
often mobile, and easily contaminated by other molecular compounds (35). The surface mosaic of the protein
monolayer is speciﬁc for the biomaterial and for the concentrations of each protein in plasma, yet the topography
of the adsorbed protein layer may not be uniform across
the biomaterial surface (33).
Furthermore, surface concentrations of adsorbed proteins may change over time (32). On most biomaterial surfaces ﬁbrinogen is selectively adsorbed (32), but von Willebrand factor (vWF), ﬁbronectin,

monocyte synthesis of tissue factor may be facilitated by
adsorbed platelets (55).

BLOOD PROTEINS AND CELLS
The interface between heparinized blood and both the
wound and perfusion circuit is the product of multiple,
separate reactions between circulating blood constituents,
nonendothelial cell tissues, and an undeﬁned monolayer
of adsorbed proteins on synthetic biomaterial surfaces. An inﬁnite number of small reactions abruptly change the
composition of circulating blood, which in turn triggers
responses from normal endothelial cells lining the heart
and blood vessels. A generalized acute inﬂammatory
reaction ensues and is appropriately described as ‘‘the
whole-body inﬂammatory response’’ (56). To varying
degrees, circulating blood cells, proteins, lipids, and other
molecules are transformed into an enzymatic stew of
activated cells and cytotoxins. ECC exposes every living
cell to injury and paradoxically turns the defense reaction
(57), which was evolved to protect against injurious
agents, against itself. As with a raging ﬁre, chaos replaces
homeostasis until subdued. The enzymatic stew produced by CPB and OHS mediates the thrombotic, embolic, bleeding, ﬂuid shifts, and
temporary organ dysfunction associated with CPB and
OHS and all applications of ECC. Platelets, endothelial
cells, neutrophils, and monocytes/macrophages are the
primary cellular contributors involved in thrombin generation and acute inﬂammation. The contact, intrinsic and
extrinsic coagulation, ﬁbrinolytic, and complement proteins are the major participating plasma systems. There
is enormous overlap between the reactions and interactions of these activated cells and reactive molecules
because most react with multiple targets. For this reason
the author has found it helpful to separate the generation of thrombin and clot formation from the acute
inﬂammatory response and to focus on principal mechanisms. This simpliﬁed presentation makes little attempt
to describe the numerically vast mediators of the inﬂam-
matory response and to catalog changes in particular hormones, peptides, cytokines, proteases, metalloproteinases,
phospholipids, eicosanoids, reactive oxygen and nitrogen
species, free radicals, cytotoxins, cellular receptors, and

are also involved in the inﬂammatory response, but their

are deﬁnitely activated during CPB and cardiac surgery;

Formation
Thrombin is the key enzyme involved in thrombosis, ﬁb-
rinolysis, and bleeding, and normally does not circulate,
but is active in clots (10). The enzyme has multiple actions, but the most important are production of ﬁbrin
from ﬁbrinogen, cross-linking ﬁbrin, activating platelets,
and stimulating the production of tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) by endothelial cells. For many years, factors XII and XI and the contact proteins, high molecular weight kininogen and prekallikrein,
were thought to activate factor IX to initiate the intrinsic coagulation pathway (57,64). Factor XIIa is generated
by a conformational change in surface-adsorbed proteins
(33,65) and by heparin (14), and can be demonstrated
in vitro in perfusion circuits (66,67), but the amount
produced is small (45,68,69). Additionally, factor XII de-
ﬁciency does not cause excessive bleeding during OHS
and CPB (70). The present paradigm (Fig. 2) assigns
the major pathway for activating factor IX to the factor VIIa/tissue factor complex, but also recognizes that
during ECC thrombin may directly activate factor XI to
produce factor IXa separately (71). Factor VIIa/tissue factor complex activates factors IX and X; factor VIIa/tissue
factor complex plus factor IX or X on a phospholipid
surface is extrinsic tenase. The assembly of factor IXa,
produced by either extrinsic tenase or factor XIa, and
factor VIIIa, (activated by thrombin) on a phospholipid
surface creates intrinsic tenase. Both tenases generate activated factor X, but intrinsic tenase activates factor X at a
much higher rate than does extrinsic tenase and therefore
predominates (2). Factor Xa forms the prothrombinase
complex with factor Va on a phospholipid surface and
cleaves prothrombin into α-thrombin, the active enzyme,
and prothrombin fragment, F1.2 (2). Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) inhibits activation of both factors IX and X by factor VIIa/tissue
factor complex and effectively slows or stops thrombin
formation (2). During OHS with CPB most thrombin is generated in
the wound by tissue factor, which exists as either cell
bound tissue factor or circulating soluble plasma tissue
factor (72–75) (Fig. 3).

In the wound, cellular tissue factor
is expressed by epicardium, adventia, muscle, fat, and
bone, but is not expressed by pericardium (76). Both
forms of tissue factor activate factor VII to form the factor
VIIa/tissue factor complex, which then activates factors
IX and X. Soluble plasma tissue factor, which contains the 166
amino acids of the extracellular domain of cellular tissue
factor, circulates in 1 to 3 pM concentrations in healthy
individuals (73,75,77,79,80), but is increased several fold
in a wide variety of diseases, including acute coronary
syndromes (81,82), sepsis (83), trauma (84), and OHS
with CPB (72,74,75,85). Soluble plasma tissue factor
requires monocytes, platelets, or microparticles (74,86)
as cofactors to activate factor VII. However, at the
concentrations of soluble plasma tissue factor measured
in patients, activated monocytes in combination with

some platelets adds coagulation factors, platelet activating factor (PAF), and a variety of inﬂammatory mediators,
including lysozymes, to the circulation (1,106,107). Electron microscopic studies demonstrate a mixture of intact

monocytes/macrophages, endothelial cells, and to a lesser extent platelets. During CPB and OHS, complement is activated three times:
in the perfusion circuit and wound (15,109,110), in the
heart after a period of ischemia followed by reperfusion
(111), and during administration of protamine after CPB
(15,17). C-reactive protein (CRP) peaks 2 days after CPB
and OHS and is a potent complement agonist, which may
contribute to delayed clinical symptoms of acute inﬂam-
mation (112). Complement is initially activated by the
classical pathway in the perfusion circuit (15) and perhaps also by conformational changes in surface-adsorbed
C3 (33). However, the alternative pathway, which has a
feedback loop that predominates in the formation of C3a
and C3b, is the major pathway during CPB (17). C3b leads
to cleavage of C5 and formation of the terminal attack
complex, C5b-9 (34). C3a, C5a, and C5b-9 are powerful
anaphylatoxins with vasoactive, cytotoxic, and cell signaling properties (34). C5a and kallikrein are major agonists
for neutrophil activation (94,113), but during CPB several other agonists also activate neutrophils (60). C5a and
C5b-9 also stimulate expression of platelet, endothelial
cell, and macrophage receptors (94). Neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and endothelial
cells are the primary blood cells involved in the acute
inﬂammatory response during ECC. When activated, these
cells express surface receptors and counter-receptors
that slow and then stop passing leukocytes on the
surface of endothelial cells. Neutrophils and peripheral
monocytes migrate into the interstitial space through
endothelial intercellular junctions following a variety
of chemoattractant cytokines, which are produced by
somatic cells, endothelial cells, and leukocytes at sites
of injury (114,115). Neutrophils contain a large variety of
powerful proteolytic and cytotoxic enzymes, chemokines,
cytokines, and arachidonate metabolites in granules that
can be quickly released (59,116), and also contain enzymes
that produce cytotoxic reactive oxidants, free radicals,
and chloramines (117). During CPB, OHS, and ECC,
neutrophils are strongly activated to release granule
contents into the systemic circulation (118–120).

Activated
neutrophils and complement anaphylatoxins are together
the principal actors in the acute inﬂammatory response to
CPB, OHS, and ECC. Monocytes/macrophages are more commonly involved
in chronic inﬂammation and immunity, but contribute
to the acute inﬂammatory reaction associated with CPB
and OHS. Monocytes/macrophages store and synthesize
a vast number of cell mediators and cytotoxins, and destroy microbes and viruses by phagocytosis and remove
particulate and cell debris. Monocytes are activated during CPB by multiple agonists including C5a, thrombin,
and bradykinin (60,75,121–123). Surface receptors are
expressed and circulating inﬂammatory mediators, including early response proinﬂammatory cytokines, are
released (59,60). Many chemokines and cytokines, plus
tissue factor, are synthesized by monocytes so that peak
levels often develop after CPB in the early postoperative
period (121,124–128). Endothelial cells, which maintain the ﬂuidity of blood
and help maintain the integrity of the vascular system,
have an important role in ﬁbrinolysis; they regulate vascular tone and capture circulating leukocytes at sites of
local injury (1). During CPB and OHS, thrombin, C5a,
proinﬂammatory cytokines, oxidants, and other agents activate endothelial cells (1). These agonists induce synthesis
of chemokines and the expression of surface receptors,
principally P- and E-selectin, and later intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and vascular cell adhesion
molecule-1 (VCAM-1), which capture and bind passing
leukocytes and facilitate transmigration into the interstitial space (1,47,129). Endothelial cells produce anticoagulants (Table 1), heparin sulfate and thrombomodulin;
adhesive proteins including vWF; protein S; tissue factor pathway inhibitor; t-PA and urokinase plasminogen
activator; and plasminogen activator inhibitor -1 (1). Endothelial cells also produce vasoactive substances, such as
nitric oxide (NO), PGI2, endothelins (130), and PAF, and
inactivate others, such as histamine, norepinephrine, and
bradykinin (2). During ECC, activated endothelial cells
synthesize tissue factor to generate thrombin, initiate ﬁb-
rinolysis, contribute to the overall acute inﬂammatory
response, and allow ﬂuid and leukocytes to enter the
interstitial space. INTENSITY OF THE DEFENSE
REACTION
Many variables affect the intensity of the defense reaction
during the various applications of ECC. These include
attributes of the perfusion circuit, duration of perfusion, anticoagulation, exposure of blood to the surgical
wound, and multiple patient factors. Therefore, the insult
to homeostasis differs among applications of ECC and
among patients. Rheology of blood ﬂowing through the
perfusion apparatus may promote thrombus formation
and injure blood elements (131–134). Perfusion circuits
need to provide smooth ﬂow paths with minimal shear

stresses and avoid areas of abrupt constriction or expansion. High shear stresses increase platelet activation and
adhesion (135). Areas of stagnation and turbulence promote thrombus; turbulence and cavitation injure blood
elements, produce hemolysis, denature proteins, and generate chylomicrons and fat emboli (103,132,134,136,137). The amount of surface area to which blood is exposed
affects the magnitude of the defense reaction. Because
oxygenators have large surface areas in contact with blood,
the magnitude of blood trauma is much higher during
CPB than in ECC systems that lack an oxygenator. The
ratio of volume ﬂow to surface area inversely affects the
concentration of active coagulation enzymes; therefore
the degree of anticoagulation may be safely reduced in
high ﬂow left and right ventricular assist devices and
artiﬁcial hearts. Likewise, large diameter aortic and major
arterial prosthetic grafts remain patent, whereas small
diameter (3–4 mm) vascular grafts invariably fail (45,138). Duration of exposure of blood to biomaterial surfaces
progressively increases trauma to red cells, proteins,
and other blood elements. Extracorporeal membrane
oxygenation (ECMO), which requires both an oxygenator
and constant blood contact over days, inﬂicts maximal
trauma and produces a consumptive coagulopathy that
requires constant transfusions of homologous blood
products for the duration of perfusion (139–147). As stated earlier, heparin does not prevent thrombin formation or ﬁbrinolysis during ECC and CPB
(21,22,148,149). Thrombin is progressively produced during CPB and OHS although activated clotting times of
more than 400 seconds are maintained. In other applications of ECC, a recent wound may be present and the
amounts of heparin reduced to maintain activated clotting
times between 180 and 220 seconds. This practice, which
generally avoids macroscopic clots and clinically recognized thrombi, nevertheless generates increased thrombin
and ﬁbrinolysis (87,148,150), which is the biochemical
deﬁnition of a consumptive coagulopathy. In adding mechanical circulatory support to a patient with a large fresh
wound, clinicians must stop wound bleeding and simultaneously suppress thrombin formation in the circuit. This
balancing act is greatly facilitated by timely measurements
of prothrombin fragment F1.2 and D-dimer. The wound is the primary site of thrombin generation during CPB and OHS. The wound also contains
high concentrations of C5a and inﬂammatory cytokines
(L. Henry Edmunds Jr., unpublished data, 2003), but nevertheless, wound blood is usually added directly to the
perfusion circuit after ﬁltration.

Washing wound blood in
a cell saver and returning only red cells to the perfusion
circuit substantially reduces the inﬂammatory response
and thrombin generation and is feasible for most surgical
procedures (3,151–153). This practice minimizes thrombin formation and ﬁbrinolysis (3,153,154) and should be
the standard of care despite the increase in costs. Patient factors also cause substantial variations in
the intensity of the inﬂammatory response. Healthy
children and adults without comorbid disease mobilize
the mediators of thrombosis and inﬂammation to greater
intensity than very ill neonates and infants, very elderly
and frail patients, patients with liver or renal disease, and
cachetic patients. Cachetic neonates or patients who have
received heparin infusions before surgery sometimes lack
sufﬁcient antithrombin to allow heparin anticoagulation
and must receive fresh frozen plasma or antithrombin III
preparations before CPB can begin (155). The presence
of comorbid diseases, particularly advanced liver disease,
renal failure, infection, and clotting disorders, affect the
intensity of the defense reaction in individual patients. COMPLICATIONS OF
EXTRACORPOREAL CIRCULATION
The bleeding complications associated with CPB and OHS
are related to pre-existing coagulation deﬁciencies, heparin, activation of platelets, and ﬁbrinolysis. Patients
with pre-existing coagulation deﬁciencies are detected and
treated preoperatively (156). CPB dilutes soluble coagulation factors, reduces factors V and VIII to concentrations
below those expected from dilution (157), but bleeding
rarely, if ever, occurs from this cause. The most common
cause of heparin-related bleeding after CPB is inadequate
neutralization of heparin with protamine. Heparin ‘‘rebound’’ describes an increase in bleeding 1 to 3 hours
after surgery owing to release of heparin bound to the
endothelial cells and macrophages after protamine has
been cleared from the circulation (158). Causes of bleeding related to platelets and ﬁbrinolysis are described in
the preceding text. Discovery of clot within the wound or either clot
or air within the perfusion circuit is an immediate
cause for alarm during cardiac surgery using CPB. The
presence of clot mandates prompt heparin administration;
discovery of air represents a technical error, which
requires immediate location of the source and removal of
the gas. Gas emboli enter from bubble oxygenators, open
stopcocks or breaks in the perfusion circuits, loose purse
string sutures, residual air in the heart, and from rapidly
introducing cold blood into a warm patient (159–161).

CPB produces a variety of large and small emboli
that are reduced but not totally prevented by ﬁltra-
tion (161,162) (Table 3). Blood activation and surgery
itself produce ﬁbrin emboli, macroaggregates of denatured proteins and lipoproteins, fat globules, and platelet
and leukocyte aggregates (136,162,163). The embolic load
is directly proportional to the duration of CPB. Foreign
material may enter the perfusion system. Stored blood
contains platelet and leukocyte aggregates, ﬁbrin, lipid
precipitates, and red cell debris, and should be ﬁltered

of perioperative strokes. before it is added to the perfusate (156,161). Crystalloid solutions may contain inorganic debris, and dust
may remain on the inside of commercially produced tubing and other heart–lung machine components. Roller
pumps cause spallation of bits of compressed tubing
(161). Bubble oxygenators produce gaseous microbubbles (164). Most particulate emboli are aspirated from the wound
by cardiotomy suckers and include ﬁbrin, fat, calcium,
cellular debris, suture material, and other foreign matter
(151,161). Aspiration of large quantities of air produces
nitrogen microbubbles, which are poorly soluble in
plasma. Because of poor solubility these microbubbles are
more dangerous than those of oxygen or carbon dioxide
(160). Blood aspirated from the wound must be ﬁltered
before addition to the perfusion circuit. The surgical procedure is the most important source
of macroemboli and microemboli that produce lasting
damage to the central nervous system (161,165–167). Cannulation and manipulation of the ascending aorta,
particularly in patients with soft atheromatous material
in the aorta, is a major source of atheromatous macroemboli (162,166–168). Microemboli are also produced during
cardiac surgery and may cause postoperative neuropsychologic deﬁcits in proportion to the numbers of emboli
(165,166). Surgical steps, particularly aortic cannulation
and manipulation of either the heart or the aorta, correlate with the highest production of microemboli (165). The
success of specially designed ﬁlters to selectively protect
against cerebral emboli has not been ﬁrmly established
(169,170). Two different types of ﬁlters are in common use: depth
and screen. A depth ﬁlter or a 40-micron (pore size) arterial
line screen ﬁlter removes most, but not all, emboli more
than 40 microns (161). Screen ﬁlters with smaller pore
sizes increase the pressure difference across the ﬁlter and
interfere with pump ﬂow, and are not generally used. During CPB, arterioles, precapillaries, and capillaries are
bombarded with microemboli (<40 µm), but cell death
is diffusely distributed and involves relatively few cells in
any one location.

For the most part, microemboli during
CPB are not detected, but can be documented by special
studies and may be related to possible postoperative
neurocognitive deﬁcits (162,165,171,172). Interstitial ﬂuid increases as capillary permeability
increases (173) in response to circulating vasoactive
substances that cause endothelial cells to contract. There
is little or no evidence that intracellular ﬂuid increases. The accumulation of extravascular water is directly
proportional to the duration of CPB and can be massive
in patients with complicated surgical procedures. In
neonatal and infant surgery, removal of ﬂuid by modiﬁed
ultraﬁltration immediately after CPB is routine in many
practices (174). In adults this ﬂuid is similarly removed by
ultraﬁltration during CPB and by diuresis during the early
postoperative period. The combination of circulating cell signaling and cytotoxic substances and microemboli, together with excess
interstitial ﬂuid, produce temporary dysfunction of essentially every organ in the immediate postoperative period
(167). Pulmonary dysfunction due to increased interstitial edema, increased alveolar–arterial oxygen difference,
pain, and decreased compliance is common, particularly
in elderly and cachectic patients. Organ dysfunction is
temporary or at least not detectable beyond the immediate postoperative period, except for the brain and possibly
the kidney. In up to 30% of patients, subtle neuropsychologic changes are demonstrable 1 year after surgery (167),
but the cause of cognitive dysfunction following CPB and
OHS remains controversial largely because of the aging
population of patients and the accelerated neurocognitive
decline caused by systemic atherosclerosis (171,172,175). Most of these changes are probably due to microemboli
(167), but other causes are not ruled out. Occurrence of
renal failure following OHS and CPB is not uncommon,
particularly in patients with reduced renal function before
surgery. Rinder et al. have shown that the inﬂammatory
response and neutrophil activation play a role (176,177). During the immediate postoperative period, heart, lung,
and kidney function are most important for survival and
must be sufﬁcient to provide an adequate, stable circulation, diuresis of excess interstitial ﬂuid, and weaning from
the ventilator. Other chapters in this book describe the
impact of CPB on various organ systems in more detail.

The previous (second) edition of this book contained
an extensive review of heparin-coated circuits (178),
which is summarized here. Cumulative evidence does
not show that either covalent- or ionic-bonded heparincoated ECC circuits reduce the rate of thrombin formation
(149,150,179,180) (Fig. 5), alter platelets (149,181,182),
or reduce postoperative bleeding or transfusion requirements (178). There is evidence that heparin-bonded circuits attenuate complement activation (109,183,184), but
no clinical beneﬁts are evident (185). There is no consistent evidence that heparin-coated ECC circuits attenuate
the inﬂammatory responses of neutrophils, monocytes,
endothelial cells, or release of circulating proinﬂamma-

lepirudin is used as the anticoagulant, in vitro studies
show complement inhibition and reduced platelet and

clinical trials are not consistent between trials and the

concept, but because direct thrombin inhibitors do not
have a fast acting inhibitor analogous to protamine, scaling the methodology to larger and more complex cardiac
procedures requires careful planning and considerable
development. Aprotinin and the ω-aminocarboxylic acids, tranexamic
acid and ε-amino caproic acid, are antiﬁbrinolytics
that reduce postoperative blood losses by 40% to 50%
after reoperative cardiac surgery with CPB in patients
taking aspirin (196). Aprotinin, a protease inhibitor
derived from bovine lungs, inhibits plasmin directly
(197); the ω-aminocarboxylic acids inhibit cleavage of
plasminogen to plasmin. Although there are differences
between these drugs, all are effective. Aprotinin given
to patients with preoperative renal dysfunction may
exacerbate the dysfunction (198,199). In high doses,
aprotinin partially inhibits kallikrein and has a platelet
sparing effect (200). Platelet anesthesia is a method for temporarily preventing or attenuating platelet activation, adhesion, and
consumption by a short-acting, reversible platelet inhibitor (201). The feasibility of this approach has been
demonstrated in a baboon model using NO and eptiﬁ-
batide (202). The main targets for selective inhibition of the in-
ﬂammatory reaction to CPB and OHS are complement,
neutrophils, and monocytes. Suppression of thrombin
formation and complement activation may or may not
suppress activation of peripheral monocytes, but are likely
to signiﬁcantly attenuate the acute inﬂammatory response,
because many of the cytokine and cytotoxin responses of
monocyte activation are delayed. Two complement inhibitors, Pexelizumab, which prevents cleavage of C5, and TP 10, which inhibits C3/C5 convertase, effectively prevent generation of C5a and C5b-9
(203,204). In clinical trials these drugs inhibit complement and are safe (203,204). The Fitch trial suggested that
Pexelizumab may reduce perioperative myocardial infarction. It was followed by a multi-institutional prospective,
randomized clinical trial having the primary outcome parameters as death or myocardial infarction within 30 days
of surgery (205). Pexelizumab showed a reduction in
perioperative mortality and acute myocardial infarction
that reached statistical signiﬁcance in a mixed group of
3,099 adult patients (205) and in some subsets of patients (206,207). A similar trial of TP 10 in 594 ‘‘high-risk’’
adult patients found a signiﬁcant reduction in a composite outcome that included a 30-day mortality and
myocardial infarction (208). However, not all subsets
showed signiﬁcant beneﬁts from the drugs (209). To date
none of these trials report changes in a selected array
of inﬂammatory response markers.

Quantitative information regarding C5a, C5b-9, neutrophil elastase, monocyte chemotactic protein-1, and inﬂammatory cytokines,
interleukin 1β (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α),
and IL-8 is needed. The neutrophil is a major actor in the inﬂamma-
tory component of the defense reaction and is therefore a primary target for inhibition. Inhibition of the
phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) family of PDEs may attenuate or suppress neutrophil activation. Rolipram is a
PDE-4 inhibitor that has been studied in a variety of
patients with acute inﬂammatory diseases. One in vitro
study demonstrated that rolipram decreased neutrophil
elastase release and receptor expression during simulated
ECC (210). CONCLUSION
Our understanding of the massive defense reaction to
continuous exposure of heparinized blood to large nonendothelial cell surfaces has steadily increased over the last
half century, and we are now on the threshold of gaining control of this autopathic disease. For the moment,
heparin is a necessary agonist. It is now clear that direct thrombin inhibitors have the potential to completely
prevent thrombin generation and ﬁbrinolysis during CPB. The surgical pericardial wound, and not the perfusion
circuit, is the primary site of both thrombin generation
and the inﬂammatory response. Perhaps the biggest disappointment is the realization that the surface chemistry
of biomaterials exposed to anticoagulated blood is overwhelmingly complex, and therefore a nonthrombogenic
biomaterial remains an elusive goal. Selective inhibition of early progenitors of the thrombotic and inﬂammatory components of the defense reaction appears to be a winning strategy. Introduction of
ﬁbrinolytic inhibitors improves hemostasis and reduces
transfusions; now anticoagulation with direct thrombin
inhibitors may pre-empt the need for antiﬁbrinolytic
drugs. Drugs to control platelet, complement, and leukocyte activation are in the pipeline, and more are under development as the basic science of cell biology and protein
chemistry discovers and fully describes the mechanisms
involved in thrombin formation and cell interactions. New
knowledge and new drugs will help future patients, but one
simple procedure will help patients currently. All blood aspirated from the surgical ﬁeld should be either washed or
sequestered whenever ECC is used. KEY POINTS
■All forms of ECC, including conventional clinical
CPB, expose the cellular, molecular, and dissolved
elements of blood to nonendothelial cells and biomaterial surfaces.

20. The Blood–Surface Interface
433
●These surfaces include all components of every extracorporeal and intracorporeal devices or systems
that are in direct contact with circulating blood. ●With blood contact, a plasma protein monolayer
is instantaneously adsorbed on every biomaterial
surface, including coated surfaces. ●Perfusion circuits constructed of biomaterials alter
ﬂow rheology at various locations within the circuit
to increase sheer stresses and induce cavitation and
stagnation. These physical phenomena produce
hemolysis and various microemboli and contribute
to activation of other blood elements, including
platelets. ■Simultaneous activation of plasma zymogens of complement, coagulation, and ﬁbrinolytic proteins, and
activation of endothelial cells, platelets, neutrophils,
and monocytes in extracorporeal perfusion circuits
trigger a massive thrombotic and acute inﬂammatory
response. ●This response produces a myriad of circulating
inﬂammatory peptides, cytokines, proteases, phospholipids, eicosanoids, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, free radicals, cytotoxins, cell signaling
peptides, and expression of cellular receptors. ●The net result is an acute, ‘‘whole-body’’ thrombotic
and inﬂammatory response of varying intensity
and production of a variety of microemboli that
are major contributors to end-organ dysfunction
and pathology associated with all applications of
ECC and CPB. ■To date, efforts to suppress the thrombotic and acute
inﬂammatory response by modiﬁcations or coatings
of biomaterial surfaces have failed. ■Emerging direct thrombin inhibitors, antiﬁbrinolyt-
ics, and temporary platelet, complement, and neutrophil inhibitors show promise of ameliorating
adverse consequences of both the thrombotic and
acute inﬂammatory responses to ECC and CPB. ■Anticoagulated blood aspirated from the surgical
ﬁeld should be sequestered and washed before red
cells are returned to the perfusate. This process
substantially reduces mediators of thrombosis and
inﬂammation and despite higher immediate costs is
recommended for all patients. REFERENCES

◗Hematologic Effects and Coagulopathy
Christine S. Rinder
Normal blood circulation maintains pro- and antithrombotic factors that are carefully balanced in number and
function to preserve blood ﬂuidity, and yet this balance
can transform instantly to seal off a site of bleeding. The
redundancy built into all aspects of clotting and endogenous anticoagulation underscores the importance of this
homeostasis, such that most heterozygous defects can be
tolerated if they occur in isolation. The ﬁrst half of this
chapter will discuss the pro- and anticoagulant factors
that make up the system of checks and balances that are
so critical to the maintenance of normal blood circulation. The second part will explore the ways in which cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) challenges this hemostatic system,
simultaneously activating coagulant and inﬂammatory
processes, creating a hemostatic impairment that can lead
to excessive bleeding and transfusion requirements. HEMOSTASIS IN THE ARTERIAL
AND VENOUS CIRCULATIONS
The arterial and venous circulations, with their widely
disparate ﬂow conditions, impose very different needs
on the coagulation system. In the ‘‘pressurized’’ arterial
system, a relatively small vascular disruption can rapidly
result in signiﬁcant blood loss and hematoma formation,
creating the need for a system that can speedily and
securely seal off bleeding sites. Platelets dominate this
‘‘rapid response team,’’ initially containing blood loss, then
providing a surface on which to localize and accelerate the
ﬁbrin formation that ultimately consolidates hemostasis. In the venous circulation, by contrast, the more leisurely
ﬂow rates diminish the need for speed, making platelets
less critical, and indeed, thrombin generation constitutes
the pivotal reaction controlling the balance of venous
hemostasis. These differences between the arterial and
venous circulation are underscored by the anticoagulant
agents that are effective for prophylaxis in these different
settings; that is, antiplatelet agents such as aspirin used
to prevent stroke and coronary thrombosis (1), and
antithrombin-based interventions such as heparin and
warfarin for the treatment of deep venous thrombosis. CPB can produce alterations that may manifest as arterial
bleeding, venous bleeding, or both. It is critical to
understand how venous and arterial hemostasis operate
in part through common pathways, and how the two
differ, to fully appreciate the manifestations of different
CPB-induced coagulation defects.

made in identifying the series of proteolytic reactions that
culminate in ﬁbrin clot. The cascade model dovetailed
well with the prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial

to guide warfarin and heparin dosing, respectively, and
these tests came to be the gold standard for measuring

workable for many clinical scenarios having to do with
