for in vivo hemostasis its shortcomings have caused it
to be abandoned except in diagnosing factor deﬁciencies
and guiding anticoagulant therapy. Recent advances in
cell-based research models have made signiﬁcant strides
in clarifying the dynamics of coagulation (4,5). Experts
agree that in vivo coagulation follows exposure of the
blood to a source of tissue factor (TF), typically on
the surface of a ﬁbroblast or other cell coming into
contact with blood through a break in the vessel wall. The intrinsic, or contact, pathway of coagulation has no
role in the earliest events in clotting in humans.

TFinitiated coagulation has two phases; one, an initiation
phase, and a second referred to as the propagation phase
(Fig. 2) (6,7). The Initiation Phase of Soluble Coagulation
The initiation phase begins as the exposed TF binds to
factor VIIa, picomolar amounts of which are present
in the circulation at all times. This factor VIIa–TF
complex (the ‘‘extrinsic’’ Xase) catalyzes the conversion
of very small amounts of factor X to Xa, which in turn
generates nanomolar amounts of thrombin. The seemingly
trivial amount of thrombin formed during the initiation
phase sparks the inception of the propagation phase,
successful completion of which culminates in explosive

21. Hematologic Effects and Coagulopathy
441
thrombin generation and ultimately ﬁbrin deposition. More than 96% of the total thrombin that is generated
during clotting occurs in the propagation phase. Notably, most of the commonly used laboratory tests of
soluble coagulation measure the kinetics of the initiation
phase only (6). The PT and aPTT both have as their endpoints the ﬁrst appearance of ﬁbrin gel, which occurs with
completion of less than 5% of the total reaction. Therefore, the ﬁbrin clotting that signals completion of either
test occurs when only minimal levels of prothrombin have
been activated. These tests are very sensitive to congenital
abnormalities associated with deﬁcits in one or more of
the clotting factors, for example, hemophilia A and B, and
in guiding traditional anticoagulant therapy; however, as
a model of the entire sequence of events necessary for
effective hemostasis and the limits on those events, they
measure only the earliest steps in the process. PT and aPTT
fail to give information relevant to thrombin generation
during the propagation phase, when the vast majority of
thrombin is generated. The propagation phase may well
determine the success or failure of thrombus formation
in vivo. The Propagation Phase of Soluble
Coagulation
Thrombin generated during the initiation phase potently
activates platelets, thereby providing both the activated
platelet surface membrane and platelet-released factor V
(which is promptly activated to factor Va by thrombin)
in abundance. Factor VIII, conveniently brought to the
bleeding site by its carrier, von Willebrand factor (vWF),
is also activated by thrombin, thereby releasing it from
vWF. FVIIIa then complexes with picomolar amounts of
factor IXa, also generated by the TF–VIIa complex during
the initiation phase, forming the FVIIIa–IXa enzyme
complex (the ‘‘intrinsic’’ tenase complex). Formation
of this complex on the platelet surface heralds the
switch of the primary path of FXa generation from
the TF–VIIa complex (extrinsic tenase) to the intrinsic
tenase. This switch in pathways incurs a signiﬁcant kinetic
advantage, with the intrinsic tenase complex exhibiting
approximately a 50-fold higher efﬁciency than extrinsic
tenase generation. The bleeding diathesis associated with
hemophilia A and B offers testament to the physiologic
importance of the step-up in thrombin generation enabled
by activity of this intrinsic tenase during the propagation
phase (8).

Although congenital deﬁciencies in factors VIII
and IX prolong the aPTT, a measure of the initiation phase
of clotting begun by an in vitro nonphysiologic activator,
it is the thrombin generation in the propagation phase, a
function not evaluated by the aPTT, that is most impaired
in these hemophilias in vivo. The activated platelet expresses receptors for factors
VIIIa and IXa. Binding of these active proteases in complex
with the negatively charged phosphatidylserine on the
platelet membrane enhances the binding of the enzyme’s
substrate, factor X. The platelet binding of each of these
proteases increases the kinetics of their contribution
to factor X activation, such that the assembly of the
entire reaction on the platelet membrane confers a 13
million-fold increase in catalytic efﬁciency over that of the
proteases that are free in solution (7). Assembly of the prothrombinase complex similarly
depends on the activated platelet surface for optimum
activity. Like the tenase complex, the membrane-bound
prothrombinase complex promotes prothrombin activation with a rate enhancement 300,000-fold higher than
the free factor Xa acting on prothrombin formed in solution. Platelet-bound factor Xa is the rate-limiting reagent
in prothrombin cleavage. The substrate for this enzyme
complex, prothrombin, binds to GPIIb/IIIa on both activated and inactivated platelets, potentially providing a
source for thrombin to be generated in both the initiation
and propagation phases of clotting. Evidence is mounting that factor XI further ampliﬁes
the propagation phase of coagulation (9,10). This is
particularly necessary to sustain the switch from extrinsic
tenase to intrinsic tenase once small amounts of factor Xa
activate the endogenous inhibitor, tissue factor pathway
inhibitor (TFPI) (11). Before TFPI activation, small
amounts of factor IXa can be generated by the activity
of the TF-VIIa complex (12), but with TFPI inactivating
the TF-VIIa complex formed during the initiation phase,
an alternative, kinetically superior source of factor IXa is
needed to meet the needs of the propagation phase. Factor
XI is another zymogen cleaved by thrombin generated
during the initiation phase, but this activation occurs only
on the surface of the activated platelet (10). Platelet-bound
FXIa is then ideally located to activate FIX, which also
binds to the platelet surface and helps focus this activity. Additionally, binding to the platelet surface protects FXIa
from its inhibitor, protease nexin 2.

Therefore, generation
of FXIa on the activated platelet appears to hold the key
to providing sufﬁcient FIXa to maintain Xa generation
through the catalytically more efﬁcient intrinsic tenase
enzyme complex. The platelet surface contributes vitally to successful
formation of a venous clot. The relative abundance of
platelets under normal circumstances ensures that decreases in platelet number or function will rarely manifest
as venous bleeding. In vitro experiments mimicking soluble coagulation in the venous circulation have shown
that the platelet number must drop below 10,000/µL
before causing any prolongation in the time to clot formation (13). By contrast, in situations that simultaneously
challenge both arterial and venous hemostasis, such as
surgery, thrombocytopenia can produce arterial bleeding at far higher platelet counts, in the neighborhood of
50,000/µL.

IV. Hematology
Hemostasis in the Arterial Circulation:
Platelet-Initiated Hemostasis
The physical forces acting on a clot being formed in
the arterial circulation are such that, had hemostasis been
identical to that in the venous system, even modest arterial
bleeding events might not be survivable. To appreciate
how specialized and ﬁnely tuned are the sequence of events
that comprise arterial hemostasis, some understanding of
the rheology of blood ﬂow is necessary. Rheology of Arterial Blood Flow
Blood moving through a vessel at the velocities typical for
arterial blood ﬂow can be modeled as concentric rings of
ﬂuid moving at different velocities (Fig. 3). The central
core of ﬂuid moves at the highest velocity. Sheathing this
central, fastest-moving ﬂuid core is a ring whose velocity
is slightly slower. Immediately outside that ring is another
that moves still more slowly, as does each successive ring
of blood all the way out to the vessel wall. The shear rate,
γ , is a measure of how rapidly these adjacent ﬂuid layers
slide past each other, and is expressed in inverse seconds
(s−1)10. The shear rate at a radial point, r (measured
from the vessel center), can be calculated according to the
following equation:
γ = dvz/dr = 4(vz)r/R2
where vz is the mass average velocity, and R is the
vessel radius. Accordingly, the shear rate is greatest at
the vessel wall (γwall = 4(vz)/R) and zero at the center
of the vessel. Given that wall shear rates are inversely
proportional to the vessel radius, R, wall shear is greatest
in arterioles, in the order of 5,000 s−1, and decreases in
progressively larger arteries, reaching a still-forceful nadir
of approximately 500 s−1 in the major arteries. Shear rates
at the interface with arteriosclerotic plaques of a modest
50% stenosis may reach 3,000 to 10,000 s−1, with even
greater shear stress in ‘‘tight’’ stenoses. In the venous system, the velocity of blood ﬂow, vz, is
low enough that shear force has a virtually negligible role
in affecting venous clotting. By contrast, the high shear
created by the arterial circulation at the perimeter of the
vessel strongly opposes any tendency of the ﬂowing blood
to clot by (a) limiting the time available for procoagulant
reactions to occur and (b) by disrupting cells or proteins
not tightly adherent to the vessel wall.

However, when
the vessel wall is damaged and bleeding occurs, these
same forces necessitate that the responding hemostatic
events rapidly and decisively repair the loss of endothelial
integrity, while simultaneously resisting the tendency to
be swept downstream by high shear stress. One of the
forces contributing to the state of hemostatic ‘‘readiness’’
in the arterial circulation is radial dispersion, or the
tendency of larger cells, for example, erythrocytes and
leukocytes, to migrate to the center of the vessel. Such
coaxial migration effectively pushes the smaller platelets
to the vessel perimeter, optimally positioning them to
respond to hemostatic challenges. This size-dependent
cellular ﬂow pattern may also explain the seemingly
paradoxical tendency of arterial bleeding accompanied
by anemia to ‘‘correct’’ with red cell transfusions (14). This effect also underscores the importance of platelets
in arterial hemostasis; reductions in platelet number or
function sufﬁcient to leave the vessel wall unguarded may
be associated with catastrophic arterial hemorrhage. The constraints imposed by dynamic ﬂow stresses
make a sequence of interrelated platelet receptor–ligand
interactions critical to the initiation of arterial hemostasis. These interactions include (a) platelet adhesion to
subendothelial proteins, (b) platelet activation and formation of stable platelet–platelet bonds, and ultimately
(c) platelet-coagulation factor interactions culminating in
the formation of ﬁbrin. Given the velocity of blood ﬂow
at an arterial bleeding site, the platelets must activate and
adhere to the injured vessel nearly instantaneously. Accordingly, the platelet has structural features that make

it uniquely suited to this critical role of ﬁrst responder to
arterial bleeding. Structure of the Resting and Activated
Platelet
Platelets are anucleate cells released from megakaryocytes
in the marrow, and to a lesser extent the lung, which
circulate in the blood for approximately 7 to 10 days. The
resting platelet is disc-shaped, with a smooth membrane
(except for invaginations known as the open canalicular
system) that permits small molecules entry into the
elaborate network of internal membranes (15). Inside
the cell are two types of granules. The most numerous
granule, the α-granule, contains adhesive ligands and
growth factors, and is the granule most readily released
from the platelet by weak agonists or low concentrations
of more potent platelet activators. The second granule,
the dense granule, so called because of its appearance
as seen by electron microscopy, is less abundant than
the α-granule. Dense granules contain calcium and two
soluble platelet agonists, adenosine diphosphate (ADP)
and serotonin, agents critical to recruiting additional
platelets to a developing platelet plug at sites of bleeding. In contrast to α-granule release, release of the dense
granule requires a more aggressive platelet stimulant or a
combination of agonists. ‘‘Platelet activation’’ in the past
was typically treated as though it were a single event, a
unimodal response to all levels of stimulation, akin to
a light switch that is either ‘‘on’’ or ‘‘off’’. Instead, we
now know that the platelet has a remarkable repertoire
of changes that may be partial and reversible or complete
and ﬁnal, depending on the strength and circumstances of
their stimulation (16). To avoid confusion in the discussion
that follows, however, the term ‘‘platelet activation’’ will
exclusively refer to the platelet response to maximal
stimulation. However, the reader should bear in mind that
more graded activation states are possible in response to
lesser stimuli, and that many in vivo activation events fall
short of the threshold needed to give rise to an effective
platelet plug, yet may still have important modulatory
effects on adjacent vascular events. Platelet activation is comprised of a series of events, beginning with shape change. The stimulated platelet loses
its discoid shape and develops a more spherical shape,
which progressively ﬂattens out, extending ﬁngerlike projections (ﬁlapods) laterally.

During this ﬂattening process,
the granules and other organelles cluster at the center
of the cell, resembling a fried egg (17). This cell spreading is accompanied intracellularly by ﬁlament assembly,
culminating in extrusion of the granule contents into the
extracellular milieu through the open canalicular system. The major platelet membrane glycoprotein (GP), αIIbβ3
(GPIIb/IIIa), in addition to undergoing the conformational changes that permit binding to ﬁbrinogen at the
cell surface (18), is also anchored in the cytosol to actin
ﬁlaments (19), which enable the platelet to develop the
force necessary for clot retraction. Platelet Adhesion
Although platelets traveling near the arterial vessel wall are
poised to respond to exposed subendothelium, the obligate
physical and biochemical changes associated with platelet activation as described earlier make the classical
platelet response sequence of ‘‘platelet stimulation →
platelet activation →platelet adhesion’’ far too slow for
the immediacy of the need. To that end, the platelet
takes advantage of the high shear properties of arterial
blood ﬂow to facilitate its own arrest at a site of arterial
bleeding. Essential to this process is the multimeric
protein, vWF (20). The base unit of vWF is synthesized
by endothelial cells (ECs) as a polypeptide of 2,813 amino
acids, and these base units are then joined by disulﬁde
bonds into dimers in the endoplasmic reticulum. These
dimers are then linked through successive N-terminal
disulﬁde bonds into multimers, ranging in mass up to
20,000 kDa. Some of these large vWF multimers are
released away from the vessel lumen into the adventitia,
some are stored in EC granules known as the Weibel-Palade
bodies, and the remainder are released in a constitutive
manner into the plasma where, over time, they are broken
down into smaller vWF units. The high multimeric nature of vWF is critical to its
ability to initiate platelet adhesion at a site of bleeding (21). In the plasma, vWF circulates as a loosely coiled molecule
with an apparent diameter of 200 to 300 nm, showing
no afﬁnity for cocirculating platelets. Disruption of the
EC layer exposes subendothelial collagen that either binds
to plasma vWF or has vWF prebound to it. Under the
inﬂuence of the high shear present along the vessel
wall (a threshold value of 1,000 s−1 is required), this
tethered vWF uncoils to lengths as great as 1,300 nm.

The
uncoiling of vWF is thought to expose a hitherto cryptic
domain in the A1 region of the molecule, a domain with
instantaneous afﬁnity for the platelet surface receptor
GPIbα (Fig. 4). The coupling of this vWF domain to
GPIbα is characterized by a high rate of bond formation. This ‘‘fast-on’’ binding tethers the platelet to the exposed
subendothelium in the face of the high velocity blood ﬂow
that would otherwise sweep the platelet past the bleeding
site. The relatively weak strength of this adhesive tethering
is soon overcome by the local shear force, and the platelet
moves on, albeit now traveling at a slower velocity but still
in proximity to the vessel wall (22). In addition to slowing the platelet’s velocity, this brief
vWF–GPIbα interaction stimulates the platelet to become
activated, causing it to release its granules and producing
a conformational change in a second platelet receptor,
GPIIb/IIIa, which allows it to bind to a different domain,

has a dual role, one of slowing the platelet and another of
inducing the conformational changes that allow it to be
cemented to the exposed subendothelium. This sequence
of events is repeated over and over until the exposed
subendothelium is covered by a monolayer of activated
platelets. Patients deﬁcient in either vWF (von Willebrand
disease) or its platelet receptor, GPIb, (Bernard-Soulier
syndrome) (24) demonstrate defective platelet adhesion
to exposed subendothelium at shear rates in the range of

and both can be associated with signiﬁcant perioperative
bleeding. Platelet Aggregation
Once the exposed subendothelium is covered by a platelet
monolayer, the next step is to extend the platelet plug
by recruiting additional platelets to its surface. Platelet
recruitment depends on stimulation of passing platelets
by agonists released from the activated platelets in the
monolayer (16).

These agonists include ADP and serotonin, released from the dense granules, and thromboxane
A2 released from the platelet cytosol. As these second-line
platelets become activated, their GPIIb/IIIa also undergoes
the conformational change that allows it to bind a bridging
ligand, in this case either vWF or ﬁbrinogen, already bound
to GPIIb/IIIa on an adherent platelet (25). Therefore, a
platelet–ligand–platelet matrix is formed at the monolayer
surface, with either vWF or ﬁbrinogen serving as the bridging ligand. In vitro studies of platelet aggregation under
low ﬂow suggest that ﬁbrinogen, perhaps because of its
greater abundance, is the major adhesive ligand participating in matrix formation in venous clots. At higher velocity
(e.g., arterial) ﬂow, however, both ﬁbrinogen and vWF take
part in the platelet–ligand–platelet aggregation that builds
up the platelet plug (26). It is this stage of platelet plug
formation that is inhibited by the platelet antagonists aspirin and clopidogrel. These agents limit extension of the
platelet plug by decreasing recruitment of passing platelets
by platelet-released thromboxane A2 and ADP, respectively, with the aspirin inhibiting thromboxane A2 release
and the clopidogrel inhibiting binding of ADP to its receptor. One additional consequence of clopidogrel’s blockade
of the ADP receptor is inhibition of the exposure of the
negatively charged phosphatidylserine that is critical to
optimum activity of both the tenase and the prothrombinase complexes (13) (described earlier in the explanations
on soluble coagulation). This inhibitory activity, together
with its antiaggregatory effects, may explain why surgery
in the presence of clopidogrel typically has greater bleeding than surgery in the presence of aspirin. Interactions between Platelets
and the Soluble Coagulation System
Deposition of ﬁbrin at the surface of the platelet plug
constitutes the next stage in the formation of a hemostatically effective arterial clot. As described earlier, platelets

21. Hematologic Effects and Coagulopathy
445
play a vital role in the effective coordination and acceleration of the soluble coagulation system even in the venous
circulation (6,27). The ability of the platelet to perform
the following functions is even more critical under the
conditions of high arterial shear: (a) provide receptors
to capture procoagulant zymogens and their enzymatically active products; (b) enrich the local concentration
of factors V, XI, XIII, and ﬁbrinogen by releasing them
from intracellular sources; (c) provide the externalized
phosphatidylserine that is essential for the tenase and
prothrombinase complexes; (d) assemble these enzyme
complexes in a spatial orientation that optimizes their
kinetics; and (e) protect bound coagulant enzymes from
inhibition/inactivation. Clot Maturation
Evidence is mounting that the formation of an initially
hemostatic thrombus does not ensure sustained hemostasis. Events initiated during thrombus generation that
operate after the clot is formed, whether ﬁbrin-rich in
the venous circulation or platelet-rich in the arterial circulation, critically impact its stability. Fibrin Clot Architecture
The architecture of a ﬁbrin clot is surprisingly variable. Although genetic factors unquestionably play a role in
determining clot structure, the environment of the developing clot appears to exert the dominant inﬂuence (28). Differing circumstances give rise to clots that vary tremendously in the thickness of the ﬁbers, the number of ﬁbers
per unit area, the degree of cross-linking between adjacent ﬁbers, and the size of the pores between ﬁbers; all
of which are features that impact vulnerability to clot
lysis. Although individual thin clot strands are highly susceptible to lysis, thicker clot ﬁbers tend to have fewer
cross-links, fewer branch points, and to be more permeable than clots composed of thinner ﬁbers. Thin strands
develop a more occlusive meshwork, and ultimately impermeable clots with higher ﬁber mass-to-length ratios
exhibit the greatest resistance to ﬁbrinolysis. A number of factors within the microenvironment of
the developing clot importantly inﬂuence clot architecture. As might be expected for a biochemical reaction, local concentrations of thrombin and ﬁbrinogen (i.e., enzyme and
substrate) dominantly impact ﬁbrin strand formation. In
a thrombin-rich environment, ﬁbrin clots that form are
generally constructed from thinner, more tightly crosslinked ﬁbers, making them virtually impermeable to lytic
enzymes. In contradistinction, clots that form in the presence of low thrombin concentrations exhibit thicker and
more porous ﬁbrin strands that are vulnerable to thrombolysis.

Similarly, when high ﬁbrinogen concentrations
are present, large thrombi form with a tight and rigid
meshwork, making the ﬁbrin clot less deformable and
more resistant to lysis. Low ﬁbrinogen concentrations,
by contrast, produce a less compact clot that is highly
lysis-prone. Fibrin Cross-Linking by Factor XIIIa
Factor XIII also plays a critical role in stabilizing the
nascent clot (29). Factor XIII circulates in the plasma
and in the platelet; indeed a full 50% of the total ﬁbrin-
stabilizing activity in blood resides in the platelets released
at sites of bleeding following platelet activation. In plasma,
factor XIII is a tetrameric molecule consisting of 2
A-subunits, containing the active site of the enzyme, and
2 B-subunits, which serve to increase the plasma half-life
of the zymogen but must be dissociated for full enzyme
activity. Platelet factor XIII, by contrast, is a dimer that
contains only the 2 A-subunits. Both forms of the zymogen
require thrombin cleavage with ﬁbrin as a cofactor for
activity, with activation of plasma factor XIII proceeding
at a considerably slower rate owing to the time it takes for
the B-subunits to dissociate. Thrombin-activated factor
XIIIa binds to ﬁbrin and forms cross-links between the
ﬁbrin units, thereby stabilizing them and rendering them
less permeable and less lysis-prone. Perhaps even more
critical to protection from ﬁbrinolysis is the ability of
factor XIIIa to cross-link the major plasmin inhibitor, α2
antiplasmin, directly to the α chain of ﬁbrin, positing it
for expeditious neutralization of any invading plasmin. Regulation and Remodeling of Vascular
Clots
The hemostatic system has evolved to ensure rapid, tenacious clot formation at sites of bleeding, whether venous
or arterial. The very aggression of that procoagulant activity requires equally vigorous endogenous anticoagulant
mechanisms to (a) prevent clot formation at nonbleeding
sites and (b) constrain the developing clot from extending into uninjured areas, potentially compromising local
blood ﬂow. Healthy ECs are the mainstay of these clot
containment systems, serving as a renewable source of
anticoagulant mediators and providing an extracellular
matrix to localize them at the vessel wall. These ECs have a
wide repertoire of anticoagulant mechanisms available to
them, and different ones are brought into play depending
on the anatomic location of the ECs.

As will be seen later
in this section, venous ECs must focus on limiting thrombin, both its rate of generation and its activity, whereas
arterial ECs need abundant, localized antiplatelet agents. However, ECs are even more specialized within the arterial
and venous systems, with larger arteries producing more
platelet-inhibiting nitric oxide than arterioles, and veins of
the upper extremities producing more tissue plasminogen
activator (t-PA) than those of the lower extremity.

Endogenous Anticoagulants Limiting Soluble
Coagulation
Endogenous anticoagulants can be divided into mediators
whose principal action is to inactivate formed thrombin
and those that prevent thrombin generation. In the former category, the most important agent is antithrombin
(AT, also known as AT III). Under circumstances of normal hemostasis, AT is present at more than twice the
concentration (3.2 µmol/L−1) of the highest local thrombin concentration reached during clotting (1.4 µmol/L−1),
and its activity against thrombin is potentiated approximately 1,000-fold by endogenous EC-associated heparan
sulfate proteoglycans. The platelet surface membrane and
platelet-released platelet factor 4 protect thrombin from
inactivation at the site of clot formation. However, in the
absence of the protection conferred by the platelet membrane, any circulating thrombin is inhibited by plasma
levels of AT with a reaction time constant that is less than
1 minute, and in the microenvironment of healthy ECs
where approximately 60,000 molecules of AT bind per
cell, thrombin is neutralized almost instantaneously. Among endogenous anticoagulants that target thrombin generation, the earliest in the coagulation process is
TFPI, which inactivates factor Xa and the TF-VIIa complex. TFPI is synthesized in ECs, and is constitutively
released by ECs into the microvasculature (12). Under normal conditions, TFPI largely localizes to the endothelial
surface by binding to EC-associated glycosaminoglycans,
and can be displaced from this site by heparin. Newly released TFPI has direct activity only against factor Xa, but
following exposure to FXa it acquires activity against the
TF-FVIIa complex (11). Therefore, this inhibitor requires
some basal coagulation activation to attain full anticoagulant activity, but once activated, it is able to inhibit the
enzymes that initiate coagulation. During the initiation
phase of coagulation, FXa binding to the platelet membrane protects this enzyme from inactivation by both TFPI
and AT. Preservation of the small amounts of FXa that are
generated during this make-or-break stage of coagulation is critical to formation of the nanomolar amounts of
thrombin needed to begin the propagation phase of clotting. Similarly, the thrombin formed during the initiation
phase depends critically on protection by the activated
platelet membrane for sufﬁcient time to transition from
the initiation phase to the propagation phase of thrombin
generation. Activated protein C (APC) is an endogenous protein
whose combined anticoagulant, anti-inﬂammatory, and
proﬁbrinolytic properties make it an important regulator
in situations where both thrombosis and inﬂammation
are prominent (30).

Like TFPI, the protein C system
becomes activated only after coagulation is partly under
way. Formed thrombin binds to thrombomodulin, a
proteoglycan associated with endothelial and monocyte
cell surfaces. Once bound, thrombin loses its ability
to activate platelets and instead activates protein C. Inactivated protein C is bound to the EC surface by
endothelial cell protein C receptor (EPCR), which posits
it for activation by the adjacent thrombomodulin-bound
thrombin (31). APC slows down the procoagulant process
by inactivating factors VIIIa and Va, critical components
of the tenase and prothrombinase complexes, respectively,
in a reaction that is also enhanced by EPCR and protein S. As with so many other coagulation factors, the activated
platelet membrane protects FVIIIa and FVa from APC
inactivation (32). In addition to its effects on thrombin generation, APC
neutralizes plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), and
thereby enhances clot remodeling. Along with these anticoagulant activities, APC has anti-inﬂammatory properties as
well (31). Recombinant APC given to endotoxin-challenged
rats resulted in reduced tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)
production, whereas heterozygous protein C–deﬁcient
mice exhibited higher levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines
upon systemic endotoxemia. Endogenous Mediators Limiting Arterial Clot
Growth
In the arterial circulation, preservation of blood ﬂow to
downstream tissues is of utmost importance. At arterial
bleeding sites, the repetitious cycle of platelet activation
→platelet activation →platelet activation, if unchecked,
could cause the platelet plug to develop into an occlusive
thrombus. The systems that work to limit growth of the
platelet aggregate can be divided into two types. One
type relies on healthy ECs at the vessel tear margins
releasing platelet inhibitors that prevent the platelet plug
from encroaching on portions of the vessel wall that
retain intact endothelium. The weak platelet inhibitors,
nitric oxide and prostacyclin, released by healthy ECs into
the microenvironment of the vessel wall stimulate cyclic
guanosine monophosphate (GMP) and cyclic adenosine
monophosphate (AMP) formation, respectively, in the
platelet cytosol, reversibly blunting its response to platelet
agonists and inhibiting adhesion. In addition, healthy ECs
release an ecto-ADPase (33), which inactivates plateletreleased ADP, also preventing activation and recruitment
of platelets in the microenvironment. The second regulatory mechanism limiting platelet
plug growth operates by limiting the availability of
the larger vWF multimers that are critical to platelet
adhesion at high shear.

vWF cleaving protease (vWF-CP),
also known as ADAMTS-13, enzymatically reduces the
larger vWF multimers into smaller, less hemostatically
effective forms (34). Synthesized by the liver, this protease
circulates in normal blood without any afﬁnity for
cocirculating vWF. However, it is hypothesized that as
the platelet plug grows and progressively narrows the

447
arterial lumen, the shear rate increases accordingly. For
the developing platelet plug, as the shear increases,
so does its dependency on larger vWF multimers for
continued growth. If unchecked, the sequence of platelet
slowing—platelet activation—and platelet adhesion that
permitted the initial monolayer to form in the face of
high shear would be continuously repeated at the surface
of the platelet plug until it threatened the patency of the
vessel lumen. However, as described earlier, multimeric
vWF uncoils at very high shear, exposing cleavage sites for
vWF-CP (34). The smaller vWF molecules subsequently
produced by this enzyme do not support platelet adhesion
at high shear, thereby checking the growth of the platelet
plug short of vessel occlusion. The importance of this
mechanism to limiting arterial thrombosis is illustrated by
thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a syndrome
that can be precipitated by loss of vWF-CP activity (35) and
producing (a) ultra-large vWF multimers in the plasma,
(b) consumption of platelets, and (c) arterial thrombosis. Therefore, vWF-CP vitally regulates platelet plug growth
to prevent development of multiple thrombi in vessels
characterized by high shear. Clot Remodeling: Fibrinolysis
The ﬁbrinolytic system operates to preserve blood ﬂu-

(Fig. 5) (36). During clot formation, the formed factor
Xa and thrombin stimulate healthy ECs to release t-PA
and urokinase-type plasminogen activator (u-PA), two enzymes capable of cleaving plasminogen into plasmin. The
vast excess of plasminogen present in the plasma dictates that under normal circumstances the concentration

1,250-fold, making this an essential cofactor and one that
is predominantly available at the blood–vessel interface. Interindividual Variability:
The Extremes of “Normal”
Laboratories establish a normal range for tests such as
the platelet count, PT, and aPTT, and the hemostatic
response to a surgical challenge is expected to be adequate
if the preoperative values for a given patient fall within
this normal range. When modeling an individual’s total
capacity to generate hemostatic mediators and critically
evaluating the formation kinetics of these mediators,
investigators ﬁnd a range of functionally competent
biologic variability that far exceeds their expectations
based on the normal range demonstrated by the PT and
aPTT. Indeed, whether measuring the total thrombin
potential and its peak rate of formation (40,41), or
the ability of maximally stimulated platelets to amplify
thrombin generation (42,43), the breadth of what would
be considered ‘‘normal’’ is remarkable. The evolution of
more sophisticated coagulation testing may demand more
than a simple ‘‘normal/not normal’’ prediction of a patient’s
response to hemostatic challenge. It may be possible to
identify patients with borderline coagulation responses
that, while adequate for most operative situations, may
not be capable of maintaining hemostasis when subjected
to extreme stressors, for example, CPB.

Summary
The chance that a clot can successfully form and arrest bleeding, while stopping short of vessel occlusion,

IV. Hematology
brings an extraordinary array of mediators into play. These mediators critically impact (a) localization of procoagulant cells and enzymes, (b) speed and efﬁciency of
thrombin generation, (c) protection of the developing clot,
and (d) conﬁnement of the clot to the site of damage. As
noted earlier, individuals vary enormously in the efﬁciency
with which these four systems operate under basal conditions. Surgery alone stresses these systems, often exposing
hitherto inapparent deﬁciencies, and perhaps more than
any other event extracorporeal circulation in conjunction
with surgery challenges the hemostatic system in ways
that are still incompletely understood. CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS:
UPSETTING THE BALANCE
CPB imposes extremes on the hemostatic system. Despite efforts aimed at improving biocompatibility, the
CPB surface is generally perceived as foreign by circulating blood elements, which attempt both to ‘‘clot it off’’
by activating hemostatic elements and to ‘‘reject it’’ by
mounting an inﬂammatory attack (see Chapter 15). During this systemic response to the bypass circuit, the host
also appears to be attacked as an ‘‘innocent bystander’’
as circulating procoagulant and proinﬂammatory mediators leave the circuit and enter the patient. Table 1 lists
some of the vascular constituents activated by CPB, together with the mediators they generate that amplify their
own or related activation pathways. Ideally, both coagulation and inﬂammatory systems could be arrested until
the need for the CPB circuit has ended; then separation from CPB would be accompanied by the full return
of coagulation and immunologic function. In reality, the
coagulation ‘‘arrest’’ achieved by current anticoagulation
techniques (see Chapter 23 for a comprehensive discussion) is partial at best, and subsequent restoration of

Bypass Affecting Hemostasis:
Heparinization, Hemodilution,
and Hypothermia
Intact ECs, as outlined earlier, actively secrete antithrombotic agents to maintain blood ﬂuidity. All synthetic
surfaces, the CPB circuit included, activate the coagulation
cascade (44) without the presence of ECs to counter this
effect. Therefore, establishment of profound anticoagulation before blood contact with the CPB circuit constitutes
an essential component of CPB (see Chapter 23). Heparin, the most widely used CPB anticoagulant, binds to
circulating AT to cause a conformational change that accelerates its binding to and inactivation of three critical
coagulation factors: thrombin, factor Xa, and factor IX. Therefore, heparinization, at doses higher than that used
for any other clinical condition, represents the ﬁrst major alteration in coagulation imposed by CPB. Although
heparin is neutralized by protamine at the end of CPB,

there may be a fraction of heparin that is unavailable
for protamine reversal because of protein binding or endothelial sequestration. This fraction may become free in
the plasma and contribute to post-CPB bleeding, a phenomenon known as heparin rebound. Heparin at CPB
doses has both direct and indirect antiplatelet effects
that may persist post-CPB. Among its antiplatelet actions,
heparin binds to vWF at a site critical for binding to
platelet GPIb (45,46); this effectively blocks vWF–platelet
interaction and can impair initial platelet rolling and adhesion to the subendothelium. This effect is seen only
at high heparin concentrations (≥2 U/mL) and does
not appear to inhibit GPIIb/IIIa-dependent platelet–vWf
interactions. However, the impairment in vWF- and GPIbdependent adhesion likely contributes to the increased
bleeding time noted during CPB when heparinization
is maximal (47). Whether this heparin–vWf interaction
plays any role in bleeding following heparin reversal, especially in the setting of heparin rebound, is not known at
this time. Once adequacy of anticoagulation by heparin is certain,
typically determined by prolongation of the activated
clotting time, the passage of blood through the CPB
circuit is initiated. Owing to the large volume of the
circuit, which must be primed with blood-compatible
ﬂuid, hemodilution represents the next challenge imposed
on the hemostatic system (see Chapter 19). The degree
of hemodilution varies with the institution, type of CPB
circuit, and size of the patient, but is in the range of
approximately 25% to 35%, and the concentration of
coagulation factors accordingly should be diluted to the
same modest degree (48). In non-CPB settings, single
soluble coagulation factor defects must result in factor
concentrations as low as 20% of normal values before
symptoms of bleeding are manifested or clotting tests
are prolonged. It has been generally assumed that the
coagulation factor dilution during CPB, bringing most
factor levels to 60% to 70% of the normal, should
not compromise coagulation. Recent advances in our
understanding of the importance of kinetics and local
thrombin concentrations for effective clot formation,
as outlined earlier, may force us to reconsider these
assumptions. A study by Davidson et al.

(49) measured

Hypothermia is the next systemic alteration frequently
imposed during CPB. The degree of systemic hypothermia achieved at different institutions varies highly, with
a trend in recent years toward more moderate hypothermia, and is accomplished by allowing the temperature
to drift downward passively. Hypothermia is known to
slow enzymatic reactions; as a general rule, for a 10◦C
decrease in temperature, enzyme activity is reduced by
approximately 50%. Accordingly, it is no surprise that
soluble coagulation, a cascade of enzymatic reactions, is
adversely affected by hypothermia. Wolberg et al. (50) recently used cell-based clotting assays and speciﬁc platelet
function tests to determine the degree to which hypothermia affects these critical aspects of coagulation. They
found that for temperatures in the range of 33◦C to
36◦C, membrane-associated coagulation enzyme activities were only minimally reduced compared with their
kinetics at 37◦C. By contrast, platelet adhesion and aggregation were signiﬁcantly reduced at 33◦C compared with
37◦C, suggesting that modest hypothermia may predominantly impair platelet-based hemostasis in the arterial
circulation.

For more severe hypothermia, that is, temperatures below 33◦C, both platelet function and coagulation
enzyme activity were impaired, likely contributing to coagulopathy under these conditions. By contrast, ﬁbrinolysis
does not appear to be affected by hypothermia, at least at
temperatures between 33◦C and 37◦C (51). Hypothermiainduced changes are reversible upon rewarming; however,
this effect may impair postoperative coagulation in patients who are inadequately rewarmed or recool after
leaving the operating room (OR) suite.

Effect of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
on Soluble Coagulation
As mentioned earlier, the passage of blood through the
extracorporeal circuit activates coagulation, hence the
need for heparin. Indeed, if the heparin dose is inadequate,
the blood in the circuit turns to gel-like clot in a matter of
seconds. However, unlike in vivo coagulation as already
described, the circuit activates the contact system of
coagulation (52), generating proinﬂammatory mediators
such as kallikrein (53) and bradykinin (54), as well as
procoagulant factors such as factor XIIa. However, at the
patients’ operative sites, TF continues to be the initiator
of clotting (55,56), and overall this appears to be the
dominant source of clotting activation during CPB (57). Nonetheless, as suggested in the preceding text, initiation
of CPB is associated with rapid and intense thrombin
(Fig. 7) and ﬁbrin generation over the ﬁrst 5 minutes to
levels 20-fold higher than that produced by surgery alone,
despite maximal heparin-induced anticoagulation (58). Following this initial burst, the rate of thrombin and ﬁbrin
generation then decreases modestly, reaching a steady
state in which it remains until restimulated by reperfusion
of the ischemic heart and by heparin neutralization. Before CPB, only approximately 1% of the ﬁbrin formed
is soluble. However, Chandler et al. (58) demonstrated
that the soluble ﬁbrin constitutes approximately 35% of
total ﬁbrin after CPB, suggesting that the ﬁbrin formed
during bypass was dysregulated and not ﬁrmly tethered to
sites of bleeding. The study by Dixon et al. supports this
concept (59). These authors measured thrombin activity
in the period surrounding CPB and found higher thrombin
activation in patients sustaining noncardiac organ injury. This suggests that CPB may induce a state akin to sepsis
in which dysfunctional ﬁbrin formation may injure or
compromise tissues remote from the operative site. The hypothesis of dysfunctional ﬁbrin formation during CPB may seem inconsistent with the CPB-induced
coagulation defect described earlier in this chapter. Effective clot formation, however, critically depends on
explosive thrombin generation accelerating ﬁbrin deposition in a highly localized reaction, protected and contained
by the activated platelet membrane. Although CPB impairs the velocity and magnitude of such focused clotting
reactions (explained later), it also renders the clot containment/remodeling systems dysfunctional; accordingly,
insufﬁcient thrombin may cause poor clots in the surgical
ﬁeld while nonoperative sites are choked by inappropriate
ﬁbrin deposition.

defects may produce bleeding that requires platelet transfusion despite seemingly adequate platelet counts (60). Several alterations in platelet function can occur in the
peri-CPB patient, with no single functional defect accounting for the preponderance of bleeding. In general, most
patients exhibit blunted platelet responses to stimulation
by agonists, without a clear cause for this dysfunction. Accordingly, after CPB, higher concentrations of ADP, collagen, thrombin, and other platelet agonists are required
to achieve irreversible platelet aggregation (61). The ability
to adhere in the presence of high shear, as in the arterial
circulation, is also decreased (62). The combination of
a decrease in platelet number and global platelet dysfunction may be responsible for a major proportion of the
blood loss associated with CPB (63,64). These observations
raise some important questions: Why are platelets often
lost out of proportion to hemodilution? What is the nature
of the platelet defect(s)? Is the process leading to platelet
loss also responsible for impaired platelet function? Studies have demonstrated that CPB activates large
numbers of platelets, measured by release of the contents
of internal granules (65,66) (Fig. 8B). These activated
platelets may then bind to exposed subendothelium, to
the CPB circuit (67), or to circulating monocytes and
neutrophils (68), potentially causing platelet numbers to
decrease beyond what would be expected from hemodilution alone. Furthermore, the activation response of still
circulating platelets is impaired.

In vitro studies have
demonstrated that stimulated platelets become refractory to repeated stimulation by the same agonist. It is
possible that the CPB-induced activation might, by ‘‘preactivating’’ platelets, produce a pool of granule-depleted,
spent platelets incapable of contributing their granule
contents to the platelet plug. Indeed, electron microscopic examination of platelets during CPB demonstrates
a heterogeneous mixture of discoid and shape-changed
platelets, in addition to partially and completely degranulated platelets (69). Investigators have attempted to ‘‘anesthetize’’ platelets better during CPB, hypothesizing that by
rendering them transiently inert to activation stimuli, their
function might be better preserved postoperatively (70). Indeed, administration of the reversible platelet inhibitor
prostacyclin (71), its analog iloprost (72), and iloprost together with nitric oxide (73), have all been associated with
some modest success in reducing chest tube drainage and
preserving platelet activity after CPB. Their reduction in
blood loss is, however, not sufﬁcient to signiﬁcantly impact
transfusions. The hypotensive side effects of these agents,
however, may preclude their widespread use. Investigators in pursuit of a more hemodynamically inert ‘‘platelet
anesthetic’’ are now turning to a class of agents known as
disintegrins (74), which compete with ﬁbrinogen and vWF
for binding sites on platelet GPIIb/IIIa receptors. However,
evidence linking the activating stimulus to subsequent
defects in the aggregation response remains indirect. Furthermore, patients exhibiting the highest percentages of
circulating activated platelets are not necessarily the ones
most affected by dysfunctional platelet aggregation (75)
(Fig. 9). It may be that platelet activation and the acquisition of the aggregation defect are distinct entities
produced simultaneously by CPB. The ability of the platelet to serve as a platform for and
integrator of soluble coagulation is critical to hemostasis. To this end, in response to maximal stimulation, the kinetic efﬁciency platelet externalizes the negatively charged
phospholipid, phosphatidylserine, to ensure peak tenase

platelet function is profoundly impaired during CPB, and
exhibits a highly variable recovery in the early postoperative period (Fig. 10). Indeed, when factored together with
the decrease in total platelet count, the inability to mobilize phosphatidylserine in a critical number of platelets
postoperatively appears to predict blood loss. The normal circulating platelet population is extremely
heterogeneous in age and function (77), with platelets recently released from the marrow exhibiting a more robust
response to stimulation than senescent ones (78,79). A
sustained, low-grade platelet-activating stimulus like CPB
may, over time, preferentially activate the younger, more
vigorous platelets, causing them to be preferentially culled
from the circulation, thereby passively increasing the proportion of ‘‘hyporesponders’’ among the still-circulating
platelets (80). In light of the increased platelet activation
seen with time, this effect would be particularly noticeable with longer bypass times. Eventually, this loss would
be compensated for by increased release of fresh young
platelets from the marrow, but this reverse selection process would still produce temporary platelet dysfunction
in the early hours after bypass, a time when coagulation function is critical. Evidence associating a reduction
in the average platelet volume, signaling loss of younger
platelets, with increased post-CPB bleeding supports this
hypothesis (Fig. 8A) (81). Catecholamines are generated in large quantities during CPB despite aggressive efforts to provide a stress-free
anesthetic. As a rule, both epinephrine and norepinephrine
are relatively weak platelet agonists in vivo. However, by binding to α-adrenergic receptors on platelets,
epinephrine and norepinephrine prime platelets for a
more exuberant response to other agonists (82), a feature
that may adversely impact postsurgical hemostasis.

number. With time on CPB, however, circulating platelets
lose their α-adrenergic receptors and are accordingly
incapable of being primed by catecholamines in the postoperative period when the need for peak platelet response
is greatest (83). Although this effect is unlikely to constitute
‘‘the post-CPB platelet defect’’ by itself, impaired adrenergic responsiveness does appear to contribute to the overall
platelet dysfunction occurring in the post-bypass period. Fibrinogen is known to bind to extracorporeal surfaces
within minutes of blood passage through the CPB circuit
(see Chapter 20). This bound ﬁbrinogen is conformationally altered such that it is capable of binding to the resting
GPIIb/IIIa receptor on platelets (84), and the resulting
tethering of platelets is one likely explanation for the excess thrombocytopenia associated with CPB. In addition,
some bound platelets break free of the circuit over time,
leaving portions of their receptors still bound to the circuit. This may be responsible for the modest decrease (in the
range of 40%–50%) in surface expression of the ﬁbrinogen
receptor, GPIIb/IIIa, on circulating platelets (85,86). Recent experience with blocking monoclonal antibodies has
demonstrated that well over 50% of GPIIb/IIIa receptors
must be blocked to produce signiﬁcant aggregation impairment (87), so this mechanism probably only modestly
contributes to post-CPB bleeding. Clot strength (88) and the related feature, clot retraction (89), are also impaired following CPB, and both of
these changes have been correlated with increased chest
tube drainage. Clot strength derives in part from factor
XIIIa–mediated cross-linking, and because 50% of factor
XIII levels are platelet-derived, it is not surprising that
platelet count, factor XIII levels, and clot strength all correlate with each other and with postoperative bleeding
(Fig. 11). Clot retraction in particular may affect the ability
of the clot to hold securely against high shear forces. Reduced thrombin production impairs the ability of plateletrich clots to undergo clot retraction (90), making clots that
form in the arterial circulation similarly vulnerable to lysis. Therefore, any decrease in clot strength after CPB, in
addition to diminishing shear resistance, may also cause
the clot to be more vulnerable to ﬁbrinolysis by plasmin. Endothelial Cell Activation
and Hyperﬁbrinolysis
Activation of ECs during CPB has been demonstrated in
animal models of bypass (91). In humans, increased release of t-PA during bypass provides indirect evidence of
EC activation (92) (Fig. 7).

As early as 5 minutes after
CPB initiation, t-PA levels increase sixfold (93), coincident
with a burst of thrombin and bradykinin generation, both
of which potently induce this proﬁbrinolytic mediator. Increased t-PA secretion continues throughout CPB and into
the post-CPB period. The major endogenous t-PA antagonist, PAI-1, is largely synthesized in the liver, and its levels
do not increase until the end of CPB. By 2 hours postCPB, PAI-1 levels are increased 15-fold, ﬁnally reducing
levels of active t-PA. However, during the bypass period
itself, proﬁbrinolytic activity is enhanced, virtually unopposed by the endogenous antiﬁbrinolytic agent normally
responsible for maintaining ﬁbrinolytic balance. Accordingly, plasmin generation increases more than
100-fold minutes after CPB initiation, in concert with
the above increases in t-PA (94). D-dimer, a breakdown
product of ﬁbrin degradation, increases 200-fold shortly
after starting CPB, in parallel to the appearance of plasmin, and generation rates of this marker of ﬁbrinolytic
activity remain 20- to 30-fold higher than normal during
the remainder of CPB. This proﬁbrinolytic state is clearly
initiated by the high levels of t-PA induced early during
CPB; however, factors impacting ﬁbrin clot architecture
may signiﬁcantly affect the vulnerability of these clots to
ﬁbrinolysis. As discussed earlier, the local concentrations
of thrombin and ﬁbrinogen present at the time of clot formation are directly proportional to the lysis-resistance of
the ﬁbrin strands that are formed. In addition to basic clot
structure, local thrombin concentrations also affect both
the degree to which factor XIII is activated to form intraﬁb-
rin cross-links and TAFI activation, both opposing ﬁbri-
nolysis of the newly formed clot. Therefore, the reductions
in thrombin potential described by Davidson et al. (49), in
addition to impairing hemostasis directly by limiting clot
formation, may also contribute indirectly by rendering the
clots that are formed more vulnerable to hyperﬁbrinolysis. In addition to directly causing ﬁbrin degradation,
plasmin has been shown in vitro to produce platelet activation (95) and platelet dysfunction simultaneously (96). The antiplatelet action of plasmin may contribute to the
dysfunction demonstrable in freely circulating platelets
during CPB, although active t-PA principally localizes onto
formed ﬁbrin. Tranexamic acid preserves platelet granule
content on CPB, possibly by preventing partial platelet
activation (97).

Such an effect of this small molecule
antiﬁbrinolytic may be much more speciﬁc than the multiplicity of actions of aprotinin in preserving platelet
number and function following CPB (see Chapter 25) (98). Plasmin in vitro has also been shown to cause internalization of platelet GPIb (99), the vWF receptor critical
for adhesion under ﬂow conditions. On average, CPB is
associated with a modest decrease, in the range of 20% to
30%, in platelet GPIb (100), and aprotinin has been shown
to preserve platelet GPIb levels (101). In the BernardSoulier syndrome, a congenital deﬁciency of GPIb, the
critical number of GPIb receptors necessary for surgical
hemostasis is unclear, but heterozygotes with approximately 50% receptor density show no predisposition to
bleeding (102). With the possible exception of children
with cyanotic congenital heart disease (103) (Fig. 12),
very few patients undergoing CPB exhibit a decrease in
GPIb into a range that would, by itself, be a major cause

of post-CPB bleeding. In association with modest thrombocytopenia and impaired platelet aggregation, however,
this GPIb-based adhesion defect may contribute to poor
platelet function overall. GPIb-dependent adhesion also depends on the presence
of high molecular weight polymers of vWF for optimal
activity, as discussed earlier. The plasma levels of these
larger polymers are regulated by low-level proteolysis,
allowing for a prompt but not pathologic response to
arterial injury. CPB causes a modest increase in vWF
proteolysis that is proportional to CPB duration, reducing
the proportion of the larger vWF multimers that are most
hemostatically effective (104). In the 25 patients studied,
levels of the larger vWF multimers did not decrease into
a range that independently produces arterial bleeding;
however, it is possible that, in concert with other multiple
defects induced by CPB, this decrease might be a factor in
suboptimal postoperative platelet performance. Complement Activation
The complement system constitutes one of the more
primitive biologic systems activated by blood contact with
foreign elements. Although traditionally considered a pro-
inﬂammatory system (105), activated complement (106)
components also exhibit activity in hemostatic pathways,
and increased markers of complement activation have in
some studies (81) correlated with post-CPB bleeding. The
alternative complement activation pathway principally activates early during CPB, resulting in formation of the opsonin C3b, the common pathway anaphylatoxins C3a and
C5a, and ﬁnally the membrane attack complex, C5b-9 (106,
107). After CPB, administration of protamine induces an
additional surge of complement activation, presumably
stemming from activation of the classical pathway by the
heparin–protamine complex (108). The formation of these
bioactive elements ampliﬁes both hemostatic and inﬂam-
matory pathways that are initially activated by exposure to
the circuit. The by-products of this inﬂammatory cascade
in turn activate leukocytes, platelets, and ECs (109,110). Studies have suggested that the complement component
C5a is principally responsible for the activation of neutrophils (111), whereas monocytes can be stimulated by
the C3a fragment also (112). The membrane attack complex, C5b-9, is a potent activator of platelets, inducing
α-granule release, formation of procoagulant microparticles, and surface exposure of the negatively charged
phosphatidylserine residues essential to the coagulation
cascade (113). In vitro, platelets activated by C5b-9 are unable to bind ﬁbrinogen to their GPIIb/IIIa receptors, so
that an aggregation defect similar to that induced in vivo
by CPB is created (114).

Clearly, the generation of complement components plays a role in platelet activation
during CPB; whether this is responsible for some of the
CPB-associated platelet dysfunction remains unknown. WBC (percentage change)

Leukocyte Activation
A number of the pathways described earlier, including
both the complement cascade and the contact system, contribute to the activation of immune cells during CPB (see
Chapter 15). Circulating monocytes and neutrophils become activated (68), which primes them to cause tissue
damage when they enter organs. Leukocyte adhesion receptors CD11b/CD18 are upregulated, so that they can bind
to ECs and migrate into extravascular tissues. Leukocytes
also release their granules on activation, liberating destructive elements including oxygen radicals, elastase, and
cathepsin G (115). In addition to having proinﬂammatory
activity, mediators such as elastase and cathepsin G are
capable of degrading ﬁbrin, potentially contributing to the
instability of newly formed clots (116). Such cell-mediated
ﬁbrinolysis may be facilitated by CD11b/CD18-dependent
adhesion to ﬁbrin (117). The contribution of cell-mediated
ﬁbrinolysis to clot instability after CPB is difﬁcult to ascertain; however, recent work has demonstrated that patients
who exhibit the greatest increase in white blood cell count
during the course of CPB are most likely to bleed during the
ﬁrst 24 postoperative hours (118) (Fig. 13). Whether these
increased numbers of white blood cells actively participate
in the bleeding diathesis or simply signal an exaggerated
inﬂammatory response remains unknown. The links between inﬂammatory and hemorrhagic processes represent
an important emerging ﬁeld of investigation. KEY POINTS
■Plasma coagulation was initially thought to reside
mainly in the soluble plasma, but further elucidation

456
IV. Hematology
of mechanisms reveals a two stage process involving
a slower phase in the soluble plasma (initiation
phase) followed by a much more explosive phase
(propagation phase) that occurs on the platelet
surface. ■Rheology plays an important role in hemostasis,
such that there are important differences in the
mechanisms of hemostasis between the venous and
arterial sides of the circulation. Traditional plasma
coagulation factors may be sufﬁcient for hemostasis
on the venous side, whereas platelet numbers and
function are critically important for hemostasis on
the arterial side. ■A variety of endogenous mediators limit clot formation or growth, among which antithrombin, activated
Protein C, von Willebrand Factor-Cleaving Protease,
and plasmin inhibitor (PAI-1) are especially important. These mediators help preserve venous and
arterial vessel patency as the forces favoring clot
formation work to seal ‘‘leaks’’ at locations where the
blood vessels are torn. ■No single entity has been identiﬁed as ‘‘the source’’
of post-CPB bleeding, but prominent contributors to
this bleeding include reduced concentrations of coagulation factors, hyperﬁbrinolysis, thrombocytopenia,
impaired platelet aggregation, platelet fragmentation
and loss of membrane receptors. ■Endothelial cell surface functions and secretory
products play an important role in the adequacy
of both the clotting response to vessel injury and in
the prevention of excessive clot propagatioin leading
to intravascular thrombosis. ■An interaction between coagulation and inﬂamma-
tion has been increasingly recognized in recent years,
such that recent evidence indicates that enhanced
inﬂammation after CPB impairs coagulation and increases blood loss. ■A variety of ‘‘extrinsic’’ factors such as residual
heparin, excessive protamine, hemodilution, and
hypothermia can also contribute importantly to postCPB bleeding. ■The list of hemorrhagic contributors is so impressive
that it makes the degree of hemostasis achieved after
CPB seem remarkable. ■A better understanding of hemostasis and the effects
of CPB on coagulation may foster improved care on
multiple fronts, including the following:
●Improving the biocompatibility of circuits
●Improving the ‘‘arrest’’ of coagulation and inﬂam-
mation during CPB
●Developing diagnostic tests to treat bleeding more
rapidly and speciﬁcally
●Developing more effective pharmacologic strategies for both prevention and treatment of bleeding. REFERENCES

◗Coagulation Testing
Jay C. Horrow and Josef Nile Mueksch
No coagulation test can duplicate the complex milieu
present at an injured vessel. Merely placing a needle or a
catheter in a vessel initiates a multitude of hemostatic responses that alter measurements on the blood sample that
has been removed. Surface activation of the clotting cascade begins when blood leaves the protective environment
of the endothelial cells and enters into collection tubes. For these reasons, coagulation tests must be viewed as an
approximation of actual events. This chapter examines the
role of coagulation tests performed at central laboratory
facilities and the changing landscape brought about by
point of care testing. CENTRALIZED COAGULATION
LABORATORY TESTS
Devices using formation of a clot as an endpoint usually
employ electrical or optical detection methods. The
classic instrument, the Fibrometer (BBL Microbiological
Systems, Cockeysville, MD), places a stationary and a
moving probe in the sample. When ﬁbrin strands bridge
the two electrodes, conductivity increases causing a
timer to halt (1). Laboratory prothrombin time (PT),
activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), ﬁbrinogen,
and thrombin time determinations use this technology. Prothrombin Time and Activated Partial
Thromboplastin Time
Figure 1 illustrates the steps in performing these tests. Each test involves centrifuging a citrated specimen of
blood. Citrate complexes calcium, a necessary cofactor in
the coagulation cascade, thereby preventing coagulation
factor activation. The supernatant obtained by centrifugation, plasma, is incubated for 3 minutes with an additive
that differs for the two tests. After addition of excess calcium with respect to citrate, the time to formation of gel
is measured. The PT, better called a complete thromboplastin time,
incubates plasma with tissue extract (thromboplastin). As a tissue product, thromboplastin supplies its own
phospholipid plus tissue factor. If the plasma sample
contains sufﬁcient factor VII and factors in the common pathway, it will gel in approximately 12 seconds. Variations in the potency and quality of thromboplastin
reagents require simultaneous determination of a control
sample and comparison of the patient’s result with the control result. Each batch of thromboplastin reagent is graded
in potency.

The international normalized ratio (INR) calculation allows for comparison of PT results from different commercial thromboplastin reagents: INR = PCRISI,
where PCR is the ratio of patient sample to control sample
PT results and ISI is the international sensitivity index,

of vitamin K–dependent factors. The higher the ISI of a
thromboplastin, the less responsive the clotting time to
changes in coagulation factors when using that thromboplastin. Therefore, a less responsive thromboplastin,
which yields a smaller PCR, carries a larger ISI, yielding
a similar calculated INR. Thromboplastin reagent manufacturers determine the ISI by comparing the reactivity of
each speciﬁc lot of thromboplastin with an international
reference preparation (2). The partial thromboplastin time (PTT) incubates
plasma with an extract of thromboplastin that contains the
phospholipid but not the tissue factor, thereby preventing
activation of extrinsic factor VII. Now entirely dependent
on surface activation alone, the gel forms slowly (73 ± 11
[SD] seconds) (3). The aPTT uses a surface activation accelerator such as kaolin, ellagic acid, silica, bentonite, or
celite, which allows gel formation to then occur in approximately 32 seconds (1). As with the PT, simultaneous
controls are required, with abnormal results at 1.5 or more
times control. Warfarin therapy, which inhibits carboxylation of the
vitamin K–dependent clotting factors, prolongs the PT
because factor VII production is most vulnerable to lack
of vitamin K. Heparin primarily affects the aPTT but not
the PT because the potent procoagulant action of the
thromboplastin reagent in the PT test easily overwhelms
any inhibition of factors Xa and thrombin from the
moderate doses of heparin used to treat venous thrombosis
or acute coronary syndrome. The less potent partial
thromboplastin reagent in the aPTT test, however, is
sensitive enough to demonstrate heparin’s anticoagulant
effects. Large doses of heparin will prolong the PT also. Thrombin Time
Adding thrombin to a plasma sample will form ﬁbrin
within 10 seconds if functionally active ﬁbrinogen is
present, heparin is absent, and ﬁbrin degradation products
(FDPs) are absent. Sensitivity of the thrombin time to
small amounts of heparin occurs because small amounts
of thrombin are added. The traditional thrombin time
is relatively insensitive to ﬁbrinogen deﬁciency and to
FDPs: detectable prolongation requires less than 0.75 g/L
ﬁbrinogen (4) or more than 200 µg/mL FDPs. Sensitivity to
FDPs increases if ﬁbrinogen concentrations are low. Also,
diluted plasma increases sensitivity of the thrombin test to
ﬁbrinogen deﬁciency. Amyloidosis prolongs the thrombin
time by inhibiting conversion of ﬁbrinogen to ﬁbrin (5).

Reptilase Time
The Reptilase time measures the interval between addition
to plasma of venom from the South American pit viper
Bothrops jararaca and formation of ﬁbrin: it is like a
thrombin time, but uses the venom instead of thrombin to
form ﬁbrin. A prolonged Reptilase time implicates reduced
or dysfunctional ﬁbrinogen or high concentrations of
FDPs as the cause of a prolonged thrombin time. Neither heparin nor direct thrombin inhibitors prolong
the Reptilase time (6). It is several-fold more insensitive to
FDPs than the thrombin time. Amyloidosis also prolongs
the Reptilase time. Fibrinogen
Most laboratories use the Clauss method for ﬁbrinogen
determination, in which a thrombin time is performed
on diluted plasma. With diluted samples, ﬁbrinogen becomes the factor limiting clot formation, so that the
clotting time varies inversely with ﬁbrinogen activity (1). The Ellis method employs undiluted plasma, smaller
amounts of thrombin, and a spectrophotometric measure of turbidity. A PT-based method adds thromboplastin
to undiluted serum, thereby using endogenously generated thrombin. Antibody-based tests for ﬁbrinogen can
distinguish among the dysﬁbrinogenemias. Decreased ﬁb-
rinogen concentration occurs in end-stage hepatic failure,
consumptive coagulopathy, and uncontrolled ﬁbrinolysis
leading to ﬁbrinogenolysis, extreme hemodilution, and
massive transfusion. Fibrin Degradation Products
Immunologic tests provide a semiquantitative determination of the various fragments resulting from ﬁbrin and
ﬁbrinogen degradation. The most common test for FDPs
uses latex agglutination of serum. Note that serum, not
plasma, is used. It provides results as either negative
(<10 µg/mL) or positive (>10 µg/mL) for antigens, which
are the breakdown products of either ﬁbrin or ﬁbrinogen. Serial dilutions of plasma yield more speciﬁc information
when the undiluted sample is positive. More expensive
quantitative analysis reveals normal serum levels of 2.1 to
2.7 µg/mL for FDPs in the absence of exercise or stress (1). This test does not differentiate the breakdown products of
ﬁbrinogen from those of ﬁbrin. D-Dimer
Molecules of two linked ‘‘D’’ domains, shown in Figure 2,
a speciﬁc degradation product of cross-linked ﬁbrin, can
be detected either semiquantitatively with a latex agglutination technique or in a fully quantitative manner with an
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Many hospital coagulation laboratories offer this test on a batched
basis. The D-dimer is more speciﬁc for secondary ﬁbrinol-
ysis than the FDP test.

appear as ﬁbrinogen equivalent units (i.e., the quantity of

The central role of platelets in coagulation and the impact
of bypass on platelet function augment the importance
of monitoring platelets during surgery. Because bypass
affects both platelet function and count, measurement
of platelet count is necessary but not sufﬁcient to assess
platelet role in coagulation. Although cell counters can
and have been made mobile (7), measurement of platelet
count has remained a central laboratory function at nearly
all centers. Platelet Aggregometry
Platelet aggregometry utilizes a photo-optical instrument
to measure light transmittance through a platelet-rich
plasma sample (8). Upon exposure to a platelet agonist,
the initially turbid sample shows increased light transmittance as platelets adhere to surfaces and one another. Impaired aggregation correlates poorly with clinical bleeding (8,9). Agonist agents include collagen, epinephrine,
and adenosine diphosphate (ADP). Owing to the technical
expertise often required to perform aggregometry, it ﬁnds
application in research rather than in routine clinical care. Ecarin Clotting Time
The injectable direct thrombin inhibitors hirudin, bivalirudin (also known as hirulog), and argatroban are
alternatives to heparin available to patients with heparininduced thrombocytopenia (HIT) (see Chapter 23). The
ecarin clotting time
(ECT) monitors the
extent of
anticoagulation from direct thrombin inhibitors.

It is
based on the conversion of thrombin to meizothrombin
by ecarin, venom from the snake Echis carinatus (10). Less procoagulant than thrombin, meizothrombin binds
to direct thrombin inhibitors in equimolar concentrations
creating a linear correlation between ECT prolongation
and thrombin inhibitor concentration (Fig. 3). With a
point of care ECT test (11–14) no longer available, each
hospital laboratory must create its own standardized version, therefore making the ECT extremely difﬁcult to
apply to the operative care of patients with HIT. Clinicians report successful cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)
using individual calibration curves for each patient (15). An alternative anticoagulation management scheme for
patients with HIT takes the functional approach using either the activated clotting time (ACT) or aPTT, as opposed
to targeting speciﬁc blood concentrations using the ECT. Only case reports exist regarding monitoring failure or
success (16–21). POINT OF CARE COAGULATION TESTS
For clinicians, the ability to obtain coagulation results
in a timely manner critically impacts the diagnosis and
treatment of speciﬁc hemostatic derangements: results
must be timely as well as accurate. Prompt turnaround
potentially saves time, which translates into ﬁnancial
savings. The desire for accurate and prompt coagulation
information has created an interest in point of care
testing (22). Point of care, also designated as ‘‘near-patient,’’ ‘‘onsite,’’ ‘‘alternate site,’’ or ‘‘bedside,’’ tests utilize whole blood
samples in close proximity to the patient, compared with
a laboratory test performed on a serum or plasma sample
at a hospital location remote from the patient. Figure 4
represents a typical point of care device. Transportation of

The real time endpoints for some point of care tests
differ from the values reported because of adjustment algorithms accounting for the difference in methodology. For
example, point of care aPTT endpoints take slightly longer
than those of the traditional laboratory-based aPTT. The
Hemochron Jr. ACT does not report actual elapsed time,
but rather calculates the ACT from an algorithm (see subsequent text). These discrepancies can confuse caregivers
unaware of the scientiﬁc foundation of the test procedures. In addition, point of care tests usually do not utilize
a coincident control sample.

Therefore, periodic quality
control assumes great importance to provide accurate
reproducible tests; this ethical and regulatory burden
falls on the caregivers by the patient’s bedside or in the
operating room. Because near-patient testing technology
undergoes rapid development, the reader should seek
additional current information when implementing it in
the operating room. With these strengths and limitations in mind, this
chapter now presents information on several point of
care tests for evaluating the coagulation status of patients
during and after CPB. Heparin Monitoring
Laboratory testing for heparin falls into two categories:
clotting function and measurements of blood or plasma
heparin concentration. Advocates of clotting time cite
the importance of assessing the clinical effect of heparin, suggesting that measuring concentration alone fails
to detect patients resistant to anticoagulation effects of
heparin (24). Proponents of concentration assays note
the changing relation between ACT and blood heparin
concentration induced by CPB, especially during hypothermia (25). Desirable characteristics of a heparin
monitor include low cost, the use of whole blood, point

463
of care availability with minimal equipment and operator
attention, precise and accurate results that are quickly
available, and the use of shelf-stable reagents (26). Activated Clotting Time
Introduced in 1966 by Hattersley (27), the ACT remains the
primary workhorse for monitoring anticoagulation during
CPB. Clinicians may now choose from a variety of devices
and reagents; the speciﬁc ones chosen will affect the degree
of automation and the normal and therapeutic ranges of
the test (28,29). Originally described using diatomaceous
earth (celite) as an activator, the operator placed whole
blood into a prewarmed tube submersed in a water bath
or placed on a heating block, and measured the time
for clot to form (27). Variation in operator attendance to
detail led to high variability in results, often explaining
the differences from one institution to another in ACT
requirements for initiation of CPB (30). The original manually performed ACT has been replaced by automated versions that minimize distraction
from the patient during CPB. Options available concurrent with publication appear in Table 1, with discussion
immediately following. The ﬁrst automated ACT utilized tubes containing celite
activator and a small cylindrical magnet (Hemochron
ACT; International Technidyne Corp., Edison, NJ) (1). The clinician starts a timer upon placing 2 mL of blood
in the tube, mixes the contents, and places it in an angled
detector well providing slow rotation. The magnet stays
in the most dependent portion of the tube as long as the
blood is liquid. When clot forms, the magnet, encased in
the clot, rotates away from a detector, which then halts the
timer and activates an audible signal. Variability using this
method remains between 4% and 8%, the higher values
occurring during heparin administration (31). Updated
versions of the original Hemochron machine now perform many point of care tests, using tubes with different
reagents (described later). Simultaneous measurement of
duplicate ACTs reduces occasional inappropriate clinical
management decisions that would occur when relying on
a single test result (32). Another automated version of Hattersley’s manual
test, the HemoTec (Medtronic, Englewood, CO) utilizes
a smaller volume of whole blood placed in a cuvette
containing kaolin activator and a plastic stirring plunger
that is lifted up in the cuvette approximately every 2
seconds (3). When the blood thickens sufﬁciently, fall
of the plunger by gravity is slowed.

Optics detects this
slower descent of the plunger and a timer is signaled. The
kaolin activator yields ACT values that are shorter than
the celite-based Hemochron device (33). Its variability is
approximately 9.2% (34). The Hemochron Jr. device moves 0.015-mL from a drop
of whole blood into a test channel (4). The sample picks up
reagent (celite or kaolin for ACT tests, depending on the
card chosen) as it moves through the card. Motion ceases
when clot forms. The device detects a mechanical endpoint
for clotting by optical means. The displayed result is not
true elapsed time; rather, it shows an equivalent ACT from
correlation analysis based on a device algorithm derived
from thousands of samples. Since its introduction (35),
the small sample volume and easy portability have made
this a popular option. Choice of Activator for Activated Clotting Time

This may arise from a heparin-like inhibitor of factor

However, the effect is small within the range of hematocrit

This effect occurs only with extreme thrombocytopenia
