rapidly hydrolyzed to thromboxane B2, which is inactive
and long-lived. Thromboxane A2 is known to be a potent
pulmonary vasoconstrictor. Pretreatment with thromboxane antagonists would seem to offer one solution
to pulmonary vasoconstrictive reactions, at least in the
animal model. However, thromboxane receptor antagonists can cause platelet dysfunction, which could lead
to increased hemorrhage following CPB. Therefore, an
extremely short-acting antagonist would be required for
clinical utility. Some thromboxane receptor antagonists are known to
inhibit platelet aggregation to collagen and arachidonic
acid stimulation and cause a brief prolongation of
bleeding times (81,85), whereas other antagonists cause
no increase in bleeding times, even at the highest dosages
used (80). Nuttall et al.

(81) showed that thromboxane
A2 receptor blockade initiated 2 minutes after protamine
administration shortened the duration of the pulmonary
hypertensive response in pigs despite similar elevations in
pulmonary artery pressures and plasma thromboxane B2
levels (Fig. 11). Although thromboxane release appears to be a central
factor in pulmonary vasoconstriction induced by heparin–protamine, the source of thromboxane is unclear. A
blood source seems doubtful, as the reaction can be produced in isolated lungs perfused with acellular media (82)
and in platelet-depleted animals (86). Endothelial cells or
more likely pulmonary intravascular macrophages (PIMs)
may be the source of the thromboxane. It has been speculated that PIMs may be the source of
the thromboxane generated in pulmonary vasoconstrictive reactions (87). These lung macrophages have been
described in sheep (88) and pigs (89) and occur less
commonly in rats (90,91) and dogs (92). They are ﬁve
times more numerous than neutrophils in sheep lung (93)
and occupy 15% of intracapillary volume (86). These
macrophages respond to the infusion of various foreign
particles by releasing vasoactive eicosanoids, particularly
thromboxane (94). Infusion of radioactively labeled protamine into rats and sheep showed uptake primarily by
the lungs in sheep with rapid development of pulmonary
vasoconstriction, in comparison with uptake primarily by
the liver in rats. On the basis of these data, it has been
hypothesized that the uptake of heparin–protamine complexes by PIMs causes the release of mediators, namely
thromboxane, with resultant pulmonary vasoconstriction. Humans have a lesser population of these macrophages
than do sheep, which may partially explain the variable
development of this syndrome in humans (85). Platelet-depleted sheep still exhibit increased thromboxane B2 levels, pulmonary vascular resistance, and
leukopenia when protamine is administered after heparin (84). These studies suggest that platelets do not cause
this adverse response.

Rate of Administration
Morel et al. (95) determined the rate of protamine
administration to be an important factor leading to
pulmonary vasoconstriction in sheep. In their study,
sheep given protamine during 3 seconds consistently
demonstrated thromboxane release, pulmonary vasoconstriction, increased pulmonary artery pressure, increased
systemic vascular resistance, and decreased cardiac output, whereas those given protamine over 30 minutes
exhibited no change. The intermediate infusion rates were
associated with variable and attenuated reactions. Site of Administration
The site of protamine administration has been considered
and studied as a triggering factor for protamine reactions. Canine studies (60,96) suggest that detrimental vasoactive
substances are released on exposure of the pulmonary
vasculature to protamine. Giving the drug on the left
side of the circulation or through a peripheral vein with
subsequent dilution was hypothesized to limit the ﬁrst-
pass pulmonary exposure. Casthely et al. (96) conﬁrmed
this hypothesis in a canine model in which protamine delivered during 4 minutes through a peripheral vein or the
left atrium proved benign, whereas delivery through central venous injection decreased systemic blood pressure
and systemic vascular resistance and increased pulmonary
vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure. These
results were not conﬁrmed by others (97,98). Frater et al. (98) demonstrated decreased systolic blood
pressure and increased plasma histamine levels in patients
given protamine through the right atrium, changes that
were not observed when protamine was administered
through the left atrium.

However, most human studies
to date have not demonstrated any advantage to left-sided
versus right-sided protamine administration (99,100). The
rate of infusion, and not the infusion site, appears to be
the more important variable to control. Lastly, because of
the risk for air embolization when a left atrial or aortic
route is used, protamine is probably best administered on
the right side of the circulation. Summary of Pulmonary Vasoconstrictive
Reactions
In summary, pulmonary vasoconstrictive protamine reactions in certain animal models result from uptake or
activation in the lung, perhaps by PIMs, of the heparin–
protamine complex. This interaction causes nonimmunologic activation of the classic complement pathway with
increased levels of C3a and C5a, which can release vasoconstrictor substances, most importantly thromboxane. The question of whether complement activation is merely
associated with the formation of heparin–protamine complexes or is a prerequisite for thromboxane generation
remains unsettled. Leukocytes do not appear to play a
crucial role, as evidenced by the work with acellular perfusates. Histamine and platelets also do not appear to be
involved. Certain drugs can block the development of this
syndrome at various points of the reaction, but because
of interference with coagulation or other problems, these
agents are not yet feasible for clinical use after CPB. Patients in whom pulmonary vasoconstriction and
bronchoconstriction developed following protamine administration at the conclusion of CPB had markedly
elevated levels of plasma thromboxane B2 and C5a in comparison with control patients in whom adverse responses
to protamine administration did not develop. The time of
peak thromboxane B2 levels corresponded to the maximum pulmonary artery pressures. These data suggest that
the activation of complement fraction C5a is associated
with thromboxane generation. Consistent with the animal
model, the same authors also documented that leukopenia
and increased C3a and C4a plasma concentrations were
universal after protamine administration, although only
patients in whom pulmonary vasoconstrictive reactions

developed had elevated concentrations of thromboxane
and C5a (101). One difference between the animal and human studies
has been that catastrophic pulmonary vasoconstriction
is demonstrated consistently in animal models, whereas
the incidence in humans is relatively low (1%–2%). This
fact suggests that different factors may play a role in
humans. Hobbhahn et al. (102) examined the effects of
protamine neutralization of heparin in 14 noncardiac
surgical patients undergoing transurethral surgery. Nine
of these 14 (64%) patients responded with increases
in mean pulmonary artery pressures, mean arterial
pressure, pulmonary vascular resistance, and increased
thromboxane B2 and C3a levels. This work conﬁrms the
relevance of the animal model to the human reaction. One interesting aspect of this syndrome is that although initial mediator release can cause catastrophic
hemodynamic changes, there are usually no long-lasting
tissue damage or sequelae if the patient can be supported
through the initial event. Diagnosis
Diagnosis of the type of protamine reaction in a patient
experiencing one is based on the clinical hemodynamic
presentation, the mediators that are present, and the
presence or absence of speciﬁc IgE or IgG antibodies. Screening for antibodies in insulin-dependent diabetics
may be a useful way to identify patients at risk for
anaphylaxis to protamine. Skin testing is available but requires a strict protocol
to yield reproducible results, is unreliable in diabetic
patients, and can cause an adverse systemic response
when an antigen is reintroduced (103). Additionally, as
stated earlier, the absence of a positive skin test reaction
does not ensure the lack of an IgE-mediated protamine
reaction. The leukocyte histamine response is an in vitro
test that has been used to detect protamine allergy in NPH
insulin–dependent diabetic patients and protect them
from adverse reactions (62). A positive response to this
standard technique in in vitro allergy study indicates
speciﬁc IgE antibodies (104). However, little evidence
supports the usefulness of this test in screening patients
at risk for adverse protamine reactions. Serum levels of
IgG or complement can be measured but are nonspeciﬁc
indicators of a potential allergic reaction, and they are
difﬁcult to interpret post hoc because of consumption
during the reaction and dilution by volume therapy during
an adverse reaction (99). The radioimmunosorbent assay is a semiquantitative
assay of a speciﬁc antibody described by Weiss et al. (65),
who used it to determine the presence of antiprotamine IgE.

The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
involves anti-IgE tagged with an enzyme that catalyzes a
photochemical reaction, and a modiﬁcation was employed
to determine IgG speciﬁc for protamine. Both tests described by Weiss et al. are probably the best currently
available for the diagnosis of protamine allergy. Prevention and Therapy
Prevention of the heparin–protamine reaction would be
the best strategy. Until a reliable screening test for antiprotamine antibodies becomes available, a history of a proven
anaphylactic reaction can be helpful. We have administered hexadimethrine for successful protamine reversal in
three protamine insulin-dependent diabetic patients who
had experienced a prior protamine reaction. A compassionate use Investigational New Drug application from
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is required
to gain permission to administer hexadimethrine bromide
in the United States. Protamine should be administered slowly. The protamine package insert suggests that infusion should not
be faster than 5 mg/min, although in practice, a rate of
15 mg/min seems to be well tolerated. Administration
should be terminated at the ﬁrst sign of any adverse
reaction. It is difﬁcult to strictly deﬁne a safe upper
limit for the rate of protamine administration, because
some patients tolerate administration rates as high as
50 mg/min with only mild vasodilatory responses, whereas
others may experience profound hypotension at rates
as low as 5 to 10 mg/min. Pharmacologic release reactions are rate-dependent, so that slow administration
prevents them. Protamine anaphylaxis is treated like any
classic anaphylactic reaction with oxygen, ﬂuids, and
epinephrine/norepinephrine. Excessive protamine doses
should be avoided because protamine has been shown
to inhibit the enzyme responsible for the inactivation of
anaphylatoxins and kinins, as mentioned earlier in this
chapter. Also, because protamine does not inhibit angiotensin I, which can also break down these compounds,
patients on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors may
be at some increased risk for pulmonary hypertensive
reactions to protamine (73). Prophylactic histamine 1 and histamine 2 blockers
and corticosteroids have not reduced the incidence of
pulmonary vasoconstrictor reactions. Histamine blockers
are known to decrease the severity of hypotension with
rapid protamine administration (55), which suggests a
role in IgE-mediated reactions, but there is no evidence to
support their routine use for this purpose. Therefore, we
do not recommend this strategy. Various supportive strategies have been used to treat
acute pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypotension, including such pulmonary vasodilators as nitroglycerin
and isoproterenol and virtually all vasoactive/inotropic
drugs.

The comparative efﬁcacy of different regimens
for these short-lived reactions has not been documented. Reinstitution of bypass may be required. It is crucial to

heparinize effectively before the reinstitution of bypass to
avoid gross clotting and the consumption of components of
coagulation, which can lead to disseminated intravascular
coagulation. Case reports suggest that the reinstitution of
bypass with heparin administration causes the reaction
to abate (105); however, it is likely that this represents
merely the conclusion of a transient reaction. The role
of thromboxane receptor blockade for treatment has not
been studied in patients. Inhaled nitric oxide has recently been reported as a
therapy for the pulmonary vasoconstrictor reactions induced by heparin–protamine complexes in lambs (106). Nitric oxide selectively produces profound relaxation of
the pulmonary vascular smooth muscle without systemic
vasodilation. In this animal model, breathing nitric oxide at 180 parts per million has been shown to attenuate
the pulmonary vasoconstrictor response markedly following heparin neutralization by protamine. Nitric oxide is
short-lived, easily administered, and effective for treating
certain types of reversible pulmonary hypertension. The
value of nitric oxide inhalation for treating protamineinduced pulmonary vasoconstriction in patients has yet
to be determined. The initial pulmonary vasoconstrictive episode usually
abates after a few minutes (3). Once this occurs, continued
inotropic infusion can result in a hyperdynamic heart, so
these agents may then need to be withdrawn. Protamine
administration may be reinstituted at a rate of 5 mg/min
following resolution of the episode and after resumption
of hemodynamic stability. FUTURE MANAGEMENT
To date there is no well-proven substitute for heparin
anticoagulation and its reversal with protamine for the
management of CPB. Research is ongoing in such areas
as total elimination of systemic heparinization through
the use of heparin-bonded bypass circuitry (107). Also,
heparin alternatives such as bivalirudin are under investigation. Research into the reversal of heparin by PF4 and
by heparinase, agents which showed considerable initial
promise, has slowed because of various combinations of
efﬁcacy limitations, side effects, and funding insufﬁciency. KEY POINTS
■Protamine, a strongly alkaline polycationic protein,
attracts the polyanionic heparin sufﬁciently to separate it from its binding site on AT III and reverse its
anticoagulant effect. ■Inhibition of plasma coagulation and platelet function
is one of the side effects of protamine, so it appears
prudent to avoid administering protamine doses
beyond the amount needed to neutralize heparin. ■Methods for calculating the protamine dose include
the following:
1. Use a ﬁxed ratio of protamine to the total or initial
dose of heparin.

2. Use the heparin–ACT dose–response to determine
the amount of circulating heparin, then assume
a protamine-to-heparin neutralization ratio of
approximately 1.1 to 1.3 mg to 100 U of heparin. 3. Measure whole blood or plasma heparin concentration, assume a protamine-to-heparin neutralization ratio, and estimate blood or plasma volume. ■A variety of methods exist for methods 2 and
3, some of which are automated. Each method
has advantages and disadvantages, and there is no
widely accepted ‘‘gold standard’’ for calculating the
protamine dose. ■Aside from commercially available protamine, other
possible approaches to heparin neutralization include the administration of hexadimethrine, PF4,
heparinase, or protamine variants (‘‘designer protamine’’), and the use of heparin-removal devices. Although some of these alternative methods are under
investigation, none is currently generally available. ■Protamine reactions can be classiﬁed as pharmacologic histamine release, true anaphylaxis, and anaphylactoid reactions. ●Pharmacologic histamine release is principally related to overly rapid administration of protamine
and can result in vasodilation and possibly myocardial depression. ●True anaphylaxis requires previous exposure to protamine, which has been conclusively demonstrated
only in diabetic patients taking intermediateduration insulin preparations that contain protamine. Even in that group of patients, the incidence
of anaphylaxis after protamine administration is
low (<3% in most studies). ●The interaction of protamine with heparin activates complement, which has been associated
with the release of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 (in sufﬁcient amounts) causes intense
pulmonary vasoconstriction. Factors predisposing
some patients to the development of this rare, lifethreatening reaction, which is predictable in some
animal species, remain ill-deﬁned. ●Antibody screening techniques may be useful for
identifying insulin-dependent diabetic patients at
risk for protamine-induced anaphylaxis. ●The treatment of protamine reactions is largely
supportive. It is possible that inhaled nitric oxide can rapidly and effectively terminate a lifethreatening pulmonary hypertensive response.

◗Pharmacologic Prophylaxis for
Post–Cardiopulmonary Bypass Bleeding
Glenn P. Gravlee and Bruce Spiess
Postcardiopulmonary bypass bleeding has complicated
cardiac surgery for its entire half-century history. The
mechanisms and treatment of this bleeding are discussed
in Chapter 21. Prevention of post-CPB bleeding may
take several nonpharmacologic forms, including avoidance of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) by using off-pump
techniques, improving the biocompatibility of artiﬁcial
surfaces, altering the conduct of CPB, and using hematologic strategies such as pre-CPB harvesting of whole
blood, plasma, or platelet-rich plasma or using transfusion algorithms to guide transfusion. Surgical technique
cannot be underestimated as a major factor in the use of
blood products and the amount of perioperative bleeding
that is encountered, nor can the importance of having
a normal hemoglobin concentration upon arrival in the
operating room. Assuming the use of relatively nontoxic
drugs, pharmacologic prophylaxis offers the appeal of
noninvasiveness and convenience. Cost-effectiveness is
also an important consideration, because the cost of the
various available agents varies considerably. Transfusion
avoidance constitutes an important goal in any surgical
intervention, but the importance of achieving this goal remains controversial. This chapter will principally address
the prophylactic use of antiﬁbrinolytic agents in cardiac
surgery. ANTIFIBRINOLYTIC AGENTS
Fibrinolysis and Antiﬁbrinolytic
Mechanisms
From the earliest days of cardiac surgery it has been known
that CPB activates protein and cellular elements that lead
to breakdown of ﬁbrinogen and other procoagulant precursors. Early leaders in cardiac surgery tried prophylactic
medications to decrease the activation of these proteins
in an attempt to ameliorate bleeding. More than 50 years
later we now know more about the causes of ﬁbrinolytic
activation, but every year new evidence converts prior
knowledge into new theories. We present our concept of
the state of knowledge, which continues to evolve at a
rapid pace. CPB anticoagulation is accomplished with high-dose
unfractionated heparin (UFH) anticoagulation. UFH has
a mild ﬁbrinolytic effect (1,2) while also stimulating the
release of serum urokinase plasminogen activator (UPA)
to mildly induce ﬁbrinolysis (3). Tissue plasminogen activator (TPA), which is far more potent than UPA, probably
serves as the primary activator of ﬁbrinolysis during heart
surgery (4). The largest surge in TPA occurs shortly after
protamine is administered to neutralize UFH (5), probably
because this is the time of highest thrombin production (6).

If thrombin generation were left unchecked by
TPA and its resultant ﬁbirinolysis, a small prothrombotic
stimulus could overwhelm the circulation and produce
large-scale clotting or diffuse intravascular coagulation. The release of TPA is accompanied by stimulation of the
protein S/C mechanism as well as an outpouring of nitric
oxide and other anticoagulant mechanisms. Thrombin is produced throughout CPB but it has
one very large surge as CPB commences and another
immediately after protamine is infused (7) (Fig. 1). Unfortunately, UFH in acting through the zymogen
antithrombin III can only attract, bind, and neutralize free
plasma thrombin. Thrombin has been widely recognized
as a key ampliﬁer protein (8,9) that activates many
different cell lines leading to inﬂammation, coagulation,
and ﬁbrinolysis, and it remains metabolically active in
sites (e.g., inside microclots) where it cannot be reached
by UFH. In a study measuring TPA and its regulating
protein plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1), it was
found that TPA on CPB varies at least 250-fold (10)
(Fig. 2). The variability of PAI-1 was more than 500-fold. Therefore, some patients experience CPB with little or
no ﬁbrinolytic response while others have a profound
response. Thrombin production drives TPA response,
whereas PAI-1 is produced principally by the liver and
endothelial cells, although platelets may release some

PAI-1 as well. PAI-1 binds to TPA as it is exported from
endothelial cells. Before TPA can create ﬁbrinolysis or
downregulate other proteins it must ﬁrst overcome the
circulating levels of PAI-1. Therefore PAI-1 forms a buffer
to surges of TPA. PAI-1, which is released in response to
inﬂammatory mediators, is highly prothrombotic because
it overcomes and suppresses the ﬁbrinolytic effects of
TPA. Genetic polymorphisms exist in both TPA and PAI-1,
which probably have implications in the epidemiology of
atherosclerosis (11). TPA directly cleaves plasminogen to plasmin (12),
which in turn has lysine binding sites where it can attach
to ﬁbrinogen and ﬁbrin. Once attached to ﬁbrinogen or
ﬁbrin, proteolytic attack leads to a number of breakdown
products. These lytic products, ﬁbrinopeptides, also serve
as serine protease inhibitors. Therefore, TPA breaks
apart ﬁbrin, which may be needed to crosslink platelets
(creating a clot) and it also inhibits coagulation precursor
reactions. These effects, if left unchecked, may be partially
responsible for post-CPB bleeding. Plasmin and plasminogen bind at a lysine-binding site
onto ﬁbrinogen and therefore it is no surprise that the
utility of some of our antiﬁbrinolytic drugs is based on
their mimicry of lysine. ε-Aminocaproic acid (ACA) is
essentially two lysine molecules stuck together. When
administered intravenously, ACA competitively binds to
the lysine-binding sites of plasminogen/plasmin and
prevents plasmin from attacking ﬁbrinogen or ﬁbrin.

Tranexamic acid (TA) is also a lysine analog. Aprotinin,
a 58-amino acid polypeptide, has a single lysine in its
chain and it is at that point that aprotinin has a very
high afﬁnity for plasmin. Aprotinin, a nonspeciﬁc serine
protease inhibitor, has several additional biologic actions
as well. Serine proteases as a group catalyze cascade
reactions of inﬂammation, coagulation, and other cellular
attack mechanisms. Lysine Analogs
ACA and TA are the two commercially available lysine
analogs. Their structural similarity to lysine is demonstrated in Figure 3. Both have been available clinically
for more than 40 years. Clinical uses have varied, but
prophylactic use in cardiac surgery dates at least to the
1960s (13). For many years the thinking was that prophylactic use should be initiated after CPB (14) or that
laboratory tests should guide their therapeutic use. In
1989, Del Rossi et al. reported a large placebo-controlled
series (350 patients) in which prophylactic pre-CPB administration of ACA decreased postoperative chest tube
drainage and transfusion without inducing hyperthrombotic complications (15). In general, lysine analog use
has proved effective in decreasing blood loss, but the
magnitude of effect and efﬁcacy in avoiding transfusion
has varied.

Pharmacology
Uptake, Distribution, and Elimination
For the purposes of cardiac surgery, only intravenous
administration applies, and uptake is immediate by this
route. Lysine analogs are small water-soluble molecules
that distribute readily into extravascular water spaces before being taken up into various cells and tissues (16–18). Speciﬁc measurements of total volume of distribution
(VD) could not be found, but one would expect initial VD
to approximate that of the extravascular water space, that
is, approximately 20% of body mass in lean adults. This
matches the ﬁndings of Butterworth et al., who also found
the expected increase in initial VD from approximately
12 L pre-CPB to approximately 15 L during CPB (19,20). A two-compartment elimination model ﬁts the ﬁndings
of Butterworth et al. (20). TA is weakly protein bound,
probably principally to plasminogen, and it crosses the
blood–brain barrier and the placenta (21). Renal excretion accounts for most elimination of the two clinically
available drugs, TA and ACA. After intravenous administration, approximately 45% of drug is recovered in the
urine after 3 hours, and approximately 90% is recovered
after 24 hours (21). The elimination half-life of both drugs
has been reported as between 1 and 2 hours following intravenous administration, and most of the drug is excreted
unchanged in the urine.

Dosing
Dosing protocols for prophylaxis have varied widely, and
are not as standardized for lysine analogs as for aprotinin,
nor have the pharmacokinetics been as well deﬁned. Perhaps the most popular dosing has been to administer
a loading dose before CPB over 1 to 15 minutes followed
by a continuous intravenous infusion. For ACA, a loading
dose of 75 to 150 mg/kg (typically 5–10 g in an adult)
has commonly been administered, typically followed by
a continuous infusion of 10 to 15 mg/kg/hr. Reports
vary about use of a priming dose for the extracorporeal
circuit, although it makes pharmacokinetic sense to add
a dose commensurate with the circuit priming volume, or
approximately 2 to 2.5 g/L of priming solution to match
the anticipated plasma concentration induced by an ACA
loading dose of 100 mg/kg. Ultraﬁltration slightly reduces
the concentration of ACA (22). Typically the infusion
continues until either the end of CPB or until protamine is
administered to neutralize heparin after CPB, but there is
no established standard for discontinuation. Some choose
to administer lysine analogs for 10 or more hours (21). Another approach is the ‘‘10-10-10’’ approach of Daily
et al., whereby 10 grams of ACA are administered as
a slow bolus (5–10 minutes) before CPB, into the CPB
priming solution, and after CPB (23). Ray et al. found that
post-CPB initiation of either aprotinin or ACA in patients
with chest tube drainage exceeding 100 mL/hr was no
better than placebo at reducing chest tube drainage or
D-dimer levels, although the study population was small
at approximately 20 patients per group (24). Bennett-Guerrero et al. measured plasma ACA concentrations in 27 patients following a standardized dosing
protocol using a loading dose of 150 mg/kg of ACA at skin

dose in the CPB circuit, plasma concentrations remained

dose of 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes followed by a maintenance infusion of 25 mg/kg/hr will achieve and maintain
target concentrations. They did not prime the CPB circuit

In an anephric patient, it seems appropriate to use a
normal or slightly reduced loading dose and a substantially
reduced continuous infusion rate (e.g., 5 mg/kg/hr for ACA
and 0.5 mg/kg/hr for TA) while monitoring antiﬁbrinolytic
efﬁcacy by periodically measuring D-dimer concentrations
or assessing ﬁbrinolysis using a thromboelastogram. Controversy exists also about the optimal time for initiation of lysine analogs for patients undergoing CPB. Often
the initial dose has been administered as early as between
anesthetic induction and surgical incision. However, case
reports of clot formation on pulmonary artery catheters as
well as electrocardiographic ST changes have caused many
to await full anticoagulation with heparin before administering these drugs (26,27). These concerns make sense,
because patients with coronary artery atherosclerosis are
at risk for arterial thrombosis, and loss of the ﬁbri-
nolytic capability in such patients theoretically increases
the risk for clinically signiﬁcant coronary arterial thrombosis. Kluger et al. therefore compared ACA initiation
before incision and after heparin to placebo in 90 primary
coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) patients (28). They
found that both ACA dosing protocols reduced chest tube
drainage compared with placebo and that there was no
difference in chest tube drainage between the two ACA
groups. It therefore appears acceptable to initiate antiﬁb-
rinolytic prophylaxis after anticoagulation for CPB but
before initiating CPB. TA dosing is typically one seventh to one tenth that
of ACA, hence a typical loading dose would be 10 to
15 mg/kg over 10 to 15 minutes followed by an infusion
of 1 to 1.5 mg/kg/hr. Fiechtner et al. (29) found that this
dosing achieved and maintained therapeutic plasma concentrations throughout CPB, and that patients with renal
insufﬁciency had increased plasma concentrations using
that dosing regimen. Dowd et al. (30) studied the clinical
pharmacokinetics of TA during CPB and recommended
a loading dose of 12.5 mg/kg or higher over 30 minutes followed by a continuous infusion of 6.5 mg/kg/hr
in addition to 1 to 2.5 g in the CPB priming solution. A dose–response study for TA indicated that a loading
dose of 10 mg/kg followed by an infusion of 1.0 mg/kg
achieved reductions in chest tube drainage, and that
higher doses did not confer additional beneﬁt (31), although some groups prefer TA loading doses as high as
100 to 150 mg/kg.

Sustained therapeutic or supratherapeutic plasma concentrations for many hours after CPB
constitute the anticipated consequence of higher dosing regimens. Such sustained high plasma concentrations
theoretically increase the risk for thromboembolic complications, but this risk has not been proved (32). Karski
et al. suggest that these higher doses improve hemostasis. We recommend the more conservative loading dose of 10
to 15 mg/kg initiated after anticoagulation, followed by
an infusion of 1 to 1.5 mg/kg/hr until the end of CPB
accompanied by a CPB priming dose of 2 to 2.5 mg/L.

Side Effects and Toxicity
When used in unanesthetized patients, a low incidence of nausea, diarrhea, and orthostatic reactions may
occur (17). In other clinical settings, ACA has been associated with rhabdomyolysis, upper urinary tract thrombosis,
anion gap acidosis, and hyperkalemia (33) When lysine
analogs are given to patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation, intravascular thrombosis may occur,
and it appears plausible that this could occur during or
after CPB, but this speciﬁc association has not been reported to date. Thromboembolic complications such as
reduced early graft patency, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolus, stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI)
are theoretically possible as a result of residual effects
of lysine analogs after heparin neutralization, but several focused reviews and meta-analyses have not found
such an association (34–37). The absence of this ﬁnding
in those studies does not necessarily exclude an association, however, because these complications have not
been rigorously pursued in large numbers of patients undergoing prospective investigation. Lysine analogs have
not been associated with an increase in the incidence
of renal dysfunction or failure or of mortality in cardiac surgery (35–38). A recent prospective investigation
including more than 1,600 patients who received ACA or
TA found no association between these agents and renal
events, cardiac events, cerebral events, or mortality (39). This multicenter study lacked random patient assignment,
but an attempt was made to compensate for this deﬁciency
using propensity analysis. Overall, although the safety pro-
ﬁle of lysine analogs in cardiac surgery lacks the beneﬁt
of large randomized prospective studies using standardized diagnostic criteria for major organ toxicities, the
likelihood that these agents cause major organ toxicity or
mortality appears low. As logic would dictate, the principal outcome beneﬁt of
transfusion avoidance or reduction can only be realized
in situations where transfusion is expected to occur. Consequently, the argument can be made that patients
who are at low risk for transfusion despite the need for
CPB might not beneﬁt from prophylactic antiﬁbrinolysis. For example, the combination of a fast surgeon whose
patients lose little blood, a patient weighing more than
80 kg, and a preoperative hematocrit exceeding 40% could
call the need for antiﬁbrinolytic pharmacoprophylaxis into
question.

Conversely, a surgeon who tends to have longer
operative and CPB times and greater blood loss operating
on a 45-kg patient with a preoperative hematocrit below
30% virtually assures a need for transfusion. In the
latter situation, pharmacoprophylaxis will reduce the
amount of transfusion and hence confer beneﬁt. In
situations between those two extremes, antiﬁbrinolytic
pharmacoprophylaxis can tip the scales toward avoiding
transfusion. Aprotinin
As already mentioned, aprotinin is different than the lysine
analogs (40). Aprotinin is a 65 amino acid polypeptide
found in all mammalian lung tissue but isolated for
pharmaceutical purposes from bovine lung. The active
site of aprotinin contains a single lysine, which appears to
be the binding site for most of the serine proteases that it
inhibits. As a nonspeciﬁc serine protease inhibitor it has
effects upon trypsin, chymotrypsin, plasmin, kallikrein,
bradykinin, TPA, urokinase plasminogen activator, and
complement. The relative strength of the effects of
aprotinin upon these various serine proteases is shown
in Table 1. In the 1960s, aprotinin was thought to have
some potential to decrease the destructive digestive effects
of pancreatic enzymes such as trypsins, but aprotinin did
not prove beneﬁcial in that setting. Also in the 1960s, some
investigators proposed using aprotinin for CPB patients,
but the dosing was low and the drug was often utilized
after pathologic bleeding was already prodigious. At that
time, prophylactic use of aprotinin was not proposed. The turning point in aprotinin use came from collaboration of three now well-known physicians in the 1980s
at the Hammersmith Hospital in London. Ben Bidstrup
and Kenneth Taylor, cardiovascular surgeons, interacted
with an anaesthetist, David Royston, in an investigation to
determine if aprotinin could decrease the frequency and
severity of postoperative lung dysfunction after CPB (41). These three investigators thought that inﬂammatory mediation through a kallikrein-initiated cascade might serve
as the trigger for post-CPB pulmonary dysfunction. These three colleagues went to a local pub, and with the
help of local brew they outlined aprotinin dosing that they
believed would dramatically inhibit kallikrein production
in circulating blood. That dosing was 2 million kallikrein
inhibiting units (KIU) infused into the patient before CPB,
plus 2 million KIU into the prime of the CPB machine
and a continuous drip of 500,000 KIU/hr to cover any
metabolism or clearance of aprotinin.

527
In the ﬁrst 20 or more patients who received aprotinin,
there appeared to be little or no effect upon pulmonary gas
exchange and postoperative lung dysfunction. However,
by pure serendipity the group agreed that the surgical
ﬁeld was dramatically dry. This led to several early
publications noting the transfusion-sparing and chest tube
bleeding reduction effects of aprotinin. Bidstrup’s ﬁrst
series notably had only 24 repeat operation patients, 15
for valve replacements or repairs and 9 for CABG (42). Royston’s ﬁrst publication similarly had few patients, 18
valve replacements and 4 CABG patients (41). Again, these
were repeat surgeries. In Bidstrup’s series the blood loss
data was dramatic: for aprotinin patients only 245 mL
and for placebo patients 1,979 mL over the ﬁrst 24 hours. Royston only used aprotinin, but in his group of 22
patients the average 24-hour blood loss was 286 mL (42). By the late 1980s a series of small studies showed dramatic
reductions in transfusion (41–43). To date there are more than 6,800 publications
about aprotinin in cardiac surgery. This chapter cannot
exhaustively summarize this literature, nor cite even a
fraction of the world’s research in the area. However,
some important studies will be examined in depth. In
Europe, aprotinin, which was already widely available,
rapidly gained acceptance in cardiac surgery. Dietrich
published his experience with more than 1,700 patients
in 1990 (44), noting dramatic decreases in transfusion as
well as blood loss. The ﬁrst large prospective U.S. Food
and Drug Administration (FDA) Phase III trial of aprotinin
was performed in patients undergoing reoperative CABG
surgery (45). The study took place at the Cleveland Clinic
under the direction of Delos Cosgrove. That study showed
differences in 24-hour chest tube drainage between a high
dose or ‘‘full Hammersmith’’ dose, a 50% reduction (‘‘halfHammersmith’’) of that dose, and a placebo (720 versus
866 versus 1,121 mL, respectively). That study has been
controversial and will be reviewed later in the chapter. Bayer Pharmaceuticals (West Haven, CT) pushed forward with two more studies in repeat CABG surgery. One
was published by Lemmer et al. and another by Levy
et al. (46,47). Levy et al.

compared three potential dosages
of aprotinin with placebo in a multicentered study of repeat CABG and found substantial reductions in chest tube
drainage, 390 mL versus 900 mL comparing high-dose (full
Hammersmith) aprotinin and placebo. The pump prime
dose utilized in Levy’s study did not show statistical difference in chest tube output from that seen with placebo. Interestingly, the half-Hammersmith dose (1 million KIU to
the patient, 1 million KIU to the pump prime and 250,000
KIU/hr as an infusion) was not statistically different from
the full dose. Levy’s study also showed a marked reduction
in overall transfusion utilization. Those patients who had
the full Hammersmith dose received on average 2.2 donor
exposures of transfusion, whereas those who had placebo
received 10.3 donor exposures. Five prospective randomized trials were completed for the purpose of ﬁling an
application to the FDA for approval of aprotinin use in cardiac surgery. Only recently has all of the efﬁcacy data and
safety data been published together in summary form (48). Mechanism of Action
As noted earlier, aprotinin exerts its actions partially by
decreasing kallikrein and by therefore reducing inﬂam-
mation (49). Kallikrein by itself does not affect bleeding,
but it does contribute to the activation of the intrinsic
cascade and therefore to some activation of coagulation
precursor proteins. More importantly, kallikrein activates
proinﬂammatory white blood cells (WBCs) and may inhibit some platelet–WBC interactions. The platelet–WBC
conjugate strongly stimulates inﬂammation. Table 1 lists the relative degrees to which each of the
known protein enzymes is downregulated or buffered by
aprotinin. Trypsin, the most easily inhibited protein, has
inﬂammatory and anticoagulation properties. It requires
only a very small amount of aprotinin to inhibit plasmin
formation. Perhaps that is why most who are experts in an-
tiﬁbrinolytic therapy will advise that there is no synergistic
advantage to combining a lysine analog and aprotinin. If
one uses reasonable does of aprotinin, all plasmin will be
inhibited, and the same holds true for the lysine analogs. Aprotinin also possesses mild antithrombin activity. It is
unclear whether this effect derives from the serine protease action or whether the decrease in kallikrein and
intrinsic coagulation cascade activation translates into
a decrease in thrombin activity. Through these multiple
mechanisms, complement and a number of interleukin
messenger proteins are decreased as well.

This inﬂamma-
tory downregulation appears to protect platelets, as glycoprotein Ib and IIb/IIIa platelet surface receptors are better
preserved when aprotinin is utilized (44,50–52) (Fig. 4). Protease activated receptors (PARs) constitute another
very important recently-discovered glycoprotein activation site on platelets and WBCs. The PAR-1 on the
surface of platelets reacts to thrombin. The fact that aprotinin maintains the PAR-1 may importantly contribute to
platelet functional preservation in patients treated with
aprotinin (53). Efﬁcacy
The literature supports the efﬁcacy of aprotinin in reducing perioperative chest tube drainage in either reoperation
CPB cases, complex CABG cases or CABG cases with
the coexistence of aspirin or other platelet inhibiting
drugs (35,36,54–56). Most studies demonstrate a 40% to
80% reduction in 24 hour-chest tube drainage as compared
with placebo. In studies carried out for FDA indications, it

that the bleeding and transfusion utilization in the control
group was considerably less than one might have expected
for a group receiving platelet inhibitors, perhaps because
the platelet inhibitors were discontinued 5 days before
surgery in the control group. The aprotinin patients had
the platelet inhibitors maintained up to the day of surgery;
hence it seems likely that the aprotinin patients would have
been at higher risk for bleeding than the control patients
at the time of surgery. Ideal study design would have also
included a group of patients who received a lysine analog.

Reoperation to investigate surgical versus microvascular bleeding or to drain a blood collection in the
mediastinum or pleural cavity adds risk and expense.

529
From the data collected in aprotinin trials, the rate of
reoperation for bleeding in placebo patients ranged from
1.4% in primary CABG patients to 1.9% in reoperation
cases. These numbers were lower than ones from contemporary literature at the time that the studies were being
conducted. With the use of aprotinin, the reoperation for
bleeding in both groups (primary and reoperation cases)
was 0.0% (n = 784 patients). Unfortunately, these clinical
trials typically did not report the frequency of severe bleeding. In one series, approximately 20% of patients were
noted to have severe bleeding and that small subgroup
of patients therefore accounted for a disproportionately
large use of blood products. The latest application of aprotinin has come in offpump coronary artery bypass grafting (OPCAB) (60). Some data supports that patients coming for CABG
surgery are intrinsically a prothrombotic group with
a selection bias for polymorphisms that would make
them hypercoagulable. An off-pump group might be at
a higher risk for perioperative graft thrombosis than an
on-pump CABG group because they would lack the mild
coagulopathy that typically follows CPB. Poston et al. conducted a prospective randomized trial of aprotinin
in primary OPCAB (60). This study assessed blood loss
and transfusion as well as graft and native vessel closure
rate using ultrafast computed axial tomographic scanning. Twenty-nine patients received aprotinin and 31 patients
received placebo. Chest tube drainage in the aprotinin
group was approximately 25% that of the placebo group
(p = 0.004). The mean use of red cells transfused was
1.3 units in the aprotinin patients and 2.3 units in
the placebo group. However, the use of an average of
2.3 units of blood in control patients exceeds that of
other reports, as one of the advantages to the off-pump
approach is a substantial reduction in blood loss and
transfusion, with transfusion commonly averaging less
than 1 unit per patient. Interestingly, Poston et al. found
lower concentrations of the prothrombin fragment F1.2 in
the aprotinin group (Fig. 5), and the blood ﬂow in grafts
was signiﬁcantly better in that group as well. Graft Patency and Myocardial Infarction Data
Poston’s study is the only one to date that examines graft
patency with and without aprotinin in the face of ‘‘offpump’’ CABG (60).

It is very easy, and probably far too
simplistic, to simply assume that any pharmacologic agent
that would decrease bleeding would increase the risk for
graft thrombosis. It is also hard for many to understand
how a drug such as aprotinin that has mild antithrombin
properties would decrease bleeding. The ﬁrst U.S.-based study of aprotinin by Cosgrove et al. raised the question of graft patency when a trend (not statistically signiﬁcant p = 0.15) was observed toward more

Perhaps
the most important point is that although Cosgrove’s graft
patency data is interesting, it comes only from autopsy
data in very few patients and it does not reach statistical
signiﬁcance. Bidstrup examined early graft closure by magnetic resonance imaging at 7 and 12 days after surgery (61). In
his 90 primary CABG patients there were no differences
in graft patency for vein grafts and all 46 of the arterial
conduits were patent at 12 days. In a similar study using
ultrafast computed tomography (CT) angiography, Lemmer et al. examined graft patency in CABG surgery (62).

A total of 151 primary and 65 reoperative CABG patients
took part in the study and had their grafts assessed at 7 and
30 days after surgery. This randomized placebo-controlled
study found no signiﬁcant difference in graft patency for
veins and internal mammary arteries but there was a trend
toward lower patency rates in the patients who received
aprotinin. There was no difference (and no trend) in MI
rates between groups in his study. In a prospective randomized trial of aprotinin in three
different dosages or placebo in repeat CABG surgery, MI
was assessed by a core laboratory (47). There was no
difference in MI rates, but there was no examination
of graft patency. Alderman prospectively examined graft
ﬂow and closure in a 13-center international study of
870 patients undergoing primary CABG surgery who
received either high-dose aprotinin or placebo (63). Electrocardiograms, myocardial enzymes, perioperative
blood loss and transfusion utilization were also assessed. As in prior studies, the use of full-dose aprotinin was
highly efﬁcacious in reducing chest tube output and
transfusion (43% reduction blood loss and 49% reduction
in transfusion p < 0.0001 for each). Approximately 703
of the 870 patients underwent graft assessment by repeat
angiography. In the overall group, 15.4% of saphenous
veins thrombosed in patients who received aprotinin
and 10.9% in those who received a placebo (p = 0.03). However, the use of aprotinin did not affect the occurrence
of MI (2.9% aprotinin versus 3.8% placebo) or mortality
(1.4% aprotinin versus 1.6% placebo). Even with the large
sample size and prospective design, some risk factors
were taken into account. The largest risk factor for graft
occlusion appears to have been site (i.e., country) of
surgery. Others included lack of aspirin therapy, female
gender, and poor target quality for graft anastomosis. The graft patency rate in U.S. centers was exactly the
same with and without aprotinin. The graft closure rate in
aprotinin patients was 9.4% and in placebo patients it was
9.5% (p = 0.72). In the two non-U.S. sites, Denmark and
Israel, the graft closure rate was 15.4% for aprotinin and
10.9% for placebo patients (p = 0.03). One explanation
often given for this discrepancy was that patients at
these two centers often had grafts attached to very small
vessels. However, other untested population differences
may have had effects as well.

For example, factor V Leiden
polymorphism or protein C/S deﬁciency may be more
common in northern Europeans or Israeli populations
than in the more heterogeneous U.S. population. Occasional case reports surface reporting sudden and
catastrophic thrombosis. These reports often note not
graft thrombosis but catastrophic large vessel, atrial, or
even whole-heart thrombosis as a patient is weaned from
CPB or after heparin neutralization by protamine has begun (64,65). Unfortunately one cannot conclude anything
about an increased or decreased thrombotic risk from
such reports. One very interesting report comes from
Canada, however, wherein a patient had undergone CPB
for CABG and had difﬁculty sustaining his myocardial
function immediately after weaning from CPB (66). He
was reheparinized and placed back on bypass. A graft
was not working well and it was redone and then another
attempt at weaning took place. Shortly after this second
attempt a transesophageal echocardiography probe was
placed and diffuse clot was seen propagating throughout
the heart and great vessels. What is striking about this case
is that (a) the patient did not receive aprotinin, and (b) the
team thought to get a heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
antibody screen. The screen came back highly positive
for such antibodies. This brings up the point that perhaps heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis
(HITT) could contribute to a prothrombotic risk that had
hitherto gone undiagnosed. In the Canadian case, HITT
was certainly the cause of sudden massive and mortal clotting within the heart and great vessels. In summary, the
evidence supporting a direct link from aprotinin to hypercoagulability or graft thrombosis is inconclusive. When
all the aprotinin prospective trials used for FDA approval
were examined, there was no difference in MI rate between those who got aprotinin and those who received
placebo (11% versus 10.4%). Two meta-analyses examined MI rates and found no
evidence for aprotinin as a risk factor for perioperative
MI. In Sedrakyan’s meta-analysis there was no overall
difference in MI (55). The Cochrane review also noted no
difference in MI rate (35). Levi et al. performed perhaps the
largest and most inclusive meta-analysis (8,409 patients)
of patients receiving either lysine analogs or aprotinin (36). Seventy-two separate trials were included. Unlike the other
meta-analyses, Levi did ﬁnd a reduction in mortality with
aprotinin [odds ratio (OR) of 0.55, conﬁdence interval
(CI) 0.34–0.90].

Treatment with aprotinin was also very
effective in reducing the incidence of reexploration for
bleeding (OR of 0.37, 95% CI 0.25–0.55). Aprotinin was
not associated with an increased incidence of MI. Other Organ Function
Levy et al., were the ﬁrst to note that the use of aprotinin
might have neurologic protective effects (47). In their
prospective randomized trial of three different dosages of
aprotinin versus placebo (DDAVP) there were no strokes
in any patient who received either mid- or high-dose
aprotinin. In the placebo group 5 of 72 patients (7%)
had strokes. In Sedrakyan and Henry’s meta-analyses,
stroke was the only thing other than blood transfusion
reduction that was decreased by aprotinin usage (35,55). In Sedrakyan’s analysis the risk of stroke was essentially
cut in half (55). Frumento et al. examined high-risk
CABG patients who received placebo, full-dose or halfdose aprotinin (67). In placebo patients the risk of stroke
was 16% and in half-dose aprotinin the risk of stroke was

alone has just been completed but is not yet published. Royston, in a meta-analysis of the Bayer data base found
that when placebo was compared with high-dose aprotinin
the stroke rate dropped from 2.4% to 1% (48). It should
be noted that stroke was not a primary outcome in these
studies, that stroke is a challenging outcome to assess,
and that sophisticated techniques for diagnosing strokes
and new neurologic deﬁcits were typically not employed
in these studies. Nevertheless, the outcomes observed
are provocative and meritorious of prospective studies
designed speciﬁcally to assess stroke and neurologic
outcomes as a primary goal. Although it might seem obvious, the patients with the
worst renal function before CPB have the greatest risk for
further impairment in renal function and for the development of renal failure requiring dialysis, with or without
aprotinin. Indeed, when stratiﬁed for estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (GFR), patients with normal GFR have
a very low risk for requiring dialysis postoperatively (68). When preoperative GFR is 50% of normal, the risk of
requiring postoperative dialysis exceeds 20%, and the risk
becomes 85% with preoperative GFR less than 20% of
normal. Both low hematocrit and transfusion to avoid
low hematocrit have been retrospectively associated with
adverse renal outcomes as well. Aprotinin must then be
examined in the context of existing literature about renal
failure (69). It has been known since the 1960s that aprotinin, as a
small polypeptide, competes with creatinine in the ascending loop of Henle for excretion. Consequently, one would
expect to see a rise in serum creatinine concentrations in
the presence of aprotinin, but this would not necessarily
denote renal damage. Lemmer et al.

ﬁrst noted that mean
serum creatinine concentrations were higher in patients
who received aprotinin as compared with those who received placebo (70). These creatinine concentrations were
higher at days 3 to 7 but the difference reached statistical signiﬁcance at day 7 (1.28 mg/dL in aprotinin-treated
versus 1.10 mg/dL in placebo patients). By days 14 to 30 of
follow-up, serum creatinine was identical in both groups. Consequently, it appears that this transient increase in creatinine levels may reﬂect competition between aprotinin
and creatinine for secretion by the tubules. In the Lemmer
study, there were three patients who went on to develop
creatinine levels above 2.0 mg/dL, all of whom received
aprotinin (p = 0.25). However, dialysis was required in
only one patient in each group. When Mangano reported
renal outcomes in a cohort of approximately 2,400 CABG
patients, she found a clinically relevant postoperative rise
in creatinine seen in just less than 8% of patients, with or
without aprotinin (71). If one reviews meta-analyses addressing this topic,
aprotinin was not associated with a signiﬁcant incremental risk of renal failure. In another study by Mora-Mangano
of 853 retrospectively analyzed thoracic aortic procedures performed at Stanford University, aprotinin was
analyzed as a potential risk factor for renal failure or dysfunction (72). In that study of patients who might well
be considered to be at high risk for renal dysfunction,
aprotinin was not implicated. Sundt et al. retrospectively
analyzed patients undergoing thoracic aortic replacement
with deep hypothermia (73). He noted that patients who
received aprotinin had a higher incidence of creatinine in
excess of 1.5 mg/dL as compared with 20 historic controls. There were differences in anticoagulation management
between these two noncontemporary groups and his data
stands in contrast to the much larger retrospective study
by Mora-Mangano. Mangano et al. reported a large retrospective analysis of
the Epi-II data from the Multicenter Study of Perioperative
Ischemia (McSPI) group (39). This was an observational
database prospectively collected from 69 or 70 centers
around the world. All patients underwent CABG on CPB;
reoperation, combined procedures and emergency procedures were also allowed. Each participating institution
had a scheme for drug randomization based on the total
number of CABG patients done per year at their institution. In this retrospective data analysis 1,295 patients
received aprotinin, 883 received ACA, 822 received TA,
and 1,374 received no antiﬁbrinolytic agent.

Mangano found that ‘‘the use of aprotinin was associated with an increased risk of renal and nonrenal
events when compared with ACA, TA, or no antiﬁbri-
nolytic therapy . . .’’ Renal events were deﬁned as a change
of at least 65 µmol/L, dialysis or death with renal autopsyproved renal failure. In the 3,013 patients undergoing
primary CABG surgery the incidence of renal events was
5.5% in patients who received aprotinin and 1.8% in patients who received no antiﬁbrinolytic. Mangano noted in
this retrospective review that there was a dose dependency,
with adverse events going up in proportion to aprotinin
dosing. A propensity analysis was done to correct for
comorbidities. The patients who received aprotinin were

IV. Hematology
more ill on average than either those who received ACA,
TA, or no antiﬁbrinolytic, so physicians were evidently
channeling sicker patients to the group that received aprotinin. Propensity analysis can modify the bias created by
the fact that those patients who received aprotinin were at
higher risk, and Mangano et al. did include more than 90
potentially confounding factors into this analysis. Consequently, Mangano et al. may have uncovered a heretofore
unknown relation between aprotinin and adverse renal
outcomes. After reporting this association, the authors unwisely concluded that aprotinin had caused this amount
of renal failure as well as other adverse outcomes. Retrospective data analysis cannot establish causation. In a somewhat similar investigation, Karkouti et al. retrospectively analyzed the data base at the University of
Toronto (74). At that institution, TA is the preferred an-
tiﬁbrinolytic agent. Four hundred and forty-nine patients
who received aprotinin were risk-matched to 449 patients
who received TA (out of the 10,870 who received TA). Like
the Lemmer report (70), Karkouti noted that there was
a transient rise in creatinine: 24% of aprotinin patients
had an increase in creatinine to a peak greater than 50%
of baseline concentrations, whereas 17% of matched TA
patients experienced this degree of rise in creatinine concentration (74). This might be interpreted as conﬁrmation
of what Mangano et al. found, but Karkouti found no
difference in either death rate or overall dialysis rate with
aprotinin or TA. In summary, aprotinin interferes with creatinine secretion in the renal tubules. The work done in randomized
prospective studies has largely excluded patients who have
moderate to severe renal dysfunction preoperatively. It remains unclear whether aprotinin adversely affects renal
function in patients whose kidneys are already at risk before surgery. Most of the evidence to date does not support
an independent and large risk for renal failure. Indeed the
Mangano paper stands in contrast to other work, not only
in its renal failure conclusion but in that it associated other
adverse outcomes with aprotinin use. Ideally, either a
blinded reanalysis of the Mangano data or further prospective trials are needed to settle this controversy. A prospective trial under way in Canada is randomly comparing the
use of aprotinin, ACA, and TA in high-risk patients. Dosage and Pharmacokinetics
A wide range of dosages has been proposed for aprotinin.

The full ‘‘Hammersmith dose’’ is perhaps the most
commonly used protocol. As mentioned earlier, this dose
was based on a goal to maximally inhibit kallikrein. The
full Hammersmith dose is: 2 million KIU in the CPB pump
prime, 2 million KIU administered intravenously to the
patient (over 30–60 minutes) and a continuous infusion of
500,000 KIU/hr for the duration of CPB. Such a dose in a
70-kg person creates a circulating plasma concentration of
approximately 4 mmol aprotinin or 200 KIU/mL. Plasmin
may be inhibited by as little as 20 KIU/mL. Plasma halflife for aprotinin with this dose regimen is approximately
5 hours. As inferred earlier, aprotinin is predominantly
excreted renally and to date there is no ability to predict the
prolongation of half-life with differing levels of decreased
glomerular ﬁltration. In combining all trials, it appeared
that blood loss and transfusion requirements are lowest
with full-dose aprotinin. Dietrich et al. recently conducted a retrospective
analysis suggesting that even higher doses of aprotinin
may further reduce bleeding (53). Nuttall et al. proposed
a dosing protocol based on patient weight, which makes
sense in view of the large variation in patient weights and
of concerns about toxicity, but their recommendations do
not appear to have deterred most centers from selecting
the full Hammersmith dosing protocol (75). In their
protocol, a plasma concentration of 200 KIU/mL was
fairly reliably achieved with a loading dose of 3.5 mg/kg
(25,000 KIU/kg), an extracorporeal circuit priming dose
of 70 mg (500,000 KIU, assumes a 2 L priming volume),
and an infusion rate of 3.5 mg/kg/hr (25,000 KIU/kg/hr)
for the ﬁrst hour, and 1 mg/kg/hr (approximately 7,000
KIU/kg/hr) for subsequent hours until completion of CPB. Allergic Reactions
Aprotinin is a foreign protein derived from bovine sources. The size of the protein is similar to that of protamine
(approximately 6,000 Da). Allergic reaction to a ﬁrst-time
dose is rare but probably does exist. This occurrence
rate can only be estimated at approximately 1 in 10,000
exposures. Those patients with a history of atopic events,
multiple drug allergies, or other anaphylactic reactions
could be suspect and treated with extra care. It is common
practice for most practitioners to administer a 1 mL test
dose of aprotinin before starting the loading dose.

This
practice is recommended in the aprotinin package insert,
along with the advice that one should wait at least 10
minutes after the test dose before beginning the loading
dose. However, there is no series that documents the
efﬁcacy of this practice in either detecting or preventing
anaphylaxis. In a retrospective review of all the cases performed
in Munich Heart Center between 1988 and 1995 (76),
Dietrich et al. examined patients who had undergone a
second exposure to aprotinin. There were 248 rexposures
to aprotinin in 240 patients and the majority (147) were
pediatric patients. Only seven reactions to aprotinin were
noted and these had a wide range of physiologic effects. If a patient had reexposure within 6 months of the
second surgery the risk was 4.5% versus approximately
1.5% for those who had reexposure after 6 months. Of the seven events, only two reacted to the test dose. The authors have recommended not only the test dose

25. Pharmacologic Prophylaxis for Post–Cardiopulmonary Bypass Bleeding
533
but also histamine blockade with both H1 and H2
blockers for reexposures. They recommend avoidance of
reexposure to aprotinin within 6 months of prior exposure. Despite Dietrich’s ﬁndings, in 2006 the FDA added an
advisory contraindicating reexposure to aprotinin within
12 months. In a pediatric study that was retrospective, 681 ﬁrst-
time exposures to aprotinin yielded a reaction rate of
1% (77). Of these the majority were severe, and in
reexposures the rate for second exposures was only slightly
higher at 1.3%. However third-time exposures had a 2.9%
reaction rate. These pediatric data contrast with the higher
ones reported by Dietrich et al., but Dietrich et al. did not
stratify the results into pediatric and adult administrations
of aprotinin (76). It seems likely that testing for aprotinin antibodies
would be useful. Skin testing before coming to surgery
had a negative predictive value of 98.9% but a positive
predictive value of only 20%. One has to wonder how
useful that data is, because the presence of a positive skin
test presumably induced either avoidance of aprotinin or
the prophylactic use of double- or triple-drug prophylaxis
against an anaphylactic response. Therefore, the 20%
ﬁgure reported is questionable. Cost Analysis
ACA, a generic drug, has an acquisition cost somewhere
between $1.50 and $10.00 per 5-gm vial. With published
dosing the acquisition cost of an entire case using
prophylactic ACA falls between $5 and $30.00. That is
a cheap drug by anyone’s standards. TA (also generic) is
more expensive and its price is more variable, so its cost for
prophylactic administration for a CPB case ranges from
$20.00 to $300.00. Aprotinin has been off patent for many
years, but, it is costly to extract and purify. Aprotinin,
although widely used for cardiac surgery in recent years,
remains a small player in the world of pharmaceuticals. Assuming 1.5 million persons undergo heart surgery
worldwide each year (crude estimate) and 33% of those
patients receive aprotinin (generous estimate), then the
500,000 dosages still represents a relatively small market
as drugs go. For comparison, clopidogrel usage is well into
millions of dosages per year, because many more patients
take the drug and they take it daily for an extended period. One can easily see why the margin of proﬁtability to
produce aprotinin is unattractive to most drug companies.

The cost of aprotinin varies somewhat with negotiation
and volume of use, but in the United States it tends to
be approximately $300 to $450.00 per bottle (considerably
lower in Europe apparently). With each patient requiring
an average of three bottles, the cost per case runs between
$1,000.00 and $1,500.00. Although that cost is generally
perceived by physicians as expensive, for comparison, a
drug such as recombinant factor VIIa costs somewhere
between $5,000 and $9,000.00 per dose for its use in a
patient with refractory bleeding after CPB, and sometimes
multiple doses are given. All too often, pharmacy committees or physician
groups look only at the cost of the drug. Antiﬁbrinolytic
agents are utilized to decrease bleeding and ultimately the
therapy for that bleeding, transfusion. A unit of packed
red blood cells (RBCs) from a blood center or the American Red Cross (more costly) generally costs between $200
and $350 (78). That same unit of RBCs cost $70 to $95
when aprotinin was ﬁrst introduced in the 1990s. The cost
of a unit of red cells is projected to exceed $500.00 by
2010. Apheresis platelet units have been recommended
to decrease donor exposure, alloimmunization and infectious disease transmission. A single-donor platelet apheresis currently costs around $850. Fresh frozen plasma,
which is overutilized in many cardiac surgery centers, is
relatively inexpensive at $35 to $55 per unit. In addition to procurement costs, overhead costs (e.g.,
processing, documentation, distribution) for a single unit
of red cells have been estimated at $450.00. Each unit
transfused carries a variety of risks. Hepatitis and human
immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) transmission are no longer
the threats that they once were, yet alloimmunization,
ABO incompatibility, and transfusion-related acute lung
injury remain on the list of transfusion complications. Blood transfusion also causes immunosuppression, which
may result from transfused WBCs that are just ‘‘along for
the ride.’’ The side effects of immunosuppresion alone
were estimated to exceed $850.00 per unit in 1998 (79). Perhaps now it is more or less as the use of leukoreduced
units has increased (in exchange for increased overhead
cost). Other costs such as that of a reoperation for bleeding
should be included in a cost analysis as well. Cost analyses
often lack societal costs such as time away from work
that could be the consequence of bleeding or transfusion
complications.

In cost analysis literature, the cost to save
one human life for a year has often been calculated and
cited. This is known as a quality-adjusted life-year (QALY),
which has not been modeled for antiﬁbrinolytic drugs in
cardiac surgery. One problem with cost analysis is the lack of agreement
about the risks and beneﬁts. It is easy to note that
prophylactic use of an antiﬁbrinolytic agent reduces red
cell utilization by 30% to 70% in reoperative cardiac
surgery patients, but after that the logic becomes less
clear. Some data shows a decrease in stroke rate with
aprotinin, which could save $100,000 or more per stroke
prevented. However, the study of Mangano et al. associates
aprotinin with increases in strokes as well as in renal
dysfunction and failure (39). For lysine analogs, there is
insufﬁcient prospective data on safety, as prospective trials
have typically been small and lacked focused on stroke,
MI, and renal failure. Although it appears that the risks
of those complications are small with lysine analogs, the

lack of large study populations renders such conclusions
tenuous. Bennett-Guerrero et al. compared aprotinin with lysine
analogs in a prospective multicenter study, and they found
a quantitative difference in bleeding and in transfusion
utilization (80). When those authors analyzed costs for
blood products, they showed that although less blood
was transfused with aprotinin than with ACA, the latter
drug was more cost effective. However, that study only
analyzed acquisition costs, not adverse event and overhead
costs. In a retrospective analysis, Smith et al. associated
aprotinin use with a decline in stroke rate (81). With these
assumptions, they showed that aprotinin was cost effective
for use in high-risk and reoperation cases. However, one
cannot rule out the possibility that lysine analogs might
also decrease stroke rates, or that aprotinin might increase
complication rates such as renal dysfunction or failure. How should the practitioner think about cost and the
use of these three drugs? There is no hard and fast
answer. Aprotinin is clearly more costly but it may be
slightly more effective in reducing bleeding. The ongoing
Canadian study should provide sufﬁcient data for a proper
in depth cost analysis. COMPARISONS AMONG
ANTIFIBRINOLYTIC AGENTS
Surprisingly few studies have directly compared clinical outcomes using prospective studies with random
patient assignment. Several focused reviews or metaanalyses have been conducted to assess and compare the
hemostatic efﬁcacy and the complications associated with
lysine analogs and aprotinin in patients undergoing CPB. Taken together, these studies contain comprehensive bibliographies for studies involving the prophylactic use of
antiﬁbrinolytic agents in cardiac surgery (35–37,55,82). Abundant evidence supports the hemostatic efﬁcacy of
prophylactic administration of lysine analogs and aprotinin in cardiac surgery involving CPB. Some evidence
supports their use in OPCAB as well, although the typical
expectation of an off-pump approach is the absence of
transfusion, and as long as this goal is achieved, the risk
and expense of adding an antiﬁbrinolytic agent appears to
exceed the beneﬁt. The ﬁrst meta-analysis was published in 1994, and
it assessed the effects of desmopressin (DDAVP, 13
studies), the use of either ACA or TA (4 studies), and
that of aprotinin (16 studies) using placebo-controlled
trials published between 1980 and 1993 (83).

Those
authors found a signiﬁcant reduction in chest tube output
versus placebo with all interventions, but therapy with
either lysine analogs or aprotinin was associated with
greater reduction in chest tube output than DDAVP. The
volume of RBC transfusion was reduced by lysine analogs
and aprotinin, and the proportion of patients receiving
RBC transfusion was reduced by aprotinin. Reduced
prevalence of mediastinal reexploration for bleeding fell
just short of statistical signiﬁcance (p = 0.07) for both
lysine analogs and aprotinin, and none of the interventions
had an effect on mortality. In 1997 Laupacis et al. reported a meta-analysis comparing placebo-controlled
trials using DDAVP, ACA, TA, and aprotinin using the
proportion of patients receiving RBC transfusion as the
primary outcome in 60 studies (84). A preponderance of
studies (47) used aprotinin (5,808 patients), whereas only
12 used TA (882 patients) and 3 used ACA (118 patients). Seven studies compared TA with aprotinin. Aprotinin
decreased the proportion of patients exposed to allogeneic
blood and the need for reoperation for bleeding. DDAVP
was ineffective. TA also decreased the proportion of
patients transfused, but ACA’s transfusion incidence did
not reach statistical signiﬁcance versus placebo (OR
for transfusion was 0.20 with ACA, 95% CI 0.04–1.12,
p = 0.07), perhaps because of the smaller number of
studies and patients. The Cochrane collaboration analyzed the effects of an-
tiﬁbrinolytic drugs on perioperative allogeneic transfusion
using randomized control trials published as recently as
1998 (35). This analysis included surgeries other than
cardiac surgery, but the vast majority of patients underwent cardiac surgery. Eighty-nine trials including 7,027
patients used aprotinin, 74 of which were conducted in
cardiac surgery. Eighteen trials including 1,342 patients
used TA, and 4 including 474 patients used ACA. Studies containing major methodological ﬂaws were excluded,
but the methodology still varied considerably, with 65%
of studies being double-blinded, 83% having a transfusion
protocol, 65 clinical trials having imperfect methods for
allocating patients to study groups, and 53 of 89 trials scoring between 1 and 3 on the 5-point (5 being highest) Jadad
quality assessment instrument for methodologic quality. In the studies containing a transfusion threshold, the postoperative transfusion threshold varied from a hemoglobin
concentration of 7.0 g/dL to 10.0 g/dL, a range that in itself imposes substantial variability in expected transfusion
outcomes.

Antiﬁbrinolytic dosing protocols also varied
considerably, but were more standardized for aprotinin
than for lysine analogs. Despite these limitations, study
quality did not appear to alter the overall results. Aprotinin reduced the relative risk (RR) of requiring
allogeneic blood in both the low-dose and high-dose
regimens (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59–0.80 and RR 0.68,
95% CI 0.62–0.75 compared with control, respectively). For TA the RR for allogeneic transfusion was similar
at 0.66 (95% CI 0.57–0.88), and that for ACA failed to
reach signiﬁcance (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.15–1.18) possibly
because of low numbers of patients studied limiting the
statistical power. Aprotinin and TA similarly reduced
volume of blood transfused by approximately 1 unit per

by the Cochrane Collaboration, and shows a variety of effects, but when pooled there was no

patient, and there was no difference in allogeneic blood
exposure between TA and aprotinin (Fig. 6). Aprotinin
reduced the need for reoperation for bleeding by 60%,
whereas TA and ACA showed insigniﬁcant trends toward
reduction. No effect on mortality, renal failure, nonfatal
MI, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolus
was found for any of the antiﬁbrinolytic drugs. The
authors noted the limitations of the data, and particularly
the lesser number of patients studied for lysine analogs. They also noted the potential impact of underpowering,
reporting bias, and of many studies containing small
numbers of patients. For example, the possibility exists
that a signiﬁcant association between lysine analogs and
reduced frequency of reexploration for bleeding was
missed because reexploration was frequency less than
5% in most studies. In 1999 Levi et al. reported a meta-analysis of 72 trials involving the use of any pharmacologic prophylactic
strategy to reduce bleeding in patients undergoing cardiac
surgery with CPB (36). As with previous meta-analyses,
prophylaxis with DDAVP was associated with a small
but clinically insigniﬁcant reduction in blood loss.

The
studies analyzed included 1,687 aprotinin-treated patients
and 604 patients who received lysine analogs. The lysine analog patients were combined into a single group. Patients were further stratiﬁed into high-risk and lowrisk categories. Aprotinin was associated with a reduction
in mortality (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90) in the overall
group. This effect narrowly missed statistical signiﬁcance
in the high-risk group, and it was not observed with lysine
analogs. Treatment with aprotinin or with lysine analogs
similarly reduced the frequency of surgical reexploration
[OR 0.37 (0.25–0.55) and 0.44 (0.22–0.90), respectively]
and the proportion of patients receiving any allogeneic
transfusion OR 0.37 (0.32–0.42) and 0.46 (0.34–0.64), respectively. Transfusion avoidance outcomes were similar
in the overall population and the high-risk population. The
seven trials that directly compared aprotinin and lysine
analogs showed a slight advantage toward aprotinin in perioperative blood loss and volume of transfusion. The conventional high-dose aprotinin protocol exhibited slightly
better bleeding outcomes than the lower-dose protocol. Surprisingly, high-dose aprotinin doubled the incidence
of perioperative MI versus low-dose aprotinin but not versus placebo. The authors speculate that this represents a
procoagulant effect of aprotinin, although laboratory studies suggest a mild anticoagulant effect. Lysine analogs did
not affect the incidence of perioperative MI. In 2004 Sedrakayan et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 randomized clinical trials involving 3,879 patients and the use of aprotinin in patients
undergoing CABG (55). Although they did not speciﬁcally
exclude OPCAB in their analysis, it seems unlikely that
signiﬁcant numbers of OPCAB patients were included. Their analysis conﬁrmed that aprotinin reduces the proportion of patients requiring allogeneic blood transfusion
[RR 0.61 (0.58–0.66)] and found no effect of aprotinin
upon mortality, MI, renal failure, or atrial ﬁbrillation
(Fig. 7). Aprotinin reduced the incidence of stroke [RR 0.53
(0.31–0.90)]. This ﬁnding is consistent with earlier studies of Levy and Frumento (47,58). One potential concern
with all three studies is that the diagnosis of perioperative
