594
V. Clinical Applications
highly sensitive to the occurrence of medical errors, not
to mention the impact of errors on the cost of health
care. The IOM deﬁned quality of care as ‘‘the degree
to which health services for individuals and populations
increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are
consistent with current professional knowledge’’. To Err is Human: Building a Safer Health System was
the ﬁrst in a series of many reports produced by the
Quality of Health Care in America project (11). It brought
attention to the fact that tens of thousands of Americans
die each year from medical errors and moved the issue of
patient safety and quality of health care to the forefront
for public and private policy makers. When the rate of
death from AEs from the HMPS was extrapolated to the
general population in 1997, there would have been an
estimated 98,000 deaths as a result of medical errors in
the United States. More people would have died from
medical errors than from motor vehicle accidents, breast
cancer, or AIDS (12). Total national costs (lost income, lost
household production, disability and health care costs) of
preventable AEs (medical errors resulting in injury) for
1997 were staggering, estimated to be between $17 billion
and $29 billion, of which more than 50% were health
care costs (13,14). An indirect cost of medical errors
is the loss of opportunity. Resources expended spent
on rediagnosing, retesting, and retreating are resources
not available for other purposes. The intangible cost of
medical error is the resulting mistrust of patients in the
health care system and the decrease in morale by health
care providers when they are unable to deliver a high
standard of care. These effects are far reaching for society. Despite resounding evidence that medical errors have
a huge and penetrating impact on the quality and
cost of health care delivered in the United States, the
efforts at organizing change have been small and slow. A comprehensive approach to improving patient safety
was suggested by the Quality of Health Care in America
Committee in To Err is Human. To err is human, but
errors can be prevented, and safety is a critical ﬁrst step
in improving quality of care.

The ﬁrst recommendation of this report was for
Congress to establish a Center for Patient Safety within
the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). Its goals would be to set the national standards for patient safety, track progress in meeting these goals, and
issue an annual report to the President and Congress on
patient safety. Second, there was a recommendation to
develop a research agenda to improve the understanding of errors in health care (with funding for Centers of
Excellence in this arena), to evaluate methods for identifying and preventing errors, and to fund dissemination
and communication activities to improve patient safety. But, in order for errors to be prevented, they must be
identiﬁed. A critical step in understanding medical errors
is to create an environment that encourages identiﬁcation
of the error, evaluate the cause and take action to prevent
its recurrence. The establishment of a nationwide mandatory reporting system was recommended for the collection
of standardized information by the state government regarding AEs that resulted in death or serious harm. All
health care organizations would be required to report
standardized information and the National Forum for
Health Care Quality Measurement and Reporting would
be responsible for promulgating and maintaining a core
set of reporting standards to be used by states. Although
AEs that result in serious harm or death should not be
protected from public disclosure, those events not falling
into this category may not be reported because of fear
of legal discoverability. To prevent the underreporting of
events, it was recommended that Congress pass legislation to protect peer reviewed data related to patient safety
and quality improvement. This subsequently became federal law as U.S. Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 5705. As a way of deﬁning the minimum standard for performance by health care organizations and professionals it
was recommended that the performance standards and
expectations focus greater attention on patient safety. Regulators and accreditors should require organizations
to implement patient safety initiatives and that public and
private purchasers should provide incentives for improvement in patient safety. Health care professional licensing
bodies should implement relicensing and reexamination,
identify unsafe providers and take action.

Professional societies should make a commitment to patient safety by
creating a committee dedicated to patient safety, deﬁne
a patient safety curriculum, disseminate information to
society members, structure practice guidelines to incorporate safety and collaborate with other societies through
a national summit on the professional’s role in patient
safety. Because a large percentage of medical errors are in
the form of medication errors, it was recommended that
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) increase
their attention to the safe use of drugs in both the pre- and
postmarketing processes. And lastly, health care organizations need to provide strong and clear attention to safety,
create a supportive environment for reporting and analyzing errors and should implement proven medication safety
practices. At the end, it was proposed that an assessment of
the progress of those recommendations be done in 5 years. Patient safety was poorly understood and was rarely the
topic of conversation until the IOM report was published
in 1999. It changed the way that health care providers and
managers think and talk about medical errors and injury
despite the fact that the national statistics do not show any
impact. An effort by the AHRQ to get a national estimate
showed little improvement, but its impact on attitudes
and organizations was profound (15). The IOM report
changed how the task of error prevention is viewed and
now few people doubt that preventable medical injuries
are a serious problem. There has been a shift from blaming

28. Primum Non Nocere: Patient Safety in Cardiopulmonary Bypass
595
bad people to blaming bad systems as the cause of most
errors and injuries to patients and that blaming people
is an ineffective approach. The most effective way of improving safety and quality is to change the system. Another
effect of the IOM report was to involve a broad array of
stakeholders. In February of 2000, the Quality Interagency
Coordination Task Force proposed landmark initiatives to
improve patient safety in order to achieve the IOM’s goal of
a reduction of medical errors by 50%. In 2001, Congress
appropriated $20 million annually for patient safety research and the establishment of the Center for Quality
Improvement and Safety; now the leader in education,
training, convening agenda-setting workshops, disseminating information, developing measures, and facilitating
the setting of standards. Hospitals participating in Medicare are required to implement error reduction programs,
which include new systems to help decrease medication
errors. Thirty-three million dollars were committed to the
FDA for the development of new standards to ensure that
pharmaceuticals are packaged and marketed to promote
patient safety. New standards to prevent medication errors caused by proprietary drug names and packaging, and
new standards that highlight common drug interactions
and dosage errors were to be implemented, and an online
serious drug AE reporting system was to be created. Unfortunately, since then most of the $20 million budget has
been earmarked toward studies of information technology
and has left investigators of patient safety without support. The Veteran’s Health Administration (VHA) surfaced as
the ﬁrst health care organization to make a public commitment to improving patient safety (16). Acknowledgment
by the VHA leadership that receiving medical care is risky
prompted steps to promote a culture of safety by allocating
resources for establishment of special patient safety centers, enhancing employee education on patient safety, and
providing incentives to promote safety. In 1998, the National Center for Patient Safety (NCPS) was established to
lead the development of a culture of safety throughout the
VHA. With contributions from quality and risk managers
in the ﬁeld, the NCPS published a patient safety handbook. The NCPS provides didactic problem-based learning
to personnel of all VHA facilities along with education on
root-cause analysis.

There are also incentives built into the
system in the way of cash rewards and nomination for a
patient safety award for anyone who designs, implements
or solves a patient safety issue. There is also a ‘‘stick’’ opposite the ‘‘carrot’’. The demonstration of improved patient
safety is incorporated into their performance measurement system. In 1997, the VHA initiated the VA Patient
Safety Event Registry. Through a mandatory reporting
system, AEs are catalogued and by systematic review of
those events, the regional and national leaders are able
to track trends and areas that would beneﬁt from focused
interventions. In addition, in a collaborative effort with
the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the
VHA has developed a voluntary Patient Safety Reporting
system using elements from the Aviation Safety Reporting
System. This system keeps the reporting source anonymous in hopes of ultimately gaining the complete picture
and relieving fears of punishment. Alongside the leading edge effort to develop a culture
of patient safety, there exist some daunting challenges. Patient safety must continue to be a top priority in every
health care system because it is an integral part of quality
of care and it cannot be allowed to fall victim to bureaucracy. It must have leadership support and the necessary
infrastructure and funding. Most importantly, the frontline providers of patient care must believe that they play a
very large part in improving patient safety and made to feel
comfortable with reporting an AE free of any penalty. One
important caveat to this philosophy is that intentionally
unsafe acts or criminal acts must not be tolerated, must
be quickly identiﬁed and separated from any adverse reporting system for separate administrative management. In October 1996, a conference ‘‘Examining Errors in
Health Care: Developing a Prevention, Education and Research Agenda’’ marked the inception of the National
Patient Safety Foundation at the American Medical Association. It was a landmark gathering of extraordinary
individuals representing all sectors; patients, practitioners, administrators, health plans, regulators, researchers,
ethicists, risk managers, and lawyers. It is an independent,
not-for-proﬁt organization devoted to assuring patient
safety during the delivery of health care, and was modeled
after the Anesthesiology Patient Safety Foundation.

Its
mission: ‘‘To improve the safety of patients’’ by creating
a core of knowledge and pathways to apply that knowledge, raise public awareness and enhance a culture of
receptivity to patient safety, and be a leader in the transition from a culture of blame to a culture of safety. The
Foundation sees itself as a resource for individuals and
organizations, and believes that patient safety is central
to quality health care, that early and appropriate response
to potential problems is the key to prevention of patient
injury. Patient involvement and development of a culture
of trust, honesty, integrity, and open communication are
key attributes of efforts to improve patient safety. Health
care systems are fallible and fundamental change, along
with an integrated body of knowledge and the infrastructure to support change processes, is necessary for the
advancement of patient safety. In 1983 40 presenters from around the world were
invited to a symposium sponsored by the Royal Society of Medicine of England and the Harvard School of
Medicine in Boston, Massachusetts. The topic of discussion: anesthesia contributory morbidity and mortality and
the morphology and teleology of anesthetic accidents. At
its conclusion, an agreement was made to continue to
share statistics and deﬁne parameters of future studies.

596
V. Clinical Applications
A year later, an idea for a patient-centered safety foundation was presented to and approved by the American
Society of Anesthesiologists House of Delegates. The Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation (APSF) was founded
in 1985. Its mission statement was: ‘‘No patient shall
be harmed from anesthesia’’. The APSF is thus far the
only organization established by a speciﬁc medical specialty dedicated to promoting patient safety in clinical
practice. The APSF attributes its success to the early identiﬁ-
cation of patient safety problems, promoting research in
patient safety, and dissemination of knowledge to members of the American Society of Anesthesiologists achieved
by the APSF Newsletter sent to every practitioner, also
available on the Internet (www.apsf.org). It has risen to
the challenge of bringing patient safety to the forefront
of awareness, and now shares equal consideration with
other traditional academic and scientiﬁc concerns of the
specialty. The IOM report ﬁndings were reviewed by the
APSF and, for the most part, found that the philosophy
of the IOM report paralleled the philosophy of the APSF. Most of the recommendations of the IOM report were incorporated into the themes that have guided the APSF and
despite the belief that some recommendations of the IOM
report may need reconsideration, both agree that medical
error is a serious issue that needs national support on every level; federal, state and local governments, health care
organizations, professional societies, private foundations,
and the public. In 1991, the Institute for Healthcare Improvement
(IHI) was founded. It is a not for proﬁt organization
based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which serves as a
worldwide knowledge source to help accelerate change
in health care in the United Sates and internationally. In
response to an increasing dissatisfaction by health care
stakeholders with the pace of healthcare improvement,
the IHI launched the 100,000 Lives Campaign in 2004. A life saved was deﬁned as a patient who survived a
hospital stay who would have died had they received that
hospital’s precampaign level of care (17). It engaged more
than 3,000 U.S. hospitals with the aim of avoiding 100,000
unnecessary deaths over 18 months by encouraging
those hospitals to adopt six evidence-based interventions
that are known to signiﬁcantly reduce harm and death,
(Table 1).

It estimated that as of April 2006, 83% of all
participating hospitals that submitted mortality data had
saved more than 84,000 lives. The campaign operated
on three levels. On the national level, IHI established
the agenda and pace to support change in the facilities. The support structure included detailed guides for each
intervention, an Internet data collection system, access to
experts, and online discussions and mentoring. At the
‘‘node’’ level, a campaign ﬁeld ofﬁce consisted of one
or more organizations that volunteered to support the
campaign activity for 50 to 100 hospitals. They provided

geography, system afﬁliation, or afﬁnity. The system level
included participating hospitals that were charged with
implementing the six interventions. The hospitals were
expected to engage all stakeholders—boards, executives,
managers, frontline providers, patients, and families. At
the end there were critical lessons learned from the
campaign. A clear and aggressive goal for the campaign
was responsible for driving the pace of work. The voluntary
nature encouraged a positive environment for proactive
change rather than to respond to a mandate from federal
or regulatory sources. There was a development of a
national infrastructure that successfully supported the
changing of care at the frontlines rather than mandating
guidelines from a distance. Along with all of the successes,
there were challenges. The campaign realized limited
success in involving patients and families, payers, and
employers, which lessened the urgency by the hospitals
to demand a high quality of care. The performance of
individual facilities was limited because the calculation
of lives saved was imprecise at the hospital level.

Finally,
the diverse and strong interests of the different parties
made it difﬁcult to maintain coalitions of partners,
participants, and nodes. It is the hope of the IHI
that there exists a national network that will sustain
efforts in advancing improvement of health care in years
to come. There is a myriad of nongovernmental organizations
that have made patient safety a priority. The Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations
(JCAHO) leads the way in requiring hospitals to implement
safe practices (www.jointcommission.org/PatientSaftey)
and assuring accountability within health care organizations. The National Quality Forum (NQF) a public–private
partnership that develops and approves measures of

597
quality of care, has developed a consensus process that
generated standards for mandatory reporting and created
a list of high-impact evidence-based safe practices that the
JCAHO and other organizations are now requiring hospitals to implement (18,19). The Centers for Medicare and
Medicaid Services and the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention have joined with other programs to reduce surgical complications. (Surgical Care Improvement Project
at www.medqic.org/scip.) The Leapfrog Group is a group
formed by a number of U.S. corporations. It is an initiative
driven by organizations that buy health care who are working to initiate breakthrough improvements in the safety,
quality, and affordability of health care for Americans. It
is a voluntary program aimed at mobilizing employer purchasing power to alert U.S. health industry that big leaps in
health care safety, quality, and customer value will be recognized and rewarded. Its mission statement: To trigger
giant leaps forward in the safety, quality, and affordability
of health care by supporting informed health care decisions by those who use and pay for health care and
promoting high-value health care through incentives and
rewards. Also instigated by the IOM report, the founders
realized that they could take ‘‘leaps’’ forward with their
employees, retirees, and families by rewarding hospitals
that implement signiﬁcant improvements in quality and
safety. Funding to set up Leapfrog came from the Business
Roundtable (BRT) and The Leapfrog Group was ofﬁcially
launched in November 2000. Leapfrog is supported by the
BRT, The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, Leapfrog
members and others (www.leapfroggroup.org). Another consequence of the IOM report was the
acceleration of the changes in practices to make health
care safe. At ﬁrst, implementation of new safe practices
was voluntary, but after the NQF published in 2002 a
list of 30 evidence-based safe practices, JCAHO required
hospitals to implement 11 of them, including improving
patient identiﬁcation, communication, and surgical-site
veriﬁcation. Since then there have been more added to the
list of safe practices to be implemented in 2005. To date
there are no large studies that verify the effectiveness of the
implementation of the safe practices required by JCAHO,
but time-series data from hospitals and systems that have
been working to improve patient safety are encouraging.

Last, but not least in response to the human side of medical errors, the teaching hospitals programs implemented
rules that limited the number of working hours of residents in 1 week based on information that a relation exists
between fatigue and errors at work (20–23). A prospective
randomized study comparing the rates of serious medical errors made by interns while they were working on a
schedule of every third day call with shifts of 24 hours or
more to an intervention schedule that eliminated extended
work shifts and decreased the number of hours worked per
week was conducted for the Harvard Work Hours, Health
and Safety Group. The results indicated that substantially more serious medical errors occurred when interns
worked frequent shifts of 24 hours or more than when
they worked shorter shifts and that eliminating extended
shifts and reducing the number of hours workedper week
will reduce serious medical errors in the intensive care
unit (24). WHAT HAS BEEN ACCOMPLISHED? ‘‘Amid signs of progress, there is a long way to go,’’ RM
Wachter (25). Where are we since the 1999 IOM report,
To Err is Human? The IOM report profoundly changed
the conversation surrounding patient safety and its effects
have impacted patient safety in three important areas. Health care professionals and managers think and talk
about medical errors and injury differently. The concept
that bad systems and not bad people are responsible for
most errors has become the mantra in health care. There
has been a recruitment of support from stakeholders. The federal government stepped up to fund research
in error prevention and patient safety and Congress
codiﬁed the AHRQ as the lead federal agency for patient
safety and established a Center for Quality Improvement
and Safety. Lastly, the pace of change in health care
safety improvement has been signiﬁcantly accelerated. The Institute for Health campaign and the list published
by the NQF of 30 evidenced-based safe practices are just
two of many examples of initiatives created to encourage
the attainment of the IOM’s goals. WHY IS HEALTH CARE NOT
DEMONSTRABLY AND MEASURABLY
SAFER? There have been many leaps forward on all fronts of health
care providers, hospital administrators, local and federal
governments, and payers of health care beneﬁts.

So why is
it so difﬁcult to implement the practices and policies that
are needed to deliver safe patient care? Part of the answer
to these questions lies in the culture of medicine itself,
a culture that is deeply rooted by custom and training
in high standards of autonomous individual performance
and a commitment to progress through research (26). Creating a culture of safety requires major changes in
behavior. This change is often perceived by professionals
as a threat to their autonomy and authority. Complexity in
the health care system and in its technology has exploded
in the recent decades and is perhaps more complex
than any other industry in terms of relations. The more
complex the system, the more chance it has to fail. An
understandable fear of punishment and liability inhibits
a willingness to discuss or expose medical errors. The

598
V. Clinical Applications
combination of the increased complexity of the health care
system, professional fragmentation with an emphasis on
individualism, enhanced by a well-entrenched hierarchical
authority structure and diffuse accountability, creates a
daunting barrier to beliefs of common purpose, teamwork,
and individual accountability. The IOM report accomplished a commendable public service by dramatizing an underappreciated public
problem: harm to patients because of medical error. It
embraced a ‘‘normal accident theory’’ hypothesizing that
modern technology systems are ‘‘error prone’’ and that
certain catastrophes can be thought of as ‘‘normal accidents’’ and that accidents and mistakes, with all of their
consequences, are not produced by individual human failings (27–29). It focused on the ‘‘system nature’’ of medical
error and suggested that through better system design,
when better reporting leads to knowledge of system defects, error would be reduced. It documented the need for
a culture of safety in medicine and proposed a number
of ways to bring this about: (a) by reducing the tolerance for and the incidence of ‘‘normal error’’ in medicine,
(b) by creating generative organizational structures that
‘‘learn’’ from past mistakes and prevent their recurrence
through better reporting, and (c) by attempting to remove
the defensive reactions of individual practitioners to error identiﬁcation and correction. Charles Bosk stated that
a second approach for understanding error was largely
unrecognized in the IOM report (30), and relies on ﬁrst-
hand observational studies. Instead of asking ‘‘How might
adverse medical events be prevented?’’ it asks ‘‘How do
workers in a medical setting deﬁne an error? How do they
understand what causes an error? And how do they respond to an error?’’ This second view concentrates on the
negotiation of the meaning of the term error on the ‘‘shop
ﬂoor’’ and that the meanings are not ﬁxed, but ﬂuid and
ﬂexible, highly dependent on context. He goes on to explain what may be the largest barriers to the IOM’s goal in
reducing the number of preventable AEs by 50% in 5 years. The ﬁrst is the professional dominance of physicians
in the organization of care. The tradition of decentralized decision making and teamwork, characteristics of
highly reliable organizations, is relatively underdeveloped
in medicine. Second, in an era of immediate cost containment, there exists little incentive for managers to consider
the long-term ﬁnancial beneﬁts of error reduction.

Third,
errors are inevitable in a system committed to aggressive
interventions. Reasonable expectations of performance
need to be communicated to the public. WHERE DO WE GO FROM HERE? Highly motivated individual stakeholders (physicians,
nurses, pharmacists, administrators, risk managers, governmental ofﬁcials and legislators, and local and federal
governments) will be instrumental in helping organizations make substantial changes. Signiﬁcant advances are
likely to occur in years to come. The time for the electronic
health care record has arrived but is long overdue. The
JCAHO and several payers continue to adopt the NQF list
of proven safe practices. Training of nurses and physicians
and other professionals to work in teams [practice-based
learning and systems-based practice have been included
by the Accreditation Council on Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) as two of the core professional skills]
is poised to effect change in the early part of training. Finally, few health care organizations reject the imperative to be honest and forthcoming with patients following
an injury. In order to respond to the IOM’s call to reduce
preventable patient injuries by 90%, every stakeholder will
need to make patient safety a top priority. PATIENT SAFETY AND
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Based on the foregoing discussion of patient safety, it can
be said that perfusion safety is a problem that encompasses a broad range of topics and for which there is
no one solution. Since the ﬁrst clinical use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) more than 50 years ago, numerous
positive changes in the engineering and manufacturing of
equipment, surgical and anesthetic techniques, education
of perfusionists and the management of perfusion has
made perfusion safer. Nevertheless, accidents/incidents
still happen (31). Perfusion safety does not refer only to
the incorporation of safety devices, but includes everything about safe conduct of CPB such as the heart–lung
machines, circuit design, ancillary equipment, perfusion
practices, surgical and anesthetic techniques, and perhaps
most importantly, the training and education of perfusionists with emphasis on vigilance and communication
with the members of the team in the operating room. The literature contains a multitude of reports describing
oxygenator failure (32–35), mechanical failure (36), electrical failure (37–40), massive air embolization (41,42),
and preventative maintenance (43,44). There are accident
surveys (45–50), comparisons of those surveys (51–53),
reviews of the risks and hazards of CPB (54–58), review of safety devices (59,60), and other aspects of safe
CPB (61,62).

Deﬁning the problem of perfusion safety
requires identifying the types of incidents and their frequency through a quantitative approach. Since the ﬁrst use of CPB in the 1953, safety in
CPB has been a prime concern. In the earliest perfusion circuits and pump mechanics, there were complex
safety feedback loops and devices incorporated into the
design. The ﬁrst heart–lung machines (HLMs) had failsafe mechanisms such as oxygenator blood level sensors,
level ﬂoats, and pressure sensors, many of which were

described in the classic perfusion textbook by Pierre Galletti in 1962, Heart–lung Bypass; Principles and Techniques
of Extracorporeal Circulation (63). As coronary artery bypass procedures increased, so did the number of cardiac
surgery programs. The need for development of simpler
systems became a necessity. The industry of producing
disposable parts for the bypass machines had to meet the
demands of the increasing numbers of open-heart procedures. Large clumsy ﬁlm oxygenators were replaced with
hard shell bubble oxygenators and ultimately evolved to
the sleek disposable, single use, self-contained hollow ﬁlter
membrane oxygenators most commonly used (in the USA)
today. Early roller became replaced by improved electromagnetically coupled centrifugal pumps. More attention
was being paid to decreasing the incidence of air embolization and monitoring anticoagulation. More recent subjects
of interest are reperfusion injury and the systemic inﬂam-
matory response elicited by the blood to foreign surface
exposure inherent in current CPB. Over the last 5 decades,
there have been many improvements in the equipment
and circuits used, but in the end, it is still difﬁcult to
mimic the anatomy and physiology of the heart and lungs. There is a large accumulation of literature regarding
CPB with particular attention paid to CPB techniques
and the equipment. The actual number of articles written
speciﬁcally addressing perfusion safety is small in comparison, although an underlying theme of safety is inferred. Palanzo searched through a database (PerfSearch, property of American Academy of Cardiovascular Perfusion,
limited to use by its members) that speciﬁcally encompasses CPB-related manuscripts that appear in journals
from cardiac surgery, anesthesiology, cardiology, perfusion, and biomedical engineering (53). The percentage of
the total of 12,000 manuscripts that were dedicated to perfusion safety was only 1.4%, a total of 165 articles. Most
of those 165 articles described air embolism, others were
reviews that included air accidents. Only 0.45% (54 of
the total) reported on safety devices or issues different
from gaseous microemboli. Some of the earliest articles addressed the prevention of air embolization (64,65). The era of the late 1950s and 1960s, produced articles
about ﬂowmeters (66), safety devices for CPB (67) were
published, mechanical failure during CPB and a left ventricular vent valve (68).

The 1970s showed a decrease in
the number of articles about perfusion safety, but popular
topics during that time described aortic vents to prevent
air embolization (69), retrograde dissection of the aorta
during CPB (70) and run away pump head (71). The next
decade witnessed an increase in the number of safety
reports secondary to a large increase in the number of
cardiac surgeons and training programs. Christman and
Kurusz published a review of safety devices available for
preventing massive gas embolization (59). The safety devices were divided into four categories: devices attached to
oxygenators, those devices used proximal and distal to the
pump head and a device that functioned as a blood pump. Reports of power failures (37,38), reviews on the risks
of CPB (54–57). Other topics reported were about preventive maintenance (43), oxygenator failure (32), safety
devices for level regulation (72), and pressure measurement (73,74). In 1988 the American Academy of Cardiovascular Perfusion devoted an entire issue in its journal
Perfusion to the many aspects of perfusion safety. The
1990s focused on a different aspect of perfusion safety. Reports on risk management (62) and quality assurance (75)
made their debut, and continue to be an important issue. In the ﬁrst 30 years of CPB, there was constant attention
paid to promoting safety in perfusion illustrated by the
previous accounting of reports describing all of the various
safety devices that were engineered and manufactured. But, it was not until 1980 when the ﬁrst hints appeared
regarding the frequency of adverse incidents occurring
during CPB. Table 2 is a summary of surveys documenting
the types and frequency of incidents. The Stoney report
was a survey of 349 cardiac surgeons between 1972
and 1977 in the United Sates and Canada to estimate
the frequency of patients injured by accidental arterial
line air embolism (45). It was the ﬁrst comprehensive
effort to determine the incidence of perfusion related
AEs. The questionnaire asked several questions about
accidents concerning the pump oxygenators, that is,
episodes of arterial line air embolism, mechanical failure
of the pump, electrical failure of the pump, disseminated
intravascular coagulation (DIC) during or after bypass and
oxygenator failure. There were a total of 1,419 accidents
that resulted in 100 permanent injuries and 264 resulting
in death (Fig. 7).

Air embolism in the arterial line was responsible for 92
deaths, and DIC was responsible for 163 deaths. Mechanical, electrical, or oxygenator failures were responsible for
nine deaths. Another common cause of accidents was the
reversal of the tubing connected to the ventricular sump,
causing air to be pumped into the left ventricle. When
asked about the usage of low-level alarms, only 42% of the
responders used them and only 20% used an alarm system that was equipped with an automatic pump shut-off. When asked about the use of an activated clotting time
(ACT) during bypass only 37% did not, but interestingly,
those using the ACT reported 313 episodes of DIC and
those that did not use the ACT reported only 57 episodes
of DIC. The authors concluded that most of the accidents
caused by arterial line air embolism were a result of human error, but could be eliminated by consistent usage of
low-level alarm systems and automatic shut-off devices. Additionally, the deaths and injuries secondary to DIC
during CPB might be avoided by consistent use of ACTs or
heparin titration. A possible disadvantage in the methodology of the survey was that the information gathered by
the questionnaire relied on the memories of the cardiac
surgeons and was not a review of past experience. This

form CPB. Mechanical failure of the HLM occurred in
170 cases resulting in three permanent injuries and one
death; roller pump stoppage was the most common form
of mechanical failure. Loss of hospital power accounted
for 326 cases of electrical failure. Profoundly inadequate
oxygenation, observed by 31% of the respondents during
506 cases, was responsible for 10 permanent injuries and
32 deaths. A switch from one oxygenator to another was
made in 365 cases with an outcome of permanent injury
or death in 27 patients. When surveyed as to the type
of oxygenators used, bubble and membrane oxygenators
were used almost equally. Several questions addressed the use of measures for the
prevention of accidents on CPB. Most of the perfusionists
who were surveyed (81%) used arterial line ﬁlters, almost
70% used low-level alarms but only one third would use
the device in the automatic pump shut-off mode, less
than 50% used air bubble detectors, and 35% used oneway pressure relief valves in the left ventricular vent line.

Less than 3% admitted to not using any safety devices
whatsoever. Those surveyed were given the opportunity
to submit their opinions regarding the effect of the use of
safety devices on vigilance, and almost 70% noted that the
use of safety devices did not lessen their vigilance, while
30% thought that vigilance was decreased by use of such
devices. When asked to comment on the effectiveness of
safety devices during a CPB accident, most felt that an
arterial line ﬁlter or an air bubble detector was functional
and effective, a low-level alarm system was effective only
approximately 50% of the time, and the one-way pressure
relief valve in the left ventricular vent line failed more often
than not. Fortunately greater than 95% of those surveyed
would have backup equipment available while on bypass
such as pump hand cranks, extratubing, IABP, and spare
oxygenators. Slightly more than half did not use a written
perfusion protocol. A prebypass checklist was used by 70%
but most went through the list in their minds as opposed
to looking at a written list or using the two-person state
and response system common in aviation. Table 3 displays
is a list of activities that the perfusionists felt lowered the
risk of perfusion accidents. Most perfusionists (72.3%) felt
that, despite the implementation of safety devices, human
error was responsible for causing accidents as opposed to
safety device failure. The last set of questions asked about the current
practice among perfusionists. For the most part, the
perfusionists controlled venous return to the pump by
tubing clamps or an occluder mechanism on the HLM,
and following CPB the perfusionist would be responsible
for clamping the venous and arterial line more than
half the time. Pressures monitored by perfusion included
radial artery, central venous, and pulmonary artery. Most

and buffers directly into the CPB lines. Answers to
questions regarding the management of blood gas values
showed no consensus of practice. Choice of equipment
was made jointly by the surgeons and perfusionists most
of the time and the majority of perfusionists were not
carrying individual liability insurance, but instead were
covered by a blanket policy. The purpose of this study was to determine if new
innovations and techniques, along with the recommendations by previous authors, had made any beneﬁcial
impact on the frequency of AEs while on CPB. Because
the sampled population was considered good, a secondary
beneﬁt resulted in documentation of ‘‘state-of-the-art’’ levels of practice. In this study, with regard to speciﬁc
types of accidents, the most frequent complication was
the so-called ‘‘protamine reaction’’ seen immediately following bypass by more than two thirds of perfusionists
surveyed. Arguably, in the immediate postbypass period,
hemodynamic instability can occur for reasons other than
a protamine reaction, but a temporal relation between
administration of protamine and unstable hemodynamics
could not be dismissed. DIC was seen much less frequently
than in earlier studies most likely due to an increase in
heparin monitoring, and gas embolization incidence fell
to 1 in every 8,000 cases, perhaps due to more perfusionists using a low-level alarm and the availability of a
secondary anti–air embolism device that when activated
shuts the pump down instantaneously. Air bubble detectors, with an arterial line ﬁlter and one-way pressure relief
valves in the left ventricular vent, considered redundant
safety devices, also contributed to the decrease of catastrophic events. The overall incidence rate of permanent
injury or death from all accidents had fallen to 1 in every
1,000 cases.

Between 1986 and 1997, there was a paucity of
formal surveys of perfusion safety despite the explosion
of advancement in technology and education since the
introduction of CPB. The literature during that interval
focused on the current trends in perfusion practices,
speciﬁcally the current perfusion practices in North
America, the United Kingdom, and Australia (76–79). In 1995 a survey conducted by O.F. Jenkins was sent
to all members of record of the three Australian perfusion
societies (49). It was a seven-page survey consisting of
a list of incidents seen and a list of safety procedures. Respondents were asked to note the numbers of times
they witnessed the occurrence of speciﬁc incidents and
the use of certain safety procedures within an 18- month
period while personally operating the HLM. The overall
response rate was 69% representing all states of Australia
and New Zealand. In the category of equipment failure,
the most frequent incident involved the heat exchanger
occurring 86 times necessitating changing to a backup
system, seen by 43% of the respondents, followed by
hospital electrical power failure seen 40 times by 26%
of the respondents. Fortunately, in anticipation of the
high frequency rate, there were backup heating/cooling
devices immediately available for 97% of the respondents. Failure of electrical power occurred less frequently,
but surprisingly, only between 29% and 36% of the
respondents had backup emergency power systems in
place. Incidents related to oxygenators; 36 membrane
leaks and the need for replacement before or during CPB
on 35 occasions, were seen by 25% of those surveyed. There were 55 incidents of air realized in the circuit,
not reaching the patient. For incidents where air was
entrained, but did reach the patient, 11 of those occurred
through the cardioplegia line and 23 through the main
circuit, including 2 incidents of massive air embolism. The most common incident related to coagulation was the
inability to maintain an ACT above 400 seconds during
CPB despite giving additional heparin. This occurred 56
times and was seen by 29% of respondents. Although
ACTs were being monitored by most of the perfusionists,
an alarmingly high percentage of those surveyed (18%),
admitted to only sometimes using ACT monitoring while
on bypass and 27% admitted to not routinely checking
for an adequately prolonged ACT before initiating CPB.

After separation from CPB, protamine-induced clotting of
the circuit occurred 39 times resulting in the need for an
urgent re-setup of a new circuit on four occasions. Other
incidents that were not under the direct control of the
perfusionists occurred fairly frequently, such as cannula
displacement, vessel dissection, gas supply failures, ﬂow
meter or vaporizer problems, and those related to drugs
(wrong drug, wrong dose), ﬂuids, and blood (wrong type,
transfusion reactions). Figure 9 illustrates the number of
consequential serious patient injuries and deaths. Serious patient injuries were deﬁned as those that sig-
niﬁcantly complicated patient recovery or that persisted
following hospital discharge. The total number of serious
injuries was 11 and total deaths were 10 in 27,048 cases,

perfusions. Of the incidents found to be responsible for serious injury or death, the category of Urgent circuit re-setup
after circuit disposal accounted for a higher frequency than

or death in this study drops to 1 in 2,459 perfusions. Earlier studies compared injury rate data for ﬁve spe-
ciﬁc events; air embolism, electrical failure, mechanical
failure, oxygenator failure and DIC (45,48,62,80,81). For
this group of ﬁve events in the Jenkins study (49), the
rate of occurrence was 1 in 27,000. Perhaps the largest
difference between the two previously mentioned studies
is the larger number of events the respondents were asked
to comment on in the Jenkins study. The rate of reporting of incidents per 1,000 perfusions in the Jenkins study
was 1 in 35 perfusions (95% CI 1:33–1:38), considerably
more than the rates of 1:98 and 1:264 in previous surveys. Although more incidents were reported in the Jenkins
study, the rate of serious injury or death per reported incident was signiﬁcantly less. There was careful avoidance
of some survey methodological shortcomings present in
previous studies. Only those engaged as primary perfusionists were surveyed, as opposed to surveying surgeons
or other perfusion department members or heads who responded on behalf of others. Fortunately, in Australia and
New Zealand, the perfusion community is small and easily identiﬁed yielding a response rate of 69%. Finally, the
reporting period was truncated at 18 months to minimize
the problem of poor recall of event details.

In this survey, at least 80% of perfusionists used
important safety devices (blood level alarms with or
without pump shut-off, high pressure alarms, arterial line
ﬁlters, oxygenators gas ﬁlter, ACT monitoring during CPB,
prebypass checklist, backup arterial pump head, backup
heater/cooler, emergency oxygen supply). Alarmingly, the
ﬂip side is that as high as 20% of perfusionists were not
using important safety devices or procedures. Admittedly,
the authors could not demonstrate a statistical association
between the number of incidents and the use of safety
devices due to such a small number of reported incidents. This is not to imply that an association does not exist. In summary, this survey reiterated conclusions found
by previous surveys. Human error is still at the root of the
majority of accidents (70%–85%). Improving perfusion
education would have the most impact on minimizing the
number of incidents due to human error. In response,
American, European, Australian, and New Zealand perfusion boards ensure that perfusionist education, practice,
experience, training, certiﬁcation, and accreditation of
training centers meets a minimum standard. In 2000, BL Mejak et al. published the results of a survey
sent to centers performing cardiac surgery in the United
States (50). Its purpose was to identify current perfusion
incident rates and safety devices used during CPB. It consisted of a four-page questionnaire mailed to 1,030 chief
perfusionists at all cardiac centers identiﬁed by Billian’s
Hospital Blue Book and were asked to comment on procedures done between July1, 1996, to June 30, 1998. Eighty
questions were divided into four categories: ‘‘Perfusion
information’’, ‘‘Hospital information’’, ‘‘Equipment information’’, and the last category was devoted to perfusion
incidents during CPB, or as a direct result. Categorization of the incidents were ‘‘no injury’’, ‘‘serious injury’’,
or ‘‘death’’. Serious injury was deﬁned as an incident that
caused the patient an extended stay in hospital. There were
524 responses representing 797 hospitals, 2,385 perfusionists, 360 perfusion assistants, and 671,290 open-heart
procedures. Figure 10 summarizes the frequencies of the
most common types of perfusion incidents and those with
death rates greater than 2%. The rate of occurrence of perfusion incidents during CPB was one incident for every 138
procedures, higher than the Kurusz or Stoney surveys, but
less than the Australian survey. The most common types of

COMPARISON OF SURVEYS
The one commonality in all of the surveys, among
the many differences, is that all were retrospective
questionnaires. The target responder populations varied
between surveys. Cardiac surgeons, as well as perfusionists and chief perfusionists were asked to answer as
individuals or as a representative of a perfusion group.
The number and type of questions also varied. The older
surveys asked about very speciﬁc types of incidents where
as the newer surveys included questions over a very broad
scope of incidents. This may be the explanation for the
increase in perfusion incidents seen in the more recent surveys, (Fig. 11). The more detailed the questions concerning

the CPB associated incident rates and the number of questions/categories on the survey (31). Comparison of the
ﬁrst national survey of CPB-related complications done
by Stoney in 1980 to the most recent survey done by
Mejak in 2000 suggests that the incidence of permanent
injury or death over the span of 20 years may have decreased, (Fig. 12). Despite the differences in results, there
are themes that have carried through time in these surveys. Protamine reactions and coagulopathies that were
prevalent in the ﬁrst survey and continue to be major problems now. Although the overall incidence has decreased,
the morbidity and mortality from protamine reactions
and coagulopathies are between 2% and 10%. Massive air
embolism still occurs albeit at a very low rate but still
carries with it mortality as high as 34%. The increased use
of arterial line ﬁlters and air bubble detectors may have
had some impact on the very low occurrence of a very
devastating event. KEY POINTS
■Is a patient undergoing a procedure requiring CPB
safer now than 30 years ago? ●Presumably as a result of improved technology,
the creation of practice guidelines and the improvement of perfusion education, time has seen
a decrease in the overall rate of perfusion related
incidents and a signiﬁcant decrease in the types of
events that have catastrophic results. ●Regardless, human error still remains a factor
that cannot be completely eliminated by using the
highest technology and adhering to the strictest of
guidelines. REFERENCES

◗Unusual Problems in Cardiopulmonary
Bypass
Ludwig K. von Segesser
The deﬁnition of ‘‘Unusual problems in cardiopulmonary
bypass (CPB)’’ is not a sharp one. However, the term selected implies some degree of unexpectedness, and under
such circumstances, if it has not been experienced before,
it can be helpful to have read about such unexpected issues. As a matter of fact, in the case of an unusual mishap,
having predetermined the potential bailout procedures
may allow for reduction of negative consequences. In addition, increased awareness of unusual problems can help
in their prevention. Unfortunately, there is no practical
way to foresee all potential issues that may occur in a
speciﬁc patient. Hence, a selection of topics had to be
made, and the following three topics shall be discussed
here:
■Air of ‘‘unknown’’ origin in the arterial line
■Unusual degree of hemolysis
■Inadequate venous drainage
AIR OF “UNKNOWN” ORIGIN
IN THE ARTERIAL LINE
Air of unknown origin in the arterial line is one of the most
catastrophic events that can occur during CPB, because
both the surgeon and the perfusionist are eventually left
without practical option to identify the source of the
problem and to take any countermeasures. As a matter of
fact, air detected by a bubble detector in the arterial line
at a pump ﬂow of 6 L/min needs little more than 1 second
to reach the patient (approximately 138 mL are required
for a 3/8 in. arterial line measuring 200 cm in length), and
therefore only immediate pump stop may give a chance to
solve the problem if its origin is readily recognized (e.g., air
entered through the venous reservoir at low blood levels). This delay may be roughly doubled if an arterial ﬁlter with
a similar priming volume is used, and some additional
time can be bought if the arterial ﬁlter is vented in an
active and/or a passive manner, which in turn may also be
a source of the air of ‘‘unknown’’ origin (e.g., inverted vent
line in the roller pump or inverted roller pump direction,
pressurized venous reservoir etc.).

It is not the purpose of this chapter to discuss the
usual causes of air on the arterial side of the pump
oxygenator from where it can travel to the patient, such as
inadequate debubbling before onset of CPB, emptying of
the hard-shell venous reservoir during perfusion (a failing
or otherwise disabled blood level detector), vortex build
up and aspiration of air at low blood levels in a hardshell venous reservoir during high pump ﬂows, inadequate
debubbling of air coming through the venous line with a
soft venous reservoir (inadequate debubbling capacity),
or as mentioned in preceding text, inverted vent lines,
pressurized reservoirs, and so on. However, there are
a number of less usual situations that may be worth
remembering. Cavitation
Creation of bubbles can occur in an airtight system like
the arterial line due to the cavitation phenomenon, which
can be produced by a sudden change in pump speed. Under certain conditions (dependant on pump speed, line
pressure, blood temperature, partial blood gas pressures,
etc.) the sudden change in velocity of a blood column
traveling at high speed within the arterial line can lead
to its interruption, and the resulting vacuum may be
ﬁlled with gases extracted from the blood, which will not
necessarily redissolve readily. Hence, gaseous emboli may
originate from a bloodline that was perfectly debubbled,
and this can occur with roller pumps, centrifugal pumps,
axial pumps, and pulsatile pumps. Cavitation has also been
described to occur at the time of closure of mechanical
heart valves in patients. Although, this phenomenon is
at a microscopic level, it can be detected by transcranial
Doppler studies, and it is also considered responsible for
some type of corrosion of heart valves made from pyrolytic
carbon. The cavitation phenomenon may be more relevant
in pulsatile mechanical circulatory support systems where
608

29. Unusual Problems in Cardiopulmonary Bypass
609
the mechanical constraints are usually higher as compared
to biological systems. Cardiotomy or Venous Reservoir Failure
Cardiotomy reservoirs are designed for effective separation of the shed blood recovered from the chest (vent lines,
open heart cavities, pericardial sac, and/or pleural space)
and the air aspirated at the same time. A large surface
area, typically made from open cell synthetic material in
conjunction with a series of ﬁlter screens, as well as the
presence of a ﬁlm of liquid ‘‘antifoam agent’’ are the key
components for effective debubbling. It is important to
know that the breakthrough of aspirated air can occur
with every cardiotomy reservoir design that we are aware
of by the simple fact that the ‘‘antifoam’’ ﬁlm is consumed
over time. Hence, in the experimental setting, it is just
a matter of blood load, air admixture, and time to reach
the point where the cardiotomy reservoir is no longer able
to work efﬁciently. At that time, the blood aspirated will
foam and there are two ways out of the reservoir: the
venous line, or the ﬂoor of the operating theater, or both. Similar mechanisms can also result in hard-shell
venous reservoir failure in open systems when signiﬁcant
amounts of air come along the venous line because of
inadequate cannulation. In contrast, closed systems with a
soft bag are not designed for handling signiﬁcant amounts
of air, and therefore the air will go right through them
from the very beginning of CPB. It is also good to know
that the less blood is in the reservoir the more easily
bubbles travel through. The most efﬁcient way to handle these situations is to
have a backup cardiotomy reservoir readily available in order to be able to add a new device at any time. This means,
in the case of integrated heat exchanger/oxygenator structures that currently have the cardiotomy reservoir usually
built into the venous reservoir, as well as perfusion circuits made from separate components, that the backup
cardiotomy reservoir should be within the active operating theater, ideally on a cart holding typical ‘‘spare parts’’
for CPB, and designed especially for this purpose. Negative Pressure in the Oxygenator
Most modern hollow ﬁber oxygenators are made from microporous hollow ﬁbers.

It is the hydrophobic nature of
the ﬁber material (e.g., polypropylene, polyethylene) that
prevents the liquid phase from traveling through the microscopic pores of the hollow ﬁbers into the gaseous phase,
and it is the positive pressure in the blood compartment
that prevents the gas from traveling in the other direction. It is for this reason that the oxygenator compartment has
always to be positioned sufﬁciently below the level of the
heart in order to maintain a positive pressure on the blood
side of the oxygenator, which must be higher than the
one on the gas side. There are a few situations where the
pressure on the blood side of the oxygenator can become
negative, with catastrophic consequences. An example for this can be augmentation of venous
return with vacuum assist in conjunction with a just
occlusive roller pump. The term just occlusive implies
that the roller pump is not calibrated in a totally occlusive
manner. Hence, if the roller pump is stopped, the arterial
and venous lines are clamped, and negative pressure is
still acting on the venous reservoir, the latter can be
transmitted to the oxygenator, which will not collapse but
rather pull gas through the pores of the hollow ﬁbers into
the blood path. Likewise, the ‘‘just occlusive’’ roller pump in conjunction with a clamped arterial line and an active vent line on
the arterial ﬁlter may result in a negative pressure in the
oxygenator and gas being pulled from the microporous
hollow ﬁbers into the blood path. This also holds true for
a centrifugal pump with a clamp on both the venous and
the arterial line and an active vent line draining potential
‘‘air’’ from the arterial ﬁlter. This phenomenon has also to be kept in mind during
perfusion with the new low prime integrated perfusion
systems, in which the well known ‘‘air handling problems’’
in relation to the air admixture coming through the venous
line have been ‘‘solved’’ with active vent systems. It should
be considered here that tubing clamps are often placed on
both sides of the tubing set, that is, by the perfusionist
and/or the surgeon, and coordination of ‘‘who does what’’
becomes increasingly difﬁcult with the complexity of the
tubing set (e.g., increasing number of pumps) as well
as the proportion of surprising events occurring during
perfusion.

Finally, positive pressure on the gas side as compared
to the blood side of the oxygenator can occur if the
oxygenator gas outlet is obstructed for some reason. A typical example for this situation is the connection
of the oxygenator gas outlet to a measuring device for
exhaust gas composition analyses. It has to be stressed
here that such devices have to be positioned in a sidearm
of the oxygenator gas outlet. A section of large-bore
extension tubing, holding several times the sampling
volume of the gas analyzer, can prevent admixture of
room air, and allows for reliable exhaust gas analysis
while accommodating the necessity for an open system. Perforation on the Inlet Side
of the Pump Body
A source of air contamination difﬁcult to spot is a small
perforation of the pump body sitting on the inlet side of
the roller pump raceway. Such a perforation can be due
to a manufacturing defect on the tubing, some damage
occurring during assembly of the tubing set or mounting
of the tubing set onto the pump console, a perforation by

610
V. Clinical Applications
a needle coming from the operating ﬁeld, fatigue, and so
on. Independent of the reason for the perforation, there
may not necessarily be a water leak at the time of priming
and recirculation with low pump speeds. However, during
the pump run at full ﬂow, there will be enough negative
pressure generated within the pump inlet with each roller
passing over this perforation, and a proportional amount
of air will be aspirated each time into the perfusion system. This is very much in contrast to a small perforation on
the outlet side of the pump body where the pressure is
positive and therefore blood leaks into the raceway, and
the problem is easily detected. Although small amounts of air can be handled by the
oxygenator (1) and the arterial ﬁlter, these structures
may be unable to handle the air loaded systematically
throughout the perfusion period, and the standard safety
systems may fail to properly detect and prevent systemic
embolization. The only way to solve this problem is a
rapid exchange of the pump body, which again means
that this small piece of tubing that is worth a few dollars
must be readily available in the operating theater. Placing
a sterile backup pump tubing under the perfusion cart is
certainly a practical solution, provided that the routines
in the perfusion team make sure that it is always there. Negative Pressure in the Arterial
System of the Patient
A different mechanism of generating air within the
circulatory system is related to an imbalance of the
available blood with reference to the set vent volumes/
pressures. Relatively low vent volumes/pressures (typically, 500 mL/min for an aortic root vent in an adult) can
draw signiﬁcant amounts of air into the aorta as long as
the latter is clamped. These include air that is aspirated
through the puncture oriﬁce in the aortic root or through a
side hole of the venting needle which is partially within the
aorta and partially outside, air that is aspirated through
opened coronaries which are not completely occluded, air
that is aspirated through porous walls of vascular grafts
which are not sealed like those used for connection of
some ventricular assist devices, or air which is aspirated
through suture lines that may be loose as long as the vessel
is not pressurized, and so on.

Excessive venting of the aortic root in such a manner that it collapses should certainly be avoided, because
under such circumstances it can become totally unpredictable what is inside the aorta and the heart at the
time of unclamping. If the systemic ﬂow is decreased for
unclamping at the same time, or if the arterial pump is
stopped for some reason (e.g., circulatory arrest), such
air in the arterial system may also contaminate in retrograde manner the arterial limb of the pump oxygenator. It can be very difﬁcult to rapidly remove air from both
the arterial system of the patient and the arterial side
of the pump oxygenator if these problems occur simultaneously. In contrast, an air-free arterial line allows for
antegrade and/or retrograde reperfusion in combination
with proper venting maneuvers. Likewise, an air-free arterial system ﬁlled with blood can be used for retrograde
repriming of the arterial line. Care has to be taken here to
avoid negative pressure in the oxygenator compartment
because this generates problems of its own as outlined
earlier. UNUSUAL DEGREE OF HEMOLYSIS
Suboptimal calibration of the roller pump, excessive use
of cardiotomy suction, and transfusion of older red cell
concentrates are the most frequent causes of clinically
manifest hemolysis in modern perfusion outside blood
matching problems, congenital red cell variations, and
reduced red cell resistance due to other causes. Although
cardiotomy suction can be avoided in some cases, and red
cell washing may be used instead, it has to be considered
here that all noncellular components of the blood as well
as the platelets are lost by the latter approach. We have
previously reported our efforts to reduce blood trauma
due to cardiotomy suction (2,3). However, on-demand
cardiotomy suction is not routine, and therefore the
most important contributor to blood trauma remains the
cardiotomy suction. However, the most obvious reason for major acute
hemolysis is the contamination of circulating blood with
pure water. In addition to the accidental injection of
distilled water (e.g., coming from a vial containing water
as solvent for a speciﬁc drug), it is certainly the water to
blood leak in the heat exchanger that has to be considered
ﬁrst if acute major hemolysis occurs.

Although modern
oxygenators are built in a way that the preferential path
in case of a leak is blood to water, this cannot be taken
for granted. An underserviced heater–cooler with a lot of
sludge in its water inlet or a kinked water drainage line
can result in water pressure buildup in the oxygenator/heat
exchanger structure. Pure water is also generated in the oxygenator itself by
condensation of vapor, which originates from the blood. This is without consequences as long as the vapor is in
the gas path and the resulting condensed water is vented
off continuously by sufﬁcient sweep gas ﬂow. However, a
restricted oxygenator exhaust, recirculation of previously
unused oxygenator compartments, for example in variable
prime systems, temporary interruption of gas ﬂow through
a temporary, partial, or total disconnection of the gas
line, and unexpected negative pressure on the blood side
of the oxygenator (pressure may be positive in absolute
values but negative with reference to the pressure on the
gas/condensate side) can lead to contamination with pure
water and massive hemolysis is the result.

29. Unusual Problems in Cardiopulmonary Bypass
611
INADEQUATE VENOUS DRAINAGE
Less Invasive Open-Heart Surgery
Limited access open-heart surgery has triggered the
development of new technologies for efﬁcient remote
arterial and venous cannulation in order to avoid partial
obliteration of the already small access. The incision
required for accessing the heart can be kept smaller
if fewer instruments are competing for space. Various
approaches have been developed for this purpose in the
past. This includes guide-wire compatible cannulae that
can be inserted through a small cut down in a remote area,
typically the femoral vein and artery. Most of the guide-wire compatible cannulae can also
be inserted in a percutaneous manner provided a kit
of dilators is available. For the latter approach, direct
puncture of the access vessel and conﬁrmed backﬂow are
followed by insertion of a guide wire and removal of the
hollow needle. A small incision is made with a blade and
the access oriﬁce is dilated in a serial manner with dilators
of increasing diameter, which are passed over the same
guide wire up to the desired cannula diameter. Finally, the
percutaneous cannula which is stiffened by its obturator
with a conical tip is inserted, secured in the optimal
position (usually the cannula tip is positioned in the right
atrium or the vena cava), the obturator is removed, and
the cannula is connected to the corresponding limb of the
bypass circuit. The main limitation of remote venous cannulation with
traditional guide wire–compatible cannulas is inadequate
ﬂow. This is due to the fact that the access vessel, that is the
femoral vein, has by deﬁnition a much smaller diameter
as compared to the two venae cava at the level of the
right atrium. Hence, either a centrifugal pump or vacuum
assistance is routinely used for augmentation of venous
return (4). Unfortunately, these adjuncts do not usually
allow for full ﬂow (5,6) and a signiﬁcant amount of blood
stays within the body and, more detrimentally, within the
heart. This is due to the traditional design of long, rectilinear
percutaneous cannula with the access vessel diameter as
the main limiting factor with regard to size. In addition,
systematic augmentation of venous drainage with vacuum
or centrifugal pump assistance increases the risk of
collapsing the venous compartment (7), with consecutive
complete shutdown of venous drainage.

Possibilities for Improved Venous
Drainage
A recently introduced innovative cannula design based on
the ‘‘collapsed insertion and expansion in situ principle’’
has been shown to solve this problem. The superior
performance of smart cannulation is based on its ability

is helpful not only in less invasive open-heart surgery,
but also in difﬁcult redo procedures (e.g., in patients with
extracardiac conduits incorporated in the sternum), heart
transplantation in assist device dependent patients, as well
as emergency procedures under critical conditions, where
remote cannulation allowing for full ﬂow can be realized
under local anesthesia. Cannulation for Intravena Caval
Procedures
Surgery within the inferior vena cava at the level of the
hepatic veins can be difﬁcult for both the surgical and the
perfusion side. As a matter of fact, venous drainage from
an open vena cava with traditional femoral cannulation is
quite delicate, because the oriﬁces of traditional designs
are at their tip and therefore in the surgical ﬁeld. A permanent struggle between a ﬂooded ﬁeld and airlock results,
and can make the surgical procedure difﬁcult. In contrast,
in smart cannulation using self expanding cannulae with
an open wall design (Fig. 4), the cannula body keeps the
vessel wall apart and the vein provides the seal, allowing
direct drainage (the blood does not have to travel along the
cannula in order to join its oriﬁces at the tip) of the venous

Typical applications for this approach are resections of intravena caval tumors (e.g., renal tumors with
extension into the vena cava), hepatoatrial anastomoses
(e.g., for Budd-Chiari syndrome) (12), and much more frequently, cavopulmonary connections (Fontan completion
for univentricular heart), or tricuspid atresia (13). At this point one may conclude that it is of prime importance that the surgeons care about perfusion technology,
and that they remain involved in its future development
in order to understand potential issues with existing and
upcoming devices. As a matter of fact, many of the socalled new designs rely on ideas that have been around for
quite some time, and a look into the past may prevent a
lot of trouble because the issue has been studied before. Likewise, it is of similar importance that the perfusion
and anesthesiology teams know what the surgical plan is
for a speciﬁc patient, and that they anticipate potential
problems coming from the surgical ﬁeld, where things are
evolving too. There can be little doubt that a smooth pump
run requires effective communication between all parties
involved in the operating theater. KEY POINTS
■Preparation for unusual occurrences in cardiac
surgery, including predetermined ‘‘bailout’’ maneuvers, may reduce the severity of such unpredictable
events. ■Unexplained air in the arterial circuit, unusual
hemolysis, and inadequate venous drainage are three
such types of occurrences. ■Unexplained air

◗Termination of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Roger L. Royster, Stephen J. Thomas, and Richard F. Davis
Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is required for many
cardiac surgical procedures and results in major physiologic abnormalities including nonpulsatile ﬂow, hypothermia, hemodilution, profound anticoagulation, electrolyte
and neuroendocrine disturbances, an inﬂammatory response and ischemia/reperfusion injury. Restoration of the
normal cardiopulmonary circulation after CPB requires
reversing many of these pathophysiologic problems. The
cardiothoracic anesthesiologist facilitates this safe transition for the patient by thorough planning and preparation
(Table 1). The termination of bypass is a team effort requiring clear communication between surgeon, perfusionist,
and anesthesiologist. SEPARATION FROM
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS:
PREPARATION
Rewarming
The patient must be rewarmed if hypothermia is used
for organ protection (1). Mild hypothermia (33◦C–35◦C)
is used for shorter cases with warm intermittent or continuous cardioplegia. Moderate hypothermia (25◦C–30◦C)
is often used to slow myocardial rewarming after cold
cardioplegia. Deep hypothermia (18◦C–22◦C) with circulatory arrest is occasionally needed for repairs of certain
congenital defects or for aortic arch reconstruction. Rewarming is initiated so that its completion coincides with
completion of the surgical procedure and is accomplished
by the heat exchanger in the bypass circuit. Temperature measurement of the arterial and venous blood is
necessary to keep the arteriovenous gradient less than
10◦C to prevent bubble formation as the blood warms
and gaseous solubility decreases (2). The temperature
required for complete rewarming is usually a nasopharyngeal or esophageal temperature of 37◦C or a bladder
or rectal temperature of 35◦C. Palpation of the patient’s
head and shoulders can be helpful in assessing the degree of rewarming. However, the high blood ﬂow to tissue
mass ratio of the head and neck region may result in
underestimation of the completeness of rewarming in
other vascular beds. Therefore, sweating of the forehead
during rewarming in CPB does not necessarily mean that
the patient is ‘‘lightly anesthetized’’ but suggests a normal
thermoregulatory response to rewarming (3). Rebound hypothermia after discontinuation of CPB
results from inadequate rewarming. This heat deﬁcit is
often compounded by further convective heat loss from
the patient into the cool operating room environment. Pharmacologic-induced vasodilation during CPB may facilitate rewarming and decrease the postbypass fall in
temperature (4). However, the use of this technique may
require more intravascular volume expansion to maintain
adequate perfusion pressure, which worsens hemodilution and tissue edema.

Inadequate rewarming while on
CPB can result in a considerable (2◦C–3◦C) drop in patient temperature from the end of CPB until arrival in
the intensive care unit. This fall in temperature can result
in shivering which increases oxygen consumption, carbon
dioxide production, and peripheral vascular resistance. Subclinical shivering in a patient who is partially paralyzed during CPB results in hypercarbia and the need for
muscle relaxation. Shivering should be anticipated when
a systemic temperature is less than 35◦C. It should be
aggressively treated with active rewarming measures. Metabolic Abnormalities
Nonpulsatile ﬂow results in vasoconstriction during CPB
and a low perfusion state especially during prolonged
cases that can cause metabolic problems. Acidemia, from
respiratory or metabolic causes, should be corrected because of its depressant effects on myocardial function, its
interference with the action of inotropic drugs and its ability to increase pulmonary vascular tone (5–7). Acidemia
and administration of cardioplegic solutions frequently
result in hyperkalemia, which has pronounced deleterious
effects on cardiac conduction including atrioventricular
conduction block (8). Atrial depolarization is especially
sensitive to hyperkalemia and failure to capture either the
atria or ventricles with pacing can be due to electrolyte
