mild hyperkalemia (<6.0 mEq/L) in the presence of normal renal function because serum potassium usually falls
after CPB due to rewarming and increased glucose utilization, renal losses from a diuresis that develops from
the hemodilution and increased catecholamines and β-2
receptor stimulation from the stress of CPB, which drives
potassium intracellularly. If hypokalemia develops after
bypass, it should be treated promptly because ventricular
and atrial arrhythmias are more prone to develop. Hypocalcemia results from hemodilution and transfusion of albumin or citrate-containing blood products. Hypocalcemia during CPB should not be treated because
normocalcemia usually occurs by the end of rewarming
due to the normal response of increased parathyroid hormone (9). If ionized hypocalcemia is present (less that
0.8 mg/dL) after rewarming is complete, then it should
be corrected with calcium chloride (5 mg/kg) to improve myocardial contractility and peripheral vascular
resistance. Otherwise calcium should not be administered
because it can theoretically worsen the reperfusion injury
that occurs after cardioplegic arrest. Hypomagnesemia
also results from hemodilution but magnesium has no
counterregulatory hormone to increase magnesium levels.

Magnesium should be administered during CPB to provide
vasodilation of coronary arteries, to attenuate post-CPB
hypertension and to prevent arrhythmias (10). Hyperglycemia is common during the hypothermic period of
CPB and usually returns to normal shortly after termination of CPB in the nondiabetic patient.However, persistent
hyperglycemia after CPB in any patient should be treated
with insulin. In diabetic patients, insulin infusions are
often needed during CPB and postoperatively for hyperglycemic control. Even mild hyperglycemia (>150 mg/dL)
has signiﬁcant adverse effects in terms of increasing
the risk of postoperative infection, wound healing, and
increased mortality (11). More severe hyperglycemia increases serum osmolarity and can cause osmotic diuresis
and central nervous system dysfunction and may increase
the susceptibility of the brain to hypoxic damage. Pump priming with crystalloid solutions results in
hemodilution. Hemodilution reduces blood viscosity and
improves microcirculatory ﬂow; however, hemodilution

616
V. Clinical Applications
decreases serum protein levels which decreases plasma
colloid osmotic pressure and increases the movement
of ﬂuid from the intravascular to the extravascular
compartments and results in tissue edema. Hemodilution
reduces hemoglobin and hematocrit concentrations. The
optimal hemoglobin concentration during CPB is usually
accepted as being 7 to 8 g/dL, although there is no
proven minimum safe level. Healthy adult patients rarely
need homologous blood transfusion with appropriate
blood conservation measures, although the chronically ill
patient may require red cell transfusion. However, blood
transfusion increases the risk of renal failure and infection
and the beneﬁts of blood transfusion in terms of increased
oxygen transport should be weighed against its risks. Heparin-induced anticoagulation should be carefully
monitored during rewarming because of the increased
metabolism of heparin at higher body temperatures and
the dangerous consequences of inadequate anticoagulation. In addition to reducing electrolyte levels and hematocrit, hemodilution reduces platelet levels by 40% and
dilutes coagulation factor levels (12). Platelet transfusions
are occasionally required, especially in patients who have
thrombocytopenia or chronic renal failure, who are receiving antiplatelet drugs, or who require repeat surgery
or lengthy procedures. Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate should be available for treating documented
factor deﬁciencies or coagulopathies. Postoperative bleeding is usually due to either inadequate surgical hemostasis,
inadequate heparin reversal, or platelet dysfunction. Anesthesia, Oxygenation
and Ventilation
The requirements for anesthetics and muscle relaxants
are greatly reduced during CPB because of the anesthetic
effects of hypothermia and decreased metabolism of most
drugs (13). However, rewarming reverses these effects,
and adequate anesthetic depth and muscle relaxation
to prevent patient awareness and shivering are a concern. Benzodiazepines, narcotics, and muscle relaxants
are empirically administered when rewarming is initiated
in anticipation of volatile agents being discontinued before termination of CPB to avoid their circulatory and
myocardial depressant effects (14,15). Failure to wean
from CPB has occurred because of the inadvertent administration of a cardiodepressant volatile anesthetic during
the weaning process. However, volatile anesthetic agents
induce vasodilation and facilitate rewarming and may be
continued if rewarming is slow but should be discontinued
approximately 10 minutes before termination of bypass. Oxygenation and ventilation must begin before discontinuation of bypass. The lungs should be manually
reinﬂated and visually inspected to document bilateral
reinﬂation and elimination of atelectasis.

Unilateral re-
inﬂation suggests mucus plugging or clot of a mainstem
bronchus or malposition of the endotracheal tube, which
may require therapeutic bronchoscopy. Suctioning should
be done carefully in the anticoagulated patient to avoid
mucosal trauma and bleeding. Occasionally a pneumothorax or blood accumulation in the pleural space may
cause problems with reinﬂation and these problems are
easily corrected by the surgeon. Mechanical ventilation
with 100% oxygen and a sufﬁcient minute ventilatory
volume to produce an arterial PCO2 of 30 to 35 mm
Hg should be initiated before beginning the weaning
process. Minute ventilation should be higher than preCPB because of the increased carbon dioxide production
during rewarming which extends into the post-CPB period. Mild hyperventilation prevents hypercapnia and
respiratory acidosis, which could result in elevated pulmonary artery pressures (PAPs) (16,17). Patients with
chronic lung disease may sometimes require positive
end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), pressure controlled ventilation, or bronchodilators. Most CPB consoles include an in-line monitor of mixed
venous blood hemoglobin oxygen saturation. Changes
in this parameter may reﬂect the adequacy of systemic
perfusion and oxygen delivery or increases in oxygen
consumption (e.g., shivering) while on CPB. Before
terminating CPB, the venous saturation and pump ﬂow
should be checked. A low saturation may indicate the
need for additional muscle relaxant, red cell transfusion,
or vasodilator therapy before weaning from bypass. CPB
should not be discontinued with an abnormally low mixed
venous oxygen saturation because it immediately requires
the heart to produce a greater than needed cardiac output
to make up for this systemic oxygen deﬁcit. Hemodynamic Monitors
Needless to say, all routine monitors need to be returned
to their full operating mode before terminating CPB. Pulse oximeter probes placed on the extremities do
not function while the patient is cold and pulseless
on CPB. Assessment of their function must wait until
partial bypass is instituted. Pressure transducers should
be zeroed and recalibrated. Frequently, the radial arterial
pressure does not reﬂect the central aortic pressure after
CPB (18–20). If there appears to be a discrepancy between
the transduced radial arterial pressure and the aortic
pressure estimated by palpation or the blood pressure cuff,
the aortic pressure can be transduced from the antegrade
cardioplegia line or stopcock on the aortic cannula once
bypass is discontinued.

Documenting an adequate central
aortic pressure compared to an inadequate radial pressure
can prevent the administration of unnecessary vasoactive
drugs. Alternatively, a femoral arterial catheter, which will
normally more closely reﬂect the central aortic pressure,
can be placed. Central and peripheral arterial pressures
usually equilibrate shortly after CPB is discontinued.

30. Termination of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
617
Pulmonary artery catheters frequently migrate distally during manipulation of the heart during cardiac
surgery (21). If the PAP waveform reﬂects pulmonary
artery occlusion pressure, the catheter should be pulled
back while on partial bypass until the phasic PAP waveform reappears. A left atrial (LA) catheter is a useful
monitor of left ventricular ﬁlling pressure if a pulmonary
artery catheter is not present. The LA catheter can also be
used as a route for administration of inotropic drugs, especially those with signiﬁcant α-adrenergic agonist properties in the context of excessive pulmonary vasoconstriction
(see subsequent text). The central venous pressure (CVP)
should be measured, especially in those patients with
pulmonary hypertension or right ventricular failure. The
appropriate right/left ventricular function balance is an
important variable in successful weaning. Urine output is routinely monitored during CPB but
low urine output during CPB is not independently predictive of postoperative renal dysfunction (22). Nevertheless,
patients with preoperative renal dysfunction or low urine
output during CPB should be treated with increased perfusion pressures on pump. Many cardiac surgical centers
have protocols for renal protection which include volume loading when possible to establish good urine output
prepump, bicarbonate infusions, additional mannitol, and
dopamine or fenoldapam; no renal protection protocol has
been proved to protect renal function during the insult of
CPB. After the resumption of pulsatile blood ﬂow, many
patients exhibit a marked diuresis due to the hemodilution
particularly if mannitol has been added to the pump prime. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) provides information that can be very useful before termination of
CPB. While on partial bypass, TEE provides an excellent
assessment of residual air in the heart after open procedures. The left ventricular short-axis view provides a useful
indicator of left ventricular size and ﬁlling. Regional wall
motion abnormalities may provide an important indicator of myocardial ischemia and inadequate ﬂow through
a speciﬁc coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). However,
regional wall motion abnormalities may also be due to
residual effects of cardioplegia, inhomogeneous myocardial temperature, or preexisting abnormalities. One of the
most useful applications of TEE before and after the termination of CPB is in evaluating valvular function after
valve replacement or repair (23). Epicardial echocardiography and TEE have proved to be useful in evaluating the
repair of complex congenital heart defects (24,25).

Also, in
contrast to routine intracardiac pressure measurements,
which do not accurately reﬂect cardiac chamber volumes,
TEE provides the capability to accurately assess biventricular ﬁlling volumes (26,27). Direct observation of the
right ventricle (RV) on the anterior surface of the heart
is a useful monitor for guiding volume infusions from
the pump and can prevent the right heart from becoming
overdistended. Heart Rate and Rhythm
After the aortic cross clamp is released and coronary
reperfusion commences, cardiac electrical activity returns. This may be in the form of ventricular ﬁbrillation, which
is likely a reperfusion arrhythmia due to calcium overload
of ischemic myocardium. Lidocaine is often given before
the cross clamp is released or in the cardioplegia and is
effective at preventing ventricular ﬁbrillation. Ventricular
ﬁbrillation during CPB may result in ventricular distension
and irreversible myocardial damage. The heart should be
electrically deﬁbrillated as soon as possible. Electrolytes
should be treated if abnormal. Recurrent ventricular
ﬁbrillation should be treated with amiodarone and repeat
deﬁbrillation. β-Adrenergic blockers are also remarkably
effective for facilitating deﬁbrillation in resistant cases. More commonly after hyperkalemic cardioplegic arrest,
the return of cardiac electrical activity is in the form of
a junctional bradycardia or sinus bradycardia with atrioventricular conduction block. Sinus bradycardia is easily
treated with atrial pacing when normal A-V conduction
is present. Sequential atrioventricular pacing is indicated
for atrioventricular conduction block or signiﬁcant ﬁrst-
degree heart block. This preserves the atrial contribution
to ventricular ﬁlling, which is a signiﬁcant advantage in the
presence of a noncompliant hypertrophied ventricle (hypertension, aortic stenosis) or enlarged ventricle (aortic or
mitral regurgitation). Ventricular pacing should be used
only when atrial or atrioventricular pacing is not feasible
(e.g., atrial ﬁbrillation or ﬂutter with a very slow ventricular
response) or in a backup demand mode when the patient is
in sinus rhythm. In patients with low ejection fractions and
preoperative conduction system abnormalities, temporary
biventricular pacing may improve postoperative hemodynamics and prevent left ventricular dyssychrony (28). All available electrocardiogram (ECG) leads should
be examined and compared with a preoperative tracing before terminating CPB to detect evidence of acute
myocardial ischemia. Temporary pacing can be momentarily discontinued to make this evaluation. Transient
ST-segment elevation is common during emergence from
CPB but usually resolves shortly thereafter (29).

Persistent ST-segment elevation suggests myocardial ischemia,
which may require surgical treatment (i.e., revision of a
graft or placement of an additional graft). Intracoronary
air embolism usually involves the right coronary artery
and resolves after a period of increased perfusion pressure. Coronary artery or internal mammary artery spasm
also produces a similar clinical picture and often responds
favorably to treatment with intravenous nitroglycerin or
to elevation of the perfusion pressure. Tachycardia before termination of CPB is more difﬁcult
to manage. Heart rate often slows with ventricular ﬁlling
and increased arterial pressure; therefore, termination of
CPB may slow sinus tachycardia. It is important to

618
V. Clinical Applications
consider and treat other common causes of tachycardia,
including hypoxemia, hypercapnia, anemia, inadequate
anesthesia, and effects of vasoactive drugs. Once these
causes are eliminated and if myocardial function is determined to be adequate, the abnormal rate can be reduced
with appropriate doses of β-adrenergic receptor or calcium channel blocking drugs. The β receptor antagonist,
esmolol, is especially useful because of its short duration
of action if adverse effects develop. Refractory supraventricular tachycardia, atrial ﬁbrillation, or ﬂutter is best
treated intraoperatively with electrical cardioversion. Ventricular Function and Prophylactic
Inotropic Support
The ischemia imposed by aortic cross-clamping can result
in considerable myocardial stunning which is prolonged
reversible acute postischemic ventricular dysfunction of
viable myocardium that follows reperfusion (30). In the
case of chronic myocardial ischemia, successful myocardial revascularization may improve ventricular function
by restoring perfusion. However, improvements in ventricular function can be delayed for hours to days because
of myocardial stunning (31). Improved ventricular function is usually obtained after aortic valve replacement
for aortic stenosis where the compensatory response to
chronic pressure overload is concentric hypertrophy of the
ventricular wall that tends to normalize wall stress (32). In contrast, myocardial dysfunction is frequently present
after valve replacement in the patient with mitral regurgitation where removing the low-pressure ejection
of blood into the left atrium increases left ventricular
afterload and frequently results in postoperative ventricular dysfunction (32,33). The degree of postoperative
dysfunction is less predictable in patients with mitral
stenosis or aortic regurgitation, but myocardial depression
may exist because of the cardiomyopathy of rheumatic
heart disease or eccentric ventricular hypertrophy, respectively. Previous myocardial infarction is an obvious
cause for irreversible myocardial dysfunction postoperatively. Procedures requiring a ventriculotomy may have
a profound impact on postoperative ventricular function because of transection of important coronary artery
branches or resection of viable myocardium with reduced ventricular compliance produced by closure of the
ventriculotomy. The prediction for the need of pharmacologic support
after CPB is usually assessed by reviewing preoperative
and prepump hemodynamic data and the intraoperative
course. Information such as the preoperative ejection
fraction, left ventricular ﬁlling pressures before and after
contrast injection during the catheterization, history of
heart failure, the prepump cardiac index, the effectiveness
of intraoperative myocardial protection, the length of time
on CPB and the adequacy of surgical repair all can affect
the decision to start inotropic drugs prophylactically.

The goal of prophylactic administration is to allow a
smooth separation from bypass without causing cardiac
distension, hypotension, and reinstitution of bypass. In a Canadian study of 12,471 patients undergoing
CABG surgery, preoperative left ventricular function was
a relevant factor in predicting outcome. In patients with
an ejection fraction of more than 40%, the predictors of
postoperative mortality were emergency surgery, female
gender, reoperation, type of myocardial protection (bloodbased cardioplegia appeared to offer greater protection
than crystalloid cardioplegia), and age. The presence of
left main coronary artery disease was a predictor of death
in patients with an ejection fraction greater than 40%. The
type of myocardial protection used remained correlated
with mortality in patients with ejection fraction between
20% and 40% (34). In patients with an ejection fraction
less than 20%, emergency surgery was the only predictor
of death (Table 2). Relatively few studies have been conducted to help
predict which patients will require pharmacologic support during and immediately after CPB. In a retrospective
analysis of patients who underwent CABG surgery, predictors of the need for inotropic support were essentially
the same as those identiﬁed for major morbidity and mortality in the previously discussed studies (35). Preexisting
low ejection fraction, a dilated left ventricle, an elevated
left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), longer
duration of aortic cross-clamp (or total bypass) time, age,
and female gender were positive predictors of the need
for postoperative inotropic support. Interestingly, in patients with normal preoperative ejection fractions (at least
55%), the presence of wall motion abnormalities and an
LVEDP greater than 10 mm Hg indicated a higher risk for
needing inotropic support similar to patients with lower
ejection fractions. In another study, left ventricular dysfunction, deﬁned by an ejection fraction less than 40%,
LVEDP more than 15 mm Hg, and abnormal systolic and
diastolic left ventricular volumes, correlated with the need
for postoperative hemodynamic support, either pharmacologic or with an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) (36). ◗TABLE 2 Christakis Study: Predictors of Mortality

decline in cardiac function postoperatively. One study
evaluated patterns of left ventricular functional recovery
after cardiac surgery. Patients with normal preoperative

of reaching a peak depression in ventricular function at

and reduced recovery as late as 24 hours postoperatively. Another study reviewed data from several previous studies
and found interesting similarities that showed a decline

CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS:
TECHNIQUE
Routine Termination of
Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Separation from bypass restores the normal circulation
to the heart and the lungs. The duration of the transitional period of partial bypass is determined by the ability
of the left ventricle and RV to sustain the entire cardiac output. Reduced left ventricular function mandates
a period of partial bypass while ventricular loading conditions are carefully adjusted by manipulations of venous
return and vascular resistance and contractility is improved by judicious selection of positive inotropic drug
therapy. During separation, ventricular distension should
be avoided and coronary perfusion pressure must be maintained. A general approach to the termination of CPB is shown
in Figure 2.

Separation is accomplished by gradual occlusion of the venous cannula, which decreases ﬂow to the
pump and allows more blood to pass through the heart
and lungs. Arterial inﬂow from the pump is then gradually reduced. Hemodynamics and ventricular function are
assessed by visual inspection of the heart and by TEE. Venous cannula clamping can be increased, arterial inﬂow
decreased, and hemodynamics reassessed. This process is
repeated until separation from CPB is complete. Hemodynamic management for every patient focuses on regulating
four primary determinants of cardiac function: rate and
rhythm, arterial pressure, preload or ventricular volume
(ventricular ﬁlling pressure), and contractility (stroke volume). An algorithm for the diagnosis and treatment of
hemodynamic abnormalities at the termination of CPB is

After CPB, the clinical management goal is to have a
systolic arterial pressure of 90 to 100 mm Hg, a normal
cardiac index (>2.0 L/min/m2) and a normal or low
ventricular ﬁlling pressures of 10 to 15 mm Hg. Additional
volume can be infused directly from the pump through
the aortic cannula until the cannula is removed usually
after protamine reversal. The need for additional volume
infusion can be judged by evaluating the arterial pressure
and ﬁlling pressure responses. Adequate ﬁlling of the heart
is assessed by direct inspection of the RV, hemodynamic
measurement, and TEE. The pulmonary artery occlusion
or pulmonary diastolic pressure is frequently used to guide
volume infusion at the conclusion of CPB. A pulmonary
artery diastolic pressure of 10 to 15 mm Hg is almost
always adequate in patients after isolated coronary artery
bypass surgery. Higher pressures may be required in
patients with valvular disease or pulmonary hypertension. However, pulmonary artery wedge or diastolic pressure correlates poorly with left ventricular end-diastolic
volume after coronary artery bypass surgery secondary
to acute decreases in left ventricular compliance (26). TEE clearly provides the best available clinical intraoperative estimate of ventricular volumes (27).

For example,
mild hypotension with measured ﬁlling pressures that are
slightly high with a TEE which reveals an underﬁlled
ventricle shortly after terminating CPB is common. These
patients can be temporarily supported with phenylephrine
to raise the coronary perfusion pressure and nitroglycerin to decrease the ﬁlling pressures. Additional volume
may then be necessary to maintain cardiac index. Often
ventricular compliance improves dramatically during the
ﬁrst 30 minutes off CPB and is manifested by a spontaneous increase in coronary perfusion pressure with a
simultaneous decrease in ﬁlling pressures. Systemic vascular resistance progressively decreases
with rewarming and continues to decrease during the
period after CPB. Pronounced vasodilation at the termination of CPB can be related to the duration of rewarming, comorbid diseases which can cause peripheral
neuropathy such as diabetes, chronic drug therapy such as
angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, or septicemia in cases of infective endocarditis. This condition
is manifested by hypotension with low ﬁlling pressures, a
normal to high cardiac index and good ventricular function on TEE. Vasoconstrictors such as phenylephrine are
effective treatment because they stimulate α-adrenergic
receptors which increase arterial blood pressure by increasing systemic vascular resistance (afterload) and by
venoconstriction which decreases venous capacitance (increasing preload). If refractory arterial vasodilation is
present or if vasodilation is combined with mildly reduced
left ventricular function, norepinephrine may be appropriate to counteract the vasodilation while providing some
degree of inotropic support to meet the increased afterload. In patients receiving ACE inhibitors who are refractory to phenylephrine and norepinephrine, vasopressin
should be considered. Some studies have shown reduced
endogenous vasopressin in these patients and a dramatic
response to exogenously administered vasopressin. Pure α receptor agonists are useful in the treatment
of hypotension in patients with good ventricular function. The beneﬁcial increase in coronary perfusion pressure

usually outweighs the negative effects of decreased cardiac
output and increased ﬁlling pressures in the patient with
coronary artery disease or ventricular hypertrophy. In
general, the use of pure α agonists to increase arterial
blood pressure in patients with poor ventricular function
or pulmonary hypertension is best avoided because
increased afterload without a compensatory increase in
contractility results in a decreased stroke volume. SEPARATION FROM
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS:
PROBLEM SITUATIONS
Left Ventricular Failure
Ventricular failure or dysfunction can be deﬁned as inadequate cardiac pump performance, despite appropriate
adjustments of preload and afterload, due to a decrease in
myocardial contractility that can be either acute (ischemia
or myocardial stunning) or chronic. If acute ischemia is
suspected, as in the situation of incomplete revascularization, nitroglycerin should be administered to maximize coronary blood ﬂow while coronary perfusion is
controlled. Calcium should be avoided with myocardial
stunning. If prophylactic inotropes were administered for
preexisting cardiac dysfunction and the hemodynamics do
not improve rapidly, additional support may be required. If additional inotropes and vasoactive drugs are not effective, partial or full bypass should be reinstituted while
therapy is optimized. This will allow the heart to recover
from a period of hypotension and cardiac distension while
additional therapy takes effect. Additional time on partial
bypass will allow more time for the postischemic recovery
of ventricular function (39). Initial therapy of left ventricular dysfunction is usually
achieved with positive inotropic drugs, of which there are
several clinically useful categories. A comparison of mild
ventricular dysfunction after separation from CPB and the
result of inotropic treatment can be analyzed by pressurevolume loops (Fig. 4). Calcium chloride or calcium
gluconate (Tables 3 and 4) have a positive inotropic effect
in the presence of hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia but
are ineffective in the presence of normal ionized calcium
concentrations and may actually be harmful because of
the detrimental effects of elevated intracellular Ca2+ in
ischemic cells after reperfusion (40). β-Adrenergic receptor agonists are the most potent and
widely used inotropes. Myocardial activation of the β1 receptor leads to modulation of the G protein system which
activates adenyl cyclase. This enzyme leads to the formation of cyclic 3′, 5′-adenosine monophosphate (AMP) from
adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

Increased intracellular concentrations of cyclic AMP lead to increased availability of
Ca2+ to the contractile apparatus in the sarcomere which

625
ventricular dysfunction after CPB. A number of different
β-adrenergic agonists are available (Table 3). These drugs
have varying actions at β1, β2, and α-adrenergic receptors. Typically, a speciﬁc drug is best selected based on the
speciﬁc hemodynamic abnormality being treated and the
drugs relative actions at each receptor type. Epinephrine and norepinephrine are useful when ventricular dysfunction is accompanied by peripheral vasodilation, because they are also potent α-receptor agonists. The vasopressor effect of norepinephrine is greater than
that of epinephrine because of the greater potency of
epinephrine at the β-2 receptors, which produce considerable vasodilation in skeletal muscle and other major
vascular beds. Dobutamine and dopamine are useful when
minimal or mild inotropic support is desired, although the
wisdom of selecting a drug with less adrenergic agonist
potency (i.e., dopamine or dobutamine) as opposed to
careful titration of a more potent drug (i.e., epinephrine)
is very debatable. Dobutamine is a β1 receptor agonist
with only minimal α receptor activity and may therefore
be useful when further vasoconstriction is undesirable. Dopamine is unique in that it stimulates renal dopamine
receptors and causes an increase in both renal blood ﬂow
and sodium excretion. It may be useful in patients with
renal dysfunction (41,42). Use of dopamine as an inotrope
at higher doses (>8 to 10 µg/kg/min) is complicated by its
increasing activity at α-adrenergic receptors, which may
produce undesirable increases in systemic and pulmonary
vascular resistance. At higher doses both dobutamine
and dopamine tend to induce tachycardia and atrial arrhythmias (43,44). At equally effective inotropic doses,
dobutamine and dopamine both appear to have stronger
arrhythmogenic potency than does epinephrine (43). The
partial dependence of the inotropic effects of dopamine
on endogenous catecholamines may also limit its efﬁ-
cacy in patients with chronic ventricular dysfunction and
after CPB. Isoproterenol is a nonselective β receptor agonist that
is a potent inotrope (β1 effect) and peripheral vasodilator
(β2 effect). The potent chronotropic effect of isoproterenol (β1 and β2 effect) is not compensated for by
the baroreceptor-mediated reﬂex bradycardia that occurs
with β receptor agonists that also possess intrinsic α receptor activity such as epinephrine and norepinephrine. Either isoproterenol or dobutamine may be useful in
patients with severe pulmonary hypertension and right
ventricular failure, because α receptor stimulation is a potent mechanism producing pulmonary vasoconstriction.

Isoproterenol is also useful for the treatment of slow ventricular rates or atrioventricular conduction disturbances
when other methods have failed because of the positive chronotropic and dromotropic effects of β-adrenergic
stimulation. These effects are also clinically useful in cardiac transplantation dealing with the acutely denervated
transplanted heart. In general, epinephrine appears to be the most useful adrenergic drug for inotropic stimulation for adult
cardiac surgical patients after CPB, perhaps because of its
combined β1, β2, and α-Adrenergic actions. Dopamine and
isoproterenol are often favored in the pediatric population
because of advantages of a higher heart rate in this group. However, patterns of inotrope use show signiﬁcant institutional variation, and the literature describing comparative
effects of the drugs in patients requiring inotropic support, especially larger scale well-designed clinical trials,
is somewhat sparse. One well-designed trial documented
the increased efﬁcacy of epinephrine as compared with
calcium chloride for increasing cardiac performance after
CPB (45). In this study, epinephrine had superior hemodynamic effects as compared with calcium. And calcium,
when given to normocalcemic patients, had no predictable
effect on cardiac output but did increase mean arterial
pressure. The use of dopamine or epinephrine as an inotrope in severe left ventricular dysfunction is limited by
dose-dependent increases in afterload and preload. These
undesirable side effects are the basis for the frequent
clinical use of combined inotropic stimulation and afterload reduction with direct acting vasodilators such as
nitroprusside or nitroglycerin (46). Another class of positive inotropic drugs, the phosphodiesterase (PDE) enzyme inhibitors, has contributed
greatly to the ability to treat myocardial failure after CPB. Although these drugs also increase the intracellular concentration of cyclic AMP, they produce this effect by an
entirely different mechanism, inhibiting the metabolic
breakdown of intracellular cyclic AMP. Several classes
of drugs have the property of PDE inhibition (Table 5). Benzylisoquinolines (e.g., papaverine) and methylxanthines (e.g., aminophylline) are examples of nonspeciﬁc
inhibitors of PDE. The PDE enzymes have several isoforms, of which type III predominates in the myocardium
and in vascular smooth muscle. The selective type III
PDE inhibitor used most often clinically is the bipyridine derivative milrinone. In vascular smooth muscle,
milrinone increases concentrations of cyclic AMP and
guanosine monophosphate (GMP), which produces sig-
niﬁcant vasodilation.

Clinically, these drugs produce mild
to moderate improvement in cardiac contraction that is
often overshadowed by the more marked improvement
in cardiac pump performance produced by the combined

inotropic, lusitropic, and peripheral vasodilation effects. The inotropic activity of the PDE III inhibitors is synergistic with that of β-adrenergic agents (Fig. 6) and may
not be associated with increased myocardial oxygen consumption; these properties have made this combination
therapy with epinephrine or norepinephrine particularly
useful in patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction (47,48). Because of the signiﬁcant vasodilation which
occurs with milrinone, an α-adrenergic vasoconstrictor,
usually phenylephrine or norepinephrine may be required
to maintain coronary perfusion pressure (49,50). Some
advocate administration of milrinone before weaning is
attempted so that the ﬂow from the pump can counteract
the vasodilation which occurs during loading. Milrinone’s inotropic effect is independent of β-
receptor activation. An important advantage of the PDE III
inhibitors is in patients where there is signiﬁcant downregulation of the β-adrenergic receptors as in chronic
ventricular failure. This downregulation may also occur
in the more acute immediate postoperative period. The
desensitization of β-adrenergic receptors that occurs in
congestive heart failure signiﬁcantly limits the efﬁcacy of
β-adrenergic agonists. Combined therapy with PDE III
inhibitors enhances the inotropic effect of β-adrenergic
receptor agonists by potentiating the rise in intracellular cyclic AMP. Such combined therapy may also permit
use of a lower dose of the β-adrenergic agonist, thereby
avoiding possible adverse side effects such as arrhythmias. If ventricular function remains inadequate despite
appropriate inotropic therapy, the addition of mechanical
support may be required to allow termination of CPB (51). An IABP should be considered in the patient with poor
preoperative ventricular function and postoperative low
cardiac output syndrome (52). If difﬁculty or failure
is encountered when terminating CPB despite maximal
pharmacologic therapy, the IABP should be inserted
while still on bypass to prevent ventricular distension.

If terminating bypass continues to be a problem despite
maximum pharmacologic therapy plus an IABP, then a
ventricular assist device (VAD) should be considered in
selected patients. Right Ventricular Failure
This condition may occur as a result of right coronary
artery damage, occlusion or embolism, inadequate intraoperative right ventricular protection, or in patients with
pulmonary hypertension. Increased pulmonary artery and
CVPs, decreased arterial pressure and cardiac output, and
a bulging RV usually characterize right ventricular failure. Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (or LA) pressure and
left ventricular volume assessed by TEE will be low or normal if right ventricular failure is associated with normal
left ventricular function. However, these measurements
will be abnormal if right ventricular and left ventricular dysfunctions coexist. The therapeutic goals in treating
right ventricular dysfunction are similar to those in treating left ventricular dysfunction; increase right ventricular
contractility and decrease afterload (PAP) while maintaining adequate preload (CVP) and coronary perfusion
pressure. It is more difﬁcult to achieve these objectives
due to the pulmonary vasoconstriction induced by most
adrenergic positive inotropes with α receptor agonist effects. It is critical to maintain adequate systemic arterial
pressure in the presence of right ventricular failure to
provide adequate coronary perfusion pressure to the distended RV, which has an elevated EDP. Because of the
relatively thin wall of the RV, intramyocardial wall tension is higher for any given level of intracavitary pressure
than is the case for the left ventricle, as predicted by the
La Place relationship. This increases oxygen consumption
and compromises coronary blood ﬂow. The goal in right ventricular failure is maintenance of a
normal systemic arterial (coronary perfusion) pressure, an
increased ventricular contractility, and a decreased right
ventricular afterload. These effects may be best achieved
by inhalation of nitric oxide combined with inotropic
drugs. Inhaled nitric oxide has been used experimentally
as a selective pulmonary vasodilator with encouraging
results (53). Unlike other vasodilators, inhaled nitric
oxide is very selective for the pulmonary circulation
because it is largely taken up by hemoglobin before
reaching the systemic circulation. Therefore, it can
decrease PAP without producing signiﬁcant systemic
vasodilation. If nitric oxide is unavailable, selective

627
infusion of pulmonary vasodilators into the right atrium
and vasopressors into the left atrium is another method
to achieve the desired goals. This has been demonstrated
by infusing prostaglandin E1 (30–50 ng/kg/min) into the
right atrium and norepinephrine into the left atrium in
patients with refractory right heart failure after mitral
valve replacement (54). The inhaled prostacyclin analogs,
repoprosternal and iloprost, have the advantage over
intravenous drugs in that their effects are limited to the
pulmonary circulation. Inhaled Iloprost has been shown to
be an effective pulmonary vasodilator in severe pulmonary
hypertension and is very useful in the treatment of
pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure after
CPB. (55). Alternatively, nitroglycerin can be infused into
the right atrium as the pulmonary vasodilator. If an LA catheter is not available, isoproterenol or dobutamine can be infused into the right atrium. Isoproterenol
may be useful for increasing right ventricular contractility
without signiﬁcantly increasing PAP (afterload), although
problems with tachycardia and arrhythmias may occur. The PDE III inhibitors are extremely useful in treating
right ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension after CPB because of their ability to increase right
ventricular contractility and reduce pulmonary vascular
resistance (56). Other manipulations to decrease pulmonary vascular resistance include hyperventilation to
induce hypocapnia, a reduction in tidal volume and inspiratory time, and avoidance of hypoxemia and acidemia. If
these measures fail, mechanical support may be required
either in the form of an IABP or a right VAD. Delayed Acute Hemodynamic
Deterioration
This critical situation can result from a number of causes
including cardiac arrhythmias, graft or valve malfunction, air embolus to the right coronary artery, reactions
to medications (often to protamine), or to the adverse
hemodynamic effects of closure of the pericardium or
the sternum. The latter can result in compression of
the heart producing a tamponade effect, which may
improve with volume infusion or inotropic support as
the heart adjusts to the altered loading conditions. The
pericardium may need to be reopened. And in severe
cases, the sternum may have to be left open for closure at a later date. Acute myocardial ischemia produced
by kinking, clotting, or embolization of a vascular graft
may require surgical revision and is usually associated
with acute changes in the ECG, often ST-segment elevation and occasionally associated with arrhythmias.

Coronary (or mammary graft) vasospasm or coronary
air is another cause of acute ischemia after CPB. Treatment of spasm includes nitroglycerin or calcium channel
blockers. Intracoronary air should be treated with an
increased coronary perfusion pressure (phenylephrine)
and nitroglycerin. Other causes of acute hemodynamic
deterioration include arrhythmias, which may be secondary to new myocardial ischemia; other metabolic or
electrolyte abnormalities; to atrial decannulation; and to
surgical manipulation of the heart. In this situation, TEE
can provide vital diagnostic information regarding new
regional wall motion abnormalities, valve function, and
ventricular ﬁlling to help determine the most appropriate
therapy. Occasionally acute hemodynamic deterioration
from any case may result in ventricular tachycardia
or ﬁbrillation. Patients will need electrical deﬁbrillation
of the heart and sometimes emergency reinstitution of
CPB if hemodynamic instability continues post deﬁbril-
lation. Postbypass Hypertension
Because it is common to turn off inhalational agents
before separating from CPB, light anesthesia often is a
contributing cause for postbypass hypertension. If inadequate anesthesia is suspected, inhalational agents for the
short term can be administered after hemodynamic stability is achieved after separation. Additional narcotics or
benzodiazepines can be administered judiciously based on
whether the patient is a candidate for ‘‘fast-track’’ extubation in the postoperative cardiac surgery unit. Intravenous
bridging medication such as propofol or dexmetatomidine, which is usually used for heavy sedation during
transport from the operating room until extubation, might
be beneﬁcial as well if administered early. Although positive inotropes are useful in improving the
contractile state of the failing ventricle, sometimes they
can contribute to postbypass hypertension in patients with
reduced compliance of their vascular system. Systemic
vascular resistance and ventricular afterload increases
which could be detrimental to myocardial function in
a failing heart. Vasodilators can not only treat postbypass
hypertension, but these drugs can improve ventricular
function by optimizing loading conditions (57). Nitroglycerin is often administered during coronary bypass surgery
to prevent myocardial ischemia or arterial conduit vasospasm. Nitroglycerin can reduce afterload as well as
preload and treat hypertension especially at higher doses. Esmolol can be effective in controlling hypertension and
tachycardia in patients requiring inotropes with careful
titration. Lower serum levels of β receptor blockers reduce
heart rate without having signiﬁcant negative inotropic
effects.

Other classes of vasodilating drugs such as calcium channel blockers (e.g., nicardipine), dopaminergic
agonists (e.g., fenoldepam) and naturetic peptides (e.g.,
nesiritide) may be used at various institutions to treat
hypertension (58–60). Occasionally, in refractory cases,
sodium nitroprusside may still be used and remains extremely effective in managing these more difﬁcult cases of
postbypass hypertension.

628
V. Clinical Applications
Hypoxemia
Hypoxemia can be a serious problem in the immediate
postbypass period if not quickly recognized and treated. A frequent etiology is atelectasis, which can be largely
corrected by vigorous lung expansion although the addition of PEEP is occasionally required. Bronchospasm
may be due to preexisting pulmonary disease or secondary to protamine administration. It is often recognized
by high peak inspiratory pressures, poor lung deﬂation,
and a shallow slope on the expiratory phase of the
capnogram. Clinically signiﬁcant bronchospasm is best
treated with aerosolized β2-adrenergic agonists, volatile
anesthetic agents if ventricular function is satisfactory,
methylxanthines, or intravenous epinephrine or isoproterenol. Right-to-left intracardiac shunt, which may occur
with congenital heart disease or in patients with a patent
foramen ovale and elevated right atrial pressure, may
require mechanical correction. Early intraoperative diagnosis is made possible by TEE. Low cardiac output may
be associated with hypoxemia, especially when accompanied by right-to-left shunting, high oxygen consumption,
and/or low oxygen delivery (anemia). Sodium nitroprusside and milrinone increase intrapulmonary shunting due
to inhibition of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema is usually secondary to
allergic reactions to drugs or blood products. Pneumothorax, hemothorax, or hydrothorax is usually evident as distended pleurae are visible in the surgical ﬁeld. Many other
causes of signiﬁcant hypoxemia after CPB are not speciﬁc
to cardiac surgery including inadequate ventilator settings, circuit disconnect, endobronchial intubation, kinking, or obstruction of the endotracheal tube with a mucus
plug or clot from bleeding during CPB. Occasionally diagnostic or therapeutic bronchoscopy is required. Arterial
blood gas should be checked soon after the termination of
CPB to assess the adequacy of ventilation and oxygenation. SEPARATION FROM
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS:
CONTROVERSIAL ISSUES
Calcium Administration
Routine administration of calcium salts at the end of CPB
is not beneﬁcial and may be harmful. Exceptions include
patients with evidence of hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia. The incidence of hypocalcemia during CPB is relatively
high, but ionized Ca2+ usually approaches normal values
immediately before termination of bypass (9). Moreover,
considerable evidence suggests that elevated intracellular
Ca2+ is correlated with increased cell death and injury
during ischemia and reperfusion, as occurs frequently
during cardiac surgery (40). One study suggests that
calcium chloride administration, during emergence from

of calcium salts at the conclusion of bypass should
be guided by determination of ionized Ca2+ levels;
signiﬁcant increases in ventricular function are produced
experimentally by Ca2+ administration in the presence
of hypocalcemia (61). Calcium salts should not be
routinely administered to patients with good ventricular
function in the absence of hypocalcemia or hyperkalemia
because of the potential detrimental effects of iatrogenic
hypercalcemia; whether this is true in cases of impaired
ventricular function remains to be determined. Use of Inotropes
Although these drugs are absolutely necessary to separate
from bypass in many patients, the routine use of these
drugs in all patients may be detrimental. Concern exists
that inotropic stimulation of the myocardium may have
deleterious effects because of increased energy consumption (62). This may be particularly relevant after cardiac
surgery with ischemic cardiac arrest, especially in the presence of residual myocardial ischemia caused by disproportionate increases in myocardial oxygen consumption

30. Termination of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
629
relative to supply (63). Animal data suggest that catecholamines should be avoided in the reperfusion period
immediately after release of the aortic cross-clamp to
facilitate metabolic recovery of the myocardium (64). Exogenous positive inotropic agents may also potentiate
damage because of the already high endogenous catecholamine levels during cardiac surgery (65). Inotropic
agents are clearly useful in discontinuing CPB and may
even expedite the recovery of stunned myocardium (66). Given their potential to increase myocardial damage,
however, their use should probably be delayed until the
heart has had a chance to recover from the ischemia immediately after aortic cross-clamp release. Animal data
suggest that in the presence of ventricular dysfunction,
the potentially deleterious effects of inotropic stimulation
on oxygen consumption may be reduced by afterloadreducing agents (67). KEY POINTS
■Systematic preparation for separation from CPB is
critical. ●Metabolic data, anesthesia/oxygenation/ventilation,
hemodynamic monitors, heart rate and rhythm,
organ function assessment, cardiac support. ■Large-scale studies include age, emergency surgery,
female gender, preoperative ventricular function, left
main coronary disease, and reoperation. ●There is a biphasic postoperative course for ventricular function: early (1 to 2 hours) improvement
relative to the end of CPB, nadir of ventricular
function 4 to 6 hours after CPB, and improvement
over next 12 to 18 hours. ■Support for ventricular function after CPB includes optimizing patient physiologic status; preparing before initiating weaning process; anticipation
of requirements; pharmacologic support with positive inotropic drugs (e.g., catecholamines, PDE III
inhibitors, calcium, cardiac glycosides); vasoconstrictors (e.g., phenylephrine, norepinephrine); vasodilators (e.g., nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, PDE III
inhibitors, prostaglandin E1, nitric oxide); and mechanical support with IABP or VAD. ■Causes for right ventricular failure include right
coronary insufﬁciency, poor right ventricular (RV)
protection, and pulmonary hypertension. ●Principle ﬁndings regarding right ventricular failure include elevated PAP, high CVP, decreased
arterial pressure, decreased cardiac output, RV
distension, and high RV wall tension. ■Treatment for right ventricular failure include elevation of perfusion pressure [LA infusion of vasoconstrictors] and pulmonary artery vasodilation (nitric
oxide, rostaglandin E1, nitrovasodilators, PDE III
inhibitors).

■Problem situations during weaning include vasodilation and hypotension (e.g., increased with long duration of rewarming and treatment with α-adrenergic
agonists); vasoconstriction and hypertension (e.g.,
inadequate rewarming, decreased cardiac output,
treatment with vasodilators); acute hemodynamic
deterioration (e.g., utility of TEE); and hypoxemia
(e.g., nitroprusside, intracardiac shunt, atelectasis,
bronchospasm, which may be produced by protamine and treated with β-2 agonists [inhaled or i.v.],
inhaled anesthetic agents [if ventricular function is

◗ECMO for Respiratory Support in Adults
Scott K. Aberegg, Stephen Kirkby, and Mark Crowley
In the 1960s, enthusiasm for the use of mechanical
devices to support failing organs gained momentum
with the introduction of renal dialysis. In 1967 Ashbaugh et al. described the adult respiratory distress
syndrome (ARDS) (1), and just 6 years later, Hill et al. reported the successful use of the Bramson membrane
lung for the prolonged treatment of an adult with
ARDS (2). The initial enthusiasm created by this report was dashed in 1979 with the publication of an
National Institutes of Health (NIH)-sponsored randomized controlled trial (RCT) of extracorporeal membrane
oxygenation (ECMO) which failed to show a mortality
beneﬁt in adult patients with severe ARDS (3). Despite this discouraging result, numerous groups persisted
and subsequently established the efﬁcacy of ECMO in
neonatal and pediatric populations where it is now an
accepted treatment for severe respiratory failure (4,5). Encouraging results in adults continue to be reported,
and a recently completed trial in the United Kingdom promises to shed new light on the efﬁcacy of
ECMO in adults with respiratory failure using modern techniques (6–9). This chapter describes the current
state of knowledge of ECMO for respiratory support in
adults. RATIONALE FOR THE USE
OF EXTRACORPOREAL MEMBRANE
OXYGENATION FOR RESPIRATORY
SUPPORT IN ADULTS
The mortality associated with ARDS appears to have declined since the ﬁrst ECMO trial (3), probably because
of improved supportive care (10–13), lung protective
ventilation strategies (14–16), improved weaning techniques (17–19), and other factors (14,20–28). Although
they have not been proved to improve mortality, therapies such as inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) (29–31), prone
positioning (32–35), and high frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) (36–40) are now being used to improve gas
exchange in severe ARDS. Nonetheless, mortality remains
unacceptably high, especially in patients with the most
severe lung injury (14,23–25). Because of this, ECMO
continues to be used in some centers as a rescue therapy for patients with severe ARDS (and other selected
conditions) who are failing to improve or are worsening despite aggressive treatment with other available
therapies.

Current approaches to the use of ECMO in adult
respiratory failure are predicated on the fact that gas
exchange sometimes cannot be supported adequately
without the use of ventilator settings that are themselves known to cause, exacerbate, and perpetuate lung
injury (41). Such ventilator parameters include high tidal
volumes and inspiratory pressures (42–47), high fractions
of inspired oxygen (FIO2) (48,49), and high respiratory
frequencies (50–53). Unfortunately, when lung injury is
severe, such ventilator settings are often necessary to
support adequate gas exchange. It is postulated that
use of ECMO to support gas exchange in severely ill
patients allows clinicians to avoid injurious respiratory
support, thereby allowing the lung to heal and recovery
to take place (54–58). In addition, venoarterial ECMO
can support circulatory failure that is sometimes coincident with lung disease. A key question is whether
these purported beneﬁts of ECMO are sufﬁcient to outweigh the known risks and complications of ECMO
itself. In the next section, we review the available evidence on the use of ECMO for respiratory support in
adults. EVIDENCE FOR THE USE
OF EXTRACORPOREAL MEMBRANE
OXYGENATION FOR RESPIRATORY
SUPPORT IN ADULTS
The evidence for ECMO in adults can be divided loosely
into three categories: (a) RCTs, (b) prospective and
retrospective series, (c) case reports and other small
series. 632

31. ECMO for Respiratory Support in Adults
633
Randomized Controlled Trials
of Extracorporeal Membrane
Oxygenation for Respiratory Support
in Adults
In 1979, Zapol et al. reported the results of a randomized,
controlled, multicenter trial of ECMO (3). In this trial,
patients with respiratory failure were randomized to
receive venoarterial ECMO in addition to conventional
care versus conventional care alone if they had a PaO2 of
less than 50 mm Hg on an FIO2 of 1.0 for 2 hours with at
least 5 cm H2O of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP);
or a PaO2 less than 50 for 12 hours on an FIO2 greater than
0.6, PEEP 5, and a transpulmonary shunt fraction (Qs/Qt)
greater than 30%. Patients were excluded if the duration
of the pulmonary insult was longer than 21 days, age was
greater than 65 years or less than 12 years, pulmonary
capillary wedge pressure was greater than 25 mm Hg, or if
they had irreversible central nervous system (CNS) injury,
chronic pulmonary disease, rapidly fatal malignancy,
chronic heart, liver or renal disease, or severe body
burns (59). Importantly, patients randomized to ECMO
continued to receive contemporaneous therapy which at
that time included ventilation with tidal volumes and
inspiratory pressures that are high by modern standards. Ninety patients were enrolled between 1975 and 1977. Patients in both groups were relatively well matched
in important baseline characteristics. The results were
disappointing: mortality in both the ECMO and the control
groups exceeded 90% with no signiﬁcant beneﬁt of ECMO
detected. These results were interpreted as demonstrating
that ECMO is not useful in the treatment of ARDS, a
conclusion that has largely persisted to this day. However,
several limitations of this trial may limit the ability
to generalize these results into current practice. These
characteristics are summarized in Table 1. In spite of these disappointing results, numerous
groups continued to use and investigate EMCO. Reports
from Italy in the mid-1980s described the successful combination of extracorporeal CO2 removal [(ECCO2R)—used
throughout this chapter synonymously with ECMO in
spite of technical differences] and pressure controlled inverse ratio ventilation (PCIRV) in the treatment of severe
ARDS (55,60). Using entry criteria similar to those of Zapol
et al., Gattinoni et al. reported survival rates of 63% and
49% in nonrandomized patients who received ECMO after
failure to improve on PCIRV (55,60).

This represented a
signiﬁcant improvement over historical mortality in the
Zapol trial, but the design of the Italian studies did not
preclude the possibility that this improvement was due
to factors other than ECMO and PCIRV, such as patient
selection, temporal trends in ARDS mortality, or advances
in the care of patients with respiratory failure. To address these concerns, Morris et al. attempted
to duplicate the Italian results in the second RCT

of Extracorporeal Membrane
Oxygenation for Respiratory Support
in Adults
Numerous uncontrolled observational studies of ECMO
use have been reported. A selection of series reporting
survival for ten or more patients is listed in Table 3. (Data
from the Zapol and Morris RCTs are included for comparison). Most of these studies used criteria to establish
the need for ECMO that were similar to those used in the
Zapol trial (3) as outlined previously.

Criteria of varying
stringency were used to exclude patients from receiving
ECMO. In most series, these were similar to the Zapol trial
and were intended to prevent use of ECMO in patients
who had little chance of survival because of irreversible
underlying disease or moribund state. Bleeding diathesis
was also used as an exclusion criterion in many of the
series. ECMO survival in these 17 observational series and
the two RCTs listed in Table 3 ranges from 10% (3) to
81% (65). Combined, these series include data on 840
adult patients who received ECMO for respiratory support
over the last 30 years. Of these 840 patients, 50% survived
(95% CI 47%–53%). This ﬁgure is similar to the 53%
survival (95% CI 50%–56%) among 972 patients reported
to the extracorporeal life support(ECLS) registry as of
June 2004 (there is doubtless overlap of patients between
the reported series and the ECLS registry) (76). These case series are useful to evaluate ECMO inclusion
and exclusion criteria that are being used by various
centers. As the technology has matured and experience
with ECMO has increased, some centers have relaxed
exclusion criteria. The University of Michigan team
attributes their plateau in ECMO survival during the last
10 years to the gradual relaxation of exclusion criteria,
such that they now do not exclude patients older than
50 or those with sepsis or who have been ventilated for
greater than 5 days (73). The uncontrolled data from these series suggest that
a survival rate of approximately 50% can be expected in
highly selected patients with severe ARDS who are treated
with ECMO using modern techniques in experienced centers (77–80). This is certainly higher than the 9% survival
in the Zapol trial, a fact often mentioned prominently by
the authors. However, extreme caution is warranted in
data interpretations that use the Zapol mortality rate as
an implicit historical control. As noted previously, that
rate may have been excessive (21), and mortality rates
in subsequent series may reﬂect regression to the mean
or temporal trends in ARDS mortality and advances in
supportive care rather than a lower mortality due to the
use of ECMO (61,81).

Indeed, many of the large series
in Table 3 selected patients based on the Zapol criteria, but progressed to ECMO only if other interventions
such as changes in ventilator mode, iNO, prone positioning, and permissive hypercapnia failed to result in
improvement or stabilization (54,60,66,68). In these trials, patients meeting Zapol entry criteria but managed
without ECMO had survival rates from 50% to 94%, generally higher than patients who went on to receive ECMO,
and certainly much higher than the 9% survival in the
Zapol trial (3,54,60,66,68). In addition, in series in which
they are reported, average APACHE II scores are less
than 20, predicting a 70% survival rate (54,68). These
data appear to undermine the validity of the frequently
invoked historical control survival rate of 9% and conclusions based on comparisons with this rate are likely to be
misleading.

V. Clinical Applications
It is notable that in the series reported by Linden
et al. oxygen saturations as low as 70% were permitted
during initiation of venovenous ECMO with no apparent
adverse consequences (70,72). This suggests the intriguing
possibility that normalization of gas exchange with ECMO
is not necessary or responsible for its beneﬁt, and that
rather it is the prevention of iatrogenic lung injury
from mechanical ventilation that is essential. PaO2 levels
much lower than 50 can be well tolerated in young
individuals (82). It remains to be seen whether a strategy
of ‘‘permissive hypoxemia’’ with or without ECMO may be
of beneﬁt in severe ARDS (83). An additional caveat regarding uncontrolled series
warrants mention. Publication bias is a concern if centers
with favorable ECMO survival rates are more likely
to report their experience than those with unfavorable
survival rates. If this occurs over a sufﬁcient period of
time, and centers with negative experiences abandon
ECMO, only centers with positive experiences will remain
(survivorship bias). Measured at any point in time, their
ECMO performance is likely to be an overestimate of
true performance. These limitations notwithstanding, the
uncontrolled series in Table 3 demonstrate that with
modern techniques in experienced centers, acceptable
survival rates can be achieved using ECMO in properly
selected patients with very severe ARDS. Case Reports of Extracorporeal
Membrane Oxygenation for Respiratory
Support in Adults
Notwithstanding the limitations of the available evidence
for ECMO, it is clear that there are indeed selected patients
in whom ECMO is a patient’s only hope for survival and
case reports often demonstrate this dramatically. A recent
report described a patient with an overdose of cardiotoxic
drugs in whom total cardiac standstill occurred for 3 hours
during ECMO treatment (84). In such extreme cases,
mortality would have been certain without ECMO. Case reports are also useful to demonstrate the range
of conditions in which ECMO has been used successfully. Table 4 lists selected disease processes that have been
successfully treated with ECMO. Apart from ARDS, a
pattern emerges of diseases which are fulminant but either
self-limited or responsive to speciﬁc treatment. Examples
include status asthmaticus, massive pulmonary embolism,
pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (treated with whole lung
lavage during ECMO), and reperfusion lung injury after
transplantation.

For these diseases, support of respiratory
failure with ECMO can ‘‘buy time’’ for speciﬁc treatment
to reverse the underlying condition while minimizing
iatrogenic lung injury. Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome is an example
of the type of disease process that may respond favorably to ECMO. At the University of New Mexico Health

with severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome since

disease enter a fulminant phase characterized by rapid
progression of pulmonary inﬁltrates, worsening gas exchange, and profound cardiogenic shock with evidence of
tissue hypoxia. These patients are very difﬁcult to support
adequately with conventional therapy, and early in the epidemic patients with such characteristics had a uniformly
fatal outcome. However, it was noted that patients who
did not enter this phase often recovered without incident. Moreover, autopsy ﬁndings in patients who succumbed
were notable for the absence of irreversible structural
changes in the heart and lungs. These observations led
to the hypothesis that if patients with a fulminant course

could be supported through this phase of the illness, they
may recover similar to patients who did not decompensate. To date, more than 30 patients have been supported
with ECMO at this center, and approximately half have
survived (Mark Crowley, personal communication, 2006). Case reports suffer from the same limitations as
observational cohort studies, and caution is warranted
in extrapolating the successful results of ECMO in
extraordinary cases to routine care. Publication bias is
of particular concern in case reports, as unsuccessful
attempts at using ECMO in the diseases in Table 4
(or others) are less likely to be reported. Nonetheless,
these reports as well as the University of Michigan series
demonstrate the breadth of diseases in which ECMO has
been used successfully (73). Patient Selection: Indications
and Contraindications
Most centers reporting large series of patients treated with
ECMO use selection criteria for ECMO that are modiﬁed
from the entry criteria of the Zapol study (Table 3). In
general, these include a PaO2 less than 50 mm Hg for
at least 2 hours in spite of a high FIO2 and the use of
PEEP. Many centers have added additional requirements
relating to lung compliance, severity of lung injury, and
other cardiopulmonary parameters (Table 3). In addition,
a number of recently reported series have added the
requirement that patients remain profoundly hypoxemic
in spite of aggressive use of other supportive measures
such as those listed in Table 5 (54,66,68,70,72). These
series had high rates of utilization of prone positioning,
diuresis to dry weight (154), and iNO. In the series by
Ullrich et al., 89% of patients were ventilated in the
prone position, 100% were therapeutically dehydrated,
and 100% received iNO. The overall survival in this series
was 83%, perhaps reﬂecting the aggressiveness of this
group in all aspects of ARDS care. Other centers utilizing

ECMO should make diligent attempts to exhaust the
therapeutic options listed in Table 5 before progressing
to ECMO. Exclusion criteria for ECMO are variable between centers and have been evolving over the last 20 years (8,73). They are generally chosen to limit the application of
ECMO in patients who are moribund or who have an
underlying condition that is not compatible with intermediate or long-term survival. Patients with signiﬁcant
underlying comorbidities (such as hemorrhagic risk or
cerebrovascular disease) that are likely to predispose them
to complications from ECMO have also been excluded. Age greater than 50 years was formerly an exclusion criteria in some centers, but this has now been raised to
70 years of age or greater in at least two centers (68,73). In
their early experience, the University of Michigan group
found that duration of mechanical ventilation greater than
5 days before ECMO initiation was correlated with a poor
outcome and used this as an exclusion criteria (160). This limit was subsequently raised to 7 days and then
to 10 days, as their experience with the technique increased (7). Tables 3 and 6 list some proposed exclusion
criteria for ECMO. On the basis of current data, it is not possible to recommend a group of patients in whom ECMO should
be routinely used. Rather, ECMO should be considered
a ‘‘rescue therapy’’ for patients in whom adequate gas
exchange cannot be achieved with noninjurious ventilatory parameters (i.e., plateau pressure <35 cm H2O

who have failed to respond to other treatment modalities
which are supported by robust evidence, are less invasive
and costly, and carry fewer risks than ECMO. Patients
considered for ECMO should have failed these therapies
and continue to have marked gas exchange abnormalities associated with evidence of tissue hypoxia. Caution
must be exercised in using abnormal blood gas values
alone to justify progression to ECMO, as values of PaO2
and PaCO2 which are markedly deranged by conventional
standards may not necessarily be associated with adverse
consequences, especially in young otherwise healthy patients (82,83,161,162). Evidence of tissue hypoxia (e.g.,
elevated lactate concentrations or reduced SvO2 values)
may allow better identiﬁcation of patients in whom gas
exchange is not adequate to meet physiologic needs (83). Future trials and experience may allow identiﬁcation of
speciﬁc groups of patients in whom ECMO has the most
favorable risk and beneﬁt proﬁle. Technical Considerations
Initiation of a successful ECMO program requires a substantial commitment of time and resources as well as
close coordination between nurses, perfusionists, surgeons, ECMO specialists, the blood bank, and other
hospital services. A substantial learning curve should be
expected while the techniques are being reﬁned. Setup of
the ECMO circuit and operation procedures have been
described in detail elsewhere and are beyond the scope of
this chapter (8,41,56,73,163). Brieﬂy, vascular cannulation
allows the patient to be connected to the ECMO circuit
which in its most basic form consists of a membrane oxygenator, roller or centrifugal pump, and heat exchanger. Systemic anticoagulation with heparin is maintained for
the duration of bypass to prevent clotting of the membrane and the delivery of microemboli to the systemic
circulation. The route of cannulation depends on whether venovenous or venoarterial ECMO is required, on individual
patient characteristics, and on surgical preference. Venovenous ECMO is preferred for isolated respiratory failure as cannulation of the low pressure venous system
carries fewer risks, and can often be achieved percutaneously. However, if patients with respiratory failure also
have signiﬁcant reversible cardiac dysfunction (e.g., due
to hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, septic shock,
overdose, or acute right heart dysfunction from pulmonary
embolism), venoarterial ECMO may be necessary to support the circulation.

Cannulation for venovenous ECMO can be achieved
using either the right internal jugular vein or femoral
vein for venous drainage and the opposite vessel for venous return (78). The relative merits of jugulofemoral
versus femorojugular are debated (78,164). If necessary,
femoral–femoral cannulation can be used, but this
approach results in reduced ﬂow due to the increased
resistance of the longer return catheter, which must be
advanced to the right atrium. Venous drainage for venoarterial ECMO is performed as with venovenous ECMO. The
main options for arterial cannulation are use of a femoral
artery or the right internal carotid artery. Femoral arterial cannulation carries the risk of distal limb ischemia,
sometimes necessitating placement of a distally directed
catheter to perfuse the limb (165–168). In addition, the
catheter must be advanced proximally to the level of the
aortic arch to assure that oxygenated blood is delivered to
the coronary and cerebral circulations. Use of the carotid
artery carries a small risk of ispilateral compromise of
cerebral perfusion, but in the absence of signiﬁcant cerebrovascular disease, collateral ﬂow is usually adequate
to prevent this (169). The artery is ligated distally and
either sacriﬁced or repaired at decannulation, although
the latter approach carries the risk of distal thromboembolism when the ligated vessel is reanastamosed. Given
these considerations, vascular catheters for infusion and
hemodynamic monitoring are preferably placed in the left
internal jugular and subclavian sites if ECMO is being
considered. The rate of venous drainage is determined by both
the caliber and length of the cannulae and by gravity. An increase in the oxygenation of drainage blood may be
due to recirculation or cannula malpositioning. It may be
necessary to raise the bed on blocks to allow for more
effective gravity drainage of blood (Fig. 1). ECMO may place signiﬁcant demands on the blood
bank. Patients are transfused to and maintained at a
normal hemoglobin concentration to enhance efﬁciency
of the membrane oxygenator and to improve oxygen

carrying capacity of the blood, thereby reducing ﬂow
requirements. Bleeding is the most frequent patientrelated complication of ECMO, and daily transfusions
are often required to maintain the hematocrit at 40%. Thrombocytopenia is common because of sepsis and
platelet activation from contact with synthetic surfaces
and platelets must be maintained near 100,000 to prevent
bleeding complications. An aggressive approach to bleeding during ECMO,
including surgery if necessary, is warranted (56,72,170). The intensity of anticoagulation can be reduced during the
procedure to minimize bleeding, albeit with a temporary
increase in the risk of circuit thrombosis. In case
of such an occurrence, a ‘‘spare’’ circuit should be
available during the procedure. The patient can be placed
back on prespeciﬁed ‘‘back-up’’ conventional ventilator
settings while the problem is corrected or the circuit is
changed. ECMO has been used in a number of patients
with ARDS associated with trauma, with the use of
heparin-bonded circuitry and by reducing or forgoing
systemic anticoagulation altogether (80,119–125). One
report describes the development of heparin-induced
thrombocytopenia in a patient on ECMO who was
successfully maintained on argatroban (79). While the patient is on bypass, current best practice
is to institute ‘‘lung rest’’ while most gas exchange is
accomplished by the ECMO circuit. This practice is based
on the known detrimental effects of high tidal volumes
and inspiratory pressures, oxygen toxicity, and respiratory
frequency in patients with ARDS. Once stable bypass is
established, the tidal volume is reduced to 4–6 ml/kg
predicted ideal body weight, or further if necessary to
limit plateau pressures to less than 30 cm H2O. FIO2
is reduced as low as possible, with a minimum goal of
FIO2 less than 50%. Respiratory frequency is decreased
to 5–10 breaths per minute and PEEP is set at 10 cm
H2O to reduce the potential for harm from repeated
opening and closing of alveolar units that are near the
closing threshold. Ventilation at low frequencies and tidal
volumes is adequate in spite of markedly increased dead
space fraction. The efﬁciency of the ECMO circuit in
removing carbon dioxide is such that CO2 must often
be added to the sweep gas to prevent severe alkalosis.

Reductions in mean airway pressure that result from
the above changes may improve venous return and
cardiac output during venovenous ECMO which can
support oxygenation even with near absence of native
lung function. The beneﬁts of preventing oversedation in critically ill
patients are well established, and probably apply to ECMO
patients as well (11). While deep sedation and muscle
paralysis were historically used during bypass, some
centers have markedly reduced sedation administered
during ECMO, and allow patients to remain awake,
interact with family members, and watch television
during bypass (72,153). This approach requires increased
nursing supervision, and may not be feasible with
venoarterial ECMO where the consequences of catheter
malposition and dislodgement are greater. Increased
sedation and muscle paralysis may also be required
if patient oxygen consumption is increased by activity
or agitation as the ﬂow capacity of the ECMO circuit
can be exceeded at high levels of oxygen consumption. Antipyretics are given for the same reason, but may not
be necessary as the heat exchanger partially regulates
body temperature. Reduction in sedation to the minimum
required for patient comfort and safety is a reasonable
approach. Some centers routinely perform tracheostomy before
or after stable bypass is established in anticipation of
greater comfort during an anticipated prolonged course
of critical illness and mechanical ventilation (72). Substantial beneﬁts of early tracheostomy (including reduced
mortality) have been recently reported in non-ECMO patients expected to require mechanical ventilation for more
than 14 days (10). This strategy also allows for reduction
in sedation, which may be responsible for some of the
beneﬁcial effects that have been observed. Strong consideration should be given to early bedside percutaneous
tracheostomy in severely ill patients being treated with
ECMO. Any complication related to critical illness can occur
during ECMO (Table 7). In addition, complications related
to the ECMO circuit itself are common. The most frequent
mechanical complications are oxygenator failure, cannulae and tubing problems, and circuit thrombosis (73,76). The most common patient-related complication is bleeding from cannulation sites, surgical sites, and the gastrointestinal tract (73,76). While cardiovascular complications
are frequently encountered with ECMO, it is difﬁcult to
separate their causes from underlying critical illness. The
most feared complications are neurologic, with cerebral
infarction, and brain death being the most common. The
latter probably results from prolonged and unrecognized
cerebral hypoperfusion or hypoxia during ECMO.

With
the exception of neurologic catastrophe, most complications can be treated, and rarely is discontinuation of
ECMO required. Weaning and discontinuation of ECMO are considered
when there is evidence of substantial improvement in the
underlying disease process and cardiopulmonary function
based on radiographs, laboratory parameters, hemodynamic parameters, and gas exchange. While monitoring
these parameters, ﬂow through the circuit can gradually be
reduced. When a reduction in ﬂow of 75% can be achieved
without changes in cardiorespiratory status, membrane
gas ﬂow can be stopped in the case of venovenous ECMO,
or the membrane lung can be bypassed by a temporary
bridge in the circuit in the case of venoarterial ECMO. If
the patient tolerates these challenges for 12 hours with

regular intervals by reducing sedation and muscle paralysis (if used) and observing for motor function and signs
of a global or focal neurologic deﬁcit (72). If evidence of
severe, irreversible compromise of neurologic function is
conﬁrmed, ECMO should be discontinued. Some centers
