and terminate ECMO when this occurs. Absent evidence
of irreversibility of the underlying disease or a supervening catastrophe, the decision to terminate ECMO for
failure to improve must be made on an individual basis. It is noteworthy that some patients have survived
after receiving ECMO for up to 30–50 days (7,70); however, such extraordinary cases should not discourage
repeated assessments of individual patients and consideration of termination of ECMO if recovery is deemed
unlikely. CONCLUSIONS
ECMO can be used to support gas exchange and circulatory
function in adult patients with severe respiratory failure
that is refractory to conventional therapy. Two RCTs of
ECMO in adults failed to demonstrate a mortality beneﬁt
from ECMO in the populations studied. These trials had
limited statistical power and may not accurately reﬂect the
potential beneﬁts of ECMO as currently practiced. Numerous observational studies have shown acceptable survival
and complication rates for appropriately selected patients
treated in experienced centers.

However, the potential for
bias in these studies and lack of suitable control groups
make these studiesinconclusive and preclude a recommendation for routine use. On the basis of available evidence,
ECMO can be recommended only as a rescue therapy in
select patients with reversible underlying illness who deteriorate despite maximal conventional therapy at or near
centers with ECMO experience. An adequately powered
and carefully designed and conducted RCT of ECMO using modern techniques and contemporary supportive care
is needed to clarify the optimal role of ECMO in the care
of adult patients with severe respiratory compromise. KEY POINTS
■ECMO as a therapy for pulmonary or cardiopulmonary failure has been clinically feasible for
30–35 years. ●Early randomized trials failed to document improved mortality from adult respiratory failure
syndrome
●Subsequent case series and isolated case reports
document that clinically relevant survival rates
may be achieved by using ECMO
■Two principle types of ECMO are venovenous and
venoarterial. ●Venovenous ECMO is useful for isolated pulmonary failure, but venoarterial ECMO is required
when combined cardiac and pulmonary failure occurs
●Venovenous ECMO returns oxygenated venous
drainage into the patients venous system, while
venoarterial is analogous to cardiopulmonary bypass with venous drainage to the ECMO apparatus
and return of arterialized blood into the patients
arterial circulation
■Selection criteria for ECMO use should include
reasonable anticipation of intermediate or long-term
survival if the acute cardiopulmonary insult can be
successfully managed. ■Complications from ECMO are numerous and include issues related speciﬁcally to the ECMO device,

◗Perfusion for Thoracic Aortic Surgery
Joseph Huh, Scott A. LeMaire, John Bozinovski, and Joseph S. Coselli
The last decade has brought many changes in the
technique and practice of perfusion for thoracic aortic
surgery. The central goal of perfusion is to enable aortic
repair while limiting ischemic injury, especially to the
central nervous system. Different perfusion strategies are
needed to achieve this goal, depending upon the portion
of the aorta that is being treated. The ascending aortic
segment begins at the aortic valve annulus and ends
just proximal to the origin of the innominate artery. The
transverse aortic arch is the segment from which the three
brachiocephalic branches arise. Perfusion techniques for
the ascending aorta and transverse aortic arch often
overlap; therefore, they are discussed together in the
following section covering proximal aortic operations. The
subsequent section covers operations involving the distal,
or descending thoracic/thoracoabdominal aortic segment,
which extends from just beyond the left subclavian artery
to the aortoiliac bifurcation. Because thoracic aortic
aneurysms and dissection often do not respect these
boundaries, perfusion and surgical techniques must be
able to cross them, as well. PROXIMAL AORTIC OPERATIONS
Selection of Technique
Proximal aortic operations are approached most commonly by median sternotomy. We use cardiopulmonary
bypass (CPB) for nonemergent operations limited to the
ascending aortic segment. In cases of aneurysm rupture or
acute dissection, however, we routinely use hypothermic
circulatory arrest (HCA) with selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP). Although acute proximal aortic
dissection can be repaired without HCA, this technique
eliminates the need for aortic clamping. The ‘‘open’’ distal
anastomosis technique—originally advocated by Cooley
and Livesay in 1981 (1)—avoids clamp injury of the fragile
dissecting membrane, allows identiﬁcation of tears within
the transverse arch, and facilitates assessment of aortic
arch diameter. Circulatory arrest is also used in graft
replacement of the transverse aortic arch. Cardiopulmonary Bypass without
Circulatory Arrest
Disease that is limited to the aortic root or ascending
aorta is approached with CPB. The arterial cannula can
be placed in the ascending aorta or transverse aortic
arch with the aortic cross-clamp applied proximal to
the innominate artery. Alternatively, the cannula can be
placed in the femoral artery, which is particularly useful
in emergency situations with hemodynamically unstable
patients.

However, because femoral cannulation creates
retrograde ﬂow in the abdominal and thoracic aorta, it is
a potential cause of embolic stroke in patients with heavy
atherosclerotic burden (2). The size of the arterial cannula is chosen to minimize
the pressure gradient across the cannula at the patient’s
calculated ﬂow rate, which is based on a standard index
of 2.2 to 2.4 L/min/m2 for adults at normothermic
temperatures. The cannula should be large enough to
provide the calculated ﬂow rate with a gradient of less
than 100 mm Hg. After this cannula is inserted into the
aorta, it is connected to the circuit tubing during a forward
pump roll to facilitate air removal at the connection. If
a femoral arterial cannula is used, it is initially attached
to the tubing and then directly inserted into the artery
during a forward pump roll. After the cannula is placed,
reverse ﬂow is brieﬂy allowed to ensure unimpeded return. Poor arterial return into the cannula during this maneuver
may indicate proximal arterial obstruction, which requires
repositioning of the cannula or changing to an alternative
cannulation site. Venous cannulation is accomplished using a right atrial
dual-stage cannula, bicaval cannulae, or a long femoral venous cannula. Like femoral arterial cannulation, femoral
venous cannulation is routinely used in hemodynamically unstable patients who require pump support before
sternotomy and is particularly useful in patients who
are at risk of aortic injury during sternotomy. This includes patients undergoing reoperation and those with
large ascending aortic aneurysms abutting the sternum. In these situations, the femoral cannula is placed before
sternotomy is performed. 647

648
V. Clinical Applications
A left ventricular sump cannula is inserted through
a purse-string suture placed at the junction of the
right superior pulmonary vein and the left atrium. The
sump minimizes preload, prevents ventricular distention,
reduces myocardial rewarming, prevents ejection of air,
and facilitates exposure of the aortic valve. An in-line
pressure relief valve is located between the sump cannula
and a roller pump, which returns the vented blood to
the bypass circuit through the cardiotomy reservoir. The
degree of sump suction is constantly regulated, because
too little suction allows ventricular distension, and too
much can cause ventricular collapse and injury. Myocardial protection is achieved using systemic hypothermia and a combination of antegrade and retrograde
cardioplegia, which facilitates adequate delivery of cardioplegia to all areas of the heart. We use a one-pass circuit to
deliver 4◦C blood-crystalloid (4:1) cardioplegia. The retrograde cardioplegia cannula is inserted into the coronary
sinus after venous cannulation, which prevents dislodgement of the coronary sinus cannula during positioning of
the venous cannula in the inferior vena cava. Antegrade
cardioplegia is delivered through either an aortic cannula
placed proximal to the aortic cross-clamp or directly into
each of the coronary ostia after opening the aorta. Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest
and Antegrade Cerebral Perfusion
Improvements in aortic arch surgery outcomes have been
partly attributed to better cerebral protection techniques. DeBakey et al. (3) ﬁrst successfully replaced the aortic
arch in 1957 using direct perfusion of the brachiocephalic
branches. The use of HCA by Griepp et al., in 1975 was a
major advance in cerebral protection (4). Soon thereafter,
Crawford and Saleh (5) adopted this technique and
reported its efﬁcacy in reducing morbidity and mortality. HCA also provides a bloodless operative ﬁeld uncluttered by brachiocephalic clamps, cannulae, and tourniquets. However, some investigators have reported that
HCA is neither completely safe nor satisfactory in abating
cerebral metabolic demands. Results of separate canine
studies by Nojima et al. (6) and Mezrow et al. (7) indicate that signiﬁcant cerebral metabolic activity occurs
at the temperatures at which HCA is routinely initiated;
this activity promotes cerebral ischemia and the accumulation of metabolic wastes (8,9). The protective limits of
HCA were further deﬁned in 1993 by Svensson et al.(10),
who reported Crawford’s experience with 656 patients
who underwent HCA during proximal aortic surgery.

The
overall rates of transient stroke, permanent stroke, and
early mortality were low, but the incidence of perioperative neurologic complications rose sharply when the
HCA time exceeded 40 minutes, and mortality increased
dramatically when HCA time exceeded 65 minutes. During the 1990s, retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP)
became popular as a means of safely extending HCA times. It was ﬁrst described in 1980 by Mills and Ochsner (11) as
a method of treating massive air embolism during CPB. However, the concept of using RCP as an adjunct to HCA
did not arise until Ueda et al. introduced RCP for neuroprotection during aortic arch surgery in 1990 (12,13). The theoretical beneﬁts of adding RCP to HCA include
more homogeneous cerebral cooling; washout of air
bubbles, embolic debris, and metabolic waste products;
prevention of cerebral blood cell microaggregation; and
delivery of oxygen and nutritional substrates to brain
tissue (14,15). Despite these potential advantages, experimental and
clinical data do not consistently support the efﬁcacy of
RCP for cerebral protection (16–21). There are questions
as to whether RCP ﬂow is adequate to meet the metabolic
demands of the brain or even whether RCP provides ﬂow
through the brain microvasculature. We used RCP during
HCA for many years; however, as evidence has mounted
for the beneﬁts of ACP, we have come to use profound
hypothermia with selective ACP almost exclusively when
repairing acute ascending aortic dissections or aortic arch
aneurysms. ACP is an older technique than RCP, dating back to
the early work of DeBakey et al. (3). Enthusiasm for
arch replacement with ACP as a stand-alone cerebral
protection strategy disappeared because of this approach’s
high mortality and the successful clinical introduction
of HCA. Frist et al.(22) revisited the concept in 1986,
using a simpliﬁed CPB circuit, moderate hypothermia,
and selective antegrade perfusion of the innominate or
left carotid artery. Later, using ACP as an adjunct to HCA
was championed by Bachet et al. (23) and Kazui et al. (24);
both groups described delivering cold cerebral perfusion
through cannulas placed into both the innominate and
left carotid arteries. Kazui (25) recently reported excellent
clinical outcomes with this technique; the incidence
of permanent neurologic dysfunction was 2.4% in 330
patients undergoing aortic arch surgery. Similarly, Di
Eusanio et al.

(26) reported a multicenter study of ACP
as an adjunct to HCA in 588 aortic arch surgery patients,
and found a permanent neurologic event rate of 3.8% and
a mortality of 7.8%. Experimental evidence supporting the efﬁcacy of ACP
includes the work by Tanaka et al. (27) in a canine
model of bilateral carotid perfusion. The degree of cerebral ischemia at moderate hypothermia was assessed
using somatosensory evoked potentials, superior sagittal
sinus blood lactate level, and histopathologic examination. These indicators showed no evidence of cerebral ischemia
when the cerebral blood ﬂow was kept above 50% of
normalized baseline, or when the mean carotid blood
pressure was maintained above 30 mm Hg. The ability
of ACP to meet cerebral metabolic needs in humans was

649
recently evaluated in a prospective randomized study by
Harrington et al. (28). They found that adjunctive use of
ACP maintained pre-HCA jugular venous saturation and
cerebral oxygen extraction in patients undergoing aortic
surgery. There has been much debate about the technical aspects of HCA and ACP. Various cannulation sites for
inducing initial circulatory arrest, as well as cannulation sites and techniques for ACP, have been described
in the literature. Furthermore, there is controversy as
to the relative effectiveness of unilateral and bilateral
ACP. Olsson and Thelin (29) recently reported that unilateral ACP is associated with a higher risk of perioperative
stroke than is bilateral ACP. In contrast, a magnetic resonance (MR) perfusion imaging study by Ye et al. (30)
found that, in porcine models of unilateral and bilateral
ACP under HCA conditions, both ACP techniques provided uniform cerebral perfusion to both hemispheres. A
follow-up study using these porcine models found unilateral and bilateral ACP to be equally effective in meeting
the metabolic needs of both cerebral hemispheres at
moderate hypothermia, according to intracellular pH and
energy metabolites measured using MR spectroscopy (31). Karadeniz et al. (32) used transcranial Doppler ultrasonography to demonstrate that unilateral ACP through
the right axillary artery can provide adequate perfusion of both the right and left cerebral hemispheres in
patients undergoing HCA. Several other authors have
also reported favorable clinical outcomes with unilateral
ACP (33–36). Technique
Performing HCA safely requires the careful monitoring of
several temperatures throughout the procedure, including
the patient’s nasopharyngeal temperature and—in the
perfusion circuit—the temperatures of the arterial blood
at the oxygenator outlet, the venous blood about to enter
the venous reservoir, and the water for the heat exchanger
unit. Ten-channel electroencephalography (EEG) is used
to monitor brain wave activity; electrocerebral silence
indicates that adequate cerebral cooling has been achieved
and that circulatory arrest can be initiated. To enhance
cerebral protection during HCA, we add 25 g of mannitol
to the pump prime and administer an intravenous dose of
dexamethasone (100 mg) before initiating CPB, although
the supporting evidence for this practice is equivocal. Arterial inﬂow has been simpliﬁed by right axillary
perfusion, which is now our preferred perfusion method
for arch operations (Fig. 1A). The artery is approached
through a 4- to 6-cm incision made at the right deltopectoral groove.

After separating the ﬁbers of the pectoralis
major muscle, the underlying pectoralis minor is divided,
exposing the fat pad lying immediately posterior to the
muscle. The brachial plexus lies beneath the fat pad, so
care must be taken to avoid causing direct trauma or electrical injury to it during cautery. The axillary vein is usually
retracted inferiorly to expose the artery. A short segment
of the artery is then mobilized and encircled with a vessel
loop. After exposing the artery, the sternum is opened
and, once sternal and mediastinal hemostasis has been

The axillary artery is then clamped. An 8-mm polyester
graft is anastomosed to the axillary artery in end-to-side
manner using running 6-0 polypropylene suture. The graft
is then secured to the inﬂow, or arterial, arm of the CPB
circuit using a plastic band and heavy silk ligature. Alternatively, the axillary artery can be cannulated directly.
Comparing direct cannulation with graft conduit access
of the axillary artery, Svensson and Sabik (37,38) have
associated using a side graft with lower rates of stroke and
arterial and brachial plexus injury.
The femoral artery can serve as an alternative cannulation site in emergent cases. When femoral artery
cannulation is used in patients with aortic dissection, careful attention is required to assure cannulation of the true
lumen. Because the false lumen usually progresses down
the left iliac artery, cannulating the right femoral artery is
preferable. Poor backﬂow into the arterial cannula during
a brief reverse ﬂow test may indicate cannulation of the
false lumen; to prevent retrograde malperfusion, the cannula should be repositioned or placed in a different vessel
before bypass is initiated.
Venous cannulation is established through the right
atrium, both cavae, or the femoral vein, depending on
need and accessibility. CPB is initiated and the adequacy
of perfusion is assessed; this is particularly important

32. Perfusion for Thoracic Aortic Surgery
651
when the femoral artery has been cannulated in a patient
with aortic dissection. A retrograde cardioplegia catheter
is placed in the coronary sinus. A left ventricular sump
catheter is placed through the right superior pulmonary
vein. This is especially important in patients who are prone
to ventricular distention, such as those with aortic valve
regurgitation. Ventricular distention can also result from
ﬁbrillation caused by systemic hypothermia; to prevent
this complication, the sump is generally placed before
systemic cooling begins. Once systemic cooling has begun, each 10◦C decrease
in body temperature reduces the rate of oxygen consumption by approximately 50%. As the temperature
and metabolic rate decrease, pump ﬂows are reduced
to 1.6 to 1.8 L/min/m2. In addition, for every 10◦C
decrease in core temperature, there is a 20% to 25%
increase in blood viscosity (39,40). In the past—before the
use of hemodilution—hypothermia-induced hyperviscosity caused substantial morbidity (eg, stroke and visceral
infarction) and mortality. Currently, patients are routinely
hemodiluted to a hematocrit below 25% until the reconstruction is completed, at which time rewarming and
hemoconcentration are initiated. Although hemodilution
decreases oxygen-carrying capacity, overall oxygen delivery is improved because the decreased blood viscosity
enhances microcirculatory ﬂow. Immediately after ﬁbrillation, 4:1 blood cardioplegia
(10–15 mL/kg) is delivered retrograde into the coronary
sinus. Despite the absence of a cross-clamp on the
aorta, this induces diastolic arrest that is maintained
by the profound hypothermia. Alternatively, if the aortic
valve is competent and the aorta can be cross-clamped
safely, cardioplegia can be given antegrade into the aortic
root. Throughout the procedure, intermittent cardioplegia
(retrograde, antegrade, or both) is used to protect the
heart. Rapid cooling is continued until the EEG shows
no cerebral electrical activity; this state of electrocerebral
silence generally takes 20 to 25 minutes to achieve and
occurs when brain temperature is reduced to 18◦C to
20◦C (41,42). Although we do not cool to a prescribed
temperature, we do not actively cool patients to less
than 15◦C. If the EEG is not silent upon reaching
15◦C, we maintain this temperature for an additional
5 minutes. When EEG is not available, cooling for at least
25 minutes to a target core temperature of 18◦C to 20◦C is
recommended.

During cooling, the innominate artery is exposed, posterior and superior to the innominate vein, and encircled
with an umbilical tape passed through a tourniquet. Once
EEG silence has been achieved, pentobarbital is given
intravenously at a dose of 500 to 1,000 mg and allowed to
circulate for 3 minutes. Ice packs are placed around the
patient’s head to assist the surface cooling of the brain,
and the patient is placed in the Trendelenburg position. CPB ﬂow is then temporarily discontinued so that the
innominate artery can be safely snared using the tourniquet. Flow is resumed at a rate of 10 mL/kg/min. This
allows retrograde blood ﬂow from the right axillary artery
into the innominate artery, which, because of the snare, diverts blood ﬂow antegrade into the right common carotid
artery, thereby providing ACP. The aorta is opened after selective ACP has started
(Fig. 1B). Back-bleeding from the left common carotid
and left subclavian arteries can obscure the operative ﬁeld. Usually, a cardiotomy suction placed in the distal arch
enables adequate visualization; occasionally, however,
this maneuver is not sufﬁcient, and a balloon occlusion
catheter must be placed in the left common carotid and
subclavian arteries to prevent back-bleeding. If there is
concern about left cerebral malperfusion, we do not
hesitate to augment ACP through a balloon perfusion
catheter placed in the left common carotid artery. In cases
in which the femoral artery was the initial cannulation site,
ACP can be delivered by one or more balloon perfusion
catheters placed in the brachiocephalic arteries. Depending upon the extent of repair needed, the end
of the polyester graft is sewn to the proximal descending
thoracic aorta, the transverse arch, or the distal ascending
aorta. For hemiarch replacements, a beveled graft is
sutured end-to-end to the arch in a manner that replaces
the lesser curvature. In cases in which the entire arch
must be replaced, the graft is sutured end-to-end to
the proximal descending thoracic aorta. If the aneurysm
extends into the descending thoracic aorta, an elephant
trunk repair is performed, leaving approximately 10 cm
of the graft suspended within the aneurysmal distal
aortic segment (Fig. 1C). In either case, after completing
the anastomosis to the descending thoracic aorta, the
brachiocephalic vessels are attached to the graft.

If none
of the brachiocephalic arteries are aneurysmal, they can
be attached as a group using an island of surrounding
aortic tissue; otherwise, each branch vessel is anastomosed
individually to a branched aortic graft. The patient is placed in a steep Trendelenburg position,
and the cardiotomy sucker is placed in the unattached
proximal end of the graft. The tourniquet on the innominate artery is released and ﬂow is slowly returned to a full
ﬂow of 50 mL/kg/min as the aorta and graft are deaired
(Fig. 1D). If the femoral artery was used for CPB inﬂow,
the arterial cannula is placed into the graft (directly or
through a side branch) so that antegrade ﬂow can be
restored. A clamp is applied to the graft and systemic
circulation is reestablished (Fig. 1E). The remainder of the procedure is focused on the
proximal aspects of the aortic reconstruction. During
proximal repair, we slowly rewarm the patient to 36.5◦C,
making sure not to exceed a gradient of 10◦C between the
arterial blood and nasopharyngeal temperatures. Once
the proximal portion of the repair has been completed,
the aorta and heart are deaired through a venting needle

652

placed in the aortic graft. The aorta is unclamped, the
retrograde cardioplegia cannula is removed, epicardial
pacing wires are attached, and the patient is weaned from
CPB. Before the patient is separated from the pump,
the aortic venting needle and left ventricular sump are
removed when the echocardiogram shows that the heart
is free of air. The venous cannula is removed, protamine is
administered, and pump blood is returned to the patient. The graft to the axillary artery is then clamped and
cut. A silk ligature is tied approximately 5 mm above
the anastomosis so as not to place excessive tension on the
suture line or narrow the vessel, and the free end of the
graft is oversewn or ligated using a polypropylene suture. Outcomes
We have operated on 1,142 patients with aortic arch
pathology since 1987. The average age of these patients was 65.3 ± 11.2 years (range, 24–76 years), and
686 (60.1%) were men. Most patients had degenerative
aneurysms without dissection (616; 53.9%). There were
221 patients (19.4%) with acute dissection and 305 (26.7%)
with chronic dissection. Mean CPB time was 127 ± 48
minutes, and mean HCA time was 34 ± 11 minutes. HCA
alone (i.e., without perfusion adjuncts) was used in 266
(23.3%) patients, RCP was used in 695 (60.9%) patients,
and ACP was used in 43 (3.8%). In the remaining 138
(12.1%) patients, we attempted to capitalize on the bene-
ﬁts of both ACP and RCP by using ACP during the arch
reconstruction and using RCP to ﬂush out debris and air
just before resuming CPB. Ninety patients died in-hospital or within 30 days of
surgery, yielding an operative mortality rate of 7.9%. Three
hundred and forty-eight (30.5%) patients had pulmonary
complications, 162 (14.2%) had cardiac complications,
43 (3.8%) had strokes, and 13 (1.1%) had renal failure
requiring hemodialysis. Additionally, 38 (3.3%) patients
were returned to the operating room because of postoperative bleeding. DISTAL AORTIC OPERATIONS
Selection of Technique
Surgical techniques and perfusion practices for the distal aortic segment have evolved tremendously in recent
years, and their use varies according to the extent of
each patient’s aortic disease. The extent of graft replacement in the distal segment ranges from a few centimeters
of the descending thoracic aorta to the entire thoracoabdominal aorta from the left subclavian artery to
the aortoiliac bifurcation.

Distinguishing descending thoracic aortic aneurysms (DTAAs) from thoracoabdominal
aneurysms (TAAAs) is important for operative planning
and risk assessment. Whereas DTAAs can involve any portion of the aorta between the left subclavian artery and
the diaphragm, TAAAs are characterized by dilatation of
the aorta within the diaphragmatic hiatus—the boundary that separates the descending thoracic and abdominal
aortic segments—with varying degrees of extension into
the chest and abdomen. Crawford’s classiﬁcation system
(Fig. 2) further deﬁnes the extent of aorta that requires

replacement and is used to plan the operative procedure,
select perfusion techniques (Table 1), and estimate surgical risks. Ischemic injuries can involve the spinal cord, kidneys,
and other abdominal viscera and often have catastrophic
consequences. Perfusion techniques play a central role in
our current multimodal approach to preventing ischemic
complications (43). The mainstay of perfusion in extensive extent I and II TAAAs is left heart bypass (LHB)
with selective visceral artery perfusion and cold crystalloid renal perfusion. Cold renal perfusion is also used
during extent III and IV TAAA repairs. Other important
adjuncts include moderate heparinization (1 mg/kg), permissive mild hypothermia (nasopharyngeal temperature,
32◦C–34◦C), cerebrospinal ﬂuid drainage (44), sequential
aortic clamping, and aggressive reattachment of segmental intercostal and lumbar arteries. This multimodality strategy is applicable to most patients undergoing surgical repair of DTAAs or TAAAs
(45–47). Particular perfusion techniques and other adjuncts are chosen according to each patient’s individual
risk factors, particularly the planned extent of aortic replacement. Additional factors that increase the risk of
ischemic complications, such as acute dissection and
preexisting renal insufﬁciency, are also important considerations in operative planning. Likewise, the selection
of surgical approach is based on several important technical considerations, most notably the ability to safely clamp
the aorta; in situations where the aorta cannot be clamped
because of proximal extension of the aortic disease into
the arch or the presence of rupture, severe calciﬁcation,
or thrombus, CPB with HCA is necessary. Left Heart Bypass
The rationale for using LHB is to provide distal aortic
perfusion while the aorta is cross-clamped, thereby
decreasing the ischemic times of distal organs, particularly
the spinal cord (Figs. 3 and 4). LHB has been shown to
improve neurologic outcomes in patients with traumatic
aortic injuries.

For example, in a pooled analysis of 20
contemporary series of traumatic aortic injury repairs,
Jahromi et al. (48) found that 84 patients treated with
LHB had no postoperative paraplegia, whereas 7% of
194 patients treated using the ‘‘clamp and sew’’ technique
had paraplegia after surgery. Additionally, Von Oppell
et al. (49) reported that, when LHB is not used, the
cumulative risk of paraplegia increases substantially if
the duration of aortic clamping exceeds 30 minutes. Several studies (50–55) support using LHB to minimize
spinal cord ischemia during TAAA repair; however,
because these studies involved many types of aneurysms,
patients with a variety of risk factors, and the various use of
other adjuncts, it is difﬁcult to draw ﬁrm conclusions from
them. Nonetheless, LHB appears to provide the greatest
beneﬁt to patients undergoing the more extensive repairs. Our own retrospective review of 1,250 consecutive extent I
or extent II TAAA repairs found that LHB, which was
used in 666 cases, reduced the incidence of spinal cord
deﬁcits in patients undergoing extent II repairs (56). By
contrast, in an analysis of 387 patients undergoing repair
of DTAAs, we found no effect of LHB on postoperative
paraplegia and paraparesis rates (45). Data from series in
which LHB and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) drainage were
used together suggest that combining these adjuncts may
enhance spinal cord protection beyond that provided by
either adjunct alone (57,58). We currently use LHB to provide distal aortic perfusion
during the proximal portion of the aortic repair. This
is achieved using a temporary bypass from the left
atrium to either the distal descending thoracic aorta
or the femoral artery (most commonly the left) with
a closed-circuit in-line centrifugal pump (Fig. 3). Our
most common indication for using LHB is extent I or II
TAAA repair. We also use LHB in patients undergoing
less extensive repairs if they have other risk factors for
ischemic complications, such as acute aortic dissection
or previous infrarenal aortic replacement. Because LHB
effectively unloads the left ventricle, it is also very useful
in patients with suboptimal cardiac reserve. Selective Visceral Perfusion and Cold
Renal Perfusion
Liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and bowel ischemia are
potential complications of TAAA repair. The effectiveness of selective visceral perfusion in preventing these
abnormalities has been shown previously (59). After distal
aortic perfusion is discontinued, the abdominal viscera
become vulnerable to ischemia.

The celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery, and renal arteries can be selectively
perfused directly through individual balloon catheters. Selective visceral artery perfusion is delivered from the LHB
circuit through a Y-limb of the return line, providing

practice is based on the results of our randomized trial of
renal perfusion with either cold lactated Ringer’s solution
or normothermic blood from the LHB circuit in patients
undergoing Crawford extent II TAAA repair; univariate
and multivariable analyses showed that cold crystalloid
solution provided superior renal protection (61). We are
currently conducting a randomized clinical trial of renal
perfusion with cold crystalloid versus cold blood.
Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest
CPB and HCA are used for DTAA and TAAA repair when
aortic disease at the proximal descending aorta precludes
clamping (Fig. 5). For example, aortic aneurysms extending into the transverse arch may necessitate an open
proximal anastomosis. Rupture or severe atherosclerosis
in this segment can also prevent safe aortic manipulation
or clamping.
Whereas we use HCA selectively, some authors have
used HCA preferentially for DTAA and TAAA repair
because of the known protective effects of hypothermia
on the central nervous system (62–64). For example,
Kouchoukos et al. (63) recently reported on their 17-year
experience with HCA for repair of extensive DTAAs and

Technique
The bypass circuit is composed of an inﬂow and an
outﬂow cannula, 3/8 in. polyvinylchloride tubing, and a
centrifugal pump (Fig. 4B). No reservoir or heat exchanger
is incorporated into the circuit. For selective visceral
perfusion, balloon perfusion catheters are connected to
the return limb using a three-way, large-bore, high-ﬂow
stopcock. Although intravenous heparin is not necessary
when using a centrifugal pump for LHB, we routinely
administer 1 mg/kg of heparin to prevent thrombosis of
the small intercostal and spinal arteries.
Proximal cannulation for LHB is usually done in the
left inferior pulmonary vein (Fig. 4B). Alternatively, the
cannula can be placed in the left superior pulmonary
vein or inserted directly into the left atrial appendage.
In either location, a 3-0 polypropylene mattress suture
with Teﬂon felt pledgets and a Rumel tourniquet are used
to secure a 26-French right-angled cannula in position,
with its tip in the left atrium. For distal cannulation, we
prefer to directly cannulate the descending thoracic aorta,

Since 1986, we have performed open surgical repair
of 2,755 DTAAs and TAAAs. There were 173 operative
deaths (6.3%), which included 130 patients (4.7%) who
died within 30 days of surgery. Paraplegia or paraparesis
occurred in 99 patients (3.6%) and renal failure requiring
hemodialysis occurred in 140 (5.1%). Return to the
operating room to treat postoperative bleeding was
required in 69 patients (2.5%). Early results stratiﬁed by the extent of repair are presented in Table 2.

Although extent I and II TAAAs comprise
53.3% of our series, this percentage reﬂects referral patterns rather than the true incidence of extensive disease. Extent II TAAA repairs, which have consistently shown
the highest morbidity and mortality in our series (67),
had a 6.0% 30-day mortality rate and a 6.3% incidence of
paraplegia or paraparesis. REFERENCES

◗Noncardiac Surgical Applications
of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
David J. Cook, Stephen Aniskevich, and Michael J. Murray
INTRODUCTION
The development of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) for
repair of cardiac anomalies during the 1950s stimulated an
appraisal of its potential in assisting with the management
of other disease processes. Complications associated
with this technique tempered the initial enthusiasm for
bypass for noncardiac applications. With time, however,
a more reasoned approach to the use of CPB for
noncardiovascular applications has developed, and many
of the early problems and complications have been
overcome. The current applications of CPB for noncardiovascular use involve four main, and one unusual area. First,
bypass is used to induce profound hypothermia so that
circulatory arrest can be instituted, for the repair of vascular abnormalities such as intracranial aneurysms and
resections of tumor/thromboses of the vena cava/right
atrium. Before the availability of CPB, surgeons did use
hypothermia, with a safe limit of 28◦to 30◦C (1), in
conjunction with cardiac inﬂow occlusion to manage
some of these cases. The application of CPB made it
possible to achieve cerebral electrical silence through
profound hypothermia for circulatory arrest (2). Second, CPB, although primarily used to facilitate cardiac
surgery, also bypasses the lungs. In fact, Gibbon developed his pump oxygenator to operate on patients with
pulmonary embolism (3). Patients with signiﬁcant pulmonary disease requiring surgery that demands a bloodless pulmonary ﬁeld constitute the second largest group
of patients beneﬁting from CPB for noncardiovascular
applications. A third group of patients undergoing CPB for noncardiac surgery includes those in whom operations on the
inferior vena cava require a bypass procedure to return
blood to the heart. Occasionally, venoarterial bypass can
be used in these patients, but more frequently, venovenous bypass is instituted. This technique uses advances
and knowledge gained with the development of CPB. Finally, patients who have a variety of unusual disease
processes may also beneﬁt from the use of bypass
techniques in managing their illness. The experience and techniques gained in the application of CPB to the ‘‘traditional’’ patient with cardiovascular
disease are used in managing all of these situations. Anesthetic Considerations
The anesthetic considerations for noncardiovascular applications of CPB are similar to those used for patients
undergoing cardiac surgery.

It is important to note, although, that bypass in noncardiac applications can be
expected to adversely affect the same organ systems that
may be impacted upon by CPB when used in cardiac
surgery. Therefore, depending on the speciﬁc application,
brain, lung, kidney, and hemostatic systems are at risk. This level of risk may be further increased when these organ systems are the focus of the operation (4). Therefore,
special care must be taken to provide relevant supplemental organ protection to these systems when indicated. These considerations will be discussed in greater detail in
the subsequent text. Surgical Considerations
While the preferred technique for the use of CPB in
cardiac surgery is a midline sternotomy with cannulation
of the right atrium and ascending aorta (5), certain
circumstances require the institution of bypass using
femorofemoral bypass (6–8). Access through the upper
extremities is not possible because the blood vessels
are too small to accept sufﬁciently large cannulas (9). Although the access site depends primarily on the surgery
being planned, femoral–femoral bypass is used more
often in CPB for noncardiovascular than for cardiac
applications. The degree of hemodilution (10,11), degree of hypothermia (12–16), pump ﬂows (17), and type of oxygenator (18),

are similar to what has previously been described for
the more common uses of CPB, although the use of
femoral–femoral bypass has the potential to limit ﬂows
because of reduced venous return and decreases cooling
efﬁciency because of remoteness from the cranial vasculature (19). Complications
Patients undergoing CPB for noncardiovascular applications experience similar complications to those experienced by cardiac surgical patients. Neurologic (20–23),
pulmonary (24,25), renal (26,27) gastrointestinal (28), cardiac (29), hematologic (30,31), immunologic (32,33), and
infectious (34) complications are probably as prevalent
in the noncardiac population as they are in the traditional cardiac patient population. Additionally, the use
of femoral arterial cannulation adds the potential for hypoperfusion, dissection of great arteries, and vascular or
neurologic injury to the lower extremity (35). Because patients undergoing noncardiovascular applications of CPB
may not have signiﬁcant cardiac disease, theoretically they
should have a lower cardiac risk. Although the incidence
of cardiac complications should be lower, if hypothermia
and circulatory arrest are used or if the pump time is long,
the risk for arrhythmias and left-ventricular dysfunction
increases (36). Personnel in the operating room involved in
the surgical monitoring and anesthetic management must
be well versed and experienced in the implementation and
use of CPB (37). Having knowledgeable and experienced
personnel available cannot be overemphasized because
these procedures may take place in ‘‘noncardiac’’ areas
where shifting of personnel and material resources will
require considerable advance planning. CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
WITH PROFOUND HYPOTHERMIA
AND CIRCULATORY ARREST
Hypothermia
Historical Perspective
In 1958, Sealy et al. (38) described open-heart surgery
using hypothermia as an adjunct to CPB. By the following
year, they had used the technique to operate on 95 patients,
with an overall survival rate of 83% (39). Also in 1959,
Drew and Anderson (16) reported three cases in which
they used cardiac bypass with profound hypothermia
and circulatory arrest. Unique to their technique was the
use of the patients’ own lungs to provide oxygenation
during surgery. Although one child died during the
perioperative period from heart block following correction
of an atrioventricular canal defect, there were minimal
complications from the hypothermia per se. During that same year (1959), Woodhall, working with
Sealy’s group, used hypothermia to repair an intracranial
vascular aneurysm (40).

Several other techniques had been
used to repair these intracranial vascular malformations,
but there were problems with all of them. Before 1959,
surface cooling to 28◦to 30◦C was used (to avoid inducing ventricular ﬁbrillation), but this limited the maximum
vascular occlusion time to 8 to 10 minutes (41). Isolated cerebral perfusion techniques with selective brain
cooling were also described (42), but it is difﬁcult to
provide uniform cerebral cooling by cannulating just the
carotid arteries. Extracorporeal perfusion with profound
hypothermia and circulatory arrest became the preferred
technique for repairing a number of neurovascular abnormalities. Initially there was a great deal of enthusiasm for
induction of hypothermia and circulatory arrest, not
only for use in neurosurgical procedures, but also for
repair of intracardiac lesions. As expertise with membrane
oxygenation improved, most cardiac cases were repaired
using CPB, an oxygenator, and moderate hypothermia, to
approximately 25◦to 30◦C. This temperature provided a
50% reduction in metabolic rate and, therefore, extended
the safe ischemic time for not only the brain and heart
but also all organ systems. There continue to be surgical
cases, however, that can be managed most effectively with
profound hypothermia and circulatory arrest. Management of Hypothermia
When using profound hypothermia, one typically cools
the patient to 15◦to 17◦C before establishing circulatory
arrest. Monitoring core temperature and neurologic function (43) intraoperatively is very important. In patients
undergoing a craniotomy, in which documentation of
electrical brain silence by electroencephalography (EEG)
is technically difﬁcult, it is of critical importance to document core temperature. Because thoracotomy is not
always surgically indicated, bypass can be established using the femoral artery and vein for access (44,45). Initially,
the Q10 for humans was thought to be approximately two
(the metabolic rate doubles for every 10◦C increase in temperature). Michenfelder and Milde (46,47) demonstrated
in dogs that the slope of the Q10 curve is non linear, becoming signiﬁcantly steeper below 27◦C. In that study,
cerebral metabolic rate was found to be approximately 3.9,
1.8 and 0.5 mL/100 g/min at 37◦C, 27◦C and 18◦C, respectively. Virtually identical numbers during CPB have been
measured more recently (48). Michenfelder attributed the
decrease in the Q10 between 37◦C and 27◦C to a reduction
in cerebral O2 demand without the inhibition of integrated
neuronal function.

Between 27◦C and 18◦C, the larger decrease in the CMRO2 (increase in the Q10) is attributed to
the inhibition of integrated neuronal function as reﬂected
in the development of an isoelectric EEG.

The lower the temperature, the lower the cerebral
metabolic rate (47). Because electrocerebral silence occurs
frequently at 20◦C, some authors have cooled patients
to 20◦C and then instituted circulatory arrest with
satisfactory results (49). However, circulatory arrest is
most often instituted, with a core temperature of 17◦C or
less. We argue this is prudent when EEG is not monitored
because under some bypass conditions the brain may
cool more slowly than the body core (Fig. 1) (50,51). Additionally, the brain may not cool homogeneously
and warmer areas are presumably at greater risk for
ischemic injury (42). The congenital heart literature
regarding circulatory arrest emphasizes slow cooling to
reduce cerebral temperature gradients before circulatory
arrest (52,53). Because of concerns about the long-term
sequelae of circulatory arrest (54), profound hypothermia
with low ﬂow and intermittent circulatory arrest is being
increasingly advocated (55). Nasopharyngeal temperature during the circulatory
arrest period may show modest increases with time. In the
absence of circulation this probably reﬂects some minor
equilibration of tissue temperatures, but an increase
secondary to air temperature may be more signiﬁcant. External cranial cooling is suggested as an important
means for the maintenance of hypothermia within the
central nervous system during circulatory arrest (56). Although this may offer advantages, surface cooling
of the brain alone does not provide adequate cerebral
protection during circulatory arrest (57). Therefore, a
method that directly cools the blood and decreases the
core temperature, in conjunction with surface cooling of
the brain, may provide the best means of establishing
and maintaining low brain temperature and extending
the safe circulatory arrest time (58). Most reports have
indicated that a nasopharyngeal temperature of between
15◦and 18◦C should be achieved before circulatory arrest
is induced while lower temperatures are associated with a
higher incidence of complications (59,60). The longer the circulatory arrest, the greater the incidence of neurologic complications even with adequate
levels of hypothermia (61).

Neurologic dysfunction correlates better with the degree of hypoxia that occurs with
extended circulatory arrest than it does with the lack of
perfusion per se (62). The safe ischemic time can be prolonged, therefore, by preliminary hyperbaric oxygenation,
but this is not usually practical (63). The safe time limit
for circulatory arrest, however, has not been fully delineated (64). Early reports demonstrated a reluctance to use
circulatory arrest for more than 30 minutes (65). Most of
the more recent reports suggest that a core temperature of
15◦C will provide up to 60 minutes of safe ischemic time
during circulatory arrest (Table 1). Management of Circulatory Arrest
Although hypothermia itself should provide maximum
cerebral protection (66), drugs such as a long-acting
muscle relaxant (pancuronium) or antibiotics should be
considered before circulatory arrest because these agents
cannot be administered once the bypass machine is turned
off. There is experimental evidence that tissue acidosis
after circulatory arrest is decreased if hyperventilation
and mild hypocapnia are induced before circulatory arrest (67). However, important work from the Boston
Children’s Hospital indicates that cerebral outcome is improved with a Ph-stat CO2 management strategy (52,68). The elevation of PaCO2 increases cerebral blood ﬂow and
may facilitate more uniform brain cooling; additionally
the relative acidosis may help shift the oxyhemoglobin
dissociation curve rightward compensating for some of
the effect of hypothermia. After the patient is on bypass,
during the induction and documentation of hypothermia,
a barbiturate should be administered for its neuroprotective effects only if there is evidence of cerebral electrical
activity on the eeg (69,70). Barbiturates may be indicated
for those patients who do not have eeg monitoring or
in whom a central nervous system temperature of 15◦C
cannot be documented, but this is controversial (71). Sig-
niﬁcant temperature gradients or reduced ﬂows during
cooling may be relative indications for the use of barbiturates. Corticosteroids and mannitol may also be given
empirically in an attempt to decrease neurologic complications, but there are no studies of patients undergoing
circulatory arrest that have demonstrated a deﬁnitive improvement in outcome with these drugs. Because of concern with steroid-induced hyperglycemia, corticosteroid
use is decreasing. Recent animal studies have suggested
that retrograde or antegrade cerebral perfusion with oxygenated compacted red blood cells (72) and intermittent

In the late 1950s, there were multiple, simultaneous developments in the ﬁeld of CPB. The studies of hypothermia
in dogs by Bigelow et al. (74) stimulated other investigators who used the animal work to serve as a basis for
clinical experimentation. In 1960, Woodhall et al. (40)
at Duke University reported the ﬁrst use of bypass and
profound hypothermia using quinidine to protect the myocardium. With a 10-minute period of circulatory arrest,
they drained a subcortical tumor-like cyst involving the
left parietal lobe. Their case stimulated Uihlein et al. (75)
at the Mayo Clinic to use extracorporeal circulation with
profound hypothermia and circulatory arrest to repair intracranial aneurysms in two patients. Although the basic
principles were the same, the reports highlight the anesthetic and surgical differences that can be found between
physicians and institutions utilizing these techniques. Other investigators, notably Patterson and Ray (44),
expanded the technique and instituted closed-chest extracorporeal circulation. Venous cannulas were advanced
into the cavae through internal jugular and femoral veins,
and an arterial cannula was placed in the femoral artery. This technique solved some of the technical difﬁculties in
performing a simultaneous thoracotomy and craniotomy
and was quickly adopted by other groups. The decision
to use thoracic or femoral cannulation sites should be
made following consultation between the members of the
neurosurgical and cardiac teams. In 5 years, between 1961 and 1966, Uihlein et al. (76),
using extrathoracic cannulation, had operated on a total
of 66 patients with intracranial aneurysms. The mortality rate, although relatively high (14.5%), was thought to
be acceptable given the alternative. Not everyone, however, was enamored with this technique for intracranial
aneurysms repair. Using the closed-chest technique, Drake
et al. (77) in London, Ontario, Canada, had difﬁculties in
10 patients with aneurysms because of poor venous return using extrathoracic cannulation. More importantly,
from their perspective cerebral arterial spasm continued
to be a problem with ruptured cerebral aneurysms, and
ﬁve of their 10 patients died within 2 to 3 months of
the operative procedure. They abandoned this technique
and developed other surgical therapies that dramatically
changed the way neurosurgeons approached intracranial
aneurysms. These new techniques, simultaneously developed by Sundt et al.

(78), led this group to also abandon
the use of profound hypothermia and circulatory arrest
for management of intracranial pathology. At the same time, Michenfelder was pioneering work
in the ﬁeld of neuroanesthesia, which would inﬂuence the
management of these patients (79). The reﬁnements of the
surgical approach to aneurysms, including the operating
microscope, withdrawal of cerebrospinal ﬂuid, controlled
hypotension, and sophisticated neuroanesthesia made
surgery for most intracranial pathology much safer
without the use of extracorporeal circulation. Beginning in
1965, most neurosurgical centers in the United States and
Canada had abandoned the intraoperative use of profound
hypothermia and circulatory arrest. In 1972, however, Sundt et al. (80) reported a case
in which an otherwise inoperable giant basilar artery
aneurysm was managed successfully with CPB, profound
hypothermia, and circulatory arrest. It was the ﬁrst case
using this technique at the Mayo Clinic since 1964. The
repair went well, and over the intervening 25 years, several
reports have delineated the limited, but important, role of
bypass, hypothermia, and circulatory arrest in managing
neurosurgical pathology. Indications
Since 1972, most cases employing circulatory arrest have
been for surgical treatment of giant basilar and cerebral
aneurysms and of hemangioblastomas, frequently of
the brain stem. In current practice, hypothermia and
circulatory arrest allow the only chance for resection in
this subgroup of patients. Baumgartner et al. (81) used a
modiﬁed hypothermic approach in managing all forms of
intracranial aneurysms, but this technique has not been
used elsewhere. Anesthetic Management
The successful management of these difﬁcult patients
mandates frequent, open communication between the
neuro- and cardiovascular-surgical and anesthesia teams. Unlike most patients presenting for cardiac surgery, many
of these patients are typically young and without coronary
artery disease. The majority, however, do have vascular
pathology, frequently a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. Therefore, careful management of the hemodynamics
to avoid hypotension and hypertension is as important
as it is in the patient with cardiac disease undergoing
CPB. Many of these patients, therefore, should receive
vasoactive drugs, most frequently β-blockers, to attenuate
hemodynamic instability. Positioning these patients can also be a major problem. While the literature shows that closed-chest techniques
were preferred in the past, several cardiac surgeons
currently cannulate the great vessels through a midline
sternotomy. There are some circumstances in which the
cranial pathology can only be approached posteriorly,
mandating that the patient be in a prone position.

Under
these circumstances, femoral cannulation is difﬁcult and
a posterolateral thoracotomy, allowing access to the atria
for venous cannulation, may be necessary.

Monitoring for these patients may include a pulmonary
artery catheter and an intrathecal catheter. A pulmonary
artery catheter is placed because myocardial dysfunction
can be a problem even in the absence of coronary artery
disease when prolonged circulatory arrest is used. Furthermore, during circulatory arrest, if the left ventricle
or pulmonary vasculature is not vented, left-ventricular
distension and/or pulmonary edema can be a serious
complication. Left-ventricular distension is a primary concern in these operations as an aortic cross- clamp is not
placed and cardioplegia is not administered. Therefore,
ventricular ﬁbrillation can occur in a ‘‘full’’ heart with serious consequences, and a preoperative echocardiographic
examination is essential in these patients to rule out aortic valvular insufﬁciency. The placement of a pulmonary
artery catheter can be an important adjunct in managing
these patients as an indicator of left-ventricular distension during CPB and hemodynamic management in the
postbypass period. Rarely, drainage of cerebrospinal ﬂuid helps the
surgeon better visualize the vascular pathology. This
beneﬁt must be weighed against the risk of an epidural
hematoma in a heparinized patient with hypothermia. In
the past, drainage was often achieved with a malleable
needle, but in current practice, catheters designed for
epidural use can be placed in the intrathecal space by the
use of an 18- or 17-gauge Tuohy needle. The catheter
is then taped to the patient’s back, allowing for the
monitoring of cerebrospinal ﬂuid pressure and withdrawal
of ﬂuid. The larger the catheter, the better the dynamic
response for pressure monitoring and the easier it is to
withdraw cerebrospinal ﬂuid. Some catheters have a spiral
wire incorporated into their walls that prevents kinking
and facilitates pressure monitoring and ﬂuid withdrawal. The maintenance of stable hemodynamics in the immediate preoperative period is a most important component
of the anesthetic protocol. Therefore, a neuroanesthetic
technique that employs controlled hypotension (using
β-blockers and nitroprusside) is often used. When intracranial hypertension is a problem, controlled hyperventilation and the use of anesthetic agents such as thiopental
and isoﬂurane are preferred. As pointed out, most of
these patients do not have coronary artery disease, and
an inhalation anesthetic can be used. More recent case
reports have described the use of an opioid technique.

The choice of an inhalation versus an opioid technique,
or a combination of the two, is at the discretion of the
anesthesiologist(s) providing care to the patient. Neurologic
dysfunction

concern, but because these patients are anesthetized,
hypothermic, and undergoing craniotomy, there is no
effective way to intraoperatively monitor neurologic function. Careful attention to detail in managing the hemodynamic response to anesthetic induction and surgery, as
well as controlling PaCO2 and core temperature, are the

of propofol in these cases has not been fully explored, but
it might be a reasonable agent to achieve these goals as
long as hypotension is avoided by titrating the propofol to
effect. Complications
Complications experienced by these patients may be similar to those experienced by other patients undergoing
CPB for cardiac procedures. Although this neurosurgical
population may be at reduced atheroembolic risk relative
to the cardiac surgical population, this patient group may
be at greater overall risk for bleeding and neurologic injury. In addition to heparinization for CPB, the profound
hypothermia required for these procedures increases the
risk of bleeding (82). Many case reports underscore the
major morbidity that these patients experience secondary
to postoperative bleeding (Table 1). The anesthesiologist
must establish baseline coagulation function on the patient’s arrival in the operating room and monitor to identify any coagulation defects as the patient comes off CPB. These defects include transfusion-related thrombocytopenia and decreased coagulation factors that may require
the use of transfused platelets, fresh-frozen plasma, or
cryoprecipitate. The use of thrombin glue by the neurosurgical team, although it does have identiﬁed risks, might
be of beneﬁt in managing these patients. Increasingly, an
antiﬁbrinolytic agent, e.g., aprotinin or one of the lysine
analogs (aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid), is used
in this patient population based on experience with CPB
and circulatory arrest for other surgical procedures (83). The incidence of neurocognitive dysfunction following
bypass for cardiac surgery can run as high as 70%
depending upon the sensitivity of the neuropsychiatric
test used (21).

Neurosurgical patients undergoing CPB
may be at risk for bypass-related neurologic injury as well
as brain injury speciﬁcally related to the neurosurgery. A
temperature probe may be necessary to document that
the temperature of the brain is, indeed, less than 15◦C, the
temperature most frequently cited as allowing maximal
cerebral protection. Finally cerebral edema may pose major neurologic
problems in patients undergoing neurosurgery with CPB. Brain swelling is common during and following intracranial surgery; CPB is also independently associated with
cerebral edema (84,85). It is the practice at the Mayo
Clinic to use relatively high doses of mannitol in these
cases anticipating some cerebral edema in all patients.

V. Clinical Applications
Finally, if an intrathoracic approach is used for venous
cannulation, special attention must be paid to right atrial
cannula position as the right atrial cannula can partially
obstruct the superior vena cava. This has marked effects
in increasing intracranial pressure (ICP) and decreasing
cerebral perfusion pressure (86). Use in Urologic Surgery
The use of CPB techniques to facilitate resection of renal malignancies came about serendipitously. Whereas
the beneﬁts of bypass with deep hypothermia and cardiac
arrest were quickly appreciated and used for resection
of intracranial aneurysms, it was not until more than
10 years of CPB use in neurosurgical procedures, that reports began to appear describing the technique of bypass
with profound hypothermia and circulatory arrest for removal of tumors invading the inferior vena cava with right
atrial extension. It had been recognized for some time that
patients with renal cell carcinomas extending into the inferior vena cava had a poor prognosis (87), but if the
tumor could be resected in its entirety, prognosis was improved (88). The critical aspect of surgery, therefore, was
the complete removal of the tumor with a technique that
did not signiﬁcantly increase morbidity. In 1970, Marshall
et al. (89) reported several cases of hypernephromas with
caval extension, including one in which they attempted to
isolate the inferior vena cava alone, and another in which
they attempted to isolate both inferior vena cava and kidney. The latter patient sustained a cardiac arrest following
caval occlusion. Pulmonary embolism was diagnosed, the
patient underwent emergency thoracotomy with cardiac
massage, and a pulmonary arteriotomy was made to remove a pulmonary thromboembolus. On the basis of this
experience, in a subsequent case the authors placed two
femoral vein cannulas below the obstructing tumor and
shunted this blood to the superior vena cava through a
cannula in the internal jugular vein. No pump was required in this case because the inferior caval pressure was
sufﬁciently elevated to allow for adequate ﬂow from the
femoral vein to the superior vena cava. During the procedure, however, the systemic arterial pressure began to
fall, so extracorporeal circulation was begun. This was the
ﬁrst time that venovenous bypass was used in resection of
kidney tumors extending into the right atrium. The second report in which bypass was used in
‘‘urologic’’ surgery was in a patient with a right atrial
tumor.

The preoperative diagnosis was myxoma; the
patient was placed on full CPB and the tumor was resected
from the atrium. The pathologic report indicated that the
resected mass was in fact a ‘‘hypernephroma’’ (90). Indications
The main indication for CPB in urologic surgery is for
resection of renal tumors, primarily renal cell carcinomas
or hypernephromas, which extend into the inferior vena
cava superiorly past the diaphragm. In children, Wilms’
tumors can present in this same way (91). Tumors not
extending above the diaphragm or into the right atrium
can be frequently resected using surgical techniques without a bypass procedure. Depending upon the extension of
the tumor, venovenous bypass can occasionally be used
to shunt blood from the inferior to the superior vena
cava. Many clinicians, however, have found that collateral circulation is sufﬁcient, so that this is not usually
necessary. The primary use for CPB in resection of caval
tumors is to allow for profound hypothermia, circulatory
arrest, and complete exsanguination for tumors extending into the right atrium. Because complete removal of
the tumor is critical to survival, several authors have
noted that a quiet, motionless, bloodless right atrium allows the best chance for complete resection (92–94). In
addition, given the high incidence of pulmonary artery
embolization associated with this surgical procedure,
bypass is occasionally instituted in those patients who
sustain an intraoperative pulmonary embolus (89,95,96),
for whom pulmonary embolectomy offers the only chance
for survival. Management
The successful management of these patients requires
communication and cooperation between the cardiac, urologic, and anesthetic teams. The anesthetic management
of these cases is infrequently described, but from available literature describing the anesthetic management, it
is obvious that an opioid anesthetic technique is most
common (97). This should not necessarily be the case,
however. An intravenous induction with thiopental and
succinylcholine has also been used, followed by maintenance of anesthesia with inhalation agents, isoﬂurane and
nitrous oxide (96). Standard monitoring of the electrocardiogram, pulse oximeter, esophageal temperature, and
systemic arterial pressures was used. A pulmonary artery
catheter is relatively contraindicated in these patients, depending on the extent and location of the tumor thrombus. Many patients with documented extension of the tumor
into the right atrium will have cardiac symptoms and
signs present before the surgical procedures (94,98).

Several case reports have documented that in positioning the
patient, the tumor can become dislodged or displaced further into the right atrium with a precipitous drop in blood
pressure. The left lateral decubitus position seems to be
the position in which this is most likely to occur (93,96). For these cases, transesophageal echocardiographic (TEE)
visualization of the right atrium and tricuspid valve can
assist in both surgical assessment and in diagnosis in the
event of sudden hemodynamic changes. TEE should probably be considered as standard monitoring in this patient
population.

33. Noncardiac Surgical Applications of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
669
After the induction of anesthesia, either a thoracoabdominal or a midline abdominal incision extended into a
sternotomy is made. While the cardiac and urologic surgical teams can begin their procedure simultaneously, the
patient is not heparinized for bypass (to avoid excessive
bleeding) until the urologist has the kidney and inferior
vena cava dissected free. Once the urologist is ready, the
patient is placed on CPB and cooled to 15◦C. Some physicians report packing the patient’s head in ice to keep the
patient’s brain at a sufﬁciently low temperature (99–101),
perhaps a worthwhile technique if inefﬁcient cooling is
anticipated from femoral arterial cannulation. However,
there are centers in which circulatory arrest is instituted
with only moderate degrees of hypothermia (approximately 25◦C) (96). From the literature, however, it is
apparent that the time necessary to resect the caval and
right atrial tumor ranges from 10 to 45 minutes (Table 2). Therefore, profound hypothermia should be instituted
when circulatory arrest is anticipated. During institution of bypass, a double ﬁlter or a
smaller pore size ﬁlter may be placed in the bypass
arterial line to prevent the embolization to the patient
of tumor emboli (102). Because of the concern about
malignant emboli, these patients have not been considered
candidates for the use of an intraoperative cell saver (96),
although the latter recommendation is not based on any
reported cases. There does not appear to be a clear
contraindication to the use autotransfusion because the
tumor is already in the bloodstream; furthermore, if
cardiotomy suckers are used on bypass, autotransfusion,
in effect, is already being used. Complications
The difﬁculties in using this technique are similar to those
described for the repair of intracranial aneurysms. The
problem of neurologic dysfunction is difﬁcult to quantify
in this patient population because most of the reports
are of single cases. There are only two series in which
more than 10 patients were studied (103,104). Bleeding,
especially from retroperitoneal beds, was the major perioperative complication in both of these series. Once the
inferior vena cava is resected, patients can develop postoperative ascites and lower extremity edema until adequate
collateral ﬂow is established. This is not a problem in
most cases, however, because sufﬁcient collateral ﬂow is
present preoperatively.

In a large series from the Cleveland Clinic, femoral venous cannulation was found to
be unnecessary as collateralization around the tumor allowed sufﬁcient venous drainage of the lower half of the
body (97). Other complications, including postoperative
pulmonary dysfunction and sepsis, are similar to those
with standard CPB. Because most of these cases include
a nephrectomy, postoperative renal failure is common. The intravenous contrast agents used preoperatively to
establish the diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma and inferior vena cava occlusion may contribute to this high
incidence of postoperative renal dysfunction. It is important for the anesthesiologist to avoid the administration
of any nephrotoxic drugs, to monitor urine output and
central venous pressure carefully, and to intervene as
appropriate if either decreases below safe levels. CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
WITHOUT CIRCULATORY ARREST
FOR THORACIC PROCEDURES
In 1959, the same year in which Woodhall et al. (40) used
CPB for excision of an intracranial aneurysm, Woods
et al. (105) used CPB for resection of a carinal tumor. The
procedure went well but was complicated by postoperative
bleeding. An obstructing blood clot was emergently
suctioned from the tracheostomy and was attributed
to the combination of the operative procedure and the
sequelae of bypass. As in other uses of CPB, problems
with coagulation remained formidable. Nissen (106) used
bypass combined with hypothermia to resect a malignant
adenoma of the trachea. A third case was reported
by Adkins and Izawa (107) in which a cylindroma
was resected using bypass. In their case report, they
emphasized the importance of having the CPB machine
primed and ready and the patient’s groin prepared. If,
during the induction of general anesthesia, the patient’s
airway becomes obstructed because of the intratracheal
tumor, femoral CPB can be instituted immediately. In 1965, Neville et al. (108) reported using bypass for
tracheal resections. They cannulated the superior vena
cava from the right atrium, drained the inferior vena
cava through a femoral venous cannula, and returned arterialized blood to their patients through a cannula in
the femoral artery. Of the 11 patients studied, they used
CPB in8 and partial CPB in3 patients. Of these patients,
two died from complications from hemorrhage, four from
pulmonary complications, and one from a myocardial infarction. The authors attempted to minimize bleeding by
completing the major portion of the operation before instituting bypass. Obviously, based on their outcomes, this
was not wholly adequate.

In addition, as noted during
CPB for cardiac and vascular procedures, postoperative
pulmonary complications were common. Other individuals continued to advocate CPB for pulmonary bypass
based on the ease with which sterility was maintained (no
manipulation of tumor or carina around a contaminated
tracheal tube), the unencumbered nature of the surgical
incision, and the ease of performance (109). An interesting report was provided in 1996 by Horita
et al. who undertook carinal reconstruction using venoveno bypass with an oxygenator using a percutaneous
femoral venous approach (110). These authors placed

As noted previously, Gibbon initially developed CPB to
manage massive pulmonary embolism (3). It was not until
1961, however, that Cooley et al. (116) reported the ﬁrst

successful use of bypass to resect a pulmonary embolus. Previously, pulmonary embolectomy was occasionally performed using cardiac inﬂow occlusion under generalized
systemic hypothermia without CPB, the same technique
that had been used to resect cardiac lesions. It was obvious
to those authors that CPB might have important advantages for resection of large pulmonary emboli, otherwise a
uniformly fatal condition. In 1966, Rosenberg et al. (117)
reviewed the experience with CPB for pulmonary embolectomy and made several recommendations. On the
basis of their review, if pulmonary embolectomy was to
be successful, resection must be attempted within 2 hours
of the embolization. In 1967, Beall and Cooley (118) summarized their
experience at the Texas Heart Institute using CPB for
resuscitation and treatment of pulmonary emboli. Their
success rate was only 33% for long-term survival, but
they believed that the technique was indicated because,
otherwise, the mortality rate would have been, in their
estimation, 100%. Sautter (119), at the Marshﬁeld Clinic, also reported
similar survival rates (4 of 11) and, based on his experience, recommended using CPB only for those patients
who were hypotensive and whose lives were immediately
threatened. He used hypothermic low-ﬂow hemodilution
because no blood was required to prime the bypass machine. Because large cannulas were unnecessary, peripheral cannulization could be used to facilitate the emergent
implementation of bypass, which he believed was most
important in managing patients and improving survival. In his experience, mortality had more to do with the underlying disease process than with the surgical procedure. He strongly recommended that bypass for pulmonary embolectomy be instituted as rapidly as possible when the
patient’s cardiopulmonary condition was still reversible,
before a series of events began which would make resuscitation impossible even following embolus resection. Garcia et al. (120), recognizing the importance of the
early use of CPB to resuscitate patients, advocated partial
bypass for resuscitation, and employing a combined
approach, used total bypass for resection of the pulmonary
embolus. In current practice, transthoracic pulmonary
embolectomy without CPB has met with such limited
success that the procedure has been all but abandoned. CPB for open pulmonary embolectomy should be used
for those patients who are hypotensive, have a PaO2 of
less than 60 mm Hg on 100% oxygen, and have a urinary
output of less than 20 mL/hr (121).

These guidelines were
developed more than 20 years ago, but are still being used
now (122). There are no prospective, controlled studies
comparing pulmonary embolectomy with and without
bypass, nor are such studies likely to be performed in the
future. Pulmonary catheter embolectomy is a newer technique
ﬁrst described by Greenﬁeld and associates (123). It
has been advocated for managing critically ill patients
with severe hemodynamic instability and an absolute
contraindication to ﬁbrinolytics, although it has been used
in conjunction with ﬁbrinolysis. A review of the few case
studies in the literature show the procedure still carries
a relatively high mortality rate varying between 9% and
30% (123–125). In summary, for those patients in whom CPB is indicated, it should be instituted as soon as possible for
resuscitation of the patient, frequently through the groin,
and then with the bypass in effect, the thromboembolus
should be resected. Problems with bleeding and postoperative pulmonary complications (pulmonary edema,
atelectasis, etc.) must be managed aggressively. Despite
the best efforts, a high mortality rate (30 days) is not
unusual, but depending on the level of experience, some
centers are reporting very good (84%) survival rates (126). Pulmonary Transplantation
Single-lung transplantation, frequently transplanting the
donor lung into the recipient’s right chest, is the most frequently used approach. This can be achieved 70% to 80%
of the time without CPB. During resection of the native
lung, the contralateral lung is ventilated through a doublelumen tracheal tube utilizing one-lung ventilation. In some
patients, however, it is impossible to provide adequate gas
exchange with one lung because of the underlying disease
process in the nonoperative side. Currently, there is no
ideal preoperative test for patients with obstructive lung
disease to predict who will require CPB. In our practice, after the patient is anesthetized and
intubated, while we wait for the ‘‘go ahead’’ from the
procurement team, we assess the effectiveness of onelung ventilation for if we are unable to maintain oxygen
saturation while ventilating the contralateral lung, we
know CPB will be required, but even this test is not
very speciﬁc. For patients with restrictive lung disease,
it is easier to use exercise tolerance and right ventricular
ejection fraction to predict preoperatively who will require
CPB intraoperatively (127).

When CPB is used, insertion
of the arterial and venous cannulae is usually through the
groin, keeping the chest free of cannulas to improve the
surgical ﬁeld (128), but many surgeons prefer a standard
approach with the cannulas in the cava and aortic root. In addition to the occasional use of bypass for
management of pulmonary transplantation, CPB has also
been used for ‘‘domino’’ procedures in which the ﬁrst
recipient’s heart and lungs are removed, en bloc, with
the (normal) heart given to a second recipient while the
ﬁrst recipient then receives a heart-lung transplant. (129)
Also, donors can be placed on bypass for procurement
of combined heart-lung preparations, allowing for the
rapid induction of hypothermia, viewed as an optimal
preservation technique for multiorgan procurement (130).

33. Noncardiac Surgical Applications of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
673
OTHER USES
There have been a few case reports in which CPB is used
for pulmonary lesions that cannot be managed by any
other means. Shuman (131) described a sarcoma of the
lung with extension into the left atrium that was successfully managed using bypass, similar to the experience
reported for resection of renal cell carcinomas that extended into the right atrium (132). In addition to elective
surgical resection of tracheal lesions, CPB has also been
used in certain airway emergencies (133,134). Maharaj
et al. (135) treated a patient who was placed on bypass for
removal of an intratracheal foreign body. Femoral CPB
has been used with traumatic tracheal disruptions (136)
and in a case of massive sand aspiration requiring bronchoscopy and pulmonary lavage (137). Similarly, several
case reports have described the use of this technique for
bilateral lung lavage in alveolar proteinosis (138,139). In
most cases, however, alveolar proteinosis can be effectively
managed without the use of CPB (140). Even patients with
a single-lung and alveolar proteinosis have been managed
by more conservative techniques (141). Anterior Mediastinal Masses
The resection of large anterior mediastinal masses may
require the use of CPB. Most commonly these masses are
teratomas, seminomas, or lymphomas (142–144) and their
presence in the mediastinum can compromise either oxygenation or cardiac output following induction of general
anesthesia (145). For patients who show respiratory distress in the preoperative period or who are unable to sleep
supine, it is prudent to have the groins prepped for femoral
cannulation before induction of anesthesia. For these patients, an awake intubation in a semisitting position may
be indicated, but placement of a tracheal tube does not
guarantee adequate gas exchange when negative pressure
ventilation ceases because airway obstruction may occur
distal to the tracheal tube. Additionally, placing the patient
in the supine position may cause acute right ventricular
failure and cardiac arrest from either pulmonary arterial
obstruction or compression of the superior vena cava and
insufﬁcient venous return to the right heart. The anesthesiologist and surgical team should review all imaging
studies (Fig. 5) and discuss these possibilities, although
the anatomy as deﬁned by the computed tomography (CT)
alone cannot clearly predict the anatomic changes that
may occur with loss of negative pressure ventilation and
the placement of the patient in the supine position.

ISOLATED LEFT HEART BYPASS
Until recently, cardiopulmonary bypass was occasionally
used in the cardiac catheterization laboratory to facilitate
