the catheterization laboratory. It is in this area that the
greatest use of bypass in noncardiac surgery is likely to
be seen in coming years. The leading technology in this
area is the TandemHeart pVAD (percutaneous ventricular
assist device; Cardiac Assist, Inc., Pittsburgh, PA, USA). The Tandem Heart device is used for left-ventricular
bypass (Fig. 6.) The femoral vein is cannulated either
openly or percutaneously and a 21-Fr catheter is threaded
into the right atrium and across the intra-atrial septum,
often with ﬂuoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance. Oxygenated blood is drained from the left atrium through
the femoral venous cannula and directed to a small
centrifugal pump. The oxygenated blood is then pumped
in a continuous, nonpulsatile manner, into a femoral
arterial cannula advanced to the iliac artery. The system
has no reservoir, no oxygenator, and is very compact. The device can deliver ﬂows between 2 and 5 L/minute
and in doing so partially or completely decompress the left
ventricle. Flow to the device is limited primarily by blood
return from the left atrium. Transesophageal echocardiographic monitoring can improve cannula position in the
left atrium, particularly if the cannula is placed in or near
the appendage and blood return is compromised. The pVAD has been used to manage cardiogenic
shock following myocardial infarction (146) as well as
a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) following cardiac surgery (147). However, it greatest application for
noncardiac surgery patients is likely to be its use in interventional cardiology. In multiple institutions (148,149),
the pVADs have been used repeatedly for percutaneus
transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) and stenting of
left main coronary lesions in patients who are not surgical

lesions, it is likely that the pVADs or similar technology

those contexts but they are very logical uses that we are

in the Catheterization Laboratory
Given the potential of left-ventricular collapse with
instrumentation of the left main coronary, it is our
practice to manage these patients with arterial and
pulmonary artery catheters. Given that asystole may occur
it is routine for us to place transvenous ventricular
pacing wires through the pulmonary artery catheter. Large-bore intravenous access is also obtained in case
emergent cardiac surgery becomes necessary. At the
authors’ institution, we heparinize patients to an activated
clotting time (ACT) of 450 seconds before initiation of
ﬂow and maintain the ACT at 250 seconds during the
procedure although lower levels of heparinization have
been safely used elsewhere. Transesophageal echocardiographic monitoring is used
intensively during cannula placement and during the
procedure. Flows on the pump are adjusted to maintain
left-ventricular decompression, manifested by a mean
arterial blood pressure and the absence of a systemic pulse. Because the right ventricle functions normally, the pulse
pressure in the pulmonary circulation should be relatively
unchanged. However, because oxygenated blood is taken
from the left atrium, successful left-ventricular bypass is
dependent on adequate right heart output and pulmonary
gas exchange. The presence of right heart failure, before
or during the procedure (left dominant system) or severe
pulmonary insufﬁciency, has the potential to result in
hypoxia or hypoperfusion. Venovenous Bypass
Marshall et al.

(89) used a passive venovenous bypass to
manage a patient with renal cell carcinoma extending into
the inferior vena cava and right atrium in 1970. The need
for a shunt that could drain blood from the lower extremities and portal system was obvious in the 1960s, but
the ﬁrst clinical trials for patients with liver disease utilizing bypass without a pump, were unsuccessful. Either
the bypass circuit clotted and did not function or clots
formed and when released from the bypass tubing caused
lethal pulmonary embolization. When heparinization was
used, the addition of anticoagulant therapy to patients
with preexisting liver-associated coagulopathy produced
unacceptable bleeding, and increased morbidity and mortality. It was not until the early 1980s that venovenous
bypass came into practice using heparin-bonded circuits
with a centrifugal pump (145,152) instead of systemic
heparinization with a roller pump. Deﬁnition
Venovenous bypass differs from CPB in many ways: (a) an
oxygenator is not used in the circuit; (b) the arterial system
is not perfused, therefore, pressures within the system are
lower; and (c) the circuit, in essence, is serving as only a
conduit for blood from one or more regions of the body to
the right heart. Therefore, venovenous bypass frequently
utilizes ﬂows less than those seen on cardiac bypass, and,
although occasionally ﬂows as high as 6 L/min can be
achieved, ﬂows between 1 and 2 L/min are more common. Indications
Venovenous bypass can be used for the treatment of
respiratory failure (extracorporeal CO2
removal, see
Chapter 25) and in the management of surgical procedures
on the liver, most frequently for liver transplantation during the anhepatic phase, and for combined resections of
the liver and vena cava.

33. Noncardiac Surgical Applications of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
675
Management
When instituting venovenous bypass, depending upon the
organ bed to be bypassed, the cannula is usually placed
in one femoral vein and advanced to the bifurcation of
the inferior vena cava. In circumstances in which the
portal system must be drained, a second catheter is placed
in the portal vein. The drainage from these cannulas is
then directed to a centrifugal pump, with return to the
patient most frequently through an axillary or internal
jugular vein. (The use of centrifugal pumps is discussed in
Chapter 3.) For procedures involving the liver, no heparin
is used. For extracorporeal CO2 removal, more aggressive
heparinization is mandatory. Venovenous bypass in this context is intended only to
return blood to the heart without the requirement for
oxygenation, CO2 removal, or systemic perfusion, ﬂows
much lower than those with CPB are employed. In our
own practice, ﬂows are considered adequate as long as
they are not less than 1 L/min (153) and cardiac preload
is maintained. Flows must be maintained to prevent
clot development in the circuit as well as to provide
adequate right heart ﬁlling, although it is not clear if
any ﬂow can guarantee that no clot will be formed in
the total absence of heparinization, even when heparin
coated circuits (standard) are used. Because there is no
reservoir in a venovenous system, the total ﬂow possible
with these systems is a function of blood ﬂow to the pump. Additionally, venovenous bypass systems are ‘‘closed’’ so
no volume can be added directly once the circuit is
primed. Decreased ﬂows usually indicate a problem with
the cannulae or some other obstruction to the venous
system although gradual decreases in ﬂows may be a
function of surgically related hypovolemia. Complications of venovenous bypass are few. Improvements in material biocompatability such as heparin
coating of catheters, tubings, and pumps, and the use
of centrifugal pumps (154) have decreased the complications of clotting or excessive bleeding that were previously
reported. Air embolism can occur in venovenous bypass (155,156), just as in CPB, with potentially lethal
sequelae. In studies of venovenous bypass, no clinically
signiﬁcant coagulopathy has been described (145,157). However, decreases in core temperature, heart rate, and
arterial pressure with increases in central venous pressure have been reported (157).

The blood volume becomes
concentrated as evidenced by increases in hematocrit,
colloid oncotic pressure, serum osmolality, and serum
sodium. These data, along with an accumulating base
deﬁcit, suggest that venovenous bypass is associated with
some hypoperfusion of the abdominal viscera and lower
extremities. Flow-dependent, third-space ﬂuid accumulation (158) may be a primary contributor to decreasing
cardiac output and pump ﬂow during the procedure.These
limitations, however, while of importance, do not limit the
use of venovenous bypass for those surgical procedures in
which it has clearly proved to be beneﬁcial. Liver Transplantation
Less than 5% of liver transplantation procedures are carried out with venovenous bypass. Originally, in the United
States, it was thought that a liver transplantation surgical
procedure would be improved by the use of a bypass technique that would shunt blood from the lower extremities
and mesenteric beds to the right atrium. For many years,
most liver transplant centers throughout the United States
and Europe used venovenous bypass (159–161). However,
as more experience was gained, surgeons have been able
to use a partial occlusion clamp on the inferior vena
cava and make their vascular anastomoses without crossclamping the entire inferior vena cava. The development
of this technique has decreased the need for venovenous
bypass, although, as stated, approximately 5% of patients
will require venovenous bypass because of severe venous
congestion and other surgical considerations. Management
Venovenous bypass has been suggested for venous decompression, improved hemodynamic stability, and decreased
intraoperative blood loss during the anhepatic phase of
liver transplantation. Because hypothermic coagulopathy
is a problem and because venovenous bypass systems
lack a heat exchanger, the maintenance of normothermia during the operative procedure is important. In many
centers, patients are positioned on a heating blanket on
the operating table. In our own practice, an air-warming
device is placed over the lower and upper extremities during surgery.

Routine hemodynamic monitoring should
include electrocardiography for measurement of heart
rate and for the presence of ischemia; a core temperature
probe; pulse oximetry; two arterial cannulas for continuous monitoring of systemic arterial pressure and for blood
withdrawal; a pulmonary artery catheter for measurement
of cardiac ﬁlling pressures, SvO2 and continuous cardiac output; and laboratory monitoring of arterial blood
gasses, complete blood count, sodium, potassium, ionized
calcium, blood glucose, and coagulation (through the use
of a thromboelastogram, prothrombin, activated partial
thromboplastin times and international normalized ratio
[INR]). These measurements are obtained at baseline and
then repeated at discrete intervals during the operative
procedure. When venovenous bypass is used for liver transplantation, it is necessary to drain both the systemic and
portal systems with cannulae in the femoral and portal
veins. In those circumstances in which the portal vein
cannot be easily cannulated, placement of catheters in
the mesenteric venous system of the abdomen has been

676
V. Clinical Applications
described (162). During the recipient hepatectomy, when
bypass is ready for implementation, the surgeon ligates the
hepatic artery and common duct and mobilizes the liver. The portal vein and femoral cannulas are inserted, allowing both the splanchnic and systemic venous drainage to
be brought into the venovenous circuit. Entry into the
proximal systemic venous system is usually through the
subclavian or internal jugular vein. The surgeon then proceeds with mobilization of the liver, dividing all structures,
including the infrahepatic vena cava. Following the initiation of bypass, there is frequently
a transient decrease in blood pressure that rarely persists
for more than 15 to 30 seconds. In one study, with the
initiation of bypass, there was a 4◦C decrease in core
temperature, a statistically signiﬁcant decrease in heart
rate, systemic arterial pressure; and an increase in
the central venous pressure (157). Electrocardiographic
changes, attributable to the effects of temperature and
alterations in potassium, were also noted. It is important
to monitor and prevent hypothermia aggressively during
the transplant procedure because heparin-less venovenous
bypass cannot use a standard heat exchanger because of
the large, potentially thrombogenic surface area of these
devices. Caval Resections
Indication
As surgical and anesthetic techniques common to transplantation of the liver improved, these advances were used
in procedures on the liver (for resections) (162), the vena
cava (for relief of obstructions) (163), and for combined
hepatic and inferior vena caval resections (164). Resection
of vena caval leiomyosarcomas (165) surgical correction
of the Budd-Chiari syndrome (166), and repair of traumatic vena caval disruption (167) have all been reported
using venovenous bypass, but in most cases, the technique
is indicated for combined hepatic and vena caval resections. Frequently, it is impossible to isolate the liver and
achieve acceptable cancer-free margins without resecting
the inferior vena cava (164). Management
During a combined liver and vena caval resection,
decompression of the portal system is not necessary. The cross-clamp time is usually only 15 to 30 minutes,
and it would be unusual for the bowel and mesentery
not to tolerate venous outﬂow obstruction for this brief
period. It is necessary, however, to shunt the lower
systemic circulation. In these circumstances, the systemic
circulation is drained through a catheter in the inferior
vena cava, and the venous efﬂuent is returned to the
patient through a large bore, internal jugular cannula.

During bypass, a ﬂow of greater than 1 L/min is the
goal. As with liver transplantation, the use of venovenous
bypass permits better surgical exposure, allowing more
meticulous dissection, resection of the tumor mass and
vena cava, and insertion of a polytetraﬂuoroethylene graft
(GORE-TEX, WL Gore, Flagstaff, AZ) when indicated. CARDIOPULMONARY
AND VENOVENOUS BYPASS
FOR OTHER INDICATIONS
Cardiopulmonary Bypass
and Accidental Hypothermia
Accidental hypothermia has been a problem for millennia. Only in the 20th century did the realization come that
many patients who might otherwise be declared dead
could be resuscitated. In 1967, Kugelberg et al. (168)
described the management of a patient who presented
to their hospital with a core body temperature of 21.7◦C. Concerns about gradually warming the patient and the risk
of cardiac arrest from ventricular ﬁbrillation stimulated
the authors to rewarm the patient rapidly with bypass
using a heat exchanger and oxygenator using the left
femoral artery and vein for cannulation. The patient
was successfully rewarmed without the development of
ventricular ﬁbrillation. The authors emphasized the use
of bypass for the management of accidental hypothermia
based on their observations that the patient could be more
rapidly rewarmed; there was diminished risk of ventricular
ﬁbrillation; and in the event of ventricular ﬁbrillation,
circulation and oxygenation could be supported until
the heart was deﬁbrillated (frequently once the core
temperature was >28◦C). In other circumstances, patients
have been more emergently managed, usually while
profoundly hypothermic, and partial bypass has been
instituted while the patient underwent cardiopulmonary
resuscitation for ventricular ﬁbrillation. Several series have examined the use of CPB in
accidental hypothermia. Following a tragedy on Mount
Hood in Oregon in which 11 patients presented to the
hospital emergency department profoundly hypothermic,
10 of the patients were warmed through bypass, and
there were2 long-term survivors (174). There were no
survivors among those patients who presented with a
core temperature less than 22◦C. This would substantiate
previous reports in which successes were rarely observed
if the core temperature was this low. The two survivors
had spontaneous respiratory activity on admission to the
hospital. The issue of age in identifying patients who are
candidates is controversial. On the basis of the Bellevue
experience, youth itself is not protective when core
temperatures are below 26◦C (168). In a series reported

33. Noncardiac Surgical Applications of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
677
from England, Duguid et al. (169) described an 87%
mortality rate in 23 elderly patients treated through active
external warming and concluded that elderly patients
should not be actively rewarmed. A review of the literature
since the initial report in 1967 from Kugelberg et al. would indicate a much higher success rate (approximately
50%–70%), but the success rate is only 50% if isolated case
reports are excluded. A recent report from Switzerland
described 32 patients in whom CPB was attempted;
15 (47%) were long-term survivors who had minimal
sequelae. Most of the patients were young (mean age
25 years), well conditioned, mountain climbers (170). On the basis of these results and other work, Lazar
advocates CPB as the treatment of choice for any patient
with accidental hypothermia, cardiac arrest, and core
temperatures of less than 32◦C. CPB should also be
considered for any patient with a core temperature less
than 32◦C even if hemodynamics are stable (because
of the risk of ventricular ﬁbrillation) (171). CPB is
contraindicated in patients with temperatures greater than
or equal to 32◦C, and in patients with serum potassium of
10 mEq/L or greater. Advanced age (older than 65 years)
is a relative contraindication (171). A review of the previous reports indicates a dire prognosis if the core temperature is less than 16◦C. The
length of time of the hypothermic insult, independent
of core temperature, is another factor in determining
the prognosis. Furthermore, prognosis for patients without some evidence of respiratory activity or with chronic
health problems is sufﬁciently poor that aggressive rewarming with bypass needs to be carefully considered
in these particular circumstances. In managing these
patients, hemoconcentration, electrolyte abnormalities,
hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, and pulmonary and cardiac
problems have been reported, and renal failure secondary
to myoglobinuria is a major concern. Whether or not CPB is useful in these profoundly hypothermic patients remains, however, controversial. A recent study from New York described 16 patients with core
temperatures of between 25◦and 32◦C. All were successfully managed using warmed intravenous ﬂuids, heated
aerosol masks, and, occasionally, warm peritoneal dialysis (172). The decision of whether to use bypass to warm a
profoundly hypothermic patient is best made by the physicians managing the patient and is based on their assessment of the patient’s status and availability of resources.

Several case reports have indicated that patients who
are hypothermic following an overdose with heroin (173)
or barbiturates can also be successfully resuscitated using
bypass (174). In contrast to patients who experience
accidental hypothermia, the patients with barbiturateinduced comas have higher core temperatures and tend to
be older patients. Outcome is improved if the patient can
be rewarmed, and one of the advantages of bypass is the
ability to include a ﬁlter to dialyze barbiturates (175). Vascular Procedures
Although uncommon, bypass with and without hypothermia has been used for a number of rare and exotic vascular
problems. These reports all include the presence of a ﬁstula
or aneurysm that would not be amenable to repair without either circulatory arrest or a degree of hypothermia
requiring bypass. There are reports of aortovenous ﬁstulas
affecting the aorta and vena cava (176), and the aorta and
renal vein (177) repaired using bypass, profound hypothermia, and circulatory arrest. A variety of aneurysms and
ﬁstulas (178,179), hemangiomas (180), and vascular malformations of the face have also been reported (181,182). Although surgical repair of renal artery abnormalities is
commonly performed in situ occasionally autotransplantation with or without extracorporeal surgery is required. In cases in which extracorporeal surgery is performed,
the kidney can be placed in a Euro-Collins slush on a
workbench and perfused with cold (4◦–7◦C) Euro-Collins
solution (183). Orthopedic Procedures
In the 1950s and 1960s, bypass techniques were used
to administer high concentrations of chemotherapeutic
agents to discrete regions of the body (184). This technique
was used most frequently on patients with neoplasms
of the lower extremities. A bypass technique was used
employing a small oxygenator in which the artery and vein
that supplied the tumor area were isolated and cannulated. For the lower extremities, the common femoral artery and
vein were most frequently cannulated. The arm could
likewise be treated utilizing an axillary artery and vein. Complete isolation of the limb was accomplished by
applying a tourniquet proximal to the cannulas. Perfusion
was usually brief, lasting from 15 to 30 minutes. Although
this technique held promise, other treatment modalities
have largely supplanted regional perfusion techniques. However, some centers continue to use this technique
experimentally.

SUMMARY
Despite enthusiasm in the 1960s for the use of CPB as
an adjunct in a variety of surgical cases, the primary
use currently is to facilitate the surgical correction of
cardiac and aortic lesions. However, bypass techniques
developed for these procedures have indications in other
cases in which they are clearly life saving. Certain neurosurgical and urologic procedures can only be undertaken
and successfully completed when CPB, profound hypothermia, and circulatory arrest are used. Furthermore,
certain pulmonary procedures are only possible when
systemic oxygenation is supplied through CPB. The principles developed for CPB have led to the development of

678
V. Clinical Applications
effective venovenous bypass techniques that have been
used in hepatic transplantation and in other procedures
involving the abdominal viscera. There are other uncommon conditions in which CPB and venovenous bypass
can be used that improve patient survival and decrease
morbidity. It is imperative that the surgical and anesthetic teams
have the necessary experience to use these techniques,
which are frequently gained in using CPB for cardiac
procedures. A well trained, experienced, and knowledgeable team signiﬁcantly decreases morbidity and improves
survival. KEY POINTS
■Principle noncardiac surgical applications of CPB
include the following:
●Induction of deep hypothermia for circulatory
arrest (DHCA)
●Pulmonary bypass for embolectomy, airway procedures or lung transplantation
●Venoarterial or venovenous bypass to facilitate
hepatic surgery
●Rewarming following accidental hypothermia
■Management of CPB per se (anesthetic, anticoagulation, monitoring, circulatory arrest, etc) is
not fundamentally different from that for cardiac
surgery. ●Pharmacologic management of DHCA (use of
barbiturates, alkalinization, steroids and mannitol)
remains controversial
■Use for neurosurgical procedures includes the following:
●Less commonly used now than in the past
●Predominant use in giant aneurysms and vascular
malformations
■Use for urological surgery procedures largely limited
to renal cell carcinomas with vena caval and/or right
atrial invasion
■Thoracic surgery uses include the following:
●Uncommonly used for tracheal or carinal surgery
●Frequently necessary for pulmonary embolectomy
●Required in approximately 5% of single-lung transplants due to inability to maintain oxygenation
with single-lung ventilation
■Rewarming following accidental hypothermia includes the following:
●Lower success rate with presenting temperatures
less than 20◦–22◦C and in the elderly
■Resurgence of use in support of interventional
procedures in the cardiac catheterization laboratory
for patients who are not surgical candidates. ●Percutaneous partial left heart bypass

◗Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Overview: State of the Art and Future
Carmen Giacomuzzi, Brian Mejak, and Irving Shen
Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is still necessary for the
repair or palliation of many congenital defects in infants
and children. The current trend in pediatric cardiac
surgery is to repair congenital heart defects early before
the heart and the patient undergo deleterious adaptation
to the abnormal physiology. However, major morbidity
can occur as a result of exposure to CPB. The exposure
to such a large foreign surface area of the CPB circuit
can lead to a substantial inﬂammatory reaction that
can create signiﬁcant hemodynamic instability and ﬂuid
shifts. Extreme variability exists in pediatric practice patterns
among both congenital heart surgeons and perfusionists. CPB strategies are rapidly changing for many practices
and it is difﬁcult to deﬁne a ‘‘standard of care’’ versus
variability of preference in pediatric CPB techniques. It is
not the aim of this chapter to deﬁne what the ‘‘standard of
care’’ should be or to provide an exhaustive and in-depth
list of all possible techniques and interventions. Rather,
our goal is to review some of the physiologic effects of CPB
on the different organ systems, the various components
of the CPB circuit, and strategies employed in the safe
application of CPB to neonates, infants and children, that
many institutions, including our own, ﬁnd useful. PHYSIOLOGIC EFFECTS OF
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Cardiopulmonary bypass for pediatric cardiac procedures
often requires the extremes of temperature, hemodilution,
and perfusion ﬂow rates. Certain anatomic features, such
as the presence of large aortoplumonary collaterals or
interrupted aortic arch, will require alterations of bypass
strategies, cannulation techniques, or the use of deep
hypothermia with circulatory arrest. As a result, CPB for
the correction of congenital cardiac defects in pediatric
patients has a profound physiologic effect on most organ
systems of the body. The deleterious effects of CPB are often more pronounced in neonates and infants than those seen in
adults. One of the reasons is because many organs like the
brain, lungs, coagulation system, and endocrine system
are still immature during infancy. Furthermore, neonates
and infants have higher metabolic demands and therefore require a higher perfusion ﬂow rate per body surface
area. This may result in higher shear stress on blood-cell
components.

Another reason why CPB can affect infants
differently when compared to adults is because of the
tremendous disparity between the CPB circuit size and
the patient. Even with the recent advances in circuit
miniaturization, the priming volume of the CPB circuit
is still often much larger than the total blood volume of
neonates and infants. This results in signiﬁcant dilution of
clotting factors, red blood cells (RBCs), and other plasma
proteins. Finally, surgical procedures to correct many congenital cardiac defects in infants often require the use of
hypothermia and low perfusion ﬂow rates to help facilitate
exposure. The physiologic effects of CPB on the various
organ systems have been studied extensively but particularly on the brain and the heart. As such, separate chapters
in this book will be devoted to the effect of CPB on these
two organ systems. Endocrine
CPB raises the level of most stress hormones in the
body with a normally functioning endocrine system. This
elevation may in part be due to surgical stress. The
level of native catecholamines, such as epinephrine and
norepinephrine, rises dramatically during the initiation
of CPB (1) and persists into the postoperative period. Hypothermia also has the effect of raising the serum catecholamine levels, not only by increasing the production,
but also by the downregulation of catecholamine receptors (2,3). Catecholamine levels tend to fall rapidly once
CPB is discontinued. The level of cortisol also increases
at the initiation of surgery but falls during CPB (2). This
685

686
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
fall is most likely secondary to hemodilution. After CPB,
the level begins to rise again and this increase continues
for approximately 24 hours after which it gradually falls
to normal levels (4). The levels of other stress hormones,
such as vasopressin (5,6), glucagons, and human growth
hormone (7), also increase during CPB. The elevation of
vasopressin level may persist for up to 48 to 72 hours
after surgery. The elevated levels of glucagon and human
growth hormone persist for only a few hours following the
termination of CPB. Hypothermic CPB can cause a decrease in insulin
level as well as a decrease in peripheral response to this
hormone (8). Therefore, it is common to see a rise in serum
glucose level during CPB. The level of insulin gradually
increases after termination of hypothermic CPB. Renal
Renal dysfunction is a major source of morbidity following
CPB. It is not uncommon to see temporary oliguric
renal dysfunction in neonates after CPB (9). The exact
mechanism of this renal dysfunction is unclear but
generally renal function will gradually improve by 24
to 48 hours after surgery. Surgical stress can result in
a decrease in renal blood ﬂow and glomerular ﬁltration
rate (10,11). This may be in part due to the elevation of
some of the stress hormones like vasopressin, epinephrine,
and norepinephrine. The pattern of blood ﬂow through
the renal parenchyma is also altered in that cortical blood
ﬂow is usually decreased in favor of more blood ﬂow to the
medulla (9,11). Finally, CPB can promote the activation
of the renin–angiotensin system (12) leading to increased
aldosterone production and ﬂuid retention. Pulmonary
Some of the alteration of pulmonary function after cardiac surgery may not be entirely attributable to the effect
of CPB. This is because many children with congenital
cardiac defects will already have abnormal respiratory mechanics before surgery due to excessive blood ﬂow through
the lung parenchyma (13–15,17). Pulmonary overcirculation can lead to pulmonary hypertension, decreased lung
compliance, and increased airway resistance. Surgery using CPB to correct these defects and decrease the amount
of pulmonary overcirculation will result in an immediate
and sustained improvement of total respiratory resistance (18,19). However, cardiac surgery using CPB on
patients with either normal or reduced pulmonary blood
ﬂow before surgery will usually cause a decrease in dynamic respiratory compliance.

The large population of
inﬂammatory cells residing in the lung parenchyma is
suspected to play a large role in mediating the mechanism
of injury seen after CPB. Hypothermic CPB can cause
leukocyte degranulation and complement activation (20). This will lead to diffuse endothelial injury (21) resulting
in increased capillary permeability and accumulation of
ﬂuid in the interstitial and alveolar space (22) and atelectasis (23). This will be seen as a reduction in static
and dynamic compliance, functional residual capacity,
and a worsening ventilation/perfusion mismatch. Because
the inﬂammatory system plays such a prominent role in
mediating the lung injury after CPB, powerful but yet non-
speciﬁc anti-inﬂammatory agents, like steroid, have been
used as an attempt to attenuate the deleterious effect of
CPB on the lungs. The use of high-dose steroid 8 hours
before exposure to CPB have been shown to reduce the
accumulation of lung water and improve post-CPB pulmonary compliance and pulmonary hypertension (24). EXTRACORPOREAL CIRCUIT
Pumps
Two types of pumps, roller and centrifugal, are currently
used for pediatric CPB. The roller pump or positive
displacement pump consists of two rollers oriented 180
degrees from one another. Each roller compresses tubing
placed in the raceway and propels the blood forward
in the tubing. Roller heads are the pumps of choice
in 90% of pediatric centers (25). One reason for this is
the roller pump delivers a precise amount of volume at
low ﬂow rates (<0.500 L/min). Roller pumps are set to
‘‘just-occlusive’’ which will promote the forward ﬂow of
blood yet reduce the amount of hemolysis and trauma to
the formed elements of blood. Historically, the drawback
to using roller pumps was that they were always in a
ﬁxed position on the base of the heart–lung machine. Newer generation heart–lung machines have alleviated
this problem by making the roller pumps mobile so
they can be placed within inches of the reservoir and
oxygenator. Centrifugal pumps are nonocclusive pumps,
which operate on the principle of entraining blood into the
pump by a vortexing action of spinning impeller blades
or rotating cones. Centrifugal pumps enjoy the aspects of
being very mobile, less traumatic on the formed elements
of blood, and will reduce its ﬂow when obstruction of
the outlet occurs.

In the past, centrifugal pumps were
used less in pediatrics because of their inaccuracy at low
ﬂow rates (<0.500 L/min) and high prime volumes. Newer
generation pumps with priming volumes of 13–32 mL
have addressed these issues and their use will most likely
increase in the future. Tubing

In the pediatric population, oxygenators must provide
efﬁcient gas exchange over a wide range of temperatures
(10◦C–40◦C), pump ﬂow rates (0–200 mL/kg/min), Hct
(15%–40%), line pressures, and gas ﬂow rates. Hollow ﬁber
oxygenators are made up of microporous polypropylene
ﬁbers in which the gas exchange occurs through pores
that are 3 to 5 µm in size (see Chapter 4). Fibers may
be treated with the same heparin-based or nonheparinbased polymers that are coated on tubing surfaces
as previously mentioned. In addition to gas exchange,
oxygenators contain an integrated heat exchanger and
can also function as an effective device for handling air. One drawback to hollow ﬁber oxygenators is that when
negative pressure develops on the blood side of the ﬁbers
or when the gas exhaust becomes obstructed, air can easily
be entrained into the blood. Newer generation oxygenators, such as the Sorin Lilliput I and Terumo BabyRx, have a lower priming volume,
less pressure drops, and higher gas transfer capability. The
Terumo BabyRx is a neonatal oxygenator with a priming
volume of 43 mL and has a maximum ﬂow rate of 1.5

volume and therefore less hemodilution. The higher ﬂow
rate allows for its usage on patients up to 12–15 kg in size. As patient size increases, larger oxygenators must be employed to satisfy increased metabolic needs of the patient. The Minimax (Medtronic), Lilliput II (Sorin), and SX10
(Terumo), and Rx15 (Terumo) are intermediate oxygenators, which can provide a maximum ﬂow range from 2.3

Hemoconcentrators used in pediatric patients range in

the condition of blood primes by removing crystalloid,
excess potassium, and lactic acid from donor blood. Cardioplegia devices are generally made up of a heat
exchanger and a luer port to monitor line pressure. Their priming volumes range from 7 mL to 35 mL. These devices can be customized to deliver various bloodto-crystalloid ratios. The Myocardial Protection System
(Quest Biomedical) is unique in that potassium and other
drugs can be added directly to the cardioplegia without
having to predilute them in a crystalloid mixture. In-line venous saturation and hematocrit monitoring
can be accomplished by placing a sensor in the venous return line. Real-time blood parameter monitoring systems
have recently gained wide acceptance. The sensors are
placed in shunt lines on either or both venous and arterial

shunt ﬂow through the sensor on the arterial line, a transonic ﬂow meter can be used to measure the precise blood
ﬂow to the patient. Another monitoring device gaining acceptance is the use of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)
to measure cerebral saturations (see Chapter 18). Prime
Development of smaller devices and reﬁnement of blood
salvaging techniques have made bloodless surgery in the
smallest of neonates an achievable goal. Priming the
bypass circuit without using blood from donors can avoid
the potential risks of allogenic blood transfusion such as
viral transmission, febrile reactions, and incompatibility
issues. It has been shown that using blood prime in the
CPB circuit is associated with a lower cardiac index,
a higher pulmonary vascular resistance, and a higher
level of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels after
surgery (30) when compared to using an asanguineous
prime. The difﬁculty is determining when the beneﬁts
of a patient receiving blood outweigh the harmful side
effects. Certainly patients with lower hematocrits, but
still able to maintain adequate venous saturations, low
lactate levels, baseline cerebral saturations, and minimal
acidosis, do not necessitate the transfusion of red blood
cells.

Patients with a hematocrit of 20% on CPB show
no difference in lactate levels, oxygen delivery, and oxygen
consumption when compared to a group with 25% as their
lowest acceptable hematocrit (31). Widespread reductions

Mannitol in the prime offers the advantages

Management of Anticoagulation
Neonates and infants are at greater risk for bleeding
diathesis following cardiac surgery due to their immature clotting system, lower levels of circulating volume of
antithrombin III (ATIII), decreased von Willebrand factor,
and reduced platelet aggregation.

Furthermore, neonates
with cyanotic heart defects have further hemostatic impairment due to polycythemia, thrombocytopenia, abnormal platelet functions, decreased levels of factors V,
VII, and VIII, and an increase in ﬁbrinolysis (38,39). Anticoagulation, however, is a critical necessity during
CPB. Providing an adequate anticoagulant environment
on CPB is further complicated in neonates and infants
when hemodilution and hypothermia can also inﬂuence
the clotting mechanism. An empirical heparin loading
dose of 300 to 400 units/kg is generally used, and maintaining the activated clotting time (ACT) greater than 480
seconds has been the gold standard for measuring adequate anticoagulation on bypass. However, neonates have
a much greater variation of response to heparin administration, which can manifest as either a greater resistance
or sensitivity to heparin (40–42). This may be due to varying levels of circulating ATIII. Rather than using a ﬁxed
dose protocol of heparin in neonates and infants, it may
be more precise to individualize heparin dose for each patient by evaluating their response to heparin, measuring
their heparin concentration during the course of CPB, and
then adjusting the dose accordingly. Although heparin is the anticoagulant of choice for
CPB, some patients are allergic to heparin and therefore
an alternative anticoagulant must be used. Two alternative
anticoagulants that have been used in adults undergoing
CPB are danaparoid and argatroban. The predictable
dose response of argatroban, its lack of renal toxicity,
and its anticoagulation effect make it an attractive
alternative to heparin (43) Argatroban can easily be
monitored by ACTs and partial thromboplastin time
(PTT). However, argatroban, with its relatively longer
half-life (39–51 minutes) and the lack of a reversal agent
that can neutralize its anticoagulation effect, will limit its
widespread use as a heparin substitute for CPB in infants
and children. Cannulation
Arterial Cannulation
In neonates and infants, the aortic cannula tip should be
small enough to facilitate insertion into a tiny aorta but
yet big enough to allow adequate arterial inﬂow from the
bypass pump without excessive perfusion pressure and
causing too much hemolysis. Furthermore, the arterial
cannula, while inside the aorta, should be small enough

690
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
so that it will not signiﬁcantly impede the normal ﬂow
of aortic blood around it. Maintaining ﬂow around
the cannula is particularly important while the arterial
cannula is inside the aorta before the initiation of CPB or
after weaning from CPB. Excessive pressure in the cannula
tip may create a powerful jet of blood, which can damage
the intima of the aorta and blood cellular elements. The arterial cannula is generally placed into the
ascending aorta; however, the anatomy of the patient
and the type of surgical procedure may inﬂuence arterial
cannula placement. For example, in hypoplastic left heart
syndrome, the ascending aorta can be 1 to 5 mm in size,
which is too small to accommodate a cannula capable
of providing systemic perfusion. As an alternative, the
arterial cannula can be placed in the main pulmonary
artery or through a side graft placed at the base of
the innominate artery. Coronary perfusion is retrograde
through the hypoplastic ascending aorta. The right and left
pulmonary arteries are occluded with snares to prevent
excessive runoff from the systemic circulation to the
pulmonary vascular bed. In newborns with transposition
of the great arteries, the arterial cannula is placed in
a more distal aspect of the ascending aorta because a
large portion of the surgery is performed on the aortic
root. Infants with interrupted aortic arch require two
aortic cannulas—one in the ascending aorta to perfuse
the head vessels and another one through the patent
ductus arteriosus to perfuse the descending aorta and
the lower body. Direct cannulation of the femoral artery
is not commonly used in neonatal or infant heart
surgery because the femoral vessels are usually too
small. However, older children who had prior cardiac
operation and are at a high risk of inadvertent injury to
vital intrathoracic vascular structures with reoperation
sternotomy, femoral or iliac arterial cannulation should
be considered. Malposition of the aortic cannula is not an uncommon
problem in neonates and infants. If the tip of the aortic
cannula is placed too distally into the aortic arch or even
in the proximal descending aorta, a Venturi effect can
be created where arterial ﬂow from the bypass pump will
preferentially go to the lower body rather than to the upper
body and the brain.

Such a scenario should be suspected
if the bladder or the rectal temperature does not fall as
quickly as the nasopharyngeal temperature during active
cooling while on CPB. Venous Cannulation
To meet the needs of different patient sizes and venous
anatomy, a large assortment of venous cannulas should
be available. The type of venous cannula used and the
amount of venous return it yields will vary depending
on cannula size, patient anatomy, site of insertion, and
adequacy of cannula position. Venous anatomy in patients with congenital cardiac
defects can be very complex. Bilateral superior vena
cava (SVC), interrupted inferior vena cava (IVC) that
drains into an azygos vein or hemiazygous vein, or
hepatic veins that drain directly into an atrial chamber
are common anatomic variations. Venous cannulation
must account for these variables if the repair is to take
place during continuous-ﬂow CPB. In contrast, a repair
under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) can be
achieved with a large single venous cannula placed in the
right atrium. Direct cannulation using right-angle venous
cannulas may provide more effective venous drainage and
less obstruction of the surgical ﬁeld. Appropriate placement of venous cannula is important
in achieving effective systemic perfusion. A poorly positioned venous cannula has the potential to cause vena
caval obstruction. A cannula in the IVC can obstruct venous return from the splanchnic bed, resulting in ascites
from increased hydrostatic pressure, or it can directly
reduce perfusion pressure across the mesenteric, renal,
and hepatic vascular beds. Likewise, obstruction of the
SVC is possible. This can elevate jugular venous pressure,
decrease cerebral perfusion pressure, and cause cerebral
edema. Monitoring SVC pressures directly through an internal jugular line or looking at the patient’s head for
venous distension may be ways to detect systemic venous
congestion after initiation of bypass. More recently, reports have shown that using NIRS can be a useful adjunct
for troubleshooting cannula-related issues (44,45). Initiation of Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Once the aortic and venous cannulas are placed and
connected to the arterial and venous limbs of the
extracorporeal circuit, CPB is initiated. Institutional
techniques for initiating bypass can vary greatly. This
can be dependent on patient body surface area, degree of
cooling desired, and degree of hemodilution or blood
conservation that can be achieved. One method for
initiating CPB in neonates and infants is to begin the
arterial inﬂow ﬁrst.

Once the arterial ﬂow through the
aortic cannula is certain, the venous line is slowly
unclamped and blood is drained out of the right atrium
into the inlet of the oxygenator reservoir. Assuring forward
ﬂow before the venous line is unclamped prevents the
potential problem of patient exsanguination in the event
of a malposition of the aortic cannula, a mechanical
pump failure, or a cannulation-induced aortic dissection. As venous blood begins to accumulate in the reservoir,
arterial pump ﬂow rates are then increased until the
desired ﬂow rate is achieved. The rate at which venous
blood is drained from the patient is determined by
the difference in height between the patient and the
oxygenator reservoir inlet, as well as the diameter and
length of the tubing. During bicaval cannulation, achieving

34. Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Bypass Overview: State of the Art and Future
691
full ﬂow rates may be difﬁcult until adequate venous
return is achieved when both cavae are cannulated. If
venous return is diminished or the arterial line pressure
is high, pump ﬂow rates must be reduced until the
problem is identiﬁed and resolved. This is usually caused
by malposition or kinking of the venous or arterial cannula
and can easily be corrected. Once CPB commences, it is
essential to observe the heart for ventricular distension. This is especially true in infants and neonates, in whom
ventricular compliance is low and the heart is relatively
intolerant of excessive preload augmentation because of
a ﬂat Starling curve. If distension occurs, the heart may
be vented or a pump sucker can be placed into the right
atrium. With the current trend towards the avoidance of intraoperative allogenic blood transfusion, the use of asanguineous primes often can be achieved through circuit
miniaturization. One of the techniques of decreasing the
priming volume is the use of vacuum-assisted venous
drainage (VAVD), where negative pressure is applied to
the venous reservoir. This technique was initially developed to facilitate venous drainage for minimally invasive
surgery. This has been gaining popularity and is becoming especially advantageous in the neonatal and pediatric
population for reducing circuit size and thereby decreasing priming volume. Furthermore, VAVD can allow the
use of smaller venous cannula in smaller neonates and it
can avoid the problem of airlock when occasional air gets
into the venous line. Although VAVD can be used routinely
and safely in pediatric perfusion, it is important to take
some precautions to avoid the various complications that
have been associated with its use (46–49). Some of these
safety precautions include monitoring both the positive
and negative pressures of the cardiotomy and regulating
the vacuum to no stronger than −20 mmHg, waiting to
apply vacuum at the initiation of CPB until some venous
return is achieved, and discontinuing vacuum before coming off bypass. With VAVD, it is theoretically not necessary
to prime the venous side of the circuit, although routine
use of this practice is currently not recommended. The technique of using RAP (see earlier discussion)
alters the sequence of events when initiating bypass. Our
preferred technique utilizes autologous venous blood to
prime most of the circuit.

This has the advantage of
producing less hemodynamic instability and offers the
option of instituting bypass immediately if doing so is not
tolerated well by the patient. When initiating bypass in this
sequence, we suggest that a test transfusion through the
arterial line be performed just before draining the patient
to assure optimal placement of the arterial cannula. Other
groups have advocated collecting approximately 10 to
20 mL/kg body weight of whole blood from patients either
before heparinization or immediately after institution of
CPB, to be transfused after the patient has been weaned
from CPB. This, in theory, returns functional platelets and
clotting factors back to the patient to aid hemostasis. We
prefer autologous blood removal before heparinization to
prevent activation of platelets by heparin. With all of the
techniques described in the preceding text, small doses
of neosynephrine may be necessary to increase blood
pressure transiently during prime and/or blood removal. Temperature Management
Hypothermia
The use of hypothermia in conjunction with CPB provides
several advantages. Hypothermia allows decreases in
pump ﬂow rates, which facilitate surgical exposure,
decreased rate of myocardial rewarming, and some
protection to other organs during periods of CPB and low-
ﬂow states. The degree of hypothermia selected depends
on the needs for reduced ﬂow to enhance surgical repair. Three ranges of hypothermia are (a) mild (30◦C–34◦C),
(b) moderate (23◦C–29◦C), and (c) deep (13◦C–22◦C). The
current trend is to perform most operative repair under
mild hypothermia in neonates and infants. More complex
procedures or in patients with signiﬁcant aortopulmonary
collaterals, moderate hypothermia with a slower pump
ﬂow rate may decrease the amount of blood return to
the heart and prevent cardiac rewarming during a longer
aortic cross-clamp period. Optimal pump ﬂow rates for children are based on
body surface area and is dependent on whether adequate
organ perfusion can be maintained as determined by
arterial blood gases, acid–base balance, and whole body O2
consumption during CPB. Recommended normothermic
pump ﬂow rates based on body weight are listed in
Table 5. At hypothermic temperatures, metabolism is
reduced and therefore pump ﬂow rates may be further
reduced accordingly. Decisions on ﬂow rates determine
the size of cannulae chosen. Deep hypothermia is used when periods of low ﬂow
or DHCA are desired.

At deep hypothermia, cellular
metabolism is so low and membrane ﬂuidity is reduced to
such a large extent that cellular basal metabolic needs can
be met and cellular membrane integrity can be maintained
for a relatively prolonged period of ischemia. The principal
clinical effect of hypothermia is the reduction in metabolic
rate and molecular movement. As the temperature is

the resting tension of the myocardium in response to
a sudden decrease in perfusion temperature. This is
referred to as a rapid cooling contracture (53), which may
be the consequence of a sudden release of intracellular
calcium stores within the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

This
cold-induced increase in resting myocardial tone may lead
to impaired recovery of systolic and diastolic function
after reperfusion, which has led some groups to avoid
cold perfusion of the heart before the aortic cross-clamp
is applied and to use warm induction cardioplegia when
possible (37,54). However, rapid cooling, when performed
in an appropriate setting, may not impair ventricular
function. With the ‘‘hypocalcemic’’ primes commonly used
in neonatal heart surgery today, rapid cooling and cold
induction of ischemia does not seem to be deleterious (55). In recent years, there has been a movement towards
avoidance of using DHCA during repair of cardiac defects
in neonates and infants. Improvements in circuit technology along with advances in cannula and vent design
have made it easier and safer to employ bicaval cannulation and continuous hypothermic low-ﬂow perfusion
to tiny patients. Concurrent improvements in myocardial
protection have allowed prolonged periods of myocardial
ischemia during moderate hypothermia with successful
outcomes (see Chapter 10). The impact of these advances
is that the simple strategy of rapidly cooling a patient
to 18◦C and turning the pump off for periods exceeding
45 to 60 minutes, have been replaced with alternative,
albeit more complex methods, which avoid the use of any
period of DHCA. Although it is indeed possible to provide continuous CPB to almost any patient, the question
of which strategy is best is not yet determined. Numerous experimental studies have clearly demonstrated that
the brain is not adequately protected by the methods of
DHCA as they were used in the 1980s and early 1990s (56). Despite the successful cardiac outcomes that were being achieved, patients were probably being neurologically
injured by the strategy of DHCA in the format it was
offered. However, continuous hypothermic low-ﬂow perfusion exposes patients to prolonged duration of CPB
and the consequences of prolonged CPB exposure have
enormous impact on postoperative convalescence. Furthermore, there is a growing body of data that continuous
hypothermic low-ﬂow CPB might lead to more soft tissue
edema, diminished pulmonary function (57), substantial
cerebral edema (58), and damage to neuronal golgi apparatus (59). Experimental data suggest that there is some
acute neurologic metabolic injury following prolonged exposure to continuous hypothermic low-ﬂow CPB that is
not apparent if the brain is exposed to short durations of

34. Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Bypass Overview: State of the Art and Future
693
DHCA (58). However, a recently published study failed to
show a signiﬁcant difference between using either strategy of DHCA or low-ﬂow hypothermic reperfusion (60). Regardless of the strategy used, both groups showed neurologic impairment, just in different areas. In a companion
article, the issue surrounding the ‘‘safe’’ period of CA was
also looked at (61). This group suggests that as long as the
arrest duration did not exceed 41 minutes, neurodevelopmental outcomes were typically not adversely affected. This is in contrast to previous evidence that the safe arrest
period is 39 to 65 minutes. An alternative strategy to both DHCA and low-ﬂow
perfusion is CA with intermittent periods of reperfusion. Langley et al., (58) and Mault et al., (62), demonstrated
that periods of DHCA of up to 60 minutes can be
associated with normal recovery of cerebral metabolism
and preservation of neural microarchitecture if the brain
is perfused for 1 minute (50 mL/kg/min) every 15 to 20
minutes. This means that sequential periods of DHCA can
be used as long as they are not prolonged beyond 15
to 20 minutes. If the brain is perfused between periods
of DHCA, the durations of the DHCA periods are not
additive (63–65). During the period of DHCA, the head
should be packed in ice to add an additional level of
protection (66). Substantial research has been performed over the last
15 years regarding how to apply the strategy of DHCA more
safely (67). This research has led to several modiﬁcations
for applying DHCA such as (a) prebypass treatment with
steroids and aprotinin (68), (b) hyperoxygenation before
the initiation of DHCA (69), (c) adequate duration of
cooling (>20 minutes) (56) to ensure more uniform and
homogeneous brain protection, (d) maintenance of higher
hematocrits during the cooling phase, (e) using pH stat
blood gas management strategy (68) during the cooling
phase especially for ‘‘high-risk’’ patients (e.g. those with
aortopulmonary collaterals or those with preoperative
cyanosis) (70,71), (f) limiting the duration of DHCA
exposure by providing intermittent cerebral perfusion for
1 to 2 minutes at 15- to 20-minute intervals (58), and
(g) the use of modiﬁed ultraﬁltration (MUF) following
CPB (72) (see Chapter 18).

Modiﬁcations in the technique
of applying DHCA have made DHCA one of the tools for
some high-risk patients and can improve the outcomes for
these patients. It is essential for surgeons to understand
the risks and beneﬁts of the various strategies available
and to learn how to use them all in the most appropriate
manner. Controversy still exists regarding what the maximum
allowable temperature gradient should be during cooling. Studies performed more than 40 years ago suggest that
arterial gas emboli can occur during cooling when cold
perfusate leaving the heat exchanger is mixed with warm
patient blood upon contact (73–75). This is because gas
has a lower solubility in cold liquid than in warm liquid. However, these studies were performed with bubble
oxygenators and without arterial line ﬁlters so it is difﬁcult
to say whether these results would still be clinically
relevant now. In fact, other studies (76,77) failed to
demonstrate any formation of gas emboli even during
rapid cooling. Despite these ﬁndings, most institutions do
follow temperature gradients upon cooling that do not
exceed 8◦C–10◦C (25). Rewarming
As in cooling, careful attention should be paid towards
following an 8◦C to 10◦C temperature gradient during
rewarming. Formation of gas emboli during rewarming
has been shown when a critical temperature gradient
has been exceeded between the perfusate temperature
leaving the heat exchanger and the patient (77,78). This
occurs as a result of gas bubbles coming out of solution
during rewarming. As mentioned previously, these studies
have been performed using a bubble oxygenator so it
is difﬁcult to say what the clinically impact would be
using newer generation of oxygenators. Geissler et al., (78)
showed that although minimal gaseous microemboli were
detected at the aortic arch at temperature gradients of
10◦C or higher, no emboli were detected at the common
carotid artery or descending aorta. This suggests that these
gaseous emboli quickly dispersed below detectable limits
and their clinical relevance thereby questionable. Despite
this, recent publications show that 100% of institutions
surveyed do follow a protocol for limiting temperature
gradients during rewarming, with the average gradient
being 9.4◦C (25,79). Patient temperature is typically monitored in at least
two different body sites during CPB: tympanic, nasopharyngeal, or esophageal (estimating cerebral temperatures),
and rectal or bladder (estimating core temperatures).

The
core temperature usually lags 2 to 3 degrees behind the
cerebral temperature during cooling or rewarming. A
larger gradient between these two temperatures may indicate problems with positioning of the temperature probes
or the aortic cannula. Pulsatile versus Nonpulsatile Flow
The difference between pulsatile and nonpulsatile perfusion has been studied extensively since the introduction
of extracorporeal circulation in the 1950s. Several investigators have shown that the use of pulsatile ﬂow may have
physiologic beneﬁts on vital organ function during and after bypass with or without the use of DHCA (80–82). Others
have found that the production of nitric oxide, a potent
vasodilator, from cultured endothelial cells is increased
during pulsatile ﬂow in comparison with nonpulsatile
ﬂow (83). This may be important at the microcirculatory

694

level affecting vascular endothelial function, thrombogenicity, and overall vascular tone. Yet others have shown
no difference in cerebral blood ﬂow either before or after
the arrest period in a neonatal porcine model of CPB and
CA (82–84). One of the main reasons for the controversy
between these two techniques appears to be the lack of
a universally accepted deﬁnition of pulsatile and nonpulsatile pressure-ﬂow waveforms for direct comparison. The
clinical superiority of pulsatile perfusion over nonpulsatile
perfusion is still debated and only a few pediatric cardiac
centers routinely use it. Acid–Base Management
There are two divergent strategies to manage blood
gas acid–base status during hypothermic CPB: α-stat
(temperature uncorrected) and pH-stat (temperature corrected) (53,68,72,85–89). These management strategies are
base on the principle that the solubility of carbon dioxide
in blood decreases with hypothermia. Therefore, blood
pH will rise with hypothermia unless exogenous carbon
dioxide is added to the oxygenator to bring the blood pH
back toward neutral. α-stat acid–base management strategy maintains a pH of 7.40, measured without mathematic
correction for the effects of temperature, whereas pH-stat
uses a mathematic correction for the effects of temperature on pH. During moderate hypothermia, selecting one
blood gas management strategy over the other appears
less critical because intracellular pH differences in the
brain are small (90,91). However, during deep hypothermia or DHCA, evidence suggests that the addition of CO2
to the oxygenator (pH-stat) causes cerebral vasodilatation
and more homogenous cerebral cooling, promotes greater
oxygen delivery by causing a rightward shift in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, and greater suppression of
cerebral metabolic rate. Moreover, cyanotic neonates and
children with known aortopulmonary collateral vessels
may especially beneﬁt from pH-stat strategy during early
cooling because less blood is shunted through the collateral vessels into the pulmonary bed in favor of more blood
going to the cerebral circulation (71). More recent animal
data also supports superior cerebral protection during
DHCA with the use of pH-stat management as compared
to α-stat (92–94). Argument for using α-stat management
during hypothermia or DHCA is that the relative alkalinity just before onset of CA is beneﬁcial. This alkaline
milieu supports a more normal cellular transmembrane
pH gradient and enzymatic function.

In an effort to gain
the beneﬁts of pH-stat on cooling and to eliminate its negative effects on enzymatic function, a combined strategy
for blood gas management can be used in which pH-stat
is used during initial cooling followed by changing to
α-stat before ischemic arrest. Despite these recent studies,
considerable controversy still exists over which strategy
is superior. In fact, some studies showed that neither
strategy is associated with improved neurodevelopmental
outcomes. Oxygenation Strategies
The utilization of different oxygenation strategies for infants has recently been gaining more interest. A number
of studies showed the potential beneﬁts of hyperoxygenation just before DHCA (69,95). Hyperoxia just before CA
takes advantage of increased oxygen solubility and reduced oxygen consumption by loading tissues with excess
oxygen. Alternative oxygen strategies for cyanotic infants
have also been explored. Previous clinical and experimental studies have shown that an unintended injury can
occur in response to sudden reoxygenation of the cyanotic
heart during the initiation of CPB using 100% oxygen (96). This injury is mediated by oxygen-free radicals and results
in signiﬁcant myocardial depression and pulmonary dysfunction. Initiating CPB at room air may reduce these
adverse effects. Weaning
Before weaning from CPB, it is important to make sure
that the patient has a satisfactory heart rate and rhythm,
the patient is fully rewarmed, the lungs are ventilated
adequately, and the patient’s electrolytes and acid–base
status are optimized. During weaning, the preload of the
heart is increased by partially clamping the venous return
line and reducing the arterial inﬂow until adequate blood
volume is achieved. Blood volume is assessed by direct
visualization of the heart and by measurement of the
right or left atrial ﬁlling pressures. When ﬁlling pressures
are adequate, the venous cannula is clamped and the
arterial inﬂow is stopped. The arterial cannula is left in
place for infusion of residual perfusate from the circuit. Direct cardiac visualization, intracardiac monitoring,
and intraoperative echocardiography (97–102) can all be
used to assess myocardial function. Low arterial oxygen
saturations or inability for the pulse oximeter to register
a pulse may be a sign of very low cardiac output and high
systemic resistance (103). Monitoring of regional cerebral
oxygen saturation (rSO2) can also be a useful method for
measuring cardiac output.

The rSO2 measures the ratio of
oxygen supply and demand in the brain and therefore
may indicate a serious imbalance (104). The relation
between the absolute lowest allowable cerebral saturation
values and outcomes in neonates is complex and not
known (105,106). It is likely dependent upon variables
such as the duration of desaturation, temperature (107),
and/or the presence of neuroprotective drugs (108). Some patients may have difﬁculty weaning from
CPB. Under these circumstances, the reason for failure
from weaning may be either (a) an imperfect surgical
repair or a residual defect that cannot be repaired,

34. Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Bypass Overview: State of the Art and Future
695
(b) pulmonary artery hypertension, and (c) right or left
ventricular dysfunction. Assessment using intraoperative
transesophageal echocardiography is extremely useful for
evaluating ventricular function and the quality of the
surgical repair. Another method utilizes intraoperative
assessment of the various cardiac chamber pressure and
O2 saturation. This can help uncover any residual pressure
gradients across valves or repaired sites of stenosis,
complications from the surgical repair, and residual
shunts. Tiny (3F) pressure catheters can be left in various
chambers through a transthoracic approach to help in
postoperative management
Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography with
Doppler color ﬂow is useful for assessing the quality of
surgical repair and ventricular function. Left ventricular
dysfunction can be treated by optimizing preload and
heart rate, increasing coronary perfusion pressure, correcting ionized calcium levels, and adding inotropic support. Inotropic support is usually begun with dopamine
(5 to 15 µg/kg/min) and milrinone (0.5 to 1.0 µg/kg/min). For signiﬁcant left ventricular dysfunction, epinephrine,
a more potent inotropes, is generally administered at
a dose of 0.05 to 0.1 µg/kg/min and titrated to effect. The combination of epinephrine and milrinone is very
effective for left ventricular dysfunction because it addresses left ventricular contractility through β-receptor
and non–β-receptor-mediated mechanisms (epinephrine:
β-receptor; milrinone: phosphodiesterase inhibition). Pulmonary artery hypertension is a common problem after
CPB in children. Reducing pulmonary vascular resistance is best accomplished by ventilatory manipulations. Various methods to control postoperative pulmonary hypertensive crisis include adequate oxygenation, hyperventilation, sedation, and use of pulmonary vasodilators such
as inhaled nitric oxide. If very high doses of inotropes
are required to wean from CPB and severe pulmonary
hypertension present, mechanical circulatory support
with extracorporeal membrane oxygenator (ECMO) or
a left ventricular assist device should be considered (see
Chapter 31)
Ultraﬁltration
Neonates and infants constitute a group who often develop excessive ﬂuid accumulation during their exposure
to CPB. Edema develops not only in the periphery but
also in vital areas such as the brain, heart, intestine, and
lungs. This can be partially controlled by limiting excessive crystalloid in the pump prime and by using colloids
when volume replacement is necessary. Excess ﬂuid can
be removed by various means to achieve an increase in
hematocrit to satisfy oxygen demands. Efforts have been
directed at removal of ﬂuid from these patients during or
immediately following CPB.

Removal of ﬂuid while still on
CPB (conventional ultraﬁltration) is difﬁcult in neonates
because removal of any ﬂuid from a miniaturized circuit
may require replacement to maintain adequate reservoir
levels. Oftentimes, the results with conventional ultraﬁltra-
tion are inconsistent (109). The technique of zero-balance
ultraﬁltration (Z-BUF) during CPB may be a more useful
method in the removal of ﬂuid and possibly some harmful
activated inﬂammatory mediators. This method involves
an isovolumetric exchange of ﬂuid, typically Normosol or
Plasmalyte, congruent with the amount of ultraﬁltrate removed. Z-BUF has been reported to reduce postoperative
blood loss, decrease time to extubation, and remove significant amount of circulating tissue necrosis factor, IL-10,

myeloperoxidase, and C3a (110,111). The most effective
form of ultraﬁltration appears to be the method as described by Elliott and Naik (112,113). This is referred to as
MUF because it is performed after the completion of CPB
while the aortic and venous cannulae are still in place. Most commonly, blood is oxygenated, concentrated, and
ﬁltered blood back to the heart through the venous cannula (arterial–venous MUF). MUF has the advantage of
ﬁltering the patient’s extracellular blood volume as well as
the residual circuit volume, which results in greater hemoconcentration (112). Both conventional and MUF has been
shown to remove inﬂammatory mediators from the circulation (114). However, MUF may be more effective in
concentrating the patient’s blood and in improving both,
pulmonary compliance, and ventricular functional recovery (113,115,116). Allowing too fast an ultraﬁltration rate
in excess of 20 mL/kg/min during arterial–venous MUF
can cause a decrease in middle cerebral artery blood ﬂow
velocities and cerebral mixed venous oxygen saturations
(Fig. 2). This may be indicative of a transient reduction
in cerebral perfusion caused by a ‘‘stealing’’ effect from
the head vessels (117). Measuring cerebral rSO2 can be
useful to help guide appropriate MUF ﬂow rates. Figure 3
shows one of a few possible schemas for the conduct of
MUF used. This circuit involves using the heat exchanger
in the cardioplegia circuit to prevent infants from cooling
down during the MUF period. Alternative circuit designs
include the use of venovenous MUF after CPB (118–120). Using variations of this technique, it is possible to
remove 500–750 mL of ﬂuid from the patient that is rich
in inﬂammatory mediators. This leads to improvements in
pulmonary, cardiac, and cerebral function (113,115,120–
123). MUF appears to be very beneﬁcial for neonates
and tiny infants and clearly results in elevation of
the hematocrit and generalized acute improvement in
pulmonary and cardiac function (109,112,115,120). In a
recent survey (25), 98% of pediatric centers contacted
employ some method of routine ultraﬁltration. Centers
using MUF increased from 43% in 1994 to 75% in 2004.

Of the centers that use MUF, 64% uses arterial–venous
MUF and 11% uses venovenous MUF. KEY POINTS
■Cardiac surgeons in the 21st century can apply far
more sophisticated CPB strategies than what they
may have been exposed to during their training. ■The ﬁeld has been research driven and many
techniques have developed from an evidence-based
format. ■Despite the large amount of information available
regarding infant CPB, there is still much room for
improvement. ■Surgical techniques have undergone evolution to
where we are capable of providing anatomic repair
or optimal palliation to most infants. ■The next horizon for signiﬁcant improvement of
surgical outcomes will be reached as we learn how
to better optimize the response of the patient to CPB
that are used during repair of cardiac defects. REFERENCES

◗Myocardial Protection and Preservation
for Neonates and Infants
Paul J. Chai
Myocardial protection is an essential component of
cardiac
surgery. The
key
principles
of
myocardial
protection—reduction of metabolic activity by hypothermia and cessation of mechanical and electrical activity
of the heart—are widely accepted principles. These principles remain important in the special circumstances of
cardiac surgery in the neonate and infant. Cardiac surgery on the neonate and infant heart differs
from cardiac surgery on the adult heart in a number of
signiﬁcant ways. The coronary arteries and myocardium
are, for the most part, normal in patients with congenital
heart disease; therefore, the congenital heart surgeon
does not need to worry about the uniform delivery of
cardioplegia or deal with signiﬁcantly scarred or impaired
regional or global ventricular function. The congenital
heart surgeon is confronted with a heart in varying stages
of maturity. This variation is signiﬁcant because, as the
myocardium matures, fundamental changes occur that
directly inﬂuence the ability of the heart to withstand
periods of ischemia and injury. The point of transition is
not well-known, but likely occurs in the ﬁrst year of life
and potentially within the ﬁrst 3 months of life. A general belief is that the normal neonatal myocardium is more resistant to ischemia and reperfusion
injury than mature adult myocardium (1,2). This added
resistance does not seem to be present in the hearts of
cyanotic neonates and children or those with acute or
chronic heart failure. These differences must be taken into
account when considering the optimal strategy for myocardial protection during cardiac surgery of the neonate
and infant. Myocardial protection techniques must be tailored with respect to the age of the patient and complexity
of the procedure to ensure the best outcomes. PHYSIOLOGIC DIFFERENCES BETWEEN
IMMATURE AND MATURE
MYOCARDIUM
There are a number of speciﬁc physiologic differences between the immature myocardium of the infant and the
mature myocardium of the adult that are important in
understanding the greater tolerance to ischemia of the pediatric heart. Table 1 (3) is a summary of these differences
and their potential impact on ischemia tolerance of the
pediatric heart. Substrate Metabolism
Myocardial energy production [adenosine triphosphate
production (ATP)] is derived from the oxidation of fatty
acids, glucose, lactate, ketone bodies, and amino acids.
