35. Myocardial Protection and Preservation for Neonates and Infants
701
The main substrate for myocardial energy production in
the adult heart is long chain fatty acids. The adult myocardium gains as much as 90% of its ATP production
from the oxidation of these fatty acids (4). In contrast,
the neonatal heart uses glucose as its main substrate. Energy production is supplemented by the use of fatty acids,
ketones, and amino acids (5). This shift in substrate preference from glucose to fatty acids occurs within the ﬁrst few
weeks of life and is caused by upregulation of 5′-adenosine
monophosphate-activated protein kinase (6). During this
period of development, the neonatal myocardium has a diminished sensitivity to insulin (7) as well as a much greater
capacity to store glycogen (8). It is generally accepted that
the immature myocardium has a greater ability to use
anaerobic metabolism. The relevance of these physiologic differences between
the neonatal and adult myocardium is not completely
understood at this time. There may be some correlation
between the neonatal heart’s increased use of glucose
with its increased tolerance to ischemia. For instance, Liu
et al. found that after a period of ischemia in the adult
heart, fatty acid oxidation rapidly normalized while glucose oxidation as well as contractile function remained
depressed (9). A positive correlation between return of
contractile function and enhanced glucose uptake was
demonstrated in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass operations (10). In different experimental settings,
activation of glucose oxidation enhanced functional recovery of cardiac muscle during or after ischemia (11,12). Doenst proposed several explanations for these ﬁnd-
ings (3). First, glucose is a more efﬁcient substrate because
it carries more of its own oxygen (4). Second, more protons
generated during ischemia are consumed when glucose
is oxidized at the pyruvate dehydrogenase step (9,12). Third, ATP generated from glycolysis supports the function of key ion pumps and calcium homeostasis (13). Fourth, metabolism of glycogen may help with the maintenance of function of sarcoplasmic reticulum (14). It is
possible that some or all of the mechanisms responsible for these ﬁndings may be already present in hearts
using glucose as a primary substrate (such as pediatric hearts) and may explain its prolonged tolerance to
ischemia. Calcium Metabolism
Pediatric myocardium is signiﬁcantly more sensitive to extracellular calcium compared to adult myocardium.

This
may be due to the underdevelopment of the sarcoplasmic
reticulum in pediatric myocardium resulting in a reduction in storage capacity of calcium. The adult heart gets
most of the calcium required for contraction from the
sarcoplasmic reticulum (15,16). In pediatric hearts, the
reduced storage capacity of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
forces much of the calcium to be provided by inﬂux of
calcium from the extracellular space (17). The activity
of sarcoplasmic calcium adenosine triphosphatase (CaATPase) (the enzyme necessary for calcium reuptake into the
sarcoplasmic reticulum) is reduced in the pediatric heart. This reduction of sarcoplasmic CaATPase activity results
in a decreased ability to release calcium upon stimulation
of the ryanodine receptor as well as a reduction in calcium
reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This biochemical variation found in the pediatric heart may explain
why postischemic calcium overload may easily occur with
the use of a perfusion medium containing high or normal
levels of calcium. Several studies have described adverse
effects using cardioplegic solutions containing high or
normal concentrations of calcium during pediatric cardiac
surgery and have recommended the use of subphysiologic
levels of calcium in cardioplegia solutions (18–20). As a
result, most cardioplegic solutions in use now contain very
low levels of calcium (21–23). Enzyme Activity
Two enzyme systems seem to be relevant to protection
of the heart during periods of ischemia. The ﬁrst of
these systems is the antioxidant system, which includes
the enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and
glutathione reductase. The activity of this enzyme system,
which is important in the protection of the heart from free
radicals, is reduced in immature myocardium (24). Free
radical generation is markedly elevated during reperfusion
following a period of ischemia and so a decreased defense
mechanism would render the heart more susceptible to
free radical injury. Children with tetralogy of Fallot are
known to have a signiﬁcant reduction in the activity of
glutathione reductase (24–26), and may be at even greater
risk from free radical damage than others. Some groups
have incorporated the use of leukocyte ﬁltration in the
cardiopulmonary bypass circuit in an attempt to reduce
the amount of free radical generation. Studies have so far
yielded mixed results (27–29). The enzyme 5′nucleotidase, which catalyzes the conversion of adenosine monophosphate (AMP) to adenosine,
is the second enzyme system of potential importance.

Although AMP is unable to pass through the plasma
membrane, adenosine easily passes through the plasma
membrane and is subsequently lost. The adenine nucleotide pool can become depleted with the production
of adenosine. The size of this adenine nucleotide pool is
important for postischemic recovery of the heart (30–32). If the pool is depleted more than 50%, immediate full recovery of contractile function is impossible. Some groups
have demonstrated improved ischemic tolerance by inhibition of this enzyme system (33–35). This enzyme system
is also reduced in immature myocardium and may be an
additional explanation as to why immature myocardium
is more tolerant to ischemia (21,34).

702
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
Catecholamine Sensitivity
The sensitivity to catecholamines is decreased in immature hearts. In vitro studies suggest that this is caused by a
decreased coupling of myocardial β-adrenergic receptors
to adenylyl cyclase at birth (36). In contrast, the kinetics
of cyclic AMP hydrolysis and the inhibitory potential of
phosphodiesterase inhibitors such as milrinone are not
affected by age. This explains the wide use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors in the postoperative care of neonates
and infants. The question as to whether this decreased sensitivity in the immature heart contributes to its increased
tolerance to ischemia is difﬁcult to answer at this time. Ischemic Preconditioning
It is striking to observe that ischemic preconditioning has
no effect in the newborn rat heart, although it is protective
in older age groups (37). This protective effect is present in
practically every animal model (including humans) (38). The mechanism for this protective effect in not clear. It
is easy to speculate, however, that this lack of effect may
be because whichever mechanisms are responsible may
already be active in the immature heart. This may add to
the understanding of the improved ischemia tolerance of
the immature heart. Summary
The preference of the immature heart for use of glucose,
the large stores of glycogen, and the low activity of
5′nucleotidase may contribute to the neonatal and infant
heart’s extended tolerance to ischemia. In contrast,
however, the reduced activity of the free radical scavenger
system, the increased sensitivity to calcium, and unknown
factors related to the unique environment of the cyanotic
heart, may serve to reduce the heart’s ischemia tolerance. The most important strategies for pediatric myocardial
protection as compared to adult myocardial protection
should include consideration of all of these ﬁndings. CLINICAL MECHANISMS
OF MYOCARDIAL PROTECTION
The most frequently applied principles for myocardial protection during pediatric cardiac surgery are hypothermia
for reduction of metabolic activity and administration of
cardioplegia for electrical and contractile arrest. There is
no clear consensus concerning the optimal strategy for myocardial protection in the neonate and infant. Strategies
vary from institution to institution as well as the composition of cardioplegia used. The general principles remain
constant, however, as most institutions incorporate both
hypothermia and the administration of cardioplegia during their pediatric cardiac procedures.

Hypothermia
Hypothermia alone can provide a signiﬁcant amount of
myocardial protection and may be the single most important factor concerning myocardial protection in the
neonate and infant. Some authors have suggested that under speciﬁc conditions, cardioplegia may in fact even be
unnecessary (3,39). This is demonstrated by a number
of studies that have shown equivalent or better myocardial protection using hypothermia alone compared
to the use of hypothermia with the addition of cardioplegia (40–43). It should be noted, however, that these
studies were performed at very low systemic temperatures
of 15◦C or less. Studies at higher temperatures do consistently demonstrate an advantage with the addition of
cardioplegia (44–46). Cooling of the human body to 32◦C reduces whole body
oxygen consumption by 45% (47). At temperatures below
12◦C, oxygen consumption of the heart is below 1% of normal and contractile function ceases (48). In one study from
Siberia, due to constraints of equipment availability, various forms of congenital heart disease were repaired using
hypothermic circulatory arrest without cardiopulmonary
bypass. Patients were packed in ice to achieve temperatures of 24◦C to 26◦C and the repair was completed within
70 minutes. Results were remarkable with mortality below
10% and neurologic complications at 13% (49). Cardioplegia
Cardioplegia provides an additional level of protection
during cardiac surgery. The essential use of cardioplegia
is for cessation of all contractile and electrical activity
of the heart. This results in a signiﬁcant reduction
of energy consumption, even at normothermia (21). Almost all cardioplegic solutions exert their protective
effects through depolarization or hyperpolarization of the
membrane and mechanical arrest of the heart. The actual
composition and method of delivery can vary signiﬁcantly
from institution to institution, as there is currently no
consensus on the type of cardioplegia that should be
used. This variation is reﬂected in the fact that more than
150 cardioplegia solutions are used clinically for cardiac
transplantation in the United States (50). Many studies
attempt to address this issue; however, these studies are
fairly contradictory in their conclusions (19,44,51–54). The primary differences in composition of cardioplegia
solution aim to address the mechanisms involved in
ischemia-reperfusion injury. These can include elevated
osmotic pressure to prevent edema formation, addition
of buffering agents to reduce acidosis, addition of free
radical scavengers, or supplementation with substrates
to improve energy production during rewarming and
reperfusion (18,22,55–57).

Indeed, the neonatal heart may
be more prone to problematic myocardial edema, which

may lead to decreased ventricular compliance, increased
ventricular stiffness, and diastolic dysfunction; therefore,
cardioplegia with normal and possibly slightly elevated
osmotic pressure may be beneﬁcial. The main studies examining the efﬁcacy of cardioplegia are summarized in Table 2 (3) with the controversial
areas highlighted. All of the studies demonstrate some
protective beneﬁt of using either hypothermia or cardioplegia or both. There is no clear conclusion as to
whether the use of hypothermia or cardioplegia alone is
superior. Figure 1 (3) plots the beneﬁt from cardioplegia against the establishment of the same temperature
by a noncardioplegic method (i.e., topical cooling, blood
perfusion etc.) as a function of myocardial temperature
during ischemia. This graphical representation indicates
that the beneﬁt of cardioplegia in the neonatal period
appears to be directly related to myocardial temperature. Baker (58) demonstrated in rabbits that the importance
of cardioplegia in addition to hypothermia increases with
age. The maintenance of deep myocardial hypothermia,
therefore, is of critical importance in the clinical setting. This can be difﬁcult to maintain in the pediatric
setting considering the small size of neonatal and infant
hearts. Multiple strategies are therefore necessary, such as
systemic hypothermia, cold ambient temperatures in the
operating room, and the periodic reinfusion of cold cardioplegia. Because the main purpose of reinfusion of cold
cardioplegia is to cool the heart, the potassium concentration is often lowered to avoid excessive hyperkalemia (18). Potassium Depolarization Arrest versus

solutions currently (59). Depolarization arrest signiﬁ-

37◦C decreases the oxygen demands of the heart by 90% to
1 mL O2/100 g/minute (60). Although depolarization arrest
has become a fundamental component of cardioplegia, the
merits of hyperpolarization arrest deserve some consideration. Certain energy-dependant processes, such as the
sarcolemmal and sarcoplamic reticular Ca2+-ATPases and
Na–K-ATPase pumps, remain active during depolarization
arrest. Some groups have argued that the energy requirements of these pumps may contribute to ischemic injury
during potassium depolarization arrest through continued
energy depletion and ionic imbalances (61). A comparison
of hyperpolarized cardioplegic arrest with a potassium
ATP channel agent versus depolarization arrest with a
traditional agent in rabbits found improved functional
outcome in the hyperpolarized group (61). These results
are intriguing and merit further exploration into possible
improvements to the traditional cardioplegic solutions in
use now. Warm Induction
A small subset of patients with left-ventricular dysfunction
was found to have a reduced tolerance to aortic clamping. This poor tolerance to myocardial ischemia was thought
to be due to depletion of myocardial energy stores. Rosenkranz et al. tested this hypothesis by depleting
myocardial energy stores in dogs using 45 minutes of
ischemia (31). The dogs were then treated with either cold
or warm induction of cardioplegia before receiving 2 hours
of aortic cross-clamping with intermittent doses of cold
cardioplegia. This group found that dogs that had received
warm induction had improved ventricular function and
improved aerobic metabolism. This ﬁnding has been
further demonstrated by other groups as well (62).

Warm blood induction is felt to be beneﬁcial in
dysfunctional hearts because arrest at 37◦C without ischemia enhances metabolic repair by channeling aerobic
ATP production to reparative processes. The use of a
warm induction dose of cardioplegia may therefore add
a further level of myocardial protection by replenishing
energy stores of previously abnormal hearts during cardiac
surgery. This technique may deserve serious consideration
in patients who come to the operating room with energydepleted hearts, such as patients with severe cyanosis,
hemodynamic instability, or heart failure. Substrate Enhancement
Further enhancements to cardioplegia solution include
the addition of substrates such as aspartate and glutamate. Studies investigating amino acid use through
anaerobic pathways found that infusion of three amino
acids—aspartate, glutamate, and ornithine—during ischemia augmented recovery of contractile function in
isolated rabbit hearts (63). Glutamate directly enters the
tricarboxylic acid cycle as α-ketoglutarate and provides for
nonglycolytic generation of ATP. Aspartate use is through
the malate-aspartate shuttle. Aspartate is converted to
oxaloacetate and then to malate. Malate enters the mitochondria where it is converted back to oxaloacetate,
which liberates the reducing equivalents needed for ATP
synthesis. The beneﬁt of using glutamate-enriched cardioplegia
solution was demonstrated by Buckberg. His group found
increased rates of contraction and relaxation, improved
stroke work index, and improved recovery of ATP using
glutamate-enriched cardioplegia (64). Engelman found
that the use of a glutamate and aspartate-enriched solution during reperfusion resulted in a reduction in infarct
size and improved levels of ATP and acetyl coenzyme A
in swine model of ischemia-reperfusion injury (65). Other
experimental studies have also suggested that including
glutamate and aspartate in the warm induction of cardioplegia and also in the reperfusate provides an additional
level of myocardial protection and recovery (44,66,67). CLINICAL TECHNIQUES
The techniques clinically used among institutions currently vary widely as was mentioned previously. Cardiac

35. Myocardial Protection and Preservation for Neonates and Infants
705
surgery in the neonate and infant is a team approach,
which makes it difﬁcult to assess clinical outcomes of
any one speciﬁc technique of myocardial protection from
another. Differences in operative techniques, operative
times, and quality of postoperative care can signiﬁcantly
camouﬂage any possible differences in myocardial protection. What may work well for one surgeon in a particular
center, may not work for another. The lack of clear and consistent data makes it difﬁcult
to recommend a single strategy of myocardial protection,
especially since primary myocardial failure after cardiac
surgery is now a rare cause of death (68,69). While myocardial failure as a cause of death remains rare, a fall
in cardiac output after pediatric cardiac surgery is fairly
common. This fall in cardiac output is especially apparent in the period between 6 and 18 hours postoperatively
as documented by multiple studies from Children’s Hospital Boston (70–73). This phenomenon would suggest
that areas of improvement remain pertaining to myocardial management techniques. Still, it is unclear whether
this fall in cardiac output 6 and 18 hours postoperatively
would be obviated by improved strategies of myocardial
protection; in fact this phenomenon may be independent
of myocardial protective strategies and instead be related
to any of a variety of alternative etiologies including a
generalized postcardiopulmonary bypass inﬂammatory
response, cytokine activity, enzymatic activity, and hormonal variations (74,75). The Boston group found that a residual volume or pressure load on the heart (i.e., an imperfect repair) was the
most important cause of an excessive drop in postoperative cardiac output (68). Other important factors included
ventricular distention during surgery (from failure to vent
the heart adequately), retraction and stretch injury to the
myocardium (from excessive retraction on tissues for exposure), coronary artery injury, ventriculotomy, edema,
perfusion factors, and reperfusion conditions (76). Cardiac Distension
In contrast to the ﬁndings that the immature myocardium
is signiﬁcantly more resistant to ischemia when compared
to the adult heart, there is a general feeling among
surgeons that immature myocardium is signiﬁcantly
more vulnerable to stretch injury. Stretch injury occurs
mainly from overdistention of the left heart and excessive
retraction on myocardial tissues. Overdistension of the
left heart can have many detrimental consequences
other than primary myocardial contractile dysfunction.

Overdistension of the left ventricle also leads to distension
of the left atrium and pulmonary veins, which eventually
results in a high transcapillary pressure in the lungs. This
elevated pulmonary transcapillary pressure eventually
leads to signiﬁcant pulmonary edema and pulmonary
dysfunction. Cardioplegia Protocols
Clinical techniques vary from groups who advocate the
use of single-dose cold cardioplegia in neonates and
infants to groups who favor a more conventional approach
adapted from use in adult cardiac surgery. The group at
Children’s Hospital Boston is one group that advocates
the use of a single dose of cold cardioplegia in speciﬁc
circumstances. Their practice is to use a single dose of
cardioplegia infusion (20 mL/kg) combined with systemic
deep hypothermia for neonatal procedures. In patients
older than 2 to 3 months of age, periodic doses of cold
cardioplegia are repeated at 20- to 30-minute intervals. Beyond 1 year of age, repeat doses of cardioplegia are
administered every 20 minutes using an initial dose of
20 mL/kg followed by subsequent doses of 10 mL/kg (76). Our group at the Congenital Heart Institute of Florida
(CHIF) currently uses a cardioplegia protocol based on the
Buckberg adult system. This involves the administration
of up to four distinct cardioplegia solutions (Table 3)
depending on the particular procedure being performed. For standard cases at mild to moderate levels of
hypothermia, a warm induction dose is given initially
(10–20 mL/kg) followed immediately by a high K cold
induction dose (20–30 mL/kg). Total induction volume is
40 mL/kg. Subsequent maintenance cardioplegia doses are
given at roughly 20-minute intervals using the low K maintenance solution at half-induction doses (10–20 mL/kg). Before the removal of the cross-clamp a ‘‘hot-shot’’
dose of physiologic K warm perfusion is administered
(10–20 mL/kg) followed by warm oxygenated blood reperfusion for 2 minutes. Patients undergoing procedures which require a period
of circulatory arrest are cooled to systemic temperatures
of 18◦Celsius. For myocardial protection, only the high K
cold induction dose is given (40 mL/kg). The warm induction dose is not administered for circulatory arrest cases. For patients undergoing cardiac transplantation, we
use initial reperfusion of the recipient heart with an
aspartate and glutamate-enriched white blood cell ﬁltered
cardioplegia (77,78). Retrograde Cardioplegia
Retrograde cardioplegia is an effective technique for
administration of cardioplegia in selective cases.

We
routinely use retrograde cardioplegia for cases involving
an open aortic root and coronary artery transfers such
as the arterial switch procedure and Ross procedure. A
retrograde cardioplegia catheter can also be placed in
cases where the ability to arrest the heart due to severe
aortic insufﬁciency is in question. The retrograde cardioplegia cannula is placed under
direct vision into the coronary sinus and secured by either
balloon insufﬂation or placement of a pursestring suture

cannula (DLP, Medtronic) is our preferred cannula
for neonatal surgery. During infusion of retrograde
cardioplegia, ﬂow through the retrograde cannula is
adjusted to result in a cardioplegia perfusion pressure
no higher than 50 mm Hg. Disadvantages for the use of retrograde cardioplegia
include the potential nonuniform distribution of cardioplegia away from portions of the right ventricle (RV) and
right atrium (RA). Patients with a left-sided superior vena
cava draining into the coronary sinus may also cause problems with the use of retrograde cardioplegia. Placement of
the retrograde cannula can be difﬁcult in the neonate and
may require a carefully placed pursestring suture around
the coronary sinus to prevent dislodgement. Care must
be taken in placement of the purse-string suture to avoid
the conduction system and prevent complete heart block. Direct coronary ostial administration of cardioplegia is
an alternative technique when retrograde cardioplegia is
difﬁcult or impossible. CONCLUSION
Cardiac surgery in the neonate and infant is a unique
process with many differences from cardiac surgery in the
adult. Myocardial protection techniques must take into
account a myriad of factors including the physical size
of the heart and operating ﬁeld as well as the physiologic
differences of the immature heart. The increased tolerance to ischemia of the immature
heart may make possible signiﬁcant changes to the
way myocardial protection is delivered to the neonate. While the use of deep hypothermia alone has certainly
been supported in some experimental studies, a general
consensus is lacking. In reality, the use of cardioplegia
is of great importance because in practical conditions
it is difﬁcult to guarantee continuous deep myocardial
hypothermia. Cardioplegia offers an additional level of
protection at higher temperatures and older age.

In 2004,
Ungerleider published a review of practice patterns in
neonatal cardiopulmonary bypass of numerous congenital
heart surgeons, as collected from surveys (the Congenital
Heart Surgeon’s Society) and from audience response
at the American Association of Thoracic Surgery (May
2003) and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (January
2004) (79). This study documented that numerous practice
patterns exist, with unanimity only in the recommended
use of cardioplegia, although the delivery, type, and
timing of doses vary (79). Therefore, current stateof-the-art for myocardial protection and preservation
for neonates and infants usually involves the use of
some form of cardioplegia, often with some degree of
hypothermia. Ongoing research will certainly encourage
further evolution of these techniques. KEY POINTS
■Basic principles of myocardial protection are similar
for adults, children, infants and neonates. ●Reduction of myocardial energy consumption
during required periods of ischemia
❍Hypothermia
❍Cessation of electrical and mechanical activity
■There are several physiological differences between
the immature myocardium of infants and neonates
and the mature adult myocardium. ●The age crossover point is uncertain but the change
to the adult form likely occurs between 3 and
12 months
●Energy production is fatty acid dependent in
adults and relies on glucose oxidation in immature
myocardium
●Immature myocardium is more sensitive to Ca++
❍Decreased sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) storage
capacity for Ca++
❍Decreased reuptake of Ca++
❍Immature myocardium is more susceptible to
postischemic Ca++ overload

◗Brain Injury Following Infant Cardiac
Surgery and Neuroprotective Strategies
Edward J. Hickey, Tara Karamlou, and Ross M. Ungerleider
The importance of neuroprotective strategies in pediatric
cardiac surgery stems from the observed association between neurologic injury and surgical repair of complex
congenital heart disease (CHD). Modern surgical techniques have only evolved through the historic use of deep
hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)—the complete
cessation of systemic and cerebral blood ﬂow (CBF) at
hypothermic temperatures. Impaired neurologic recovery
has therefore become causally linked to cerebral ischemia
sustained during DHCA. Considerable time and energy
has consequently been spent reducing or eliminating periods of cerebral ischemia during cardiopulmonary bypass
(CPB) through the use of novel continuous perfusion
techniques. These include circulatory arrest with intermittent perfusion (IP), continuous low-ﬂow CPB, antegrade
selective cerebral perfusion (SCP), retrograde cerebral perfusion and more recently normothermic full-ﬂow CPB. The multitude of techniques perhaps implies that they all
have limitations. Evidence is gradually accumulating to suggest that
numerous nonsurgical factors predispose to the initiation
and progression of brain injury in the neonatal period. The
fact that the incidence of neurologic injury has remained
little changed despite attempts to avoid DHCA, supports
the notion that factors other than ischemia per se may
be of greater importance. Furthermore, multivariable
regression analyses studying the entire neonatal period
demonstrate that intraoperative factors account for less
than 20% of the variance in neurologic dysfunction (1). An
understanding of these risks, together with the particular
vulnerability of the immature brain, is therefore necessary
to continue the pursuit of improved neurologic outcomes
following infant cardiac surgery. HISTORY
Although frequently considered a subsequent development, (deep) hypothermic circulatory arrest was developed
in parallel to CPB, and rapidly became intertwined. Separate from the developments in CPB, Bigelow et al. in 1950 initially introduced the concept of cooling in cardiac surgery by demonstrating that moderate hypothermia
to 30◦C would permit circulatory arrest for 10 minutes. Experiments in dogs were used to study progressively
deeper hypothermia in an attempt to permit longer arrest
durations, and indeed surface cooling to 20◦C did allow
survival following 15 minutes of total circulatory arrest (2).

It was quickly apparent, however, that progressive cooling
was a precarious business, as bradycardia and inadequate inotropy resulted in hypoxemia in warmer organs
or rendered the circulation at risk of complete collapse
through ﬁbrillation. Experimental observations indicated
that quinidine or supplemental carbon dioxide could be
used to avert ﬁbrillation, but this did not correct the circulatory inadequacy at deep hypothermia, which in addition
made rewarming extremely difﬁcult. Nevertheless, this
notion was soon applied clinically, in conjunction with in-
ﬂow occlusion, for the successful repair of an atrial septal
defect in a 5-year-old girl by Lewis and Tauﬁc (3), and
success was also independently reported by others (4). The marriage of hypothermia and CPB came about in
the 1950s when the possibility was raised that damage
supposedly attributed to the early oxygenators might
be averted through the use of cooling. Much of the
early work was undertaken by an overlooked physiologist
in Nashville named Frank Gollan. Using a gas-bubble
oxygenator, he reported perfusion cooling to 4◦C and
even as low as 0◦C (5). In eerie resemblance to practice
40 years later, he primed with Ringer’s solution to
produce hemodilution, and corrected the hematocrit
by transfusing donor blood after separation from CPB. This remarkable work culminated in a presentation
to the American Association of Thoracic Surgeons in
1955 describing a successful series of experimental
left atriotomies in animals cooled to 13◦C using his
oxygenating device (6). Despite detailed descriptions of
the clear and unencumbered operating ﬁeld—in contrast

711
to the beating-heart and bloody conditions otherwise
experienced by surgeons of the day—his efforts (as a
physiologist) were largely ignored. In Europe at the same time, Juvenelle (7), and later
Ake Senning, were investigating the impact of cooling on
physiologic parameters, and in particular showed that
hypothermic ventricular ﬁbrillation could be tolerated
for prolonged periods, even using an aortic cross-clamp
to successfully induce myocardial isolation for almost
an hour—almost certainly the ﬁrst application of this
maneuver (8). By the late 1950s, with the concept of cooling becoming more widespread, the team at Duke University
collaborated with the radiator division of General Motors
to develop a circuit heat-exchanger, and described clinical use of circuits close in overall design to those in use
currently. Their standard protocol proposed maintaining
esophageal temperature at 28◦C to 30◦C, although they
also described successful surgery on a child with severe
tetralogy of Fallot who was cooled to 10◦C. Technical problems encountered during this tetralogy repair necessitated
the complete cessation of the circulation for several periods totaling 22 minutes—perhaps the earliest description
of DHCA (9). Not all investigators pursued hypothermia in conjunction with full CPB. Charles Drew was a surgeon
from Westminster, London, who, despite having visited
both Minneapolis and Minnesota to witness the pumpoxygenators these pioneering groups were using, was
convinced that the morbidity and mortality they experienced was associated with the use of an oxygenator. He was, however, convinced by the merits of profound
hypothermia, and therefore concentrated on developing
dual-chamber bypass pumps that made use of the patient’s lungs as the oxygenator. Blood from each atrium
was drained and pumped, after cooling, into the corresponding outﬂow artery. The efforts spent by his team
perfecting this technique on animals in a disused billiards
room on the sixth ﬂoor of Westminster Hospital in London made way for a 22-year career using this technique
for intracardiac repair. He was invited to present his system at a Hunterian Lecture in 1961, and despite artiﬁcial
oxygenators proving safe, never relinquished his novel
biventricular bypass technique (10). The successful introduction of hypothermic CPB, and
in particular DHCA, changed the course of surgical repair
of congenital lesions. From the mid-1950s through the
next three decades, DHCA enabled progressively more and
more complex defects to be addressed.

Lesions otherwise
incompatible with life were routinely offered the chance
of survival into adolescence and beyond. During this
era—the birth of congenital cardiac surgery—emphasis
was understandably almost entirely placed on achieving
early operative survival. It was only once surgical mortality approached 5% (and currently just <2% in selected
units (11)) that attention began to shift toward the longterm quality of life of these patients. The realization that
neurologic dysfunction remains a common occurrence attributable to events spanning the entire neonatal period
has led to a surge of interest in attempting to understand
the mechanisms involved and devising future neuroprotective strategies. NEUROLOGIC OUTCOMES IN MODERN
PRACTICE: THE SIZE OF THE PROBLEM
Few studies have described the acute postoperative
neurologic status using standardized techniques. In young
infants (<6 months), hypotonia appears to be common
(68% at the end of the ﬁrst postoperative week and 34%
remained hypotonic at discharge) and seizures have been
documented in as many as 15% before discharge. In the
same report, only 81% of the 91 infants were fully alert by
discharge (12). Late neurologic outcomes following cardiac surgery
have been studied in greater detail. Severe neurologic
deﬁcits, such as cerebral palsy, mental retardation and
epilepsy are fortunately not common overall—5% to 9%
of recent cohorts if hypoplastic left heart is excluded. Nevertheless, more subtle developmental, behavioral, cognitive, and motor abnormalities are reported frequently. The applicability of reports in the literature is somewhat
limited by era effects, heterogeneity between the CHD lesions studied and the age at which the children have been
studied. This latter point relates to the important observation that neurobehavioral tests performed in infancy and
early childhood have only limited predictive validity for
later learning difﬁculties (13). Low mean intelligence quotients (IQ) are commonly
reported (typically in the low-to-mid 90s), as are language
delays. Low IQ of a sufﬁciently low level to be categorized
as intellectual dysfunction occurs in approximately 5% to
25% (14), and is particularly associated with postoperative complications such as cardiorespiratory arrest and
continued symptomatic compromise (15). Parental IQ is
also a strong predictor of the IQ of a child with CHD. Sophisticated testing has identiﬁed a particular pattern of
problems involving attention, hyperactivity, visual-motor
integration, and executive functioning. Interestingly, this
is a pattern frequently associated with normal children
born prematurely (13).

Preschool children appear to function well within
the family after cardiac surgery, whereas at school age
they have been reported to be socially and emotionally maladjusted compared with controls. Behavioral
and social problems can be exacerbated by maternal feelings of emotional maladjustment and guilt. In
fact, maternal feelings and attitudes may carry greater
inﬂuence in behavioral and social development than

the severity of the underlying congenital heart lesion (16). Considerable insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes has been provided by the Boston circulatory arrest
trial (17–19). Patients with CHD functioned as a group
signiﬁcantly worse than age-matched normals in terms of
motor skills, speech and language development, and IQ at
4 years. Neurobehavioral abnormalities were observed in
as many as a third of all subjects. By 8 years, although
these deﬁcits were now closer to normal children (IQ
98 versus 100), speciﬁc problems in the execution of complex problems persisted. Visual-spatial and visual-memory
skills, memory, attention, and hypothesis generation were
all signiﬁcantly deﬁcient. More than 10% had repeated a
grade and more than one third were requiring speciﬁc
educational intervention. Neurologic outcomes appear to be comparable across
the range of congenital lesions, with the exception of hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS), which is especially
associated with intellectual dysfunction and neurodevelopmental abnormalities (20). How CHD children with
genetic syndromes compare in their neurodevelopmental
status is not currently clear. THE VULNERABLE BRAIN
Neonatal Vulnerability
to Hypoxia-Ischemia and
Periventricular Leukomalacia
Prematurity as an independent cause of perinatal brain
injury is of enormous importance. Therefore, of the
57,000 infants born in the United States each year with
a birth weight below 1,500 g (21), 90% will now survive
the neonatal period, but 10% of these will later display
spastic motor deﬁcits (cerebral palsy), and as many as
25% to 50% (22) will manifest cognitive or behavioral
problems that interfere with educational progression. This
signiﬁcant morbidity is primarily due to the particular
vulnerability of the immature human brain to hypoxic,
chemical, and inﬂammatory injury. Developing white
matter (WM) appears especially at risk and speciﬁc
‘‘temporal windows’’ of this susceptibility to injury are
now being recognized. The most dangerous period is
preterm at 32–34 weeks’ gestation, and injury in this
window results in cystic necrosis and gliosis in the
periventricular WM regions: periventricular leukomalacia
(PVL), (Fig. 1). Nevertheless, this window of vulnerability
has been shown to extend later into gestation and the early
post-term period. The fact that many infants born with
complex CHD exhibit microcephaly and developmental
immaturity has led some authors to speculate that they
display the same vulnerability extending well into the
neonatal and operative window (13).

Recent magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) studies have conﬁrmed that
new WM lesions do indeed occur in the periventricular
regions of post-term infants undergoing cardiac surgery. The fact that young age is a major component of WM
injury in CHD patients is corroborated by these studies. Evidence of PVL was seen in 54% neonates after cardiac
surgery, compared with 4% of older infants (23). The neuropathology of PVL consists of localized necrosis of all cellular elements deep in the cerebral WM, with
subsequent cyst formation. A more diffuse gliosis (without cystic necrosis) is associated with less severe injury. Both types are associated with developmentally immature
oligodendrocye precursors (24). Mature oligodendrocytes
form the myelin of cerebral WM. Oligodendrocyte-related
injury is therefore characterized by a deﬁciency in cortical myelination, loss of WM volume, and the clinical
manifestation of spastic motor disorders. Oligodendrocyte precursors appear unable to adequately process activated oxygen species (24), whereas
by contrast mature oligodendrocytes are relatively resistant to such attack (25). Accumulation of oxygen-free
radicals results in the liberation of the lethal hydroxyl
radical through the iron-catalyzed Fenton reaction. The
experimental application of iron chelators to immature
oligodendrocytes has conferred resistance to hypoxiaischemia (25) and represents exciting avenues for future
research. The blood supply to the cerebral WM is precarious and
contributes to the pathogenesis of PVL. Short penetrating
arteries supply the superﬁcial WM, and sparse longpenetrating arteries supply the deeper regions. Many
of these arteries are still developing in the post-term
neonatal period. The vulnerability of deep cortical WM has
been conﬁrmed by positron emission tomography data
revealing that even in normal or near-normal preterm

WM, CBF values are frequently measured as less than
5 mL/100 g/min (the threshold for viability in the adult
brain is approximately 10 mL/100 g/min). Some studies
have reported ranges as low as 1.6–3.0 mL/100 g/min (26). Therefore, there exists a minimal margin safety for deep
cortical WM oxygen delivery. CEREBRAL INFLAMMATION
Systemic inﬂammation is now recognized to be a trigger for PVL. A number of clinical and epidemiologic
series suggested a link between maternal/fetal infection
and PVL (27). Similarly the induction of maternal intrauterine infection in fetal rabbits has resulted in WM
lesions (28). In cell culture models, either tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) or interferon-γ (IFN-γ ) alone (in
the absence of hypoxia-ischemia) can trigger apoptotic
cell death, and TNF-α potentiates the toxicity of IFN-γ
(29,30). Perhaps more important in the context of CPB-related
brain injury is the role of the cerebral inﬂammatory response in the progression of established ischemic brain
injury. The onset of CPB is associated with generalized activation of the innate immune system (31), and
this phenomenon appears to be exaggerated at the extremes of age (32). No facet of the inﬂammatory response
is spared: neutrophils become primed, complement and
kallikrein-kinin systems are activated, inﬂammatory (and
anti-inﬂammatory) cytokines are generated and activated
platelets litter the surface of the extracorporeal circuit
resulting in coagulation disturbances and thrombocytopenia (31,33–35). These processes have a direct role
in commonly encountered postoperative complications
including capillary leak syndrome, acute lung injury, systemic inﬂammatory response syndrome, coagulopathies,
and multiorgan failure (31,36). In addition, recent studies
have demonstrated that inﬂammation contributes exigently to postCPB cerebral dysfunction. Inﬂammatory cytokines are liberated by numerous
stimuli including complement activation, activated neutrophils, activated endothelium, platelets and ischemia. Interleukin (IL)-1β and TNF-α are both apical cytokines
recognized to be central to the progression of neuronal
loss following periods of cerebral ischemia in virtually
every model studied (37–39). TNF-α in particular is now
being implicated as one of the major determinants of
progression of injury following cerebral ischemia. Exogenous TNF-α increases infarct size in experimental stroke
and its antagonism reduces it. TNF-α is elevated with
CPB (40–42), and in proportion to CPB duration and remains so for the ﬁrst 24 hours. Prolonged ischemia during
CPB also results in the do novo production of TNF-α
within the brain.

The chemokine IL-8 is also consistently
raised during CPB and is primarily a trigger of neutrophil
activation and chemotaxis (40–42). Platelet-activating
factor (PAF), so named because of its effects on platelets
actually has numerous (probably more important) roles
as a chemoattractant of neutrophils and the monocytemacrophage lineage, and has been implicated in both
myocardial and pulmonary ischemia-reperfusion injury
during CPB (43). PAF represents a signiﬁcant potential
therapeutic target in this respect. Certainly in the context of cerebral no-reﬂow, PAF-antagonism improves the
cerebral recovery following DHCA (44). The cytokine network is extremely complex. For
example TNF-α is also involved in protective mechanisms:
TNF-α knock-out mice exhibit more severe injury following experimental stroke, and mild TNF-α liberation is
now understood to be an obligatory step in producing
delayed tolerance to injury through preconditioning. The
cytokine network is further complicated by the role of anti-
inﬂammatory mediators (e.g., IL-10). IL-10 suppresses the
production of IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8, and its release
has been demonstrated during CPB (40,45). Overall, in the
sea of interacting mediators, general sway in one direction
or another is likely to be more important than attempting
to isolate individual culprits. THE ENDOTHELIAL UNIT
AND NO REFLOW
The endothelial unit is a uniquely structured arrangement
of vascular endothelium, perivascular membrane and
astroglial cells. This unit is the blood–brain barrier
(BBB), and serves as a gatekeeper between the blood
and the extracellular cerebral environment. It is only
selectively permeable—characterized by low levels of
vesicular transport with tightly juxtaposed endothelial
cells—such that speciﬁc membrane transport proteins are
necessary to allow for the controlled passage of molecules
including glucose, amino acids, lipoproteins, hormones,
and drugs. The endothelial unit is activated rapidly upon the
initiation of CPB. Contrary to earlier reports, studies
with (BBB impermeable) labeled protein chasers have
clearly shown that BBB disruption occurs within 15
minutes of normothermic full-ﬂow CPB, increases with
duration of CPB and may be exacerbated by periods
of ischemia. Scanning electron microscopy has shown
that DHCA causes rapid changes in the endothelial
unit morphology, including membrane invaginations,
endothelial cell contraction, microvillar formation, and
loss of astrocyte foot processes (AsP). Loss of BBB
integrity results in loss of extracellular homeostasis,
exposure to noxious inﬂammatory mediators, leukocyte
inﬁltration, and edema. BBB injury following clinical
cerebral ischemia is increasingly being linked with poor
outcome. In the context of cardiac surgery, the relative

importance of CPB and DHCA in causing BBB injury
has not been fully delineated. Preliminary piglet studies
using (BBB impermeable) gadolinium MRI has suggested
that 2 hours of normothermic full-ﬂow CPB may be more
injurious than 1 hour uninterrupted DHCA with 1 hour
spent cooling and rewarming; however, further studies are
clearly needed. A second important consequence of activation of the
endothelial unit is the initiation of the local inﬂammatory
response and microvascular perfusion abnormalities. The
concept of ‘‘no-reﬂow’’ was introduced following early
perfusion studies involving dye tracers (46). It was noted
that after periods of ischemia, despite restoring the blood
ﬂow to preischemic levels, some areas of the myocardium
remain unperfused. This was termed no-reﬂow and was
deﬁned . . . ‘‘. . . the inability to perfuse previously ischemic myocardium, even when blood ﬂow has been restored to the
large arteries supplying the tissue.’’
Cerebral no-reﬂow is now recognized to be a common
feature of cerebral ischemia during CPB, particularly in
relation to DHCA (44,47). The pathogenesis of cerebral
no-reﬂow appears to involve several aspects, and an activated endothelial unit is central (48). There are two
main components to no-reﬂow: (1) a ‘‘physiologic’’ component characterized by a sustained vasoconstriction (or
impaired vasodilatation); (2) a ‘‘mechanical’’ component
characterized by obstructed capillary beds (49). Physiologic No-Reﬂow
Endothelin-1 is a potent long-acting vasoconstrictor that is
elevated by both CPB and ischemia (50) and may be partly
responsible for the sustained depression in postischemic
depression in myocardial blood ﬂow following periods of
ischemia (51). Because endothelin concentrations are elevated following ischemia, investigators have examined its
role following cerebral ischemia. Endothelin-1 is indeed
elevated following DHCA (52), and in fact techniques that
reduce the overall circulating levels of endothelin-1 following DHCA (such as ultraﬁltration of the perfusate during
the circulatory arrest period) are believed to be associated with improved cerebral outcome. The arachadonic
acid metabolite thromboxane A2 (vasoconstrictor) has also
been implicated, as its direct inhibition has been shown
to reduce cerebral no-reﬂow in neonatal piglet models of
DHCA (53). Furthermore, thromboxane A2 release may
be mediated in part by endothelin-1, exacerbating the
overall vasoconstrictor response following periods of ischemia (54). Downregulation of counteracting vasodilator mechanisms may also contribute. Endothelium releases PGI2,
adenosine, and nitric oxide (NO), all of which act on underlying precapillary sphincters to augment blood ﬂow.

Following ischemia, endothelial generation of prostanoid
vasodilators may be impaired, allowing unopposed vasoconstriction to occur. The common pathway for mediation
of vasodilatation is through the production of NO. Certainly following periods of ischemia or hypoxia, the NO
axis appears to by dysregulated (55) and NO synthase,
which mediates the production of NO through the conversion of the amino acid L-arginine to L-citrulline is deﬁcient
following ischemia-reperfusion (56). Free radicals and activated oxygen species are potent inhibitors of NO (57)
and it may be that arteriolar constriction may be fundamentally due to this inability for NO vasodilatation to be
triggered. Mechanical No-Reﬂow
A feature of the no-reﬂow phenomenon appears to be
capillary plugging by adherent neutrophils. Neutrophil
elastase has been suggested as a mechanism of proteolytic
endothelial basement membrane degradation leading to
detachment, swelling, and destruction of endothelial cells,
contributing to the cellular debris occluding capillary
beds (58). In addition, in non-CPB stroke models, endothelial cells have been shown to undergo apoptosis,
a process leading to impaired capillary function (59),
and perhaps obstruction through endothelial casts or
tissue edema. Platelets, which become activated upon exposure to the inanimate surface of the extracorporeal
circuit, are also believed to adhere to capillary endothelium, disrupting the microvascular perfusion (60,61). Monoclonal antibodies antagonizing tissue factor reduces
myocardial no-reﬂow (61). Direct inhibition of platelet activation through antagonism of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa has
recently been shown to reduce cerebral no-reﬂow following DHCA (62). Overall, the contribution of adherent
leukocytes and platelets, endothelial edema and casts, and
inﬂammatory debris (ﬁbrin) have collectively believed to
result in mechanically occluded capillary beds that contribute to reperfusion abnormalities following periods of
either total or relative ischemia during CPB. PREOPERATIVE BRAIN INJURY
Congenital Brain Abnormalities
CHD is frequently associated with genetic or chromosomal abnormalities. The incidence of extracardiac anomalies—including central nervous system dysfunction—is
therefore higher than in the general population (63–66). Abnormalities in embryogenesis occurring in early pregnancy probably impact detrimentally on systems other
than exclusively the heart. The precise interplay between
potential teratogens is largely unknown, although in utero
exposure to rubella antigens illustrates this concept. The
rubella embryopathy is characterized by cognitive impairment and microcephaly in addition to congenital heart

defects (patent ductus arteriosus, septal defects, and pulmonary artery stenosis) (66). Certain syndromes predictably involve the heart and
central nervous system—the most notable being trisomy
21. The neuroanatomic abnormalities peculiar to Down
syndrome include a disproportionately small cerebellum
and brainstem and a narrow superﬁcial temporal gyrus,
although these features do not speciﬁcally imply a
functional deﬁcit. Abnormalities in dendritic morphology
and synaptic function have been demonstrated, which are
believed to account for the developmental delay observed
in these children. Deletions of chromosome 22q11 are
believed to be present in as many as 5% of infants
born with CHD (67) and are associated with DiGeorge,
CATCH-22, and velocardiofacial syndromes. The cerebral
consequences of chromosome 22q11 deletions include
microcephaly in 40%, mental retardation in 40% to 50%,
psychiatric disorders in 10% and learning difﬁculties in
almost everyone (68). Other rarer genetic causes of CHD
known to have neurologic associations include myotonic
muscular dystrophy, dystrophinopathies, mitochondrial
disorders, and abnormalities in the β-oxidation of fatty
acids (66). Abnormal Baseline Cerebral Perfusion
CBF and autoregulation are abnormal in many patients
with CHD, and these abnormalities precede interventional procedures and CPB. In fact, in a series of 25
term infants with CHD, mean CBF was only 40% of the
normal mean value, and 5 children exhibited CBF less
than 10 mL/100 g/min (69), which is a threshold known
to cause ischemic injury in piglets (70). Potential reasons
for an impaired baseline CBF include cerebrovascular developmental abnormalities, inadequate systemic cardiac
output, and regional systemic blood ﬂow distribution. Of
particular importance, however, is that the (usually powerful) CBF response to hypercarbia was demonstrated to
be deﬁcient in children with CHD (69). Furthermore, both
lower baseline CBF and impaired hypercarbic vasodilatation were signiﬁcantly associated with demonstrated WM
injury on MRI (69). Baseline preoperative CBF appears to
be especially low in infants with a ductus-dependent circulation. The most studied patients are those with HLHS,
who consistently have abnormally low CBF in the region
of 30–40 mL/100 g/min. Preoperative Cyanosis
Cyanosis is intrinsic to almost 40% of infants born with
CHD. It may occur abruptly upon either during transition from the fetal to independent circulation, or during
ductus closure, or otherwise more gradually with age due
to progressive right ventricular hypertrophy and the resulting right-to-left shunting.

Compensatory polycythemia
typically develops, which may lead to an elevated risk of
thrombosis and stroke (66). The cerebral consequence
of chronic cyanosis is not clear. In vitro models using
cultured rat neurons exposed to prolonged oxygen deprivation demonstrated an elevated rate of apoptosis (71),
but more recently, an in vivo rat model in which rats
were placed in a 10% O2 atmosphere immediately at birth
to mimic cyanotic heart disease failed to demonstrate
an increased rate of apoptosis. Studies in children with
cyanotic CHD indicate that although the cerebral oxygen extraction remains fairly constant (∼30%), cerebral
oxygen saturation (ScO2) correlates directly with arterial
saturation (SaO2). The critical ScO2 that is capable of
initiating ischemic brain injury is uncertain. Experimental work suggests it to be in the vicinity of 30%, and
Kurth et al. (72) demonstrated ScO2 below 40% in 13% of
preoperative children with CHD using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS). An important consequence of reduced
tissue oxygenation is a smaller safety margin in the event
of cardiorespiratory embarrassment. Clinical Injury in the Preoperative Infant
with Congenital Heart Disease
Although the neurologic assessment of neonates is dif-
ﬁcult, several studies have conﬁrmed that infants with
congenital cardiac disease have a signiﬁcant incidence
of brain injury preoperatively. In a study of 131 infants,
neurobehavioral problems were present in as many as
50% (73). The advent of MRI has introduced a safe and
sensitive method by which subtle neurologic lesions can
be identiﬁed (Fig. 2). Mild ischemic lesions (in the form of
PVL—see subsequent text) were present in 16% of a series
of infants undergoing surgical repair (which increased to
>50% postoperatively) (74), an observation subsequently
conﬁrmed in repeated studies (23). An MRI study of
ten infants undergoing arterial switch operation revealed
preoperative lesions in four (75). Detailed neurobehavioral assessment of neonates is difﬁcult, but standardized
neurologic examination of 56 consecutive infants with
CHD referred to Montreal Children’s Hospital revealed
abnormalities in more than one third (73). Manifestations
included commonly hypotonia, irritability, microcephaly
and developmental delay, and less commonly hypertonia
and seizures. Recently, the preoperative window has been scrutinized
for speciﬁc events that could potentially trigger ischemic
brain injury. Any episode giving rise to acute hypoxia or
hypotension—such as a cardiac arrhythmia—is a potential
risk.

Interestingly, percutaneous balloon atrial septostomy
has been shown to be a major predictor for preoperative
focal brain injury in patients with transposition of the
great arteries, suggesting that interventions other than
open surgery utilizing CPB may be important (76,77). In a series of 29 term neonates with transposition of

Hypothermia
The importance of the preservation of tissue viability
through the use of hypothermia cannot be overstated
in modern surgical practice. It is an integral part of
tissue protection and organ support in widely contrasting
areas of medicine, and its role in functional recovery
following prolonged hypothermic cardiac arrest are well
known. Considerable energy is being spent trying to
establish protocols for the controlled use of hypothermia
following stroke, cardiac arrest, and even in combination
with postsurgical extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
(ECMO). However, no uniform strategy has yet emerged
for the management of therapeutic hypothermic therapy. The mechanisms whereby hypothermia exerts its neuroprotective effects have not fully been elucidated. The
effects on reducing total oxygen consumption and preserving high-energy tissue phosphates are now well known
following the pioneering work in the 1950s by Wilfred Bigelow (2), subsequently conﬁrmed by others (78)
(Fig. 3). It should be pointed out that these initial studies
opposed the prevailing opinion of the day, which noted
that tissue metabolic oxygen consumption increased during hypothermia. It was only through careful anesthetic
regulation and elimination of shivering that the true effects of temperature on tissue metabolic requirements
were realized. Hypothermia causes a reduction in the
reaction kinetics of mitochondrial respiration and energy utilization. This is a central prerequisite to whatever
other protective properties hypothermia conveys, because
unless intracellular ATP concentrations remain within
physiologic constraints, neuronal viability will not be
preserved. The onset of hypothermia is initially accompanied by a
rise in mean arterial blood pressure due to a sympathetic
response in association with shivering.

In the context
of CPB, this may be masked by the anesthetic state,
but thereafter a fall in mean pressure is observed (79). Although some animals, for example the rat, can maintain
unaltered perfusion pressures at temperatures as low as
27◦C, temperatures lower than 33◦C to 34◦C in humans
is associated with progressively worsening hemodynamic
compromise, and eventually ﬁbrillation. In Bigelow’s
experiments using dogs, he was frequently able to topically
cool to as low as 18◦C to 20◦C (albeit with a signiﬁcant
attrition rate during rewarming) before the onset of
ﬁbrillation, and certain hibernating animals achieve core
temperatures as low as 3◦C (80). Arterial oxygen tensions

with the rate of metabolic oxygen consumption (79). However, in the context of CPB, this linear relation is
sometimes lost, and several reports describe an elevation
in CBF with progressive cooling (81). The reason for this
is not known, although some have attributed it to localized hyperemia resulting from regional ischemia from
microemboli, although this is mere supposition. At approximately 28◦C, a state of ‘‘cold narcosis’’ develops and
consciousness is lost even in the absence of anesthetics. Below 28◦C, decreases in cerebral metabolic rate are larger
than those in blood ﬂow, and therefore the oxygen delivery
capacity of the cerebral circulation is in a metaphoric state
of excess where supply increasingly exceeds demands (82). This is the reason for the descriptions of extremely low-
ﬂow rates (<5 mL/100 g/min) in meeting cerebral energy
demands during deep hypothermic continuous low-ﬂow
CPB (83). During periods of ischemia, hypothermia slows the
breakdown of high-energy phosphate compounds (adenosine triphosphate, adenosine diphosphate, adenosine
monophosphate), as well as the rate of formation of
lactate (and inorganic phosphates), and this effect is
related to the depth of hypothermia. Whether this relation is exponential or linear is not precisely known because few studies have examined numerous temperature
points.

Overall, however, the breakdown of high-energy
phosphates (and overall metabolic oxygen consumption)
appears to be slowed by two- to threefold for a 10◦C
drop in core temperature (similar to the rule-of-thumb 7%
drop in basal metabolic rate for each 1◦C drop from normothermia) (84). The preservation of energy stores has
equally been demonstrated following deep hypothermic
CPB strategies (85). How the reduction in basal metabolic rate recovers
during and after rewarming is not completely understood,
especially with regard to the inﬂammatory consequences
of CPB. For example, although mild hypothermia has
been shown in some non-CPB models be protective
following head trauma, in others it has been shown to
prolong the activation of nuclear factor-κ B (NFκB) and
augment the generation of cytokines (86). Similarly in
one model of DHCA, mild post-CPB hypothermia delayed
the recovery from lactic acidosis and energy deﬁcit (87). These observations may imply that although hypothermia
may confer a theoretic protection from severe ischemia,
the inﬂammatory and metabolic consequences may just
reﬂect slower kinetics. The inﬂammatory response may be
of no lesser amplitude, but simply more drawn out: lactic
acidosis may take longer to develop, but may also take
longer to recover. In fact, it is difﬁcult to differentiate the hypothermic
effect on biomolecular reaction kinetics from other possible effects on neuronal ultrastructure and function. For
example, dendritic spines at neuronal synapses are motile
structures whose shape can alter rapidly within seconds
or minutes, and are believed to be inﬂuential in wider
brain function. Progressive hypothermia profoundly affects dendritic spine morphology, ultimately leading to
their disappearance (88) (Fig. 4). Although this appears
to be a reversible process, it illustrates the high degree
of neuronal plasticity that can occur with hypothermia. Another synaptic consequence of hypothermia is reduced
presynaptic neurotransmitter release, which may have a
central role in the neuroprotective effects (89). Furthermore, although the cell cycle continues at a signiﬁcantly
retarded rate at hypothermia, cultured cells frequently fail
to divide, resulting in the formation of giant cells instead. Interestingly, the protective effects of hypothermia
do not appear to be restricted to the CPB window. Brief (20 minutes) periods of moderate hypothermia
have been shown to elicit delayed protection against
subsequent hypoxic-ischemic injury lasting for as long
as a week, similar in concept to delayed preconditioning
from ischemia, hypoxia, endotoxin, or pharmacologic
means (90).

The impact of hypothermia in clinical situations is
of huge interest, but its use in CPB remains a subject of considerable debate. Normothermic strategies
have gained increasing support on the basis of being more ‘‘physiologic’’ (91), while others contend that

ECMO (100). Postischemic hyperthermia has been shown
to have a detrimental effect on histologic outcome (101),
and should therefore be avoided. There clearly remains much to be learned about the
mechanisms and applications of hypothermia in clinical
neuroprotection—including the context of CPB. There
has been a gradual shift away from deep (16◦C–20◦C)
and profound (11◦C–16◦C) hypothermia during CPB, in
the empirical belief that ‘‘warmer is better.’’ The shift
is not based on sound evidence but rather through
individual speculation or the drive to shorten rewarming
durations. Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest
DHCA involves the complete uninterrupted cessation of
CPB ﬂow after a period of perfusion cooling to a predetermined target temperature. The advantages of DHCA
include its ease and simplicity combined with unparalleled clarity of a surgical ﬁeld free of blood and ancillary
equipment. In addition, it is worth considering that DHCA
typically involves a shorter dynamic exposure to CPB
than continuous perfusion techniques. The ‘‘ideal’’ target
temperature has not been established, but should offset
potential harmful consequences of severely unphysiologic
temperatures against the necessary reduction in cerebral
metabolic oxygen consumption. A typical target temperature of between 16◦C and 20◦C has emerged through
anecdotal practice, although this may vary from as low as
11◦C (profound hypothermia) to as high as 25◦C (moderate hypothermia). Uneven cooling is generally perceived
to be a risk factor for injury. Large temperature gradients
should therefore be avoided (102).

The temperature gradient between venous-line blood and arterial-line blood
is usually kept within approximately 4◦C to 6◦C and certainly not more than 10◦C to avoid ‘‘crash-cooling,’’ which
has been linked with neurologic dysfunction (103). For
prolonged (>40 minutes) exposure to circulatory arrest,
it is generally recommended that cooling duration should
be for a minimum of 20 minutes, and the head should
be packed in ice for the entire ischemic period to reduce the ambient temperature. Electroencephalography
has been used to demonstrate that ‘‘electrocerebral silence’’ is achieved after cooling over 27 minutes to a ﬁnal
temperature of 17.8◦C (104). After the reinstitution of CPB, rewarming is initiated
by removing the ice and warming the CPB perfusate. Particular attention should be paid to the temperature
gradient—which should not exceed 10◦C between venous
and arterial blood—during rewarming because there is a
real risk of liberating dissolved gases in the form of air
emboli, which are recognized to result in microvascular
obstruction. It is widely accepted that rewarming should
be more gradual, over a minimum period of approximately 30 minutes, to prevent rebound hypothermia once
separated from CPB. Considerable energy has been spent attempting to identify the minimum ‘‘safe’’ duration of DHCA—the threshold
beyond which the hazard for sustaining neurologic dysfunction begins to rise signiﬁcantly. The observed link between cardiac surgery and neurologic injury was historically interpreted as a causal
link to DHCA. Experimental studies were energetically

719
undertaken to investigate the effects of DHCA on cerebral
physiology and neuronal injury. Cerebral reperfusion
anomalies (no-reﬂow) are a consistent feature of DHCA,
and have been interpreted as an indicator of poor neurologic outcomes, although this link has not been well
established. Nevertheless, interventions that alleviate no-
reﬂow including steroids (105), leukocyte ﬁltration (106),
PAF antagonism (44), circuit miniaturization (107), and
IP (47) are all considered to be beneﬁcial to subsequent
recovery. In the 1990s, several groups used histologic models in
neonatal piglets to conﬁrm that DHCA initiated diffuse
neuronal death throughout the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and hippocampus (108–111). However, these models
required lengthy (60–120 minutes) uninterrupted DHCA
and the animals frequently received no cardiorespiratory
support postoperatively. The relevance of these studies
to the modern application of DHCA is therefore dubious, and more recent histologic studies using meticulous
perioperative support have failed to demonstrate histologic neuronal apoptosis after 60 minutes of uninterrupted
DHCA (112). Nevertheless, DHCA has progressively fallen
out of favor with many surgeons who have adopted novel
continuous perfusion techniques instead. The Boston Circulatory Arrest trial represents an impressive attempt to examine the impact of DHCA on
neurologic outcome in a carefully controlled prospective manner, and provides the best insight into ‘‘safe’’
durations of DHCA on functional outcome. The investigators chose to study (113) patients with D-transposition
of the great arteries (18). This diagnosis is associated
with an extremely low incidence of cardiac and noncardiac anomalies, and because they have essentially
normal hemodynamic physiology after successful arterial switch operation they are ideally suited for studying
neurologic outcomes. After randomizing patients to surgical repair using either uninterrupted DHCA or deep
hypothermic continuous low-ﬂow CPB (50 mL/min/kg),
the children have been subsequently followed up to 8 years
with detailed neurofunctional assessment. Overall, despite
lengthy DHCA durations (mean 53 minutes, maximum 70
minutes), the children did not perform signiﬁcantly worse
in Wechsler academic achievement tests, neuropsychological testing or speech and language development when
compared with children exposed to continuous low-ﬂow
CPB. More importantly, both groups of children faired
signiﬁcantly worse than age-matched controls, supporting
the idea that factors other than ischemia during DHCA
are alone important.

Careful analysis of the impact of
uninterrupted DHCA duration on neurodevelopmental
outcome implied a threshold of approximately 40 minutes, beyond which the risk of permanent cerebral injury
is signiﬁcantly elevated (19). This is consistent with earlier
observational and anecdotal reports suggesting a threshold of 45 minutes (114). At present, there is no clinical
evidence to suggest that DHCA for durations shorter than
this are associated with greater neurologic impairment
than any other CPB strategy. Nevertheless, few topics
raise more debate (115) than differences between perfusion strategies. A reasonable summary would be that (a) prolonged uninterrupted DHCA (longer than 60 minutes) is universally
perceived to be detrimental; (b) DHCA beyond 40 minutes
is associated with increasing risk of neurologic injury;
(c) continuous perfusion techniques or IP (see subsequent
text) should be employed if lengthy repairs are anticipated; (d) if DHCA is to be used, intermittently perfusing
makes intuitive sense and has considerable experimental
support; (e) many who continue to use DHCA actually
use a combination of DHCA and SCP (e.g., cannulating
the neoaorta during stage I Norwood) to limit cerebral ischemia durations to 20–25 minutes; and (f) the incidence
of subtle neurodevelopmental abnormalities is approximately 30% regardless of perfusion strategy employed. Finally, for all the debate and controversy, it remains
especially pertinent that recent anonymous audience response sessions at major international cardiac surgery
meetings indicate that almost all surgeons retain DHCA in
their armamentarium and approximately 20% frequently
use it (116). INTERMITTENT PERFUSION
Analogous to the wisdom behind the administration of
blood cardioplegia intermittently, in the late 1990s the
concept of IP emerged (47). Experimental studies demonstrated that ultrastructural abnormalities sustained during
uninterrupted circulatory arrest could be avoided by intermittently perfusing at full pump ﬂows for 2 minutes
every 20 minutes (Fig. 5). Experimental studies have indicated that IP reduces cerebral no-reﬂow and reduces
the astroglial ultrastructural changes associated with
DHCA (47). Many surgeons who employ DHCA have embraced this concept either by adhering to a predetermined
IP regimen or otherwise more commonly by administering
brief periods of systemic ﬂow at convenient interludes in
the surgical procedure. The required rate of systemic ﬂow
during the period of IP necessary to prevent the increase
of harmful metabolic products has recently been shown to
be approximately 80 mL/kg/min (117).

The clinical impact
of IP protocols on functional neurologic recovery has not
been formally characterized. The introduction of IP strategies has raised the possibility that cooling to deep and profound hypothermic
temperatures may not be necessary. Target temperatures
in the region of 20◦C to 25◦C (moderate hypothermia) have
several theoretical advantages. The most obvious are the
shorter durations required for cooling and rewarming and
therefore potentially shorter overall durations of CPB. In

Regional, Low Flow and Selective
Cerebral Cardiopulmonary Bypass
The relation between reduced cerebral metabolic oxygen consumption and hypothermia prompted the notion
that greatly reduced cerebral ﬂow rates during CPB
might nevertheless provide sufﬁcient oxygenated blood
to prevent accumulation of anaerobic metabolic products. Therefore, the concept of low-ﬂow CPB emerged in the
early 1990s (118) to reduce cerebral ischemic injury while
avoiding some of the technical incumbencies of full-ﬂow
CPB. Experimentally, low-ﬂow CPB is usually administered at a rate of 50 mL/kg/min through the aorta (14)
(delivering approximately 40%–50% normal CBF). In clinical practice, low-ﬂow CPB is more frequently administered
through a cannula inserted in the innominate artery and
therefore is more accurately regional or SCP (Fig. 6). Further confusion arises because 50 mL/kg/min to the cerebral
circulation actually represents quantitatively normal CBF. Nevertheless, despite being quantitatively normal overall,
regional distribution of CBF during regional perfusion abnormalities still result in no-reﬂow phenomena (119). This
may be because CBF at hypothermia is pressure dependent rather than ﬂow dependent (120). The use of carotid
artery pressure lines or NIRS to dictate innominate artery
ﬂow rates seems sensible (121). Continuous low ﬂow and SCP are associated with
preservation of cerebral energy stores (118), improved
cerebral reperfusion (107), improved histologic outcome,
and improved neurologic function (122) when compared
with prolonged (60–120 minutes) uninterrupted DHCA
in the experimental setting. However, these inordinately
lengthy DHCA durations represent a signiﬁcant departure
from clinical practice and therefore the relevance of

above baseline during hypothermic low-ﬂow CPB, regional
perfusion abnormalities do occur, which gives rise to the
potential for regional ischemic injury. Consequently, no-
reﬂow may occur following low-ﬂow CPB, although less
consistently and to a lesser extent than DHCA (107). In
addition, we have compared the systemic inﬂammatory
response during deep hypothermic CPB and found low

DHCA (107,125). This may be attributable to the longer
dynamic exposure to CPB associated with continuous

An obvious prerequisite for low CPB is that perfusion
cannulas must necessarily remain within the surgical ﬁeld
for the duration of CPB. This represents a disadvantage
when compared with DHCA, where the uncluttered operative ﬁeld is a major attraction. In addition, empirically
one might ask—if the perfusion cannulas must remain in
place—why not remain at full ﬂow, and why cool to deep
hypothermia? Most who use ‘‘low-ﬂow CPB’’ are probably
actually providing normal or near-normal CBF through
selective cannulation of the head and neck vessels (SCP)
and are cooling to reduce ischemic injury to the rest of the
body. Normothermic Full-ﬂow
Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Several groups have recently advocated the use of normothermic CPB strategies for the repair of complex CHD
on the empirical assumption that it represents a more
‘‘physiologic’’ and less inﬂammatory state (91,126–128). Angelini’s group reported lower troponin levels following
normothermic CPB, although when adjusted for duration
of aortic cross-clamp, this observation was no longer sig-
niﬁcant (127). Moreover, levels of activated complement
C3a, and IL-6 and IL-8 were not different. Pouard et al. similarly reported lower levels of troponin, and a non-
signiﬁcant trend toward shorter intensive care stay with
normothermic CPB (126). However, the long-term and cerebral effects of using
normothermic CPB have not been assessed, and there is a
signiﬁcant body of evidence to suggest that normothermic
temperatures may not be advantageous. Higher CPB
temperatures are associated with leukocyte activation
and elevated numbers of rolling and adherent leukocytes
on intravital microscopic evaluation of the cerebral
circulation (129). In preliminary studies, we have shown
that BBB permeability to gadolinium is signiﬁcantly
elevated when compared with deep hypothermic CPB
(E. Hickey, M. Jerosch-Herold, J. You, et al., unpublished
data, 2005). Furthermore, normothermic temperatures
require high ﬂow rates, which increase the risk of
microemboli, increases left heart return and the need
for suction, reduces intracardiac exposure, and reduces
