the safety margin in the advent of equipment failure. Therefore, despite considerable opinion and debate, the
subject of normothermic full-ﬂow CPB is largely a matter
of personal preference. ACID–BASE MANAGEMENT
The role of CO2 management in CPB has been studied
extensively both in animal models and in prospective
randomized trials in pediatric patients (130,131). Two
different blood gas management strategies have been
advocated based on the effect of CO2 on arterial and intracellular pH at hypothermic temperatures: α-stat strategy
maintains a pH of 7.40 measured without mathematic
correction for temperature effects, whereas pH-stat uses
a nomogram-based mathematic correction for the alkalotic effects of hypothermia. Using pH-stat strategy, CO2
is added to maintain a temperature corrected pH of 7.40. The addition of CO2, however, lowers the intracellular pH,
resulting in impaired intracellular enzymatic function. In
addition, the loss of electrochemical neutrality is rendered
more problematic because at hypothermic temperatures,
the normal buffering systems (NH3−, HCO3−) become ineffective. At hypothermia, buffering capacity is limited to
negative charges of the amino acids composing intracellular proteins. The amino acid histidine, which contains
an α imidazole ring, is the most important buffer at hypothermic conditions. The principal advantage of α-stat
strategy, therefore, is in preserving intracellular electrochemical neutrality, maintaining appropriate intracellular
pH, and improving the efﬁcacy of intracellular enzymatic
function (132). During moderate hypothermia, selecting
one blood gas management strategy over the other appears
less critical, because brain intracellular pH differences
are small (133,134). During deep hypothermia (with or
without DHCA), the addition of CO2 during active brain
cooling could potentially improve the distribution of the
cold perfusate to deep brain structures. α-Stat strategy became the preferred approach in many
centers based on experimental ﬁndings suggesting that
α-stat preserved cerebral autoregulation and maintained
coupling between ﬂow and metabolism down to low
cerebral perfusion pressures near 20 mm Hg (135). The
experimental data was, in part, supported by three trials
in adult patients demonstrating improved cognitive outcomes with α-stat management (136,137). These data were
never conﬁrmed in the pediatric population, however. Virtual epidemics of choreoathetosis following a switch
in perfusion protocols from pH-stat to αstat prompted
a reinvestigation of the optimum blood gas strategy. Several studies suggested that pH-stat management enhances the distribution of extracorporeal perfusate to the
brain and may help cool the brain more thoroughly and
rapidly (138,139).

Although improved cooling was seen in
these studies, metabolic recovery after circulatory arrest
was shown to be impaired suggesting that the acid load
induced by pH-stat had a negative effect on enzymatic
function after cerebral rewarming. A prospective clinical
trial of α-stat versus pH-stat at Boston Children’s Hospital demonstrated decreased morbidity, and a trend toward
decreased mortality in infants randomized to pH-stat management (130). Numerous clinical and laboratory studies
from other centers in recent years have conﬁrmed the advantages of the pH strategy for pediatric bypass (140–143). The group at Duke in 2000, based on their experimental
work in a neonatal piglet model, advocated a combined
blood gas management strategy using pH-stat during
cooling, followed by α-stat management before initiation
of circulatory arrest (138). The authors of this study
hypothesized that such a successive strategy would allow
the beneﬁcial effects of more uniform cooling along with
avoidance of intracerebral acid-load during rewarming. On the basis of the collective body of experimental
and clinical evidence, we would advocate the use of pHstat management for hypothermic CPB in infants, at least
during the period of perfusion cooling. Current trends to
reduce the degree of hypothermia, shorten the duration
of circulatory arrest, and prolong the time allocated for
rewarming may reduce the relative importance of one
management strategy versus another. Hematocrit and Hemodilution
Hemodilution during CPB was initially introduced to
reduce allogeneic blood requirement in combination with
the large early CPB circuits. In addition, hemodilution
was proposed to improve ﬂow in the microcirculation. In
past decades, standard practice would involve lowering
the hematocrit during CPB to 25% or even as low as
20%. However, severe hemodilution is not only a problem
for red cell–dependent gas transport, but also for platelet
and humoral factor–dependent coagulation and proteindependent intravascular oncotic pressure. The threshold
for ‘‘unacceptable’’ hematocrit is not clearly deﬁned, but
several studies indicate that oxygen delivery, tissue blood
ﬂow, and clinical outcome may only be affected at levels
below 14% to 17% (144,145) for extended periods of time. Several animal studies have revisited the issue and
increasingly suggest that higher hematocrits (30%) are
instead preferable (146–148). Not only is tissue ﬂow and
metabolism improved but leukocyte and endothelial cell
activation is also reduced (147). Jonas’ group undertook
a randomized clinical trial comparing hemodilution to
20% or 30% (149).

Intraoperative data were comparable
but psychomotor development scores were signiﬁcantly
worse in the lower hematocrit group. However, mental
development scores were not different, nor were the incidences of abnormal neurologic examinations. Therefore,
the evidence is not ﬁrm enough to categorically advocate

36. Brain Injury Following Infant Cardiac Surgery and Neuroprotective Strategies
723
one category over the other, but a gradual shift away
from lower hematocrits toward 25% to 30% and higher is
occurring. CIRCUIT MINIATURIZATION AND
ELIMINATION OF ALLOGENEIC BLOOD
Conventional neonatal CPB requires the use of a blood
prime to prevent unacceptable hemodilution (Fig. 7). Accumulating evidence surrounding the deleterious effects
of blood use has prompted the investigation of circuit
miniaturization for infant CPB. Aside from the risk of
transmission of blood-borne diseases, allogeneic transfusion is now recognized to incite a potent inﬂammatory
response (150–154). Silliman et al. have shown that blood
transfusion is a major risk factor for postinjury multiorgan system failure, including transfusion-related acute
lung injury, especially in certain susceptible patients, including patients with trauma, infants, and those exposed
to CPB (152,154). They have also shown that the risk of
transfusion-related morbidity is highly correlated with the
duration of blood storage. The neutrophil has been implicated as a primary
effector cell in the pathogenesis of transfusion-mediated
injury (150). The plasma from stored red blood cells
directly primes neutrophils for cytotoxicity, prompting
the release of lytic enzymes. (154). Additionally, recent
studies have documented delayed apoptosis of neutrophils
in patients receiving blood transfusions. These ﬁndings
may explain the association between fresh whole blood
transfusions and lengthier intensive care stays (113). Bloodless

was similarly shown by Fromes et al. who incorporated
biocompatible components into a minimal extracorporeal
circuit in adult patients (158). Most impressively, Merke
et al. have reported a series of infants as small as 3.4 kg
placed on CPB with a crystalloid prime of 190 mL, all
of whom recovered uneventfully (159). Assessment of the
clinical beneﬁts has yet to be undertaken. Ultraﬁltration and Leukocyte Reduction
Leukocyte ﬁltration during CPB was initially tested in animals in the early 1990s and subsequently used in humans
undergoing cardiac surgery (160). When leukocyte ﬁl-
ters are incorporated into the extracorporeal circuit, total
leukocyte count and CD18-mediated neutrophil adhesion
are signiﬁcantly attenuated compared to control patient
groups, but this has not translated into clinical beneﬁt. In
particular, parameters of myocardial and lung function,
including respiratory index, blood PaO2, spirometry and
pulmonary vascular resistance, and myocardial-bound
creatine kinase (CK-MB) levels were not affected by the
use of a leukocyte ﬁlter (161,162). Equivocal ﬁndings,
however, are difﬁcult to interpret because ischemiareperfusion injury can be mediated initially by other
effector cells, and therefore occurs independent of neutrophil participation (163). Intraoperative ultraﬁltration, using a conventional or
modiﬁed approach, has been reported to reduce the rise
in total body water following CPB in pediatric patients,
as well as the duration of mechanical ventilation (164). Modiﬁed ultraﬁltration has the advantage of ﬁltering
only the patient’s extracellular blood volume, resulting in
greater hemoconcentration efﬁcacy and more rapid recovery of ventricular function (165). Similar to the data with
leukocyte depletion, however, reduction of inﬂammatory
markers with ultraﬁltration have been inconsistent and
have not provided durable clinical beneﬁt, likely because
many factors including choice of ﬁlter and pore size, the
hemoﬁltration rate, and the timing of the procedure importantly inﬂuence outcome (40). In addition, the removal
of certain anti-inﬂammatory cytokines, such as IL-10, may
actually produce deleterious effects (166). Anti-inﬂammatory Strategies: Steroids
and Aprotinin
Steroids. Many clinical and laboratory studies have suggested that corticosteroid usage improves the postoperative course after CPB (105,167,168). These salutary effects
have mainly included a reduction in myocardial injury
with improved cardiac output and decreased pulmonary
edema (168,169). Glucocorticoids blunt neutrophil upregulation, inhibit the expression of adhesion molecules
produced by the activated endothelial cells, including
endothelial-leukocyte adhesion molecule-1 (ELAM-1) and
intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1), and therefore reduce diapedesis of leukocytes into injured areas
(170,171).

Whether the corticosteroid provides enhanced
neuroprotection following DHCA is more controversial (172). A recent study by Schubert et al. showed no
attenuation of neuronal injury following 120 minutes of
DHCA in a neonatal piglet model using 30 mg/kg of methylprednisolone administered 24 hours before surgery. In
fact, these authors showed both increased rates of necrotic
neuronal cell death and apoptosis at 6 hours following separation from CPB (173). In contrast, Langley et al. demonstrated improved recovery of CBF following 60 minutes
of DHCA in their neonatal piglet model wherein methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg) was administered at 8 hours and
2 hours before surgery (105). Given the disparate experimental ﬁndings, it is not surprising that current steroid
administration practices (type, dosing, route, and timing)
during the conduct of pediatric open heart surgery are
highly variable. Ungerleider’s group (105,168) has extensively studied the timing of steroid administration and
found that premedication with methylprednisolone (Solumedrol) 30 mg/kg 12 hours preoperatively is beneﬁcial
relative to isolated administration in the pump prime. Bronicki et al. demonstrated that preoperative administration of dexamethasone (1 mg/kg) intravenously 1 hour
before the pump run in children produced an eightfold
decrease in IL-6 and a threefold decrease in TNF-α, which
improved convalescence (167). Given the lack of consensus
regarding steroid administration and the wide variations
in practice among large centers in North America, it is
clear that a multicenter clinical trial to investigate the
potential impact of corticosteroids and their optimum
administration is indicated. Aprotinin. Aprotinin is a serine protease inhibitor that
inhibits kallikrein and plasmin, resulting in suppression
of multiple systems involved in the inﬂammatory response, including inhibition of factor XII, bradykinin,
anaphylatoxins as well as activation of leukocytes and
platelets (174). Aprotinin has known efﬁcacy in reducing
the bleeding diathesis that frequently accompanies the
use of CPB. Costello et al. reported reduced operative
closure time and blood product exposure in a matched
prospective study of 36 patients less than 6 months of
age (175). It is possible, given the deleterious effect of
blood product exposure and extended operative time, that
aprotinin may exert a beneﬁcial effect in pediatric CPB. Accordingly, aprotinin has shown promise in reducing
capillary leak, reducing biochemical markers of inﬂam-
mation, and improving myocardial recovery following
CPB (176).

Aprotinin has also been shown to result in
more rapid recovery of cerebral energy metabolism following DHCA in animal models and is associated with a
decrease in neurologic complications of patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (177). Jonas’ group has
recently demonstrated improved neurologic function after

36. Brain Injury Following Infant Cardiac Surgery and Neuroprotective Strategies
725
deep hypothermic CPB in piglet survival models (178), but
clinical studies are awaited. To achieve adequate plasma levels of aprotinin (200
KIU/m–400 KIU/m), the dose must be calculated on either
the patient’s weight or body surface area, and must include
an appropriate dose in the circuit prime. Aprotinin will
prolong the activated clotting time and an alternative
method to determine adequacy of heparinization during
CPB is necessary. Anaphylactic reactions are exceedingly
uncommon (0.3%–0.6%), but have been reported (179). CEREBRAL RECOVERY FOLLOWING
CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS
Reperfusion Injury
The period of early reperfusion following hypoxiaischemia is now recognized to be of paramount importance to the progression of injury. Reinstigating capillary
ﬂow results in a ﬂood of oxygenated blood containing in-
ﬂammatory mediators, activated and primed leukocytes,
and oxygen (48). Leukocytes adhere and transmigrate, amplifying the inﬂammatory response to injury that we now
know contributes to the magnitude of both pathologic and
functional injury sustained. Neurophils exhibit an oxidative burst resulting in the liberation of free radicals and
activated oxygen species. These highly labile molecules
initiate a self-perpetuating cascade of lipid-membrane perixoidation resulting in loss of cellular integrity, an inﬂux
of cytosolic calcium, and cell death. Techniques to reduce
the circulating leukocyte pool through the use of leukocyte
ﬁlters in the CPB circuit reduce leukocyte adherence in the
reperfusion phase, reduce no-reﬂow (probably by reducing
microvascular obstruction by leukocytes), and are associated with improved clinical recovery following DHCA. Similarly, containing the reperfusion oxidative burst by
antagonizing superoxide dismutase or administering free
radical scavengers reduces cerebral injury following both
DHCA and other situations of hypoxia-ischemia. The magnitudes of both the cellular and cytokine loads of the
postischemic inﬂammatory response are now clearly recognized to be directly proportional to the subsequent
neurologic dysfunction. Interestingly, systemic methods
of delayed preconditioning render leukocytes refractory to
activation and thereby reduce the inﬂammatory response
during reperfusion. Postoperative hemodynamic instability may further
contribute to the initiation and progression of injury in a
vulnerable brain. Prolonged stay in intensive care is therefore associated with poorer neurologic outcomes (180). The consistent demonstration of a no-reﬂow effect following CPB strategies involving partial or total cerebral ischemia has generated interest in the impact this
may have early in intensive therapy unit (ITU).

injury sustained during prolonged DHCA (181), probably
because of dysfunctional cerebral autoregulation (182). Both hypercapneic and hypoxemic cerebral vasodilatation
is deﬁcient following DHCA (Fig. 9). Norwood patients are
necessarily hypoxemic and are therefore in a precarious
position until cerebral autoregulation returns (probably
at least 8–12 hours later). This does not mean that DHCA
must be avoided, but rather that conscious efforts should
be directed at maximizing cerebral oxygen delivery in this
period—perhaps through the use of ECMO or ventricular assist devices (VADs) (183). Recognizing such ‘‘at-risk’’
groups and tailoring postoperative cerebral support represents an important future area for research and clinical
improvement. MECHANICAL ASSIST FOLLOWING
HYPOTHERMIC CARDIOPULMONARY
BYPASS
Though data are limited at present, one intriguing idea
to mitigate neurologic injury following periods of hypothermic CPB is to improve CBF by mechanical assistaugmented cardiac output (184). Use of mechanical
support—VADs and ECMO—also simpliﬁes the postoperative care of infants following the Norwood procedure
because of the enhanced cardiac output and oxygen

726
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
delivery. Initial results with VAD were disappointing
because it was used to salvage neonates who developed
refractory hemodynamic deterioration and because of
troublesome bleeding complications (185). Subsequent
modiﬁcations have instead resulted in considerably more
successful application. Speciﬁcally, these modiﬁcations
include: (a) elimination of an oxygenator in the ECMO
circuit in patients with patent systemic-pulmonary artery
shunt by harnessing the patient’s own lungs to provide gas
exchange; (b) further reducing the level of anticoagulation
required by increasing VAD-ﬂow rates to approximately
twice systemic cardiac output; and (c) routinely using
mechanical assist rather than utilizing it as a salvage
option. Laboratory studies in neonatal piglets have conﬁrmed
that augmentation of cardiac output from 100 mL/kg/min
to 200 mL/kg/min, especially in severely hypoxemic
piglets, increased CBF and cerebral oxygen delivery (186). A subsequent multi-institutional study has suggested that
routine VAD use immediately following CPB and ultraﬁl-
tration leads to measurable neurologic beneﬁt in following
the Norwood operation for HLHS (187). Sixteen of the 18
patients survived and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior
Scale were normal for all infants tested. A more detailed examination of outcomes is clearly warranted in
a larger controlled study. Of course, the potential neurologic beneﬁts will be offset by the morbidity associated
with prolonged extracorporeal support. However, the concept of mechanically augmenting CBF and oxygenation
is supported by the conﬁrmed loss of cerebral autoregulation (182), no-reﬂow and dangerously low cerebral
tissue oxygenation early postoperatively following Norwood operations (188). A reasonable strategy may include
reserving postoperative VAD use to neonates with severe
preoperative hypoxemia, those in whom prolonged hypothermic CPB was necessary, or in those institutions
with suboptimal current outcomes following Norwood
operation. RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
IN CEREBRAL MONITORING:
NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY
NIRS is an FDA-approved noninvasive optical technique
that can provide continuous real-time assessment of
microcirculatory oxygenation at the patient’s bedside. Biological tissues are relatively transparent to nearinfrared light (700–900 nm). Within this range of optical
wavelengths, oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin
have different absorption spectra. The attenuation of light
from the emitter is detected and from this a value for
the tissue (cerebral) oxygen saturation (rSO2) can be
calculated. This is the same principle by which pulseoximetry works, except that pulse-oximetry measures
the pulsatile—and therefore arterial—component.

NIRS
instead provides a ‘‘weighted average’’ of the tissue
circulation: 75% to 85% of the signal is contributed to
by venules. Because mixed venous saturations (SvO2) vary
according to cardiac output, NIRS potentially can provide
real-time information about both tissue oxygenation and
tissue perfusion. Deciphering the relative contribution of
each of these components (hemoglobin oxygen saturation
and blood ﬂow) is not possible from the NIRS calculation
alone. Although isolated values are therefore not especially
helpful, its use as a trend monitor has been shown to be
useful for identifying abrupt changes in tissue oxygen
delivery that should be addressed to minimize ischemic
injury. NIRS has been applied both in the operating room
while on CPB and postoperatively in the intensive care. Preliminary studies have investigated the potential
use of NIRS during hypothermic CPB. For example,
Tweddell’s group conﬁrmed that the use of regional
cerebral perfusion (RCP) was successful in maintaining
high (80% versus 65% baseline) cerebral ScO2, although
after CPB they fell to levels below baseline (∼53%) (189). The authors additionally recognized that the risk of
cerebral desaturation was signiﬁcantly increased in the
early postCPB period. Studies of this kind will prove
important in determining the reference normal patterns
during and after surgery. In the operating room, NIRS can be used to identify regional perfusion anomalies (e.g., by misplaced cannulae)
either by revealing abnormally low values or otherwise
through asymmetric readings between bilateral monitors (190). This latter circumstance is presently a matter
of contention (191) because signiﬁcant bilateral disparity
(>10%) has been reported within individuals in whom no
injury was sustained (192). In one case, the bilateral cerebral NIRS readings were signiﬁcantly different throughout
the procedure (including preoperatively) and were resistant to repeated interventions aimed at improving the
lower reading (193). Because no injury was sustained, the
inference is that considerable variations exist within individual patients, and therefore the value of using bilateral
monitors is currently not fully understood. Alternatively, NIRS can be utilized during periods of
reduced CPB ﬂow—or circulatory arrest—to indicate the
point at which tissue levels of oxygenation have fallen to a
threshold that might be injurious (generally considered
to be 20% below baseline (191)). Once this point is
reached, intervention can be directed toward restoring
tissue oxygenation (temporarily increasing pump ﬂow rate
or intermittently perfusing the head and neck).

A similar
application has been the use of lumbar NIRS during
surgical repairs of coarctation of the aorta where distal
perfusion techniques are being employed: dangerously
low values imply a risk of ischemic injury to the
spinal cord (194). Of course, the central premise behind
this practice is that by intervening on the basis of

727
NIRS readings, clinical neurologic outcome is improved. Evidence is accumulating to corroborate this practice:
Kurth et al. reported that low intraoperative NIRS
values may predict worse neurologic recovery (195),
Austin’s group reported that by intervening at threshold
levels, recovery can be improved (196). However, these
experiences are small and retrospective. There is clearly
the need to more formally assess the issue in a prospective
controlled manner in addition to clarifying normative
values and trends. The increasing scrutiny of the postoperative period in
the etiology of brain injury has led to early attempts
at using NIRS in intensive care to monitor cerebral
oxygenation. A prerequisite requires an understanding
of the ‘‘normal’’ trends in postoperative cardiac surgery
patients. Early studies on infants undergoing Norwood
procedures have indicated that the ScO2 typically falls
from a baseline value of 65% to 70% pre-CPB to
approximately 50% in the ﬁrst 12 hours (consistent with a
no-reﬂow effect or elevated cerebral oxygen extraction
recovering from metabolic acidosis) before gradually
increasing to approximately 55% at 72 hours (188). More than one third of the measurements in these
infants were below the previously reported critical level
of 48% (197,198) (Fig. 10). Proposed use of NIRS
in the postoperative period is supported by studies
investigating the association between postoperative mixed
venous saturations and functional neurologic outcome. Hoffman et al. undertook repeated sampling of mixed

Preconditioning and Pharmacologic
Induction of Tolerance
The search for pharmacologic methods of neuroprotection has largely been driven by the huge burden of adult
stroke. However, a signiﬁcant problem with neuroprotective strategies in adult stroke is the lack of a well-deﬁned
preaura. This typically precludes the administration of
agents in the preischemic window. In contrast, neurologic complications of both adult and congenital cardiac
surgery are ideally suited to preemptive neuroprotection. Unfortunately, decades of research have revealed several
means of experimental neuroprotection, but all have failed
to translate into treatments for patients. The bulk of
this work has centered on the blockade of ‘‘excitotoxicity’’ where the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate
is released and causes postsynaptic opening of calcium
channels. Toxic intracellular calcium accumulation results in cell death. Many reasons for the failed clinical
application of these previous strategies exist, including
severe side effects, poor trial design or dose–response
issues. Preconditioning is a concept whereby brief exposure
to a harmful stimulus in a dose below the threshold
for causing tissue injury provides robust protection—or
tolerance—against the injurious effect of a subsequent
more severe insult (200). The primary stimulus can include
a wide variety of insults, including hypoxia, ischemia,
seizures, noxious drugs, or toxins. A central prerequisite
is that the primary stimulus must be administered in a
very brief and low dose. Two main types of preconditioning exist: early preconditioning occurs minutes to hours following the stimulus

728
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
and lasts for a few hours, whereas delayed preconditioning
occurs 1 to 3 days after the stimulus and the protection
persists for up to 10 days (200). Delayed preconditioning
is an active process, dependent on protein synthesis and
induces a complete switch in the genetic response to injury that mimics the hibernating state (201). There is a
metabolic downregulation of activity and household gene
expression (before ischemic injury). After delayed preconditioning, if a severe ischemic insult is sustained the
expression of inﬂammatory and injurious gene expression
is greatly reduced. Interestingly, circulating leukocytes
are also affected, and although they still accumulate in the
infarct zone, they are refractory to activation (202). Several agents can induce powerful delayed preconditioning, but the most closely studied is bacterial endotoxin
(and its relatives). In tiny doses, endotoxin induces robust and sustained protection against systemic sepsis and
brain, myocardial, renal, and hepatic ischemia (203–205). Endotoxin preconditioning acts through an evolutionary
historic Toll-like receptor signaling axis (206). It is likely
that local products released during delayed ischemic preconditioning also act through this common pathway. It
is hoped that less toxic Toll-like receptor ligands will
be identiﬁed to test this concept in early clinical trials. Already the application to CPB-related injury has
been made: endotoxin preconditioning has been shown
to signiﬁcantly reduce neuronal loss after experimental
DHCA (207). Nonhuman primate dose–response studies
are presently under way to more accurately determine
the therapeutic window for humans (M. Stenzel-Poore,
personal communication, 2007). The principal attractions of delayed preconditioning
techniques are that they provide systemic multiorgan
protection, they render the innate inﬂammatory response
refractory to activation and the window of tolerance
extends for as long as 10 days (200). The potential exists,
therefore, to pharmacologically protect against the entire
operative and early intensive care period. CONTINUING THE PURSUIT
OF CIRCUIT MINIATURIZATION
To capitalize on the considerable achievements in reducing blood priming volumes in infant CPB, a systematic
approach needs to be adopted to all CPB components,
including tubing, pumps, oxygenators/heat exchangers,
cardiotomy suction, and ﬁlters. Tubing length and diameter are two important factors
when trying to minimize circuit priming volume. Downsizing from 1/4 to 3/16 in. tubing almost halves the volume
to 1.73 mL per 10-cm length. Some centers apparently
even employ 1/8 in.

tubing for arterial lines in very small
neonates with a volume of 0.75 mL/10 cm (159). Tubing
length can be signiﬁcantly reduced by repositioning the
venous reservoir and arterial roller pump console closer
to patient. Alternatively, a conventional console with a
mast-mounted arterial roller pump has resulted in a 29%
reduction of priming volume (208). Suction and venting
lines can hold a substantial volume, which can impact on
the dynamic priming of the extracorporeal circuit as it
needs to be replaced during CPB. Poiseuille’s Law states
that ﬂow is proportional to the fourth power of radius,
and therefore small decreases in diameter can drastically
reduce ﬂow. Drainage may therefore need to be encouraged through the use of kinetic-assisted venous return
(KAVD) or VAVD. These techniques introduce potential
risks of air aspiration should venous return become momentarily insufﬁcient. However, with the use of automated
reservoir sensor levels, this risk should be minimized. We have routinely used VAVD both clinically and in our
experimental model at—20 mm Hg without untoward
effects. The arterial pump in our experimental circuit was a
COBE roller pump with 3/8 in. tubing and 40-cm boot
length, yielding a pump prime of 6 mL. Theoretically
a shorter raceway would allow for further reductions in
tubing length, but the higher revolutions per minute would
make hand-cranking more difﬁcult in the event of power
failure. Although centrifugal pumps are used in pediatric
patients, none are available with 1/4 or 3/16 in. connectors,
precluding their use in miniaturized circuits. The priming volume of oxygenators has been tremendously reduced because the screen-type oxygenator was
used for the ﬁrst successful open heart surgery in 1953. Current oxygenators for neonatal perfusion have static
priming volumes of 43 mL (Capiox RX 05, Terumo,
Japan), 52 mL (Safe Micro, Polystan, Denmark) and 60 mL
(Lilliput I, Dideco, Italy). Recently, Fuji Systems successfully developed a thin silicone rubber hollow-ﬁbber
oxygenator with no plasma leakage, better blood compatibility, low blood prime, and low-ﬂow resistance in
the ex vivostudies (209,210). Silicon is generally perceived to be more biocompatible than polyethylene or
plastic. An arterial-line ﬁlter is a safety device used in a high
percentage of pediatric patients (211). Some departments,
however, have eliminated arterial-line ﬁlters because
they have priming volumes comparable to oxygenator
modules (159) (Dideco D 736 Newborn 40 mL, and
Terumo Capiox AF02 40 mL).

However, removal of arterial
ﬁlter would increase the chances of microemboli and
sacriﬁce the bubble purge line, which is usually connected
from ﬁlter to reservoir, necessitating an additional bubble
sensor ﬁlter. A new arterial ﬁlter is predicted to become
available in 2007 with a priming volume of only 12 mL. Potential volume reductions may also be possible for other
integral parts of neonatal circuits, including hemoﬁlters
and cardioplegia systems and need to be targeted by the
biomedical corporations.

36. Brain Injury Following Infant Cardiac Surgery and Neuroprotective Strategies
729
SUMMARY: A MODEL
OF THE COMBINED RISKS
Infants with complex CHD are neurologically abnormal
long before arrival in the operating room. A hypothetical
model drawing together the current understanding would
suggest that early in gestation teratogens that interfere
with cardiovascular development may also interfere with
noncardiac embryogenesis and result in possible cerebrovascular or parenchymal brain abnormalities. As a
result, even at term the incidence of microcephaly and
neurologic immaturity is high. Some of the microglial
and neuronal vulnerability displayed by normal preterm
infants may therefore be present in a neonate with CHD. The child may be cyanotic with low baseline tissue oxygenation and therefore a small safety margin for cerebral
oxygen delivery. The CBF is likely to be lower than normal, especially if the circulation is ductus dependent. At
the same time, the already precarious deep cortical WM
vascular supply is still not fully developed, placing this
area at particular vulnerability. The neonatal period may
be interspersed with episodes of cardiorespiratory embarrassment attributable to their functional morphology, and
may periodically initiate early ischemic injury in these vulnerable regions. Interventional procedures will likely be
necessary and are now being recognized as a major cause
of ischemic brain injury in these critically ill preoperative
infants. When the need for surgical intervention is reached,
the child is then placed on CPB. Generalized activation of
the innate inﬂammatory response takes place within 10–15
minutes, resulting in leukocyte activation, endothelial unit
activation, and liberation of apical cytokines. Exposure
to allogeneic blood products in the disproportionately
large extracorporeal circuit further ampliﬁes the systemic
inﬂammatory response. Harnessing this response through
pharmacologic means and eliminating the use of blood
products is a major potential therapeutic avenue. Systemic
inﬂammation disrupts the integrity of the BBB, triggering
local tissue edema and exposing the cerebral parenchyma
to harmful products of inﬂammation. Even without
cooling or ischemia (DHCA), this inﬂammatory response
is itself capable of initiating irreversible neuronal injury. Furthermore by avoiding DHCA, the inﬂammatory load
may be greater and the total CPB duration longer. During cooling, profound changes in neuronal metabolism, synaptic function, and dendritic ultrastructure all
occur. Alterations in perfusion, acid–base balance and
hematocrit are all superimposed and periods of total or
relative ischemia may then be initiated.

During these
ischemic episodes, basal aerobic metabolism persists,
albeit at a greatly reduced rate. Ensuring maintenance
of hypothermia is important and intermittent or low-
ﬂow techniques may be beneﬁcial in this regard. NIRS
represents a potential method of monitoring gradual
declines in cerebral oxygenation during ischemic periods. Upon reintroduction of cerebral perfusion and rewarming,
the microvascular capillary bed is occluded with cellular casts, ﬁbrin, and inﬂammatory debris. The denuded
endothelium is dysfunctional and resistant to NO and
prostacyclin-mediated vasodilatation and vasoconstriction from endothelin-1 predominates: cerebral autoregulation has been lost and no-reﬂow has been established. Methods of reducing this phenomenon include the use of
leukocyte ﬁlters, steroids, free radical scavengers, eliminating blood prime, inhibiting platelet activation and IP
during DHCA. Nevertheless, the reintroduction of oxygen
delivery fuels an oxidative burst with hydroxyl radicals
wreaking havoc through self-perpetuating lipid peroxidation and cell membrane disintegration. The rewarming
period carries the potential threat of gaseous microemboli from dissolved gases. Oxygen delivery is now plentiful
while on CPB, allowing the oxygen deﬁcit incurred during
periods of reduced perfusion to be partially recuperated. However, after separation from CPB, both cardiac
output and oxygenation are potentially under threat. The loss of cerebral autoregulation is now of central
importance because CBF will vary in parallel with
episodes of low cardiac output. Similarly, hypoxemia
following staged cyanotic palliation is unable to induce
the required elevations in CBF. Both cardiac output
and tissue oxygenation are low in the ﬁrst 24 hours
postoperatively and NIRS monitors conﬁrm that levels
consistent with ischemic injury are frequent in this
period. Methods to maximize cerebral oxygen delivery
(e.g., ECMO) are likely to be especially beneﬁcial during
this window. Nevertheless, the threat of primary ischemic
events continues for the entire intensive care duration, and
neurologic dysfunction therefore correlates with its length. Only by appreciating the wider picture and addressing
threats throughout the neonatal period are we likely to
make signiﬁcant inroads into the neurologic morbidity
of infants with CHD. The particular importance of the
preoperative and postoperative components should result
in the gradual introduction of therapy speciﬁcally tailored
to cerebral protection, such as identifying the high-risk
groups, maximizing and continuously monitoring cerebral
oxygen delivery, harnessing the systemic inﬂammatory
response, inducing tolerance through preconditioning and
identifying speciﬁc risks within intensive care.

KEY POINTS
■The neonatal brain is especially vulnerable to ischemic and inﬂammatory injury
●Preoperative injury is common
●Both open and percutaneous procedures are initiators of injury

●Elimination of DHCA has not reduced the incidence of neurologic injury
●Uninterrupted DHCA greater than 40 minutes is
associated with elevated risk
■There is no clinical evidence that DHCA lesser than
40 minutes poses greater risk than any other CPB
strategy
■Intermittent
or
continuous
perfusion
strategies
should be employed if lengthy DHCA is anticipated
■Cerebral tissue oxygen levels are frequently dangerously low in the early postoperative period

◗ECMO for Infants and Children
D. Michael McMullan, Martin J. Elliot, and Gordon A. Cohen
The modern era of cardiovascular surgery began with John
Gibbon’s pioneering work in developing extracorporeal
cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) technology that enabled
surgeons to begin to perfect many of the surgical
techniques used now. In the years following Gibbon’s
ﬁrst successful atrial septal defect closure utilizing CPB
in 1953 (1), much experience has been gained with
this innovative technology. By 1958, John Kirklin had
performed open-heart surgery on more than 240 patients
utilizing CPB (2). In the intervening years, every facet of
CPB has been examined and reﬁned. Improvements in
CPB techniques have provided surgeons the opportunity
to tackle the most complex anatomic anomalies in even
the smallest babies. Likewise, advances in methods of
extracorporeal support methods have enabled clinicians
to expand clinical indications and implementation in the
intensive care unit (ICU). Although the initial experience with extracorporeal
membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in adult patients was
discouraging (3), improved outcomes were observed in
newborns, older infants, and children with respiratory
failure (4,5). Respiratory failure remained the primary
indication for ECMO until the late 1980s. As preoperative
care, anesthesia, CPB, and surgical techniques evolved and
improved, the ECMO for isolated cardiac or combined
cardiorespiratory failure expanded, usually as a last
ditch effort for the dying infant or child. With growing
experience, cardiac ECMO has begun to make the
transition from ‘‘rescue’’ therapy, to ‘‘therapeutic’’ and
even ‘‘preventive’’ therapy. Coincident with advances
in pharmacologic and mechanical ventilatory support
strategies for respiratory failure, the use of ECMO in the
cardiac surgery patient population has steadily increased
as a proportion of the Extracorporeal Life Support
Organization (ELSO) registry (Fig. 1). In 1985 there
were only 32 cardiac ECMO cases versus 385 neonatal
(noncardiac) cases, increasing to 548 cardiac cases versus
751 neonatal cases in 2003 (6). TYPES OF MECHANICAL SUPPORT
Several methods have evolved to provide mechanical
cardiopulmonary support outside the operating room
(OR). In general, ventricular assist devices (VADs) are
used to provide mechanical cardiac support alone, whereas
ECMO is used to provide either combined cardiopulmonary or isolated pulmonary support. Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) provides
total cardiopulmonary support by removing deoxygenated
blood from the venous circulation, exchanging oxygen and
carbon dioxide, and then pumping it back into the patient’s arterial circulation.

Because this method of support
bypasses the patient’s entire central cardiopulmonary circulation, adequate end-organ oxygen delivery is possible
even in the setting of combined respiratory and cardiac
failure. Studies have shown that temporary total cardiopulmonary support providesan environment that isconducive
to myocardial and lung recovery (7). In contrast, venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO)
provides primarily pulmonary support by withdrawing deoxygenated blood from the venous system, exchanging
oxygen and carbon dioxide, and then returning the blood
to the venous system. This is generally the best modality for
treatingpatientswithseverehypoxemiainthesettingofadequate native cardiac output. In certain clinical situations,
ECMO may also be used to provide primarily circulatory
support. The type of mechanical support utilized within
an individual institution will undoubtedly be inﬂuenced
by availability, overall familiarity, and experience with
various devices. However, several forms of mechanical assistance are generally present in tertiary centers, allowing a
more selective approach to mechanical cardiopulmonary. Ideally, the type of mechanical support used should be
based on a careful consideration of the clinical scenario,
underlying cause of the failure, status of the lungs and pulmonary circulation, presence of intracardiac shunts, and
the beneﬁts and limitations of each support strategy. 735

The decision-making process involved in selecting
either ECMO or VAD assistance for use in patients with
postcardiotomy heart failure is often complex. Several
etiologic factors may contribute to postcardiotomy heart
failure, which typically manifests as hypoxemia, acidosis,
pulmonary hypertension, and low urine output. VA-ECMO
is generally an appropriate form of mechanical assistance
for patients with multiple organ system dysfunction as
it allows the greatest versatility of support. VA-ECMO
is necessary in patients with severe cardiac dysfunction.

patients requiring VA-ECMO support in the postoperative

anatomic diagnosis and predicted recoverability from the

MEMBRANE OXYGENATION SUPPORT
The indications for ECMO in pediatric patients may be
broadly classiﬁed as primary respiratory failure, primary
cardiac failure, or combined cardiopulmonary failure. The efﬁcacy of ECMO in supporting neonates with primary respiratory failure has been clearly established. In the newborn, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, meconium aspiration, and sepsis lead to increased pulmonary
artery pressure, resulting in intrapulmonary shunting and
right-to-left shunting at the level of a patent foramen
ovale and ductus arteriosus. As progressive hypoxia and
acidosis develop, the immature myocardium is incapable
of maintaining adequate tissue oxygen delivery, rapidly
leading to complete cardiovascular collapse. Initiation of
ECMO support in these patients provides a therapeutic
window that may allow recovery of native lung function
and thereby reverse the deleterious cycle.

As the underlying cause of lung injury resolves, native lung function
recovers, allowing discontinuation of ECMO support. Pulmonary hypertension, in particular, is a common cause of
morbidity and mortality in pediatric patients, especially
following cardiac surgery (8). Infants with unrepaired
cyanotic heart disease who acquire common viral respiratory illnesses are also at increased risk (8–11). In
these patients, VV-ECMO improves oxygenation, corrects
respiratory acidosis, and reduces pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in increased pulmonary blood ﬂow,
decreased right ventricular strain, better left-sided ﬁlling,
enhanced myocardial oxygenation, and improved cardiac
output with reduced inotropic support. Imamura, et al. reported their experience with patients placed on VV-ECMO
for acute viral pneumonia or inadequate pulmonary blood
ﬂow at the Arkansas Children’s Hospital (8). In their report, VV-ECMO was a successful bridge to recovery or
surgical intervention, and overall hospital survival was
95% in these groups of patients. VV-ECMO is beneﬁ-
cial when cardiac function is adequate to support the

738
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
circulation. Cardiac failure in many of these patients is
related to the severe hypoxemia that accompanies the
underlying disease and once oxygenated blood is infused
into the right side of the heart, and perfused through the
lungs into the left heart, the oxygenated blood getting
to the coronary arteries often results in improved cardiac
function. VV-ECMO requires that the only support needed
is oxygenation. If substantial mechanical circulatory support is needed, then VV-ECMO (which only oxygenates
blood on the right side of the circulation) may not be successful. Cardiac indications for mechanical assist include
treatment of acute myocarditis (12,13), bridging to heart
transplantation (14), treatment of intractable ventricular
arrhythmias (15), pulmonary hypertension, and cardiac
resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest (16,17). ECMO
can also be a very useful supportive measure in children
with cardiovascular collapse secondary to overwhelming
sepsis (18) and in these circumstances, the nature of the
myocardial dysfunction may be so severe that mechanical
assist in the form of VA-ECMO may be essential. Acute heart failure is an uncommon occurrence in
children without underlying congenital heart pathology. When acute heart failure is present in pediatric patients,
aggressive therapy is justiﬁed because of the high potential
for complete recovery. The most common cause of acute
heart failure in children is congenital heart disease and
the most common indication for instituting mechanical
circulatory support in these patients is low cardiac
output following cardiac surgery. It is clinically useful
to categorize these patients with regard to the onset of
acute heart failure: those with failure occurring acutely
after surgical repair and those with failure unrelated to
surgical repair (Table 1). Determining which cardiac patients are appropriate
candidates for ECMO support is complicated. On the basis
of univariate and multiple logistic regression analysis of
retrospectively collected data in 218 patients, Trittenwein
et al. proposed that criteria for placement on ECMO
should include threshold lactate level and central venous
oxygen saturation (19). We believe that such criteria are
restrictive and not universally applicable. Such attempts

to create strict inclusion or exclusion criteria can be
extremely difﬁcult and imprecise. It is probably most
important to provide thoughtful consideration of each
unique clinical scenario in the context of an individual
institution’s experience. Low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) is one of the
most common reasons to consider ECMO support in
postoperative cardiac patients (20,21). The etiology of
postcardiotomy LCOS is often multifactorial. It may occur
in patients with good preoperative myocardial function as
a result of one or more perioperative insults, including prolonged CPB, deep hypothermic circulatory arrest, complex
surgical repair and manipulation of the heart, exaggerated
inﬂammatory response, or inadequate myocardial protection. Alternatively, some patients undergoing surgical
repair have preexisting myocardial dysfunction related to
the underlying anatomic defect. These patients may have
difﬁculty separating from CPB after even a short period of
bypass and they may experience early postoperative myocardial dysfunction. Moreover, acute heart failure may
occur in response to altered myocardial workload related
to newly created anatomy and physiology despite excellent myocardial preservation (e.g., left ventricular failure
following late arterial switch operation). The cardiac insult sustained in these patients is often reversible, which
increases the theoretic potential for myocardial recovery. Clinically, LCOS manifests as poor peripheral perfusion,
oliguria, and lactic acidosis despite adequate intravascular volume. Elevated ventricular ﬁlling pressures are
common. Decreased mixed venous oxygen saturation, due
to inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery, is often an important indicator of LCOS. Traditional therapy
for perioperative cardiogenic shock involves correcting
anemia, hypoxia, obstructive cardiac disease, and optimizing pharmacologic support. Pharmacologic agents act
through a variety of mechanisms, but most contribute to
increased biventricular afterload and heart rate, which increases myocardial workload and oxygen consumption
in the setting of preexisting compromised myocardial
oxygen supply. This exacerbates myocardial ischemia, delaying or preventing myocardial recovery. ECMO is a
useful therapeutic intervention to support the acutely failing myocardium and to reverse the downward spiral of
increasing myocardial oxygen debt. ECMO unloads the
distended and poorly contractile heart, which decreases
ventricular wall stress and myocardial workload, creating a favorable environment for myocardial recovery (22). Consequently, the timing of initiation of ECMO is critically
important in these patients. Earlier institution of mechanical support maintains adequate perfusion of the heart,
brain, kidneys, and other vital organs while minimizing
ongoing myocardial insult and enhancing myocardial recovery.

Several groups have reported improved survival
in patients placed on ECMO in the OR as compared to
those cannulated in the ICU (23–25). This supports the

notion that early initiation of ECMO in the OR in patients
at high risk of LCOS avoids the negative sequela of inadequate postoperative oxygen delivery during the critical
early postoperative period. In 1987, Kanter et al. reported the successful use of
ECMO to treat with postcardiotomy heart failure, with
6 of the 13 patients surviving to hospital discharge (26). Since this initial report, the literature is replete with institutional series of ECMO use in patients with structural
cardiac anomalies. Recently, Morris et al. at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia reported their experience
with 137 cardiac patients supported with ECMO between
1995 and 2001 (27). The patients exhibited a spectrum of
congenital cardiac malformations, including single ventricle with intracardiac mixing and single ventricle with
separate circulations, as well as children with structurally
normal hearts. Overall survival to hospital discharge was
39%. Two thirds of the patients were supported with
ECMO following a cardiac surgical procedure, with 40%
of postcardiotomy patients surviving to discharge. Risks
factors for mortality in this subset of patients included age
younger than 1 month, male gender, increased duration of
mechanical ventilation before initiation of ECMO, and the
development of renal or hepatic dysfunction while being
supported with ECMO. Importantly, failure to separate
from CPB was not identiﬁed as a predictor of mortality, suggesting that ECMO was a life-saving therapeutic
intervention in those cases. In addition, the presence of
single-ventricle physiology was also not identiﬁed as a
risk factor for increased hospital mortality in this series
despite historical bias against the use of ECMO to support these patients. None of the factors analyzed were
predictive of increased mortality in the nonpostoperative
subset of patients, which exhibited 35% survival to hospital discharge. The authors concluded that, ‘‘it is imprudent
to impose strict indications for, or contraindications to
ECMO support’’ considering the fact that many of the
survivors would likely have otherwise died without mechanical support. In another report describing 74 patients
supported with cardiac ECMO between 1995 and 2001
at the University of Michigan, overall hospital survival
was 50% (24). In this series, patients with single-ventricle
physiology exhibited increased mortality when compared
to those with two ventricles (34% versus 58%). Increased
mortality was also observed in patients who developed
renal insufﬁciency (35% required hemoﬁltration).

More
recent reports are ﬁnding improved survival in patients
with single-ventricle physiology, possibly related to recognition of keeping the shunt open to maintain pulmonary
parenchymal perfusion during ECMO support in these
patients (28). Chaturvedi et al. reported their experience with 81
cardiac patients with two-ventricle anatomy who were
managed with ECMO at the Great Ormond Street Hospital
in London between 1992 and 2000 (25). More than
half of these patients were placed on ECMO in the
OR following unsuccessful separation from CPB. Overall
hospital survival was 49%. Hospital survival was 64% in
the group of patients who were placed on ECMO in the
surgical suite compared to 29% in those cannulated in the
ICU. Renal failure was also identiﬁed as a signiﬁcant risk
factor for mortality in this series. Additionally, the ﬁndings
from this series and others indicate that the presence
of a residual anatomic cardiac lesion is associated with
poor outcome and is, therefore, a contraindication for
initiation of ECMO support. Clearly, it is critical to
identify etiologic residual structural lesions that are
amenable to immediate surgical repair before initiating
mechanical support. However, we feel that ECMO is a
useful ‘‘bridge’’ to return to the OR or to transfer a
very unstable patient to the catheterization laboratory
in order to evaluate possible residual cardiac lesions not
identiﬁed by other methods of assessment. When possible,
transesophageal echocardiography should be performed
to carefully evaluate cardiac function and anatomy before
initiating postoperative ECMO support (20). In general, ECMO is a useful therapeutic intervention
for hemodynamically unstable patients in whom delay
to surgical intervention is unavoidable or when aggressive resuscitation is necessary before undertaking surgical
correction such as is often seen with obstructed total
anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. Furthermore, mechanical support may be very helpful when confronted
with speciﬁc types of congenital cardiac defects. There is
growing evidence that supports the use of a centrifugal
VAD during the perioperative period in patients with an
anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery
and in patients undergoing late single-stage arterial switch
operation. Neonates with refractory congenital cardiomyopathy or dysrhythmia may beneﬁt from ECMO support
while diagnostic studies and therapeutic interventions are
pursued. Data from the ELSO registry (Table 2) demonstrates
that in patients placed on extracorporeal life support
(ECLS) for cardiac failure, 57% of neonates and 58%
of pediatric patients survived ECLS.

Furthermore, 38%
of neonates and 43% of pediatric patients survived to
hospital discharge or transfer to another facility (6). Single-institution data over a 6.5-year period on 137

of Philadelphia essentially mirrors the ELSO registry
data (27). Although the mortality rate in these patients is
signiﬁcant, the expected mortality rate in this group would
have approached 100% without mechanical support. The
use of mechanical cardiac assistance can dramatically
reduce mortality in children with acute heart failure. More
liberal use could potentially achieve even better outcomes
in these patients. In patients with acute heart failure secondary to viral myocarditis or end-stage cardiomyopathy, the clinical
course may progress rapidly and ultimately lead to death. ECMO is an important life-saving therapeutic maneuver that facilitates recovery of myocardial function or
serves as a bridge to cardiac transplantation, which is
the only deﬁnitive therapeutic option currently available for children. Duncan et al. reported 83% survival
in 12 pediatric patients with refractory myocarditis who
were supported with ECMO (12). When all 15 patients
in this study were examined (12 ECMO, 3 VAD), 47%
recovered native ventricular function and 33% were successfully bridged to cardiac transplantation with ECMO. This contrasts sharply with pre-ECMO era in which only
pharmacologic support was available to these patients and
the reported mortality rate for acute myocarditis was as
high as 100% (29). Similarly, Marx et al. reported 67%
survival in patients with acute myocarditis and 62% survival in patients with cardiomyopathy who were supported
with ECMO (21). Insufﬁcient donor organ availability is
a major problem in both adult and pediatric transplant
programs. However, limitations related to donor-recipient
size mismatch disproportionately affects organ availability for pediatric recipients. This results in prolonged time
between listing and transplantation, with the potential for
acute deterioration while awaiting a donor organ. In this
circumstance, mechanical cardiac assist has been successfully used as a bridge to transplantation. There are several
series that describe the successful use of ECMO as a bridge
to transplantation (30–35). Goldman et al. (14) reviewed
the U.K. experience with mechanical assist as a bridge
to transplantation. In this series, 77% of patients were
successfully bridged to transplantation and survived to
hospital discharge, with better results observed in patients
supported with ECMO than those supported with paracorporeal VAD. Kirshbom et al. at the Children’s Hospital of
Philadelphia described 31 patients supported with ECMO
as a bridge to cardiac transplantation (35).

They found
no difference in long-term survival between patients supported with ECMO and those not supported with ECMO
before heart transplantation. Six of the 31 patients were
reported to have had sufﬁcient recovery of cardiac function to be weaned from ECMO and discharged from the
hospital (bridge to recovery). Twelve of the 31 patients underwent cardiac transplantation. Overall survival to hospital discharge was 48% (15 of 31). Interestingly, only 18%
of the postsurgical patients survived to transplant versus
64% of the nonsurgical patients. Several patients in this
series survived after more than 250 hours of ECMO support, including four that were successfully transplanted
after 500 hours of support and one that was supported
for 1,126 hours before transplantation. This experience
suggests that there is not universally deﬁned period of
support before transplantation beyond which survival is
unlikely. Ideally, ECMO should be initiated before complete cardiovascular collapse in patients with progressive
or chronic heart failure. However, several reports suggest
that the initiation of ECMO following cardiac arrest is
not associated with poorer outcome following transplantation (24,32,36). ECMO can also be an effective strategy
for managing hemodynamic stability in postoperative patients following transplantation. Kirshbom reported 22%
hospital survival in patients requiring early ECMO support
following transplantation, whereas 67% of patients who
required ECMO support later during their postoperative
course survived to hospital discharge (35). TIMING OF MECHANICAL CARDIAC
ASSIST
Survival following mechanical cardiac assistance
in
postcardiotomy patients is often poorer than would be
expected in the setting of acute myocardial injury or dysfunction. This is probably related to the importance that
timing of initiation of mechanical circulatory support has
on ameliorating the negative effects of ongoing cardiopulmonary failure. In a review of 81 cardiac patients placed
on perioperative VA-ECMO over a 100-month period at
Great Ormond Street Hospital, Chaturvedi et al. reported
that patients placed on ECMO in the OR demonstrated
a 64% incidence of hospital survival compared with 29%
in patients placed on ECMO in the cardiac ICU (25). Although these ﬁndings may reﬂect intraoperative selection bias toward patients who may not have otherwise
required mechanical support, the data supports earlier
initiation of ECMO to facilitate more complete myocardial recovery. Along these lines, Shen et al. reported 87%
hospital survival in 23 patients who were routinely converted directly from CPB to VAD support in the OR after
undergoing the Norwood procedure (37).

Although many
of these patients would likely have survived without circulatory support, the authors assert that some patients might
have otherwise developed acute heart failure and therefore beneﬁted from early implementation of mechanical
cardiac assistance, especially in the setting of hypoxemia
that is associated with all Norwood patients. Research
has demonstrated that in the setting of hypoxemia, the
brain is extremely vulnerable to diminished cerebral oxygen delivery that can accompany a fall in systemic cardiac
output (38). In the setting of hypoxemia, augmentation

37. ECMO for Infants and Children
741
of cardiac output in the initial hours following exposure
to CPB can have important effects on brain protection
and may be particularly beneﬁcial to infants following
Norwood (39). Such aggressive use of perioperative ventricular assistance in these high-risk patients supports the concept of
improved patient survival with the early use of mechanical
circulatory support. The rationale for improved survival with early mechanical support is based on early correction of cardiac
and systemic pathophysiologic states. Acute heart failure,
manifest as a low cardiac output state, produces a critical
mismatch between the tissue oxygen demand and delivery. This mismatch affects both the systemic circulation and
the myocardium. Traditional pharmacologic therapy for a
low cardiac output state typically increases heart rate and
systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance. Tachycardia
and increased afterload result in greater cardiac workload with concomitantly increased myocardial oxygen
demand at a time when myocardial oxygen delivery is maximally compromised. These stresses result in signiﬁcant
ongoing myocardial injury that may prevent or compromise myocardial recovery. When utilized in the setting of
severely depressed cardiac output, mechanical circulatory
support reduces myocardial workload while maximizing
myocardial oxygen delivery. When employed in this setting, mechanical devices often enable rapid weaning, and
even complete discontinuation of inotropic agents, which
results in further reduction in myocardial oxygen demand. In addition, mechanical assistance facilitates ventricular
decompression, which reduces myocardial wall tension,
further decreasing myocardial oxygen demand. Mechanical cardiac assistance may be considered an important
tool in the armamentarium of the surgeon to address severe heart failure rather than as therapeutic intervention
used solely for ‘‘rescue’’ therapy. As such, earlier use of mechanical support should be considered to increase hospital
survival following acute heart failure in these patients. Rapid-deployment ECMO or ECLS refers to the use of
ECMO as an immediate life-sustaining therapy in the setting of acute cardiopulmonary failure. Early reports of the
use of ECMO for this purpose involved the use of a standard ECMO circuit to resuscitate patients who developed
cardiovascular collapse following cardiac surgery (30,40). A modiﬁed rapid-deployment ECMO circuit for use in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
was introduced at Boston Children’s Hospital in 1996 (16). Designed to enable the initiation of total cardiopulmonary
support within 15 minutes, the circuit is maintained in the
ICU and was easily transportable throughout the hospital.

The circuit is stored in the primed state, using vacuum and
Normosol solution (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL). Blood is added to the circuit at the time of cannulation if
available. Otherwise blood is added later and ultraﬁltra-
tion is performed to optimize the patient’s ﬂuid-volume
status. By institutional policy, a rapid-resuscitation ECMO
team is notiﬁed after a patient with heart disease has
undergone 10 minutes of standard CPR. In an early retrospective review of 11 patients, 10 patients (91%) were
successfully weaned from ECMO, 7 patients (64%) were
successfully discharged from the hospital, and 6 patients
(55%) are described as long-term survivors. One child
developed mild neurologic impairment and another developed moderate neurologic impairment. In another review
of patients who underwent ECMO support during active
CPR, the median duration of chest compressions was 45
minutes (range, 5–105 minutes) in the survivors and 50
minutes (range, 15–90 minutes) in the nonsurvivors (27). Fifty-one percent of patients were weaned from ECMO,
and 37% were discharged from the hospital. Almost half
of the patients who received CPR for greater than 60 minutes survived to discharge. Although all patients had ice
applied to their heads during resuscitation, two patients
developed new-onset seizure activity before discharge. Long-term neurologic outcome in patients who require
ECLS remains to be determined. Because rapid-deployment ECMO can potentially improve survival following cardiopulmonary arrest, this
therapeutic option is being adopted by a growing number of institutions. However, this approach requires the
presence of an in-house team that is capable of initiating
ECMO support within a very short period of time. The increased costs and manpower associated with ECLS make
this is resource unavailable to many institutions. As the trend toward earlier surgical intervention for
congenital heart disease continues, the use of perioperative mechanical circulatory support will undoubtedly play
an increasingly important role in the management of these
patients. Despite increasing surgical complexity and more
complicated perioperative care, patients and families will
continue to expect excellent clinical results. Mechanical
cardiac assistance is a critically important therapeutic
option in the treatment of perioperative low cardiac output. Early implementation of mechanical support provides
numerous physiologic advantages when compared with
pharmacologic support alone and frequently leads to improved clinical outcome. EQUIPMENT
The typical ECMO circuit is comprised of three main components: pump, oxygenator, and heat exchanger.

Additional components include tubing and monitoring devices
to ensure safe operation of the ECMO circuit. Regardless
of the type of ECMO utilized, the basic principles of the
circuit remain the same (Fig. 3). Deoxygenated blood is
removed from the patient, accelerated by an in-line pump,
oxygenated, heated, and then returned to the patient. Tubing size, oxygenator volume, and requisite ﬂow rates will

circuit priming volume for neonates is frequently twice
that of the patient’s circulating blood volume, whereas
circuits used for adults generally require less than half the
equivalent of the patient’s blood volume for priming (41). Platelet consumption is a common problem, which is
related to direct blood contact with foreign material. Consequently, the immune response associated with platelet
activation and consumption is increased in proportion to
surface area of the oxygenator (41). The following sections will discuss the details related to
pumps, oxygenators, heat exchangers, tubing, and safety
and monitoring devices. Pumps
First developed by Gibbon in 1950, the standard roller
pump (Fig. 4) has been the device most widely used ECMO
pump over the last 30 years. Its popularity is based on the
fact that it is a relatively inexpensive and reliable device
with a simple design that responds well to servocontrol. Blood ﬂow is generated by sequential linear tubing
compression by a roller that forces blood forward. As each
roller completes its compressive phase, another begins
its compressive phase, providing near constant forward
blood ﬂow. Tube compression is carefully adjusted to
avoid complete tube occlusion to minimize hemolysis and
tubing wear (42). Although the roller pump is generally
a reliable pump for use in ECMO circuits, it does have
FIGURE 4. Roller pump. several signiﬁcant limitations. It is dependent upon gravity
drainage from the venous system to maintain adequate
inﬂow pressure. It requires continuous servoregulation
and pressure monitoring to prevent the development
of excessively negative or positive pressure within the
circuit. Excessive negative circuit pressure may result
in cavitation, causing air to be drawn out of solution. Furthermore, excessive negative pressure may result in
hemolysis, damage to venous and/or atrial structures near
the site of cannulation (41). An in-line bladder is generally
utilized to assist in the monitoring and servoregulation of
the ECMO circuit to prevent excessive negative pressure. Excessively elevated circuit pressure may result in circuit
rupture. When the system is compromised, the roller
pump has the potential to pump a large volume of air,
leading to massive air embolism.

Long-term use of the
roller pump may cause spallation of the tubing within
the pump housing, potentially resulting in embolization
of particulate matter or even complete circuit rupture due
to repetitive occlusions. Owing to these concerns with roller pumps, investigators have experimented with the use of centrifugal pumps. Centrifugal pumps (Fig. 5) propel blood by forced vortex
pumping utilizing rotating cones within a rigid conical
housing. In general, these pumps are less traumatic to
formed elements in the blood, although increased turbulence and shear stress at very low or high ﬂow rates
increases damage to blood elements. Additionally, ﬁbrin
deposits within the pumping chamber often limit the functional life of these pumps to 5 to 7 days (43). Unlike roller
pumps, inﬂow occurs independent of gravity, enabling
these pumps to be positioned at any height relative to
the patient. Centrifugal pumps are sensitive to preload
and afterload, either of which will signiﬁcantly impact
pump ﬂow. Like roller pumps, centrifugal pumps are capable of generating signiﬁcantly negative line pressure,

pumps have not been widely adopted at ECMO centers
due to compatibility issues with membrane oxygenators
related to increased intrinsic resistance to ﬂow and associated hemolysis. Recently, there has been renewed interest
in the use of centrifugal pumps, due to development of
newer-generation hollow ﬁber oxygenators, that exhibit
less resistance to ﬂow and appear to interface much better
with centrifugal pumps. Despite the unique theoretic advantages and disadvantage of roller and centrifugal pumps used in ECMO circuits, neither pump has proven superior to the other (44). Oxygenators
The artiﬁcial oxygenator, like the lungs, facilitates gas exchange, introducing oxygen and removing carbon dioxide
from circulating blood. Ideally, an extracorporeal gas exchange devise should be noncompliant to allow constant
blood volume, thereby minimizing the risk of thrombosis
and hemolysis (41). In modern oxygenators, blood ﬂows
into the manifold region of a rigid housing, from which it
disburses to either a diffusion membrane in the case of a
membrane oxygenator, or to microporous ﬁbers in a hollow ﬁber oxygenator. Oxygenated gas is directed through
the oxygenator in a direction that is countercurrent to the
ﬂow of blood through the device. The movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the diffusion membrane or
microporous ﬁbers is facilitated by the gradients created
by the countercurrent nature of gas and blood ﬂow, the
constant partial pressure of the introduced gasses, and ongoing consumption of oxygen and production of carbon
dioxide by the patient. The net effect of diffusion is that
oxygen diffuses into the circulating blood as carbon dioxide is eliminated. Because these devices characteristically
exhibit very efﬁcient carbon dioxide diffusion capacity,
carbon dioxide must occasionally be added to the gas
mixture to maintain normal carbon dioxide concentration
within the blood. By contrast, the relative diffusion coefﬁ-
cient of oxygen is signiﬁcantly lower and oxygen transfer is
substantially dependent upon the duration of hemoglobin
transit through the oxygenator. As a result, oxygenators
are relatively limited in their capacity to exchange oxygen. Each oxygenator has an intrinsic ﬂow rate, above which it
is no longer able to increase venous blood saturation from
70% to 95% (45).

Like the lungs, oxygenators are susceptible to structural defects, extravascular ﬂuid accumulation, loss of
circulating blood products, and thrombosis, which may
lead to ventilation/perfusion mismatch (45,46). Water,
plasma, and blood may collect in the gas phase of the
oxygenator, decreasing the efﬁciency of carbon dioxide
exchange. Accordingly, PCo2 is a sensitive indicator of
ﬂuid accumulation within the oxygenator that decreases
the functional surface for gas exchange. Similarly, clot
formation and ﬁbrin deposition are not an uncommon
cause of oxygenator failure. Elevated preoxygenator circuit pressures (>400 mm Hg), falling postoxygenator PO2,
and evidence of worsening gas exchange by analysis of the
patient’s blood gas are important indicators of mechanical
obstruction within the oxygenator by one or more of these
factors. Currently, two types of oxygenators are used; membrane
oxygenators and hollow ﬁber oxygenators. The membrane
oxygenator (Fig. 6) was based on the spiral-wound silicone
membrane lung developed by Kolobow in 1963 (47) and
is the most commonly used oxygenator for ECMO in the
United States (48). The gas exchange unit is a long, spirally
wound envelope of silicone rubber contained within a
semirigid housing. Gas and blood ﬂow through the series
of winding spirals, which separate them. The long series

Heat exchangers (Fig. 8) are necessary to maintain the
temperature of blood returning to the patient within a limited physiologic range and are particularly important in
the management of neonatal patients due to their propensity for heat loss and inefﬁcient thermoregulatory ability. To prevent unnecessary heat loss, the heat exchanger is
generally placed distally in the circuit just to warm the
blood as it is being returned to the patient. A series of
silicone-coated, nonpermeable stainless steel tubes allow
warm water to ﬂow in a countercurrent manner to blood
ﬂowing through the ECMO circuit.

Blood is heated as it
ﬂows from the higher to more dependent portion of the
vertically oriented heat exchange unit, permitting air bubbles to be trapped in the upper section (46). Failure of
the heat exchanger occurs in approximately 1% to 2% of
ECMO cases (56), most commonly, due to leakage of water
from the device’s inﬂow and outﬂow connectors. Leakage
of blood within the heat exchanger is uncommon, as is
leakage of water into the blood phase of the unit because
of the differential ﬂuid pressures within the ECMO circuit (46). In a survey conducted in 2002, Lawson found
that 82% of ECMO centers used the Medtronic ECMOtherm heat exchanger, 15% used a Gish heat exchanger, and
3% used the Dideco D720 heat exchanger (48). The Jostra
Quadrox D oxygenator combines hollow ﬁber technology

Cannulae
Appropriate choice of cannulae is critically important to
maximize ECMO efﬁciency and limit hemolysis. The size
of cannulae used is based on patient body weight and
the size of the vessels to be cannulated (Table 3). Several
types of cannulae are currently used for ECMO. Each
type of cannula is associated with distinct advantages
and disadvantages; there is no perfect cannula. Arterial
cannulae (VA-ECMO) are available in sizes ranging from
8 Fr to greater than 23 Fr to accommodate vessels ranging
from even the smallest carotid artery to an adult ascending
aorta. Because they are essentially incompressible and
resist kinking, wire-reinforced cannulae are especially
well suited for ECMO. Smaller arterial cannulae are often
packaged with a specialized stylet to facilitate cannulation
of small vessels. Venous cannulae used for VA-ECMO
contain multiple fenestrations to improve venous return
to the circuit. Some cannulae feature a malleable distal
tip that enables the cannula to be tailored to the unique
geometry of the heart during chest cannulation. Largerdiameter, dual-lumen cannulae are designed to allow
VV-ECMO support through a single cannulation site. Tubing
Circuit tubing has improved signiﬁcantly since the advent
of ECMO 30 years ago. Most of the circuit consists of
polyvinyl chloride tubing. A controversial disadvantage of
polyvinyl chloride tubing is the release of the plasticizer
di(2-ethylexyl)phthalate (DEHP), which is associated with
decreased fertility, reduced sperm production, and ovarian
dysfunction in animal studies (58–60). However, a recent
study by Khodayar et al. failed to demonstrate an
adverse effect on somatic growth, pubertal maturity, or
liver, thyroid, renal, or gonadal function in adolescents
who were exposed to DEHP during neonatal ECMO
support; (61) however, the limited durability of polyvinyl
chloride tubing makes it inadequate for use in the
‘‘raceway’’—the portion of the circuit passing through the
roller pump housing. Instead, most ECMO centers utilize
Super Tygon tubing, S-65 HL, in the ‘‘raceway,’’ as it is
more resistant to rupture and has been shown to minimize
