Bladder Reservoir
A recent Duke University survey by Lawson et al. found
that 92% of American ECMO centers utilize a bladder
reservoir (Fig. 9) in the ECMO circuit (48). The inline bladder is situated just proximal to the pump and
serves a several purposes. The bladder provides access to
blood ﬂowing through the circuit, whereby pharmacologic
agents, blood products, and ﬂuid may be administered. Aspiration ports incorporated into the bladder allow
for removal of air that may be inadvertently been
introduced into the circuit. Prebladder circuit pressure is
routinely transduced to provide a quantiﬁable estimation
of the pressure (volume) of the venous blood returning
to the circuit. Servoregulated pumps may be used to
decrease or completely stop blood pump ﬂow if ﬂuid
pressure within the bladder approaches or falls below a
predetermined critical value. The relatively small volume
FIGURE 9. Bladder reservoir. of a bladder is frequently incapable of handling large ﬂow
rates and pressure (volume) ﬂuctuations associated with
older patients. In this situation, the ECMO circuit may
incorporate a parallel segment of tubing to allow blood to
bypass the bladder and be diverted directly into the pump. Pressure Transducers
Circuit pressure is generally monitored prebladder (‘‘in-
ﬂow’’) and between the pump and patient (‘‘line’’) in most
ECMO centers (65). Pre- and postoxygenator pressures are
usually monitored in particular, to detect a changes indicative oxygenator circuit thrombosis or kinking of the tubing. Isolated increases in preoxygenator pressure, in the
setting of a normal postoxygenator pressure, suggest the
development of occlusive thrombus within the oxygenator. Increasing pressure gradient across the oxygenator often
portends eminent oxygenator failure. Excessive pressure
within the circuit may lead to catastrophic tubing rupture.

Risk of circuit disruption is increased as preoxygenator
pressures increase beyond 400 mm Hg, whereas rupture
is probable when pressures increase beyond 500 mm Hg
and imminent above 600 mm Hg. Bubble Detectors
Although the bladder, oxygenator, and heat exchanger,
are capable of trapping large bubbles within the circuit,
in-line bubble detectors are frequently incorporated into
the circuit near the site of blood return to the patients to
decrease the likelihood of air embolism. The pump may
be set to automatic shutoff in the event that bubbles are
detected. After cessation of pump ﬂow, air bubbles rise to
the top of the heat exchanger, where they may be safely
removed through integrated aspiration ports. The Bridge
A short segment of tubing may be incorporated to allow
direct communication between the arterial and venous
limbs of the ECMO circuit near the patient. The main
function of such a ‘‘bridge’’ is to allow continuous blood
ﬂow through the ECMO circuit during temporary periods
during which the patient is removed from ECMO support,
such as during emergency situations or trial periods off
ECMO support following weaning. The bridge is clamped
(occluded) during normal periods of ECMO support. The
inﬂow and outﬂow tubing is clamped near the patient and
the bridge is unclamped to allow continued circuit ﬂow
during temporary periods off ECMO support. The bridge is
generally temporarily opened (‘‘ﬂashed’’) at approximately
30-minute intervals during ECMO support to prevent
stagnation of blood and possible thrombosis within the
bridge segment. Temporarily ﬂashing the bridge creates
a direct arteriovenous shunt within the circuit, which

MEMBRANE OXYGENATION SUPPORT
Supporting a patient with ECMO requires a cohesive
team of surgeons, cardiologists, perfusionists, ECMO
specialists, nurses, and intensive care specialists. The use
of ECMO is fraught with potential complications, each of
which may result in severe morbidity or morality. Clear
communication and constant vigilance by all members of
the team are critical to ensuring patient safety and optimal
clinical outcome. Cannulation
The cannulation strategy for ECMO must be based on
the type of support to be provided (VA-ECMO versus VVECMO), the age and weight of the patients, and underlying
structural or functional cardiac abnormalities. When providing complete cardiopulmonary support (VA-ECMO),
the arterial cannula is generally introduced into the ascending aorta, right common carotid artery, or either
femoral artery. Other cannulation sites occasionally may
be used depending on unique anatomic considerations. The importance of proper cannula selection and quality
of the cannulation to successful ECMO support cannot
be overemphasized. The right common carotid artery is
generally the ideal site for peripheral arterial cannulation
in neonates and infants because of the vessel’s diameter and the fact that relatively direct access to the right
atrium makes the right internal jugular vein the optimal
site of venous cannulation. The optimal cannula size must
take into consideration the size of the carotid artery and
the projected amount of blood ﬂow through the cannula. Cannulation with an oversized cannula should be avoided
to prevent injury to the carotid endothelium or complete
and catastrophic vascular disruption. The cervical arterial cannula is inserted into the common carotid under
direct vision using a limited neck incision. The cannula
is advanced so that the tip lies at the base of the innominate artery.

It is important to avoid advancing the
cannula too far into the aorta to prevent partial occlusion
of the aortic arch, injury to the facing aortic wall, or
retrograde orientation of the cannula into the ascending
aorta. The latter puts unnecessary mechanical stress of
the aortic valve that may lead to injury to the delicate
valve leaﬂets or valvular insufﬁciency. When cannulating
the carotid artery, the surgeons should consider the potential for carotid reconstruction once ECMO support is
discontinued. Although prior neck cannulation does not
preclude subsequent use of the carotid artery, occlusion
of either carotid artery is an obvious contraindication to
cervical arterial cannulation. Carotid artery reconstruction at the time of decannulation can be performed if
cannulation techniques are employed that are conducive
for this. Several reports have demonstrated very good
short- and long-term patency following post-ECMO arterial reconstruction (69,70). Carotid reconstruction is not
performed by all centers and may not always be possible. There are no data demonstrating an advantage with
respect to long-term neurologic function in patients with
as opposed to without carotid reconstruction. Long-term
neurologic outcome may be more related to the condition
of the patient at the time of initiation of ECMO as well
as to other factors related to their underlying condition
(such as hypoxemia and adequacy of cerebral blood ﬂow). Despite the lack of conclusive data, carotid reconstruction
has advocates and is generally recommended if feasible. Direct cannulation of the ascending aorta is generally
performed in patients who require emergent circulatory
support in the immediate postoperative period. This approach enables the clinician to evaluate the mediastinum
for evidence of tamponade and perform direct cardiac
massage when needed. The principles of aortic cannulation used during cardiac surgery are applicable to ECMO
patients. The site of cannulation should be above the sinotubular junction to avoid injury or distortion of the aortic
valve, which may lead to valvular insufﬁciency. The cannula is secured with a purse-string suture and ﬂexible
tourniquet. It is important to direct the tip of the cannula away from the aortic valve while avoiding injury
to the back wall of the aorta. Oversizing the cannula or
advancing the cannula too far into the aorta may cause
a mechanical obstruction to antegrade ﬂow through the
aortic arch and can contribute to difﬁculties in weaning
ECMO support before decannulation.

Femoral artery cannulation is useful in larger patients
and in patients with compromised carotid blood ﬂow. Either femoral artery may be cannulated under direct
vision or using percutaneous Seldinger technique. The
cannula is advanced so that the tip lies in the descending
aorta. We advocate direct suture repair of the femoral
artery at time of decannulation to limit subsequent
limb morbidity related to vascular insufﬁciency. In some
patients, it may be safer to sew a side graft onto the femoral
artery and place the cannula into this side graft. This may

be especially useful in patients with small femoral arteries
in whom placement of an adequate size cannula would
otherwise be hazardous. For example, a 5-mm side graft
is large enough to allow insertion of a 14-mm cannula
and an 8-mm side graft would easily accommodate a
22-mm cannula. This technique can be extremely valuable
in selected cases and greatly reduces the risk of dissection
of the femoral or iliac vessels during cannula insertion. Venous cannulation is generally performed through
the right internal jugular vein, either femoral vein, or the
right atrial appendage. However, as with arterial cannulation, certain anatomic considerations may require the
clinician to adopt unique venous cannulation strategies,
such as is seen in patients who require support following superior cavopulmonary (Glenn) shunt. In patients
requiring VV-ECMO support, the specialized dual chamber venous cannula is inserted through the right internal
jugular vein and advanced so that the tip lies at the inferior cavoatrial junction. Although this may be performed
using the percutaneous Seldinger technique, we prefer to
perform venous cannulation under direct visualization to
prevent unnecessary injury to the vascular structures in
the neck and chest. Some centers insert a second smaller
retrograde jugular cannula that lies near the base of the
skull. This cannula provides improved venous drainage
of the cerebral circulation and may be used to monitor
cerebral venous saturation during ECMO support. Jugular vein reconstruction is generally not performed at time
of decannulation because of dismal short- and long-term
patency. The technique for VA-ECMO jugular venous cannulation is similar. Femoral venous cannulation may be
performed through either femoral vein. We prefer the
percutaneous Seldinger technique of cannulation when
possible. The femoral venous cannula is advanced until
the tip lies within the right atrium. Placement must be
conﬁrmed by chest radiography. Cannulation involving
both femoral vessels in one leg or either femoral vessel in
each leg is possible. Femoral vein reconstruction is generally not necessary after removing a venous cannula. The
technique for right atrial cannulation is similar to that
used in the OR for CPB. A variety of cannulae may be
used. Care must be taken to avoid injury to the sinoatrial
node or the tricuspid valve during cannulation.

Aortic valve insufﬁciency and increased systemic arterial pressure may contribute to left ventricular distention,
particularly in the setting of poor ventricular function
The subsequent increase in wall tension and myocardial oxygen demand will ultimately impede myocardial
recovery. The presence of any degree of aortic insufﬁ-
ciency exacerbates this process. Improper carotid and
aortic cannulation can be important contributing factors
by generating a ﬂow jet that is directed toward the aortic
valve. This creates additional afterload for the left ventricle, leading to ventricular distension. When necessary,
decompression of the left ventricle may be accomplished
in several ways. In the setting of a closed chest, left
ventricular decompression may be accomplished by creating, or augmenting, an interatrial communication. When
present, a patent foramen ovale can be enlarged at the
bedside by balloon septostomy under echocardiographic
guidance. Alternatively, blade or balloon septostomy may
be performed in the catheterization laboratory, even in the
absence of a preexisting interatrial communication. Recently, Cheung et al. have described an alternative method
of left heart decompression, utilizing a percutaneous technique for inserting a vent into the left ventricle that is
connected to the venous arm of the ECMO circuit (71). More options are available for decompressing the
left heart when the chest is open. Since many of these
patients are placed on ECMO in the OR, a cannula can
be placed directly into the left atrium and connected to
the venous return of the ECMO circuit. This cannula
can be placed through the left atrial appendage or in the
space between the two right-sided pulmonary veins. Either
site is easily accessible and readily visualized in an ICU
setting if reexploration for any reason becomes necessary. However, an open chest also provides the option to
create a surgical atrial level communication by atrial
septectomy, precluding the need for additional cannulae. Irrespective of the technique used, we believe it is
important that left ventricular decompression is achieved
soon after initiating ECMO support in patients with
severely depressed left ventricular function. In addition to
decreasing the likelihood recovery of ventricular function,
left ventricular distension may lead to increased left atrial
pressure, causing fulminant pulmonary edema to rapidly
ensue.

Additionally, the relative amount of coronary blood
ﬂow derived from the ECMO circuit (aortic or carotid
cannula) or the lungs (through antegrade ﬂow through
the aortic valve) is dependent upon the amount of cardiac
support provided by the ECMO circuit. At lower levels
of support, the blood delivered to the coronary arteries
is predominately derived from the left ventricle, whereas
all coronary blood ﬂow is derived from the ECMO circuit
during periods of total cardiopulmonary support and the
absence of left ventricular ejection (72). Even at high
ECMO ﬂow rates, the coronaries preferentially receive
blood supplied by the left ventricle blood. Effective leftsided decompression ensures that adequately oxygenated
blood derived from the ECMO circuit will preferentially
perfuse the coronaries in the setting of severely depressed
lung function. This is an important consideration when
weaning ECMO support. Moderate levels of mechanical
ventilation must be continued during partial ECMO
support and lung function must be adequate to wean
ECMO support. Left ventricle decompression can be a
source of air being introduced into the ECMO circuit and
the ECMO technicians need to be aware of this possibility. The decision to utilize left ventricular decompression
is one that is dependent on the circumstances of the

center. Excellent results can be achieved in centers where
left ventricular decompression is used sparingly, if at all. In
fact, left ventricle decompression in the setting of severe
aortic insufﬁciency may simply set up a ‘‘recirculation’’
circuit and in these cases, ECMO may be contraindicated
in lieu of aortic valve replacement or repair. EXTRACORPOREAL MEMBRANE
OXYGENATION MANAGEMENT
Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane
Oxygenation
VA-ECMO is used to provide broad spectrum of cardiopulmonary support, ranging from partial cardiac support in
patients with depressed ventricular function following a
prolonged period of CPB to total cardiopulmonary support in patients with complete cardiovascular collapse due
to severe lung infection. The ECMO management strategy
must take into consideration the degree of native cardiac and lung function and the projected length of ECMO
support. The optimal ECMO ﬂows rate should provide adequate end-organ blood ﬂow while limiting unnecessary
turbulence and pressure gradients within the ECMO circuit which increase hemolysis. Clinical parameters, such
as urine output and body temperature, provide important
information about the overall state of end-organ perfusion. Likewise, biochemical markers such as arterial lactate and
mixed venous oxygen saturation provide and estimation
of the adequacy oxygen delivery and should be scrutinized
at regular intervals. In general, the amount of ECMO ﬂow
to achieve total cardiopulmonary support is determined
by the patient’s body surface area (Table 4). Neonates may
require ECMO ﬂows of up to 200 mL/kg/min to achieve
adequate tissue oxygen delivery, whereas adults generally
require ﬂow rates of approximately 80 mL/kg/min. Target
ﬂow rate must be adjusted in unusual clinical circumstances, such as the infant with single ventricle and a
surgically created aortopulmonary shunt or patent ductus
arteriosus. Considerably higher ECMO ﬂow rates may be
required in these infants because of the inefﬁciency of

to avoid clipping or ligating recently constructed aortopulmonary shunts when possible and there is good evidence
that this may not only be unnecessary (28) but it may also

Most centers now avoid ligating or clipping
aortopulmonary shunts in single ventricle patients who
require ECMO, and this has probably contributed to the
improved survival in this group of patients. Extracorporeal gas exchange is regulated by the relative
concentrations and rate of gas ﬂow through the oxygenator. Typically, the added gas mixture is a combination
of oxygen and air. The exchange of oxygen occurs down
the concentration gradient within the oxygenator. Modern oxygenators are capable of very efﬁcient gas exchange,
resulting in 100% saturation of the blood leaving the
oxygenator. Similarly, carbon dioxide exchange occurs
down the concentration gradient within the oxygenator
that favors carbon dioxide removal. The extent of carbon
dioxide removal is largely dependent upon the ﬂow rate
of the ventilatory gas supplied to the oxygenator. At lower
gas ﬂow rates equilibration across the exchange surface
occurs, which limits carbon dioxide removal, whereas
carbon dioxide removal is increased with higher gas ﬂow
rates. Consequently, the overall ventilatory gas ﬂow rate
or ‘‘sweep rate’’ is used to regulate carbon dioxide gas exchange and, therefore, carbon dioxide levels in the blood. Using a blender, carbon dioxide is added to the ventilatory
gas to decrease carbon dioxide exchange within the oxygenator. Altering the gas admixture in this way enables
precise regulation of blood carbon dioxide level and is
very useful in the setting of systemic hypocarbia related
to high ventilatory gas ﬂow rates. As native cardiac and lung function improve, ECMO
support is decreased. The process of weaning ECMO
involves continuous careful assessment of measured respiratory and hemodynamic parameters and biochemical
markers. It is not uncommon for the pressure tracing
of a peripheral arterial catheter to be relatively ﬂat or
exhibit minimal pulsatile deﬂections during full ECMO
support. Increased arterial pulsatility on the pressure
monitor during ECMO support may indicate improved
ventricular compliance, contractility, or both. Such functional indications of returning native cardiac function are
useful during weaning from ECMO support. However,
it is important to remember that a malpositioned aortic
or carotid cannula may hinder left ventricular ejection. Likewise, a signiﬁcant collection of mediastinal blood can
inhibit cardiac performance when an attempt is made to
wean the patient from ECMO. Serial echocardiography
is helpful in following improvement in cardiac function
over time, particularly in the setting of right ventricular
failure.

The use of pulmonary vasodilators such
as inhaled nitric oxide are often beneﬁcial when weaning
from ECMO. Anticoagulation
Although much of our current understanding about
the activation of blood components in this setting has
been extrapolated from experience with CPB in the
OR, there is a growing body of literature speciﬁc to
ECMO. During extracorporeal support, the patient’s entire
circulating blood volume is exposed to the foreign
material that leads to activation of the inﬂammatory
cascade (74). Over time, equilibrium between activation
and neutralization of inﬂammatory blood elements must
be established for successful extracorporeal support to
occur. Initial contact activation of the blood elements
within the ECMO circuit leads to adsorption of plasma
proteins by all nonendothelial surfaces (75,76). These
proteins become tightly packed, irreversibly bound, and
stationary. Fibrinogen is also adsorbed by the hydrophobic
surface of biomaterials within the circuit (76). Circulating
monocytes elaborate tissue factor which contributes
to activation of the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation
pathways (77). The resulting cascade eventually stimulates
clot formation and activates a series of cascades and
blood elements, including the contact system, intrinsic and
extrinsic coagulation pathways, ﬁbrinolysis, complement,
platelets, endothelial cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and
lymphocytes. As platelets adhere to the ECMO circuit, they
become activated, leading to degranulation and further
platelet activation (78). This process is accentuated by
the action of thrombin and plasma protein systems. Activated platelets undergo morphologic change and
express GPIIb/IIIA receptors that facilitate platelet binding
with ﬁbrinogen (77). Once bound to biomechanical
surfaces, platelets may detach and fragment, reducing
in the number of functional platelets within the vascular
bed (79). Ongoing activation of the coagulation system
may lead to abnormal feedback loops and unbalanced
consumption and production of clotting factors, causing
systemic disseminated intravascular coagulation. Achieving a balance between adequate anticoagulation
and overanticoagulation is critical to prevent thrombus
formation within the ECMO circuit and hemorrhagic

complications, respectively. Heparin, the most commonly
used anticoagulant, binds to and activates antithrombin III, which in turn inactivates thrombin, factor Xa, and
other proteases involved in the coagulation cascade. Although heparin inhibits thrombin activity, it has no effect
on thrombin formation or platelet activation. More than
half of the heparin molecules administered during ECMO
are eliminated by the ECMO circuit itself or by blood
components within the circuit. Consequently, relatively
large doses of heparin needed are required to maintain
adequate anticoagulation during ECMO support (80). Serial measurements of activated clotting time (ACT) are
generally used to titrate heparin therapy. Although ACT
is a relatively crude measure of the effect of heparin on
whole blood, its ease of use in point of care testing makes
it the preferred method in most ECMO centers. Before
cannulation, 75 to 100 units/kg of heparin are administered to patients who are not otherwise anticoagulated. After initiation of ECMO, a continuous heparin infusion
is used to maintain the ACT between 180 and 220 seconds. Patients who are placed on ECMO immediately following
cardiac surgery frequently do not require heparin administration before the initiation of ECMO and may require
very little heparin during the subsequent 24 to 48 hours of
support. Protease inhibitors, such as aprotinin or aminocaproic
acid (Amicar), have been successfully used to inhibit the
ﬁbrinolytic system and modulate the coagulation system
during CPB and may be useful adjuncts in ECMO patients. When used in CPB, they have been shown to signiﬁcantly
reduce bleeding and the use of blood products. When
used during ECMO, Amicar has been reported to decrease
in the incidence of intracranial hemorrhage and other
hemorrhagic complications (81). Additional reports in the
cardiac ECMO literature indicate that Amicar is a useful
adjunct for postoperative patients with signiﬁcant postoperative bleeding who require mechanical support (82). Although there is less experience with the use of aprotinin during ECMO support, there is evidence that it is
beneﬁcial in the setting of life-threatening bleeding on
ECMO (83). Additional agents with anticoagulant properties may
also be useful adjuncts to modulate the coagulation system during ECMO. Argatroban is a potent and reversible
direct thrombin inhibitor that may be beneﬁcial in patients who develop heparin sensitivity.

In an in vitro
study of ECMO anticoagulation, argatroban did not initiate clot formation and was associated with decrease
thrombin formation when compared to heparin, suggesting that it may be useful as an alternative to heparin (84). Clinically, it has been used during CPB in a heparinsensitized individual (85) and during ECMO in a patient
with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (86). Nafamostat
mesilate is a protease inhibitor that has been shown to
reduce postoperative blood loss following CPB (87). The
very short duration of the anticoagulant properties of
this agent appears to facilitate selective suppression of
contact protein activation within the ECMO circuit (88). The concomitant use of nafamostat mesilate reduces the
overall heparin requirement, and allows for the maintenance of lower ACT within the patient but normal ACT
within the ECMO circuit (89). More recently, the presence
of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia/thrombosis (HITT)
has been described in pediatric patients as occurring with
an incidence similar to that seen in adult patients (90). The development of HITT on ECMO has occurred and
is an extremely challenging problem. It should be suspected in patients who have persistent thrombocytopenia
and/or thrombosis while on ECMO. When suspected, a
heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) assay should be
performed and if positive, then anticoagulation needs to
be switched from heparin to argatroban. Recently, biotechnology companies have focused on
altering the structural properties of the circuit itself in
order to reduce anticoagulation requirements and associated risk of hemorrhage. Heparin-bonded circuits,
developed using either covalent (Cardmeda systems) or
ionic (Duraﬂo II, Baxter) bonding techniques, provide
antithrombin-mediated inhibition of thrombin and factor
Xa along within the lumen of the ECMO tubing. Thrombin–antithrombin complexes bind to the tubing surface
without functionally blocking the activity of immobilized
heparin, decreasing exogenous heparin requirements (78). In a comparison of heparin-coated and noncoated systems, coagulation system activation and D-dimer formation were signiﬁcantly more delayed in the heparin-coated
group (91). However, no differences between the groups
were detectable after 6 hours and biochemical markers examined had returned to near baseline values after
24 hours. Although the authors concluded that heparinbonded circuits provide only limited advantage during
long-term use for ECMO, they may be beneﬁcial in patients with increased risk of bleeding because of the
reduced heparin requirement.

A new centrifugal pumpdriven ECMO system is being developed in Japan that
utilizes a conduit system with a newly developed heparin
(Toyobo-NCVC) coating and a hollow ﬁber oxygenator
with an ultrathin dense layer in contact with blood to
prevent plasma leak (92). In animal trials, VA-ECMO has
been successfully sustained for 34 days without the use
of systemic anticoagulation. Initial studies indicate only
minimal thrombus formation and no signiﬁcant plasma
leakage from the oxygenator. Nutrition
Critically ill patients on ECMO support typically have
signiﬁcant nutritional requirements. Nutritional requirements are especially increased during the postoperative
period due to increased catabolic rate and the burden

752
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
of wound healing. Parenteral nutrition has traditionally
been the primary source of calories provided to patients
supported with ECMO because of concern for suboptimal splanchnic perfusion. However, enteral nutrition has
been shown to be beneﬁcial by maintaining gut mucosal
integrity, improving gastrointestinal immunologic function, and reducing septic morbidity (93–95). Although no
studies have exclusively examined the impact of enteral
versus parenteral nutrition on cardiac ECMO patients, a
large retrospective study demonstrated enteral feeding tolerance without serious adverse events in a heterogeneous
group of critically ill neonates supported with ECMO (93). Similarly, there is evidence that initiation of early enteral
nutrition is safe and beneﬁcial in adult patients supported
with ECMO (96). When used, intralipids should be administered directly to the patient through through a separate
venous catheter rather than infused through the ECMO
circuit. An in vitro analysis of fat emulsion infused directly into ECMO circuits, mimicking clinical conditions,
found layering (separation of fat emulsion from blood)
and agglutination at 24 hours and adhesion of the emulsion to the circuits (97). This study, along with anecdotal
experience at many other ECMO centers, suggest that fat
emulsions should be infused through separate intravenous
sites whenever possible. Immunologic Factors
Many centers routinely administer immunosuppressive
steroids before the initiation of ECMO support and during subsequent circuit changes to reduce the inﬂammatory
cascade that is triggered upon exposure of the patient’s
blood components to the foreign surfaces of the ECMO circuit. In a recent randomized, double-masked, controlled
trial examining the use of dexamethasone versus placebo
in infants supported with ECMO for respiratory failure, patients receiving dexamethasone exhibited improved
lung injury scores on day 3 of support (98). However, clinical outcome and duration of ECMO support was similar
for both groups. Although the use of steroids appears to
ameliorate some of the inﬂammatory sequela of ECMO,
the long-term beneﬁt is unclear. Hypothermia is routinely
utilized in CPB and appears to play a role in modify
of the immune response to the CPB circuit. Systemic
hypothermia has been shown to alter the neutrophil activity, decreasing endothelial adherence and the release of
L-selectin (99–101). Such observations are intriguing and
suggest temperature regulation may be a useful means of
modulating the immunologic response to ECMO.

Neurologic Sequelae of Extracorporeal
Membrane Oxygenation
While assessing neurologic outcomes related to ECMO in
cardiac patients is complex due to the many confounding
variables inherent to this patient population, the potential
long-term neurologic sequelae of ECMO can be devastating and should therefore bear considerable weight in the
decision to initiate ECMO support. Neurologic outcome
may be in part related to the condition of the patient at the
time they are placed on ECMO (102). Cerebral blood ﬂow
on VA-ECMO may also be related to controllable factors
such as carbon dioxide levels (103). Cyanotic heart disease alone is frequently associated
with neurodevelopmental abnormalities (104–107). In addition, the association between CPB and the subsequent
development of gross and ﬁne-motor deﬁcits, as well
as behavioral and cognitive impairment, has been well
documented in both adults and children (108–110). Furthermore, neurobehavioral and functional deﬁciencies
have been described in patients following ECMO support during the neonatal period (111–119). It is difﬁcult to
determine the extent to which ECMO plays a role in the development of neurodevelopmental abnormalities in these
heterogeneous patient populations with preexisting risk
factors for neurodevelopmental and cognitive abnormalities. A report from the University of Michigan describing
neurologic changes in cardiac patients following ECMO
support describes a 14% incidence of seizures and 7%
incidence of central nervous system (CNS) injury by diagnostic radiography (24). Hamrick et al. have described
long-term neurologic impairment following ECMO in cardiac patients (120). In their 11-year experience with 53
infants supported with ECMO following cardiac surgery,
7 of the 14 surviving patients who were available for longterm follow-up were found to be completely neurologically
intact. Early recognition of neurologic impairment and
prompt initiation of rehabilitation is critical in this highrisk patient population (121). The use of bispectral index
monitoring and near infrared spectroscopy is becoming
increasingly common in the postoperative critical care
setting and the role these tools will play in the management of these patients is evolving. Although cranial
ultrasonagraphy is not always feasible before initiation of
ECMO, serial cranial ultrasonagraphy should be obtained
throughout the period of ECMO support to evaluate the
patient for gross intracranial hemorrhage or infarct (120). CONCLUSIONS
Exciting advances in extracorporeal membrane support
equipment, techniques, and experience, have led to a blossoming of its use in the pediatric cardiac population.

Consideration of earlier initiation of support is warranted
based on outcomes reported in the literature, as well as
the theoretic advantage of avoiding multiorgan dysfunction associated with the LCOS. Furthermore, improved
myocardial repair and recovery is possible when demands on the ailing heart are decreased. Nevertheless,

37. ECMO for Infants and Children
753
thoughtful, realistic consideration of the myriad clinical
and programmatic issues associated with cardiac ECMO
must be pursued on a case-by-case basis to ensure its
judicious use, and to avoid offering false hope to families. REFERENCES

Chitra Ravishankar and J. William Gaynor
While conventional therapy with inotropic support and
afterload reduction remains the mainstay of treatment
for the failing heart, mechanical circulatory support is
being increasingly used in the pediatric population (1–5). When combined with an active transplantation program,
mechanical circulatory support can have a signiﬁcant
impact on survival. Most pediatric experience consists
of use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). However, with the advent of new technology, ventricular
assist devices (VADs) are being increasingly used in
infants, children, and young adults for resuscitation,
as a bridge to transplantation, and as a bridge to
recovery (6–8). In this chapter, we review the types
of mechanical circulatory support, the indications, the
currently available systems, the pediatric experience with
the use of VAD, the mechanical circulatory support
experience in patients with a univentricular circulation,
and emerging new technology. Table 1 lists the short-term and long-term devices
available for mechanical circulatory support in children. A COMPARISON OF
EXTRACORPOREAL MEMBRANE
OXYGENATION VERSUS
VENTRICULAR ASSIST DEVICE
SUPPORT
Despite recent advances in VAD technology, ECMO remains the most common circulatory assist system in
use for pediatric patients. The advantages of ECMO include its familiarity among practitioners, ability to provide
biventricular support and respiratory support, universal
availability across all pediatric age groups, and relative
low cost. Unlike adults in whom pure left ventricular failure is the common indication for mechanical circulatory
support, cardiopulmonary support is more commonly required in children due to a combination of pulmonary dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular
dysfunction This is particularly true in the immediate
postoperative period. ECMO is obviously the mechanical support of choice for rapid deployment during cardiopulmonary arrest. However, ECMO has a number of
disadvantages, including the need for a dedicated team
of ECMO specialists, immobilization, requirement for intensive care monitoring, risks of bleeding, thrombosis,
infection, and multiorgan failure. These attendant disadvantages increase over time and hamper the use of ECMO
for long-term support. The short-term VADs with a roller
pump or centrifugal pump have many of the disadvantages
of ECMO including shorter duration of use, occasional
thrombus in the circuit and nonpulsatile ﬂow. Advantages
include easy implantation, fast setup time, low priming
volume, low-level anticoagulation, and lower cost.

The advantages of long-term implantable VAD include
less trauma to blood cells (lack of membrane oxygenator) thereby decreasing the need for anticoagulation, and
decreased risk of infection compared to ECMO where
the system is more open with multiple access ports. Implantable VADs also allow greater mobility for cardiac rehabilitation and have chronic support capability
as bridge to transplantation. The disadvantages of VAD
include the need for transthoracic cannulation, while
ECMO can be initiated with peripheral cannulation. In
addition, biventricular support with VAD requires four
cannulas, whereas ECMO provides biventricular support
with two cannulas. VAD does not provide respiratory support and cannot be used in the presence of respiratory
failure. ◗TABLE 1 Types of Mechanical Circulatory Support

Table 2 lists the indications for mechanical circulatory

in the nonsurgical patient. Cardiac Surgery
Preoperative Stabilization
Mechanical circulatory support is occasionally required
in neonates who present with profound cyanosis and/or
cardiogenic shock (9). A classic example is a patient with
obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
who presents in extremis, and may require preoperative
stabilization with ECMO support (10). Similarly, patients
may present with respiratory failure secondary to critical airway especially with tetralogy of Fallot with absent
pulmonary valve syndrome or pulmonary artery sling. Pulmonary hypertension refractory to conventional therapy
can occur in neonates with transposition of great arteries and there are several reports of the successful use
of ECMO for preoperative stabilization (11,12). Another
example is the neonate with severe Ebstein anomaly of
the tricuspid valve and functional pulmonary atresia with
ductal-dependant pulmonary blood ﬂow who has a circular shunt from a wide open ductus arteriosus, and will
beneﬁt from ECMO support while the pulmonary vascular
resistance declines (13). Postcardiotomy Ventricular Dysfunction
Mechanical circulatory support may be required in the
postoperative period either due to the inability to separate
from cardiopulmonary bypass, or a progressive low cardiac output syndrome due to a number of factors such
as ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension or
intractable arrhythmias. In this group of patients, it is important to rule out residual anatomic reasonswithechocardiography and if necessary cardiac catheterization. Anomalous left coronary artery from pulmonary artery
(ALCAPA) is a classic example of postcardiotomy pure left
ventricular dysfunction where VAD support is particularly
effective. del Nido et al. described the use of a centrifugal pump for mechanical support in seven infants unable
to be weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass after primary repair of ALCAPA (14). The median age at operation
was 89 days (48–243 days) and the median weight was
4.8 kg (4.1–6.2 kg). All patients received left ventricular
assist without requiring biventricular support.

Mechanical support was required for a median of 43.5 hours
(2.4–80 hours), with return of cardiac ejection in four of
ﬁve survivors within 24 hours and within 48 hours in the
other surviving patient. Five patients were successfully
weaned from VAD and were discharged home. There are
other reports regarding the successful use of mechanical support after repair of ALCAPA (15). ECMO is often
the preferred type of mechanical circulatory support for
postcardiotomy myocardial dysfunction as pulmonary hypertension (e.g., obstructed total anomalous pulmonary
venous return), biventricular dysfunction, or hypoxemia
often contributes to failure to separate from bypass. Similarly in single ventricle patients requiring mechanical
circulatory support after the Norwood operation, ECMO
with or without the membrane oxygenator can be used
(16–20, discussed later). Cardiopulmonary Arrest
del Nido et al. initially described the use of rapid resuscitation ECMO after cardiopulmonary arrest in the postoperative period (21). Many centers now have the capability of
rapid deployment of mechanical circulatory support and
current survival for this indication is 40% to 50% (22). One
such system utilizes a modiﬁed, portable ECMO circuit
that is maintained primed in the cardiac intensive care
unit. Another system utilizes a hollow-ﬁber membrane
oxygenator and a centrifugal pump (23). The simplicity of
this system and the avoidance of the blood-priming step
enable setup time to be as brief as 5 minutes. Rapid institution of circulatory support with modiﬁed ECMO systems
can be lifesaving with better preservation of end-organ
function in these patients. In a large single center study
evaluating risk factors for cardiac ECMO, duration of cardiopulmonary resuscitation did not inﬂuence survival (24). Rapid resuscitation ECMO can be lifesaving in single
ventricle patients as well, especially when used for
otherwise lethal conditions such as acute occlusion
of aortopulmonary shunt or transient depression of
ventricular function. In a recent report of the use of
ECMO in patients with hypoplastic left heart syndrome
and variants after the Norwood operation, 14 of 36 or 39%
survived to discharge (17). In this study, all ﬁve patients
diagnosed with shunt occlusion were resuscitated with
ECMO and survived to discharge.

VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
Noncardiac Surgery
Myocarditis and Cardiomyopathy
In children with acute myocarditis, mechanical circulatory
support can be used as a ‘‘bridge to recovery’’ or ‘‘bridge
to transplant.’’
Bridge to Recovery
Children with acute fulminant myocarditis can beneﬁt
greatly from mechanical circulatory support with eventual myocardial recovery. Similar to the adult experience,
survival is excellent in the pediatric population as well. Duncan et al. reported 88% survival for 15 children who
required mechanical circulatory support for acute fulminant myocarditis over an 8-year period (25). All 15
patients had rapidly progressive ventricular dysfunction
with a clinical picture consistent with acute fulminant
myocarditis. Twelve patients were supported with ECMO,
and the remaining three were supported with a centrifugal VAD. The median duration of support was 140 hours
(48–400 hours). Nine patients (60%) had sufﬁcient recovery of ventricular function to allow weaning from
mechanical circulatory support with seven survivors. Six
patients were successfully bridged to cardiac transplantation with ﬁve survivors. Of all diagnostic groups, the
Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) reports
the highest survival for myocarditis with 58% being successfully weaned from ECMO (26). Hence in children with
acute myocarditis, persistent low cardiac output syndrome
despite escalating inotropic support should be an indication for mechanical circulatory support (27–29). ECMO is
the mechanical support of choice in these patients because
of the speed with which it can be instituted and its easy
reversibility. However, there are several reports of VAD
being successfully used as a ‘‘bridge to recovery’’(30,31). Bridge to Heart Transplantation
Mechanical circulatory support can also be used as a
bridge to transplantation in children with irreversible myocardial dysfunction. This includes patients with dilated
cardiomyopathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, end-stage
congenital heart disease, and chronic graft dysfunction
post-transplantation. ECMO has been the mainstay of
therapy especially in infants (32). In a retrospective study
of 31 patients placed on ECMO and listed for heart transplantation, 6 were weaned from ECMO and survived to
discharge, and 12 patients were successfully bridged to
heart transplant (33). In this study, ECMO in the pretransplant period did not have an impact on long-term
survival post-transplantation. One-year actuarial survival
was 83% for the 12 ECMO patients versus 73% for the 48
non-ECMO patients during the study period (p = 0.68). Recently, long-term VADs are being increasingly used in
children for this indication with good results (34,35).

With
the advent of new technology, pulsatile devices are available for use in infants (Berlin Heart and Medos), and
older children (Thoratec, Heartmate, Abiomed). Advantages of implantable VAD include its capability for chronic
use, ambulation, and cardiac rehabilitation. VAD support
should be anticipated and every attempt must be made to
initiate VAD support ‘‘urgently’’ rather than ‘‘emergently’’
before the presence of end-organ dysfunction or circulatory collapse. In an emergency, these patients can be
resuscitated with ECMO and subsequently transitioned to
a long-term VAD after a period of stability. Mechanical circulatory support can also be utilized
after heart transplantation. Indications for mechanical
circulatory support post-transplantation include failure to
separate from cardiopulmonary bypass and progressive
low cardiac output syndrome in the immediate postoperative period, and circulatory collapse due to rejection
or graft vasculopathy late after transplant. Most of this
experience is with the use of ECMO (33,36,37). Right
heart failure/pulmonary hypertension is often responsible
for inability to separate from cardiopulmonary bypass,
and hence ECMO is the mechanical circulatory support
of choice. Pure left heart failure is usually predominant in
late rejection or graft vasculopathy, and one could make a
case for the use of VAD especially if the process is thought
to be irreversible. Pulmonary Hypertension Refractory
to Medical Therapy
Select patients with pulmonary hypertension refractory to
medical therapy will beneﬁt from ECMO support (38). A
classic example is obstructed total anomalous pulmonary
venous connection for preoperative stabilization when a
patient is in extremis, and in the postoperative period
when the pulmonary vascular resistance may be transiently elevated. In this group of patients, it is important
to rule out any residual pulmonary venous obstruction as
a cause of pulmonary hypertension. Mechanical circulatory support is controversial for
patients with irreversible pulmonary hypertension such
as primary pulmonary hypertension, as the likelihood of
survival as a bridge to lung transplantation or heart–lung
transplantation is minimal (33). Intractable Arrhythmias with Hemodynamic
Compromise
In select patients with malignant tachyarrhythmias and
bradyarrhythmias, a short trial of mechanical circulatory
support may be warranted to prevent circulatory collapse
while medical therapy is being optimized or before an
attempt at radiofrequency ablation. Patients who have
beneﬁted from the use of mechanical circulatory support

for this indication include those with lethal arrhythmias secondary to acute myocarditis or cardiomyopathy,
supraventricular tachycardia, junctional ectopic tachycardia or ventricular tachycardia after cardiac surgery,
and recalcitrant supraventricular tachycardia in Ebstein
anomaly of the tricuspid valve (39,40). It is important to
rule out residual lesions or coronary ischemia in the postcardiotomy patients. ECMO has mostly been used for this
indication, although there are occasional reports of the
use of VAD effectively as well (31). Respiratory Failure
Patients with congenital heart disease can develop respiratory failure due to parenchymal lung disease from viral
infections such as respiratory syncytial virus, adeno virus
etc., or due to severe tracheobronchomalacia as seen in the
severest form of tetralogy of Fallot with absent pulmonary
valve syndrome. In the latter group, respiratory failure
requiring ECMO support can occur due to the massively
dilated pulmonary arteries compressing the airways, and
can help stabilize these neonates before surgical intervention. ECMO can also be used to provide short-term
ventilatory support to allow time for deﬁnitive tracheal
surgery in infants and children in whom it would otherwise not be possible to achieve adequate gaseous exchange
because of major airway disease and disruption as seen
with long segment tracheal stenosis (41). CURRENTLY AVAILABLE SYSTEMS

The pediatric experience with long-term pulsatile devices
has been growing. Advantages of these devices include
their chronic support capability, ease of use, capability for
biventricular support without an oxygenator, mobility for
cardiac rehabilitation, need for low-level anticoagulation,
and pulsatile ﬂow nature with the pulsatile devices. Disadvantages include a propensity to have thromboembolic
complications, difﬁculty of implantation/explantation, cumulative cost, exteriorization of the cannulas, ventricular
apical cannulation in most patients, increased risk of
presensitization, and size limitation especially with biventricular support. Infection is also a serious complication;
the risk can be minimized by immobilization of the
driveline as close to the exit site as possible with a
binder. Pulsatile Devices
The Berlin Heart is a paracorporeal pneumatically driven
pulsatile device that has been available for use in a
miniaturized version since 1992. The inlet is cannulation
through the ventricular apex, and the outlet is to the aorta
or pulmonary artery with both cannulas exteriorized. The
polyurethane pumps have a wide range of stroke volumes
of 10, 12, 15, 25, 30, 50 and 80 mL (Figs. 3 and 4). Three

There is some pediatric experience in adolescents with the

Although the pediatric experience with axial ﬂow devices
such as the DeBakey device is limited to a few adolescents,
its smaller size holds promise for future pediatric use (44). This class of devices consists of relatively small axial
pumps that involve an impeller with its housing that is
entirely implantable. The advantages of such an axial
system are the relative ease of implantation, decreased

throughout the cardiac cycle. Its disadvantage is the need
for a large-sized ventricular apical cannulation, and higher
incidence of hemolysis. The MicroMed DeBakey is a small titanium axial device
with inﬂow from the left ventricle and outﬂow to the

and up to 10 L/min (Fig. 6). This was the ﬁrst long-term

VENTRICULAR ASSIST DEVICE
PLACEMENT
In the immediate postoperative period, patients on VAD
need to be fully ventilated and oxygenated. It is also
important to remember that output from the VAD is dependant on both preload and afterload. Although most
children with end-stage cardiomyopathy or congenital
heart disease have biventricular dysfunction, the ventricular unloading provided by the ‘‘left’’ or ‘‘systemic’’
VAD has generally made biventricular assist uncommon. It is important to appreciate that the right ventricular
output is the preload to the left ventricular assist device (LVAD). Inadequate ﬁlling of LVAD may be from
low intravascular volume, tamponade, right ventricular
dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and arrhythmias. Monitoring of central venous pressure is critical in these
patients, and there should be frequent echocardiographic
assessment of right ventricular function and estimated

762
VI. Neonates, Infants, and Children
right ventricular pressure. Right ventricular dysfunction
and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance need to be
treated in a timely manner with pharmacological agents
such as milrinone, isoproterenol, prostacycline, or inhaled
nitric oxide. With the long-term VADs, most patients including
infants can be extubated. Older children and adolescents
can be ambulatory and eventually regain near normal
activity with good nutrition and physical rehabilitation. ANTICOAGULATION FOR
VENTRICULAR ASSIST DEVICE
Heparin is used in the immediate postoperative period
once bleeding is well controlled. A continuous infusion
of heparin is used to maintain an activated clotting time
(ACT) between 180 and 220 seconds or partial thromboplastin time (PTT) between 60 and 85 seconds. For the
long-term devices, aspirin is added once the platelet count
has stabilized. In older children and adolescents with
implantable VAD, long-term anticoagulation can be maintained with Coumadin alone aiming for an international
normalized ratio (INR) of 2 to 2.5, or a combination of
Coumadin and antiplatelet agents such as aspirin, dipyridamole, or clopidogrel. In neonates and infants with a
Berlin Heart or Medos, low molecular weight heparin can
be used subcutaneously along with aspirin for long-term
anticoagulation. The goal is to maintain a therapeutic
anti-factor Xa level of 0.5 to 1 unit/mL. However in cases
where thrombus accumulates in the pump head, a more
aggressive approach may be required with a combination of a continuous infusion of intravenous heparin,
aspirin, and dipyridamole. Persistence of thrombus despite this aggressive strategy may necessitate replacement
of the pump. COMPLICATIONS
Major complications include infection, postoperative
bleeding, neurologic complications and thromboembolic
events. In a retrospective study of 58 children and adolescents supported with the Thoratec VAD in 27 centers, 28
patients or 52% had one or more infections (35). Infection
at the cannula site occurred in four patients. Postoperative
bleeding requiring surgical re-exploration occurred in 16
patients (33%). Neurologic events occurred in 15 patients
(27%) including embolic/ischemic stroke in 10 patients
and intracerebral hemorrhage in 5 patients. In this study,
atrial rather than apical cannulation was a risk factor for
neurologic events. Other thromboembolic events included
a femoral embolus in one patient and intestinal infarction
in another patient. Hypertension requiring treatment was
seen in nine patients (18%). PEDIATRIC EXPERIENCE AFTER

Thuys et al.

reported the use of the Biopump (Medtronic

3.7 kg (1.9–5.98 kg) (45). Sixty-three percentage of patients
were successfully decannulated from VAD support and
31% survived to hospital discharge. In a large series,
116 infants and children underwent centrifugal pump
VAD support postcardiotomy from 1989 to 2005 (46,47). Median age was 3 months (2 days to 19 years) and the
median weight was 4.6 kg (1.9–70). The probability of

was 43% (conﬁdence limits 31%–55%). The median
support time was 75 hours (range 19–428 hours). The centrifugal pump can be used either alone or as
part of ECMO circuit without the membrane oxygenator. The latter is particularly true of neonates with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and variants requiring mechanical
circulatory support after stage I reconstruction (discussed
later). Berlin Heart and MEDOS
These devices have been available in a miniaturized
version in Europe since the 1990s. Survival has been
reported to be 52% in 28 patients with ages ranging from
6 days to 16 years for a mean support of 17 days (12 hours
to 98 days). Ishino et al. reported the use of the Berlin
Heart in 14 children with an average age of 1 month
(2 weeks to 15 years) and average weight of 14.9 kg
(3.2–52 kg) (48). Complications included mediastinal
exploration for bleeding in 6 patients, and three pump
changes for thrombus visualized in the pump. Eight
patients were transplanted with four survivors, and three
were decannulated due to recovery of ventricular function
with one survivor. Stiller et al. reported the use of the
Berlin Heart for four children with acute myocarditis (30). The duration of support was 11 to 21 days. Three of four
patients were successfully weaned from VAD support, and
the fourth patient was bridged to transplantation. Survival with the Medos VAD has been reported to
be 36.2% in children up to 16 years of age, including
an infant with a BSA less than 0.3 m2. Konertz et al. described a series of six children supported with this
device (49). The patients’ age ranged from 5 days to
8 years, and their weight ranged from 3.1 to 20 kg.

Aspirin
and heparin were used for anticoagulation. Four of six
patients (67%) survived to discharge, two patients were

38. Circulatory Assist Devices for Infants and Children
763
bridged to transplantation, and two were weaned from
the device. These devices are not FDA approved for use in the
United States. However, the Berlin Heart has been
successfully used as a bridge to transplantation after
applying to the FDA for a HDE on a case-by-case basis. Thoratec Ventricular Assist Device
In a large series of 209 pediatric patients supported with
the Thoratec device, survival was 68% (50). Mean age
was 14.5 years (5–18 years), mean weight was 57 kg
(17–118 kg), and mean BSA was 1.6 m2 (0.7–2.3 m2). Indications for mechanical circulatory support included
cardiomyopathy in 55%, myocarditis in 25%, and endstage congenital heart disease in 6% of patients. The
average duration of support was 44 days (0–434 days). Survival rates were higher for patients with myocarditis
(86%), cardiomyopathy (74%), compared with patients
with congenital heart disease (27%). On performing a
subanalysis of children with BSA of less than 1.3 m2,
there was a higher proportion of children with congenital
heart disease (51). The smallest child in this series was
17 kg with a BSA of 0.7 m2. Survival for this group
was 52%. In another series, 12 children and adolescents
with an average BSA of 1.7 m2 (1.1–1.9 m2) underwent
implantation of Thoratec biventricular assist devices for
refractory heart failure (43). Overall survival was 83%
with nine patients successfully bridged to transplantation
(75%). Complications included bleeding requiring reexploration in three patients, driveline infections in two,
stroke in one, and device malfunction in one patient. The Heartmate is a pulsatile implantable VAD that
is only applicable to large adolescents. Helman et al. described the use of this device in 12 adolescents (BSA
of 1.4–2.2 m2); most of these patients had a dilated
cardiomyopathy (52). As in the adult population, most
children supported with the vented electrical model were
discharged home and resumed normal activity. The FDA has recently granted an HDE to the MicroMed
DeBakey VAD Child. The ﬁrst pediatric implantation of this
device in the United States was recently reported in a 10-
year-old patient with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy
(BSA 1.2 m2) who was then successfully bridged to
transplantation (53). EFFECTS OF EXTRACORPOREAL
MEMBRANE OXYGENATION AND
VENTRICULAR ASSIST DEVICE ON
RECOVERY OF VENTRICULAR
FUNCTION
Mechanical circulatory support with VAD leads to direct ventricular decompression and thereby reduction of
wall stress.

Experimental studies have shown that venting of the left atrium during ECMO support can provide
the same degree of ventricular decompression with the
equivalent likelihood of myocardial recovery. This can be
accomplished by direct left atrial venting during transthoracic cannulation, and by balloon atrial septostomy in the
cardiac catheterization laboratory for peripheral cannulation (54). With the use of a VAD, the inﬂow cannula in
infants and children often involves cannulation of the left
ventricular apex, and decannulation will involve the loss
of myocardium carved out from the apex of the ventricle. Removal of an assist device is a procedure of signiﬁcant
magnitude, requiring the use of cardiopulmonary bypass. ECMO is probably the mechanical circulatory support of
choice when used as a bridge to recovery, although VAD
has also been successfully used for this indication. Mechanical Circulatory Support
in Patients with a Univentricular
Circulation
Most children with the functionally univentricular circulation undergo a three-stage reconstruction to achieve
completion of the Fontan circulation. The syndrome of
low cardiac output is quite common in this population
through all three stages of reconstruction, and some of
these patients will eventually require heart transplantation. While conventional therapy with inotropic support
and afterload reduction remains the mainstay of therapy
for the failing heart in these children, mechanical circulatory support is being increasingly used in this patient
population as well (20). The ELSO registry recently reported the outcome
of ECMO for neonates with cardiac indications from
1996 to 2000 (55). The registry recorded 740 neonates
who were placed on ECMO for cardiac indications
at less than 30 days. There were 118 neonates with
hypoplastic left heart syndrome. There was no signiﬁcant
difference in survival between patients with hypoplastic
left heart syndrome compared with other defects. For
those with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, placement on
extracorporeal life support at greater than 15 days of age
was signiﬁcantly associated with better survival. For the
whole group, placement on extracorporeal life support at
less than 3 days of age was signiﬁcantly associated with
better survival. Survivors also had a shorter duration of
support. A recent report reviewed a large single-center experience with ‘‘nonelective’’ ECMO after stage I reconstruction
for hypoplastic left heart syndrome and its variants over
a period of 7.5 years (17).

Of the 382 infants who underwent stage I reconstruction during the period, 36
required ECMO in the postoperative period. These included 22 infants with hypoplastic left heart syndrome. Indications for ECMO included inability to separate from

764

cardiopulmonary bypass in 14 infants, and cardiopulmonary arrest due to circulatory failure or severe hypoxemia in 22. Of this group, 14 of 36 or 38.8% survived
to hospital discharge or transfer. Longer duration of cardiopulmonary bypass, the need for ECMO early in the
postoperative period, and longer duration of support were
associated with worse survival. All ﬁve infants who had a
cardiac arrest due to thrombosis of a shunt survived, as
opposed to one third of those arresting due to other causes. The mean duration of support was signiﬁcantly less for
those who survived. As with the report from the registry,
there was a trend toward a longer time to ECMO after
stage I reconstruction among survivors. Of the early survivors, half of the infants are alive at a median follow-up
of 20 months. Ungerleider et al. have suggested that mechanical assistance should be routine after stage I reconstruction,
arguing that this approach simpliﬁes postoperative management and improves hospital survival (19). They have
used their protocol in 18 consecutive patients undergoing
the Norwood operation, with a mean duration of mechanical support of 3 plus or minus 0.1 days. Survival to
discharge was 87%, with improved early neurodevelopmental outcomes. Such routine mechanical support after
the Norwood operation is a novel approach that addresses
the increased cardiac output demands in the immediate
postoperative period, and as argued, simpliﬁes postoperative care. The approach, nonetheless, will likely increase
cost and the need for additional support personnel. Further studies are needed to deﬁne the role of this strategy
in the postoperative period after stage I reconstruction. It is possible to use a standardized circuit, including
a servoregulated system driven by a roller pump or a
centrifugal pump, for mechanical support. The aortopulmonary shunt can be left open as long as the ﬂows are
adjusted to maintain adequate systemic blood pressure,
tissue perfusion, and gas exchange. Owing to signiﬁcant
runoff through the shunt towards the pulmonary circulation, some patients may require ﬂows as high as 150 to
200 mL/kg/min. In most patients, the membrane can be
isolated, and the circuit utilized as a VAD. There is very limited experience with mechanical circulatory support in patients with cavopulmonary connections. The registry of Extracorporeal Life Support reported
survival in one fourth of patients with this physiology.

The
largest single-center experience reported is a series of 20
patients with cavopulmonary connections supported with
ECMO from 1984 to 2002 (56). In patients with a bidirectional Glenn, only one of six patients survived, and
this patient sustained severe neurologic damage. In those
with the Fontan circulation, half survived to discharge,
and one third are alive at follow-up. This report highlights
some of the technical difﬁculties in this challenging group
of patients. Patients with cavopulmonary connections
are difﬁcult to resuscitate effectively with conventional
cardiopulmonary resuscitation. During resuscitation, the
increase in intrathoracic pressure may restrict effective
ﬂow of blood to the lungs and oxygenation, as well as
increasing cerebral venous pressure that may further limit
cerebral perfusion. This study also demonstrates the inability to maintain adequate venous drainage and systemic
perfusion in these patients. Therefore mechanical circulatory support, although
technically challenging, is possible in patients with a
univentricular circulation, and can be lifesaving especially
when used for otherwise lethal conditions such as
acute occlusion of aortopulmonary shunt or transient
depression of ventricular function. Long-Term Follow-Up with Mechanical
Circulatory Support
In a recent report, 37 children (26 ECMO and 11
VAD survivors) were followed for an average of more
than 4 years (57). Only one patient died in either
group for an overall long-term survival of 95%. Eighty
percent of children in both groups were reportedly
in excellent general condition, and ventricular function
by echocardiographic evaluation was normal in all the
ECMO survivors and in 90% of the VAD survivors. More
than 60% of ECMO-supported children had moderate
to severe neurologic impairment, whereas only 20%
of the VAD survivors demonstrated the same degree
of neurologic impairment. These results may suggest
an advantage for VAD support possibly because of
decreased requirements for anticoagulation with less risk
for intracranial hemorrhage. However, these results must
be interpreted with caution as the ECMO-supported group
had a higher proportion of critically ill neonates with more
complex underlying cardiac conditions. Destination Therapy
There is a rapidly growing clinical experience with
implantable VADs among the adult population. The
Randomized Evaluation of Mechanical Assistance for the
Treatment of Congestive Heart Failure (REMATCH) trial
in adults who were ineligible for heart transplantation
illustrated a signiﬁcant improvement in quality of life
with the use of VAD as destination therapy (58).

This
strategy may be applicable in the future for some patients
with ‘‘end-stage congenital heart disease.’’
FUTURE DIRECTIONS
AND CONCLUSION
Experience with mechanical circulatory assist devices in
infants and children is increasing with improvement in
clinical results. With the introduction of miniaturized

38. Circulatory Assist Devices for Infants and Children
765
assist devices, it is now possible to provide VAD support across all pediatric age groups. Currently, there
is a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-sponsored development effort to design and perform clinical testing
of new pediatric devices. The Pediatric Circulatory Support initiative from the National Heart, Lung and Blood
Institute (NHLBI) of the NIH represents a landmark development in this ﬁeld. Funds from this program are
aimed to support early stage development of novel pediatric circulatory support devices. The support of early
development efforts provided by this program will hopefully yield several devices that are clinically useful within
the next 5 years. While the availability of devices such as
the DeBakey VAD child and Berlin Heart VAD provides
immediate options for children, funding for the development of these innovative designs by the NHLBI helps to
ensure that technologically advanced pediatric circulatory
support systems will be available in the future (59). KEY POINTS
■As the overall survival of children with congenital
heart defects improves, the indications for VAD
placement are likely to increase in the long term. ■This includes a growing population of patients with
univentricular circulation developing ‘‘heart failure’’
through all stages of Fontan completion. ■These patients are anatomically challenging. ■Many of these patients are ‘‘high-risk’’ candidates
for heart transplantation both medically and psychosocially, and may beneﬁt from VAD support as
‘‘destination therapy.’’
■One may speculate that in patients with a failing
Fontan circulation due to ventricular dysfunction or
protein-losing enteropathy, there may be a role for
elective rather than emergency circulatory support
with an implantable VAD, either as a bridge to
transplantation or as deﬁnitive ‘‘destination’’ therapy
in patients who are not suitable candidates for heart
transplantation. REFERENCES

1c6dd439-d759-4808-b474-3645b5251da4_p5_.text:
Foreword 
Medical technology is so deeply indebted to so many scientific creditors that a 
late-coming analyst cannot easily trace the movements of intellectual capital that 
bankrolled a successful clinical enterprise. Cardiopulmonary bypass is one of the 
triumphs of medical technology, both in terms of volume (approaching one million 
procedures a year worldwide) and cost-effectiveness. If John Gibbon stands out as 
the tenacious broker who transformed a laboratory curiosity into a tool that surgeons would buy and use, contributions from many others - engineers, physiologists, and internists of all kinds - can also be recognized in the many facets of 
cardiopulmonary bypass. As its acceptance and use continue to expand, further 
investments of technology and clinical wisdom are still needed. The Emory authors of this textbook have benefited from a long-standing local 
tradition of investigative work, clinical audit, and postgraduate education. Thirty 
years ago, in the pioneer days of cardiopulmonary bypass, attention was, of necessity, focused on devices and components, and on the degree of physiologic damage 
that could be tolerated to see the patient through a dangerous procedure. Nowadays, the emphasis is on the patient-or, more precisely, on the clinical impact of 
any procedure, material, component, or monitoring system that over the years has 
found its place in the care of cardiac patients. The mechanics of cardiopulmonary bypass reflect the convergence of the efforts 
of several device manufacturers on a limited number of blood-contracting materials 
and gas-exchange and pumping systems, as well as much closer attention to quality 
control and cost containment. The procedure of cardiopulmonary bypass is reasonably well standardized. Physiology remains the frontier. New technology allows us 
to question accepted procedures, as exemplified by the advent of continuous-flow 
centrifugal pumps, warm retrograde cardioplegia, and normothermic body perfusion techniques. Yet innovation must be placed in the perspective of welldocumented earlier experience, with proper attention to second-order effects on all 
organ systems. The physiologic consequences of cardiopulmonary bypass are much 
more extensive than was once thought, even though the morbidity of the procedure 
has been considerably reduced. A better appreciation of the potential and the limits of cardiopulmonary bypass 
has allowed its recent application to special patient populations other than candidates for cardiac surgery.

Its use as a mechanical or metabolic aid, after many false 
starts, now appears firmly established, even though the volume of cases in which its 
use is indicated is still quite small. All of these issues are addressed in this text, which places innovation in the 
context of well-established knowledge. As a long-term observer of medical science

1c6dd439-d759-4808-b474-3645b5251da4_p7_.source: Pierre M. Galletti, Christina T. Mora (auth.), Christina T. Mora M.D., Rober.pdf
1c6dd439-d759-4808-b474-3645b5251da4_p7_.text:
Preface 
Although the basic concept of extracorporeal circulation is almost 200 years old, the 
technique of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) has been used routinely in surgical 
procedures for only about 40 years. During the latter part ofthis century, however, 
the heart-lung machine has enabled the rapid growth of heart surgery, so that, by 
1995, over 500,000 cardiac operations using CPB will have been performed in the 
United States alone. The last decade has also witnessed an increase in the use of extracorporeal technology in the non-cardiac surgery patient. Cardiologists have brought the bypass 
circuit to the angioplasty suite; circulatory arrest is being used to facilitate intracranial surgery; and clinical trials to assess an intravenous oxygenator are underway. Although fatalities directly attributable to modern CPB techniques are remarkably 
few, extracorporeal support of cardiorespiratory function is still associated with 
multiple pathophysiologic processes and attendant morbidity. But with continued 
research and acquired knowledge, the adverse events that often accompany these 
life-saving techniques can be eliminated. With that goal in mind, Cardiopulmonary 
Bypass has been designed to provide a compendium of the current knowledge regarding the clinical practice, pathophysiology, and future direction of extracorporeal circulation. The text is presented in seven parts. Part I, authored by a pioneer in the field of 
extracorporeal technology, recounts the history of the development of CPB. Part II 
outlines the physiology and pathophysiology of CPB. These chapters discuss both 
hemostasis and myocardial protection during bypass, and detail the effects of perfusion on the central nervous, respiratory, renal, hepatic, and immune systems and 
endocrine axis. Parts III and IV focus on the mechanics and conduct of bypass. These chapters describe the components of the heart-lung machine (oxygenators, 
pumps, heat exchange devices, etc.) and the procedural aspects of perfusion (cannulation, initiation and maintenance of bypass, discontinuation of bypass support, 
and management of perturbations). CPB in specific patient populations is explored 
in Parts V and VI. The use of extracorporeal circuits and oxygenators is increasing 
in non-cardiac surgery (intracranial, thoracic, liver transplantation, and high-risk 
angioplasty patients) and outside the operating room (ventricular assist devices in 
bridge-to-transplant patients or patients recovering from myocardial failure; extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in the pediatric and adult patient). Because the 
conduct of CPB in pediatric, obstetric, and thoracic surgery patients requires special 
expertise, the care of these patients during perfusion is considered in detail in Part 
V.

Preface 
for surgeons, perfusionists, and anesthesiologists. This somewhat difficult task is 
accomplished by presenting both basic concepts and detailed knowledge on a given 
subject in language intended for all readers. A specific chapter may be of greater 
interest to one group, but every chapter contains essential information. For example, a grasp of basic pharmacokinetic principles (Chapter 4) is necessary to the 
perfusionist who requires a fundamental understanding of drug disposition during 
bypass, but who may be less likely to study the effect of bypass on a certain 
antibiotic. Similarly, the surgeon and anesthesiologist should understand the basic 
principles of extracorporeal oxygenation (Chapter 10) and heat exchange (Chapter 
14), but may not need to know the specific thermal constants of the materials used 
in heat exchange devices. Several chapters, however - such as Chapter 17, on the 
discontinuation of bypass support, and Chapter 18, on the management of perturbations - will be vital to all readers. These chapters emphasize the importance of 
communication among the surgeon, perfusionist, and anesthesiologist during these 
critical events. I would like to thank those who provided valuable assistance in the preparation 
of this text. I have been privileged to work with members of the Emory University 
School of Medicine, Department of Anesthesiology and the Division of Cardiothoracic Surgery; many of these colleagues gave generously of their time and support. Pierre Galletti, author of Heart Lung Bypass (1962), which served as the 
inspiration for this work, provided both direction and moral support during the 
course of this project. J. Devn Cornish kindly allowed me to recruit his expert help 
in editing many of the chapters on the technical aspects of perfusion, and the text 
benefited greatly from his contribution. The day-to-day progress on this text was ensured by my secretary, Louise Evans, 
and I feel fortunate to have worked with this dedicated and tenacious individual. Helen Fontsere, editor for the Emory Department of Anesthesiology, polished each 
chapter and provided invaluable help in citing references, obtaining letters of permission, and addressing the myriad of tasks required to make a manuscript publisher-ready. Mary Lopez and Michele Mitchell offered encouragement and administrative support. Members of the Emory Department of Medical Illustration 
created many of the illustrations and photographs; Patsy Bryan, Nancy Mathews, 
Benjamin King, Jack Kearse, and Chuck Bogle never grumbled when I requested
